lessons.title: Propositional logic and proof
lessons.prerequisite: Comfort with true/false statements and basic algebra.
lessons.intuition: A proposition has a definite truth value. Logic asks whether the structure of an argument is valid, independently of the subject matter. First translate sentences into symbols; then reason about all possible assignments, not just one convenient example.

sections.title: Connectives and implication
sections.body: AND is true only when both operands are true; OR is inclusive and false only when both are false. Negation reverses the truth value. \(P\to Q\) is equivalent to \(\neg P\lor Q\): the promise fails only when P is true and Q is false. \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) requires equal truth values. XOR requires unequal values.

sections.title: Equivalence and normal forms
sections.body: Two expressions are equivalent if their truth-table columns match for every assignment. De Morgan’s laws change ¬(\(P\land Q\)) to ¬P∨¬Q and ¬(\(P\lor Q\)) to ¬P∧¬Q. Distribute AND over OR to obtain disjunctive normal form, or OR over AND for conjunctive normal form. A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false; a satisfiable expression is true for at least one assignment.

sections.title: Checking an argument
sections.body: An argument with premises A₁,…,Aₖ and conclusion C is valid if (A₁∧…∧Aₖ)→C is a tautology. To refute validity, find an assignment making all premises true and the conclusion false. The contrapositive \(\neg Q\to\neg P\) is equivalent to \(P\to Q\); the converse \(Q\to P\) is not generally equivalent.

sections.title: Necessary versus sufficient: translating words
sections.body: “P only if Q” means that whenever P holds, Q must hold: \(P\to Q\). “P if Q” means Q is enough to establish P: \(Q\to P\). For example, “a number is divisible by 4 only if it is even” states divisibility by 4 implies evenness; the reverse is refuted by 6. A necessary condition can hold even when the target property does not. To test a proposed equivalence, translate each direction separately and look for a counterexample. In proofs, modus ponens uses P and \(P\to Q\) to infer Q, while modus tollens uses ¬Q and \(P\to Q\) to infer ¬P. Inferring P merely from Q is the invalid pattern called affirming the consequent.

examples.prompt: Show why \(P\to Q\) and its converse differ

steps.title: Choose a distinguishing assignment
steps.explanation: Choose the antecedent of the first implication false and its consequent true. This is deliberately asymmetric; P=Q would not expose the difference.

steps.title: Evaluate the original implication
steps.explanation: Material implication excludes only a true antecedent with a false consequent. A false antecedent therefore makes this implication true.

steps.title: Evaluate the converse
steps.explanation: Reversing the implication changes which statement is the antecedent. Here the converse asserts that a true Q forces a false P.

steps.title: Draw the logical conclusion
steps.explanation: Equivalence requires agreement on every assignment. One disagreement is enough to refute it; no full truth table is necessary.

examples.given: P and Q can independently be true or false.
examples.goal: Decide whether an implication is equivalent to its converse.
examples.strategy: Disprove equivalence by finding one truth assignment where the two expressions disagree.
examples.answer: The implication and its converse are not equivalent.
examples.verification: The contrapositive \(\neg Q\to\neg P\) is true on this assignment, consistent with its equivalence to \(P\to Q\).

examples.prompt: Test: \(P\to Q\), \(Q\to R\), therefore \(P\to R\)

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: A false implication requires a true antecedent and false consequent. These values are forced by the attempted counterexample.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Since P is true, the first premise can remain true only if Q is also true.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: The second premise then forces R true, contradicting the R=false requirement. No satisfying assignment to the premises falsifies the conclusion.

examples.strategy: Try to make the conclusion false while keeping both premises true.
examples.answer: \(Q\to R\) then forces R=true, a contradiction. No counterexample exists; the argument is valid.
examples.verification: This is implication chaining, also called hypothetical syllogism. The counterexample test verifies it without presuming the conclusion.

pitfalls: Necessary and sufficient are directional: P sufficient for Q means \(P\to Q\).
“Only if Q” introduces Q as a necessary condition.
A true implication does not mean both P and Q are true.
revision: Contrapositive preserves meaning; converse need not.

checks.prompt: Which statement is equivalent to \(P\to Q\)?
checks.hint: Think about the contrapositive.
checks.explanation: The contrapositive preserves the implication: \(\neg Q\to\neg P\) is equivalent to \(P\to Q\). Reversing alone gives the converse, which is not equivalent.

checks.prompt: For how many assignments to P,Q is \(P\to Q\) true?
checks.hint: Identify its sole false case.
checks.explanation: TT, FT and FF make the implication true. TF makes it false, so 3 assignments work.

lessons.concept: A proposition has a definite truth value. Logic asks whether the structure of an argument is valid, independently of the subject matter. First translate sentences into symbols; then reason about all possible assignments, not just one convenient example.
lessons.method:
A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value. “7 is prime” is a proposition; “x is prime” depends on x and is a predicate; a command has no truth value. Symbols P and Q let us reason about statement structure without repeatedly discussing their subject matter. Negation reverses a truth value; conjunction requires both inputs true; disjunction requires at least one true. Mathematical OR is inclusive unless stated otherwise.
A truth table enumerates all assignments. With n independent propositions there are \(2^n\) rows, because each independently has two choices. Create columns for smaller subexpressions before the final expression. Parentheses determine grouping, so calculate inside them first. A tautology is true on every row, a contradiction false on every row, and a contingent formula true on some rows and false on others.
For GATE, “always true” requires every row, while refuting it requires just one false row. Do not confuse a proposition’s actual real-world truth with a formula’s truth under arbitrary assignments. A table is also a proof: it exhausts the finite cases rather than testing a few favorable examples. Implication \(P	o Q\) says that a true P cannot coexist with a false Q. It does not assert that P is true, or that Q can occur only because of P. Its truth-table definition is \(P	o Q\equiv
eg P\lor Q\). A false antecedent satisfies this constraint, which is why an implication can be true when its antecedent is false. “P only if Q” makes Q necessary for P; “P if Q” makes Q sufficient for P and translates as \(Q	o P\).
Two formulas are logically equivalent when they agree on every assignment. The contrapositive \(
eg Q	o
eg P\) is equivalent to \(P	o Q\); the converse \(Q	o P\) generally is not. Biconditional \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) requires both implication directions and holds exactly when the truth values agree.
To test an argument, assume every premise true and attempt to make the conclusion false. A successful assignment is a counterexample; proving no such assignment exists establishes validity. This differs from checking whether a conclusion happens to be true. In MCQs, check direction words before simplifying, and distinguish equivalence of formulas from implication in just one direction. Two propositional formulas are logically equivalent when their truth values agree for every assignment to their variables. This is stronger than finding one assignment where both happen to be true. It is also different from a one-way implication: an implication can hold even when the formulas do not always agree. Write an equivalence with the symbol \(\equiv\), or show that their biconditional is a tautology.
For a small number of variables, a truth table gives a complete proof. List all \(2^n\) assignments, evaluate the inner expressions first, and compare the final columns row by row. A single disagreement disproves equivalence; complete agreement proves it. De Morgan's laws exchange AND with OR when a negation is pushed inside, and negate each operand. Parentheses matter: negating a whole conjunction differs from negating just its first operand. In the example, do not assume the law from its name; compute both sides so that the conclusion follows from all four cases. AND is true only when both operands are true; OR is inclusive and false only when both are false. Negation reverses the truth value. \(P	o Q\) is equivalent to \(
eg P\lor Q\): the promise fails only when P is true and Q is false. \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) requires equal truth values. XOR requires unequal values. Two expressions are equivalent if their truth-table columns match for every assignment. De Morgan’s laws change ¬(\(P\land Q\)) to ¬P∨¬Q and ¬(\(P\lor Q\)) to ¬P∧¬Q. Distribute AND over OR to obtain disjunctive normal form, or OR over AND for conjunctive normal form. A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false; a satisfiable expression is true for at least one assignment. An argument with premises A₁,…,Aₖ and conclusion C is valid if (A₁∧…∧Aₖ)→C is a tautology. To refute validity, find an assignment making all premises true and the conclusion false. The contrapositive \(
eg Q	o
eg P\) is equivalent to \(P	o Q\); the converse \(Q	o P\) is not generally equivalent. “P only if Q” means that whenever P holds, Q must hold: \(P	o Q\). “P if Q” means Q is enough to establish P: \(Q	o P\). For example, “a number is divisible by 4 only if it is even” states divisibility by 4 implies evenness; the reverse is refuted by 6. A necessary condition can hold even when the target property does not. To test a proposed equivalence, translate each direction separately and look for a counterexample. In proofs, modus ponens uses P and \(P	o Q\) to infer Q, while modus tollens uses ¬Q and \(P	o Q\) to infer ¬P. Inferring P merely from Q is the invalid pattern called affirming the consequent. Think of a compound proposition as a small circuit whose inputs are truth values and whose gates are connectives. Translating a sentence therefore requires identifying its grouping, not just replacing every “and” or “or” with a symbol. A valid argument preserves truth from premises to conclusion under every assignment; it need not have premises that actually hold in the world. To analyze an argument, search specifically for an assignment making all premises true and the conclusion false. If none exists, the argument is valid. This method assumes classical two-valued logic and inclusive OR. A true conclusion on one assignment cannot repair an invalid argument structure. A truth table is exhaustive enumeration, so its main discipline is keeping assignments and intermediate columns consistent. With n distinct variables there are exactly 2 to the n rows regardless of how often a variable occurs in the expression. Repeated occurrences must share one truth value on a row. Number the rows systematically, compute negations and parenthesized parts first, and use the final column to count satisfying assignments or classify the formula. When an expression has several clauses, a short case split can independently check that count. This assumes all variable assignments are allowed; restricting the inputs by additional premises changes which rows are relevant to an argument. Read an implication as excluding a single forbidden combination: its premise holds but its promised consequence does not. This explains both its direction and its behavior when the premise fails. “P only if Q” places Q after the arrow because Q is necessary for P; “P if Q” places Q before it because Q is sufficient. For chained rules, track what becomes guaranteed after each true antecedent. To refute a proposed implication, produce one true antecedent with a false consequent. Material implication is a truth-functional mathematical convention; it does not assert causation or establish the antecedent itself. Negating an implication means asserting precisely its forbidden combination. Equivalence permits replacing a subexpression inside any larger propositional formula without altering truth values. Algebraic laws such as absorption and distributivity therefore function as proof steps, but each step must preserve every assignment. Keep equivalence separate from implication: simplifying a formula to a stronger sufficient condition can discard satisfying rows. A useful verification is to compare cases based on a variable rather than assume a familiar identity. In exam simplification, eliminate implications first, move negations inward with De Morgan’s laws, and then use identities or absorption. These transformations apply to classical Boolean formulas; ordinary arithmetic addition and multiplication do not obey exactly the same laws.

gateGuide.recognize: Use truth assignments when a question asks whether an implication or argument is always valid. Use algebraic equivalence when an expression needs simplifying.
method: Mark which words express necessary or sufficient conditions before translating to symbols.
To refute validity, force every premise true and the conclusion false. If these requirements contradict, no counterexample exists.
For several options, compare their false cases instead of building four complete truth tables; verify any shortcut against the full logical conditions.

traps.claim: Affirming the consequent
traps.why: From “divisible by 4 implies even” and “6 is even,” you cannot infer divisibility by 4. The conclusion adds information the premise never promised.

traps.claim: Treating implication as AND
traps.why: With P false and Q false, P implies Q is true while P AND Q is false. Implication excludes only a broken promise with true antecedent and false consequent.

formulas.meaning: The single false case is P=true,Q=false.
Use this form when constructing a counterexample.
Contrapositive, unlike converse, preserves equivalence.

example.prompt: Classify P∨¬P and P∧¬P.
example.strategy: Enumerate → Evaluate OR → Evaluate AND

steps.title: Enumerate
steps.explanation: There is one variable, so exactly two rows are needed.

steps.title: Evaluate OR
steps.explanation: The disjunction is true in both assignments.

steps.title: Evaluate AND
steps.explanation: The conjunction is false in both assignments.

example.answer: P∨¬P is a tautology; P∧¬P is a contradiction.
example.verification: No assignment was omitted; each formula’s classification holds over the complete table.

examples.prompt: Let P be true and Q false. Evaluate (\(P\lor Q\))∧¬Q.
examples.strategy: Inner disjunction → Negate Q → Combine

steps.title: Inner disjunction
steps.explanation: Inclusive OR needs only one true input.

steps.title: Negate Q
steps.explanation: Negation reverses the false value of Q.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: Both conjuncts are true, so the whole proposition is true.

examples.answer: True.
examples.verification: Rewriting the expression as (P∧¬Q)∨(Q∧¬Q) gives true OR false, again true.

examples.prompt: A system satisfies \(P\to Q\) and P. Must Q hold?
examples.strategy: Assume a failing conclusion → Use the second premise → Test the first premise

steps.title: Assume a failing conclusion
steps.explanation: Validity is tested by trying to falsify the conclusion while retaining the premises.

steps.title: Use the second premise
steps.explanation: The premise P rules out every assignment with a false antecedent.

steps.title: Test the first premise
steps.explanation: The remaining candidate violates \(P\to Q\), so no counterexample satisfies both premises.

examples.answer: Yes; the inference is valid modus ponens.
examples.verification: The only assignment satisfying both premises has P=Q=T; exhaustive two-variable checking agrees.

examples.prompt: Is the inference from \(P\to Q\) and Q to P valid?
examples.strategy: Try a false conclusion → Make the second premise true → Check the implication

steps.title: Try a false conclusion
steps.explanation: An invalidity witness must make the proposed conclusion false.

steps.title: Make the second premise true
steps.explanation: This assignment satisfies the premise Q.

steps.title: Check the implication
steps.explanation: Both premises are true while P is false, furnishing a counterexample.

examples.answer: Invalid: affirming the consequent.
examples.verification: For example, rain may imply a wet road, but a sprinkler can make the road wet without rain.

examples.prompt: Build the final column of (\(P\lor Q\))∧¬(\(P\land Q\)), in row order TT,TF,FT,FF.
examples.strategy: Compute the disjunction → Compute the negated conjunction → Combine columns

steps.title: Compute the disjunction
steps.explanation: At least one true input makes OR true.

steps.title: Compute the negated conjunction
steps.explanation: Only the first row has a true conjunction.

steps.title: Combine columns
steps.explanation: AND keeps only rows where both intermediate columns are true.

examples.answer: The column is F,T,T,F: exactly one input must be true.
examples.verification: Directly counting assignments with unequal truth values gives precisely TF and FT.

examples.prompt: How many of the eight assignments satisfy (\(P\lor Q\))∧(¬P∨R)?
examples.strategy: Split on false P → Split on true P → Add disjoint cases

steps.title: Split on false P
steps.explanation: Q must be true, while R is free, giving two rows.

steps.title: Split on true P
steps.explanation: R must be true, while Q is free, giving two more rows.

steps.title: Add disjoint cases
steps.explanation: Every assignment belongs to exactly one P case.

examples.answer: Four satisfying assignments.
examples.verification: They are (F,T,F),(F,T,T),(T,F,T),(T,T,T), an explicit enumeration without duplicates.

examples.prompt: Do \(P\to Q\) and \(Q\to P\) have identical truth tables?
examples.strategy: Choose an asymmetric row → Evaluate forward → Evaluate reverse

steps.title: Choose an asymmetric row
steps.explanation: A row with unequal inputs can distinguish implication directions.

steps.title: Evaluate forward
steps.explanation: A true antecedent and false consequent violate the forward implication.

steps.title: Evaluate reverse
steps.explanation: A false antecedent satisfies the reverse implication.

examples.answer: No; they disagree on this row and also on P=F,Q=T.
examples.verification: Their columns in TT,TF,FT,FF order are T,F,T,T and T,T,F,T.

tutorials.title: Implication, equivalence and proof by counterexample
tutorials.body:
Implication \(P	o Q\) says that a true P cannot coexist with a false Q. It does not assert that P is true, or that Q can occur only because of P. Its truth-table definition is \(P	o Q\equiv
eg P\lor Q\). A false antecedent satisfies this constraint, which is why an implication can be true when its antecedent is false. “P only if Q” makes Q necessary for P; “P if Q” makes Q sufficient for P and translates as \(Q	o P\).
Two formulas are logically equivalent when they agree on every assignment. The contrapositive \(
eg Q	o
eg P\) is equivalent to \(P	o Q\); the converse \(Q	o P\) generally is not. Biconditional \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) requires both implication directions and holds exactly when the truth values agree.
To test an argument, assume every premise true and attempt to make the conclusion false. A successful assignment is a counterexample; proving no such assignment exists establishes validity. This differs from checking whether a conclusion happens to be true. In MCQs, check direction words before simplifying, and distinguish equivalence of formulas from implication in just one direction.

example.prompt: Does “divisible by 4 implies even” imply its converse?
example.strategy: Original → Candidate converse → Counterexample

steps.title: Original
steps.explanation: Any multiple of four is twice an integer, so the original implication holds.

steps.title: Candidate converse
steps.explanation: This would require every even integer to be divisible by four.

steps.title: Counterexample
steps.explanation: The converse has a true antecedent and false consequent.

example.answer: The converse is false; the original implication remains true.
example.verification: A counterexample to the converse does not refute the original direction.

For chained rules, track what becomes guaranteed after each true antecedent. To refute a proposed implication, produce one true antecedent with a false consequent. Material implication is a truth-functional mathematical convention; it does not assert causation or establish the antecedent itself. Negating an implication means asserting precisely its forbidden combination.

examples.prompt: Translate “a candidate is eligible only if the candidate completed training,” then identify the violating case.
examples.strategy: Name the statements → Translate necessity → Identify the failure

steps.title: Name the statements
steps.explanation: Use separate symbols before deciding direction.

steps.title: Translate necessity
steps.explanation: Training is required whenever eligibility holds.

steps.title: Identify the failure
steps.explanation: Being eligible without training is the single forbidden truth combination.

examples.answer: E→T; eligible and untrained violates the rule.
examples.verification: ¬E∨T has the same values and is false only in that violating case.

examples.prompt: Given \(P\to Q\) and \(Q\to R\), prove \(P\to R\).
examples.strategy: Assume the target antecedent → Apply the first rule → Apply the second rule

steps.title: Assume the target antecedent
steps.explanation: Only assignments with true P could violate the desired implication.

steps.title: Apply the first rule
steps.explanation: The first premise forces Q true.

steps.title: Apply the second rule
steps.explanation: The second premise forces R true, so the target cannot fail.

examples.answer: \(P\to R\) follows from the premises.
examples.verification: If P is false the target already holds; if P is true the chain forces R, covering both cases.

examples.prompt: Evaluate “if 9 is even, then 9 is prime” in classical propositional logic.
examples.strategy: Evaluate the antecedent → Evaluate the consequent → Apply implication

steps.title: Evaluate the antecedent
steps.explanation: Nine is odd, so the antecedent is false.

steps.title: Evaluate the consequent
steps.explanation: Nine equals three times three, so the consequent is false.

steps.title: Apply implication
steps.explanation: A material implication fails only with a true antecedent and false consequent.

examples.answer: The implication is true, although both component claims are false.
examples.verification: Using \(\neg P\lor Q\) gives true OR false, independently confirming the result.

tutorials.title: Proving logical equivalence across every assignment
tutorials.body:
Two propositional formulas are logically equivalent when their truth values agree for every assignment to their variables. This is stronger than finding one assignment where both happen to be true. It is also different from a one-way implication: an implication can hold even when the formulas do not always agree. Write an equivalence with the symbol \(\equiv\), or show that their biconditional is a tautology.
For a small number of variables, a truth table gives a complete proof. List all \(2^n\) assignments, evaluate the inner expressions first, and compare the final columns row by row. A single disagreement disproves equivalence; complete agreement proves it. De Morgan's laws exchange AND with OR when a negation is pushed inside, and negate each operand. Parentheses matter: negating a whole conjunction differs from negating just its first operand. In the example, do not assume the law from its name; compute both sides so that the conclusion follows from all four cases.

example.prompt: Prove that ¬(\(P\land Q\)) is logically equivalent to ¬P∨¬Q.
example.strategy: List the cases → Evaluate the left side → Evaluate the right side → Compare columns

steps.title: List the cases
steps.explanation: Two independent propositions give four assignments; none may be omitted.

steps.title: Evaluate the left side
steps.explanation: The conjunction is true only in the first row, and its negation reverses that column.

steps.title: Evaluate the right side
steps.explanation: Both negations are false only when P and Q are both true.

steps.title: Compare columns
steps.explanation: The final columns agree in every row, proving equivalence.

example.answer: The formulas are logically equivalent.
example.verification: Their biconditional is true on all four assignments. For P=T,Q=F, both sides are true even though \(P\land Q\) is false.

examples.prompt: Simplify P∨(\(P\land Q\)) and prove the result.
examples.strategy: Case true P → Case false P → Compare with P

steps.title: Case true P
steps.explanation: The first disjunct already makes the expression true.

steps.title: Case false P
steps.explanation: Both disjuncts are false regardless of Q.

steps.title: Compare with P
steps.explanation: The two exhaustive cases reproduce P itself.

examples.answer: It simplifies to P by absorption.
examples.verification: The conjunction \(P\land Q\) never contributes a true row that P has not already contributed.

examples.prompt: Find a conjunction equivalent to ¬(\(P\to Q\)).
examples.strategy: Eliminate the implication → Move negation inward → Remove double negation

steps.title: Eliminate the implication
steps.explanation: Replace \(P\to Q\) by its equivalent disjunction.

steps.title: Move negation inward
steps.explanation: De Morgan changes OR to AND and negates both operands.

steps.title: Remove double negation
steps.explanation: Classical double negation restores P.

examples.answer: P∧¬Q.
examples.verification: Both formulas are true only when the implication fails: P true and Q false.

examples.prompt: Can \(P\lor Q\) be replaced by \(P\leftrightarrow Q\)?
examples.strategy: Choose unequal inputs → Evaluate OR → Evaluate biconditional

steps.title: Choose unequal inputs
steps.explanation: Equivalence must hold on every assignment, so one discriminating row suffices.

steps.title: Evaluate OR
steps.explanation: One true operand makes the disjunction true.

steps.title: Evaluate biconditional
steps.explanation: A biconditional requires equal operand truth values.

examples.answer: No; the formulas are not logically equivalent.
examples.verification: On FF, OR is false but the biconditional is true, giving a second independent disagreement.

lessons.title: First-order logic and quantifiers
lessons.prerequisite: Propositional logic; understand a variable and a set.
lessons.intuition: A predicate becomes a proposition when its variables are given values or bound by quantifiers. The domain matters: “every number has a multiplicative inverse” changes truth when zero is included. Quantifier order expresses who gets to choose a value first.

sections.title: Meaning and scope
sections.body: ∀x P(x) requires P for every domain element; ∃x P(x) requires at least one witness. A bound variable lies within a quantifier’s scope; a free variable remains unspecified. Write brackets to show scope. “Every student knows some language” is ∀s ∃l Knows(s,l); it does not promise the same language for everyone.

sections.title: Negation
sections.body: Negating ∀ changes it to ∃ and negates the predicate: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). Similarly ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). For multiple quantifiers apply this from the outside inward. Negating a conjunction or implication inside the predicate still requires propositional rules.

sections.title: Order and witnesses
sections.body: ∃y∀x R(x,y) selects one y that works for all x. \(\forall x\exists y\ R(x,y)\) permits y to depend on x. The former implies the latter on the usual nonempty domains, but not conversely. To disprove a universal statement provide a counterexample; to prove an existential statement provide a witness.

sections.title: Choosing witnesses and refuting nested statements
sections.body: For \(\forall x\exists y\ R(x,y)\), an explicit witness formula y=g(x) can prove the claim. To refute it, find one x for which every possible y fails. For ∃y∀x R(x,y), the witness must be chosen independently of x; refuting it requires showing that each candidate y fails for some x. Over integers, ∀x∃y(y>x) is true with y=x+1, but ∃y∀x(y>x) is false because for any proposed y, choosing x=y violates strict inequality. These are different orders of dependency, not different spellings of the same statement. When translating “only students passed,” write Passed(x)→Student(x); it does not assert that all students passed.

examples.prompt: Negate “every student passed at least one exam”

steps.title: Translate the original statement
steps.explanation: The exam can depend on the student. The sentence does not require one common exam passed by everyone.

steps.title: Negate the universal quantifier
steps.explanation: A universal statement fails if there is at least one counterexample student.
steps.equation: \neg(\forall s\exists e\ Passed(s,e))\equiv\exists s\neg(\exists e\ Passed(s,e))

steps.title: Negate the existential quantifier

lessons.concept: A predicate becomes a proposition when its variables are given values or bound by quantifiers. The domain matters: “every number has a multiplicative inverse” changes truth when zero is included. Quantifier order expresses who gets to choose a value first.
lessons.method:
A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is assigned a value or bound by a quantifier. Always state the domain: “every x has a square root” can be false over real numbers and true over complex numbers. Universal quantification ∀x requires every domain element; existential quantification ∃x requires at least one witness. A universal claim is refuted by one counterexample, whereas an existential claim is refuted by showing every possible witness fails.
Quantifier order records dependencies. In \(\forall x\exists y\ R(x,y)\), choose x first and then permit y to depend on it. In ∃y∀x R(x,y), one fixed y must work for all x. These statements are not freely interchangeable. Scope parentheses also matter: bound variables only belong to the quantifier’s subformula, and free variables leave a predicate rather than a closed sentence.
Negation swaps each quantifier while retaining order and negating the inner predicate: \(\neg\forall x\exists yR(x,y)\equiv\exists x\forall y\neg R(x,y)\). Over an empty domain a universal formula is vacuously true and an existential formula false; most numerical examples instead specify a nonempty domain. A predicate is a statement template containing one or more variables. It does not have a fixed truth value until the variables receive values or are bound by quantifiers. For example, “x is greater than two” becomes true at x=5 and false at x=1. A proposition has a definite truth value; an open predicate still depends on its free variables. Always specify a domain because the possible satisfying values come from that domain.
The satisfaction set of a one-variable predicate is the set of domain elements that make it true. To determine it, translate the condition into mathematics, solve it, and check both that the candidates work and that no others were lost. Substitution then evaluates individual instances. For polynomial equations, factoring can expose every root without testing an arbitrary list of numbers. A root is a satisfying input, not a truth value itself. Distinguish the predicate P(x), the proposition P(2), and the set of all inputs satisfying P. ∀x P(x) requires P for every domain element; ∃x P(x) requires at least one witness. A bound variable lies within a quantifier’s scope; a free variable remains unspecified. Write brackets to show scope. “Every student knows some language” is ∀s ∃l Knows(s,l); it does not promise the same language for everyone. Negating ∀ changes it to ∃ and negates the predicate: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). Similarly ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). For multiple quantifiers apply this from the outside inward. Negating a conjunction or implication inside the predicate still requires propositional rules. ∃y∀x R(x,y) selects one y that works for all x. \(\forall x\exists y\ R(x,y)\) permits y to depend on x. The former implies the latter on the usual nonempty domains, but not conversely. To disprove a universal statement provide a counterexample; to prove an existential statement provide a witness. For \(\forall x\exists y\ R(x,y)\), an explicit witness formula y=g(x) can prove the claim. To refute it, find one x for which every possible y fails. For ∃y∀x R(x,y), the witness must be chosen independently of x; refuting it requires showing that each candidate y fails for some x. Over integers, ∀x∃y(y>x) is true with y=x+1, but ∃y∀x(y>x) is false because for any proposed y, choosing x=y violates strict inequality. These are different orders of dependency, not different spellings of the same statement. When translating “only students passed,” write Passed(x)→Student(x); it does not assert that all students passed. First order logic talks about objects and relations between objects, rather than treating every sentence as an indivisible Boolean input. Its interpretation supplies a domain, meanings for predicate symbols, and any functions or constants. Quantifiers range over that domain; restrictions such as “students” are normally expressed through predicates unless separate typed domains are stated. To translate a sentence, identify which objects are chosen universally, which witnesses may depend on them, and the scope of every condition. Universal restrictions usually use implication, whereas existential restrictions use conjunction. Evaluate a finite model by checking its actual predicate instances. The same formula can be true in one interpretation and false in another. A universal statement requires coverage of the whole stated domain, not just many successful samples. For an infinite numerical domain, an algebraic argument or exhaustive structural cases can cover every input at once. For a finite domain, checking every member is a complete proof. One failing member refutes the statement regardless of how many others pass. Quantified implications require attention to their antecedents: elements failing a restriction do not violate the implication. When negating a universal, preserve its domain and exhibit an existential counterexample to the inner condition. Nonempty-domain assumptions matter if existence is inferred from universality; universal truth alone does not supply an object. An existential statement is proved by supplying a witness in the domain and verifying the entire required condition. A witness can depend on variables quantified earlier, but not on variables universally chosen later. To refute existence, rule out every candidate through a bound, contradiction, or exhaustive finite check. Be careful with conjunction inside the quantifier: the same witness must satisfy all conjuncts. Separate existential statements may use different witnesses, so their conjunction does not automatically combine into one witness satisfying everything. Algebraic construction is often more convincing than a few guesses. State the domain before choosing a witness, because an integer, real, or nonnegative restriction can change whether the construction works. A predicate’s inputs have roles and domains, so arity and argument order are part of its meaning. A binary predicate R(x,y) may express divisibility, adjacency or precedence; swapping x and y can change its truth value. For a fixed assignment, evaluate the stated relation, not a related informal claim. Its satisfaction set can be described by solving a condition or by listing true tuples in a finite domain. Before evaluating an expression, ensure every operation is defined for the supplied input. A formula involving division by zero cannot be labeled false simply because its arithmetic is undefined. Domain restrictions turn such an expression into a well-defined predicate.

A predicate is a statement template containing one or more variables. It does not have a fixed truth value until the variables receive values or are bound by quantifiers. steps.title: Evaluate a failing input

steps.title: Evaluate a satisfying input
steps.explanation: P(2) is true, agreeing with the computed satisfaction set.

lessons.title: Sets, relations and functions
lessons.intuition: Sets describe collections, relations describe permitted pairs, and functions choose one output for every input. Keep those three objects separate: a function is a special relation, but a general relation may connect an element to many others or none.

sections.title: Sets and counting
sections.body: A∪B includes elements in either set; A∩B includes elements in both; A−B removes B from A. A power set contains every subset, so |P(A)|=2^|A|. The Cartesian product A×B consists of ordered pairs and has |A|×|B| elements for finite sets. Inclusion–exclusion gives \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\).

sections.title: Properties of relations
sections.body: On A, reflexivity means aRa for every a. Symmetry means aRb implies bRa. Antisymmetry means aRb and bRa imply a=b. Transitivity means aRb and bRc imply aRc. Reflexive+symmetric+transitive defines an equivalence relation, whose equivalence classes partition A. Test the properties individually; loops and pair direction matter.

sections.title: Functions and inverses
sections.body: A function \(A\to B\) is total and single-valued. Injectivity forbids two distinct inputs sharing an output; surjectivity requires every codomain element to be reached. Bijectivity combines both and permits a two-sided inverse. On finite sets of equal size, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent; that shortcut depends on finiteness and equal cardinality.

sections.title: Relation matrices and composition
sections.body: For a finite set {a₁,…,aₙ}, represent a relation by a Boolean matrix M where \(M_{ij}=1\) iff \(a_iRa_j\). Reflexivity requires diagonal 1s; symmetry requires \(M=M^T\); antisymmetry disallows simultaneous off-diagonal 1s in symmetric positions. Transitivity requires that every two-edge path implies its direct relation pair. Relation composition uses Boolean matrix multiplication, where products use AND and sums use OR. The transitive closure adds all pairs reachable by paths, and need not add loops unless a path or reflexive closure requires them. For function composition \(g\circ f\), apply f first and then g; the right-hand function acts first. If both functions are injective, their composition is injective, but properties of a composition do not freely imply every property of each component.

examples.prompt: Partition integers by congruence modulo 3

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: Zero is divisible by three, proving reflexivity for every integer a.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Negating a multiple of three gives another multiple, proving symmetry.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: Adding the two differences gives a−c, proving transitivity. These three properties establish equivalence; its classes are residues 0, 1 and 2.

examples.strategy: Verify each equivalence axiom under divisibility of the difference.
examples.answer: The classes are residues 0,1,2, so the relation is an equivalence relation.
examples.verification: Any integer has exactly one remainder modulo three, so the three classes are disjoint and cover the integers.

examples.prompt: Count functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set

steps.title: Count independent assignments
steps.explanation: A function chooses exactly one output for each input; inputs may share outputs, so multiply two choices three times.

steps.title: Describe failure of surjectivity
steps.explanation: With only two outputs, missing an output means all inputs select the other one. These are the two constant functions; there is no third failure case.

steps.title: Subtract and check injectivity
steps.explanation: Three inputs cannot have pairwise distinct images inside two outputs. Onto and one-to-one are different conditions.

examples.given: Three distinct inputs and two distinct outputs. All functions are permitted.
examples.goal: Count total, surjective and injective functions.
examples.strategy: Count all functions, subtract those missing an output, then use the pigeonhole principle.
examples.answer: 8 total functions; 6 surjections; 0 injections.
examples.verification: Onto assignments split the inputs 1+2 or 2+1 across the outputs: choosing the isolated input and its output gives 3×2=6.

pitfalls: Antisymmetric does not mean “not symmetric”; identity relations satisfy both.
The codomain is part of a function definition; changing it can change surjectivity.
revision: Number of functions from m inputs to n outputs is nᵐ.
Equivalence classes are disjoint and cover the underlying set.

lessons.concept: Sets describe collections, relations describe permitted pairs, and functions choose one output for every input. Keep those three objects separate: a function is a special relation, but a general relation may connect an element to many others or none.
lessons.method:
A set records membership, not order or repetition: {1,2,2} and {2,1} describe the same set. A subset A⊆B means every member of A belongs to B; proper subset additionally requires inequality. The empty set is a subset of every set, but it is not necessarily an element of a set. This distinction separates ∅⊆A from ∅∈A.
Union collects membership in either operand; intersection requires both; difference A−B keeps members of A absent from B. A complement needs a stated universe. Cartesian product A×B consists of ordered pairs, so swapping the operands can change it even when their sizes agree. A power set contains all subsets and has size \(2^{|A|}\), including the empty and full subsets.
When counting a union, adding sizes counts intersection members twice. Subtracting the intersection once gives \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\). Do not confuse elements with subsets in a power-set question. If an object is itself a set, carefully check which level of braces the statement is about before choosing an option. A relation from A to B is any subset of A×B. Unlike a function, it may give an input no partner or many partners. On one set A, reflexivity requires every (a,a), symmetry requires (b,a) whenever (a,b) occurs, and transitivity requires (a,c) whenever both (a,b) and (b,c) occur. Antisymmetry is different from “not symmetric”: it permits two-way pairs only when the endpoints are equal.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Its class [a] contains all elements related to a. Classes are either identical or disjoint, and partition the original set; choosing a different representative from the same class changes no class. In finite matrices, reflexivity uses diagonal ones, symmetry uses mirrored entries, and transitivity uses all two-edge paths.
To disprove a property, exhibit its exact missing requirement: a missing loop for reflexivity, an unmatched reversed pair for symmetry, or a two-step path lacking its shortcut for transitivity. Checking only selected pairs cannot prove a universal axiom. Equivalence classes and connected components are not interchangeable for an arbitrary non-equivalence relation. A function f:\(A\to B\) assigns exactly one element of B to every element of A. A is its domain, B its codomain, and the attained values form its image, which need not equal B. Injective means different inputs never share an output; surjective means every codomain element is attained; bijective means both. A bijection has a two-sided inverse function, but a many-to-one map cannot recover an input uniquely.
For finite sets with m inputs and n outputs, there are \(n^m\) total functions because output choices are independent. An injection requires m≤n and uses decreasing choices n(n−1)…; a surjection requires m≥n. Equal finite sizes let injection and surjection imply each other, but infinite domains need separate reasoning.
Composition \(g\circ f\) applies f first. The intermediate domain/codomain must be compatible. Composition preserves injectivity when both functions are injective and preserves surjectivity when both are surjective, but one cannot infer every component property from the composite. In questions involving a named codomain, do not quietly replace it by the image to make a map onto. A∪B includes elements in either set; A∩B includes elements in both; A−B removes B from A. A power set contains every subset, so |P(A)|=2^|A|. The Cartesian product A×B consists of ordered pairs and has |A|×|B| elements for finite sets. Inclusion–exclusion gives \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\). On A, reflexivity means aRa for every a. Symmetry means aRb implies bRa. Antisymmetry means aRb and bRa imply a=b. Transitivity means aRb and bRc imply aRc. Reflexive+symmetric+transitive defines an equivalence relation, whose equivalence classes partition A. Test the properties individually; loops and pair direction matter. A function \(A\to B\) is total and single-valued. Injectivity forbids two distinct inputs sharing an output; surjectivity requires every codomain element to be reached. Bijectivity combines both and permits a two-sided inverse. On finite sets of equal size, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent; that shortcut depends on finiteness and equal cardinality. For a finite set {a₁,…,aₙ}, represent a relation by a Boolean matrix M where \(M_{ij}=1\) iff \(a_iRa_j\). Reflexivity requires diagonal 1s; symmetry requires \(M=M^T\); antisymmetry disallows simultaneous off-diagonal 1s in symmetric positions. Transitivity requires that every two-edge path implies its direct relation pair. Relation composition uses Boolean matrix multiplication, where products use AND and sums use OR. The transitive closure adds all pairs reachable by paths, and need not add loops unless a path or reflexive closure requires them. For function composition \(g\circ f\), apply f first and then g; the right-hand function acts first. If both functions are injective, their composition is injective, but properties of a composition do not freely imply every property of each component. Set operations can be verified through membership conditions before counting anything. An element belongs to a union if it passes at least one membership test, to an intersection if it passes both, and to a difference if it passes the first but fails the second. Complements require a fixed universe; changing it changes the answer. Nested sets require distinguishing an object from a subset containing that object. For finite sets, explicit enumeration gives an independent check of identities and power-set sizes. Remember that membership ignores repetition and order, whereas Cartesian products preserve coordinate order. Empty-set membership and empty-set inclusion answer different questions and therefore must be tested separately. A finite relation can be viewed as a directed edge set, an adjacency matrix, or a table of ordered pairs. Each representation encodes the same yes-or-no predicate, but property checks require the correct pattern. Reflexivity examines every diagonal pair; symmetry pairs each arrow with its reversal; antisymmetry permits arrows in both directions only on a loop. Transitivity checks every two-step route and demands its shortcut. Do not replace this universal route check with a claim that a diagram looks connected. A relation from A to B need not assign partners to every input and need not be single-valued. Those additional requirements belong to functions, not arbitrary relations. An equivalence relation formalizes sameness with respect to one selected feature, even when the objects themselves differ. Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity jointly ensure that choosing a different representative does not alter an equivalence class. To construct classes on a finite set, place related elements together, then check that the resulting blocks are disjoint and cover the domain. Conversely, a partition defines an equivalence relation by declaring two elements related exactly when they share a block. A relation that groups some similar-looking pairs without transitivity may fail to produce genuine classes. In modular examples, residues determine the feature of sameness; the difference of related integers must be divisible by the modulus. The domain and codomain are part of a function’s specification, even when a familiar algebraic formula is used. Surjectivity compares the image with the declared codomain; injectivity compares outputs of distinct domain inputs. To prove an algebraic map injective, set two outputs equal and show their inputs must match. To prove surjectivity, start with an arbitrary codomain value and construct a permitted preimage. For a finite map, count or list preimages instead. Composition applies the inner map first, so a proposed inverse must return each input and each codomain value in the appropriate direction. gateGuide.recognize: First classify the object: set, relation or function. For a relation test each required axiom; for a function distinguish domain, image and codomain.
method: List allowed pairs or use a relation matrix for small finite domains. Do not infer transitivity from checking only consecutive-looking labels.
For injectivity compare equal outputs; for surjectivity solve for an input reaching an arbitrary codomain element.
For counting, identify independent choices. A relation from A to B chooses a subset of their Cartesian product, whereas a function chooses exactly one output per input.

traps.claim: Confusing relations with functions
traps.why: With m inputs and n outputs, arbitrary relations have 2^(mn) possibilities, but total functions have n^m. A function must cover every input with exactly one output.

traps.claim: Antisymmetric means asymmetric
traps.why: The identity relation is both symmetric and antisymmetric. Antisymmetry only rules out two opposite directed pairs between distinct elements.

formulas.meaning: Finite Cartesian-product size.
Relations choose pairs independently; functions choose one output per input.
Subtract overlap to avoid double counting.

tutorials.title: Sets, operations and counting overlap
tutorials.body:
A set records membership, not order or repetition: {1,2,2} and {2,1} describe the same set. A subset A⊆B means every member of A belongs to B; proper subset additionally requires inequality. The empty set is a subset of every set, but it is not necessarily an element of a set. This distinction separates ∅⊆A from ∅∈A.
Union collects membership in either operand; intersection requires both; difference A−B keeps members of A absent from B. A complement needs a stated universe. Cartesian product A×B consists of ordered pairs, so swapping the operands can change it even when their sizes agree. A power set contains all subsets and has size \(2^{|A|}\), including the empty and full subsets.
When counting a union, adding sizes counts intersection members twice. Subtracting the intersection once gives \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\). Do not confuse elements with subsets in a power-set question. If an object is itself a set, carefully check which level of braces the statement is about before choosing an option.

example.prompt: Let A={1,2,3}, B={3,4}. Find their union, intersection and |A×B|.
example.strategy: Union → Intersection → Product count

steps.title: Union
steps.explanation: Collect each distinct member once: A∪B={1,2,3,4}.

steps.title: Intersection
steps.explanation: Only 3 belongs to both, giving A∩B={3}.

steps.title: Product count
steps.explanation: Each first coordinate has two possible second coordinates.

example.answer: Union size 4, intersection {3}, Cartesian-product size 6.
example.verification: Inclusion–exclusion gives 3+2−1=4, matching explicit union enumeration.

depth.body: Set operations can be verified through membership conditions before counting anything. An element belongs to a union if it passes at least one membership test, to an intersection if it passes both, and to a difference if it passes the first but fails the second. Complements require a fixed universe; changing it changes the answer. Nested sets require distinguishing an object from a subset containing that object. For finite sets, explicit enumeration gives an independent check of identities and power-set sizes. Remember that membership ignores repetition and order, whereas Cartesian products preserve coordinate order. Empty-set membership and empty-set inclusion answer different questions and therefore must be tested separately.

examples.prompt: Let U={1,2,3,4,5}, A={1,3,5}, B={3,4}. Find A∖B and the complement of A in U.
examples.strategy: Apply the difference condition → Apply the complement condition → Check disjointness

steps.title: Apply the difference condition
steps.explanation: Remove three from A because it also belongs to B.

steps.title: Apply the complement condition
steps.explanation: Keep universe members absent from A.

steps.title: Check disjointness
steps.explanation: An element cannot simultaneously belong and fail to belong to A.

examples.verification: A∪Aᶜ={1,2,3,4,5}=U, confirming that the complement uses the stated universe.

examples.prompt: A set A has four elements. How many subsets contain a fixed element a?
examples.strategy: Fix the required membership → Choose the other members → Count the subsets

steps.title: Fix the required membership
steps.explanation: The element a must appear, so it contributes no independent choice.

steps.title: Choose the other members
steps.explanation: Each of the other three elements may independently be included or omitted.

steps.title: Count the subsets
steps.explanation: All eight choices give distinct subsets containing a.

examples.answer: Eight subsets.
examples.verification: There are sixteen total subsets; pairing every subset with the result of toggling a divides them equally into containing and excluding a.

examples.prompt: For A={∅,{1}}, decide whether ∅∈A, ∅⊆A, and {1}⊆A.
examples.strategy: Check empty-set membership → Check empty-set inclusion → Check singleton inclusion

steps.title: Check empty-set membership
steps.explanation: The empty set is explicitly one of the two elements.

steps.title: Check empty-set inclusion
steps.explanation: There is no element of the empty set that could violate inclusion.

steps.title: Check singleton inclusion
steps.explanation: A contains the set {1}, not the number one itself.

examples.answer: True, true, false.
examples.verification: The statement {1}∈A is true, illustrating why membership of a set differs from inclusion of its members.

tutorials.title: Relations, axioms and equivalence classes
tutorials.body:
A relation from A to B is any subset of A×B. Unlike a function, it may give an input no partner or many partners. On one set A, reflexivity requires every (a,a), symmetry requires (b,a) whenever (a,b) occurs, and transitivity requires (a,c) whenever both (a,b) and (b,c) occur. Antisymmetry is different from “not symmetric”: it permits two-way pairs only when the endpoints are equal.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Its class [a] contains all elements related to a. Classes are either identical or disjoint, and partition the original set; choosing a different representative from the same class changes no class. In finite matrices, reflexivity uses diagonal ones, symmetry uses mirrored entries, and transitivity uses all two-edge paths.
To disprove a property, exhibit its exact missing requirement: a missing loop for reflexivity, an unmatched reversed pair for symmetry, or a two-step path lacking its shortcut for transitivity. Checking only selected pairs cannot prove a universal axiom. Equivalence classes and connected components are not interchangeable for an arbitrary non-equivalence relation.

example.prompt: On {1,2,3}, relate numbers having the same parity.
example.strategy: Reflexivity → Symmetry and transitivity → Classes

steps.title: Reflexivity
steps.explanation: Every number has the same parity as itself.

steps.title: Symmetry and transitivity
steps.explanation: Parity equality reverses and chains, so both axioms hold.

steps.title: Classes
steps.explanation: Odd and even membership partitions the set.

example.answer: It is an equivalence relation with two classes.
example.verification: The classes are disjoint and their union is {1,2,3}; 1 and 3 are different representatives of one class.

depth.body: A finite relation can be viewed as a directed edge set, an adjacency matrix, or a table of ordered pairs. Each representation encodes the same yes-or-no predicate, but property checks require the correct pattern. Reflexivity examines every diagonal pair; symmetry pairs each arrow with its reversal; antisymmetry permits arrows in both directions only on a loop. Transitivity checks every two-step route and demands its shortcut. Do not replace this universal route check with a claim that a diagram looks connected. A relation from A to B need not assign partners to every input and need not be single-valued. Those additional requirements belong to functions, not arbitrary relations.

examples.prompt: On {1,2}, let R={(1,1),(2,2),(1,2)}. Is it reflexive, symmetric and antisymmetric?
examples.strategy: Inspect the diagonal → Inspect reversal → Inspect two-way distinct pairs

steps.title: Inspect the diagonal
steps.explanation: Both required loops are present, so reflexivity holds.

steps.title: Inspect reversal
steps.explanation: The missing reversal disproves symmetry.

steps.title: Inspect two-way distinct pairs
steps.explanation: There are no opposite arrows between different elements, so antisymmetry holds.

examples.answer: Reflexive and antisymmetric, but not symmetric.
examples.verification: The relation is the ordinary ≤ relation restricted to {1,2}, consistent with these properties.

examples.prompt: On {a,b,c}, R={(a,b),(b,c)}. What pair must be added to make this relation transitive?
examples.strategy: Find a two-step chain → Add its shortcut → Recheck all chains

steps.title: Find a two-step chain
steps.explanation: The middle endpoint b matches, so transitivity imposes a requirement.

steps.title: Add its shortcut
steps.explanation: This pair satisfies the only existing two-step route.

steps.title: Recheck all chains
steps.explanation: No pair leaves c and none enters a, so the added shortcut creates no further missing two-step requirement.

examples.answer: Add (a,c); no other pair is necessary.
examples.verification: The transitive closure has exactly the three ordered pairs corresponding to reachability in the chain a→b→c.

examples.prompt: Can a relation be both symmetric and antisymmetric? Use the equality relation on {1,2,3}.
examples.strategy: List equality pairs → Check symmetry → Check antisymmetry

steps.title: List equality pairs
steps.explanation: Equality includes only diagonal pairs.

steps.title: Check symmetry
steps.explanation: Reversing a loop produces the same pair, so every reverse exists.

steps.title: Check antisymmetry
steps.explanation: Whenever both directions hold, the endpoints are already equal.

examples.answer: Yes; equality is both symmetric and antisymmetric.
examples.verification: There are no distinct mutually related elements. Antisymmetric means a precise restriction, not merely “not symmetric.”

depth.body: An equivalence relation formalizes sameness with respect to one selected feature, even when the objects themselves differ. Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity jointly ensure that choosing a different representative does not alter an equivalence class. To construct classes on a finite set, place related elements together, then check that the resulting blocks are disjoint and cover the domain. Conversely, a partition defines an equivalence relation by declaring two elements related exactly when they share a block. A relation that groups some similar-looking pairs without transitivity may fail to produce genuine classes. In modular examples, residues determine the feature of sameness; the difference of related integers must be divisible by the modulus.

examples.prompt: On {0,1,2,3,4,5}, define aRb when a≡b (mod 3). List the equivalence classes.
examples.strategy: Use remainder zero → Use the other remainders → Check coverage

steps.title: Use remainder zero
steps.explanation: These elements differ from zero by a multiple of three.

steps.title: Use the other remainders
steps.explanation: The other two residue values form their own blocks.

steps.title: Check coverage
steps.explanation: The blocks are disjoint and together contain all six elements, so they are the complete classes.

examples.verification: Every within-block difference is divisible by three; every cross-block difference has a nonzero remainder.

examples.prompt: A six-element set is partitioned into blocks of sizes 3,2,1. How many ordered pairs are in the induced equivalence relation?
examples.strategy: Count within the first block → Count the other blocks → Add disjoint pair sets

steps.title: Count within the first block
steps.explanation: Every first element can be paired with every element in its own three-member block.

steps.title: Count the other blocks
steps.explanation: The same Cartesian-product rule applies independently within each block.

steps.title: Add disjoint pair sets
steps.explanation: No related pair crosses between blocks.

examples.answer: Fourteen ordered pairs.
examples.verification: The six diagonal pairs are included; off-diagonal counts 3·2+2·1+1·0=8 give the same total 14.

examples.prompt: On {1,2,3}, define aRb when |a−b|≤1. Is this an equivalence relation?
examples.strategy: Check easy axioms → Find a chain → Test the shortcut

steps.title: Check easy axioms
steps.explanation: The relation is reflexive and symmetric.

steps.title: Find a chain
steps.explanation: Both adjacent differences equal one.

steps.title: Test the shortcut
steps.explanation: The required pair 1R3 fails, disproving transitivity.

examples.answer: No; transitivity fails.
examples.verification: The supposed neighborhoods [1]={1,2} and [2]={1,2,3} overlap without being identical, which genuine equivalence classes cannot do.

tutorials.title: Functions: injective, surjective and compositional behavior
tutorials.body:
A function f:\(A\to B\) assigns exactly one element of B to every element of A. A is its domain, B its codomain, and the attained values form its image, which need not equal B. Injective means different inputs never share an output; surjective means every codomain element is attained; bijective means both. A bijection has a two-sided inverse function, but a many-to-one map cannot recover an input uniquely.
For finite sets with m inputs and n outputs, there are \(n^m\) total functions because output choices are independent. An injection requires m≤n and uses decreasing choices n(n−1)…; a surjection requires m≥n. Equal finite sizes let injection and surjection imply each other, but infinite domains need separate reasoning.
Composition \(g\circ f\) applies f first. The intermediate domain/codomain must be compatible. Composition preserves injectivity when both functions are injective and preserves surjectivity when both are surjective, but one cannot infer every component property from the composite. In questions involving a named codomain, do not quietly replace it by the image to make a map onto.

example.strategy: Check totality → Check injectivity → Check surjectivity

steps.title: Check totality
steps.explanation: All three inputs have exactly one output, so this is a function.

steps.title: Check injectivity
steps.explanation: Distinct inputs collide, disproving injectivity.

steps.title: Check surjectivity
steps.explanation: Both declared codomain elements have preimages.

example.answer: Surjective, not injective, and therefore not bijective.
example.verification: Changing the codomain to {a,b,c} would destroy surjectivity without changing the three assignments.

depth.body: The domain and codomain are part of a function’s specification, even when a familiar algebraic formula is used. Surjectivity compares the image with the declared codomain; injectivity compares outputs of distinct domain inputs. To prove an algebraic map injective, set two outputs equal and show their inputs must match. To prove surjectivity, start with an arbitrary codomain value and construct a permitted preimage. For a finite map, count or list preimages instead. Composition applies the inner map first, so a proposed inverse must return each input and each codomain value in the appropriate direction. Restricting the domain can remove collisions; enlarging the codomain can destroy surjectivity without changing the formula.

examples.prompt: For f:{1,2,3}→{a,b,c} with f(1)=b,f(2)=c,f(3)=a, determine injectivity and surjectivity.
examples.strategy: Compare outputs → Compare image and codomain → Combine the properties

steps.title: Compare outputs
steps.explanation: The three outputs b,c,a are all distinct, so no two domain inputs collide.

steps.title: Compare image and codomain
steps.explanation: Every declared target has a preimage.

steps.title: Combine the properties
steps.explanation: The map is both injective and surjective, hence bijective.

examples.answer: Bijective.
examples.verification: The inverse assigns a→3,b→1,c→2 and recovers each original input.

examples.prompt: Show that f:ℝ→ℝ, f(x)=3x−4, is bijective and find its inverse.
examples.strategy: Prove injectivity → Construct every preimage → Write the inverse

steps.title: Prove injectivity
steps.explanation: Equal outputs force equal inputs.

steps.title: Construct every preimage
steps.explanation: This real input exists for every real codomain value.

steps.title: Write the inverse
steps.explanation: The preimage is unique, so the inverse is a function.

examples.answer: Bijective; f⁻¹(y)=(y+4)/3.
examples.verification: Composing gives 3((y+4)/3)−4=y and ((3x−4)+4)/3=x.

examples.prompt: Is f:ℝ→ℝ, f(x)=x², a bijection?
examples.strategy: Find an input collision → Find an unattained target → Distinguish a repaired specification

steps.title: Find an input collision
steps.explanation: Different real inputs share an output, so injectivity fails.

steps.title: Find an unattained target
steps.explanation: The negative codomain value −1 has no preimage, so surjectivity fails.

steps.title: Distinguish a repaired specification
steps.explanation: Restricting both domain and codomain to nonnegative reals yields a bijection, but that is a different function specification.

examples.answer: No; it is neither injective nor surjective as stated.
examples.verification: Its image is [0,∞), and every positive image value has two real preimages.

lessons.title: Partial orders and lattices
lessons.intuition: An order need not compare every pair. A dependency graph of tasks can say one task comes before another while leaving independent tasks incomparable. A lattice adds a reliable way to combine any two elements using their closest common upper and lower bounds.

sections.title: Partial order and diagrams
sections.body: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. If every pair is comparable, it is a total order. A Hasse diagram omits loops and edges implied by transitivity; lower-to-higher paths imply the order. An edge represents a cover relation: no element lies strictly between its endpoints.

sections.title: Extremal elements
sections.body: A least element is below every element and is unique if it exists; a minimal element has no strictly smaller element and several may exist. Greatest and maximal are dual. An upper bound of a pair lies above both; the least upper bound is the smallest among those bounds, not just any convenient upper bound.

sections.title: Lattice operations
sections.body: A lattice requires every pair to have a unique least upper bound (join) and greatest lower bound (meet). In a power-set lattice ordered by inclusion, join is union and meet is intersection. For positive divisors of an integer ordered by divisibility, join is lcm and meet is gcd. A finite lattice has top and bottom elements.

sections.title: Finding bounds without confusing numeric order
sections.body: To find an upper bound of a,b in an arbitrary poset, list elements x for which a≤x and b≤x according to the defined relation. Among these candidates, a least upper bound must be below every other upper bound. A merely minimal upper bound might fail that requirement; two incomparable minimal upper bounds mean there is no join. For a Hasse diagram, follow upward paths from both elements and intersect their reachable sets. Repeat downward for lower bounds. In a finite poset, having a top and bottom alone does not make it a lattice: the pairwise meet and join requirement still needs checking. In subset inclusion, these constructions reduce to union and intersection because those sets satisfy the universal bound definitions.

examples.prompt: Find meet and join of 4 and 6 among divisors of 12

steps.title: Find lower bounds
steps.explanation: A lower bound must divide both numbers and belong to the poset. Among these, 1 divides 2, so 2 is the greatest lower bound.

steps.title: Find upper bounds
steps.explanation: An upper bound must be divisible by both 4 and 6. Within this set 12 is the only candidate, and therefore the least upper bound.

steps.title: Express the operations
steps.explanation: The gcd/lcm shortcut is justified here because the poset of all divisors of 12 contains these bounds.

examples.given: The set is all positive divisors of 12; the order relation is divisibility.
examples.goal: Find the meet and join of 4 and 6.
examples.strategy: Use the relation’s bound definition, not ordinary numerical minimum and maximum.
examples.answer: Meet 2; join 12.
examples.verification: 4 is not a lower bound of 6, and 6 is not an upper bound of 4: neither number divides the other.

examples.prompt: Identify minimal versus least in {2,3,6}, ordered by divisibility

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: Neither 2 nor 3 has a distinct predecessor in {2,3,6}. They are incomparable, not ordered by their numerical sizes.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: A least element would have to divide both 2 and 3. No member of the given set does, although two minimal elements exist.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: Six is above every member under divisibility, so it is greatest. The absent integer 1 cannot be used as the set’s least element.

examples.strategy: Use divisibility comparisons inside the given set only.
examples.answer: There is no least element; 6 is greatest because both 2 and 3 divide it.
examples.verification: Minimality rules out an element strictly below that candidate; leastness requires that candidate below every element. The two definitions are unequal.

pitfalls: Do not draw all transitive edges in a Hasse diagram.
Minimal does not imply least.
revision: Join is least upper bound; meet is greatest lower bound.

checks.prompt: Which condition is required for a poset to be a lattice?
checks.hint: The requirement concerns pairwise bounds.
checks.explanation: Every pair needs a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. Total comparability is unnecessary; a subset-inclusion lattice can have incomparable elements.
options: It has at least one minimal element
Every pair has a meet and a join

checks.prompt: How many elements are in the power-set lattice of a 3-element set?
checks.hint: All subsets are nodes.
checks.explanation: There are \(2^3=8\) subsets.

lessons.method:
A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. It permits incomparable elements: neither a≤b nor b≤a may hold. A total order additionally compares every pair. The order symbol describes the stated relation, which can be divisibility or set inclusion rather than ordinary numeric size.
A Hasse diagram omits reflexive loops and edges implied by transitivity. Draw b above a when a<b and no intermediate element lies between them; these are covering pairs. An upward path still proves comparability even without a direct edge. Minimal means no distinct element lies below the candidate; least means the candidate lies below every element. Multiple minimal elements may exist, whereas a least element, if present, is unique. Maximal and greatest are the dual notions.
To recover a relation from the diagram, include equality and all upward reachability, not just drawn edges. For upper bounds of a pair, intersect their upward-reachable sets. A common upper bound need not be the least one. In divisor diagrams numeric placement is merely visual; every asserted comparison must satisfy divisibility. For a,b in a poset, a lower bound lies below both and an upper bound above both. The meet a∧b is the greatest lower bound: every other lower bound must lie below it. The join a∨b is the least upper bound: it must lie below every other upper bound. Having several incomparable minimal upper bounds gives no join, even though upper bounds exist.
A lattice requires a meet and join for every pair. A top and bottom do not alone prove this pairwise property. In a power set ordered by inclusion, intersection is meet and union join; their bound definitions prove these formulas. Among all positive divisors of a fixed integer ordered by divisibility, gcd and lcm supply meet and join and remain in the set. A restricted subset of divisors may lose the needed elements.
Bounds use the poset’s order, not numerical min/max. To test a proposed answer, first prove it is a bound, then prove it compares correctly with every other bound. This second step distinguishes “a common upper bound” from “the least upper bound” and often removes a plausible GATE distractor. A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. If every pair is comparable, it is a total order. A Hasse diagram omits loops and edges implied by transitivity; lower-to-higher paths imply the order. An edge represents a cover relation: no element lies strictly between its endpoints. A least element is below every element and is unique if it exists; a minimal element has no strictly smaller element and several may exist. Greatest and maximal are dual. An upper bound of a pair lies above both; the least upper bound is the smallest among those bounds, not just any convenient upper bound. A lattice requires every pair to have a unique least upper bound (join) and greatest lower bound (meet). In a power-set lattice ordered by inclusion, join is union and meet is intersection. For positive divisors of an integer ordered by divisibility, join is lcm and meet is gcd. A finite lattice has top and bottom elements. To find an upper bound of a,b in an arbitrary poset, list elements x for which a≤x and b≤x according to the defined relation. Among these candidates, a least upper bound must be below every other upper bound. A merely minimal upper bound might fail that requirement; two incomparable minimal upper bounds mean there is no join. For a Hasse diagram, follow upward paths from both elements and intersect their reachable sets. Repeat downward for lower bounds. In a finite poset, having a top and bottom alone does not make it a lattice: the pairwise meet and join requirement still needs checking. In subset inclusion, these constructions reduce to union and intersection because those sets satisfy the universal bound definitions. Partial orders compare objects through a specified relation, so ordinary numerical size may be irrelevant. Divisibility and inclusion allow some pairs to remain incomparable while still satisfying reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity. To identify a least element, test whether it lies below every object; being minimal only excludes a strictly smaller object. These conditions differ precisely because incomparability is permitted. The dual distinction holds for greatest and maximal elements. On a finite set, listing each object’s predecessors and successors can settle the questions without relying on a sketch. A strict order deliberately removes equality and therefore is not reflexive; it must not be checked against the non-strict partial-order axioms unchanged. A Hasse diagram stores only cover relations, making it a compressed representation of a finite partial order. A cover has no intermediate object between its endpoints; any comparison recoverable through an upward path is omitted as an edge. Recovering the full relation therefore requires reflexive pairs and transitive reachability. Edge counts in the drawing are not counts of all ordered comparable pairs. For inclusion, covers add one element; for divisibility within a restricted domain, covers depend on which intermediate divisors are present. Verify an edge by checking the stated order and the absence of an intermediate element, rather than by geometric closeness. Vertical placement records order direction, while horizontal placement has no algebraic meaning. A lattice makes two binary operations available from order alone: meet selects the greatest common lower bound and join the least common upper bound. Existence of some bound does not prove that the required extremal bound exists. In a finite poset, collect all common bounds, then check whether one compares correctly with all the others. In familiar lattices, domain closure remains essential: the gcd or union computed algebraically must actually belong to the poset. Meet and join need not equal numerical minimum and maximum because the order may be divisibility or inclusion. Counting join outcomes in a power-set lattice can be done element by element, using independent membership choices.

Find all common upper/lower bounds by paths, then check whether a candidate is below/above every other bound.
