lessons.title: Limits, continuity and differentiability
lessons.intuition: A limit describes nearby behaviour, while a function value describes the point itself. Continuity joins those ideas. Differentiability asks for one consistent local slope, a stronger requirement than having no break in the graph.

sections.title: Evaluating limits
sections.body: A two-sided limit exists when left and right limits agree. Try substitution first; an indeterminate 0/0 asks for simplification, not an answer. Factor and cancel on a punctured neighbourhood, rationalize radicals, or use standard limits such as sin x/x→1 in radians. Cancellation does not redefine the function at the removed point.

sections.title: Continuity
sections.body: At a, require f(a) to be defined, limₓ→ₐf(x) to exist, and both to agree. For piecewise functions check both sides and the assigned point value. A removable discontinuity can be repaired by defining the missing value to equal the limit; jump discontinuities cannot be repaired by one point assignment.

sections.title: Derivative from definition
sections.body: f′(a)=limₕ→₀[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h. Left and right derivative limits must agree. Continuity does not imply differentiability: a corner can have conflicting one-sided slopes.

sections.title: Piecewise continuity and matching slopes
sections.body: Consider f(x)=ax+b for x<1 and f(x)=x² for x≥1. Right-side value and limit at 1 are both 1. Continuity requires a+b=1. The left derivative is a while the right derivative is 2, so differentiability additionally requires a=2, hence b=−1. Matching values alone leaves many continuous choices, but only the matching slope gives differentiability here. For limits involving infinity, divide polynomial numerator and denominator by their highest relevant power of x to compare growth. A limit can exist even when the function is undefined at the point. Neither observing a plot nor substituting a few nearby values proves the exact limiting behaviour.

A sharp corner can remain continuous. lessons.title: Derivatives, extrema and the mean value theorem
lessons.intuition: Derivatives reveal change, but a zero slope alone does not identify a maximum. The mean value theorem connects average change over an interval to an instantaneous slope inside it, under precise continuity and differentiability assumptions.

sections.title: Derivative rules
sections.body: Differentiate sums termwise; the product rule is (uv)′=u′v+uv′, not u′v′. The chain rule multiplies outer derivative by inner derivative. For a quotient use (u′v−uv′)/v² where v≠0. sections.title: Finding extrema
sections.body: On a closed interval, a continuous function attains absolute extrema. List endpoints and interior critical points where derivative is zero or undefined; compare function values. A sign change from + to − in f′ gives a local maximum, from − to + a local minimum. If f′(c)=0, positive f″ gives a local minimum and negative f″ gives a maximum; f″=0 is inconclusive.

sections.title: Rolle and mean value theorems
sections.body: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), Rolle gives f′(c)=0 inside. The MVT removes the equal-endpoint requirement and gives f′(c)=[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a). Verify assumptions before solving the slope equation; functions with corners can violate the conclusion.

sections.title: Classifying a stationary point by signs
sections.body: For f(x)=x³−3x, derivative is 3x²−3, vanishing at x=−1 and x=1. On x<−1 the derivative is positive, on −1<x<1 it is negative, and on x>1 it is positive. Thus −1 is a local maximum and 1 a local minimum. The second derivative 6x gives the same classification, but the sign test also handles cases where f″ is zero. To find absolute extrema over a given closed interval, compare only critical points inside that interval plus its endpoints. Rolle’s theorem is MVT with equal endpoint values: the average slope becomes zero. A nondifferentiable corner can invalidate the hypothesis even if endpoints match.

lessons.title: Integration and accumulated quantities
lessons.intuition: Integration sums contributions over a continuum. A definite integral is signed accumulation; area below the axis contributes negatively. An antiderivative reverses differentiation, but definite integrals become useful only after applying limits consistently.

sections.title: Fundamental theorem and basic rules
sections.body: If f is continuous, an antiderivative F satisfies ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx=F(b)−F(a). The indefinite integral includes an arbitrary constant C. For n≠−1, ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C; ∫1/x dx=ln|x|+C on intervals avoiding zero. Definite integral limits have orientation: reversing them changes the sign.

sections.title: Substitution and parts
sections.body: For a composite expression, choose u=g(x) and du=g′(x)dx. In definite integrals, either transform both limits into u or substitute back before using original limits. Integration by parts is ∫u dv=uv−∫v du and is useful for products such as x eˣ or x ln x. Choose a differentiable part that simplifies.

sections.title: Symmetry and improper cases
sections.body: On [−a,a], an odd function integrates to zero and an even function integrates to twice the integral on [0,a]. This requires an integrable function; a singularity cannot be dismissed just by symmetry. For improper integrals use one-sided limits at singularities or infinity and require convergence.

sections.title: Integration by parts with actual evaluation
sections.body: To evaluate ∫₀¹xeˣdx, choose u=x and dv=eˣdx. Then du=dx and v=eˣ. Integration by parts gives [xeˣ]₀¹−∫₀¹eˣdx=e−(e−1)=1. The choice simplifies the polynomial factor under differentiation. For area between a curve and the x-axis, split intervals at sign changes and integrate absolute contributions; the integral of x on [−1,1] is zero but geometric area is 1. An improper integral such as ∫₁∞1/x²dx is a limit: ∫₁ᴹ1/x²dx=1−1/M tends to 1. ∫₁∞1/x dx instead grows as ln M and diverges; formally writing an antiderivative is not proof of convergence.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: The fundamental theorem converts the integral to upper-minus-lower values.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: Since the integrand is nonnegative on the interval, the signed integral here also equals geometric area. This equivalence fails when positive and negative regions cancel.

lessons.concept: Integration sums contributions over a continuum. A definite integral is signed accumulation; area below the axis contributes negatively. An antiderivative reverses differentiation, but definite integrals become useful only after applying limits consistently.
lessons.method:
An antiderivative F satisfies F′=f. The indefinite integral records all such functions as F+C on an interval. A definite integral instead measures accumulated signed contribution across bounds and is a number. Under the fundamental theorem’s conditions, it equals F(b)−F(a); a common constant cancels.
Positive and negative regions contribute opposite signs. Thus the integral is not automatically geometric area, which requires integrating |f| or separating sign intervals. Reversing bounds changes sign, and splitting an interval adds its pieces. Symmetry can simplify: odd integrable functions cancel over [−a,a], while even integrable functions double their contribution over [0,a]. Check integrability before using those rules near singularities.
For improper integrals, replace a singular endpoint or infinite bound by a limit and evaluate convergence. A formally written antiderivative does not make a divergent integral finite. In GATE, track whether the requested quantity is a signed integral, enclosed area, or probability mass; the same expression may require different handling of negative regions. Substitution reverses the chain rule. Choose u=g(x) so du=g′(x)dx replaces the derivative factor, and rewrite the whole integrand in u. For a definite integral transform endpoints as well, or return entirely to x before applying original endpoints; mixing new variables with old bounds is an error. Merely naming u without removing every x does not finish the substitution.

tutorials.title: Antiderivatives and signed definite integrals
tutorials.body:
An antiderivative F satisfies F′=f. The indefinite integral records all such functions as F+C on an interval. A definite integral instead measures accumulated signed contribution across bounds and is a number. Under the fundamental theorem’s conditions, it equals F(b)−F(a); a common constant cancels.
Positive and negative regions contribute opposite signs. Thus the integral is not automatically geometric area, which requires integrating |f| or separating sign intervals. Reversing bounds changes sign, and splitting an interval adds its pieces. Symmetry can simplify: odd integrable functions cancel over [−a,a], while even integrable functions double their contribution over [0,a]. Check integrability before using those rules near singularities.
For improper integrals, replace a singular endpoint or infinite bound by a limit and evaluate convergence. A formally written antiderivative does not make a divergent integral finite. In GATE, track whether the requested quantity is a signed integral, enclosed area, or probability mass; the same expression may require different handling of negative regions.

example.strategy: Signed integral → Left absolute area → Right absolute area

steps.title: Signed integral
steps.explanation: Opposite contributions cancel.

steps.title: Left absolute area
steps.explanation: Absolute value changes the sign on the negative half.

steps.title: Right absolute area
steps.explanation: Add the nonnegative areas.

example.answer: Signed integral 0; total geometric area 1.
example.verification: Odd symmetry explains the signed zero, while two triangles each have area 1/2.

lessons.title: Probability, conditional probability and Bayes
lessons.intuition: A conditional probability changes the population under consideration. Once B is known, count only outcomes inside B. Bayes reverses a conditioning direction by combining prior frequencies with evidence; a high detection rate need not imply a high probability that a detected condition is real.

sections.title: Events and conditioning
sections.body: A probability measure assigns nonnegative values totaling 1 to the sample space. For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). The multiplication rule gives P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B). Mutually exclusive nonzero-probability events cannot be independent, because their intersection is empty.

sections.title: Total probability and Bayes
sections.body: If B₁,…,Bₖ form a partition, P(A)=ΣP(A|Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ). Bayes gives P(Bⱼ|A)=P(A|Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ)/P(A). Construct the denominator from every way the evidence can occur. Use a frequency table when fractions feel abstract: population counts often make false positives obvious.

sections.title: Independence
sections.body: A and B are independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when defined. Pairwise independence among three events is weaker than mutual independence: the triple intersection must also factor. Do not infer independence from different-looking descriptions.

sections.title: A table prevents reversed conditioning
sections.body: Use rows for cause classes and columns for evidence outcomes. For prevalence 0.2, sensitivity 0.8 and false-positive rate 0.1, among 1000 cases there are 200 positives-by-condition, of which 160 test positive; among the 800 without the condition, 80 test positive. Hence P(test positive)=240/1000 and P(condition|test positive)=160/240=2/3. The denominator is everyone with the evidence, not everyone with the condition. The formula agrees: 0.8×0.2/[0.8×0.2+0.1×0.8]. Independence can also be tested by checking whether conditioning leaves the probability unchanged. Sampling without replacement often destroys that equality because the first draw changes the remaining population.

examples.prompt: A test has sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 10%, and prevalence 1%. Find \(P(\text{condition}\mid\text{positive})\)

steps.title: Label events and joint probabilities
steps.explanation: D means having the condition. Sensitivity is P(+|D), not the posterior probability being asked for.

steps.title: Count positives without the condition
steps.explanation: The large noncondition population can contribute more positives despite its smaller per-person positive rate.

steps.title: Normalize within all positives
steps.explanation: The denominator is total positive probability. Omitting false positives or the prevalence changes the event being computed.

examples.given: Prevalence 0.01; sensitivity 0.90; false-positive rate 0.10.
examples.goal: Find the probability of the condition given a positive test.
examples.strategy: Account for both sources of positive tests, then restrict to the positive population.
examples.answer: Approximately 8.33%.
examples.verification: Among 10,000 people: 90 true positives and 990 false positives; 90/1080 reproduces the posterior.

examples.prompt: Draw two cards without replacement; find probability both are aces

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: A₁ is an ace on the first draw. The standard deck has four aces among 52 cards.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Conditioned on an ace already being removed, three aces remain among 51 cards. The draws are not independent.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: The multiplication rule uses a conditional second factor. Reusing 4/52 would silently change the experiment to replacement.

examples.strategy: Multiply a marginal probability by the correct conditional probability.
examples.answer: Multiply \(\frac4{52}\frac3{51}=\frac1{221}\). Treating the draws as independent would use the wrong second factor.
examples.verification: An unordered count gives C(4,2)/C(52,2)=6/1326=1/221, agreeing with the sequential calculation.

Disjointness and independence are different.

Cannot be determined even with disjointness

checks.hint: Multiply independent probabilities.

Bayes reverses a conditioning direction by combining prior frequencies with evidence; a high detection rate need not imply a high probability that a detected condition is real.

Probability assigns normalized weights to events. Conditional probability P(A|B) restricts attention to outcomes in B and renormalizes by P(B), so P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. The multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B) does not require independence.
Independence means the intersection probability factors as P(A)P(B), equivalently conditioning on one nonzero-probability event does not change the other’s probability. Disjoint events instead cannot occur together and have zero intersection. Two disjoint events with positive probabilities are therefore dependent, not independent. Draws without replacement usually change remaining probabilities and require conditional factors.
For a chain of events, multiply each probability conditional on earlier events. For unions, use inclusion–exclusion rather than summing overlapping probabilities. Describe the sample space and whether outcomes are equally likely before using favorable/total counts. GATE distractors often invert A|B or reuse the original denominator after a removal; a count-based interpretation of the condition makes both errors visible. Bayes’ theorem derives from calculating an intersection two ways: P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A). Reversing a conditional therefore needs prior probabilities, not just swapping letters. With mutually exclusive exhaustive causes Bᵢ, total probability P(A)=ΣP(A|Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ) supplies the denominator.
The posterior for cause Bⱼ is its joint contribution to the observed event divided by every cause’s contribution. In testing, sensitivity P(positive|condition) is not \(P(\text{condition}\mid\text{positive})\). Even a good test can produce many false positives when the condition’s prior prevalence is low. A hypothetical population converts percentages into counts and often makes this effect intuitive.
Draw a tree with first branches for prior causes and second branches for evidence likelihoods. Multiply down branches for joint probabilities and sum across evidence-compatible leaves. Only afterward normalize the requested branch. Priors must sum to one and the evidence probability must be nonzero. Keep the full denominator when several machines, boxes or populations can produce the same observed outcome. Two events A and B are independent when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). If B has positive probability, the same condition says \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\): learning B does not change the probability of A. Independence is a property of the specified events and probability model. It is not established merely because two events sound unrelated, and it differs from disjointness. Disjoint positive-probability events cannot be independent, because their intersection has probability zero while the product of their probabilities is positive.
For equally likely finite outcomes, count the sample space, each event, and their intersection. Use the same underlying outcomes for every count, then compare the probabilities exactly. Events defined using the same experiment can still be independent, as the dice example demonstrates. Conversely, independent individual dice do not make every pair of events involving them independent. Identify the conditions precisely: a sum being even means the two dice have matching parity, which lets the joint event be counted without enumerating all 36 pairs one by one. Construct the denominator from every way the evidence can occur. Use a frequency table when fractions feel abstract: population counts often make false positives obvious. A and B are independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when defined. Pairwise independence among three events is weaker than mutual independence: the triple intersection must also factor. Do not infer independence from different-looking descriptions. Use rows for cause classes and columns for evidence outcomes. For prevalence 0.2, sensitivity 0.8 and false-positive rate 0.1, among 1000 cases there are 200 positives-by-condition, of which 160 test positive; among the 800 without the condition, 80 test positive. Hence P(test positive)=240/1000 and P(condition|test positive)=160/240=2/3. The denominator is everyone with the evidence, not everyone with the condition. The formula agrees: 0.8×0.2/[0.8×0.2+0.1×0.8]. Independence can also be tested by checking whether conditioning leaves the probability unchanged. Sampling without replacement often destroys that equality because the first draw changes the remaining population. Conditioning changes the reference population to the outcomes where the given event occurred. The numerator counts outcomes satisfying both the target and the condition; the denominator normalizes by the condition, which must have positive probability. In equally likely finite models, this is a ratio of counts within the reduced sample space. Without replacement, later draws depend on earlier ones, so compute joint events through sequential probabilities rather than assuming independence. The direction of conditioning matters because changing the denominator changes the question. Always translate “given” into a specific event before calculating, and verify that the final value lies between zero and one. Bayes' theorem updates competing explanations after evidence arrives. Multiply each hypothesis’s prior probability by its likelihood for the evidence, then normalize those contributions by their sum. A likelihood is not a posterior: high sensitivity or a high probability of evidence under a hypothesis does not by itself make that hypothesis likely after observing evidence. Repeated observations must use a likelihood for the full observed sequence, with conditional independence stated when products are used. For a finite exhaustive hypothesis partition, total probability provides the denominator. Posterior probabilities should sum to one, and hypotheses with zero prior remain zero unless the model itself is changed. Independence compares a joint probability with a product of marginal probabilities, not with zero overlap. Positive-probability disjoint events are dependent because learning one excludes the other. For three or more events, pairwise independence checks only two-event products; mutual independence additionally checks every larger intersection. A construction from a few fair bits can expose that distinction exactly. Events arising from one experiment may be independent, while events defined from independent inputs can still share a dependent condition. Name the events precisely and compute the intersections using the same outcome model. For zero-probability conditions, the product definition remains meaningful even when a conditional probability ratio is undefined.

tutorials.title: Conditioning, intersections and independence
tutorials.body:
Probability assigns normalized weights to events. Conditional probability P(A|B) restricts attention to outcomes in B and renormalizes by P(B), so P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. The multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B) does not require independence.
Independence means the intersection probability factors as P(A)P(B), equivalently conditioning on one nonzero-probability event does not change the other’s probability. Disjoint events instead cannot occur together and have zero intersection. Two disjoint events with positive probabilities are therefore dependent, not independent. Draws without replacement usually change remaining probabilities and require conditional factors.
For a chain of events, multiply each probability conditional on earlier events. For unions, use inclusion–exclusion rather than summing overlapping probabilities. Describe the sample space and whether outcomes are equally likely before using favorable/total counts. GATE distractors often invert A|B or reuse the original denominator after a removal; a count-based interpretation of the condition makes both errors visible.

example.prompt: A fair die shows an even value. What is the probability it exceeds 3?
example.strategy: Conditioned sample space → Intersection → Normalize

steps.title: Conditioned sample space
steps.explanation: Only even outcomes remain, each equally likely.

steps.title: Intersection
steps.explanation: These outcomes are both even and greater than three.

steps.title: Normalize
steps.explanation: Divide by the condition’s probability.

example.verification: Using 3/6 would calculate unconditioned P(value>3), a different question.

depth.body: Conditioning changes the reference population to the outcomes where the given event occurred. The numerator counts outcomes satisfying both the target and the condition; the denominator normalizes by the condition, which must have positive probability. In equally likely finite models, this is a ratio of counts within the reduced sample space. Without replacement, later draws depend on earlier ones, so compute joint events through sequential probabilities rather than assuming independence. The direction of conditioning matters because changing the denominator changes the question. Always translate “given” into a specific event before calculating, and verify that the final value lies between zero and one.

examples.prompt: Draw one card uniformly from a standard 52-card deck. Given that it is a king, what is the probability it is red?
examples.strategy: Restrict the sample space → Count favorable conditioned outcomes → Normalize

steps.title: Restrict the sample space
steps.explanation: The condition leaves the four kings, each equally likely.

steps.title: Count favorable conditioned outcomes
steps.explanation: The heart and diamond kings are red, so two of those four outcomes qualify.

steps.title: Normalize
steps.explanation: Use the conditioned four-card population rather than all fifty-two cards.

examples.answer: One half.
examples.verification: The joint probability is 2/52 and the king probability 4/52; their ratio is again one half.

examples.prompt: An urn has three red and two blue balls. Draw two without replacement. Given at least one is red, find the probability the first is red.
examples.strategy: Compute the conditioning probability → Compute the intersection → Normalize

steps.title: Compute the conditioning probability
steps.explanation: The excluded event is two blue draws.

steps.title: Compute the intersection
steps.explanation: If the first draw is red, at least one red is automatic.

steps.title: Normalize
steps.explanation: The joint probability is divided by the actual conditioning probability.

examples.answer: Two thirds.
examples.verification: Among twenty equally likely ordered ball pairs, eighteen contain red and twelve start red; 12/18=2/3.

examples.prompt: Among 100 people, 20 belong to A, 50 belong to B, and 10 belong to both. Are P(A|B) and P(B|A) equal?

steps.title: Find the shared numerator
steps.explanation: The intersection event is identical in both directions.

steps.title: Condition on B
steps.explanation: The denominator uses the fifty B members.

steps.title: Condition on A
steps.explanation: Reversing the question changes the reference population.

examples.answer: No; they are 1/5 and 1/2.
examples.verification: Multiplying each conditional by its own condition probability gives the same joint value 1/10.

tutorials.title: Bayes’ theorem: reverse a conditional using base rates
tutorials.body:
Bayes’ theorem derives from calculating an intersection two ways: P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A). Reversing a conditional therefore needs prior probabilities, not just swapping letters. With mutually exclusive exhaustive causes Bᵢ, total probability P(A)=ΣP(A|Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ) supplies the denominator.
The posterior for cause Bⱼ is its joint contribution to the observed event divided by every cause’s contribution. In testing, sensitivity P(positive|condition) is not \(P(\text{condition}\mid\text{positive})\). Even a good test can produce many false positives when the condition’s prior prevalence is low. A hypothetical population converts percentages into counts and often makes this effect intuitive.
Draw a tree with first branches for prior causes and second branches for evidence likelihoods. Multiply down branches for joint probabilities and sum across evidence-compatible leaves. Only afterward normalize the requested branch. Priors must sum to one and the evidence probability must be nonzero. Keep the full denominator when several machines, boxes or populations can produce the same observed outcome.

example.prompt: Machine A makes 60% of items with 2% defects; B makes 40% with 5% defects. Given a defect, find P(B).
example.strategy: Joint defect contributions → Total defect probability → Posterior

steps.title: Joint defect contributions
steps.explanation: Weight each defect rate by production share.

steps.title: Total defect probability
steps.explanation: Either machine can explain the defect.

steps.title: Posterior
steps.explanation: Normalize B’s contribution among defective items.

example.answer: P(B|defect)=0.625.
example.verification: Despite producing fewer items, B contributes more defects; the posterior need not equal its 40% production share.

examples.prompt: Choose one of two boxes with equal probability. Box A is one-quarter red; box B is three-quarters red. After drawing red, find the posterior probability of B.
examples.strategy: Compute joint contributions → Find total red probability → Normalize B’s contribution

steps.title: Compute joint contributions
steps.explanation: Weight each red likelihood by the box-selection prior.

steps.title: Find total red probability
steps.explanation: The two box explanations are exhaustive and disjoint.

steps.title: Normalize B’s contribution
steps.explanation: The posterior compares B’s contribution with all observed-red outcomes.

examples.answer: Three quarters.
examples.verification: A has posterior one quarter, so the updated probabilities sum to one and preserve the three-to-one likelihood ratio.

examples.prompt: Choose a fair coin or a double-headed coin with equal probability. Toss the chosen coin twice, independently conditional on its type, and observe HH. Find the probability it was double-headed.
examples.strategy: Calculate the sequence likelihoods → Weight by the priors → Normalize

steps.title: Calculate the sequence likelihoods
steps.explanation: The two fair tosses multiply, while the double-headed coin always gives heads.

steps.title: Weight by the priors
steps.explanation: Both coin types initially have probability one half.

steps.title: Normalize
steps.explanation: Use the likelihood of the full two-toss evidence.

examples.answer: Four fifths.
examples.verification: After one head the posterior is 2/3; updating with the second head gives (2/3)/((2/3)+(1/3)(1/2))=4/5.

examples.prompt: A hypothetical condition has prevalence 0.001. A test detects every case but falsely flags 0.01 of noncases. Does a positive result establish the condition with certainty?
examples.strategy: Compute the true-positive contribution → Compute the false-positive contribution → Normalize the posterior

steps.title: Compute the true-positive contribution
steps.explanation: Perfect sensitivity does not change the small prior prevalence.

steps.title: Compute the false-positive contribution
steps.explanation: Noncases are numerous, so this contribution exceeds true positives.

steps.title: Normalize the posterior
steps.explanation: The denominator includes both explanations of a positive result.

examples.answer: No; the posterior is 100/1099, about 9.10%.
examples.verification: In 100,000 modeled people, there are 100 true positives and 999 false positives, giving the same count ratio.

tutorials.title: Checking independence by comparing joint and marginal probabilities
tutorials.body:
Two events A and B are independent when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). If B has positive probability, the same condition says \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\): learning B does not change the probability of A. Independence is a property of the specified events and probability model. It is not established merely because two events sound unrelated, and it differs from disjointness. Disjoint positive-probability events cannot be independent, because their intersection has probability zero while the product of their probabilities is positive.
For equally likely finite outcomes, count the sample space, each event, and their intersection. Use the same underlying outcomes for every count, then compare the probabilities exactly. Events defined using the same experiment can still be independent, as the dice example demonstrates. Conversely, independent individual dice do not make every pair of events involving them independent. Identify the conditions precisely: a sum being even means the two dice have matching parity, which lets the joint event be counted without enumerating all 36 pairs one by one.

example.prompt: Roll two independent fair six-sided dice. Let A mean the first die is even, and B mean the sum is even. Are A and B independent?
example.strategy: Count the first event → Count an even sum → Count the intersection → Compare the product

steps.title: Count the first event
steps.explanation: The first die has three even values and the second can be any of six values.

steps.title: Count an even sum
steps.explanation: An even sum arises from two even values or two odd values; those cases are disjoint.

steps.title: Count the intersection
steps.explanation: If the first die is even and the sum is even, the second die must also be even.

steps.title: Compare the product
steps.explanation: The defining equality holds, proving independence of these two events.

example.answer: A and B are independent.
example.verification: Conditioning on an even sum leaves 18 equally likely pairs, nine with an even first die, so P(A|B)=9/18=1/2=P(A). The events overlap and are not disjoint.

Positive-probability disjoint events are dependent because learning one excludes the other. For three or more events, pairwise independence checks only two-event products; mutual independence additionally checks every larger intersection. A construction from a few fair bits can expose that distinction exactly. Events arising from one experiment may be independent, while events defined from independent inputs can still share a dependent condition. Name the events precisely and compute the intersections using the same outcome model. For zero-probability conditions, the product definition remains meaningful even when a conditional probability ratio is undefined.

examples.prompt: On a fair die, let A mean even and B mean divisible by three. Are the events independent?
examples.strategy: Count the marginals → Count the intersection → Compare the product

steps.title: Count the marginals
steps.explanation: The event sets are {2,4,6} and {3,6}.

steps.title: Count the intersection
steps.explanation: Only outcome six meets both conditions.

steps.title: Compare the product
steps.explanation: The defining joint-product equality holds.

examples.answer: Yes.
examples.verification: Given B, the outcomes are {3,6}; one of two is even, so P(A|B)=1/2=P(A).

examples.prompt: Two independent fair bits are generated. Let A mean first bit zero, B mean second bit zero, and C mean equal bits. Are the three events mutually independent?
examples.strategy: Find the marginals → Check pairs → Check the triple

steps.title: Find the marginals
steps.explanation: Each event contains two of the four equally likely bit pairs.

steps.title: Check pairs
steps.explanation: Each pair intersection contains only 00, so pairwise independence holds.

steps.title: Check the triple
steps.explanation: The triple product fails despite all pairwise checks.

examples.answer: Pairwise independent, but not mutually independent.
examples.verification: Knowing both A and B determines C with certainty, revealing the remaining dependence directly.

examples.prompt: On a fair coin toss, are H and T independent because they are mutually exclusive?
examples.strategy: Compute their positive marginals → Compute the joint → Compare the required product

steps.title: Compute their positive marginals
steps.explanation: Both events have nonzero probability.

steps.title: Compute the joint
steps.explanation: One toss cannot be both heads and tails.

steps.title: Compare the required product
steps.explanation: Disjointness contradicts independence here.

examples.answer: No; they are dependent.
examples.verification: P(H|T)=0 differs from P(H)=1/2, confirming that learning tails changes the chance of heads.

lessons.title: Random variables and descriptive statistics
lessons.intuition: A random variable attaches a number to an outcome. The distribution tells you how often values occur; expectation, variance, and quantiles summarize different aspects. An average alone cannot tell you whether values are tightly concentrated or widely spread.

sections.title: PMF, PDF and CDF
sections.body: For discrete X, p(x)=P(X=x) is a probability mass function and its values sum to 1. For continuous X, a density f integrates to 1; probabilities are areas, so P(X=x)=0 at individual points. The cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) works in both cases and is nondecreasing.

sections.title: Expectation and dispersion
sections.body: For discrete X, \(E[X]\)=Σxp(x); for continuous X, integrate xf(x). E[aX+b]=a\(E[X]\)+b without needing independence. Var(X)=\(E[X^2]\)−\(E[X]\)² and Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X). Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variances of sums add for independent variables; otherwise covariance terms matter.

sections.title: Mean, median and mode
sections.body: The arithmetic mean uses every observation and is sensitive to outliers. Median splits the ordered data into halves and resists extreme values. Mode is a most frequent value and need not be unique. Distinguish population variance, with divisor n, from the conventional unbiased sample variance, with divisor n−1, when the question specifies a sample estimator.

sections.title: Deriving variance and using linearity
sections.body: Variance is E[(X−μ)²], where μ=\(E[X]\). Expand the square: E[X²−2μX+μ²]=\(E[X^2]\)−2μ\(E[X]\)+μ²=\(E[X^2]\)−μ². This explains why the second moment, not just the mean, is needed. For a count X=I₁+…+Iₙ of indicator variables, \(E[X]\)=ΣE[Iᵢ]=ΣP(Iᵢ=1), even when the events are dependent. Variance addition requires checking covariance: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independent variables have covariance zero, but zero covariance alone does not establish independence in general. Scaling all observations by 3 scales deviations by 3 and squared deviations by 9, while adding a constant leaves deviations unchanged.

examples.prompt: Compute moments when X is 0 or 2 with equal probability

steps.title: Compute the mean
steps.explanation: Expectation is the probability-weighted value, which need not itself be a possible outcome.

steps.title: Compute the second moment
steps.explanation: Square each outcome before averaging. Squaring the mean would instead give 1 and is not the second moment.

steps.title: Compute spread
steps.explanation: Variance is in squared units; standard deviation is the nonnegative square root in the original units.

examples.given: X takes 0 and 2, each with probability 1/2.
examples.goal: Find mean, variance and standard deviation.
examples.strategy: Compute first and second moments separately, then subtract the squared first moment.
examples.answer: Mean 1, variance 1, standard deviation 1.
examples.verification: The deviations from mean are −1 and +1, so their squared values are both 1; their weighted average confirms variance 1.

examples.prompt: Summarize the data 1,2,2,3,12

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: The mean includes every observation, so the large final value has considerable influence.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: For five sorted observations the third is the median. The value two also has the largest occurrence count.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: The difference between mean and median signals this sample’s right-skewed extreme observation; the statistics need not coincide.

examples.strategy: Calculate mean, median and mode according to their distinct definitions.
examples.answer: The large observation shifts the mean away from the typical central values.
examples.verification: Removing 12 changes the mean to 2 while the central repeated values remain near 2, illustrating the mean’s sensitivity.

\(E[X^2]\) is not generally \(E[X]\)².

lessons.concept: A random variable attaches a number to an outcome. The distribution tells you how often values occur; expectation, variance, and quantiles summarize different aspects. An average alone cannot tell you whether values are tightly concentrated or widely spread.
lessons.method:
A random variable maps outcomes to numbers; it is not itself a probability. A discrete variable has a probability mass function whose nonnegative masses sum to one. A continuous variable has density integrating to one; interval probability is area, and a single exact value has probability zero in a continuous distribution.
Expectation is the probability-weighted value. It can fall between possible outcomes and obeys linearity without independence. Variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean, equivalently \(E[X^2]\)−\(E[X]\)². Standard deviation is its nonnegative square root, using the original units; variance uses squared units. Adding a constant changes the mean but not variance, while multiplying by a scales variance by a².
For sums, covariance determines whether variances add; independence is a sufficient condition for zero covariance, whereas expectation always adds. In sample statistics distinguish dividing by n for a population variance from n−1 for the conventional unbiased sample estimator. A supplied distribution question normally uses its theoretical expectation/variance, not an estimator convention chosen without explanation. For a finite dataset, the arithmetic mean is sum divided by count. The median is a middle location after sorting: for odd count use the central observation, and for even count the usual numerical median averages the two central observations. The mode is a most frequent value; it may be nonunique or absent under a convention requiring repetition.
These statistics need not agree. A large outlier can move the mean substantially while scarcely changing the median. The mode records concentration at a value rather than balancing numerical distances. Sorting is essential for median but does not change mean or frequencies. For a frequency table, weight each value by its count and locate median positions using cumulative counts rather than taking the median of category labels alone.
Combining datasets requires a count-weighted mean; simply averaging two means works only with equal sample sizes. Do not assume symmetry or a normal distribution from one summary statistic. A GATE question may deliberately provide repeated observations or uneven group sizes to test whether each definition, rather than a familiar slogan about an “average,” is being used. A random variable is a function that assigns a numerical value to every outcome of a random experiment. The variable is not itself an event or a probability. Different outcomes may produce the same value, so the probability of a value is the total probability of every outcome mapped to it. A discrete random variable has a probability mass function, written \(p_X(x)=P(X=x)\), whose values are nonnegative and sum to one.
Start with a clearly specified sample space and outcome probabilities. Define what number the variable records, map each outcome to that number, and group outcomes sharing a value. Then add probabilities within each group. Equal probability of basic outcomes does not imply equal probability of random-variable values, since groups may have different sizes. The support contains the attainable values; all other values have probability zero. Checking normalization verifies that no experiment outcome was omitted or counted twice. In the coin example, the two distinct ordered outcomes HT and TH both map to one head, which makes that value more likely than zero or two heads. For discrete X, p(x)=P(X=x) is a probability mass function and its values sum to 1. For continuous X, a density f integrates to 1; probabilities are areas, so P(X=x)=0 at individual points. The cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) works in both cases and is nondecreasing. For discrete X, \(E[X]\)=Σxp(x); for continuous X, integrate xf(x). E[aX+b]=a\(E[X]\)+b without needing independence. Var(X)=\(E[X^2]\)−\(E[X]\)² and Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X). Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variances of sums add for independent variables; otherwise covariance terms matter. The arithmetic mean uses every observation and is sensitive to outliers. Median splits the ordered data into halves and resists extreme values. Mode is a most frequent value and need not be unique. Distinguish population variance, with divisor n, from the conventional unbiased sample variance, with divisor n−1, when the question specifies a sample estimator. Variance is E[(X−μ)²], where μ=\(E[X]\). Expand the square: E[X²−2μX+μ²]=\(E[X^2]\)−2μ\(E[X]\)+μ²=\(E[X^2]\)−μ². This explains why the second moment, not just the mean, is needed. For a count X=I₁+…+Iₙ of indicator variables, \(E[X]\)=ΣE[Iᵢ]=ΣP(Iᵢ=1), even when the events are dependent. Variance addition requires checking covariance: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independent variables have covariance zero, but zero covariance alone does not establish independence in general. Scaling all observations by 3 scales deviations by 3 and squared deviations by 9, while adding a constant leaves deviations unchanged. The mean balances weighted values, with observation counts or probabilities supplying the weights. Combining groups therefore requires weighting each group’s mean by its size; a simple average of means works only for equal sizes. Expectation is linear even without independence, but it does not commute with a general nonlinear transformation such as squaring. The mean may be absent from the support because it summarizes the distribution rather than selecting an actual outcome. Check a finite-data mean by verifying that deviations sum to zero, and check a weighted mean by ensuring the weights sum to one. These examples distinguish an arithmetic population summary from a probabilistic expectation while using the same weighted-sum principle. Standard deviation measures spread in the original measurement units by taking the nonnegative square root of variance. First calculate the mean, then average squared deviations using probabilities or the appropriate population denominator. Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean equally, leaving deviations unchanged; multiplying by a scalar scales standard deviation by that scalar’s absolute value. A negative scalar cannot produce a negative spread. For observations treated as a sample, the conventional sample variance divides by n−1 rather than n; distinguish that estimator from population variance before computing. The square root of the unbiased variance estimator is not itself generally an unbiased standard-deviation estimator. The median is determined by sorted positions, not by the numerical midpoint of the smallest and largest observations. Frequency tables require cumulative counts to identify the central observations in the expanded dataset. With an even number of numerical observations, use the average of the two central values under the usual convention. Large outliers may leave those central positions unchanged, explaining the median’s resistance to extreme values. Medians of separate groups cannot generally be averaged to recover the combined median because their counts and full ordering matter. A verification should locate how many observations lie on each side of the proposed middle, counting equal values carefully. The mode identifies a most frequent value and does not involve numerical distance or averaging. Build a frequency table before choosing it; several values can tie for the largest count, giving multiple modes. Under a convention requiring repetition, a dataset of entirely distinct values has no mode, whereas a pure frequency-maximizer convention calls all values tied modes. State that convention in such an edge case rather than silently changing definitions. A large value is not automatically modal, and a mean need not be a mode even when it occurs in the dataset. For categorical observations, the mode remains meaningful where arithmetic mean and median may not be defined. A random variable compresses experiment outcomes into numerical information, and its distribution results from that mapping. If the map is many-to-one, combine the probabilities of all preimages of each value. For transformations such as a minimum, a cumulative or survival probability may count those preimages more easily than a direct list. Once a survival function is known for an integer-valued variable, subtract consecutive tails to obtain its mass function. Continuous variables require a density or cumulative function instead of a point-mass table; a density value itself is not the probability of an exact outcome. Keep the underlying experiment and the recorded quantity distinct when interpreting support or events.

steps.explanation: The larger lower-scoring group receives greater weight.

examples.answer: Sixty-five.
examples.verification: The weighted average (3/4)60+(1/4)80=65 agrees; the unweighted mean seventy would incorrectly treat the groups as equally large.

examples.prompt: X equals −1 or 1 with probability one half each. Is \(E[X^2]\)=(\(E[X]\))²?
examples.strategy: Compute the mean → Transform before averaging → Compare the operations

steps.title: Compute the mean
steps.explanation: The opposite values cancel.

steps.title: Transform before averaging
steps.explanation: Squaring removes the sign before expectation.

steps.title: Compare the operations
steps.explanation: Nonlinear transformation does not commute with expectation.

examples.verification: Their difference is variance one, independently confirming that the second moment differs from the squared mean.

depth.body: Standard deviation measures spread in the original measurement units by taking the nonnegative square root of variance. First calculate the mean, then average squared deviations using probabilities or the appropriate population denominator. Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean equally, leaving deviations unchanged; multiplying by a scalar scales standard deviation by that scalar’s absolute value. A negative scalar cannot produce a negative spread. For observations treated as a sample, the conventional sample variance divides by n−1 rather than n; distinguish that estimator from population variance before computing. The square root of the unbiased variance estimator is not itself generally an unbiased standard-deviation estimator.

examples.prompt: Treat data {1,3} as a complete population. Find its standard deviation.
examples.strategy: Find the mean → Average squared deviations → Take the nonnegative root

steps.title: Find the mean
steps.explanation: Both population members carry equal weight.

steps.title: Average squared deviations
steps.explanation: Divide by the full population count.

steps.title: Take the nonnegative root
steps.explanation: Standard deviation returns to the data’s original units.

examples.answer: One.
examples.verification: The second moment is (1²+3²)/2=5; subtracting μ²=4 also gives variance one.

examples.prompt: A random variable X has standard deviation 2. For Y=−3X+7, find Var(Y) and its standard deviation.
examples.strategy: Read the original variance → Apply the affine scaling rule → Take the square root

steps.title: Read the original variance
steps.explanation: Variance is the square of standard deviation.

steps.title: Apply the affine scaling rule
steps.explanation: The translation seven leaves spread unchanged.

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.explanation: The negative multiplier reverses order but not the sign of spread.

examples.answer: Variance 36; standard deviation six.
examples.verification: Every centered deviation is multiplied by −3, so its magnitude and the standard deviation are multiplied by three.

examples.prompt: Observations are 0,2. Compare population standard deviation with the conventional sample standard deviation.
examples.strategy: Compute the common deviation sum → Use the population denominator → Use the sample denominator

steps.title: Compute the common deviation sum
steps.explanation: Both conventions center at the same mean.

steps.title: Use the population denominator
steps.explanation: The complete two-member population divides by n.

steps.title: Use the sample denominator
steps.explanation: The conventional sample variance divides by n−1.

examples.answer: Population standard deviation one; sample standard deviation √2.
examples.verification: The difference comes entirely from the stated denominator, so the convention must be identified before reporting a number.

tutorials.title: Mean, median and mode summarize different aspects
tutorials.body:
For a finite dataset, the arithmetic mean is sum divided by count. The median is a middle location after sorting: for odd count use the central observation, and for even count the usual numerical median averages the two central observations. The mode is a most frequent value; it may be nonunique or absent under a convention requiring repetition.
These statistics need not agree. A large outlier can move the mean substantially while scarcely changing the median. The mode records concentration at a value rather than balancing numerical distances. Sorting is essential for median but does not change mean or frequencies. For a frequency table, weight each value by its count and locate median positions using cumulative counts rather than taking the median of category labels alone.
Combining datasets requires a count-weighted mean; simply averaging two means works only with equal sample sizes. Do not assume symmetry or a normal distribution from one summary statistic. A GATE question may deliberately provide repeated observations or uneven group sizes to test whether each definition, rather than a familiar slogan about an “average,” is being used.

example.prompt: Dataset: 1,2,2,5,10,10. Find mean, median and modes.
example.strategy: Mean → Median → Modes

steps.title: Mean
steps.explanation: All six observations contribute.

steps.title: Median
steps.explanation: The sorted third and fourth positions are central.

steps.title: Modes
steps.explanation: Both 2 and 10 occur twice, more often than the others.

example.answer: Mean 5; median 3.5; modes 2 and 10.
example.verification: An even-count median can be a value absent from the data; neither mode must equal the mean.

depth.body: The median is determined by sorted positions, not by the numerical midpoint of the smallest and largest observations. Frequency tables require cumulative counts to identify the central observations in the expanded dataset. With an even number of numerical observations, use the average of the two central values under the usual convention. Large outliers may leave those central positions unchanged, explaining the median’s resistance to extreme values. Medians of separate groups cannot generally be averaged to recover the combined median because their counts and full ordering matter. A verification should locate how many observations lie on each side of the proposed middle, counting equal values carefully.

examples.prompt: Find the median of the unsorted data 9,1,5,3,7.
examples.strategy: Sort the observations → Locate the middle position → Read the middle value

steps.title: Sort the observations
steps.explanation: The original entry order has no statistical role.

steps.title: Locate the middle position
steps.explanation: An odd count has one central observation.

steps.title: Read the middle value
steps.explanation: The third sorted observation is five.

examples.answer: Five.
examples.verification: Two observations lie below five and two above it, directly confirming the middle position.

examples.prompt: A frequency table has value 1 occurring twice, value 4 five times, and value 10 once. Find the median.
examples.strategy: Count the dataset → Locate cumulative ranges → Read positions four and five

steps.title: Count the dataset
steps.explanation: An even total requires two central positions.

steps.title: Locate cumulative ranges
steps.explanation: Value one occupies positions 1–2, four occupies 3–7, and ten occupies position eight.

steps.title: Read positions four and five
steps.explanation: Both central observations belong to the value-four block.

examples.answer: Four.
examples.verification: The expanded list 1,1,4,4,4,4,4,10 has the same two central values.

examples.prompt: Group A is {0,0,0} and group B is {100}. Is the combined median the average of the group medians?
examples.strategy: Compute separate medians → Merge and sort → Apply the combined definition

steps.title: Compute separate medians
steps.explanation: The medians are zero and one hundred.

steps.title: Merge and sort
steps.explanation: The combined list is 0,0,0,100, so positions two and three are both zero.

steps.title: Apply the combined definition
steps.explanation: Averaging the group medians would instead give fifty.

examples.answer: No; the combined median is zero.
examples.verification: The median depends on the middle observations of the full list, not on treating unequal groups as two equally weighted observations.

depth.body: The mode identifies a most frequent value and does not involve numerical distance or averaging. Build a frequency table before choosing it; several values can tie for the largest count, giving multiple modes. Under a convention requiring repetition, a dataset of entirely distinct values has no mode, whereas a pure frequency-maximizer convention calls all values tied modes. State that convention in such an edge case rather than silently changing definitions. A large value is not automatically modal, and a mean need not be a mode even when it occurs in the dataset. For categorical observations, the mode remains meaningful where arithmetic mean and median may not be defined.

examples.prompt: Find the mode of 3,3,4,4,4,8.
examples.strategy: Tally frequencies → Find the largest frequency → Select its value

steps.title: Tally frequencies
steps.explanation: Count repetitions without regard to magnitude.

steps.title: Find the largest frequency
steps.explanation: Three occurrences exceed the other counts.

steps.title: Select its value
steps.explanation: Only the value four has this frequency, so the mode is unique.

examples.answer: Four.
examples.verification: The six tally counts sum to six observations; the largest numerical value eight appears only once.

examples.prompt: A frequency table has values 2,3,4 with counts 5,3,5. Identify every mode.
examples.strategy: Compare the counts → Identify the tie → Report both values

steps.title: Compare the counts
steps.explanation: The central value three has fewer occurrences.

steps.title: Identify the tie
steps.explanation: Both outer values attain the maximum frequency.

steps.title: Report both values
steps.explanation: There is no basis to discard one tied maximizer or average them into a new mode.

examples.answer: Modes two and four.
examples.verification: The value three is their average but appears only three times, so averaging tied modes would produce a nonmodal value.

examples.prompt: Under the convention that a mode must repeat, what is the mode of 1,2,3? Is its mean two automatically a mode?
examples.strategy: Count each value → Apply the stated convention → Distinguish the mean

steps.title: Count each value
steps.explanation: All observations are distinct.

steps.title: Apply the stated convention
steps.explanation: No value repeats, so the dataset has no mode.

steps.title: Distinguish the mean
steps.explanation: The arithmetic mean does not satisfy the repetition requirement.

examples.answer: No mode under the stated convention; the mean is two.
examples.verification: Under a frequency-maximizer convention all three values tie instead. Neither convention makes two a uniquely determined mode.

tutorials.title: Building a random variable and its probability mass function
tutorials.body:
A random variable is a function that assigns a numerical value to every outcome of a random experiment. The variable is not itself an event or a probability. Different outcomes may produce the same value, so the probability of a value is the total probability of every outcome mapped to it. A discrete random variable has a probability mass function, written \(p_X(x)=P(X=x)\), whose values are nonnegative and sum to one.
Start with a clearly specified sample space and outcome probabilities. Define what number the variable records, map each outcome to that number, and group outcomes sharing a value. Then add probabilities within each group. Equal probability of basic outcomes does not imply equal probability of random-variable values, since groups may have different sizes. The support contains the attainable values; all other values have probability zero. Checking normalization verifies that no experiment outcome was omitted or counted twice. In the coin example, the two distinct ordered outcomes HT and TH both map to one head, which makes that value more likely than zero or two heads.

example.prompt: Toss a fair coin twice independently. Let X be the number of heads. Construct the probability mass function of X.
example.strategy: List the experiment outcomes → Define the numerical map → Group equal values → Check normalization

steps.title: List the experiment outcomes
steps.explanation: Independence and fairness give four equally likely ordered outcomes.

steps.title: Define the numerical map
steps.explanation: The variable records the head count rather than the ordered toss sequence.

steps.title: Group equal values
steps.explanation: Add the probabilities of all basic outcomes that map to each value.

steps.title: Check normalization
steps.explanation: The groups account for the entire sample space without overlap.

example.answer: The support is {0,1,2}, with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 respectively; other values have probability zero.
example.verification: The event X=1 consists of HT and TH, while X≥1 consists of HH,HT,TH and therefore has probability 3/4. This agrees with 1−P(X=0).

depth.body: A random variable compresses experiment outcomes into numerical information, and its distribution results from that mapping. If the map is many-to-one, combine the probabilities of all preimages of each value. For transformations such as a minimum, a cumulative or survival probability may count those preimages more easily than a direct list. Once a survival function is known for an integer-valued variable, subtract consecutive tails to obtain its mass function. Continuous variables require a density or cumulative function instead of a point-mass table; a density value itself is not the probability of an exact outcome. Keep the underlying experiment and the recorded quantity distinct when interpreting support or events.

examples.prompt: Roll a fair die and let X be zero for even outcomes and one for odd outcomes. Find the distribution of X.
examples.strategy: Define the two preimages → Add their probabilities → Check the support and total

steps.title: Define the two preimages
steps.explanation: The numerical map groups three outcomes under each value.

steps.title: Add their probabilities
steps.explanation: Each underlying die face has probability one sixth.

steps.title: Check the support and total
steps.explanation: Only zero and one are attainable, and their two masses sum to one.

examples.answer: X has support {0,1}, each with probability one half.
examples.verification: The event X=1 is exactly the odd-die event, providing a direct event-based check.

examples.prompt: Roll two independent fair dice and let M be their minimum. Find P(M=k) for k=1,…,6.
examples.strategy: Count the survival event → Subtract consecutive tails → Simplify

steps.title: Count the survival event
steps.explanation: Both dice must land among k,…,6.

steps.title: Subtract consecutive tails
steps.explanation: Remove cases where both dice exceed k.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.explanation: The masses are 11,9,7,5,3,1 divided by thirty-six.

examples.answer: (13−2k)/36 for k=1,…,6; zero elsewhere.
examples.verification: The numerators sum to 36; the tail at k=4 is (3/6)²=1/4, matching (5+3+1)/36.

examples.prompt: X is continuous uniform on [0,1], so its density is one. Is P(X=0.5)=1?
examples.strategy: Distinguish density from mass → Measure the singleton → Compute an interval for comparison

steps.title: Distinguish density from mass
steps.explanation: Density must be integrated over an interval to obtain probability.

steps.title: Measure the singleton
steps.explanation: A single point has zero width.

steps.title: Compute an interval for comparison
steps.explanation: A positive-width interval, rather than one point, carries positive probability.

examples.answer: No; the exact-value probability is zero.
examples.verification: The CDF is continuous at 0.5, so its jump there, which would represent a point mass, is zero.

lessons.title: Binomial and Poisson distributions
lessons.intuition: The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent identical trials. Poisson models event counts in a window with a specified mean rate. Identify the experiment first: fixed trials and success probability suggest binomial; an event rate over time suggests Poisson.

sections.title: Binomial construction
sections.body: X~Binomial(n,p) has P(X=k)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. The combination chooses success positions; multiplying gives the probability of a specific ordering. \(E[X]\)=np and Var(X)=np(1−p). At least one success is conveniently 1−(1−p)ⁿ.

sections.title: Poisson counts
sections.body: X~Poisson(λ) has P(X=k)=e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!, k≥0. Its mean and variance are both λ. If the rate is r per unit time, a duration t has λ=rt under the homogeneous Poisson-process model. Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with summed means.

sections.title: When approximation is sensible
sections.body: For many independent trials with small p and moderate np, Binomial(n,p) can be approximated by Poisson(np). It is an approximation, not a rule replacing all binomial questions. Check the event and units; changing a 1-minute window to 3 minutes multiplies λ by three, not p by three.

sections.title: Deriving binomial moments with indicators
sections.body: Write the success count X as the sum of n independent Bernoulli indicators Iᵢ. Each has mean p and variance p(1−p), so expectation is np and independent variances sum to np(1−p). The mass formula contains C(n,k) because there are that many ways to place k successes among n positions. For Poisson with rate 3/hour, a 20-minute interval has λ=1, not λ=3: converting the window is part of specifying the distribution. Then P(exactly two)=e⁻¹/2. A binomial n=1000,p=0.001 has mean 1; its zero-count probability (0.999)^1000 is close to e⁻¹, illustrating the rare-event approximation without treating it as an exact equality.

examples.prompt: Fair coin tossed four times: exactly two heads

steps.title: Identify the model
steps.explanation: There are a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same head probability. These assumptions justify the binomial model.

steps.title: Count successful sequences
steps.explanation: Choose the two head positions; order of choosing these positions does not matter.

steps.title: Weight each sequence
steps.explanation: Each length-four sequence has probability 1/16. The six sequences are disjoint, so add their probabilities.

examples.given: Four independent fair coin tosses; exactly two heads required.
examples.goal: Find the probability.
examples.strategy: Count valid head positions and multiply by the probability of each disjoint ordering.
examples.verification: The five binomial counts are 1,4,6,4,1; summing gives 16 equally likely outcomes.

examples.prompt: Calls arrive with rate 2 per minute. Find mean and zero-call probability in 3 minutes

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: The Poisson model parameter is expected events over the entire interval, not the per-minute rate by itself.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: For a Poisson count, both mean and variance equal its parameter. Standard deviation is √6, not six.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: At zero, both the power and factorial equal one. The resulting probability is about 0.00248 under the homogeneous Poisson assumptions.

examples.strategy: Convert the rate into a mean for the stated time window before using the PMF.
examples.answer: \(P(X=0)=e^{-6}\frac{6^0}{0!}=e^{-6}\); the duration must be included before using the formula.
examples.verification: A longer interval has a larger mean and a smaller no-event probability; using e⁻² would describe one minute rather than three.

pitfalls: Binomial trials need the same p and independence.
Poisson λ belongs to the actual time window.

checks.prompt: Which experiment directly fits a binomial model?
checks.hint: Identify fixed trials, independence and a common p.
checks.explanation: Binomial counts successes under those three assumptions. A rate-based event count may instead use Poisson, and waiting time may be continuous.
options: A fixed number of independent equal-probability success/failure trials
A continuous value uniformly sampled from an interval

checks.prompt: A Poisson process has rate 4 per hour. What is the count variance over 2 hours?
checks.hint: Compute the window mean first.
checks.explanation: λ=4×2=8; Poisson variance equals λ.

lessons.concept: The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent identical trials. Poisson models event counts in a window with a specified mean rate. Identify the experiment first: fixed trials and success probability suggest binomial; an event rate over time suggests Poisson.
lessons.method:
A binomial variable counts successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability p. Fixed trial count, independence and identical p are all model assumptions. Exactly k successes can occupy C(n,k) subsets of positions. Each ordering has probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, and disjoint orderings add to the binomial mass.
The mean np follows by writing the count as a sum of success indicators. Independence makes their variances add, giving np(1−p). At least one success is often easiest as one minus zero successes: 1−(1−p)ⁿ. “At most k” instead requires summing masses from zero through k, not inserting k into the exactly-k formula.
Sampling without replacement is generally not binomial because probabilities and dependence change; use conditional counting or the relevant finite-population model. Degenerate p=0 or p=1 cases deserve interpretation rather than blindly using a formula involving zero powers. A small-case enumeration can verify combinatorial factors and expose counting ordered successes twice. A Poisson count models events in an interval under a constant-rate process with independent increments and the standard rare-single-event local assumptions. Its parameter λ is the expected count in the whole interval, so rate r over duration t gives λ=rt. The mass is e⁻λ λᵏ/k! for nonnegative integer k, and both mean and variance equal λ.
Probability of zero events is e⁻λ; at least one is its complement. Counts over disjoint independent Poisson intervals add, with parameters adding too. The distribution is unbounded in count even though the time interval is fixed, unlike a binomial variable’s maximum n. A binomial can be approximated by Poisson when n is large, p small and np remains moderate; this is an approximation, not an identity for arbitrary trials.
Keep units consistent before computing λ: a rate per minute cannot multiply a duration in seconds without conversion. Distinguish event count from waiting time, which is exponential under a Poisson process. Standard deviation is √λ, not λ. Those interpretation checks often matter more than factorial arithmetic. X~Binomial(n,p) has P(X=k)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. The combination chooses success positions; multiplying gives the probability of a specific ordering. \(E[X]\)=np and Var(X)=np(1−p). At least one success is conveniently 1−(1−p)ⁿ. X~Poisson(λ) has P(X=k)=e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!, k≥0. Its mean and variance are both λ. If the rate is r per unit time, a duration t has λ=rt under the homogeneous Poisson-process model. Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with summed means. For many independent trials with small p and moderate np, Binomial(n,p) can be approximated by Poisson(np). It is an approximation, not a rule replacing all binomial questions. Check the event and units; changing a 1-minute window to 3 minutes multiplies λ by three, not p by three. Write the success count X as the sum of n independent Bernoulli indicators Iᵢ. Each has mean p and variance p(1−p), so expectation is np and independent variances sum to np(1−p). The mass formula contains C(n,k) because there are that many ways to place k successes among n positions. For Poisson with rate 3/hour, a 20-minute interval has λ=1, not λ=3: converting the window is part of specifying the distribution. Then P(exactly two)=e⁻¹/2. A binomial n=1000,p=0.001 has mean 1; its zero-count probability (0.999)^1000 is close to e⁻¹, illustrating the rare-event approximation without treating it as an exact equality. A binomial count can be written as a sum of success indicators, making its mean and variance transparent. Fixed trial count and identical success probability determine the marginals; independence permits multiplying sequence probabilities and adding indicator variances. Cumulative questions such as “at most one” require adding disjoint masses, while “at least one” often favors a complement. Before applying the model, inspect whether sampling changes the population or success probability. Without replacement from a small population, the count is generally hypergeometric instead. A numerical check can enumerate sequences for a small experiment or calculate the same event through conditional draw probabilities rather than assuming the binomial formula. A Poisson parameter is the expected event count over the specified interval, not the rate by itself. Multiply rate by duration after matching units. Independent Poisson counts add into another Poisson count with summed parameters, which makes combining separate streams straightforward under the independence assumption. The probability mass uses a factorial for an exact count; a tail probability usually sums masses or uses a complement. Mean and variance equal the parameter, while standard deviation is its square root. This equality of count moments does not describe waiting-time moments, which belong to an exponential model. Verify a probability through a recurrence between adjacent masses or through the independent-stream zero-event calculation.

gateGuide.recognize: Match the experiment to the distribution: fixed independent equal-p trials for binomial; event counts with a specified window rate for Poisson.
method: Write n,p or the actual window mean λ before plugging in a mass formula.
For at least one event, compute one minus zero instead of summing every positive count.
For independent counts use indicators or distribution addition, but treat Poisson approximation as an approximation and retain the correct time-unit conversion.

traps.claim: Poisson rate equals mean for every window
traps.why: A rate of 6 per hour has mean 2 in 20 minutes. The rate must be multiplied by the duration in consistent units.

traps.claim: Any sequence of trials is binomial
traps.why: Changing success probabilities or dependence invalidates the elementary binomial model even when outcomes are successes/failures.

Binomial moments.
