tutorials.title: Binomial counts from independent fixed trials
tutorials.body:
A binomial variable counts successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability p. Fixed trial count, independence and identical p are all model assumptions. Exactly k successes can occupy C(n,k) subsets of positions. Each ordering has probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, and disjoint orderings add to the binomial mass.
The mean np follows by writing the count as a sum of success indicators. Independence makes their variances add, giving np(1−p). At least one success is often easiest as one minus zero successes: 1−(1−p)ⁿ. “At most k” instead requires summing masses from zero through k, not inserting k into the exactly-k formula.
Sampling without replacement is generally not binomial because probabilities and dependence change; use conditional counting or the relevant finite-population model. Degenerate p=0 or p=1 cases deserve interpretation rather than blindly using a formula involving zero powers. A small-case enumeration can verify combinatorial factors and expose counting ordered successes twice.

example.prompt: Three independent trials succeed with p=1/4. Find P(exactly one) and P(at least one).
example.strategy: One-success arrangements → Exactly one → At least one

steps.title: One-success arrangements
steps.explanation: Choose its position.

steps.title: Exactly one
steps.explanation: Every other trial must fail.

steps.title: At least one
steps.explanation: Subtract the single zero-success event.

example.answer: Exactly one: 27/64. At least one: 37/64.
example.verification: The second probability must be larger because it also includes two and three successes.

depth.body: A binomial count can be written as a sum of success indicators, making its mean and variance transparent. Fixed trial count and identical success probability determine the marginals; independence permits multiplying sequence probabilities and adding indicator variances. Cumulative questions such as “at most one” require adding disjoint masses, while “at least one” often favors a complement. Before applying the model, inspect whether sampling changes the population or success probability. Without replacement from a small population, the count is generally hypergeometric instead. A numerical check can enumerate sequences for a small experiment or calculate the same event through conditional draw probabilities rather than assuming the binomial formula.

examples.prompt: Toss a fair coin four times independently. Model the head count X and find its mean and variance.
examples.strategy: Check the binomial conditions → Add indicator means → Add independent variances

steps.title: Check the binomial conditions
steps.explanation: The trial count is fixed, each trial is fair, and independence is explicitly given.

steps.title: Add indicator means
steps.explanation: Each head indicator has expectation one half.

steps.title: Add independent variances
steps.explanation: Independence removes covariance terms.

examples.answer: X is Binomial(4,1/2), with mean two and variance one.
examples.verification: Its masses have numerators 1,4,6,4,1 over sixteen; their weighted mean and squared deviations give the same two and one.

examples.prompt: Five independent components each fail with probability 0.2. Find the probability that at most one fails.
examples.strategy: Count zero failures → Count one failure → Add disjoint masses

steps.title: Count zero failures
steps.explanation: All five components must work.

steps.title: Count one failure
steps.explanation: Choose the failed component, and require the others to work.

steps.title: Add disjoint masses
steps.explanation: Exactly zero and exactly one cannot occur together.

examples.verification: The complement probability of at least two failures is 0.26272; the two probabilities sum to one.

examples.prompt: Draw two balls without replacement from three red and two blue. Is the red count Binomial(2,3/5)? Test two reds.
examples.strategy: Compute the actual joint probability → Compute the claimed binomial mass → Compare the results

steps.title: Compute the actual joint probability
steps.explanation: After one red draw only two red balls remain among four.

steps.title: Compute the claimed binomial mass
steps.explanation: This incorrectly keeps the second success chance fixed.

steps.title: Compare the results
steps.explanation: The changing probability and dependence violate the binomial assumptions.

examples.answer: No; the without-replacement count is not binomial here.
examples.verification: Choosing two red balls among all two-ball subsets gives C(3,2)/C(5,2)=3/10, confirming the actual probability.

tutorials.title: Poisson counts and converting rate to interval mean
tutorials.body:
A Poisson count models events in an interval under a constant-rate process with independent increments and the standard rare-single-event local assumptions. Its parameter λ is the expected count in the whole interval, so rate r over duration t gives λ=rt. The mass is e⁻λ λᵏ/k! for nonnegative integer k, and both mean and variance equal λ.
Probability of zero events is e⁻λ; at least one is its complement. Counts over disjoint independent Poisson intervals add, with parameters adding too. The distribution is unbounded in count even though the time interval is fixed, unlike a binomial variable’s maximum n. A binomial can be approximated by Poisson when n is large, p small and np remains moderate; this is an approximation, not an identity for arbitrary trials.
Keep units consistent before computing λ: a rate per minute cannot multiply a duration in seconds without conversion. Distinguish event count from waiting time, which is exponential under a Poisson process. Standard deviation is √λ, not λ. Those interpretation checks often matter more than factorial arithmetic.

example.prompt: Events arrive at 3 per hour. Find probability of no event in 20 minutes.
example.strategy: Convert duration → Interval mean → Zero events

steps.title: Convert duration
steps.explanation: Match the rate unit.

steps.title: Interval mean
steps.explanation: Expected count in this window is one.

steps.title: Zero events
steps.explanation: Zero factorial and zero exponent each give one.

example.verification: Using e⁻³ would describe a full hour, not the requested twenty-minute interval.

depth.body: A Poisson parameter is the expected event count over the specified interval, not the rate by itself. Multiply rate by duration after matching units. Independent Poisson counts add into another Poisson count with summed parameters, which makes combining separate streams straightforward under the independence assumption. The probability mass uses a factorial for an exact count; a tail probability usually sums masses or uses a complement. Mean and variance equal the parameter, while standard deviation is its square root. This equality of count moments does not describe waiting-time moments, which belong to an exponential model. Verify a probability through a recurrence between adjacent masses or through the independent-stream zero-event calculation.

examples.prompt: If X is Poisson with parameter two, find P(X=2).
examples.strategy: Use the exact-count mass → Insert the count → Simplify

steps.title: Use the exact-count mass
steps.explanation: The parameter is already an interval mean.

steps.title: Insert the count
steps.explanation: Two factorial equals two.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.explanation: The probability is approximately 0.2707.

lessons.title: Uniform, exponential and normal distributions
lessons.intuition: Continuous probabilities are interval areas. Uniform gives equal density over a bounded interval; exponential models waiting time with a constant hazard; normal describes symmetric variation around a mean. Each has a different support and interpretation.

sections.title: Uniform[a,b]
sections.body: The density is 1/(b−a) inside [a,b] and zero outside. An interval probability is its overlapping length divided by b−a. Mean=(a+b)/2 and variance=(b−a)²/12. Equal density does not mean a positive probability at each exact point; any one point still has probability zero.

sections.title: Exponential rate λ
sections.body: The density is λe^(−λx) for x≥0; survival P(X>t)=e^(−λt). Mean=1/λ and variance=1/λ². Memorylessness follows because P(X>s+t|X>s)=e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs)=e^(−λt). The rate parameter is the reciprocal of the mean, so check which parameterization the question uses.

sections.title: Normal(μ,σ²)
sections.body: The density is symmetric around μ, so mean=median=mode=μ. Standardize using Z=(X−μ)/σ, not σ². Probabilities reduce to standard normal CDF Φ: P(a<X<b)=Φ((b−μ)/σ)−Φ((a−μ)/σ). Independent normal variables have normal sums with means and variances added.

sections.title: Normalize a density before calculating probabilities
sections.body: If f(x)=cx on [0,2] and zero outside, normalization requires ∫₀²cx dx=2c=1, so c=1/2. Then P(1<X<2)=∫₁²x/2 dx=3/4, and \(E[X]\)=∫₀²x²/2 dx=4/3. This distribution is not uniform because density grows with x. For exponential waiting time, conditional survival divides two survival probabilities and cancels the elapsed factor, explaining memorylessness directly. For normal variables, convert an interval using standard deviation before looking up Φ. If Y=aX+b for a negative a, inequality direction reverses when standardizing an event; keeping the event itself visible avoids sign errors.

examples.prompt: For \(X\sim U[2,8]\), find P(3<X<5)

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Both event bounds lie inside the support; otherwise first intersect with [2,8]. A density value is not itself an interval probability.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: Multiply constant density by interval length. Strict versus non-strict endpoints do not change a continuous distribution’s interval probability.

examples.strategy: Integrate constant density over the part of the support that satisfies the event.
examples.answer: Probability=2/6=1/3; the density 1/6 alone is not the answer.
examples.verification: The event spans two of the support’s six units, so its probability must be 2/6. The entire support has probability 6/6=1.

steps.title: Translate the event
steps.explanation: The scale is positive, so the inequality direction stays the same. Φ denotes the standard-normal CDF; use a supplied table when a numeric approximation is requested.

Uniformity means equally long subintervals have equal probability, not that each real-number outcome has some identical positive mass. A discrete uniform choice among integers is different and requires counting points rather than lengths. In GATE, identify which model is stated before converting a range into a numerator; mixing inclusive integer counts with continuous widths produces off-by-one errors. The parameters specify location and scale; many texts write N(μ,σ²), so read whether the second parameter is variance or standard deviation before calculation. Standardizing Z=(X−μ)/σ produces the standard normal with mean zero and variance one.
Use its cumulative function Φ to express P(X≤x)=Φ((x−μ)/σ), and subtract two CDF values for an interval. Symmetry gives Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z). A continuous probability at exactly the mean is zero even though the density there is largest. Mean, median and mode all equal μ for this distribution, which is a model-specific fact rather than a general rule for every dataset.
When a table is supplied, check whether it reports full left-tail probability or area between zero and z. For a numeric answer without a table, retain the exact Φ expression unless an accepted approximation is specified. Changing variance alters standardized distance by its square root, not by variance itself; GATE distractors commonly divide by the wrong parameter. An exponential variable with rate λ>0 models nonnegative waiting time in a constant-rate Poisson process. Its density is λe⁻λt for t≥0, its survival probability P(T>t)=e⁻λt, mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ². Rate and scale are reciprocal conventions; a parameter described as mean waiting time must not be used as a rate without inversion.

This does not say every real-world waiting process is memoryless; an aging device or fixed appointment schedule may not fit this model.
Interval probabilities subtract survival or CDF values, and probabilities for negative waiting times are zero. Keep λ’s time unit reciprocal to t’s unit. Do not use the Poisson count PMF to answer a waiting-time question; the process relates the two distributions, but one counts events and the other measures elapsed time. The density is symmetric around μ, so mean=median=mode=μ. Standardize using Z=(X−μ)/σ, not σ². Probabilities reduce to standard normal CDF Φ: P(a<X<b)=Φ((b−μ)/σ)−Φ((a−μ)/σ). Independent normal variables have normal sums with means and variances added. If f(x)=cx on [0,2] and zero outside, normalization requires ∫₀²cx dx=2c=1, so c=1/2. Then P(1<X<2)=∫₁²x/2 dx=3/4, and \(E[X]\)=∫₀²x²/2 dx=4/3. This distribution is not uniform because density grows with x. For exponential waiting time, conditional survival divides two survival probabilities and cancels the elapsed factor, explaining memorylessness directly. For normal variables, convert an interval using standard deviation before looking up Φ. If Y=aX+b for a negative a, inequality direction reverses when standardizing an event; keeping the event itself visible avoids sign errors. Continuous uniform probability is proportional to length within its support. Its cumulative function rises linearly over that interval, and conditioning on a subinterval produces another uniform distribution on that restricted interval. This makes interval intersections a convenient way to compute conditional probabilities. Equal-length regions have equal probability, but individual real points have zero mass. A discrete uniform distribution on integers uses counts instead of lengths and includes endpoints as actual positive-mass outcomes. Read which model is specified before choosing a numerator. Means and variances provide additional checks on location and support width, while conditional calculations must divide by the length of the allowed region rather than the original whole support. Normal calculations become simpler after separating location from scale. Symmetry supplies probabilities at the mean directly, while other thresholds require subtracting the mean and dividing by standard deviation. The notation N(μ,σ²) uses variance as its second parameter in these examples. Independent normal sums and differences remain normal, with means combining algebraically and variances adding when the variables are independent. A negative sign changes a variable’s mean contribution but not its variance contribution. Without independence, covariance must be included. Keep exact answers in terms of the standard-normal CDF when no table is provided, and verify whether the requested event is a lower tail, upper tail or interval before using a table entry. An exponential waiting time has constant hazard: conditional chance of surviving an additional interval depends on its length rather than the already elapsed wait. Its rate is inverse time, while mean and median are times and are not equal. Conditioning on an elapsed event-free period shifts an absolute deadline into a remaining-time interval. A normal variable has bell-shaped density centered at μ with standard deviation σ>0. The parameters specify location and scale; many texts write N(μ,σ²), so read whether the second parameter is variance or standard deviation before calculation. Standardizing Z=(X−μ)/σ produces the standard normal with mean zero and variance one.

For a numeric answer without a table, retain the exact Φ expression unless an accepted approximation is specified. Changing variance alters standardized distance by its square root, not by variance itself; GATE distractors commonly divide by the wrong parameter.

tutorials.title: Exponential waiting time and memorylessness
tutorials.body:
An exponential variable with rate λ>0 models nonnegative waiting time in a constant-rate Poisson process. Its density is λe⁻λt for t≥0, its survival probability P(T>t)=e⁻λt, mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ². Rate and scale are reciprocal conventions; a parameter described as mean waiting time must not be used as a rate without inversion.
Memorylessness means P(T>s+t|T>s)=P(T>t). Conditioned on already waiting s without an event, the remaining wait has the same distribution. Derive it by dividing e⁻λ(s+t) by e⁻λs. This does not say every real-world waiting process is memoryless; an aging device or fixed appointment schedule may not fit this model.
Interval probabilities subtract survival or CDF values, and probabilities for negative waiting times are zero. Keep λ’s time unit reciprocal to t’s unit. Do not use the Poisson count PMF to answer a waiting-time question; the process relates the two distributions, but one counts events and the other measures elapsed time.

name: Digital Logic
description: From Boolean expressions to working circuits

lessons.title: Boolean algebra and algebraic minimization
lessons.intuition: Boolean simplification preserves a function while reducing the gates required to implement it. Work with identities valid for every input. Boolean addition is OR, so 1+1=1; ordinary numerical cancellation cannot be imported without checking it.

sections.title: Basic identities
sections.body: Identity laws give A+0=A and A·1=A; domination gives A+1=1 and A·0=0. Complement gives A+¬A=1 and A¬A=0. Idempotence gives A+A=A and AA=A. Absorption A+AB=A removes a redundant condition. De Morgan moves negation through a gate and swaps AND with OR.

sections.title: Canonical forms
sections.body: A minterm specifies every variable and is true on exactly one truth-table row. Sum the minterms where the function is 1 to obtain canonical SOP. A maxterm is false on exactly one row; multiply maxterms for rows where the function is 0 to obtain canonical POS. Ordinary simplified SOP need not contain every variable in every term.

sections.title: Simplifying systematically
sections.body: Combine terms differing in only one literal: AB+A¬B=\(A(B+\overline B)=A\). Remove absorbed terms and apply the consensus rule XY+¬XZ+YZ=XY+¬XZ. Confirm the result with a truth table when unsure. Fewer literals and fewer gates are related but distinct implementation cost measures.

examples.prompt: Simplify \(F=AB+A\overline B+AC\)

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Factor the first two terms: \(A(B+\overline B)=A\). Complementarity makes B+¬B=1 for either Boolean B; multiplication by A then leaves A.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Now \(F=A+AC\). The removed terms together cover every case where A is true. Keep the remaining AC term until absorption is justified.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Absorption removes AC, leaving F=A for all inputs. When A=0, both terms are zero; when A=1, the first term already forces output one. Thus C cannot change the result.

examples.strategy: Use a Boolean identity at each transformation, rather than ordinary arithmetic.
examples.answer: Absorption removes AC, leaving F=A for all inputs.
examples.verification: Try A=0 and A=1 with both C values; the output always equals A. Boolean + is OR, so 1+1=1 here.

examples.prompt: Build SOP for a 2-variable function true on 01 and 11
steps: The corresponding minterms are ¬AB and AB.
\(F=\overline AB+AB=B(\overline A+A)\).
The simplified expression is B, so the output ignores A.

pitfalls: Boolean OR is not arithmetic addition.
A canonical term must contain every variable.

checks.hint: The second term is already contained in the first condition.
checks.explanation: Absorption removes AB because whenever AB is true, A is already true; it adds no new accepting assignments.

checks.hint: B and C remain unconstrained.
checks.explanation: Fix A=1; B and C each have 2 choices, yielding 4.

lessons.concept: Boolean simplification preserves a function while reducing the gates required to implement it. Work with identities valid for every input. Boolean addition is OR, so 1+1=1; ordinary numerical cancellation cannot be imported without checking it.
lessons.method:
Boolean variables take only zero and one; + means OR, multiplication means AND, and a bar means NOT. These are not ordinary arithmetic operations: A+A=A and A·A=A. Identity laws include A+0=A and A·1=A; complement laws include A+Ā=1 and AĀ=0. De Morgan complements both operands while swapping AND and OR.
Minimize by applying an identity to an entire matching subexpression and preserve the original truth table. Factoring can expose complements; absorption A+AB=A removes a term already covered by another. Consensus can remove a redundant bridge term, but dropping a literal without justification can add unwanted true inputs. Complementing a sum requires complementing every term, not only one.
For GATE, write one justified transformation per line and verify on a truth assignment that stresses the changed term. Algebraic minimization seeks simpler implementation but a minimal expression need not be unique. Count literals or gates under the specified hardware cost; the fewest algebraic terms need not always mean the cheapest realization. A sum of products ORs together AND terms; a product of sums ANDs together OR terms. Canonical SOP uses minterms, each containing every variable and true on exactly one input row. For a minterm, a row’s zero bit uses a complemented literal and its one bit an uncomplemented literal. Canonical POS uses maxterms false on exactly one row, reversing that literal convention within an OR term.
Build SOP from true rows and POS from false rows. A noncanonical simplified expression may omit variables. The notation Σm lists true minterm indices and ΠM lists false maxterm indices under a stated variable bit order. Changing bit order changes indices even when the function’s words remain the same.
To verify an expression, test its output on both listed and unlisted rows. A frequent trap uses the minterm convention when writing a maxterm and therefore selects the opposite row. tutorials.title: Boolean identities and algebraic minimization
tutorials.body:
Boolean variables take only zero and one; + means OR, multiplication means AND, and a bar means NOT. These are not ordinary arithmetic operations: A+A=A and A·A=A. Identity laws include A+0=A and A·1=A; complement laws include A+Ā=1 and AĀ=0. De Morgan complements both operands while swapping AND and OR.
Minimize by applying an identity to an entire matching subexpression and preserve the original truth table. Factoring can expose complements; absorption A+AB=A removes a term already covered by another. Consensus can remove a redundant bridge term, but dropping a literal without justification can add unwanted true inputs. Complementing a sum requires complementing every term, not only one.
For GATE, write one justified transformation per line and verify on a truth assignment that stresses the changed term. Algebraic minimization seeks simpler implementation but a minimal expression need not be unique. Count literals or gates under the specified hardware cost; the fewest algebraic terms need not always mean the cheapest realization.

tutorials.title: Canonical SOP/POS and minterms/maxterms
tutorials.body:
A sum of products ORs together AND terms; a product of sums ANDs together OR terms. Canonical SOP uses minterms, each containing every variable and true on exactly one input row. For a minterm, a row’s zero bit uses a complemented literal and its one bit an uncomplemented literal. Canonical POS uses maxterms false on exactly one row, reversing that literal convention within an OR term.
Build SOP from true rows and POS from false rows. A noncanonical simplified expression may omit variables. The notation Σm lists true minterm indices and ΠM lists false maxterm indices under a stated variable bit order. Changing bit order changes indices even when the function’s words remain the same.
To verify an expression, test its output on both listed and unlisted rows. A frequent trap uses the minterm convention when writing a maxterm and therefore selects the opposite row. Don't equate “product of sums” with complementing an SOP without the required De Morgan transformation.

steps.title: Identify false row
steps.explanation: Only one maxterm is required.

steps.title: Construct maxterm
steps.explanation: Both literals evaluate to zero at 01.

steps.title: Verify other rows
steps.explanation: At 00,10,11 at least one literal is one.

example.verification: The complementary true-row SOP is Σm(0,2,3), recognizing the same function.

Simplified POS factors can exclude several false rows at once. NOR gates naturally implement POS by first complementing each sum and then NORing those complements. steps.explanation: A product uses a complemented literal exactly where its row has a zero.

lessons.title: Karnaugh maps and the tabular method
lessons.intuition: Adjacent minterms differ in one variable, so combining them eliminates that variable. Karnaugh maps make this adjacency visual; the tabular method performs the same operation symbolically and scales without relying on a drawing.

sections.title: K-map layout and grouping
sections.body: Use Gray-code labels such as 00,01,11,10 so neighbours differ in one bit. Group 1s in rectangles with 1,2,4,8,… cells. Edges wrap around and corners may be adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent. A group with 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables. Overlap is allowed and often necessary; every required 1 must be covered.

sections.title: Prime and essential implicants
sections.body: A prime implicant cannot be enlarged into another valid group. An essential prime implicant covers a minterm covered by no other prime implicant and must be selected. After selecting essentials, cover remaining minterms with a low-cost collection. Don’t-care cells may be included as 1s to enlarge a group or ignored; there is no requirement to cover them.

sections.title: Quine–McCluskey
sections.body: Write minterms in binary, group by number of 1s, and combine terms differing in one specified bit, replacing that bit by a dash. Repeat until no more combinations are possible. Uncombined terms are prime implicants. Build a chart mapping primes to covered required minterms and select a cover. This separates implicant generation from the covering problem.

examples.prompt: Minimize \(F(A,B,C)=\sum m(0,1,2,3)\)

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The minterms are 000,001,010,011. Use ABC bit order consistently: changing the assumed variable order changes the resulting literal.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Across the four-cell group B and C take both values but A stays 0. The group is a complete power-of-two block, so all four B,C combinations are represented. A varying literal is unnecessary.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Eliminate B,C to get \(F=\overline A\). The literal is complemented because the retained A bit is zero, not one.

examples.answer: Eliminate B,C to get \(F=\overline A\).
examples.verification: ¬A is true exactly for minterms 0 through 3, and false for minterms 4 through 7; this checks the entire truth table.

lessons.concept: Adjacent minterms differ in one variable, so combining them eliminates that variable. Karnaugh maps make this adjacency visual; the tabular method performs the same operation symbolically and scales without relying on a drawing.
lessons.method:
A Karnaugh map places minterms in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ in one variable. Edges wrap: opposite borders are adjacent, while diagonal cells generally are not. A valid group contains a power-of-two rectangle of adjacent cells. A group of 2ᵏ minterms eliminates k varying literals, retaining variables fixed throughout it.
For SOP, cover every required one without covering a required zero. Groups may overlap and can be as large as permitted; a cell need not be covered exactly once. A don't-care marks an input whose output is unspecified under the model. It may be treated as zero or one to improve simplification, and does not have to be covered. It cannot overwrite a specified output.
Begin with essential groups and choose remaining groups to meet the stated cost. A visually large collection is invalid if it is not a permitted rectangle or power-of-two size. Always translate the selected group back to its constant-bit literals and check the represented minterms rather than relying on a diagram’s appearance alone. The tabular method systematically combines minterms rather than relying on a spatial map. Group binary terms by number of ones and combine terms differing in exactly one retained bit, replacing that position by a dash. Repeat combinations only when dash positions agree and the remaining patterns differ in one bit. Combined terms cover all assignments to their dashed positions.
A prime implicant cannot be further enlarged without entering a required-zero case. Mark every term used in a combination; unused terms at the end of each stage are candidates for the prime set. Don’t-cares can participate in combining but the final chart needs to cover only required ones. An essential prime covers a required minterm no other prime covers.
Select all essentials, then cover remaining columns according to the cost objective. Finding every prime does not mean every prime belongs in the final expression. A minimum cover can be nonunique. In GATE, distinguish one legal simplified cover from a proof of minimality and inspect whether cost is number of terms, literals or actual gates. An implicant is a product term whose covered input rows all belong to the function’s true set, or to allowed don’t-care rows. A prime implicant is an implicant that cannot be enlarged by removing another literal without covering a required zero. Being prime does not mean a term must appear in every minimum expression. Essential prime implicants have the stronger property that they alone cover at least one required minterm.
After generating all prime implicants, construct a chart with one column for every required true minterm and one row for each prime. Mark the minterms each prime covers. Any column having only one mark forces that row into the expression. Remove all columns covered by selected essentials and solve any remaining cover according to the stated cost, such as number of terms followed by number of literals.
Don’t-care columns are not required in the final chart even though they can help form larger primes. A chosen prime may overlap another chosen prime; overlapping coverage is legal. Verify the cover both for completeness and for exclusion of required zeros, because merely covering all listed ones does not justify a term that also turns a specified zero into one. Use Gray-code labels such as 00,01,11,10 so neighbours differ in one bit. Group 1s in rectangles with 1,2,4,8,… cells. Edges wrap around and corners may be adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent. A group with 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables. Overlap is allowed and often necessary; every required 1 must be covered. A prime implicant cannot be enlarged into another valid group. An essential prime implicant covers a minterm covered by no other prime implicant and must be selected. After selecting essentials, cover remaining minterms with a low-cost collection. Don’t-care cells may be included as 1s to enlarge a group or ignored; there is no requirement to cover them. Write minterms in binary, group by number of 1s, and combine terms differing in one specified bit, replacing that bit by a dash. Repeat until no more combinations are possible. Uncombined terms are prime implicants. Build a chart mapping primes to covered required minterms and select a cover. This separates implicant generation from the covering problem. The geometry of a Karnaugh map encodes a binary adjacency relation rather than ordinary numeric order. Gray-code neighbors differ in one bit, including the wrap across opposite edges. A legal rectangle has a power-of-two number of cells and changes every eliminated variable through all its combinations. The retained literals are exactly the variables constant throughout that rectangle. For SOP group ones; for POS group zeros and choose a sum factor that vanishes on the group. Large-looking diagonal patterns may not be rectangles at all. Check the binary assignments represented by a proposed group and verify both required coverage and exclusion of forbidden rows before claiming a simplification. A don’t-care is freedom in a specification, not a third physical logic value. The implemented circuit still returns zero or one at that input, but either output is accepted because the system promises that the input is irrelevant or unreachable. Use optional rows only when they enlarge a useful group or reduce cost; covering all of them is unnecessary. The promise matters: if an invalid code can occur through a fault or transient, the simplified circuit may behave differently from another legal realization. List required ones, required zeros and optional rows separately. Check every required row after minimization, and explain any operating assumption that makes the optional rows genuinely unconstrained. The tabular method represents groups as binary patterns with dashes. A dash means that both values of that variable are included, so each extra dash doubles the represented rows. Combining two patterns is legal only if their dash positions match and exactly one remaining bit differs. Keep a record of the minterms covered by every pattern, because duplicate combinations can arise through different routes. Mark combined terms and retain uncombined ones as prime candidates. Don’t-cares may enlarge combinations but must not become mandatory chart columns. The method separates generating prime implicants from selecting a cover; stopping after a first combination can leave a correct but unnecessarily expensive expression. Prime implicants are maximal safe groups, while essential primes are unavoidable members of a cover. These are different claims: a prime may be omitted when other primes cover all its required rows. In a chart, unique coverage proves essentiality and a lower bound on the number of selected terms. When no column is unique, choose a cover by an explicit criterion rather than assuming the absence of essentials means the function is empty. A prime chart can contain ties and multiple optimal covers. Don’t-care rows help determine which groups are maximal but are excluded from mandatory coverage. Verify minimality using forced columns or a coverage lower bound, not merely the appearance of a concise expression.

Find largest valid power-of-two rectangles, including wraparound, then identify essential prime implicants.

traps.claim: Diagonal cells are adjacent
traps.why: A diagonal can change two input bits, so combining it does not eliminate just one literal.

traps.claim: All don’t-cares must be covered
traps.why: They represent unconstrained outputs. Covering unnecessary ones can make the implementation larger instead of smaller.

A Karnaugh map places minterms in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ in one variable. Edges wrap: opposite borders are adjacent, while diagonal cells generally are not. A valid group contains a power-of-two rectangle of adjacent cells. A group of 2ᵏ minterms eliminates k varying literals, retaining variables fixed throughout it.
For SOP, cover every required one without covering a required zero. Groups may overlap and can be as large as permitted; a cell need not be covered exactly once. A don't-care marks an input whose output is unspecified under the model. It may be treated as zero or one to improve simplification, and does not have to be covered. It cannot overwrite a specified output.
Begin with essential groups and choose remaining groups to meet the stated cost. A visually large collection is invalid if it is not a permitted rectangle or power-of-two size. Always translate the selected group back to its constant-bit literals and check the represented minterms rather than relying on a diagram’s appearance alone.

example.prompt: Minimize F(A,B,C)=Σm(0,2), with don’t-cares 1,3.
example.strategy: Available grouping → Identify fixed bit → Write product

steps.title: Available grouping
steps.explanation: The required ones and optional cells together cover 000,001,010,011.

steps.title: Identify fixed bit
steps.explanation: The four-cell group eliminates B and C.

steps.title: Write product
steps.explanation: This agrees with required ones and keeps required zeros false.

example.answer: \(F=\overline A\) is a valid minimized realization.
example.verification: Its values on 1 and 3 are allowed to be one because those rows were unspecified, not required zero.

depth.body: The geometry of a Karnaugh map encodes a binary adjacency relation rather than ordinary numeric order. Gray-code neighbors differ in one bit, including the wrap across opposite edges. A legal rectangle has a power-of-two number of cells and changes every eliminated variable through all its combinations. The retained literals are exactly the variables constant throughout that rectangle. For SOP group ones; for POS group zeros and choose a sum factor that vanishes on the group. Large-looking diagonal patterns may not be rectangles at all. Check the binary assignments represented by a proposed group and verify both required coverage and exclusion of forbidden rows before claiming a simplification.

examples.prompt: In a three-variable map, group the ones at minterms 0 and 4; all other rows are zero.
examples.strategy: Write binary rows → Use edge adjacency → Keep fixed literals

steps.title: Write binary rows
steps.explanation: Only A changes between the two true assignments.

steps.title: Use edge adjacency
steps.explanation: In the Gray-code map these cells are adjacent across the appropriate boundary, so a two-cell group is legal.

steps.title: Keep fixed literals
steps.explanation: Eliminate A while retaining the zero values of B and C.

examples.answer: F=¬B¬C.
examples.verification: The resulting product covers exactly 000 and 100; it includes no required-zero row.

examples.prompt: Use zero grouping to minimize a four-variable function whose only zeros are 0,2,8,10; variable order is A,B,C,D.
examples.strategy: Inspect zero rows → Form a wrapped four-cell group → Write a POS factor

steps.title: Inspect zero rows
steps.explanation: A and C vary through all combinations while B=D=0.

steps.title: Form a wrapped four-cell group
steps.explanation: The corner/edge arrangement is one legal rectangle in Gray-code order, eliminating A and C.

steps.title: Write a POS factor
steps.explanation: This sum is zero exactly when B and D are both zero.

examples.answer: The minimum POS is the single factor B+D.
examples.verification: There are four assignments with B=D=0; these are precisely the specified zero indices, and every other assignment makes the sum one.

examples.prompt: Can two one-cells at 00 and 11 in a two-variable map be grouped into a term with no literals?
examples.strategy: Check bit distance → Check what a zero-literal term means → Test an omitted zero row

steps.title: Check bit distance
steps.explanation: These cells are diagonal rather than adjacent.

steps.title: Check what a zero-literal term means
steps.explanation: Eliminating both variables would cover all four rows.

steps.title: Test an omitted zero row
steps.explanation: The original function is zero there, but the proposed constant is one.

examples.answer: No; the two diagonal cells remain separate minterms, yielding ¬A¬B+AB.
examples.verification: The correct expression has outputs 1,0,0,1; grouping the diagonal would incorrectly set the middle two rows to one.

depth.body: A don’t-care is freedom in a specification, not a third physical logic value. The implemented circuit still returns zero or one at that input, but either output is accepted because the system promises that the input is irrelevant or unreachable. Use optional rows only when they enlarge a useful group or reduce cost; covering all of them is unnecessary. The promise matters: if an invalid code can occur through a fault or transient, the simplified circuit may behave differently from another legal realization. List required ones, required zeros and optional rows separately. Check every required row after minimization, and explain any operating assumption that makes the optional rows genuinely unconstrained.

examples.prompt: F(A,B)=1 at minterm 1, has don’t-care 3, and is zero at 0 and 2. Choose a simple realization.
examples.strategy: Identify available group → Eliminate varying bit → Check required outputs

steps.title: Identify available group
steps.explanation: The optional row can join the required one.

steps.title: Eliminate varying bit
steps.explanation: The two-row group retains only B.

steps.title: Check required outputs
steps.explanation: Rows 0 and 2 have B=0, while required row 1 has B=1.

examples.answer: F=B is a valid realization.
examples.verification: At optional row 3 the output is one, which is allowed; the specified rows remain correct.

examples.prompt: A BCD input A,B,C,D must output one for odd digits 1,3,5,7,9; digits 10–15 are don’t-cares. Minimize the odd-digit detector.
examples.strategy: Interpret valid digits → Extend into optional region → Check all valid codes

steps.title: Interpret valid digits
steps.explanation: For every valid BCD digit, oddness is exactly the least significant bit D.

steps.title: Extend into optional region
steps.explanation: This also marks 11,13,15 as one, but those inputs are unconstrained.

steps.title: Check all valid codes
steps.explanation: Even digits 0,2,4,6,8 have D=0 and odd digits have D=1, so one wire implements the valid specification.

examples.answer: The detector is F=D, assuming inputs are valid BCD or invalid-code outputs are unconstrained.
examples.verification: Enumerating digits 0 through 9 confirms parity; no assertion is made about a required safe output for codes 10 through 15.

examples.prompt: A student declares a required-zero row a don’t-care to create a larger K-map group. For F=Σm(1), required zero 3, is F=B valid in variables A,B?
examples.strategy: Inspect the specification → Evaluate the shortcut → Keep the needed literal

steps.title: Inspect the specification
steps.explanation: Only 01 is true, while 11 is explicitly false and cannot be reclassified.

steps.title: Evaluate the shortcut
steps.explanation: The proposed wire turns the required-zero row on.

steps.title: Keep the needed literal
steps.explanation: A complement separates row 01 from forbidden row 11.

examples.answer: No; \(F=\overline A\)B is required when row 3 is specified zero.
examples.verification: The simplified wire is legal only for a different specification where row 3 is optional; the original truth table forbids it.

tutorials.title: Quine–McCluskey and the prime-implicant chart
tutorials.body:
The tabular method systematically combines minterms rather than relying on a spatial map. Group binary terms by number of ones and combine terms differing in exactly one retained bit, replacing that position by a dash. Repeat combinations only when dash positions agree and the remaining patterns differ in one bit. Combined terms cover all assignments to their dashed positions.
A prime implicant cannot be further enlarged without entering a required-zero case. Mark every term used in a combination; unused terms at the end of each stage are candidates for the prime set. Don’t-cares can participate in combining but the final chart needs to cover only required ones. An essential prime covers a required minterm no other prime covers.
Select all essentials, then cover remaining columns according to the cost objective. Finding every prime does not mean every prime belongs in the final expression. A minimum cover can be nonunique. In GATE, distinguish one legal simplified cover from a proof of minimality and inspect whether cost is number of terms, literals or actual gates.

example.prompt: Combine 000,001,100,101 for variables A,B,C.
example.strategy: First combinations → Second combination → Interpret

steps.title: First combinations
steps.explanation: C varies in each pair.

steps.title: Second combination
steps.explanation: Dash positions agree and only A differs.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.explanation: Only B remains fixed at zero.

example.answer: One implicant −0−, corresponding to ¬B.
example.verification: It covers exactly all four inputs with B=0, with no required-zero input included.

depth.body: The tabular method represents groups as binary patterns with dashes. A dash means that both values of that variable are included, so each extra dash doubles the represented rows. Combining two patterns is legal only if their dash positions match and exactly one remaining bit differs. Keep a record of the minterms covered by every pattern, because duplicate combinations can arise through different routes. Mark combined terms and retain uncombined ones as prime candidates. Don’t-cares may enlarge combinations but must not become mandatory chart columns. The method separates generating prime implicants from selecting a cover; stopping after a first combination can leave a correct but unnecessarily expensive expression.

examples.prompt: Run tabular combination for F(A,B,C)=Σm(4,5), with all other rows zero.
examples.strategy: Group binary terms → Combine one-bit difference → Stop and interpret

steps.title: Group binary terms
steps.explanation: The terms lie in adjacent one-count groups.

steps.title: Combine one-bit difference
steps.explanation: The last position varies while A=1 and B=0 remain fixed.

steps.title: Stop and interpret
steps.explanation: No other true row permits enlarging this pattern.

examples.answer: The prime pattern is 10−, corresponding to A¬B.
examples.verification: Expanding its dash gives only rows 100 and 101, so the expression covers precisely the two required minterms.

examples.prompt: For F(A,B,C)=Σm(0,1,2,3,6,7), find the final tabular cover.
examples.strategy: Generate first-round pairs → Combine matching dash patterns → Cover the true set

steps.title: Combine matching dash patterns
steps.explanation: The two four-row primes are ¬A and B.

steps.title: Cover the true set
steps.explanation: The union of their coverage is {0,1,2,3,6,7}.

examples.answer: A minimum cover is ¬A+B.
examples.verification: At rows 4 and 5, A=1 and B=0, making the expression zero; every other row satisfies at least one term.

examples.prompt: May patterns 0−1 and −01 be combined into −−1?
examples.strategy: Check dash alignment → Enumerate actual coverage → Expand the proposed pattern

steps.title: Check dash alignment
steps.explanation: The first pattern varies B; the second varies A. Their dash positions do not match.

steps.title: Enumerate actual coverage
steps.explanation: Their union has three rows, not a four-row binary cube.

steps.title: Expand the proposed pattern
steps.explanation: It adds minterm 7, which could be a required zero.

examples.answer: No; the proposed combination is invalid unless further terms independently justify the missing row.
examples.verification: A function true only at 1,3,5 is a counterexample: the combined pattern wrongly turns row 7 on.

tutorials.title: Use a prime-implicant chart to identify essential terms
tutorials.body:
An implicant is a product term whose covered input rows all belong to the function’s true set, or to allowed don’t-care rows. A prime implicant is an implicant that cannot be enlarged by removing another literal without covering a required zero. Being prime does not mean a term must appear in every minimum expression. Essential prime implicants have the stronger property that they alone cover at least one required minterm.
After generating all prime implicants, construct a chart with one column for every required true minterm and one row for each prime. Mark the minterms each prime covers. Any column having only one mark forces that row into the expression. Remove all columns covered by selected essentials and solve any remaining cover according to the stated cost, such as number of terms followed by number of literals.
Don’t-care columns are not required in the final chart even though they can help form larger primes. A chosen prime may overlap another chosen prime; overlapping coverage is legal. Verify the cover both for completeness and for exclusion of required zeros, because merely covering all listed ones does not justify a term that also turns a specified zero into one.

example.prompt: For F(A,B,C)=Σm(0,1,2,5), the prime implicants are ¬A¬B, ¬A¬C and ¬BC. Find the essential primes and a minimum SOP.
example.strategy: Build coverage → Find unique columns → Finish cover

steps.title: Build coverage
steps.explanation: Translate each product into the exact rows it covers.

steps.title: Find unique columns
steps.explanation: Minterm 2 is covered only by ¬A¬C; minterm 5 is covered only by ¬BC. Both terms are essential.

steps.title: Finish cover
steps.explanation: Those two essentials also cover 0 and 1, so no remaining column needs ¬A¬B.

example.answer: The essential primes are ¬A¬C and ¬BC; their sum is a minimum two-term SOP.
example.verification: Their covered sets unite to {0,1,2,5}. Both are forced by unique columns, so a one-term cover is impossible and the third prime is redundant.

depth.body: Prime implicants are maximal safe groups, while essential primes are unavoidable members of a cover. These are different claims: a prime may be omitted when other primes cover all its required rows. In a chart, unique coverage proves essentiality and a lower bound on the number of selected terms. When no column is unique, choose a cover by an explicit criterion rather than assuming the absence of essentials means the function is empty. A prime chart can contain ties and multiple optimal covers. Don’t-care rows help determine which groups are maximal but are excluded from mandatory coverage. Verify minimality using forced columns or a coverage lower bound, not merely the appearance of a concise expression.

examples.prompt: For F(A,B)=Σm(0,1), determine its prime implicants and essential primes.
examples.strategy: Combine true rows → Rule out enlargement → Inspect chart uniqueness

steps.title: Combine true rows
steps.explanation: Both true assignments have A=0, so the largest safe group is ¬A.

steps.title: Rule out enlargement
steps.explanation: Removing A would include required-zero rows 10 and 11, so ¬A is prime.

steps.title: Inspect chart uniqueness
steps.explanation: Both required columns are covered only by ¬A, making that prime essential.

examples.answer: The only prime implicant is ¬A, and it is essential.
examples.verification: The candidate covers both true rows and no zeros; every valid cover must cover minterm 0, which has no alternative prime.

examples.prompt: For F(A,B,C)=Σm(0,1,2,5,6,7), the prime chart contains pairs {0,1},{0,2},{1,5},{2,6},{5,7},{6,7}. Identify essential primes and a minimum SOP.
examples.strategy: Inspect column counts → Choose a complete cover → Prove the lower bound

steps.title: Inspect column counts
steps.explanation: Each required minterm belongs to exactly two listed pairs, so no prime is essential.

steps.title: Choose a complete cover
steps.explanation: The corresponding terms are ¬A¬B, B¬C and AC.

steps.title: Prove the lower bound
steps.explanation: Every prime covers two required minterms, so at least three primes are needed to cover six distinct columns.

examples.answer: There are no essential primes; \(F=\overline A\)¬B+B¬C+AC is a minimum three-term SOP.
examples.verification: The three selected pairs are disjoint and cover all six ones. Each listed pair is a maximal legal binary group because any four-cell enlargement would include zero row 3 or 4.

examples.prompt: For F(A,B,C)=Σm(0,1,2,5), is prime ¬A¬B necessarily required because it covers two minterms?
examples.strategy: List its coverage → Find alternatives → Form a cover without it

steps.title: List its coverage
steps.explanation: Being a two-cell prime does not establish unique coverage.

steps.title: Find alternatives
steps.explanation: Each row of the first prime is also covered elsewhere.

steps.title: Form a cover without it
steps.explanation: The alternatives cover every required minterm.

examples.answer: No; ¬A¬B is prime but not essential and may be omitted.
examples.verification: The two alternative sets unite to {0,1,2,5}; minterms 2 and 5 force those alternatives, so adding ¬A¬B would be redundant.

lessons.title: Designing combinational circuits
lessons.intuition: A combinational circuit has no memory: outputs are determined by current inputs. The design process starts with a behavioural specification, translates it to a truth table, simplifies the output equations, and maps them to available gates or modules.

sections.title: Adders and arithmetic building blocks
sections.body: A half adder produces sum A⊕B and carry AB. A full adder includes Cin: sum=A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout=AB+ACin+BCin. Cascading full adders yields a ripple-carry adder whose worst delay grows with the carry path length. A carry-lookahead adder uses generate G=AB and propagate P=A⊕B to compute carry dependencies more directly.

sections.title: Multiplexers and decoders
sections.body: A 2ᵏ:1 multiplexer selects one of 2ᵏ data inputs using k select bits. A decoder maps k inputs to up to 2ᵏ one-hot outputs. Implement a Boolean function with a mux by assigning select variables, then making each data input the residual function of remaining variables. Decoder minterm outputs can be ORed for SOP implementation.

sections.title: Design and timing
sections.body: Validate all input combinations, including active-high/active-low control conventions. Gates have propagation delays; the longest input-to-output path determines worst-case settling. Logical equivalence alone does not remove hazards caused by unequal physical path delays. Combinational feedback without carefully defined storage is not ordinary combinational design.

examples.prompt: Full adder with A=1,B=1,Cin=0

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: \(S=1\oplus1\oplus0=0\). XOR represents addition modulo two, so the sum bit records the parity of the three inputs.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: \(C_{out}=AB+AC_{in}+BC_{in}=1+0+0=1\). Each product tests one pair of high inputs. OR of these products is one precisely when at least two inputs are high.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The pair Cout,S represents binary 10, correctly summing decimal 2. Carry is the higher-weight bit; reversing the pair would incorrectly turn decimal two into one.

examples.strategy: Evaluate sum and carry independently, then read them as a two-bit number.
examples.answer: The pair Cout,S represents binary 10, correctly summing decimal 2.
examples.verification: Direct arithmetic gives 1+1+0=2; binary Cout,S=10 has the same value.

examples.prompt: Implement XOR using a 2:1 mux
steps: Select S=A.
If A=0, output should equal B, so I₀=B.
If A=1, output should equal ¬B, so I₁=¬B. The mux equation \(\overline AI_0+AI_1\) yields XOR.

pitfalls: Output bit width must allow carry if the specification requires it.
Check active-low enables before using a decoder table.

checks.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a combinational circuit?
checks.hint: Separate current-input dependence from stored state.
checks.explanation: A combinational function depends on current inputs. Physical propagation delay exists, but there is no designed state memory.
options: It necessarily stores prior input values
Its output depends on current inputs under the ideal settled model
It requires a clock for every output change
It is the same as a flip-flop

checks.prompt: How many output lines does a complete 3-to-8 decoder have?
checks.hint: One output per input combination.
checks.explanation: \(2^3=8\) outputs.

lessons.concept: A combinational circuit has no memory: outputs are determined by current inputs. The design process starts with a behavioural specification, translates it to a truth table, simplifies the output equations, and maps them to available gates or modules.
lessons.method:
A combinational circuit’s current outputs depend only on current inputs. Design starts by specifying a truth table, deriving expressions and realizing them with gates. A half adder adds two bits: XOR gives sum and AND gives carry. A full adder adds two operand bits and a carry-in; sum is their XOR and carry is one when at least two are one.
Multi-bit ripple addition chains each carry-out into the next more significant carry-in. Its long carry propagation limits delay; carry-lookahead computes carries using generate/propagate structure. A truth-table-correct circuit can still have propagation delay and transient hazards, so Boolean function and timing behavior are separate design aspects.
For signed addition, overflow occurs when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result, or equivalently when carry into the sign position differs from carry out. Carry-out alone reports unsigned behavior and is not the signed-overflow test. Always state bit width and whether operands are unsigned or two’s-complement before interpreting the result bits. A multiplexer selects one data input using binary select bits. A 2-to-1 mux outputs I₀ when S=0 and I₁ when S=1, so Y=¬S·I₀+S·I₁. A 2ᵏ-to-1 mux uses k select bits; data inputs can be constants or expressions in remaining variables to implement a function by Shannon expansion.
A decoder activates an output corresponding to its input code. An n-to-2ⁿ decoder provides one minterm per output under an active-high enabled convention. ORing selected minterm outputs implements SOP. Active-low outputs or enables change the connecting logic, so inspect the specification before assuming output ones.
To realize a function by a mux, choose select variables, evaluate the desired function under each select assignment, then use each residual function as a data input. Do not confuse decoder outputs with mux select lines. These components are combinational unless a register is explicitly added; neither stores a previous input merely because it has several terminals. A decoder converts an n-bit input code into one selected output among 2ⁿ possibilities. For an enabled active-high decoder, output Yᵢ is one exactly when the binary input value is i; every other output is zero. Thus each output already implements a canonical minterm. A decoder is combinational: changing its inputs changes the selected output after propagation delay, with no stored previous input.
To implement a Boolean function, assign its variables to the decoder inputs in the specified bit order and combine the outputs corresponding to the function’s true minterms. Active-high outputs normally feed an OR gate. With active-low decoder outputs, the appropriate combining logic is often a NAND because the selected line goes low; the active levels must be stated rather than guessed. An enable pin can disable every output, so it must also be driven to its asserted level.
Trace at least one selected input and one unselected input to verify the wiring. Using the correct output numbers with reversed input order realizes a different function. A decoder does not choose a data input as a multiplexer does: its output identity is determined by the input code itself, which makes minterm realization a direct connection between a truth table and hardware. A half adder produces sum A⊕B and carry AB. A full adder includes Cin: sum=A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout=AB+ACin+BCin. Cascading full adders yields a ripple-carry adder whose worst delay grows with the carry path length. A carry-lookahead adder uses generate G=AB and propagate P=A⊕B to compute carry dependencies more directly. A 2ᵏ:1 multiplexer selects one of 2ᵏ data inputs using k select bits. A decoder maps k inputs to up to 2ᵏ one-hot outputs. Implement a Boolean function with a mux by assigning select variables, then making each data input the residual function of remaining variables. Decoder minterm outputs can be ORed for SOP implementation. Validate all input combinations, including active-high/active-low control conventions. Gates have propagation delays; the longest input-to-output path determines worst-case settling. Logical equivalence alone does not remove hazards caused by unequal physical path delays. Combinational feedback without carefully defined storage is not ordinary combinational design. A combinational design is a function of its present inputs, so start with a precise input/output contract before choosing gates. Translate verbal conditions into a truth table or equations, simplify, then verify the implementation on boundary cases. No clock edge or remembered state is available unless storage is explicitly added. Gate propagation delay means output changes are not instantaneous, but delay by itself does not make a circuit sequential. Multiple paths can briefly disagree and produce hazards even when their final truth table is correct. Distinguish functional correctness from timing correctness, and state active levels or validity assumptions whenever signal names such as enable, alarm or ready could otherwise be ambiguous. Binary addition can be understood one column at a time: count the true operand and carry-in bits, write the parity as the sum bit and propagate a carry when at least two are true. A full adder therefore combines a three-input parity function with a majority carry function. Chaining full adders creates word addition, where carry propagation determines timing. Unsigned carry and signed overflow answer different questions about the same bit result. To analyze signed overflow, inspect operand signs and result sign, or compare carries entering and leaving the sign bit. State width, extension rules and carry-in before calculating; extra result bits should be interpreted deliberately rather than silently discarded. A multiplexer implements a conditional choice: fixing the select bits leaves one data input connected to the output. To realize a function, choose selects and calculate its residual function separately for every select assignment. This is Shannon decomposition, and the residual can be a constant, a remaining variable, its complement or a smaller circuit. The number of data inputs is a power of two for a complete binary select space. Data width is independent of the number of choices, so a four-way eight-bit selector is eight parallel four-to-one muxes with shared selects. Verify wiring by branch evaluation; confusing select order or treating a data input as a select creates a valid circuit for the wrong function. A decoder separates input codes into distinct output lines. Its active-level convention determines whether the selected line becomes one or zero, and an enable determines what happens when decoding is disabled. This makes polarity part of the logic, not a cosmetic wiring label. Hierarchical decoding can expand input width by using high bits to enable one lower-bit decoder bank. In minterm realization, combine exactly the selected lines corresponding to required true codes, then account for any output inversion. Address-decoding applications also require that inactive banks release a shared bus; the decoder selects a device but does not itself guarantee correct data-bus electrical behavior or store an earlier selection.

gateGuide.recognize: Translate the specification into output functions first. A multiplexer is a function implementation tool, not merely a selector to memorize.
method: Build the truth table and separate each output, such as sum and carry.
For a mux choose select variables and substitute each selector combination to find residual data-input functions.
For delay, trace the longest dependent gate path rather than adding delays of independent parallel branches.

traps.claim: XOR and OR are interchangeable in an adder
traps.why: For inputs 1,1, a half-adder sum is 0, while OR would give 1. Carry separately represents the value 2.

traps.claim: Mux inputs must be constants
traps.why: Residual functions can be B, its complement, or other available signals when only some variables are selectors.

formulas.meaning: Full-adder outputs.
Two-to-one mux equation.

example.prompt: Add 7 and 1 in 4-bit two’s complement.
example.strategy: Encode → Add → Interpret signed result

steps.title: Encode
steps.explanation: Both operands are positive.

steps.title: Add
steps.explanation: Ripple carries propagate through the lower three bits.

steps.title: Interpret signed result
steps.explanation: Two positives produced a negative code, proving signed overflow.

example.answer: The bit result is 1000, with signed overflow.
example.verification: The mathematical answer 8 exceeds the signed range −8…7, although it fits four-bit unsigned representation.

Translate verbal conditions into a truth table or equations, simplify, then verify the implementation on boundary cases. No clock edge or remembered state is available unless storage is explicitly added.
