example.prompt: An 8-bit signed fixed-point format has four fractional bits. Interpret code 11101000.
example.strategy: Decode signed integer → Apply scale → Resolution

steps.title: Decode signed integer
steps.explanation: The leading one indicates a negative two’s-complement integer.

steps.title: Apply scale
steps.explanation: Four fractional bits imply division by 2⁴.

steps.title: Resolution
steps.explanation: Adjacent codes differ by 0.0625 in represented value.

example.answer: Value −1.5; resolution 1/16.
example.verification: Encoding +1.5 gives integer code 24; taking its eight-bit two’s complement gives 232, the observed bit pattern.

depth.body: A bit pattern has no signedness without a representation rule. Unsigned decoding adds positive positional weights; two’s-complement decoding subtracts 2ⁿ when an n-bit code has its sign bit set. Widening a signed value repeats the sign bit because the new negative high-order weight is balanced by the inserted ones. Widening an unsigned value inserts zeros instead. The most negative two’s-complement value is asymmetric: its positive magnitude is outside the same-width signed range. State width at every encode, negate, compare and extend operation. Verify conversions by reconstructing the numeric value, not merely by recognizing a familiar-looking sequence of bits.

examples.prompt: Encode −13 in eight-bit two’s complement.
examples.strategy: Encode positive magnitude → Invert all eight bits → Add one

steps.title: Encode positive magnitude
steps.explanation: Use the target width before negating.

steps.title: Invert all eight bits
steps.explanation: Bitwise inversion alone gives one less than the desired two’s-complement code.

steps.title: Add one
steps.explanation: The low eight bits encode the negative value.

examples.verification: Unsigned code 243 minus 256 gives −13; adding code 13 wraps to zero modulo 256.

examples.prompt: Interpret eight-bit 10010110 as signed, then widen it to sixteen bits. Compare with zero extension.
examples.strategy: Decode signed value → Sign-extend → Contrast zero-extension

steps.title: Decode signed value
steps.explanation: The sign bit is one, so unsigned decoding must be adjusted.

steps.title: Sign-extend
steps.explanation: Repeating the sign bit preserves the signed value.

steps.title: Contrast zero-extension
steps.explanation: Zero extension preserves the unsigned interpretation instead.

examples.answer: Signed widening gives 1111111110010110 (0xFF96), still −106; zero extension gives +150.
examples.verification: The signed sixteen-bit code is 65430, and 65430−65536=−106, while the zero-extended code is 150.

examples.prompt: Negate signed eight-bit 10000000 using invert-and-add-one. Is the mathematical positive magnitude representable?
examples.strategy: Interpret the starting code → Apply fixed-width negation → Check mathematical target

steps.title: Interpret the starting code
steps.explanation: The signed range is −128 through 127.

steps.title: Apply fixed-width negation
steps.explanation: The bit operation wraps back to the same pattern.

steps.title: Check mathematical target
steps.explanation: The desired positive value cannot be encoded at this width.

examples.answer: The bit result remains 10000000, and signed negation overflows.
examples.verification: The asymmetric signed endpoints explain why this single nonzero code equals its own modular negation.

depth.body: The binary point is an interpretation attached to an integer code, not necessarily a bit stored alongside it. Increasing fractional precision reduces the step size but narrows the value range at fixed total width. Operations combining different formats must align their scales before addition, comparison or assignment. Conversion to fewer fractional bits discards information and therefore needs a specified rounding rule, especially for negative values. An arithmetic right shift usually rounds negative integers downward, while division truncated toward zero can yield a different result. Treat the destination format’s signed integer range and scale separately: a perfectly aligned computation can still overflow its final storage width.

examples.prompt: An unsigned code 00101101 has three fractional bits. Find its value and the spacing between adjacent codes.
examples.strategy: Decode integer code → Apply implicit scale → Find one-code increment

steps.title: Decode integer code
steps.explanation: The bit pattern first represents an ordinary unsigned integer.

steps.title: Apply implicit scale
steps.explanation: Three fractional positions give a denominator of eight.

steps.title: Find one-code increment
steps.explanation: Changing the stored integer by one changes the value by one scale unit.

examples.answer: Value=5.625; spacing=0.125.
examples.verification: Binary interpretation 00101.101 equals 5+1/2+1/8=5.625.

examples.prompt: Add fixed-point code 6 with two fractional bits to code 20 with four fractional bits, storing the result with four fractional bits in signed eight-bit storage.
examples.strategy: Decode input scales → Align to finer scale → Add and check

steps.title: Decode input scales
steps.explanation: The numeric codes cannot be added directly because their units differ.

steps.title: Align to finer scale
steps.explanation: Code 24 at scale 1/16 represents the first input exactly.

steps.title: Add and check
steps.explanation: The code fits signed eight-bit storage.

examples.answer: Output code 44 (00101100), representing 2.75.
examples.verification: Adding the decoded values gives 1.5+1.25=2.75; directly adding unaligned codes would incorrectly give 26/16=1.625.

examples.prompt: Convert signed code −3 with two fractional bits to one fractional bit, rounding toward zero. Is an arithmetic right shift by one the correct operation?
examples.strategy: Find exact destination code → Apply specified rounding → Compare arithmetic shift

steps.title: Find exact destination code
steps.explanation: The value −0.75 lies halfway between destination codes −2 and −1.

steps.title: Apply specified rounding
steps.explanation: Rounding toward zero chooses value −0.5.

steps.title: Compare arithmetic shift
steps.explanation: The shift rounds downward and instead gives destination value −1.

examples.answer: No; round-toward-zero requires code −1, while arithmetic shifting yields −2.
examples.verification: The respective value errors are +0.25 and −0.25; the direction of the error reveals the different rounding conventions.

tutorials.title: Floating-point fields, normalization and special values
tutorials.body:
Floating point stores sign, exponent and significand to represent a wide dynamic range. A normalized binary value has form (−1)ˢ(1.f)₂2ᵉ. IEEE single precision stores 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits, using exponent bias 127 for normal values and an implicit leading one. Effective significand precision is therefore 24 bits for normals.
Stored exponent zero represents zero or subnormal values, which use a different leading-bit/exponent rule. All-one exponent represents infinity for zero fraction or NaN for nonzero fraction. Do not apply the normal-value formula to those reserved fields. Positive and negative zero have distinct sign codes but compare equal under ordinary equality semantics.
Addition aligns exponents before combining significands, then normalizes and rounds. Large exponent gaps can erase a small addend, so floating addition need not be associative. Overflow, underflow and rounding are distinct. In GATE, decode exponent bias and hidden bit explicitly, and identify whether the problem uses IEEE fields or a custom format with different widths or conventions.

example.prompt: Decode a normal single-precision value with sign 0, exponent 128 and fraction .100…0.
example.strategy: Unbias exponent → Decode significand → Combine

steps.title: Unbias exponent
steps.explanation: The stored exponent is not the actual power.

steps.title: Decode significand
steps.explanation: Include the implicit leading one.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: The sign is positive.

example.answer: Value 3.
example.verification: If the hidden bit were forgotten, the incorrectly decoded significand 0.5 would give 1 instead.

depth.body: Floating-point spacing depends on magnitude because the exponent scales a finite-precision significand. Normalization chooses a standard leading bit, while reserved exponent patterns encode zero, subnormals, infinities and NaNs rather than ordinary normalized values. To encode a finite normal number, write it in binary, move the point to follow the first one, store a biased exponent and retain the specified fraction bits. Arithmetic must align exponents and round the significand afterward. An exact real answer may lie halfway between representable numbers, so the tie rule matters. Specify precision as total significand bits or stored fraction bits explicitly; the implicit leading one makes those counts differ for normal values.

examples.prompt: Encode positive 6.5 in IEEE single precision, giving sign, biased exponent and leading fraction bits.
examples.strategy: Convert and normalize → Encode sign and exponent → Store the fraction

steps.title: Convert and normalize
steps.explanation: Normalization separates significand and exponent.

steps.title: Encode sign and exponent
steps.explanation: The stored exponent includes the bias.

steps.title: Store the fraction
steps.explanation: The normalized leading one is implicit rather than stored.

examples.prompt: A binary floating format retains three total significand bits and rounds to nearest, ties to even. Add 1.00×2³ and 1.00×2⁰.
examples.strategy: Align exponents → Form exact sum → Resolve the tie

steps.title: Align exponents
steps.explanation: Both operands need the same exponent before addition.

steps.title: Form exact sum
steps.explanation: The exact significand requires a bit beyond the three-bit precision.

steps.title: Resolve the tie
steps.explanation: Representable neighbors are 1.00×\(2^3=8\) and 1.01×2³=10. The retained low bit of 1.00 is even, so the tie rounds to 8.

examples.answer: The rounded sum is 8 even though the exact sum is 9.
examples.verification: The two representable neighbors are each one unit from 9; the even retained-bit rule chooses the lower neighbor in this particular tie.

examples.prompt: An IEEE single-precision code has sign 1, exponent field zero and fraction zero. May the normal formula with hidden leading one be applied?
examples.strategy: Identify reserved exponent → Inspect zero fraction → Apply special interpretation

steps.title: Identify reserved exponent
steps.explanation: An all-zero exponent is outside the normal-number field rule.

steps.title: Inspect zero fraction
steps.explanation: With exponent and fraction both zero, the encoding represents zero; the sign distinguishes its signed code.

steps.title: Apply special interpretation
steps.explanation: There is no implicit leading one in this zero encoding.

examples.answer: It represents negative zero; the normal hidden-one formula is invalid.
examples.verification: Applying the normal formula would invent a nonzero negative value. Under ordinary IEEE equality, −0 compares equal to +0 despite distinct sign bits.

tutorials.title: Multiply fixed-point values without losing the scale
tutorials.body:
Fixed-point arithmetic operates on integer codes whose interpretation includes an implicit power-of-two scale. If a signed code I has f fractional bits, its represented value is I/2ᶠ. Addition of equal-scale operands can directly add codes, subject to overflow, but multiplication changes the scale: codes with f fractional bits each produce a raw product with 2f fractional bits. Keeping the original scale requires dividing the raw integer product by 2ᶠ.
Use a widened signed product before rescaling. Multiplying only at the original storage width can discard high bits before the scale correction, yielding a wrong answer even when the final mathematical value would fit. When rescaling discards nonzero low bits, apply the stated rounding rule; for negative values, truncation toward zero and an arithmetic right shift need not produce the same integer.
After rescaling, check that the final signed code lies within the destination width’s range. Overflow refers to inability to represent the result, while rounding error comes from discarding fractional precision. Verify the calculation by decoding the final code and comparing it to multiplication of the decoded input values, allowing only the rounding error specified by the format.

example.prompt: In signed 8-bit fixed point with four fractional bits, multiply values 1.5 and −0.5 using a widened product and store the result at the same scale. No rounding is needed here.
example.strategy: Encode operands → Multiply widened codes → Restore destination scale → Decode and check

steps.title: Encode operands
steps.explanation: The stored codes represent values divided by 16.

steps.title: Multiply widened codes
steps.explanation: The raw product has eight fractional bits, so its value is −192/256.

steps.title: Restore destination scale
steps.explanation: Dividing by 16 leaves four fractional bits and is exact because P is divisible by 16.

steps.title: Decode and check
steps.explanation: The signed code −12 fits the eight-bit range, so no overflow occurs.

example.answer: The result is −0.75, stored as code −12 (11110100 in eight-bit two’s complement).
example.verification: Direct value multiplication gives 1.5×(−0.5)=−0.75; decoding 11110100 gives (244−256)/16=−0.75.

depth.body: Hardware arithmetic produces a fixed-width bit result whose numeric interpretation must then be checked. Unsigned operations follow arithmetic modulo 2ⁿ when high bits are discarded; signed operations use the same low bits but have a different representability test. Subtraction can reuse addition by complementing the subtrahend and adding one, provided all operands use the same width. Multiplication needs more result bits before truncation or fixed-point rescaling, because a narrow intermediate can destroy information that the final format would need. Interpret carries, borrows, signed overflow and rounding as separate outcomes. A useful check compares the decoded bit answer with exact arithmetic and explains any mismatch using the stated storage convention.

examples.prompt: Compute −3−4 with a four-bit two’s-complement adder.
examples.strategy: Encode at common width → Prepare subtraction → Add and retain

steps.title: Encode at common width
steps.explanation: These codes represent −3 and +4.

steps.title: Prepare subtraction
steps.explanation: Adding the two’s-complement negation of B implements A−B.

steps.title: Add and retain
steps.explanation: The low four bits represent −7, which fits the signed range.

examples.answer: Result=1001, representing −7, with no signed overflow.
examples.verification: Exact arithmetic gives −3−4=−7; decoding code 9 as signed gives 9−16=−7.

examples.prompt: Multiply unsigned four-bit values 12 and 3. Find the full product and the result if only four low bits are retained.
examples.strategy: Compute exact product → Encode the widened result → Apply four-bit storage

steps.title: Compute exact product
steps.explanation: An eight-bit intermediate can represent any product of two four-bit unsigned operands.

steps.title: Encode the widened result
steps.explanation: The full product retains both high and low parts.

steps.title: Apply four-bit storage
steps.explanation: Discarding high bits changes the represented mathematical value.

examples.answer: The full product is 00100100; the retained four-bit result is 0100 (4), with unsigned overflow.
examples.verification: 12×(2+1)=24+12=36; the retained code satisfies 36=2×16+4.

examples.prompt: Add signed four-bit 0101 and 0100. The carry-out is zero; can that prove no overflow?
examples.strategy: Interpret operands → Compute bit result → Check sign condition

steps.title: Interpret operands
steps.explanation: The exact sum exceeds the four-bit signed maximum 7.

steps.title: Compute bit result
steps.explanation: The retained signed code is −7 despite positive inputs.

steps.title: Check sign condition
steps.explanation: Two positive operands produced a negative result, proving signed overflow even without final carry.

examples.answer: No; signed overflow occurs although carry-out is zero.
examples.verification: Carry into the sign bit is one and carry out is zero, so their XOR is one, agreeing with the sign-based test.

name: Computer Organization & Architecture
description: Understand what happens beneath your code

lessons.title: Instruction sets, addressing modes and CPU time
lessons.intuition: An instruction is a compact command that tells a processor what operation to perform and where operands come from. Addressing modes separate operand-location rules from the operation itself. CPU performance follows the total work and cycles, not clock rate alone.

sections.title: Instruction structure
sections.body: An instruction can contain an opcode, register identifiers, addressing-mode bits and immediate/displacement fields. Load/store architectures generally operate on registers and use separate memory-transfer instructions; other architectures may permit memory operands directly. The program counter identifies instruction flow, and branches update it differently from ordinary sequential execution.

sections.title: Effective addresses
sections.body: Immediate addressing embeds the operand, not an address. Register addressing reads the register value. Direct addressing uses an explicit address; indirect addressing follows a pointer to the operand. Base+displacement computes EA=base+offset; indexed modes add an index, sometimes scaled by element size. PC-relative addressing uses a displacement from a specified PC reference point; conventions matter.

sections.title: Performance equation
sections.body: CPU time=instruction count×average CPI×cycle time=IC×CPI/frequency. For instruction classes, average CPI=Σfractionᵢ×CPIᵢ. A new design may use fewer instructions but more cycles each. Compare complete execution time and use speedup=old time/new time.

examples.prompt: Address an array element using base 1000, index 3 and 4-byte elements

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The byte displacement is 3×4=12. The address space is byte-addressed. An index counts elements, so multiplying by four converts it into bytes.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: \(EA=1000+12=1012\). The base addresses element zero; index three is the fourth element and lies twelve bytes beyond that base.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Using raw index 3 as a byte offset would fetch the wrong location. Pointer arithmetic must use units consistently: element indices cannot be added as unscaled byte offsets.

examples.strategy: Scale an element index by element width before adding the base address.
examples.answer: Using raw index 3 as a byte offset would fetch the wrong location.
examples.verification: Elements start at 1000, 1004, 1008 and 1012, so index 3 corresponds to 1012.

examples.prompt: Compute time for 2 million instructions, CPI 3, clock 1 GHz
steps: Total cycles=\(2\cdot10^6\cdot3=6\cdot10^6\).
Cycle time is \(1/10^9\) seconds.
CPU time=0.006 s=6 ms.

pitfalls: Bytes, words and elements are different address units.
Average CPI must weight instruction frequencies.

checks.prompt: With base 2000 and byte displacement 24, what is the effective address?
checks.hint: Add the displacement.

checks.prompt: A program needs 6 million cycles at 2 GHz. What is its time in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Divide cycles by cycles per second, then convert.

lessons.method:

Instruction encoding width and field sizes determine how many operation/operand choices can be named. A program’s meaning follows the instruction semantics, not the appearance of an assembly mnemonic alone.
An addressing mode tells how to obtain the operand or its effective address. Immediate uses a value in the instruction; register uses a register value; direct uses a stated memory address; indirect follows an address through a register or memory. Base-plus-displacement adds an offset, indexed/scaled modes add an element index times element width, and PC-relative uses a defined PC reference.
Separate effective-address computation from fetching memory contents at that address. A question saying register R contains 1000 does not say memory[1000] contains 1000. PC-relative reference may use the next instruction address under the ISA, so check the stated convention. For encodings, account for unused field patterns and variable instruction formats before multiplying apparent possibilities. CPU execution time is instruction count times average cycles per instruction divided by cycles per second. Instruction count depends on the program and ISA/compiler choices; CPI depends on instruction mix and implementation; clock rate converts cycles to time. A higher frequency alone does not guarantee a faster program if CPI or instruction count also changes.
Weighted CPI uses dynamic instruction fractions: ΣpᵢCPIᵢ. Static source counts do not measure how often loops execute. Speedup is old time/new time, so a value above one means improvement. Amdahl’s law limits gains when only a fraction of execution is accelerated; time outside that fraction remains.
Convert GHz to 10⁹ cycles/s and keep instructions, cycles and seconds separate. Do not average performance rates where elapsed times should be added. For comparing architectures, calculate complete program time under each instruction count and CPI before taking their ratio. A “20% faster” rate and a “20% less time” statement are not identical percentages. An instruction can contain an opcode, register identifiers, addressing-mode bits and immediate/displacement fields. Load/store architectures generally operate on registers and use separate memory-transfer instructions; other architectures may permit memory operands directly. Register addressing reads the register value. Direct addressing uses an explicit address; indirect addressing follows a pointer to the operand. Base+displacement computes EA=base+offset; indexed modes add an index, sometimes scaled by element size. PC-relative addressing uses a displacement from a specified PC reference point; conventions matter. CPU time=instruction count×average CPI×cycle time=IC×CPI/frequency. For instruction classes, average CPI=Σfractionᵢ×CPIᵢ. A new design may use fewer instructions but more cycles each. Compare complete execution time and use speedup=old time/new time. An ISA defines the software-visible contract: instruction encodings, operand interpretation, register effects and exceptional behavior. A microarchitecture chooses how to implement that contract and can change pipeline depth or CPI without changing what a valid instruction means. Encoding questions are allocation problems: identify the bits available for opcodes and operands, count patterns, then account for reserved formats. Expanding opcodes reuse space from instructions needing fewer operands, but a prefix already assigned to a longer-operand instruction cannot be reused ambiguously. Signed immediate ranges depend on the specified field interpretation, not on total instruction width. Verify an allocation by tracing how a decoder distinguishes every instruction format before examining its remaining operand bits. An addressing mode is a recipe for obtaining an operand, and not every recipe produces a memory address. Immediate mode supplies a constant; register mode supplies a register value; memory modes first compute an effective address and then access its contents. Indirection introduces an additional address lookup, while scaled indexing combines a base with an index expressed in elements. PC-relative addressing requires a declared reference PC and displacement unit. Keep a small table of intermediate values to avoid confusing an address with data stored there. Negative offsets must be sign-extended according to their field width, and byte-addressed versus word-addressed conventions can change a target even when the encoded numbers look identical. Execution time is a chain of units: executed instructions become cycles through average CPI, then cycles become seconds through clock rate. Dynamic instruction frequencies determine the weights in average CPI; counting source lines or distinct opcodes gives different data. Speedup compares complete old and new elapsed times, including unchanged work. When only one fraction improves, express its new contribution as original time divided by the improvement factor and leave the other contribution alone. Rates should be combined according to the workload: sequential jobs require adding their times before computing total throughput. State whether memory stalls are already included in CPI to avoid adding the same penalty twice.
lessons.example: Address an array element using base 1000, index 3 and 4-byte elements

gateGuide.recognize: Performance questions combine instruction count, instruction mix, CPI and frequency. A clock-rate comparison alone is incomplete.
method: Compute effective addresses in the machine’s addressing units, including index scaling by element size.
Find weighted CPI using instruction fractions, then total cycles.
Divide by clock frequency and convert units at the end; compare old/new times for speedup.

traps.claim: Lower CPI always means faster
traps.why: A design with CPI 1 at 1 GHz is slower per instruction than CPI 1.5 at 2 GHz; instruction counts may also differ.

traps.claim: Index means byte displacement
traps.why: Array index 3 for 4-byte elements means displacement 12 bytes, not 3.

formulas.meaning: CPU time and weighted average cycles/instruction.
For the specified scaled base/index addressing form.

tutorials.title: Instruction semantics and effective addresses
tutorials.body:
An instruction set specifies visible operations, operand forms and architectural state. An opcode selects an operation; operands may be registers, immediate constants or memory references. Instruction encoding width and field sizes determine how many operation/operand choices can be named. An addressing mode tells how to obtain the operand or its effective address. example.prompt: R=1000, displacement=12, memory[1012]=42. What does a base-displacement load obtain?
example.strategy: Address → Memory access → Contrast immediate

steps.title: Address
steps.explanation: Base and displacement locate the memory cell.

steps.title: Memory access
steps.explanation: The load reads its contents, not the address itself.

steps.title: Contrast immediate
steps.explanation: An immediate 12 would supply the constant 12 without this memory lookup.

example.answer: The loaded operand is 42.
example.verification: 1012 is the effective address, not the fetched value; confusing them changes the instruction’s meaning.

depth.body: An ISA defines the software-visible contract: instruction encodings, operand interpretation, register effects and exceptional behavior. A microarchitecture chooses how to implement that contract and can change pipeline depth or CPI without changing what a valid instruction means. Encoding questions are allocation problems: identify the bits available for opcodes and operands, count patterns, then account for reserved formats. Expanding opcodes reuse space from instructions needing fewer operands, but a prefix already assigned to a longer-operand instruction cannot be reused ambiguously. Signed immediate ranges depend on the specified field interpretation, not on total instruction width. Verify an allocation by tracing how a decoder distinguishes every instruction format before examining its remaining operand bits.

examples.prompt: A sixteen-bit instruction has a five-bit opcode, a three-bit register field and an eight-bit signed two’s-complement immediate. Find the field capacities.
examples.strategy: Check total width → Count opcode and register names → Interpret immediate range

steps.title: Check total width
steps.explanation: All instruction bits are accounted for.

steps.title: Count opcode and register names
steps.explanation: Each binary field names one pattern per bit combination.

steps.title: Interpret immediate range
steps.explanation: The sign bit gives a range of −128 through 127 rather than 0 through 255.

examples.answer: At most 32 opcode patterns and 8 register names; signed immediates range from −128 to 127.
examples.verification: The three field spaces contain 32×8×256=65536 patterns, exactly 2¹⁶ before any reserved encodings.

examples.prompt: A sixteen-bit ISA uses six-bit operands. Twelve two-operand opcodes use twelve of the sixteen high-four-bit prefixes. Use expanding opcodes to support 200 one-operand instructions; how many zero-operand instructions can remain?
examples.strategy: Count available one-operand opcodes → Reserve one-operand patterns → Expand zero-operand encodings

steps.title: Count available one-operand opcodes
steps.explanation: Each free high-four-bit prefix can extend through six additional opcode bits while retaining one six-bit operand.

steps.title: Reserve one-operand patterns
steps.explanation: These unassigned ten-bit prefixes can be extended further.

steps.title: Expand zero-operand encodings
steps.explanation: With no operand field, all remaining low-six-bit patterns become opcode extensions.

examples.answer: At most 3584 zero-operand instructions remain under this allocation.
examples.verification: Two-operand instructions consume 12×4096 patterns and one-operand instructions consume 200×64; subtracting both from 65536 leaves 3584.

examples.prompt: Two processors implement the same ISA. One uses microcoded execution and the other a deeper pipeline. Must a valid ADD instruction produce different arithmetic results because their CPI differs?
examples.strategy: Identify the architectural contract → Separate implementation timing → Apply identical input state

steps.title: Identify the architectural contract
steps.explanation: The ISA specifies operands, result width and visible effects of ADD.

steps.title: Separate implementation timing
steps.explanation: Microsteps and pipeline overlap change how long the operation takes, not its specified arithmetic semantics.

steps.title: Apply identical input state
steps.explanation: Given the same architectural input state and specified conditions, both implementations must produce the same ADD result.

examples.answer: No; CPI can differ while ISA-visible arithmetic behavior remains identical.
examples.verification: A difference in the result for a valid, fully specified ADD would indicate an implementation error or a different ISA contract, not merely a performance difference.

depth.body: An addressing mode is a recipe for obtaining an operand, and not every recipe produces a memory address. Immediate mode supplies a constant; register mode supplies a register value; memory modes first compute an effective address and then access its contents. Indirection introduces an additional address lookup, while scaled indexing combines a base with an index expressed in elements. PC-relative addressing requires a declared reference PC and displacement unit. Keep a small table of intermediate values to avoid confusing an address with data stored there. Negative offsets must be sign-extended according to their field width, and byte-addressed versus word-addressed conventions can change a target even when the encoded numbers look identical.

examples.prompt: A PC-relative branch adds a signed byte displacement −8 to the next-instruction PC, which is 1004. Find its target.
examples.strategy: Choose the defined reference → Interpret displacement units → Compute target

steps.title: Choose the defined reference
steps.explanation: The instruction specifies next-instruction PC rather than the branch’s own address.

steps.title: Interpret displacement units
steps.explanation: No instruction-size scaling is applied because the offset is already in bytes.

steps.title: Compute target
steps.explanation: The signed displacement points backward.

examples.answer: The branch target is byte address 996.
examples.verification: Moving eight bytes forward from 996 returns the specified reference 1004; using a different PC would violate the stated ISA convention.

examples.prompt: A byte-addressed load uses base 2000, element index 7 scaled by 4 bytes, and displacement 12. Memory at the effective address contains 42. Find address and loaded value.
examples.strategy: Scale the element index → Add base and displacement → Fetch contents

steps.title: Scale the element index
steps.explanation: The register index counts elements rather than bytes.

steps.title: Add base and displacement
steps.explanation: All combined quantities now use byte-address units.

steps.title: Fetch contents
steps.explanation: The load obtains the value stored at that address.

examples.answer: Effective address=2040; loaded operand=42.
examples.verification: The address difference 2040−2000 equals seven four-byte elements plus twelve bytes; 2040 and 42 serve different roles.

examples.prompt: A memory-indirect operand is defined as memory[memory[100]]. Given memory[100]=200 and memory[200]=37, is the operand 200?
examples.strategy: Perform the address lookup → Perform the operand lookup → Classify the mistaken answer

steps.title: Perform the address lookup
steps.explanation: The first memory value supplies the effective address.

steps.title: Perform the operand lookup
steps.explanation: The mode requires a second access for actual data.

steps.title: Classify the mistaken answer
steps.explanation: Returning 200 stops after address indirection and omits the required data fetch.

examples.answer: The operand is 37; 200 is its effective address.
examples.verification: Replacing the inner memory expression by its supplied value gives memory[200], whose contents are independently specified as 37.

tutorials.title: Instruction count, CPI and clock-rate comparisons
tutorials.body:
CPU execution time is instruction count times average cycles per instruction divided by cycles per second. Instruction count depends on the program and ISA/compiler choices; CPI depends on instruction mix and implementation; clock rate converts cycles to time. A higher frequency alone does not guarantee a faster program if CPI or instruction count also changes.
Weighted CPI uses dynamic instruction fractions: ΣpᵢCPIᵢ. Static source counts do not measure how often loops execute. Speedup is old time/new time, so a value above one means improvement. Amdahl’s law limits gains when only a fraction of execution is accelerated; time outside that fraction remains.
Convert GHz to 10⁹ cycles/s and keep instructions, cycles and seconds separate. Do not average performance rates where elapsed times should be added. For comparing architectures, calculate complete program time under each instruction count and CPI before taking their ratio. A “20% faster” rate and a “20% less time” statement are not identical percentages.

example.prompt: A executes 1 million instructions at CPI 2 and 1 GHz; B at CPI 3 and 2 GHz with the same count.
example.strategy: Time A → Time B → Speedup

steps.title: Time A
steps.explanation: Count cycles then divide by rate.

steps.title: Time B
steps.explanation: Its higher CPI partly offsets its clock gain.

steps.title: Speedup
steps.explanation: Compare elapsed times.

example.answer: B is faster by a speedup of 4/3.
example.verification: B’s twofold clock rate does not yield twofold program speed because each instruction uses more cycles.

depth.body: Execution time is a chain of units: executed instructions become cycles through average CPI, then cycles become seconds through clock rate. Dynamic instruction frequencies determine the weights in average CPI; counting source lines or distinct opcodes gives different data. Speedup compares complete old and new elapsed times, including unchanged work. When only one fraction improves, express its new contribution as original time divided by the improvement factor and leave the other contribution alone. Rates should be combined according to the workload: sequential jobs require adding their times before computing total throughput. State whether memory stalls are already included in CPI to avoid adding the same penalty twice.

examples.prompt: A program executes two million instructions: 40% have CPI 1 and 60% CPI 3. The clock is 2 GHz. Find average CPI and CPU time.
examples.strategy: Weight by dynamic fractions → Count cycles → Convert cycles to time

steps.title: Weight by dynamic fractions
steps.explanation: The average reflects how often each class executes.

steps.title: Count cycles
steps.explanation: Multiply executed instructions by their average cycle cost.

steps.title: Convert cycles to time
steps.explanation: The clock supplies two billion cycles per second.

examples.answer: Average CPI=2.2; execution time=2.2 ms.
examples.verification: Class counts give 0.8 million one-cycle instructions plus 1.2 million three-cycle instructions, totaling 4.4 million cycles.

examples.prompt: A change accelerates the part responsible for 80% of a program’s original time by a factor of four. Find overall speedup.
examples.strategy: Normalize original time → Compute new contributions → Take time ratio

steps.title: Normalize original time
steps.explanation: The accelerated and unchanged contributions are 0.8 and 0.2.

steps.title: Compute new contributions
steps.explanation: Only the accelerated part is divided by four.

steps.title: Take time ratio
steps.explanation: Overall performance is limited by unchanged work.

examples.answer: Overall speedup is 2.5, not four.
examples.verification: An original 100-second run becomes 20 seconds for improved work plus 20 unchanged seconds, giving 40 seconds and the same ratio.

examples.prompt: Two equal-sized jobs run sequentially, one in 1 second and the other in 3 seconds. Is overall throughput the arithmetic mean of 1 and 1/3 jobs per second?
examples.strategy: Add elapsed times → Count completed work → Compute total rate

steps.title: Add elapsed times
steps.explanation: Both jobs must finish in sequence.

steps.title: Count completed work
steps.explanation: The numerator covers the same complete workload.

steps.title: Compute total rate
steps.explanation: The arithmetic mean of per-job rates incorrectly gives equal time weight to unequal durations.

examples.answer: Overall throughput is 0.5 jobs per second.
examples.verification: A repeated pair completes four jobs in eight seconds, again giving 0.5 rather than the arithmetic rate mean 2/3.

lessons.title: ALU design and hardwired/microprogrammed control
lessons.intuition: The datapath performs operations; the control unit chooses which operation happens and when. Keeping those roles separate makes it possible to trace an instruction as a sequence of register transfers instead of treating the CPU as a black box.

sections.title: ALU and status flags
sections.body: An ALU combines an adder, logic functions and selection hardware. Subtraction can reuse addition by complementing the second operand and setting carry-in: A−B=A+¬B+1. Flags may record zero, sign, carry and signed overflow. Signed comparison cannot rely on the sign of a wrapped subtraction without considering overflow.

sections.title: Register-transfer sequencing
sections.body: An instruction fetch can involve MAR←PC, memory read, IR←memory data and PC advancement. Execution then reads operands, activates the ALU, and writes a destination. Control signals choose mux inputs, register write enables, ALU function and memory actions. A single-cycle design combines actions in one long cycle; multicycle designs reuse hardware across shorter steps.

sections.title: Control implementation
sections.body: Hardwired control uses finite-state logic and decoding to generate signals, often with low latency but less flexibility. Microprogrammed control stores control words in a control memory; a sequencer chooses subsequent microinstructions using opcode and conditions. Horizontal microcode exposes more parallel control bits, while encoded vertical microcode reduces width at the cost of decoding.

examples.prompt: Compute 5−3 using 4-bit adder hardware

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Represent 5=0101 and 3=0011. Both operands fit in four-bit signed representation; retain that width throughout the bit calculation.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Invert 3 to 1100 and add carry-in 1: 0101+1100+1=10010. Bitwise inversion plus the carry-in forms −3 modulo 16. Include the extra carry in the intermediate sum before truncating.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Discard the carry beyond 4 bits; result 0010 is 2. The carry flag and signed-overflow flag are interpreted separately. An n-bit adder returns its low n result bits. Carry out does not by itself indicate signed overflow.

examples.strategy: Implement subtraction as addition of the width-limited two’s complement of the subtrahend.
examples.answer: Discard the carry beyond 4 bits; result 0010 is 2. The carry flag and signed-overflow flag are interpreted separately.
examples.verification: Low four bits 0010 represent +2, and +5−3 lies within the signed range −8…7, so signed overflow does not occur.

examples.prompt: Estimate control-store capacity
steps: Suppose there are 128 microinstructions, each 40 bits wide.
Storage is \(128\cdot40=5120\) bits.
Divide by 8 to obtain 640 bytes; sequencing circuitry is additional hardware.

pitfalls: Microinstructions and machine instructions are different levels.
Overflow interpretation depends on signedness.
revision: Datapath computes; control selects and sequences.

checks.prompt: A control store has 256 words of 32 bits. How many bytes does it occupy?
checks.hint: Multiply words by bits per word, then divide by 8.

checks.prompt: How many bits are needed to select one of 8 ALU operations?
checks.hint: Use log₂ of the number of choices.
checks.explanation: \(2^3=8\), so 3 selection bits.

lessons.concept: The datapath performs operations; the control unit chooses which operation happens and when. Keeping those roles separate makes it possible to trace an instruction as a sequence of register transfers instead of treating the CPU as a black box.
lessons.method:
An ALU combines operand paths for arithmetic and bitwise logic, selecting one output using control signals. An n-bit adder can support subtraction by conditionally inverting the second operand and inserting carry-in one, because A−B=A+¬B+1 modulo 2ⁿ. Separate AND/OR/XOR networks implement bitwise operations; a result multiplexer chooses the requested function.
Carry chains determine addition delay; faster structures use propagate/generate relationships. Flags describe different aspects of the result: zero checks all result bits, sign reads the leading bit, carry concerns unsigned arithmetic and overflow concerns signed representability. Shifts need stated logical or arithmetic fill behavior; arithmetic right shift normally repeats the sign bit.
Control decoding must drive both operand transformation and output selection consistently. A circuit giving correct low bits can still set a wrong overflow flag. In a trace, use the exact width and operation convention. Two’s-complement subtraction’s final carry interpretation depends on whether the architecture treats carry as no-borrow or exposes a separate borrow flag. The control unit schedules datapath actions such as register loads, ALU selections and memory reads. Hardwired control implements a state machine using combinational decoding and state registers. It can be fast but changing the instruction sequencing often requires changing hardware logic. Microprogrammed control stores sequences of microinstructions in a control memory and uses a microsequencer to choose their order.
A microinstruction can assert several independent control signals during one microcycle, provided the datapath supports them without conflict. Horizontal formats use wider explicit controls; vertical formats encode groups more compactly and need decoding. Control-store capacity is number of stored words times word width, not the architectural program-memory capacity.
An ISA instruction may execute several microinstructions, and their count need not equal the number of assembly instructions. A microprogram does not remove the need for datapath hardware or timing constraints. Compare the chosen design’s speed, encoding and modifiability rather than claiming every microprogrammed machine is necessarily slow. Trace which register updates occur simultaneously and which require a later microstep. A hardwired control unit produces datapath control signals using logic gates, a state register and any required instruction decoding. Its state records which part of instruction execution is in progress. The current state and inputs determine the next state, while the control logic asserts signals such as memory read, instruction-register load, ALU operation selection and destination-register write. There is no stored microinstruction word to fetch for each step.
Start from the datapath’s permitted actions and the controller’s state table. Encode each state, build a truth table for each output signal, then simplify the output functions. Several signals can share the same state decode when they are needed together. A minimal Boolean expression still must be checked against every encoded state, including reserved or unused codes under the specified behavior.
State encoding affects the resulting logic: binary encoding saves flip-flops but usually requires more decoding; one-hot encoding uses more state bits and may simplify control equations. Neither encoding alone establishes performance. The key distinction from microprogrammed control is where the sequencing and output decisions are implemented. To verify a hardwired design, substitute each state code into the Boolean outputs and confirm that only the intended datapath actions are enabled. An ALU combines an adder, logic functions and selection hardware. Subtraction can reuse addition by complementing the second operand and setting carry-in: A−B=A+¬B+1. Flags may record zero, sign, carry and signed overflow. Signed comparison cannot rely on the sign of a wrapped subtraction without considering overflow. An instruction fetch can involve MAR←PC, memory read, IR←memory data and PC advancement. Execution then reads operands, activates the ALU, and writes a destination. Control signals choose mux inputs, register write enables, ALU function and memory actions. A single-cycle design combines actions in one long cycle; multicycle designs reuse hardware across shorter steps. Hardwired control uses finite-state logic and decoding to generate signals, often with low latency but less flexibility. Microprogrammed control stores control words in a control memory; a sequencer chooses subsequent microinstructions using opcode and conditions. Horizontal microcode exposes more parallel control bits, while encoded vertical microcode reduces width at the cost of decoding. An ALU combines candidate arithmetic and logic results with control decoding that selects one operation. Subtraction commonly shares an adder by XORing the second operand with a subtract-control bit and using that bit as carry-in. Logical operations apply independently at each bit, whereas arithmetic operations couple positions through carries. Flags must be derived under the chosen operation and number interpretation: negative reports the sign bit, zero tests the entire result, and carry or borrow conventions are architecture-specific. Shift hardware also needs a distinction between arithmetic and logical right shifts. Verify both the selected result and its flags; checking a correct low-bit result alone does not validate the surrounding control or status logic. Microprogrammed control represents sequencing as words in a control store. Each word selects datapath actions and either names or helps compute the next microinstruction address. A sequence must respect data dependencies and resource conflicts even when a wide horizontal word can assert many control bits. Encoding mutually exclusive choices compresses a vertical word but requires decoding before driving the datapath. Account separately for control fields, branch-condition fields and next-address fields when calculating width. The architectural instruction count is not the microinstruction count, and a memory operation may require waiting under the stated device timing. Verify a microsequence by following the values available at each step rather than assuming all register transfers can occur together. Hardwired control turns state and instruction conditions into Boolean control and next-state signals. Outputs answer which datapath actions happen now; next-state equations answer which execution phase follows at the next clock edge. Derive these separately because a state may assert the same output under several conditions while branching differently afterward. Binary state encodings require decoding, whereas one-hot state bits can directly select phases; changing encoding changes hardware equations but not the intended sequence. Reset and illegal states also require explicit policies. A control table is an implementation specification, not just a list of mnemonics. Verify every guarded action using both the state code and its opcode or readiness condition.

gateGuide.recognize: Trace an instruction as register transfers and control choices. Separate datapath work from the sequencing that selects it.
method: List operands and destination, then identify the ALU operation, mux choices and write enables.
For subtraction use the fixed-width complement-plus-one construction and inspect flags separately.
For microcode storage multiply word count by control-word width; sequencing logic is separate from stored bits.

traps.claim: Microinstructions equal program instructions
traps.why: A machine instruction may require many internal microinstructions. They are different abstraction levels.

traps.claim: Signed comparison uses result sign alone
traps.why: Wrapped signed subtraction can overflow, so sign without overflow information can give the wrong comparison.

formulas.meaning: Fixed-width subtraction through an adder.
Control-memory capacity excluding additional hardware.

tutorials.title: ALU design: arithmetic, logic and flags
tutorials.body:
An ALU combines operand paths for arithmetic and bitwise logic, selecting one output using control signals. An n-bit adder can support subtraction by conditionally inverting the second operand and inserting carry-in one, because A−B=A+¬B+1 modulo 2ⁿ. example.prompt: Subtract 3 from 5 using a four-bit adder.
example.strategy: Prepare operands → Add with carry-in → Retain result

steps.title: Prepare operands
steps.explanation: Invert 0011 at the same width.

steps.title: Add with carry-in
steps.explanation: This implements subtraction modulo 16.

steps.title: Retain result
steps.explanation: Discard the fifth result bit but analyze flags separately.

example.answer: Result 2, with no signed overflow.
example.verification: The true signed result lies in −8…7; carry-out is not a reason to label it signed overflow.

depth.body: An ALU combines candidate arithmetic and logic results with control decoding that selects one operation. Subtraction commonly shares an adder by XORing the second operand with a subtract-control bit and using that bit as carry-in. Logical operations apply independently at each bit, whereas arithmetic operations couple positions through carries. Flags must be derived under the chosen operation and number interpretation: negative reports the sign bit, zero tests the entire result, and carry or borrow conventions are architecture-specific. examples.prompt: For eight-bit operands A=10101010 and B=11001100, compute the ALU’s bitwise AND and XOR results.
examples.strategy: Apply AND columnwise → Apply XOR columnwise → Interpret operation control

steps.title: Apply AND columnwise
steps.explanation: A result bit is one only where both corresponding input bits are one.

steps.title: Apply XOR columnwise
steps.explanation: A result bit is one where exactly one input bit is one.

steps.title: Interpret operation control
steps.explanation: Selecting AND or XOR chooses different combinational result paths for the same operands.

examples.verification: Hexadecimal checking gives 0xAA AND 0xCC=0x88 and 0xAA XOR 0xCC=0x66.

examples.prompt: An eight-bit ALU subtracts 9 from 6 using A+¬B+1. Carry-out means no unsigned borrow. Find result, carry, zero and negative flags.
examples.strategy: Prepare subtract input → Add with carry-in → Set defined flags

steps.title: Prepare subtract input
steps.explanation: Complement the eight-bit subtrahend 00001001.

steps.title: Add with carry-in
steps.explanation: The sum is below 256, so there is no ninth-bit carry.

steps.title: Set defined flags
steps.explanation: The result is nonzero with its sign bit set; zero carry means an unsigned borrow under the stated convention.

examples.answer: Result=11111101 (signed −3); C=0, Z=0, N=1, and no signed overflow.
examples.verification: 6−9=−3 lies in the signed range; unsigned subtraction needs a borrow, agreeing with the specified no-borrow carry flag.

examples.prompt: Right-shift eight-bit 10000000 by one. Can an arithmetic shift and a logical shift be used interchangeably for signed values?
examples.strategy: Apply logical shift → Apply arithmetic shift → Compare signed intent

steps.title: Apply logical shift
steps.explanation: Zero enters the high bit, producing unsigned/signed value 64.

steps.title: Apply arithmetic shift
steps.explanation: The sign bit is replicated, producing signed value −64.

steps.title: Compare signed intent
steps.explanation: Only the arithmetic shift preserves the signed division interpretation in this exact even case.

examples.answer: No; logical shifting gives +64, while arithmetic shifting gives −64.
examples.verification: Signed decoding of 11000000 is 192−256=−64; decoding 01000000 is +64.

tutorials.title: Hardwired versus microprogrammed control units
tutorials.body:
The control unit schedules datapath actions such as register loads, ALU selections and memory reads. Hardwired control implements a state machine using combinational decoding and state registers. It can be fast but changing the instruction sequencing often requires changing hardware logic. Microprogrammed control stores sequences of microinstructions in a control memory and uses a microsequencer to choose their order.
A microinstruction can assert several independent control signals during one microcycle, provided the datapath supports them without conflict. Horizontal formats use wider explicit controls; vertical formats encode groups more compactly and need decoding. Control-store capacity is number of stored words times word width, not the architectural program-memory capacity.
An ISA instruction may execute several microinstructions, and their count need not equal the number of assembly instructions. A microprogram does not remove the need for datapath hardware or timing constraints. Compare the chosen design’s speed, encoding and modifiability rather than claiming every microprogrammed machine is necessarily slow. Trace which register updates occur simultaneously and which require a later microstep.

example.prompt: A control memory has 256 microinstructions, each 48 bits. Find storage bytes.
example.strategy: Count bits → Convert → Identify scope

steps.title: Count bits
steps.explanation: Every stored word uses 48 bits.

steps.title: Convert
steps.explanation: Eight bits form one byte.

steps.title: Identify scope
steps.explanation: This excludes sequencer and decoder circuitry and any additional metadata.

example.answer: 1536 bytes, or 1.5 KiB.
example.verification: The address field needs eight bits to select 256 words; that is not the width of each microinstruction.

depth.body: Microprogrammed control represents sequencing as words in a control store. Each word selects datapath actions and either names or helps compute the next microinstruction address. A sequence must respect data dependencies and resource conflicts even when a wide horizontal word can assert many control bits. Encoding mutually exclusive choices compresses a vertical word but requires decoding before driving the datapath. Account separately for control fields, branch-condition fields and next-address fields when calculating width. The architectural instruction count is not the microinstruction count, and a memory operation may require waiting under the stated device timing. Verify a microsequence by following the values available at each step rather than assuming all register transfers can occur together.

examples.prompt: A simple load microsequence uses μ₀: MAR←Rbase; μ₁: MDR←memory[MAR]; μ₂: Rdest←MDR. Rbase=120 and memory[120]=77; each memory read completes within its stated microstep. Trace the result.
examples.strategy: Address setup → Memory transfer → Destination transfer

steps.title: Address setup
steps.explanation: At μ₀, MAR receives the base register value 120, selecting the memory location.

steps.title: Memory transfer
steps.explanation: At μ₁, the completed read places memory[120]=77 into MDR.

steps.title: Destination transfer
steps.explanation: At μ₂, the destination register receives MDR=77; the architectural load is now complete.

examples.answer: The destination register becomes 77 after three specified microsteps.
examples.verification: Substituting the register values along the microsequence gives Rdest=memory[Rbase]=memory[120]=77, while the address 120 remains separate from the data.

examples.prompt: A control word chooses one of 6 ALU operations, 4 bus sources and 8 destinations, plus a six-bit next address. Compare encoded fields with separate one-hot fields for these groups over 64 words.
examples.strategy: Calculate encoded controls → Include next address → Count storage

steps.title: Calculate encoded controls
steps.explanation: Each group is mutually exclusive, permitting binary encoding.

steps.title: Include next address
steps.explanation: Both designs retain the same sequencer field.

steps.title: Count storage
steps.explanation: The example counts only control-store bits, allowing packed storage.

examples.answer: Encoded storage=112 bytes; one-hot field storage=192 bytes under the supplied format.
examples.verification: The difference is 64×10=640 bits=80 bytes; encoded patterns outside the six ALU choices need a defined invalid-code policy.

examples.prompt: A horizontal microinstruction on a single shared bus asserts both R1out and R2out, where R1=5 and R2=9. Does its wide word make this simultaneous transfer valid?
examples.strategy: Inspect the physical resource → Compare driven values → Repair the microsequence

steps.title: Inspect the physical resource
steps.explanation: Both output controls enable different registers to drive the same bus.

steps.title: Compare driven values
steps.explanation: The drivers request incompatible bit values on at least some bus lines.

steps.title: Repair the microsequence
steps.explanation: Select only one source per microstep or provide a datapath with independent buses; word width cannot create a second bus.

examples.answer: No; this word causes a bus-source conflict in the stated datapath.
examples.verification: A destination has no defined single bus value when conflicting drivers are simultaneously active, so the transfer cannot be validated as an ordinary register assignment.

tutorials.title: Derive control signals from encoded controller states
tutorials.body:
A hardwired control unit produces datapath control signals using logic gates, a state register and any required instruction decoding. Its state records which part of instruction execution is in progress. The current state and inputs determine the next state, while the control logic asserts signals such as memory read, instruction-register load, ALU operation selection and destination-register write. There is no stored microinstruction word to fetch for each step.
Start from the datapath’s permitted actions and the controller’s state table. Encode each state, build a truth table for each output signal, then simplify the output functions. Several signals can share the same state decode when they are needed together. A minimal Boolean expression still must be checked against every encoded state, including reserved or unused codes under the specified behavior.
State encoding affects the resulting logic: binary encoding saves flip-flops but usually requires more decoding; one-hot encoding uses more state bits and may simplify control equations. Neither encoding alone establishes performance. The key distinction from microprogrammed control is where the sequencing and output decisions are implemented. To verify a hardwired design, substitute each state code into the Boolean outputs and confirm that only the intended datapath actions are enabled.

example.prompt: A controller uses q₁q₀=00 for idle, 01 for fetch, 10 for register ADD and 11 for halt. MemRead and IRWrite are asserted only in fetch; ALUAdd and RegWrite only in ADD. Derive the four control equations.
example.strategy: Decode fetch → Decode execution → Drive controls → Check inactive states

steps.title: Decode fetch
steps.explanation: The product is true at state 01 and nowhere else.

steps.title: Decode execution
steps.explanation: The product selects exactly state 10.

steps.title: Drive controls
steps.explanation: Each paired signal shares the state in which the specified action occurs.

steps.title: Check inactive states
steps.explanation: At 00 and 11 both F and E are zero, so all four outputs are inactive.

example.answer: MemRead=IRWrite=¬q₁q₀; ALUAdd=RegWrite=q₁¬q₀.
example.verification: Substitution at 01 enables only fetch controls, at 10 only ADD controls, and at idle/halt none. These are direct combinational state decodes rather than control-store lookups.

depth.body: Hardwired control turns state and instruction conditions into Boolean control and next-state signals. Outputs answer which datapath actions happen now; next-state equations answer which execution phase follows at the next clock edge. Derive these separately because a state may assert the same output under several conditions while branching differently afterward. Binary state encodings require decoding, whereas one-hot state bits can directly select phases; changing encoding changes hardware equations but not the intended sequence. Reset and illegal states also require explicit policies. A control table is an implementation specification, not just a list of mnemonics. Verify every guarded action using both the state code and its opcode or readiness condition.

examples.prompt: A binary controller asserts RegWrite only in state q₁q₀=10 when opcode condition ADD=1. Derive RegWrite and evaluate state 10 with ADD=0.
examples.strategy: Decode execution state → Include instruction condition → Evaluate excluded opcode

steps.title: Decode execution state
steps.explanation: The state product selects code 10 exactly.

steps.title: Include instruction condition
steps.explanation: Entering the state alone is insufficient unless the correct opcode is active.

steps.title: Evaluate excluded opcode
steps.explanation: The guard blocks an unintended register update.

examples.answer: RegWrite=q₁¬q₀·ADD; it is zero for the supplied non-ADD case.
examples.verification: Substitution at all other state codes also yields zero; only the specified state/opcode combination enables writing.

examples.prompt: An idle/busy hardwired controller uses Q=0 for idle and Q=1 for busy. Start begins work only while idle; Done ends it only while busy. Derive Q⁺ and trace (Start,Done)=(1,0),(0,0),(0,1) from idle.
examples.strategy: Derive idle branch → Derive busy branch → Combine and trace

steps.title: Derive idle branch
steps.explanation: A start request enters busy state.

steps.title: Derive busy branch
steps.explanation: Busy remains asserted until completion.

steps.title: Combine and trace
steps.explanation: The three sampled pairs produce states 1,1,0.

examples.answer: Q⁺=¬Q·Start+Q·¬Done; the state trace is busy,busy,idle.
examples.verification: The middle step ignores Start while busy and holds until Done; the last step consumes completion rather than waiting for a new start.

examples.prompt: A controller uses only gates and state flip-flops. Can editing program RAM rewrite its next-state function, so the same encoded state and opcode now produce a different next state?
examples.strategy: Locate transition implementation → Separate program input from control logic → Identify an actual modification

steps.title: Locate transition implementation
steps.explanation: Next-state and control-output functions reside in logic gates, not in a fetched microinstruction table.

steps.title: Separate program input from control logic
steps.explanation: New instruction bytes can select already-supported opcode cases but do not rewrite the controller’s Boolean equations.

steps.title: Identify an actual modification
steps.explanation: Changing the execution sequencing rules requires changing the hardware logic or a separately specified programmable mechanism.

examples.answer: No; program RAM contents do not themselves rewrite a purely hardwired control unit.
examples.verification: The same state and decoded-input combination still feeds the same gates after the RAM edit, so its prescribed transition remains unchanged.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy and cache mapping
lessons.prerequisite: Binary address splitting and CPU performance.
lessons.intuition: Caches exploit repetition and neighbourhood in memory accesses. A small fast store holds copies of slower memory blocks. Mapping decides where a block may go; replacement decides which resident block leaves when those allowed locations are full.

sections.title: Hierarchy and locality
sections.body: Temporal locality reuses recently accessed data; spatial locality accesses nearby addresses. Transfers occur in blocks, so one miss may bring several adjacent words. A larger block can improve spatial reuse but reduces the number of resident blocks at fixed capacity and increases transfer cost. Separate compulsory, capacity and conflict misses when reasoning about changes.

sections.title: Address partition
sections.body: In a byte-addressed system with 2ᵇ-byte blocks, the lowest b bits are block offset. A cache with S sets needs log₂S index bits; remaining high bits form the tag. Direct mapping has one line per set; W-way associativity has W lines per set. Sets=capacity/(block size×ways). Fully associative caches have one set and no index bits.

sections.title: Writes and performance
sections.body: Write-through updates lower memory on writes; write-back marks lines dirty and writes them on eviction. Write-allocate versus no-write-allocate controls write misses independently. Single-level AMAT=hit time+miss rate×miss penalty, where the penalty is the additional miss cost. Multilevel formulas require using local versus global miss rates consistently.

examples.prompt: Split a 32-bit address for a 16 KiB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks

steps.title: Convert capacity and count lines
steps.explanation: KiB is binary here. Data capacity excludes tag/valid metadata; do not subtract those bytes from C.

steps.title: Count sets
steps.explanation: Each set holds four lines. Index selects a set; associativity is not another independent address field.

steps.title: Find low-order fields
steps.explanation: Byte offset selects one of 64 bytes inside a block. Set index selects one of 64 sets.

steps.title: Allocate remaining address bits
steps.explanation: Tag is what remains after identifying a byte and a set. The tag comparison distinguishes different memory blocks mapping to that set.

examples.given: 32-bit byte addresses; 16 KiB data capacity; 4-way associativity; 64-byte blocks.
examples.goal: Find tag, index and offset bits.
examples.strategy: Determine sets from data capacity first, then take powers-of-two logarithms.
examples.answer: 20 tag bits, 6 index bits, 6 offset bits.
examples.verification: Reconstruct data capacity: 2⁶ sets ×4 ways ×2⁶ bytes=16,384 bytes; the fields sum to 32 bits.

examples.prompt: Compute AMAT for hit time 2 ns, miss rate 4%, penalty 50 ns
steps: Miss contribution is \(0.04\cdot50=2\) ns.
Add the baseline hit time 2 ns.
\(AMAT=4\) ns; do not multiply the hit time by hit rate in this penalty-based convention.

pitfalls: Cache capacity usually excludes tag/valid/dirty storage unless specified.
Use number of sets, not total lines, for index bits.

checks.prompt: Which quantity determines cache index bits?
checks.hint: A set-associative cache indexes a set, then compares tags within it.
checks.explanation: Index width is log₂(number of sets). Number of sets equals lines divided by ways; total lines works only in direct mapping.

checks.prompt: A hit takes 1 ns, miss rate 0.1, extra penalty 30 ns. What is AMAT in ns?
checks.hint: Use the penalty convention.

lessons.concept: Caches exploit repetition and neighbourhood in memory accesses. A small fast store holds copies of slower memory blocks. Mapping decides where a block may go; replacement decides which resident block leaves when those allowed locations are full.
lessons.method:
A hierarchy trades small fast storage against larger slower storage. Temporal locality predicts reuse of recently accessed data; spatial locality predicts access to nearby locations. A cache transfers blocks rather than individual requested bytes so it can exploit both. A hit finds the block in cache; a miss fetches it from a lower level and may evict another block.
Average access time depends on how miss cost is defined. With hit time Tₕ and additional penalty P, AMAT=Tₕ+miss_rate·P, since every access pays the baseline and misses add penalty. If instead supplied hit and miss times are complete mutually exclusive path times, use hit_rate·T_hit+miss_rate·T_miss. Mixing these conventions double-counts or omits time.
Multiple levels require conditional miss rates: an L2 local miss rate is among requests reaching L2, not among all CPU references. Dirty write-back blocks can add eviction work; write-through and write-allocate choices alter traffic. State what capacity and timing include before calculating. A high hit rate can still have poor AMAT when rare misses are exceptionally costly. A byte-addressed cache divides an address into block offset, set index and tag. Offset chooses a byte within a block; index chooses a set; tag distinguishes different memory blocks using that set. For data capacity C, block bytes B and W ways, there are C/B lines and C/(BW) sets. With power-of-two sizes the corresponding bit counts are logarithms.
Direct mapping has one way per set, fully associative mapping one set, and set associativity several candidate lines per indexed set. Replacement selects among ways of the chosen set, not arbitrary lines from the whole cache. LRU records recent references within that set. Valid bits prevent an uninitialized tag from being mistaken for resident data.
For a reference trace, first divide byte address by block size to identify block number, then take modulo set count. Nearby bytes in one block can hit after one miss.
