gateGuide.recognize: Address-bit questions require capacity, block size, associativity and address width. AMAT questions require a clear miss-penalty convention.
method: Convert capacity and block size to bytes, compute lines, then divide by ways to get sets.
Allocate low offset bits, then set index bits, and use remaining high bits for tag.
For access time distinguish additional miss penalty from total miss service time. If multilevel, identify local versus global miss rates.

traps.claim: Use total lines for index bits in every cache
traps.why: A four-way cache has one quarter as many sets as lines. Indexing lines instead of sets steals two bits incorrectly from the tag.

traps.claim: Double-count hit time
traps.why: If miss penalty is additional cost, hit time is already paid for every access and is added once.

formulas.meaning: Byte-addressed cache: capacity C, block bytes B, ways W, address bits A.
Additional miss penalty convention.

tutorials.title: Memory hierarchy and average access time
tutorials.body:
A hierarchy trades small fast storage against larger slower storage. Temporal locality predicts reuse of recently accessed data; spatial locality predicts access to nearby locations. A cache transfers blocks rather than individual requested bytes so it can exploit both. A hit finds the block in cache; a miss fetches it from a lower level and may evict another block.
Average access time depends on how miss cost is defined. With hit time Tₕ and additional penalty P, AMAT=Tₕ+miss_rate·P, since every access pays the baseline and misses add penalty. If instead supplied hit and miss times are complete mutually exclusive path times, use hit_rate·T_hit+miss_rate·T_miss. Mixing these conventions double-counts or omits time.
Multiple levels require conditional miss rates: an L2 local miss rate is among requests reaching L2, not among all CPU references. Dirty write-back blocks can add eviction work; write-through and write-allocate choices alter traffic. State what capacity and timing include before calculating. A high hit rate can still have poor AMAT when rare misses are exceptionally costly.

example.prompt: Hit time 1 ns, miss rate 5%, extra miss penalty 60 ns.
example.strategy: Baseline → Expected extra cost → Total

steps.title: Baseline
steps.explanation: Every access first spends 1 ns in the cache lookup.

steps.title: Expected extra cost
steps.explanation: Only the miss fraction pays the additional penalty.

steps.title: Total
steps.explanation: Add baseline and expected increment.

example.answer: \(AMAT=4\) ns.
example.verification: Complete miss path is 61 ns; 0.95×1+0.05×61 also yields 4 ns.

depth.body: A cache performance calculation is a weighted account of costs and events. Decide whether miss time includes the hit lookup or is an extra penalty, then use one consistent convention. If cache stalls are converted into CPI, count memory references per instruction and multiply by the miss fraction and penalty in cycles. Instructions and data accesses can contribute separate streams, and writes may have additional policy-dependent costs. Improving one number, such as hit latency, can worsen overall time if misses become more common. Validate a result using a finite reference population or a complete-path weighted sum, and keep cycle penalties separate from nanosecond penalties until a clock period explicitly connects the units.

examples.prompt: Hits take a complete 2 ns and misses a complete 42 ns. The hit rate is 90%. Find average access time.
examples.strategy: Use mutually exclusive paths → Weight each path → Add costs

steps.title: Use mutually exclusive paths
steps.explanation: The supplied miss time already includes the whole miss path.

steps.title: Weight each path
steps.explanation: Ninety percent pay the hit path and ten percent the complete miss path.

steps.title: Add costs
steps.explanation: No additional baseline is added afterward.

examples.answer: Average access time is 6 ns.
examples.verification: The equivalent incremental penalty is 42−2=40 ns, giving 2+0.1×40=6 ns.

examples.prompt: Base CPI excludes memory stalls and equals 1. Each instruction fetches once; 25% also access data once. All accesses miss at rate 4%, with an extra 40-cycle penalty and no overlap. Find effective CPI.
examples.strategy: Count references per instruction → Compute expected stall cycles → Add baseline

steps.title: Count references per instruction
steps.explanation: Instruction fetches occur for all instructions and data accesses for the stated fraction.

steps.title: Compute expected stall cycles
steps.explanation: Every expected miss adds its nonoverlapped penalty.

steps.title: Add baseline
steps.explanation: The base cost and extra memory stalls are disjoint by specification.

examples.answer: Effective CPI is 3.
examples.verification: For 100 instructions there are 125 references, five expected misses and 200 extra cycles; adding 100 base cycles gives 300 total.

examples.prompt: Cache A has hit time 2 ns, miss rate 2%, extra penalty 50 ns. Cache B lowers hit time to 1 ns but misses 10%, with the same penalty. Is B faster on average?
examples.strategy: Calculate original average → Calculate redesigned average → Compare actual request time

steps.title: Calculate original average
steps.explanation: The small miss fraction adds only one nanosecond.

steps.title: Calculate redesigned average
steps.explanation: The faster hit is outweighed by expected miss cost.

steps.title: Compare actual request time
steps.explanation: The redesigned cache doubles average access time under this workload.

examples.answer: No; B averages 6 ns versus A’s 3 ns.
examples.verification: The one-nanosecond hit saving is smaller than the four-nanosecond increase in expected penalty, leaving a net three-nanosecond regression.

tutorials.title: Direct, associative and set-associative mapping
tutorials.body:
A byte-addressed cache divides an address into block offset, set index and tag. Offset chooses a byte within a block; index chooses a set; tag distinguishes different memory blocks using that set. For data capacity C, block bytes B and W ways, there are C/B lines and C/(BW) sets. With power-of-two sizes the corresponding bit counts are logarithms.
Direct mapping has one way per set, fully associative mapping one set, and set associativity several candidate lines per indexed set. Replacement selects among ways of the chosen set, not arbitrary lines from the whole cache. LRU records recent references within that set. Valid bits prevent an uninitialized tag from being mistaken for resident data.
For a reference trace, first divide byte address by block size to identify block number, then take modulo set count. Nearby bytes in one block can hit after one miss. Cache capacity normally means data capacity unless metadata is explicitly included. Distinguish compulsory, conflict and capacity misses; increasing associativity targets conflicts without necessarily changing the block offset.

example.prompt: An initially empty direct-mapped 16-byte cache uses 4-byte blocks. Access byte addresses 0,3,16,0.
example.strategy: Sets → First two accesses → First reference to block four → Return to block zero

steps.title: Sets
steps.explanation: There is one line per set.

steps.title: First two accesses
steps.explanation: Addresses 0 and 3 are block 0, set 0: the first is a compulsory miss and the second hits.

steps.title: First reference to block four
steps.explanation: This compulsory miss brings in a new block and evicts block 0 from set 0.

steps.title: Return to block zero
steps.explanation: The final address 0 misses because block 4 evicted block 0. A fully associative cache with the same four-line capacity would retain both blocks, so this is a conflict miss.

example.answer: Miss, hit, miss, miss; the misses are compulsory, compulsory and conflict respectively.
example.verification: Only two distinct blocks are referenced, fewer than the four-line capacity. The first access to each is compulsory; the final return misses solely because both blocks compete for direct-mapped set 0.

depth.body: Cache mapping limits the candidate locations for a memory block, while replacement chooses a victim within those candidates. Derive the block number before considering placement, since byte offset bits do not participate in tag matching. Set count depends on data capacity, block size and associativity; increasing ways at fixed capacity reduces index bits and increases tag bits. Trace replacement order within each set independently. A miss on the first reference to a block is compulsory even if its insertion evicts another block. To distinguish later conflict misses from capacity misses, compare against a fully associative cache with the same capacity and replacement assumption, rather than treating every same-set eviction as the same miss category.

examples.prompt: A byte-addressed 32-bit system has a 4 KiB, two-way cache with 16-byte blocks. Find offset, index and tag widths; capacity counts data only.
examples.strategy: Compute set count → Allocate offset and index → Allocate remaining bits

steps.title: Compute set count
steps.explanation: There are two data lines per set.

steps.title: Allocate offset and index
steps.explanation: Low bits choose bytes and sets.

steps.title: Allocate remaining bits
steps.explanation: Tag bits distinguish blocks mapping to the same set.

examples.answer: Offset=4 bits, index=7 bits, tag=21 bits.
examples.verification: 128 sets×2 ways×16 bytes=4096 bytes, and the three address fields sum to 32 bits.

examples.prompt: An initially empty cache has two sets and two ways per set, using LRU. Trace block numbers 0,2,4,0 and classify the final miss against an equal-capacity fully associative LRU cache.
examples.strategy: Map blocks → Trace set-local LRU → Compare equal capacity

steps.title: Map blocks
steps.explanation: All three distinct blocks compete in set zero.

steps.title: Trace set-local LRU
steps.explanation: After 0 and 2, the set holds both, with 0 older. Bringing in 4 evicts 0; returning to 0 therefore misses.

steps.title: Compare equal capacity
steps.explanation: The fully associative four-line cache retains all three distinct blocks, so its final access to 0 hits.

examples.answer: The trace is miss,miss,miss,miss; the final miss is a conflict miss.
examples.verification: The three first references are compulsory. Three blocks fit in the four-line total capacity, so the final miss comes from placement restriction rather than total capacity.

examples.prompt: A fully associative cache uses 64-byte blocks in a 32-bit byte-addressed system. Does having no set index mean it also needs no tag?
examples.strategy: Allocate block offset → Remove only the index field → Retain block identity

steps.title: Allocate block offset
steps.explanation: Six low bits identify a byte within a block.

steps.title: Remove only the index field
steps.explanation: Any cache line may hold any block, so no address bits select a set.

steps.title: Retain block identity
steps.explanation: Tags still distinguish which of the many memory blocks each line holds.

examples.answer: It needs 26 tag bits per stored block identity, despite having zero index bits.
examples.verification: Addresses 0 and 64 share offset zero but name different blocks; tags must distinguish them when placement alone does not.

tutorials.title: Follow conditional accesses through two cache levels
tutorials.body:
A memory hierarchy places fast, small storage near the processor and slower, larger storage farther away. A request first checks the nearest cache. A miss sends the request to the next level; only a miss there reaches main memory. Consequently the traffic observed by a lower cache is a subset of the processor’s requests. If every access pays the L1 lookup time, every L1 miss pays an additional L2 lookup, and every L2 miss pays an additional memory penalty, average time is the sum of each incremental cost weighted by its probability of occurring.
Time conventions matter: an additional penalty excludes earlier work, whereas a complete path time includes it. Mixing those descriptions can count the same lookup twice. Cache capacity and locality affect rates, but the arithmetic must use the rates supplied for the stated workload. Verify a hierarchical calculation using expected request counts over a convenient number of accesses and comparing those counts with the probability model.

example.prompt: L1 lookup is 1 ns with miss rate 10%. An L1 miss adds a 4 ns L2 lookup. L2 has a local miss rate 20%; an L2 miss adds 50 ns for memory. For 1000 accesses, find memory requests and AMAT.
example.strategy: Trace L1 traffic → Trace memory traffic → Weight incremental costs

steps.title: Trace L1 traffic
steps.explanation: Only L1 misses reach the second cache.

steps.title: Trace memory traffic
steps.explanation: The local L2 miss rate applies to its 100 incoming requests, giving a global memory rate 2%.

steps.title: Weight incremental costs
steps.explanation: Every access pays L1; smaller conditional subsets pay the later costs.

example.answer: Expected memory requests: 20; AMAT: 2.4 ns.
example.verification: Total expected lookup/penalty time is 1000×1+100×4+20×50=2400 ns; dividing by 1000 yields 2.4 ns.

depth.body: The purpose of a hierarchy is to exploit locality while limiting expensive lower-level accesses. Temporal locality concerns reuse of the same item; spatial locality concerns nearby items brought in together by a block transfer. Trace which level sees each request before applying a miss rate. Global and local rates share a numerator but use different denominators, so their relationship follows directly from traffic counts. Inclusion is a separate policy: an inclusive lower cache guarantees that upper-cache blocks also appear below, and a lower-level eviction may therefore require an upper-level invalidation. Do not assume inclusion, equal block sizes or free writebacks unless the problem explicitly supplies those conditions.

examples.prompt: An initially empty cache fetches aligned 16-byte blocks. Read byte addresses 0,4,8,12 with no intervening eviction. Explain the hierarchy benefit.
examples.strategy: Identify the common block → Fetch on first request → Reuse neighboring data

steps.title: Identify the common block
steps.explanation: All four addresses belong to one transferred block.

steps.title: Fetch on first request
steps.explanation: The access to address 0 misses and brings bytes 0–15 from the lower level.

steps.title: Reuse neighboring data
steps.explanation: The remaining three accesses hit, exploiting spatial locality rather than requiring three more lower-level transfers.

examples.answer: One block fetch serves all four references: miss,hit,hit,hit.
examples.verification: The number of lower-level reads is one although four different byte addresses are requested, directly illustrating the block-transfer advantage.

examples.prompt: An L1 cache misses on 20% of processor references. L2 misses on 5% of all processor references. Find L2’s local miss rate.
examples.strategy: Choose a reference count → Count L2 misses globally → Condition on reaching L2

steps.title: Choose a reference count
steps.explanation: Only L1 misses reach L2.

steps.title: Count L2 misses globally
steps.explanation: The supplied five-percent rate uses all processor references as denominator.

steps.title: Condition on reaching L2
steps.explanation: Local rate divides by actual L2 requests.

examples.answer: The L2 local miss rate is 25%.
examples.verification: Multiplying L1’s 0.20 miss fraction by local L2 rate 0.25 recovers the given global miss fraction 0.05.

examples.prompt: In an inclusive L1/L2 hierarchy with equal block size, may L2 evict block X while leaving a valid copy of X in L1?
examples.strategy: Apply inclusion invariant → Consider the proposed eviction → Maintain the invariant

steps.title: Apply inclusion invariant
steps.explanation: Every valid L1 block must also be present in L2.

steps.title: Consider the proposed eviction
steps.explanation: Removing X only from L2 would leave an L1 block absent from the required lower-level superset.

steps.title: Maintain the invariant
steps.explanation: The hierarchy must invalidate the upper copy or use another specified inclusion-preserving action when X is evicted below.

examples.answer: No; leaving the L1 copy valid would break the stated inclusive policy.
examples.verification: After the upper invalidation, the set of valid L1 blocks is again a subset of L2’s blocks; an exclusive hierarchy would have a different contract.

lessons.title: Memory interfacing, interrupts and DMA
lessons.intuition: A processor must select the correct memory device and coordinate data transfer. I/O introduces devices whose speed and readiness differ from the CPU. Polling, interrupts and DMA assign different amounts of coordination work to software and hardware.

sections.title: Memory organization and decoding
sections.body: A memory specified as N×w stores N locations of w bits each. Address bits select locations; data pins carry width w. To expand width, connect chips to different data-bit lanes while sharing address lines. To expand depth, decode extra high address bits into chip-select signals. Byte addressing may require multiple byte lanes and enables.

sections.title: Polling and interrupts
sections.body: Polling repeatedly checks a device status register and spends CPU cycles waiting. An interrupt lets a device request attention; the CPU saves required execution state, enters an interrupt handler, services the event and returns. Masking, priority and nesting determine which interrupts can be serviced. Interrupt latency includes finishing or suspending permitted work and reaching the handler.

sections.title: DMA
sections.body: A DMA controller transfers blocks between a device and memory after the CPU configures addresses, length and direction. Burst mode may occupy a bus for a sequence; cycle stealing interleaves transfers with CPU activity. DMA reduces per-byte CPU overhead but does not imply zero setup cost or unlimited bandwidth. Shared caches can require coherency handling for DMA buffers.

examples.prompt: Build 4K×16 memory from 1K×8 chips

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Width expansion requires 16/8=2 chips in parallel per bank. Two chips receive the same address and supply different byte lanes to build each 16-bit word.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Depth expansion requires 4K/1K=4 banks. Four independent banks provide four times the word count. Bank selection must enable only the addressed bank.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Total=2×4=8 chips; two extra address bits select the bank, while ten bits select a location inside a chip. Multiplying the two expansion factors counts all physical chips; address bits select words, not individual bit lanes.

examples.strategy: Separate word-width expansion from the number of addressable words.
examples.answer: Total=2×4=8 chips; two extra address bits select the bank, while ten bits select a location inside a chip.
examples.verification: Eight chips each store 1024×8 bits, totaling 65536 bits; the target 4096×16 bits has the same capacity.

examples.prompt: Compare one-byte interrupts with DMA for 4096 bytes
steps: An interrupt per byte produces 4096 service events.
A DMA block can use one setup and a completion interrupt under the simple model.
The CPU saves many handler invocations, although memory-bus transfer time remains.

pitfalls: Chip width and depth expansion are separate factors.
DMA still competes for memory bandwidth.
revision: Total chips=(desired depth/chip depth)×(desired width/chip width).
Interrupts request service; DMA performs data movement.

checks.prompt: What is the primary role of DMA?
checks.hint: The CPU configures transfer work but need not move each byte.
checks.explanation: DMA transfers between devices and memory with controller support. Setup/completion overhead and bus competition still remain.
options: Transfer blocks with reduced per-byte CPU involvement

checks.prompt: How many address bits select one location in a 4K-location chip?
checks.explanation: 4096=2¹², requiring 12 address bits.

lessons.concept: A processor must select the correct memory device and coordinate data transfer. I/O introduces devices whose speed and readiness differ from the CPU. Polling, interrupts and DMA assign different amounts of coordination work to software and hardware.
lessons.method:
A chip described as D×W stores D addressable words, each W bits. To increase width, connect chips in parallel to common address signals and use different data-bit lanes. To increase depth, create banks and use higher address bits to enable the selected bank. These operations are independent, so compatible expansion factors multiply.
Address bits select word locations, not individual stored bits unless the chip is bit-addressed. Within a power-of-two depth D, log₂D bits address each location. Bank-select bits are additional to within-chip bits. Read/write and chip-enable signals must prevent several banks from driving the same data bus simultaneously.
Check unit conventions: a 1K×8 chip has 1024 byte-wide words, whereas 1K×1 has 1024 single-bit words. A target capacity expressed in bytes needs conversion to its access width before choosing factors. Unused address ranges and partial decoding can create aliases; the desired memory map may require full decoding rather than just enough pins to store the requested bit count. An I/O interface exposes device data, status and control registers, reached through memory-mapped or separate I/O addressing. Programmed polling repeatedly reads status until the device is ready, then the CPU transfers data. Interrupt-driven I/O lets the device request service, so the CPU can do other work rather than poll continuously; the interrupt handler still performs work and has entry/exit overhead.
DMA allows a controller to transfer a block between device and memory after CPU setup. It needs bus arbitration and can occupy memory bandwidth; the CPU is not necessarily idle or entirely unaffected during transfer. Completion can raise an interrupt. DMA reduces per-unit CPU transfer involvement, not the physical number of bytes moved.
Trace who copies data, who controls the address/count and when the CPU is notified. An interrupt is a control event, not automatically a DMA transfer. Bus stealing can delay CPU memory accesses even while saving software overhead. In performance questions include setup, transfer and completion costs exactly as specified instead of assuming one mode has zero overhead. An I/O interface provides a defined way for processor instructions to interact with a device. In memory-mapped I/O, some addresses select device registers instead of ordinary RAM. A status register reports conditions such as ready or busy; a data register transfers the payload; a control register may start an operation or select its mode. The instruction still performs a load or store, but the selected device determines what that access means.
Treat device-register semantics as part of the problem specification. Reading a data register can clear a ready flag or consume a queued byte; writing a control register can initiate work. Such accesses may have side effects and cannot generally be reordered or repeated as if they were ordinary memory reads. Polling repeatedly checks status until the specified ready condition holds, then accesses the appropriate data register.
Keep address, register contents and individual status bits separate. A nonzero status value does not necessarily mean the particular ready bit is set, so test the stated mask. Interrupts and DMA change how readiness and transfer work are scheduled, but they still rely on an interface with defined registers or descriptors. Verify a polling trace by explaining which accesses touch status, which consume data, and whether any side effect changes later observations. A memory specified as N×w stores N locations of w bits each. Address bits select locations; data pins carry width w. To expand width, connect chips to different data-bit lanes while sharing address lines. To expand depth, decode extra high address bits into chip-select signals. Byte addressing may require multiple byte lanes and enables. Polling repeatedly checks a device status register and spends CPU cycles waiting. An interrupt lets a device request attention; the CPU saves required execution state, enters an interrupt handler, services the event and returns. Masking, priority and nesting determine which interrupts can be serviced. Interrupt latency includes finishing or suspending permitted work and reaching the handler. A DMA controller transfers blocks between a device and memory after the CPU configures addresses, length and direction. Burst mode may occupy a bus for a sequence; cycle stealing interleaves transfers with CPU activity. DMA reduces per-byte CPU overhead but does not imply zero setup cost or unlimited bandwidth. Shared caches can require coherency handling for DMA buffers. A memory chip’s depth and word width are independent dimensions. Parallel chips widen each addressed word, while banks selected by higher address bits increase the number of locations. Identify whether the CPU addresses bytes or complete words before assigning address pins: byte lanes can use low CPU address bits that never reach the chip’s word-address input. Chip-enable decoding should choose a bank without enabling competing drivers on the same data lane. Partial decoding can cause aliases, where multiple CPU addresses reach the same physical location. Verify an arrangement by multiplying chip count by per-chip bit capacity and by tracing one complete CPU address into bank, chip location and lane selection. An interrupt is a control transfer that lets a device or event request processor attention. Servicing requires preserving the interrupted architectural context, identifying and acknowledging the source, performing the required work and restoring execution. Entry latency differs from handler duration: masking or a higher-priority handler can delay entry even when the eventual handler is short. Level-triggered requests remain asserted until the source condition is removed, so returning without acknowledgment can immediately retrigger service. An interrupt does not by itself move an entire data block; software or DMA still performs the transfer. State priority, masking and acknowledgment assumptions when computing response time or counting service events. DMA separates processor setup from the controller’s repeated data transfers. The controller needs source or destination addresses, length, direction and a valid ownership/coherence protocol. Trace how addresses advance with each transfer beat and distinguish byte counts from word counts. DMA reduces per-byte software work but still consumes bus or memory bandwidth, so cycle stealing can slow processor memory accesses. In systems without automatic cache coherence, memory updates made by a DMA device may not immediately appear in a processor’s cached copy; cache maintenance or an uncached buffer policy is then part of correct use. Compute CPU overhead and transfer elapsed time separately because they measure different benefits and costs. An I/O register defines an interaction with a device, including any side effects of reads and writes. The same load/store instruction used for RAM may therefore have a very different meaning at a device address. Read-modify-write is safe only when the register’s semantics permit reading and rewriting unchanged bits. A write-one-to-clear status register illustrates the danger: writing an old one back actively clears that event. Decode register offsets and transfer widths carefully, and preserve alignment when the interface requires full words. Describe which values are addresses, which are control masks and which are returned data. Correct interface use follows its register contract, not a general assumption that every mapped address behaves like ordinary storage.

gateGuide.recognize: Memory-chip construction separates depth from width. I/O questions compare CPU service overhead and shared-bus transfer, not just labels.
method: Expand width with parallel data lanes and depth with selected banks; determine address bits from location count.
For interrupts count handler invocations and any per-event work under the model.
For DMA include setup/completion costs and bus occupancy; controller movement does not eliminate physical transfer time.

traps.why: The CPU configures transfers and handles completion, and DMA can compete for memory bandwidth.

traps.claim: Chip count depends only on bytes
traps.why: Two organizations with the same byte capacity may need different bank/wiring arrangements when depth and width are specified.

example.prompt: Construct 8K×16 from 2K×8 chips.
example.strategy: Width expansion → Depth expansion → Total and addressing

steps.title: Width expansion

steps.title: Depth expansion

steps.title: Total and addressing

example.verification: 8×2048×8 bits equals 8192×16 bits, confirming total capacity.

depth.body: A memory chip’s depth and word width are independent dimensions. Parallel chips widen each addressed word, while banks selected by higher address bits increase the number of locations. Identify whether the CPU addresses bytes or complete words before assigning address pins: byte lanes can use low CPU address bits that never reach the chip’s word-address input. Chip-enable decoding should choose a bank without enabling competing drivers on the same data lane. Partial decoding can cause aliases, where multiple CPU addresses reach the same physical location. Verify an arrangement by multiplying chip count by per-chip bit capacity and by tracing one complete CPU address into bank, chip location and lane selection.

examples.prompt: A chip is specified as 4K×8, with K=1024 and word addressing. Find address-input count and byte capacity.
examples.strategy: Count locations → Find address pins → Convert capacity

steps.title: Count locations
steps.explanation: Depth is the number of independently addressed words.

steps.title: Find address pins
steps.explanation: Twelve binary inputs select one chip word.

steps.title: Convert capacity
steps.explanation: Each word is exactly one byte wide.

examples.answer: Twelve address inputs and 4 KiB of stored data.
examples.verification: 2¹² distinct word addresses each select eight data bits, totaling 32768 bits.

examples.prompt: Construct 16K×32 memory from 4K×8 chips. Find chip count, bank selection and the CPU byte-address width if every byte is addressable.
examples.strategy: Expand width and depth → Count chips and word addresses → Account for byte lanes

steps.title: Expand width and depth
steps.explanation: Each bank uses four parallel chips, and four banks supply depth.

steps.title: Count chips and word addresses
steps.explanation: Twelve bits address within a chip and two select a bank.

steps.title: Account for byte lanes
steps.explanation: Two low byte-address bits identify a lane within each 32-bit word.

examples.answer: Sixteen chips; two bank bits and twelve within-chip address bits; sixteen CPU byte-address bits overall.
examples.verification: 16×4096×8 bits equals 16384×32 bits. Four bytes per word explain the extra two CPU address bits rather than two extra chip depth bits.

examples.prompt: Eight 1K×1 chips share address lines and drive separate data-bit lanes. Does this arrangement create 8K addressable words?
examples.strategy: Identify connection type → Count locations → Count resulting width

steps.title: Identify connection type
steps.explanation: Common address inputs with separate data lanes widen the selected word rather than creating more addresses.

steps.title: Count locations
steps.explanation: All eight chips select the same numbered location simultaneously.

steps.title: Count resulting width
steps.explanation: Together they provide one byte at each of the existing 1024 addresses.

examples.answer: The arrangement is 1K×8, not 8K×1 or 8K words.
examples.verification: There are still only ten address bits, yielding 1024 addresses; total bit capacity is 8192, but bit count is not address count.

tutorials.title: Programmed I/O, interrupts and DMA
tutorials.body:
An I/O interface exposes device data, status and control registers, reached through memory-mapped or separate I/O addressing. Programmed polling repeatedly reads status until the device is ready, then the CPU transfers data. Interrupt-driven I/O lets the device request service, so the CPU can do other work rather than poll continuously; the interrupt handler still performs work and has entry/exit overhead.
DMA allows a controller to transfer a block between device and memory after CPU setup. It needs bus arbitration and can occupy memory bandwidth; the CPU is not necessarily idle or entirely unaffected during transfer. Completion can raise an interrupt. DMA reduces per-unit CPU transfer involvement, not the physical number of bytes moved.
Trace who copies data, who controls the address/count and when the CPU is notified. An interrupt is a control event, not automatically a DMA transfer. Bus stealing can delay CPU memory accesses even while saving software overhead. In performance questions include setup, transfer and completion costs exactly as specified instead of assuming one mode has zero overhead.

example.prompt: Transfer 4096 bytes with one interrupt per byte versus one DMA block completion.
example.strategy: Byte service count → DMA setup → DMA completion

steps.title: Byte service count
steps.explanation: Each byte separately asks the CPU for service.

steps.title: DMA setup
steps.explanation: The CPU supplies starting address, length and direction to the controller.

steps.title: DMA completion
steps.explanation: One block completion notification replaces thousands of byte handlers under this model.

example.answer: DMA greatly reduces CPU service events; all 4096 bytes still cross the transfer path.
example.verification: Saving handler work does not mean the device-to-memory transfer itself took zero time.

depth.body: An interrupt is a control transfer that lets a device or event request processor attention. Servicing requires preserving the interrupted architectural context, identifying and acknowledging the source, performing the required work and restoring execution. Entry latency differs from handler duration: masking or a higher-priority handler can delay entry even when the eventual handler is short. Level-triggered requests remain asserted until the source condition is removed, so returning without acknowledgment can immediately retrigger service. An interrupt does not by itself move an entire data block; software or DMA still performs the transfer. State priority, masking and acknowledgment assumptions when computing response time or counting service events.

examples.prompt: An interrupt is accepted between instructions, with saved next PC=200 and handler entry address 128. After a correct return-from-interrupt, where does execution resume?
examples.strategy: Save the interrupted context → Enter the handler → Restore on return

steps.title: Save the interrupted context
steps.explanation: The next PC=200 identifies the instruction that should execute when service finishes.

steps.title: Enter the handler
steps.explanation: The interrupt vector supplies a temporary control-transfer target, not the continuation address.

steps.title: Restore on return
steps.explanation: Return-from-interrupt restores the saved continuation and required processor state.

examples.answer: Execution resumes at address 200.
examples.verification: The handler’s own last instruction address is unrelated to the saved continuation; restoring 128 would simply reenter the handler.

examples.prompt: An interrupt arrives just after interrupts are masked for a maximum 120 μs critical section. Entry overhead is 8 μs, and the first device-service operation occurs 3 μs after entry. Find worst-case time to first service, assuming no other delays.
examples.strategy: Count masking delay → Include context-entry work → Include handler prefix

steps.title: Count masking delay
steps.explanation: Arrival at the start of the maximum masked interval is the worst case.

steps.title: Include context-entry work
steps.explanation: Service cannot begin before the processor enters the handler.

steps.title: Include handler prefix
steps.explanation: The first service operation follows the specified three-microsecond prefix.

examples.answer: Worst-case time to first device service is 131 μs.
examples.verification: An arrival after the masked interval would need only 11 μs; the extra 120 μs is blocking delay rather than handler execution time.

examples.prompt: A level-triggered device keeps its interrupt line high until its pending flag is acknowledged. A handler returns without clearing that flag. Will there necessarily be only one interrupt?
examples.strategy: Inspect source condition → Restore acceptance → Remove the cause

steps.title: Inspect source condition
steps.explanation: The device’s pending flag remains set, so its request line remains high.

steps.title: Restore acceptance
steps.explanation: After return reenables acceptance, the still-asserted level can again request service.

steps.title: Remove the cause
steps.explanation: The handler must perform the specified device acknowledgment, not merely return or clear a CPU-local entry indicator.

examples.answer: No; the uncleared level can immediately retrigger the handler.
examples.verification: Clearing the pending device flag deasserts the line and prevents repeated service for the same unchanged source condition.

depth.body: DMA separates processor setup from the controller’s repeated data transfers. The controller needs source or destination addresses, length, direction and a valid ownership/coherence protocol. Trace how addresses advance with each transfer beat and distinguish byte counts from word counts. DMA reduces per-byte software work but still consumes bus or memory bandwidth, so cycle stealing can slow processor memory accesses. In systems without automatic cache coherence, memory updates made by a DMA device may not immediately appear in a processor’s cached copy; cache maintenance or an uncached buffer policy is then part of correct use. Compute CPU overhead and transfer elapsed time separately because they measure different benefits and costs.

examples.prompt: A DMA controller copies 12 bytes from source address 400 to destination 800 using four-byte beats and incrementing addresses. List beat addresses.
examples.strategy: Count beats → Trace source progression → Trace destination progression

steps.title: Count beats
steps.explanation: The byte count is exactly divisible by the transfer width.

steps.title: Trace source progression
steps.explanation: The three beats begin at source addresses 400,404 and 408.

steps.title: Trace destination progression
steps.explanation: The matching destinations are 800,804 and 808, covering destination bytes 800 through 811.

examples.verification: Each four-byte beat covers a disjoint range; their union contains exactly twelve source and twelve destination bytes.

examples.prompt: A cycle-stealing DMA reserves 20% of bus cycles. A processor workload continuously needs the bus and previously completed at one memory operation per cycle. Ignore endpoint effects and other bottlenecks; find its steady-state slowdown.
examples.strategy: Allocate remaining bandwidth → Relate work to elapsed cycles → Compute slowdown

steps.title: Allocate remaining bandwidth
steps.explanation: The processor can use only the non-DMA fraction.

steps.title: Relate work to elapsed cycles
steps.explanation: The same operation count now requires more total cycles.

steps.title: Compute slowdown
steps.explanation: DMA saves CPU copying work elsewhere but constrains this bus-bound workload.

examples.answer: The processor workload takes 1.25 times as long in the stated steady-state model.
examples.verification: Across five recurring bus slots, four serve CPU operations and one serves DMA, giving four operations per five cycles rather than one per cycle.

examples.prompt: A noncoherent processor cache holds an old clean copy of a buffer. DMA writes new bytes into main memory. Can the CPU read the buffer immediately and assume it sees the new bytes?
examples.strategy: Locate the DMA update → Follow a cached CPU read → Apply required protocol

steps.title: Locate the DMA update
steps.explanation: The controller changed main memory, while the noncoherent cache received no automatic update.

steps.title: Follow a cached CPU read
steps.explanation: A cache hit can return the old resident bytes without consulting main memory.

steps.title: Apply required protocol
steps.explanation: Use the platform’s cache invalidation/synchronization or a suitable uncached buffer policy before consuming the DMA result.

examples.answer: No; a stale cached copy can hide the new DMA data.
examples.verification: Once the clean stale line is invalidated and the read fetches the updated memory block, the CPU can observe the new bytes; dirty-line cases need additional protocol care.

tutorials.title: Read status and data through a memory-mapped interface
tutorials.body:
An I/O interface provides a defined way for processor instructions to interact with a device. In memory-mapped I/O, some addresses select device registers instead of ordinary RAM. A status register reports conditions such as ready or busy; a data register transfers the payload; a control register may start an operation or select its mode. The instruction still performs a load or store, but the selected device determines what that access means.
Treat device-register semantics as part of the problem specification. Reading a data register can clear a ready flag or consume a queued byte; writing a control register can initiate work. Such accesses may have side effects and cannot generally be reordered or repeated as if they were ordinary memory reads. Polling repeatedly checks status until the specified ready condition holds, then accesses the appropriate data register.
Keep address, register contents and individual status bits separate. A nonzero status value does not necessarily mean the particular ready bit is set, so test the stated mask. Interrupts and DMA change how readiness and transfer work are scheduled, but they still rely on an interface with defined registers or descriptors. Verify a polling trace by explaining which accesses touch status, which consume data, and whether any side effect changes later observations.

example.prompt: A memory-mapped device has STATUS at 0x1000 and DATA at 0x1004. STATUS bit 0 indicates ready. Consecutive STATUS reads return 0x04 then 0x05. When ready, DATA returns 0x41 and reading it clears ready. What does the polling routine obtain?
example.strategy: Test first status → Test second status → Consume data

steps.title: Test first status
steps.explanation: Another status bit is set, but the ready bit is zero, so the routine keeps polling.

steps.title: Test second status
steps.explanation: The ready bit is now set, permitting a DATA read.

steps.title: Consume data
steps.explanation: A load from 0x1004 returns byte 0x41 and clears STATUS bit 0 under the stated interface semantics.

example.answer: The routine obtains 0x41 after two status reads and one data read.
example.verification: 0x04 being nonzero is insufficient to signal ready. The data address 0x1004 differs from its returned contents 0x41, and a second read is not guaranteed to return the same byte after ready is cleared.

depth.body: An I/O register defines an interaction with a device, including any side effects of reads and writes. The same load/store instruction used for RAM may therefore have a very different meaning at a device address. Read-modify-write is safe only when the register’s semantics permit reading and rewriting unchanged bits. A write-one-to-clear status register illustrates the danger: writing an old one back actively clears that event. Decode register offsets and transfer widths carefully, and preserve alignment when the interface requires full words. Describe which values are addresses, which are control masks and which are returned data. Correct interface use follows its register contract, not a general assumption that every mapped address behaves like ordinary storage.

examples.prompt: An ordinary read/write control register is initially 0x02. Set enable bit 3 while preserving other bits; reads have no side effects. Find the written value.
examples.strategy: Build enable mask → Read current control value → Merge requested bit

steps.title: Build enable mask
steps.explanation: Bit numbering starts at zero.

steps.title: Read current control value
steps.explanation: The supplied value 0x02 already has bit 1 set, which must be preserved.

steps.title: Merge requested bit
steps.explanation: OR sets bit 3 without clearing other set bits.

examples.answer: Write 0x0A to the control register.
examples.verification: Binary 00000010 becomes 00001010, changing only the requested enable bit under the stated ordinary read/write semantics.

examples.prompt: A 32-bit memory-mapped interface starts at 0x40000000: CTRL is offset 0, STATUS offset 4 and DATA offset 8. A program adds an offset of two to the base to read DATA. Correct the address and explain the width issue.
examples.strategy: Interpret register offsets → Calculate actual data address → Diagnose the shortcut

steps.title: Interpret register offsets
steps.explanation: The interface specifies byte offsets, so DATA is eight bytes from the base.

steps.title: Calculate actual data address
steps.explanation: This is aligned to a four-byte word.

steps.title: Diagnose the shortcut
steps.explanation: Adding two directly gives byte address 0x40000002, which is not DATA. Two register positions must be scaled by four bytes.

examples.answer: Read DATA at 0x40000008, using the interface’s specified 32-bit transfer width.
examples.verification: Register-number two multiplied by four-byte spacing yields offset eight; address low bits 00 confirm full-word alignment.

examples.prompt: A write-one-to-clear STATUS register currently reads 1010. Clear only bit 1. Is writing the read value 1010 back safe?
examples.strategy: Apply register semantics → Construct the requested mask → Compare writeback behavior

steps.title: Apply register semantics
steps.explanation: A written one clears its corresponding pending bit; zero leaves that bit unchanged.

steps.title: Construct the requested mask
steps.explanation: Only the requested bit should receive a clearing one.

steps.title: Compare writeback behavior
steps.explanation: Writing 1010 would clear both bits 3 and 1, losing the separate event at bit 3.

examples.answer: Write 0010; ordinary read-modify-write using the whole read value is unsafe here.
examples.verification: Under write-one-to-clear semantics, 1010 AND NOT 0010 gives remaining status 1000, whereas writing 1010 would give 0000.

lessons.title: Instruction pipelining and hazards
lessons.intuition: Pipelining overlaps different instructions in different stages. It increases completed instructions per unit time, while each individual instruction still passes through every stage. Hazards arise when that ideal overlap would violate resource limits or program dependencies.

sections.title: Ideal timing
sections.body: For k equal-latency stages and n instructions, an initially empty ideal pipeline takes k+n−1 cycles. The first instruction fills the pipeline; each subsequent one then finishes one cycle later. Clock period is determined by the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead, not average stage delay. Unequal stages reduce ideal speedup.

sections.title: Data and structural hazards
sections.body: A structural hazard occurs when simultaneous operations need the same unavailable resource. A RAW dependency requires a consumer to receive the producer’s value; forwarding can route it before register writeback. A load-use pair can still stall if data arrives after the consumer needs it. WAR and WAW are naming/order hazards relevant to designs that reorder reads or writes; simple in-order pipelines handle them differently.

sections.title: Control hazards
sections.body: A branch may make fetched instructions wrong-path work. Waiting, predicting, or delayed-branch mechanisms handle this in different models. A misprediction flushes invalid instructions and adds cycles. To compute effective CPI, add expected stall cycles per instruction from hazards without double-counting overlapping penalties.

examples.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline runs 12 instructions with 3 total stall cycles

steps.title: Count the ideal cycles
steps.explanation: The first instruction needs five cycles. Each remaining instruction adds one cycle in this single-issue, balanced-stage model.

steps.title: Include stalls
steps.explanation: The question supplies total actual stalls, so add them once. They are not three stalls per instruction.

steps.title: Convert cycles to time
steps.explanation: Pipeline overlap changes instruction throughput; multiplying every instruction by all five stage times would erase that overlap.

examples.given: Five stages; 12 instructions; three actual stall cycles; cycle time 2 ns.
examples.goal: Find elapsed time including fill and drain.
examples.strategy: Count pipeline cycles before multiplying by the cycle duration.
examples.answer: 19 cycles, 38 ns.
examples.verification: With one instruction and no stalls the same formula gives five cycles, matching its complete path through the stages.

examples.prompt: A branch frequency is 20%, misprediction rate 10%, penalty 3 cycles
steps: Mispredictions per instruction=\(0.2\cdot0.1=0.02\).
Expected additional CPI=\(0.02\cdot3=0.06\).
If baseline CPI is 1 and there are no other stalls, effective CPI=1.06.

pitfalls: Dependency does not automatically mean a stall if forwarding meets timing.
Pipeline speedup is not simply stage count for short sequences.
revision: Clock period follows the slowest stage.

checks.prompt: Does a RAW dependency necessarily cause a stall?
checks.hint: Distinguish logical dependency from timing availability.
checks.explanation: Forwarding can resolve many RAW dependencies without a stall. A load-use timing gap may still require one in the specified pipeline.
options: No; forwarding may deliver the value on time

checks.prompt: A sequence ideally needs 20 cycles and adds 4 nonoverlapping stalls. What is its total?
checks.hint: Add actual stalls once.
checks.explanation: 20+4=24 cycles.

lessons.concept: Pipelining overlaps different instructions in different stages. It increases completed instructions per unit time, while each individual instruction still passes through every stage. Hazards arise when that ideal overlap would violate resource limits or program dependencies.
lessons.method:
A pipeline partitions instruction processing into stages and overlaps different instructions at those stages. It improves throughput without necessarily reducing an individual instruction’s latency. With k balanced stages and n instructions in an initially empty ideal single-issue pipeline, completion takes k+n−1 cycles: the first instruction uses k and each later one adds one.
The clock period must accommodate the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead. Dividing unpipelined work into k stages does not guarantee k-fold speedup when delays are unbalanced, n is small or overhead matters. Fill/drain effects are significant for short sequences, while long ideal sequences approach one instruction per cycle.
Stalls insert bubbles and increase elapsed cycles. Flushes discard incorrectly fetched work and can add costs. Count actual extra cycles once under the stated model; do not multiply a total stall count by every instruction. GATE questions may ask cycles, nanoseconds, throughput or speedup, so convert only after deciding which quantity the model gives. A structural hazard arises when overlapping instructions require the same unavailable resource. A data hazard arises when an instruction needs a value before the producing instruction can supply it. A control hazard arises when the next instruction address depends on an unresolved branch. These categories describe causes; bubbles, duplication and prediction are remedies with specific limits.
Forwarding bypasses a value from a producing stage to a consuming stage without waiting for register-file writeback. It cannot send a value before it exists, so a load-use dependency may still need a stall when memory data arrives too late. In a basic in-order pipeline, common operand dependencies are read-after-write; other hazard types depend on ordering and execution structure.
For branches, a misprediction flushes wrong-path work. Expected added CPI can be branch fraction times conditional misprediction fraction times penalty cycles, provided costs are modeled without overlap. Trace stage timing before asserting that forwarding eliminates every dependency stall, and distinguish branch frequency from misprediction frequency among branches. Forwarding routes an instruction’s newly produced result directly to a later instruction’s operand input, bypassing register-file writeback. In a five-stage IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB pipeline, an ALU instruction normally produces its result at the end of EX. The next instruction can use that value at EX in the following cycle through an EX/MEM bypass. This removes a read-after-write delay only when the required value exists before the consumer uses it.
A load produces its data at the end of MEM. An immediately following instruction would reach EX in that same cycle, too early to use a value that arrives only at its end. Under this conventional timing model, one stall holds the consumer in ID and inserts an EX bubble. The consumer then uses the loaded data in EX during the next cycle via forwarding. The pipeline’s exact bypass paths and timing assumptions must be specified before counting stalls.
Draw a stage trace, mark when each producer generates its result and when each consumer needs it, then delay only dependencies that lack a timely path. Later ALU-to-ALU dependencies may still need no extra bubble after a load-use stall. Total cycles equal ideal fill-and-drain cycles plus actual inserted stall cycles; a forwarding benefit should never be assumed to create a value earlier than its producing stage. For k equal-latency stages and n instructions, an initially empty ideal pipeline takes k+n−1 cycles. The first instruction fills the pipeline; each subsequent one then finishes one cycle later. Clock period is determined by the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead, not average stage delay. Unequal stages reduce ideal speedup. A structural hazard occurs when simultaneous operations need the same unavailable resource. A RAW dependency requires a consumer to receive the producer’s value; forwarding can route it before register writeback. A load-use pair can still stall if data arrives after the consumer needs it. WAR and WAW are naming/order hazards relevant to designs that reorder reads or writes; simple in-order pipelines handle them differently. A branch may make fetched instructions wrong-path work. Waiting, predicting, or delayed-branch mechanisms handle this in different models. A misprediction flushes invalid instructions and adds cycles. To compute effective CPI, add expected stall cycles per instruction from hazards without double-counting overlapping penalties. Pipelining overlaps stages from different instructions; it does not make one instruction skip its stages. Determine the clock from the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead, then count fill, successive issues and any inserted bubbles. In a finite sequence, the first completion pays the whole stage count, so short workloads do not reach the ideal asymptotic throughput. Comparing against an unpipelined machine requires an explicit serial latency and the same workload. Extra stages may improve combinational balance while adding register overhead and branch recovery cost. Report whether a question asks total completion time, individual latency or steady-state completion interval, since these quantities can move in different directions. A hazard is a timing conflict in overlapping execution, not necessarily an incorrect instruction ordering in the program. Structural hazards contend for a resource, data hazards need a not-yet-available value, and control hazards depend on an unresolved next PC. Remedies must match the cause: duplicating memory ports does not supply an unavailable register value, and forwarding does not resolve a branch direction by itself. Draw stage occupancy and mark the stage where data is required under the implementation’s rules. Simple in-order pipelines with fixed read and write stages avoid some hazards that out-of-order machines must handle. State register-file half-cycle behavior, memory-port count and bypass paths before converting a dependence into a stall count. A branch changes control flow according to an instruction-defined condition and target computation. Prediction selects a provisional direction or target before resolution; its correctness is measured against the eventual architectural decision. A saturating predictor is a small state machine, so trace prediction from the old counter state before updating it with the actual outcome. A wrong prediction can flush younger work, but those wrong-path instructions do not become additional retired program instructions. Their cost appears as lost cycles under the recovery model. Distinguish taken rate, branch frequency and misprediction rate, and state the branch-resolution stage and prediction policy before inferring either the number of discarded instructions or the penalty. Forwarding chooses the youngest preceding instruction that has produced the required operand in time for the consumer. Matching a register number is necessary but not sufficient: the producer must actually write that register, its value must be ready and the selected bypass must reach the consuming stage. When multiple older instructions target the same register, a nearer valid result must take priority over a stale farther result. A scheduling gap can eliminate a load-use stall because memory finishes before the later consumer reaches EX. These examples assume a five-stage in-order pipeline, ALU results at the end of EX and load data at the end of MEM; same-cycle end results cannot be consumed at the beginning of EX.
lessons.example: A 5-stage pipeline runs 12 instructions with 3 total stall cycles

gateGuide.recognize: Pipeline timing requires fill, steady-state work and actual hazards. Read whether stage delays are equal and whether forwarding is available.
method: Find the clock period from the slowest stage plus register overhead; do not use average stage delay.
Count ideal fill/drain cycles, then add specified nonoverlapping stalls/flushes.
For branch CPI multiply branch frequency, conditional misprediction rate and penalty; a dependency stalls only if data cannot arrive on time.

traps.claim: Every dependency causes one stall
traps.why: Forwarding can remove stalls for ALU chains, while a load-use pair may still require waiting under the timing model.

traps.claim: Throughput improvement means equal latency reduction
traps.why: An instruction still traverses every stage; pipelining overlaps different instructions rather than skipping stages.

formulas.meaning: Initially empty k-stage ideal pipeline for n instructions.
Expected branch penalty with nonoverlapping modelled costs.

tutorials.title: Pipeline fill, steady throughput and drain

example.prompt: Four stages each clocked at 3 ns run ten instructions without stalls.
example.strategy: Ideal cycles → Elapsed time → Single instruction latency

steps.title: Ideal cycles
steps.explanation: Include first-instruction fill.

steps.title: Elapsed time
steps.explanation: Every cycle has the stated period.

steps.title: Single instruction latency
steps.explanation: This differs from the steady completion interval of 3 ns.

example.answer: Total 39 ns; individual ideal latency 12 ns.
example.verification: For n=1 the same formula gives four cycles, establishing that pipeline fill was included.

depth.body: Pipelining overlaps stages from different instructions; it does not make one instruction skip its stages. Determine the clock from the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead, then count fill, successive issues and any inserted bubbles. In a finite sequence, the first completion pays the whole stage count, so short workloads do not reach the ideal asymptotic throughput. Comparing against an unpipelined machine requires an explicit serial latency and the same workload. Extra stages may improve combinational balance while adding register overhead and branch recovery cost. Report whether a question asks total completion time, individual latency or steady-state completion interval, since these quantities can move in different directions.

examples.prompt: Three pipeline stages have logic delays 2,5,3 ns; every pipeline register contributes 1 ns overhead. Find clock period, single-instruction latency and ideal completion interval.
examples.strategy: Find slowest stage → Count one instruction’s stages → Use ideal steady issue

steps.title: Find slowest stage
steps.explanation: All stages share a clock that accommodates the largest stage plus register overhead.

steps.title: Count one instruction’s stages
steps.explanation: The instruction advances through three separate cycles.

steps.title: Use ideal steady issue
steps.explanation: After filling, one instruction can complete every 6 ns in a balanced single-issue schedule without stalls.

examples.answer: Clock=6 ns; individual latency=18 ns; ideal steady completion interval=6 ns.
examples.verification: The 2 ns and 3 ns stages wait for the common clock boundary; summing only their logic delays would ignore stage quantization and overhead.

examples.prompt: A four-stage pipeline clocks at 2 ns and runs 20 instructions from empty, with three total bubble cycles. An unpipelined machine takes 8 ns per instruction. Find time and speedup.
examples.strategy: Count ideal and stalled cycles → Convert pipeline time → Compare complete serial workload

steps.title: Count ideal and stalled cycles
steps.explanation: Add pipeline fill and the actual total bubbles once.

steps.title: Convert pipeline time
steps.explanation: Every scheduled cycle uses the specified clock.

steps.title: Compare complete serial workload
steps.explanation: Both times include all twenty instructions.

examples.answer: Pipeline time=52 ns; speedup=40/13≈3.077.
examples.verification: With no bubbles the run would need 23 cycles; the three extra cycles add 6 ns rather than three penalties per instruction.

examples.prompt: A 10 ns operation is split first into five balanced stages, then ten balanced stages. Register overhead is 1 ns in each design. Does doubling stages double steady throughput?
examples.strategy: Compute five-stage period → Compute ten-stage period → Compare throughputs

steps.title: Compute five-stage period
steps.explanation: The overhead is added to the two-nanosecond logic slice.

steps.title: Compute ten-stage period
steps.explanation: One nanosecond of logic still pays one nanosecond of register overhead.

steps.title: Compare throughputs
steps.explanation: Throughput improves by 1.5, not two, even before hazards.

examples.answer: No; ideal steady throughput improves by only 1.5 under these delays.
examples.verification: Single-instruction latency also rises from 5×3=15 ns to 10×2=20 ns, showing why stage count alone does not determine all performance measures.
