Expected added CPI can be branch fraction times conditional misprediction fraction times penalty cycles, provided costs are modeled without overlap. Trace stage timing before asserting that forwarding eliminates every dependency stall, and distinguish branch frequency from misprediction frequency among branches.

example.prompt: Base CPI 1; branches 25%, prediction wrong on 20% of branches, penalty 4 cycles.
example.strategy: Mispredictions per instruction → Added cycles per instruction → Effective CPI

steps.title: Mispredictions per instruction
steps.explanation: The two probabilities refer to different populations.

steps.title: Added cycles per instruction
steps.explanation: Multiply conditional event frequency by penalty.

steps.title: Effective CPI
steps.explanation: No other stalls are assumed.

example.answer: Effective CPI 1.2.
example.verification: Applying the 20% rate to all instructions would overcount because only one quarter are branches.

depth.body: A hazard is a timing conflict in overlapping execution, not necessarily an incorrect instruction ordering in the program. Structural hazards contend for a resource, data hazards need a not-yet-available value, and control hazards depend on an unresolved next PC. Remedies must match the cause: duplicating memory ports does not supply an unavailable register value, and forwarding does not resolve a branch direction by itself. Draw stage occupancy and mark the stage where data is required under the implementation’s rules. Simple in-order pipelines with fixed read and write stages avoid some hazards that out-of-order machines must handle. State register-file half-cycle behavior, memory-port count and bypass paths before converting a dependence into a stall count.

examples.prompt: In a five-stage IF,ID,EX,MEM,WB pipeline, one shared single-port memory serves both instruction fetch and load/store access. I₁ is a load; can I₄ fetch in cycle 4 without a conflict?
examples.strategy: Locate load access → Locate younger fetch → Apply resource limit

steps.title: Locate load access
steps.explanation: With no earlier stalls, I₁ is in MEM during cycle 4 and requests the memory port.

steps.title: Locate younger fetch
steps.explanation: I₄ would normally enter IF in that same cycle and request the same port.

steps.title: Apply resource limit
steps.explanation: One port cannot service both requests simultaneously, so the schedule needs a structural stall or a separate memory resource.

examples.answer: No; the two requests create a structural hazard in cycle 4.
examples.verification: The registers may be independent and there may be full data forwarding; neither change removes this physical memory-port conflict.

examples.prompt: A five-stage pipeline has no forwarding. Registers write in the first half of WB and read in the second half of ID. Trace ADD r1,r2,r3 followed by SUB r4,r1,r5, starting empty.
examples.strategy: Trace producer → Hold consumer until writeback → Complete consumer

steps.title: Trace producer
steps.explanation: ADD uses IF1,ID2,EX3,MEM4,WB5; r1 becomes readable during cycle 5.

steps.title: Hold consumer until writeback
steps.explanation: SUB has IF2 and reaches ID3, but must remain through cycles 3 and 4 before reading r1 in ID5.

steps.title: Complete consumer
steps.explanation: SUB then uses EX6,MEM7,WB8, inserting two bubbles beyond the ideal two-instruction completion at cycle 6.

examples.answer: Two data-hazard stall cycles; final completion is cycle 8.
examples.verification: Five stages and two instructions give six ideal cycles; waiting for the cycle-5 register read adds two, matching the explicit trace.

examples.prompt: In the same fixed-stage in-order pipeline, I₁ reads r2 and younger I₂ later writes r2. Does this create a write-after-read stall?
examples.strategy: Place older read → Place younger write → Compare temporal order

steps.title: Place older read
steps.explanation: I₁ reads its register operands in ID, normally cycle 2 when it starts at IF1.

steps.title: Place younger write
steps.explanation: I₂ writes only in its later WB stage, normally cycle 6 when it starts at IF2.

steps.title: Compare temporal order
steps.explanation: The older read already occurred before the younger write, preserving the required old value without a WAR stall.

examples.answer: No WAR stall is needed in this stated fixed-stage in-order model.
examples.verification: The apparent register name overlap is real, but the stage ordering guarantees read-before-write; a reordered implementation could require additional handling.

depth.body: A branch changes control flow according to an instruction-defined condition and target computation. Prediction selects a provisional direction or target before resolution; its correctness is measured against the eventual architectural decision. A saturating predictor is a small state machine, so trace prediction from the old counter state before updating it with the actual outcome. A wrong prediction can flush younger work, but those wrong-path instructions do not become additional retired program instructions. Their cost appears as lost cycles under the recovery model. Distinguish taken rate, branch frequency and misprediction rate, and state the branch-resolution stage and prediction policy before inferring either the number of discarded instructions or the penalty.

examples.prompt: A four-byte branch at byte address 40 uses next-PC-relative byte offset +12. It branches when r1=0, and r1 is currently zero. Find next architectural PC.
examples.strategy: Evaluate condition → Choose reference PC → Apply byte offset

steps.title: Evaluate condition
steps.explanation: The instruction’s stated condition is true.

steps.title: Choose reference PC
steps.explanation: The four-byte branch’s next instruction begins four bytes after address 40.

steps.title: Apply byte offset
steps.explanation: A taken branch selects the computed target rather than fall-through 44.

examples.answer: The next architectural PC is 56.
examples.verification: The target is twelve bytes beyond the supplied next-PC reference; a false condition would instead select address 44.

examples.prompt: A two-bit saturating predictor uses 00,01 to predict not-taken and 10,11 to predict taken. It starts at 01, increments on taken and decrements on not-taken. Trace actual outcomes T,T,N,T.
examples.strategy: Predict before first update → Process the opposite outcome → Finish and count

steps.title: Predict before first update
steps.explanation: State 01 predicts N, so the first T misses and increments to 10; state 10 then correctly predicts the second T and becomes 11.

steps.title: Process the opposite outcome
steps.explanation: State 11 predicts T for the third outcome N, misses, and decrements to 10.

steps.title: Finish and count
steps.explanation: State 10 correctly predicts the final T and becomes 11. Two of the four predictions were wrong.

examples.answer: Predictions are N,T,T,T; mispredictions=2/4=50%; final state=11.
examples.verification: Counter states after outcomes are 10,11,10,11. Predictions use their preceding states, preventing the common error of predicting after updating.

examples.prompt: A branch resolves at end of EX in a five-stage pipeline, flushing two younger wrong-path instructions in IF and ID. Should those two instructions increase the program’s retired instruction count?
examples.strategy: Identify discarded work → Define retired instruction count → Account for performance cost

steps.title: Identify discarded work
steps.explanation: The younger IF/ID instructions belong to the incorrectly predicted path and are canceled before architectural completion.

steps.title: Define retired instruction count
steps.explanation: Only instructions that complete on the architectural execution path count toward the executed program’s retired instruction total.

steps.title: Account for performance cost
steps.explanation: The lost fetch/decode work contributes recovery cycles under the specified pipeline model, rather than two extra retired instructions.

examples.answer: No; the flushed instructions add recovery cost but do not count as retired program instructions.
examples.verification: An architectural instruction trace excludes the canceled operations, while a cycle trace records their wasted pipeline occupancy; the two measurements intentionally differ.

tutorials.title: Trace forwarding and the unavoidable load-use bubble
tutorials.body:
Forwarding routes an instruction’s newly produced result directly to a later instruction’s operand input, bypassing register-file writeback. In a five-stage IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB pipeline, an ALU instruction normally produces its result at the end of EX. The next instruction can use that value at EX in the following cycle through an EX/MEM bypass. This removes a read-after-write delay only when the required value exists before the consumer uses it.
A load produces its data at the end of MEM. An immediately following instruction would reach EX in that same cycle, too early to use a value that arrives only at its end. Under this conventional timing model, one stall holds the consumer in ID and inserts an EX bubble. The consumer then uses the loaded data in EX during the next cycle via forwarding. The pipeline’s exact bypass paths and timing assumptions must be specified before counting stalls.
Draw a stage trace, mark when each producer generates its result and when each consumer needs it, then delay only dependencies that lack a timely path. Later ALU-to-ALU dependencies may still need no extra bubble after a load-use stall. Total cycles equal ideal fill-and-drain cycles plus actual inserted stall cycles; a forwarding benefit should never be assumed to create a value earlier than its producing stage.

example.prompt: Use a five-stage, single-issue in-order pipeline with full EX-input forwarding. ALU results are ready at end of EX, loads at end of MEM; data cannot arrive and be consumed in the same cycle. Trace LW r1,0(r0); ADD r2,r1,r3; SUB r4,r2,r5 from an empty pipeline.
example.strategy: Trace the load → Insert load-use stall → Forward the ALU result → Count completion

steps.title: Trace the load
steps.explanation: LW uses IF1, ID2, EX3, MEM4 and WB5. Its r1 value becomes available only at the end of cycle 4.

steps.title: Insert load-use stall
steps.explanation: ADD has IF2 and ID3, stays in ID during cycle 4, then uses EX5, MEM6 and WB7. The bubble prevents its planned EX4 from reading r1 before it exists.

steps.title: Forward the ALU result
steps.explanation: SUB has IF3, is held during cycle 4, then ID5, EX6, MEM7 and WB8. ADD produces r2 at the end of EX5, so EX/MEM forwarding supplies SUB in EX6 without another stall.

steps.title: Count completion
steps.explanation: Three instructions need seven ideal cycles plus the single load-use bubble.

example.answer: One stall; final completion is cycle 8. LW→ADD uses load-data forwarding after the bubble, and ADD→SUB uses ALU-result forwarding without a second bubble.
example.verification: Without the bubble, ADD would require r1 during EX4 while LW only produces it at the end of MEM4. With the bubble, ADD’s EX5 and SUB’s EX6 each have their input value available beforehand.

depth.body: Forwarding chooses the youngest preceding instruction that has produced the required operand in time for the consumer. Matching a register number is necessary but not sufficient: the producer must actually write that register, its value must be ready and the selected bypass must reach the consuming stage. When multiple older instructions target the same register, a nearer valid result must take priority over a stale farther result. A scheduling gap can eliminate a load-use stall because memory finishes before the later consumer reaches EX. These examples assume a five-stage in-order pipeline, ALU results at the end of EX and load data at the end of MEM; same-cycle end results cannot be consumed at the beginning of EX.

examples.prompt: With full EX-input forwarding, trace ADD r1,r2,r3; SUB r4,r1,r5; AND r6,r4,r7 in a five-stage pipeline from empty. ALU results are ready at end of EX.
examples.strategy: Place first production → Forward consecutive dependencies → Count the unstalled run

steps.title: Place first production
steps.explanation: ADD reaches EX3 and produces r1 at the end of cycle 3.

steps.title: Forward consecutive dependencies
steps.explanation: SUB consumes r1 in EX4 and produces r4 at its end; AND consumes that r4 in EX5.

steps.title: Count the unstalled run
steps.explanation: Each result exists before the next instruction’s consuming EX cycle.

examples.answer: No data stalls are needed; the three instructions finish by cycle 7.
examples.verification: The two producer/consumer pairs cross adjacent EX cycles, each with an available EX/MEM forwarding result.

examples.prompt: Trace LW r1,0(r0); ADD r8,r9,r10; AND r2,r1,r3 with full EX-input forwarding. The middle ADD is independent; memory returns load data at end of MEM.
examples.strategy: Trace load readiness → Use the independent gap → Forward the available load

steps.title: Trace load readiness
steps.explanation: LW uses EX3 and MEM4, so r1 exists at the end of cycle 4.

steps.title: Use the independent gap
steps.explanation: The middle ADD uses EX4, while the dependent AND is scheduled for EX5.

steps.title: Forward the available load
steps.explanation: At EX5, load data from the preceding MEM4 is available through the MEM/WB path; no load-use bubble is required.

examples.answer: No data stall is needed; final completion is cycle 7.
examples.verification: The dependent instruction’s EX occurs one cycle after the load’s MEM, unlike an immediately following consumer whose EX would occur too early in cycle 4.

examples.prompt: I₁ and I₂ both write r1, producing values 10 and 20 in EX3 and EX4. I₃ consumes r1 in EX5. Both older pipeline registers match r1; may forwarding choose I₁’s value?
examples.strategy: Identify architectural ordering → Locate ready candidates → Apply priority rule

steps.title: Identify architectural ordering
steps.explanation: I₂ is the most recent preceding write to r1, so I₃ must observe its value 20.

steps.title: Locate ready candidates
steps.explanation: At cycle 5, I₂’s EX/MEM result and I₁’s farther MEM/WB result can both be available.

steps.title: Apply priority rule
steps.explanation: Choose the nearer valid writer I₂ rather than selecting an arbitrary matching register tag.

examples.answer: Forward 20 from I₂; selecting 10 would violate sequential instruction semantics.
examples.verification: Executing the instructions serially leaves r1=20 before I₃, providing an independent reference for the forwarding choice.

name: Programming & Data Structures
description: Build a strong foundation in C and structures

lessons.title: C types, expressions, pointers and memory
lessons.intuition: C exposes the relationship between a value and its storage. A pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the object there. Tracing code requires tracking types, lifetimes and sequencing, rather than assuming every expression has a predictable machine result.

sections.title: Types and evaluation
sections.body: Integer promotions and conversions affect arithmetic. Integer division truncates toward zero; floating operands change division behaviour. Logical AND and logical OR short-circuit, evaluating the right side only when necessary. sizeof measures bytes and normally does not evaluate its operand, except relevant variable-length-array cases. Do not assume int is always four bytes unless the question states the machine model.

sections.title: Pointers and arrays
sections.body: For a pointer p to T, p+1 advances by sizeof(T) bytes within a valid array range. An array expression usually decays to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual in-scope array returns full array size. Function parameters written as arrays are adjusted to pointers. Dereferencing a one-past-the-end pointer is invalid even though forming it is permitted.

sections.title: Lifetime and undefined behaviour
sections.body: Automatic local objects cease to exist after their scope exits; returning their addresses creates dangling pointers. Dynamically allocated storage survives until freed and must be checked for allocation failure. Out-of-bounds accesses and unsequenced conflicting modifications can be undefined behaviour. For such programs, reporting a single numerical output is not a valid analysis.

sections.title: A safe pointer trace
sections.body: Use a table of variable, type, value and referenced object. In the example, a is an array object, p points to its second element, and *p refers to a[1]. After *p=9, the array changes without changing p. Moving p by one advances to a[2]; it does not increase the integer stored at a[1]. A pointer may be formed one past the array, but that location is not an element to dereference. The code deliberately separates updates into sequenced statements to avoid unsequenced modification traps.

examples.prompt: Trace an array with sizeof(int)=4

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: For int a[5], sizeof(a)=5×4=20 bytes while a remains an array in scope. sizeof sees an actual array object in this scope and counts all five elements, with no array-to-pointer conversion.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: If p=&a[1], p+2 points to a[3], advancing 8 bytes. Adding two to an int pointer advances by two int objects, not two bytes. The resulting pointer remains inside the array.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Inside a function f(int a[]), sizeof(a) is pointer size, not 20. An array-form parameter declaration is adjusted to a pointer parameter. Its sizeof therefore uses the platform’s pointer width.

examples.strategy: Track array extent, pointer scaling and parameter adjustment as separate C rules.
examples.answer: Inside a function f(int a[]), sizeof(a) is pointer size, not 20.
examples.verification: From &a[1], two further element positions lead to &a[3]; byte displacement is 2×4=8.

examples.prompt: Evaluate 7/2 versus 7/2.0
steps: 7 and 2 are integer operands, so 7/2 gives 3.
2.0 is floating; 7 is converted and division gives 3.5.
Assigning the first expression to double afterward produces 3.0; conversion does not restore the discarded fraction.

pitfalls: Address arithmetic scales by pointed-to type size.
Do not compute outputs for undefined behaviour.
Assignment target type does not retroactively change integer division.
revision: sizeof(array)=element count×element size in array scope.
C arguments are passed by value; a copied pointer can still mutate its pointee.

checks.prompt: A C function parameter is written int a[]. Inside the function, what is a’s adjusted parameter type?
checks.hint: Array parameter syntax is adjusted.
checks.explanation: The parameter is adjusted to int*. sizeof(a) there measures pointer size, not the original caller array storage.

checks.prompt: In C, what is the value of 9/4 when both operands are int?
checks.hint: Integer division truncates toward zero.
checks.explanation: 9/4 is 2, with remainder 1.

lessons.concept: C exposes the relationship between a value and its storage. A pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the object there. Tracing code requires tracking types, lifetimes and sequencing, rather than assuming every expression has a predictable machine result.
lessons.method:
C expressions are evaluated according to operand types, operator rules and sequencing guarantees. Integer division truncates toward zero; an operation using a floating operand normally performs a floating conversion before arithmetic. Assigning an already computed integer quotient to double converts the truncated result and cannot recover its discarded fraction. Operator precedence determines grouping, not necessarily temporal evaluation order.
Some expressions have undefined behavior, such as accessing beyond an array, signed integer overflow, or certain unsequenced modifications of one object. Undefined behavior does not have one deterministic answer to “trace” across compilers. Implementation-defined behavior instead requires a documented platform choice; unspecified behavior permits several allowed choices. Character and integer widths, signedness and pointer sizes should follow the supplied machine model.
Short-circuit && and || sequence their left operand before a conditionally evaluated right operand. Bitwise & and | do not provide that same control-flow behavior. Parenthesize a complex expression to determine its parse, then analyze conversions and sequencing separately. GATE code problems can test whether a proposed output is even defined, not merely whether arithmetic is correct. An array stores a fixed sequence of contiguous elements of one type. Its index-zero address is the base, and index i lies i times the element width beyond it. In most expressions an array converts to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual array object obtains its entire storage extent rather than pointer size. An array-form function parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter.
A pointer stores an address with a pointed-to type. Adding j advances by j elements, not j raw bytes; subtracting pointers within one array gives an element difference. A one-past pointer may be formed and compared under the language rules but cannot be dereferenced. Access outside the permitted object range is not repaired by memory happening to exist nearby.
Distinguish a pointer variable’s storage from the pointed-to object. Passing a pointer copies the address value, permitting modification of that object, but reassigning the parameter alone does not change the caller’s pointer variable. Track lifetime: pointers to automatic locals become invalid when those objects cease to exist. Array-to-pointer conversion does not imply arrays and pointer variables are identical types. Scope tells where a name is visible; lifetime tells when its object exists. Automatic locals typically exist during a block activation, with a distinct instance in each recursive call. Static-duration objects exist for the program’s execution; a static local keeps its value across calls despite its name having local scope. Dynamically allocated objects persist until released, independent of the block containing the pointer variable.
Uninitialized automatic scalar values are indeterminate, while static-duration objects without explicit initializers are initialized to zero. Allocation failure must be checked before dereferencing a returned pointer. A freed object cannot be validly read just because its former bytes have not visibly changed; double-free and use-after-free are invalid operations.
For tracing, maintain separate objects and name bindings. A local variable shadowing a global accesses a different object unless the code explicitly obtains the global through another means. “Global,” “heap” and “stack” are implementation concepts related to these rules but not a substitute for the language lifetime specification. Function-return questions commonly expose pointers to dead automatic storage rather than a legitimate returned array. A C program executes statements according to its control flow, while expressions compute values used by those statements. A for loop first runs its initialization, then tests its condition before each iteration. After the body, its update expression runs and the condition is tested again. A false initial condition means the body never runs. Variables declared in the loop initializer have that loop's scope.
An if statement chooses its branch from a condition: zero is false and a nonzero scalar value is true. The remainder operator on positive integers is useful for parity tests. A continue in a for loop skips the rest of the current body but still proceeds to the loop update; break instead exits the loop. Confusing these two changes both the trace and the result.
Build a trace table containing the loop variable, condition result, selected branch and persistent accumulator. Update only statements that actually execute. Count the final failed condition separately from successful iterations. For a well-defined C question, derive the output from language rules rather than from one compiler run, and check that all reads use initialized objects. Integer promotions and conversions affect arithmetic. Integer division truncates toward zero; floating operands change division behaviour. Logical AND and logical OR short-circuit, evaluating the right side only when necessary. sizeof measures bytes and normally does not evaluate its operand, except relevant variable-length-array cases. Do not assume int is always four bytes unless the question states the machine model. For a pointer p to T, p+1 advances by sizeof(T) bytes within a valid array range. An array expression usually decays to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual in-scope array returns full array size. Function parameters written as arrays are adjusted to pointers. Dereferencing a one-past-the-end pointer is invalid even though forming it is permitted. Automatic local objects cease to exist after their scope exits; returning their addresses creates dangling pointers. Dynamically allocated storage survives until freed and must be checked for allocation failure. Out-of-bounds accesses and unsequenced conflicting modifications can be undefined behaviour. For such programs, reporting a single numerical output is not a valid analysis. Use a table of variable, type, value and referenced object. In the example, a is an array object, p points to its second element, and *p refers to a[1]. After *p=9, the array changes without changing p. Moving p by one advances to a[2]; it does not increase the integer stored at a[1]. A pointer may be formed one past the array, but that location is not an element to dereference. The code deliberately separates updates into sequenced statements to avoid unsequenced modification traps. Analyze an expression in three passes: determine its grouping, determine the operand types at each operator, then check evaluation and sequencing rules. Parentheses can clarify grouping without imposing an evaluation order between independent operands. Logical operators produce an int truth value of zero or one, whereas bitwise operators combine the individual bits of integer operands. Short-circuit operators also decide whether their right operand executes. Integer promotions happen before arithmetic on narrow types, and assignment can perform a further conversion afterward. Distinguish a legal conversion with a defined wrap from signed overflow or an unsequenced conflicting access; those latter cases do not supply a portable numeric answer. A pointer expression must be interpreted relative to the object and pointed-to type, not merely as an integer address. Keep an alias diagram connecting each pointer variable to its current target. A write through an alias updates that shared object, whereas assigning a new address to the pointer changes only the alias. Pointer differences within one array count elements and already account for element width. The permitted range includes a one-past value for comparison or subtraction, but excludes dereferencing it. A pointer's numeric-looking value cannot establish lifetime or bounds; determine both from the originating object and its allocation before following it. An array type fixes both its element type and extent, and a multidimensional array is an array whose elements are themselves arrays. C lays out each complete inner row contiguously, followed by the next row. Derive offsets from the declared inner extent instead of assuming that two indices contribute equally. Most expression contexts convert an array to its first-element pointer, but sizeof applied directly to an array object uses its complete storage. Array-form parameters are adjusted to pointers, so the same-looking spelling inside a function does not retain the caller's extent. Bounds belong to each subarray as well as to the enclosing object. Use two parallel timelines when reasoning about storage: one for name visibility and another for object existence. Entering a nested block can hide a name without destroying the outer object. Each ordinary function activation creates its own initialized automatic locals, while a static local belongs to one persistent object shared by all activations of that function. Dynamic storage follows explicit allocation and release rather than lexical block entry and exit. Initialization and lifetime must be checked independently; a surviving pointer can outlive its target. Never derive an output by reading a dead object simply because its previous bytes might still occupy the same address. To trace a C program, separate the values of objects from the path of execution. Give every declaration its own object, including a parameter that copies a caller's value. Record a loop's condition before entering its body and its update after completing or continuing the body. Function calls can modify an object through a copied pointer even though ordinary scalar parameters remain independent. Check the control statement's actual rule: switch selects an entry label but falls through subsequent statements until a break or the end. Assume initialized values, valid addresses and arithmetic representable in the stated types before assigning a deterministic result.

gateGuide.recognize: Do not assign a numerical output to undefined behaviour. First determine types, storage lifetime and which object each pointer references.
method: Create a trace table for variables, types, values and pointer targets; use the stated machine-size assumptions.
Evaluate promotions, integer division and short-circuiting before assignment conversions.
Check bounds and lifetime at every dereference, and sequencing for competing updates. Undefined behaviour stops a unique-output analysis.

traps.claim: Assignment to double changes earlier division
traps.why: For double x=7/2, integer division already produced 3, then conversion yields 3.0.

traps.claim: sizeof on an array parameter gives caller array size
traps.why: The parameter is adjusted to a pointer. Actual array scope and adjusted parameter scope differ.

formulas.meaning: Contiguous array addressing in bytes.
Only within the permitted object/one-past range.

example.prompt: Compare double a=7/2; and double b=7/2.0;.
example.strategy: Integer operation → Assignment conversion → Floating operation

steps.title: Integer operation
steps.explanation: Both operands are int, so fractional remainder is discarded.

steps.title: Assignment conversion
steps.explanation: Conversion happens after that division.

steps.title: Floating operation
steps.explanation: The floating operand changes the arithmetic before division.

example.verification: The destination type alone does not determine the earlier subexpression’s arithmetic type.

Parentheses can clarify grouping without imposing an evaluation order between independent operands. Logical operators produce an int truth value of zero or one, whereas bitwise operators combine the individual bits of integer operands. Short-circuit operators also decide whether their right operand executes. Integer promotions happen before arithmetic on narrow types, and assignment can perform a further conversion afterward. Distinguish a legal conversion with a defined wrap from signed overflow or an unsequenced conflicting access; those latter cases do not supply a portable numeric answer.

examples.prompt: For initialized ints x=6 and y=3, find x&y and x&&y.
examples.strategy: Write bit patterns → Apply bitwise AND → Apply logical AND

steps.title: Write bit patterns
steps.explanation: The nonzero values have different sets of one bits.

steps.title: Apply bitwise AND
steps.explanation: Only the shared middle bit survives, giving two.

steps.title: Apply logical AND
steps.explanation: Both operands are true, so the logical result is exactly one.

examples.verification: The bitwise result has value two, while every logical-AND result belongs to {0,1}.

examples.prompt: Trace int x=0,y=5; int z=(x!=0)&&(y/x>1). Does division execute?
examples.strategy: Evaluate the left operand → Use short circuit → Assign the result

steps.title: Evaluate the left operand
steps.explanation: The comparison is false because x is zero.

steps.title: Use short circuit
steps.explanation: Logical AND skips its right operand after a false left operand.

steps.title: Assign the result
steps.explanation: No division occurs, so this expression does not divide by zero.

examples.answer: z=0; x=0 and y=5 remain unchanged.
examples.verification: Replacing && by bitwise & would evaluate the right-side division and lose this protection.

examples.prompt: With eight-bit unsigned char and a 32-bit int, trace unsigned char u=0; u--; Is this signed overflow?
examples.strategy: Promote the operand → Compute before conversion → Store in the narrow unsigned type

steps.title: Promote the operand
steps.explanation: The arithmetic uses int because it can represent all unsigned-char values.

steps.title: Compute before conversion
steps.explanation: This int result is representable and does not overflow.

steps.title: Store in the narrow unsigned type
steps.explanation: The assignment conversion wraps to the unsigned-char range.

examples.answer: u=255; the operation is defined under the supplied widths.
examples.verification: Adding one modulo 256 returns zero, confirming the wrap; no out-of-range signed arithmetic was performed.

tutorials.title: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and bounds
tutorials.body:
An array stores a fixed sequence of contiguous elements of one type. Its index-zero address is the base, and index i lies i times the element width beyond it. In most expressions an array converts to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual array object obtains its entire storage extent rather than pointer size. An array-form function parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter.
A pointer stores an address with a pointed-to type. Adding j advances by j elements, not j raw bytes; subtracting pointers within one array gives an element difference. A one-past pointer may be formed and compared under the language rules but cannot be dereferenced. Access outside the permitted object range is not repaired by memory happening to exist nearby.
Distinguish a pointer variable’s storage from the pointed-to object. Passing a pointer copies the address value, permitting modification of that object, but reassigning the parameter alone does not change the caller’s pointer variable. Track lifetime: pointers to automatic locals become invalid when those objects cease to exist. Array-to-pointer conversion does not imply arrays and pointer variables are identical types.

example.prompt: For int a[5] and sizeof(int)=4, p=&a[1]. Where does p+2 point?
example.strategy: Locate current index → Apply element scaling → Determine target

steps.title: Locate current index
steps.explanation: p refers to element one, not the beginning of the array.

steps.title: Apply element scaling
steps.explanation: Two int-sized steps are eight bytes.

steps.title: Determine target
steps.explanation: The index advances from one to three within bounds.

example.answer: a[3], eight bytes beyond p.
example.verification: Subtracting (p+2)−p yields 2 elements, not 8 bytes.

depth.body: A pointer expression must be interpreted relative to the object and pointed-to type, not merely as an integer address. Keep an alias diagram connecting each pointer variable to its current target. A write through an alias updates that shared object, whereas assigning a new address to the pointer changes only the alias. Pointer differences within one array count elements and already account for element width. The permitted range includes a one-past value for comparison or subtraction, but excludes dereferencing it. A pointer's numeric-looking value cannot establish lifetime or bounds; determine both from the originating object and its allocation before following it.

examples.prompt: For int a[]={10,20,30}, int *p=a,*q=p; execute *q=11; p++; *p=22. Find a and both targets.
examples.strategy: Create aliases → Move only p → Write the new target

steps.title: Create aliases
steps.explanation: Initially p and q both designate a[0]. Writing through q changes a[0] to 11.

steps.title: Move only p
steps.explanation: p++ advances p to a[1]; q still designates a[0].

steps.title: Write the new target
steps.explanation: *p=22 changes a[1], leaving a[2] unchanged.

examples.answer: a=[11,22,30]; p targets a[1], q targets a[0].
examples.verification: Reading *q gives 11 and p−q gives one element, consistent with distinct current targets.

examples.prompt: A valid int a[6] has base byte address 1000 and sizeof(int)=4. p=&a[4], q=&a[1]. Find p−q and their byte separation.
examples.strategy: Locate each address → Subtract typed pointers → Separate byte distance

steps.title: Locate each address
steps.explanation: Scale the two indices by four bytes from the same base.

steps.title: Subtract typed pointers
steps.explanation: C pointer subtraction reports element count within this array.

steps.title: Separate byte distance
steps.explanation: Byte separation is the element count multiplied by element width.

examples.answer: p−q=3 elements; byte separation is 12.
examples.verification: q+3 equals p; multiplying the typed difference by sizeof(int) reproduces the address difference.

examples.prompt: For int a[3], p=a+3. Classify forming p, comparing p==a+3, and reading *p.
examples.strategy: Form the boundary → Compare the boundary → Check dereference

steps.title: Form the boundary
steps.explanation: a+3 is the permitted one-past pointer for this array.

steps.title: Compare the boundary
steps.explanation: Equality comparison with the same one-past expression is valid and true.

steps.title: Check dereference
steps.explanation: There is no a[3] element, so *p cannot be read as an array value.

examples.answer: Formation and comparison are valid; dereferencing p has undefined behavior.
examples.verification: The valid element indices are 0,1,2. Permission to represent the end does not create an additional element.

depth.body: An array type fixes both its element type and extent, and a multidimensional array is an array whose elements are themselves arrays. C lays out each complete inner row contiguously, followed by the next row. Derive offsets from the declared inner extent instead of assuming that two indices contribute equally. Most expression contexts convert an array to its first-element pointer, but sizeof applied directly to an array object uses its complete storage. Array-form parameters are adjusted to pointers, so the same-looking spelling inside a function does not retain the caller's extent. Bounds belong to each subarray as well as to the enclosing object.

examples.prompt: For int a[2][3] at byte address 200 with four-byte ints, locate a[1][2].
examples.strategy: Count complete rows → Add the column → Scale to bytes

steps.title: Count complete rows
steps.explanation: The first index skips one entire row of three ints.

steps.title: Add the column
steps.explanation: Column two is two additional elements within the second row.

steps.title: Scale to bytes
steps.explanation: Multiply the total element offset by the int width.

examples.answer: a[1][2] begins at byte address 220.
examples.verification: The six element addresses are 200,204,208,212,216,220, so the target is the final element.

examples.prompt: On a machine with four-byte ints and eight-byte pointers, compare sizeof a for int a[7] with sizeof b inside void f(int b[7]).
examples.strategy: Use the actual object → Adjust the parameter → Measure that parameter

steps.title: Use the actual object
steps.explanation: a in the caller is an array object containing seven ints.

steps.title: Adjust the parameter
steps.explanation: The array-form parameter b has type pointer to int in the function.

steps.title: Measure that parameter
steps.explanation: sizeof sees a pointer object, not the caller's full array.

examples.answer: The sizes are 28 bytes and 8 bytes.
examples.verification: Changing the caller array extent changes its object size but does not change the adjusted parameter pointer width.

examples.prompt: Given int a[2][3], is a[0][3] a valid way to read a[1][0] because rows are adjacent?
examples.strategy: Identify the inner object → Check its index → Separate layout from permission

steps.title: Identify the inner object
steps.explanation: a[0] is an array containing exactly three ints.

steps.title: Check its index
steps.explanation: Index three is one past that row and cannot be dereferenced.

steps.title: Separate layout from permission
steps.explanation: Contiguous neighboring storage does not extend the first row's indexing bounds.

examples.answer: No: a[0][3] is out of bounds; use a[1][0].
examples.verification: The legitimate column indices in each row are 0 through 2; both indices of a[1][0] obey their extents.

tutorials.title: Scope, lifetime and storage duration in C
tutorials.body:
Scope tells where a name is visible; lifetime tells when its object exists. Automatic locals typically exist during a block activation, with a distinct instance in each recursive call. Static-duration objects exist for the program’s execution; a static local keeps its value across calls despite its name having local scope. Dynamically allocated objects persist until released, independent of the block containing the pointer variable.
Uninitialized automatic scalar values are indeterminate, while static-duration objects without explicit initializers are initialized to zero. Allocation failure must be checked before dereferencing a returned pointer. A freed object cannot be validly read just because its former bytes have not visibly changed; double-free and use-after-free are invalid operations.
For tracing, maintain separate objects and name bindings. A local variable shadowing a global accesses a different object unless the code explicitly obtains the global through another means. “Global,” “heap” and “stack” are implementation concepts related to these rules but not a substitute for the language lifetime specification. Function-return questions commonly expose pointers to dead automatic storage rather than a legitimate returned array.

example.prompt: A function uses static int x=0; then increments and returns x on each call.
example.strategy: Initialization → First call → Second call

steps.title: Initialization
steps.explanation: x is initialized once to zero, not once per call.

steps.title: First call
steps.explanation: The object persists after return.

steps.title: Second call
steps.explanation: The next call sees the previously stored value.

example.answer: The first two returns are 1 and 2.
example.verification: Replacing static with an initialized automatic local would instead restart at zero on every call.

depth.body: Use two parallel timelines when reasoning about storage: one for name visibility and another for object existence. Entering a nested block can hide a name without destroying the outer object. Each ordinary function activation creates its own initialized automatic locals, while a static local belongs to one persistent object shared by all activations of that function. Dynamic storage follows explicit allocation and release rather than lexical block entry and exit. Initialization and lifetime must be checked independently; a surviving pointer can outlive its target. Never derive an output by reading a dead object simply because its previous bytes might still occupy the same address.

examples.prompt: A global int x=5 is shadowed by int x=2 inside a block; the block increments its x once. What values exist inside and after the block?
examples.strategy: Create separate objects → Execute the local increment → Leave the scope

steps.title: Create separate objects
steps.explanation: The block declaration creates a new automatic x while the global x remains five.

steps.title: Execute the local increment
steps.explanation: The visible name binds to the local object, so the global is untouched.

steps.title: Leave the scope
steps.explanation: The local lifetime ends and the outer binding becomes visible again.

examples.answer: Inside the block local x=3; afterward global x=5.
examples.verification: Only one assignment targeted the local object; no statement named the hidden global during the block.

examples.prompt: In f(n), execute int local=n; static int s=0; s+=n; if(n>0) f(n−1); then print(local,s). Trace f(2), with s initially zero.
examples.strategy: Descend with separate locals → Print the deepest frame → Resume callers

steps.title: Descend with separate locals
steps.explanation: Frames retain local values 2,1,0 while their additions make shared s=3.

steps.title: Print the deepest frame
steps.explanation: f(0) prints (0,3); its local disappears on return.

steps.title: Resume callers
steps.explanation: f(1) prints (1,3), then f(2) prints (2,3), because s belongs to one persistent object.

examples.answer: Printed pairs are (0,3),(1,3),(2,3).
examples.verification: The shared sum is independently 2+1+0=3, while each retained local still equals its own argument.

examples.prompt: int *make(void){int a=6; return &a;} Can the caller safely read *make()?
examples.strategy: Locate the target → End its lifetime → Classify the read

steps.title: Locate the target
steps.explanation: a is an automatic local object belonging to make's activation.

steps.title: End its lifetime
steps.explanation: Returning ends that activation and a's lifetime; returning its address does not extend it.

steps.title: Classify the read
steps.explanation: The caller has no live pointed-to object from which to obtain six.

examples.answer: No; dereferencing that returned address is invalid and has no defined result.
examples.verification: A static local or suitably managed dynamically allocated object would have a different lifetime; this automatic a does not.

tutorials.title: C control flow: trace the loop and each branch
tutorials.body:
A C program executes statements according to its control flow, while expressions compute values used by those statements. A for loop first runs its initialization, then tests its condition before each iteration. After the body, its update expression runs and the condition is tested again. A false initial condition means the body never runs. Variables declared in the loop initializer have that loop's scope.
An if statement chooses its branch from a condition: zero is false and a nonzero scalar value is true. The remainder operator on positive integers is useful for parity tests. A continue in a for loop skips the rest of the current body but still proceeds to the loop update; break instead exits the loop. Confusing these two changes both the trace and the result.
Build a trace table containing the loop variable, condition result, selected branch and persistent accumulator. Update only statements that actually execute. Count the final failed condition separately from successful iterations. For a well-defined C question, derive the output from language rules rather than from one compiler run, and check that all reads use initialized objects.

example.prompt: Trace: int total=0; for (int i=1; i<=4; ++i) { if (i%2==0) continue; total+=i; } printf("%d",total); Assume printf is declared.
example.strategy: Initialize and visit one → Skip even iterations → Visit three → Terminate and print

steps.title: Initialize and visit one
steps.explanation: The condition is true and the odd branch reaches the addition.

steps.title: Skip even iterations
steps.explanation: The remainder is zero, so continue skips addition but does not skip ++i.

steps.title: Visit three
steps.explanation: The next odd iteration adds three to the value retained from the first iteration.

steps.title: Terminate and print
steps.explanation: The failed condition exits the loop; the printed accumulator is four.

example.answer: The program prints 4.
example.verification: The executed additions are exactly 1 and 3. Counting two successful additions separately from four loop iterations confirms the result.

depth.body: To trace a C program, separate the values of objects from the path of execution. Give every declaration its own object, including a parameter that copies a caller's value. Record a loop's condition before entering its body and its update after completing or continuing the body. Function calls can modify an object through a copied pointer even though ordinary scalar parameters remain independent. Check the control statement's actual rule: switch selects an entry label but falls through subsequent statements until a break or the end. Assume initialized values, valid addresses and arithmetic representable in the stated types before assigning a deterministic result.

examples.prompt: Trace int x=3,s=0; while(x>0){s+=x; --x;} What are final x and s?
examples.strategy: First iteration → Remaining iterations → Stop

steps.title: First iteration
steps.explanation: The initial true condition permits addition before decrement.

steps.title: Remaining iterations
steps.explanation: The next bodies use x=2 and x=1, then leave x=0.

steps.title: Stop
steps.explanation: The condition is checked again without executing another body.

examples.answer: x=0 and s=6.
examples.verification: The accumulator equals the independent sum 1+2+3; there are three decrements.

examples.prompt: void change(int v,int *p){v=9; *p=7;} Called as change(x,&a[0]) with x=2 and a=[4,5], what remains?
examples.strategy: Bind arguments → Execute assignments → Return

steps.title: Bind arguments
steps.explanation: v copies x=2; p copies the address of a[0].

steps.title: Execute assignments
steps.explanation: v=9 changes the local parameter. Writing *p=7 changes the caller's array element.

steps.title: Return
steps.explanation: The local v disappears while x and a remain live in the caller.

examples.verification: Only a[0] was reachable through p; neither x nor a[1] was assigned by the function.

examples.prompt: Trace int y=0; switch(2){case 1:y+=1; case 2:y+=2; case 3:y+=3; break; default:y=9;}
examples.strategy: Select entry → Follow fallthrough → Exit at break

steps.title: Select entry
steps.explanation: The controlling value is two, so execution starts at case 2.

steps.title: Follow fallthrough
steps.explanation: Without a break after case 2, case 3 also executes.

steps.title: Exit at break
steps.explanation: The break leaves the switch before default, whose statement is never reached.

examples.answer: y=5, rather than 2 or 9.
examples.verification: The executed additions are exactly +2 and +3; case labels themselves do not end a branch.

lessons.title: Recursion and stack-frame tracing
lessons.intuition: A recursive call is another invocation with its own local state. You can reason inductively about the returned value or mechanically trace stack frames. Both require knowing where recursion stops and how an argument gets closer to that base case.

sections.title: Call and return model
sections.body: Each call creates a frame with parameters, locals and return information. A recursive call suspends its caller until it returns. For factorial, fact(n) waits for fact(n−1), then multiplies. Statements before recursion run on descent; statements after recursion run during unwinding. Shared global state differs from per-frame locals.

sections.title: Correctness and termination
sections.body: State a base case and a decreasing measure bounded below, such as remaining input length. An induction proof assumes smaller calls work and verifies the current combination. Recursion over graph edges needs a visited set when cycles are possible; merely calling neighbours is not guaranteed to terminate.

sections.title: Time versus space
sections.body: Count the total calls for time and maximum simultaneous active frames for stack space. Factorial takes \(\Theta(n)\) time and \(\Theta(n)\) stack. A balanced divide recursion can take \(\Theta(n)\) total work but \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack depth. Naive Fibonacci revisits subproblems exponentially; memoization stores repeated results and reduces time to \(\Theta(n)\).

sections.title: A recursion template you can trace
sections.body: The base case returns before making another call. For n>0, n−1 is a smaller nonnegative input, so the decreasing argument guarantees reaching zero. The multiplication waits for the child call to return. This mathematical template assumes the answer fits in the return type: a real C implementation can overflow for sufficiently large n, and the allowed range must be part of its contract.

examples.prompt: Trace f(n): if n=0 return; print n; f(n−1); print n, starting at 2

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Call f(2) prints 2, then calls f(1), which prints 1. The first print occurs before recursion, so descending calls produce decreasing values.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: f(0) immediately returns; f(1) then prints 1. The base case prints nothing. Returning resumes f(1) after its call statement, rather than restarting the function.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: f(2) resumes and prints 2, giving 2,1,1,2. The final print belongs to the suspended outer frame; it runs only after the inner call has completed.

examples.strategy: Maintain one program position per active call and resume after the recursive call returns.
examples.answer: f(2) resumes and prints 2, giving 2,1,1,2.
examples.verification: Each nonbase call prints twice. Two such calls give four values, and the before/after arrangement makes 2,1,1,2 symmetric.

examples.prompt: Count calls in factorial(4) with base factorial(0)
steps: The active call chain is 4→3→2→1→0.
There are 5 calls and maximum stack depth 5 under this model.
Unwinding returns 1,1,2,6,24. Do not count only the 4 multiplications as the number of calls.

pitfalls: Count base-case invocations too.
Total call count and stack depth need not have the same asymptotic size.
revision: Recursion needs a base case and progress.
Time counts work; stack space counts the deepest active chain.

checks.prompt: Which determines auxiliary recursive stack use?
checks.hint: Frames are released when calls finish.
checks.explanation: Stack space follows simultaneously active frames. Many sequential recursive calls may reuse storage, so total calls alone does not give stack size.
options: Maximum simultaneous call depth and per-frame storage

checks.prompt: A recurrence T(n)=T(n−1)+1 has T(0)=1. What is T(8)?
checks.hint: One unit is added for each level.

lessons.concept: A recursive call is another invocation with its own local state. You can reason inductively about the returned value or mechanically trace stack frames. Both require knowing where recursion stops and how an argument gets closer to that base case.
lessons.method:
A recursive function calls itself on smaller or otherwise progressing instances. A base case ends the descent, and a progress measure must guarantee that calls eventually reach it for the permitted input. A recursive call does not replace all state of the caller: each active call retains parameters, locals and a return position until its child returns.
To trace output, separate statements before the recursive call from those after it. Before-call prints occur while descending; after-call prints occur while unwinding. Draw an activation stack and resume each frame after its call statement. Multiple recursive branches execute according to the language’s sequencing, and total calls can greatly exceed maximum simultaneous depth.
A return value flows into the suspended caller’s expression; a print statement and a returned value are different observations. Tail recursion has no remaining work after the recursive call, but C does not generally guarantee elimination of its stack frame. Do not assume constant stack just because a source function is tail-recursive; follow the problem’s implementation model. Recursive complexity counts total work across the whole call tree, while stack space counts the largest simultaneously active path. For one child per call with decreasing n and constant local work, the call tree is a chain and time and depth are linear. For two child calls, the tree can grow exponentially even if each root-to-leaf path has only linear depth.
Write a recurrence from the actual child sizes and nonrecursive work. Count base calls too when the question asks invocations. Memory per frame matters: a recursion of logarithmic depth can still use more than logarithmic space if each frame stores a large array. Sequential child branches typically do not coexist as complete subtrees in memory.
For naive Fibonacci, repeated subproblems cause exponential calls; memoization changes this by storing results. For factorial, a chain down to zero contains n+1 calls but n multiplications. Asymptotic notation and exact counts answer different questions. State whether memory includes the input/output storage and whether the implementation performs tail-call optimization before giving an auxiliary-space bound. Each call creates a frame with parameters, locals and return information. A recursive call suspends its caller until it returns. For factorial, fact(n) waits for fact(n−1), then multiplies. Statements before recursion run on descent; statements after recursion run during unwinding. Shared global state differs from per-frame locals. State a base case and a decreasing measure bounded below, such as remaining input length. An induction proof assumes smaller calls work and verifies the current combination. Recursion over graph edges needs a visited set when cycles are possible; merely calling neighbours is not guaranteed to terminate. Count the total calls for time and maximum simultaneous active frames for stack space. Factorial takes \(\Theta(n)\) time and \(\Theta(n)\) stack. A balanced divide recursion can take \(\Theta(n)\) total work but \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack depth. Naive Fibonacci revisits subproblems exponentially; memoization stores repeated results and reduces time to \(\Theta(n)\). The base case returns before making another call. For n>0, n−1 is a smaller nonnegative input, so the decreasing argument guarantees reaching zero. The multiplication waits for the child call to return. This mathematical template assumes the answer fits in the return type: a real C implementation can overflow for sufficiently large n, and the allowed range must be part of its contract. A recursive definition becomes an executable algorithm only after its domain, stopping rule and decreasing measure are clear. Track the argument of every child call, not an informal claim that the input becomes smaller. Returned values are combined by the caller after the child finishes; printed effects occur at the exact statement where they are written. Multiple children can represent different subproblems or duplicate the same one. A function's name does not determine its recurrence: changing a child argument changes the mathematics even when the code still terminates. Use small inputs to expose the complete call structure, then check the result against the problem's independent definition. A call stack records pending work, not merely the argument values currently being visited. Each frame retains its own local variables, return location and information needed after its child finishes. Sketch frames from oldest at the bottom to newest at the top, and remove only the frame that returns. Sequential child calls do not keep both completed subtrees on the stack; after the first child returns, its space can be reused by the second. A recursive call does not reset the caller's local variable or mutate it just because a child uses the same name. Maximum simultaneous frames therefore differs from total invocations and from the final value returned. Derive recursive time from the whole invocation tree and recursive space from the maximum live path plus retained allocations. The number and sizes of children determine the recurrence; their execution order determines which frames or buffers coexist. Include base invocations in an exact call count, even if they perform no recursive work. A logarithmic recursion depth does not guarantee logarithmic memory when large buffers remain live. Conversely, exponential invocation count can coexist with only linear stack depth because sibling calls execute sequentially. State whether inputs are powers of two, how small states terminate, and what work the base performs before summing a recursion tree or claiming a tight bound.
lessons.example: Trace f(n): if n=0 return; print n; f(n−1); print n, starting at 2

gateGuide.recognize: Separate descent from return-time work. Trace invocations, not just function names, because each call has its own frame.
method: Write the base case and decreasing measure, then draw the active call chain or tree.
Execute statements before recursion on descent and after recursion while unwinding.
Count total call/work nodes for time, but only the maximum simultaneous active chain for stack space.

traps.claim: Call count equals stack depth
traps.why: A branching recursion may make many sequential calls while retaining only one root-to-leaf chain at a time.

traps.claim: A recursive formula guarantees termination
traps.why: If arguments do not decrease to a valid base case, it may loop or exhaust stack rather than compute the intended sequence.

formulas.meaning: Linear-depth, constant-work-per-frame recurrence.
Stack use follows maximum depth h and frame size.

example.prompt: Trace f(n): if n=0 return; print n; f(n−1); print n, for n=2.
example.strategy: Descend → Base case → Unwind

steps.title: Descend
steps.explanation: f(2) prints 2, and f(1) prints 1 before calling f(0).

steps.title: Base case
steps.explanation: f(0) returns without printing, restoring the suspended f(1).

steps.title: Unwind
steps.explanation: f(1) prints 1; then f(2) prints 2.

example.answer: Output sequence 2,1,1,2.
example.verification: There are two nonbase calls and each prints twice; four values must appear.

depth.body: A recursive definition becomes an executable algorithm only after its domain, stopping rule and decreasing measure are clear. Track the argument of every child call, not an informal claim that the input becomes smaller. Returned values are combined by the caller after the child finishes; printed effects occur at the exact statement where they are written. Multiple children can represent different subproblems or duplicate the same one.
