examples.prompt: Let digitSum(n)=0 if n=0, otherwise n%10+digitSum(n/10), using nonnegative integer division. Evaluate digitSum(123).
examples.strategy: Decompose successive inputs → Return the base value → Combine while returning

steps.title: Decompose successive inputs
steps.explanation: Calls use 123,12,1,0, retaining final digits 3,2,1 in the callers.

steps.title: Return the base value
steps.explanation: The descent stops instead of recursing on zero again.

steps.title: Combine while returning
steps.explanation: Each caller adds its saved digit to the returned sum.

examples.answer: digitSum(123)=6.
examples.verification: Direct addition of the decimal digits 1+2+3 also gives six.

examples.prompt: Solve three-disk Tower of Hanoi from A to C using B. State the recursive move sequence and move count.
examples.strategy: Move the smaller pair → Move the largest disk → Move the pair onto it

steps.title: Move the smaller pair
steps.explanation: The first two-disk subproblem uses moves \(A\to C\), \(A\to B\), C→B, freeing disk three.

steps.title: Move the largest disk
steps.explanation: Move disk three \(A\to C\) exactly once before solving the second subproblem.

steps.title: Move the pair onto it
steps.explanation: Use B→A, \(B\to C\), \(A\to C\). The full sequence has seven moves.

examples.answer: Moves: \(A\to C\),\(A\to B\),C→B,\(A\to C\),B→A,\(B\to C\),\(A\to C\); count 7.
examples.verification: The recurrence M(3)=2M(2)+1=2·3+1=7 agrees; every smaller disk stays above larger disks.

examples.prompt: A function has f(n)=1 for n≤1, otherwise f(n)=f(n−1)+f(n−1). Evaluate f(3) and decide whether it is Fibonacci.
examples.strategy: Evaluate the smaller state → Evaluate the requested state → Check the intended recurrence

steps.title: Evaluate the smaller state
steps.explanation: Both children have argument one.

steps.title: Evaluate the requested state
steps.explanation: The caller adds two identical state results.

steps.title: Check the intended recurrence
steps.explanation: Fibonacci would use distinct arguments n−1 and n−2, so this function solves another recurrence.

examples.answer: f(3)=4; this is not the Fibonacci recurrence.
examples.verification: For n≥1 this definition gives 2^(n−1), confirming four at n=3 without relying on the function name.

depth.body: A call stack records pending work, not merely the argument values currently being visited. Each frame retains its own local variables, return location and information needed after its child finishes. Sketch frames from oldest at the bottom to newest at the top, and remove only the frame that returns. Sequential child calls do not keep both completed subtrees on the stack; after the first child returns, its space can be reused by the second. A recursive call does not reset the caller's local variable or mutate it just because a child uses the same name. Maximum simultaneous frames therefore differs from total invocations and from the final value returned.

examples.prompt: f(n) stores local=n+10; if(n>0) f(n−1); then prints local. Trace f(2) without frame optimization.
examples.strategy: Push distinct frames → Return the deepest call → Resume saved work

steps.title: Push distinct frames
steps.explanation: The active frames retain local values 12,11,10 for arguments 2,1,0.

steps.title: Return the deepest call
steps.explanation: The n=0 frame prints ten and is popped, exposing the suspended n=1 frame.

steps.title: Resume saved work
steps.explanation: The next frames print eleven and twelve using their own unchanged locals.

examples.answer: Output is 10,11,12; maximum simultaneous frames is three.
examples.verification: There are three independent locals, and unwind order is the reverse of the descent argument order.

examples.prompt: g(n) calls g(n−1) twice sequentially for n>0 and returns immediately at n=0. For g(2), compare total calls with maximum frames.
examples.strategy: Count the invocation tree → Identify the longest active chain → Reuse returned space

steps.title: Count the invocation tree
steps.explanation: The root has two children, each of which has two base children.

steps.title: Identify the longest active chain
steps.explanation: A path is g(2)→g(1)→g(0), containing three frames.

steps.title: Reuse returned space
steps.explanation: The second child starts after the first returns, so completed sibling subtrees are not simultaneously stacked.

examples.answer: Seven calls occur, but at most three frames coexist.
examples.verification: Counting root-to-leaf length gives three independently of the seven-node call-tree size.

examples.prompt: Caller f has local x=4 and calls h; h has local x=9 and returns. With no pointer arguments, what is f's x afterward?
examples.strategy: Bind the caller object → Create and remove the child → Resume the caller

steps.title: Bind the caller object
steps.explanation: f's x belongs to the still-active caller frame.

steps.title: Create and remove the child
steps.explanation: h's separate x=9 exists only in h's frame and disappears when h returns.

steps.title: Resume the caller
steps.explanation: Execution resumes with f's own x=4; equal spellings do not create aliases.

examples.answer: The caller still has x=4.
examples.verification: No statement supplied h with the address of f's object or assigned to that caller object.

tutorials.title: Call count, recursion depth and auxiliary space
tutorials.body:
Recursive complexity counts total work across the whole call tree, while stack space counts the largest simultaneously active path. For one child per call with decreasing n and constant local work, the call tree is a chain and time and depth are linear. For two child calls, the tree can grow exponentially even if each root-to-leaf path has only linear depth.
Write a recurrence from the actual child sizes and nonrecursive work. Count base calls too when the question asks invocations. Memory per frame matters: a recursion of logarithmic depth can still use more than logarithmic space if each frame stores a large array. Sequential child branches typically do not coexist as complete subtrees in memory.
For naive Fibonacci, repeated subproblems cause exponential calls; memoization changes this by storing results. For factorial, a chain down to zero contains n+1 calls but n multiplications. Asymptotic notation and exact counts answer different questions. State whether memory includes the input/output storage and whether the implementation performs tail-call optimization before giving an auxiliary-space bound.

example.prompt: Factorial(n) calls factorial(n−1), with base factorial(0). Find calls and stack depth at n=4.
example.strategy: Chain → Count invocations → Maximum depth

steps.title: Chain
steps.explanation: The active values descend 4,3,2,1,0.

steps.title: Count invocations
steps.explanation: Include the base call.

steps.title: Maximum depth
steps.explanation: All five calls can be simultaneously active immediately before the base returns.

example.answer: Five invocations and maximum depth five, assuming one frame per call.
example.verification: Only four multiplications occur; operations and function-call count are not interchangeable.

depth.body: Derive recursive time from the whole invocation tree and recursive space from the maximum live path plus retained allocations. The number and sizes of children determine the recurrence; their execution order determines which frames or buffers coexist. Include base invocations in an exact call count, even if they perform no recursive work. A logarithmic recursion depth does not guarantee logarithmic memory when large buffers remain live. Conversely, exponential invocation count can coexist with only linear stack depth because sibling calls execute sequentially. State whether inputs are powers of two, how small states terminate, and what work the base performs before summing a recursion tree or claiming a tight bound.

examples.prompt: A procedure makes two calls on n−1 until n=0. Find exact invocations and depth for n=3.
examples.strategy: Count each level → Sum invocations → Count active levels

steps.title: Count each level
steps.explanation: Levels correspond to arguments 3,2,1,0.

steps.title: Sum invocations
steps.explanation: The eight base invocations still count as calls.

steps.title: Count active levels
steps.explanation: One root-to-base path contains four calls.

examples.answer: 15 invocations; maximum depth 4 frames.
examples.verification: The recurrence C(0)=1, C(n)=1+2C(n−1) gives C(3)=15.

examples.prompt: For n=8, each nonbase call splits into two halves and performs n units of local work; size-one calls cost one. Find exact total work.
examples.strategy: Charge internal levels → Charge leaves → Combine the costs

steps.title: Charge internal levels
steps.explanation: There are three internal levels, and their subproblem sizes sum to eight at each.

steps.title: Charge leaves
steps.explanation: Eight size-one subproblems each contribute one base unit.

steps.title: Combine the costs
steps.explanation: Internal work and base work are separate contributions.

examples.answer: Total work is 32 units, with \(\Theta(n\log n)\) growth for powers of two.
examples.verification: T(2)=4, T(4)=12 and T(8)=2·12+8=32 reproduce the tree sum.

examples.prompt: A halving recursion retains an array of length n in each active frame, then calls on n/2. Is its auxiliary space \(\Theta(\log n)\)?
examples.strategy: Count depth → Count retained storage → Establish the lower bound

steps.title: Count depth
steps.explanation: Halving creates logarithmically many frames.

steps.title: Count retained storage
steps.explanation: The parent buffers remain live during the child, so frame sizes are not constant.

steps.title: Establish the lower bound
steps.explanation: The initial buffer alone needs linear space.

examples.answer: Auxiliary space is \(\Theta(n)\), despite \(\Theta(\log n)\) frame depth.
examples.verification: For n=8 with lengths 8,4,2,1, live buffers total 15, between n and 2n.

lessons.title: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues
lessons.intuition: Data structures trade access speed against update cost. A complexity statement must specify what information you already possess: inserting after a known linked-list node is cheap, but finding that node may dominate the operation.

sections.title: Arrays and linked lists
sections.body: Contiguous arrays allow constant-time indexed access because address=base+index×element size. Middle insertion shifts a suffix, taking \(\Theta(n)\). A singly linked list stores a next pointer and supports \(O(1)\) insertion after a known node. Finding a predecessor or an indexed element takes \(O(n)\). Doubly linked lists store previous links too, enabling deletion of a known node without a predecessor search.

sections.title: Stacks and queues
sections.body: Stacks remove the most recently inserted item and support recursion, expression evaluation and DFS. Queues remove the oldest and support BFS. A linked queue can enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head in \(O(1)\) with both pointers. Reversing these ends in a singly linked list makes tail deletion expensive.

sections.title: Circular arrays
sections.body: Advance queue indices modulo capacity. Empty and full can both appear as head=tail unless you track a count, a full flag, or leave one slot unused. A capacity-n array with an unused-slot convention holds only n−1 elements. Carefully check whether an index denotes the next free location or the last occupied location.

sections.title: Linked queue operation sequence
sections.body: To enqueue a node, initialize its next pointer to NULL, attach it after the current tail if one exists, or make it the head for an empty queue; then update tail. To dequeue, read the head node, advance head to its next, and if the queue becomes empty set tail to NULL as well. Save the returned value before freeing the removed node. These pointer operations are \(O(1)\) because no predecessor search is required. A nonempty invariant is that tail points to the final node and tail.next is NULL. The empty invariant has both pointers NULL. Missing the final tail reset leaves a dangling pointer after removing the last node.

examples.prompt: Evaluate postfix “2 3 + 4 *”

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Push 2 then 3; + pops both and pushes 5. Operands are pushed in encounter order. Addition removes two values and replaces them with one, reducing stack size by one.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Push 4; * pops 4 and 5 and pushes 20. The earlier addition’s result is an operand for multiplication, so postfix order directly represents evaluation dependencies.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The final stack contains 20. For subtraction preserve left/right operand order when popping. A well-formed binary postfix expression finishes with exactly one value. The first popped operand is the right operand.

examples.strategy: Trace a stack after every token; operators consume operands and push their result.
examples.answer: The final stack contains 20. For subtraction preserve left/right operand order when popping.
examples.verification: The equivalent infix expression is (2+3)×4=20. For “2 3 −”, correct popping gives 2−3=−1, not 1.

examples.prompt: A queue has capacity 5 and next-free tail index 4. Enqueue twice
steps: The first insertion uses slot 4 and advances tail to (4+1)%5=0.
The second uses slot 0 and advances tail to 1.
The wrap is arithmetic modulo capacity; valid insertion also requires checking available space.

pitfalls: List insertion is not \(O(1)\) if the position first needs a search.
Circular queue capacity depends on the chosen full/empty convention.

checks.prompt: To implement a singly linked queue efficiently with head/tail pointers, which ends are used?
checks.hint: Tail deletion needs finding its predecessor in a singly linked list.
checks.explanation: Tail insertion and head deletion take \(O(1)\) with maintained pointers. The reverse requires predecessor traversal for dequeue.
options: Search the entire list for every enqueue

checks.prompt: A queue tail index is 7 in a capacity-8 ring. What index follows one increment?
checks.hint: Use modulo 8.

lessons.concept: Data structures trade access speed against update cost. A complexity statement must specify what information you already possess: inserting after a known linked-list node is cheap, but finding that node may dominate the operation.
lessons.method:
A linked list stores nodes connected by pointers rather than one contiguous indexed array. A singly linked node points forward; a doubly linked node also points backward. Head references the beginning, and a null link convention marks the end unless the structure is circular. Nodes can be individually allocated and need not have neighboring addresses.
Insertion after a known node is constant time by updating a few pointers; locating the kth node takes traversal. Deleting a singly linked node generally needs its predecessor to repair the incoming link. Head and empty-list cases need separate updates. In a doubly linked list, neighbor pointers enable constant-time deletion when the node is known, but both directions must be repaired.
Big-O claims must state what is already given. “Delete a key” includes search unless a node reference is supplied. Compared with arrays, lists allow local structural updates without shifting a suffix but pay pointer overhead and weaker locality. A circular list needs a stopping condition other than null to avoid an infinite traversal. Preserve references before changing links, or an allocated suffix can become unreachable. A stack is last-in-first-out. Push adds to the top, pop removes the top, and peek reads it without removal. An array implementation tracks a top index and capacity; a linked implementation uses a head pointer. Underflow means removing from an empty stack; overflow depends on the representation’s capacity or allocation limits.
Stacks support nested operations such as balanced-parenthesis checking, recursion and postfix expression evaluation. For postfix, push operands; on a binary operator pop right operand first, then left, compute left operator right and push the result. The order is essential for subtraction and division. A valid complete expression leaves exactly one value, and no operator can require more operands than available.
Balanced-parenthesis algorithms push open symbols and match each closing symbol against the top, detecting incorrect nesting as well as unmatched count. Equal numbers of open and close symbols alone do not establish correctness. Complexity is linear in input length when each symbol is pushed/popped at most once, with stack space proportional to maximum nesting or pending operands. A queue is first-in-first-out: enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes at the front. An array queue can waste released prefix space if indices only move forward; a circular queue wraps them modulo capacity. A linked queue usually retains both head and tail for constant-time endpoint operations.
Full/empty representation is a design choice. If head and tail coincide when empty, using the same condition for full is ambiguous unless a count or separate full flag exists. A common alternative reserves one slot, making usable capacity N−1; that is not a universal property of every circular queue. A stored count permits all N slots and distinguishes the cases.
Trace whether tail denotes last occupied or next free; update formulas differ between conventions. Enqueue requires available capacity and dequeue requires nonemptiness before moving indices. Circular indexing changes placement, not FIFO order. When calculating complexity, exclude resizing or include its amortized effect if the implementation grows; a fixed-capacity queue has straightforward constant-time successful endpoint operations. An array stores equal-sized elements in consecutive locations, so its index identifies an offset from the base address. Direct access to an existing element is constant time when the machine supports that addressing. The allocated capacity and the number of logically stored elements are separate quantities; a partly filled array can contain unused slots without those slots being members of the sequence.
Insertion at position p must preserve the order of the old suffix. First check that capacity exceeds logical length and that p is between zero and length inclusive. Shift existing elements from the end toward p, working right to left, and then write the new element. Shifting left to right overwrites values before they have been copied. Increase logical length only after constructing the expanded sequence.
Insertion near the front can move a linear number of elements even though each individual indexed read or write is constant time. Appending into available capacity moves none. Deletion uses the opposite direction to close a gap. Verify bounds, preservation of every original item, the new length and the insertion position rather than treating an array's fast indexing as proof that all its operations are constant time. Contiguous arrays allow constant-time indexed access because address=base+index×element size. Middle insertion shifts a suffix, taking \(\Theta(n)\). A singly linked list stores a next pointer and supports \(O(1)\) insertion after a known node. Finding a predecessor or an indexed element takes \(O(n)\). Doubly linked lists store previous links too, enabling deletion of a known node without a predecessor search. Stacks remove the most recently inserted item and support recursion, expression evaluation and DFS. Queues remove the oldest and support BFS. A linked queue can enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head in \(O(1)\) with both pointers. Reversing these ends in a singly linked list makes tail deletion expensive. Advance queue indices modulo capacity. Empty and full can both appear as head=tail unless you track a count, a full flag, or leave one slot unused. A capacity-n array with an unused-slot convention holds only n−1 elements. Carefully check whether an index denotes the next free location or the last occupied location. To enqueue a node, initialize its next pointer to NULL, attach it after the current tail if one exists, or make it the head for an empty queue; then update tail. To dequeue, read the head node, advance head to its next, and if the queue becomes empty set tail to NULL as well. Save the returned value before freeing the removed node. These pointer operations are \(O(1)\) because no predecessor search is required. A nonempty invariant is that tail points to the final node and tail.next is NULL. The empty invariant has both pointers NULL. Missing the final tail reset leaves a dangling pointer after removing the last node. Treat a linked-list operation as a change to graph edges between node objects. Before overwriting a link, retain every node or suffix still needed for the operation. The head is an incoming reference too, so deleting or inserting the first node requires updating it instead of an ordinary predecessor field. For reversal, maintain a reversed prefix, the current node and the untouched suffix; saving the next link is what keeps the suffix reachable. Complexity claims depend on supplied references. A known singly linked tail still lacks its incoming predecessor reference, and constant-time deletion by copying a successor cannot handle that tail or preserve arbitrary node identity requirements. A stack models pending work whose newest unresolved item must be handled first. Write the entire stack with its top convention when tracing, because an unordered set cannot capture operand order or nesting. Parenthesis checking needs symbol types as well as counts; each closer must match the most recent unmatched opener. Expression conversion uses precedence to decide which operators remain pending, while evaluation uses the right-then-left pop order. Before every pop, establish that a value exists. A malformed expression can have balanced final size yet require an earlier underflow, so validate the sequence of operations rather than only counting net pushes and pops. A FIFO queue preserves arrival order even when its physical storage or implementation changes. Keep a logical front-to-rear sequence separate from internal arrays or stacks. A queue built from two stacks accumulates new arrivals in an input stack and removes older records from an output stack. Transfer input to output only when output is empty, reversing the current batch exactly once. Each item can be charged for one input push, one transfer pair and one output pop, giving constant amortized operations although a particular dequeue can move many items. Empty-state handling matters because removing an absent item is not a legitimate FIFO operation or a numerical return value. A circular buffer reuses released slots by reducing index updates modulo physical capacity. First specify whether rear means last occupied or next free, and whether fullness uses a count, a flag or one reserved slot. These choices change both formulas and usable capacity. Under a count convention, all physical slots are usable and equal head/rear indices can describe either empty or full. Under a reserved-slot convention, equality means empty and the next rear position colliding with head means full. Trace the logical sequence alongside indices, because numerical index order does not describe FIFO order after wrapping. Test capacity before writes and size before reads. Array updates must preserve the logical sequence as well as stay inside allocated capacity. Distinguish a slot containing a leftover value from an element that belongs to the current sequence. When closing a deletion gap, copy the suffix left from low indices upward; when opening an insertion gap, copy right from high indices downward. The safe direction prevents a source from being overwritten before it is read. A sorted merge into spare capacity can also work backward because the largest remaining value belongs at the latest available destination. Establish the unread-source and completed-destination regions, then count movement from the actual affected suffix rather than assigning constant cost to every indexed operation.

gateGuide.recognize: Complexity depends on whether a position or predecessor is already known. Stack/queue traces depend on removal order and empty/full conventions.
method: Identify representation and which pointers/indices are maintained.
Draw affected links before mutating a list, or trace head/tail modulo capacity for a ring.
For expressions, preserve operand order on popping; for queues check the last-removal case resets both pointers.

traps.claim: Linked insertion is always O(1)
traps.why: Finding the kth node first takes O(n); only insertion after an already-known node is constant time.

traps.claim: Stack subtraction pops left operand first
traps.why: For postfix a b −, pop b as the right operand and a as the left; reversing gives the wrong sign.

formulas.meaning: Circular-array index update.
Only for the convention that reserves one slot to distinguish full from empty.

example.prompt: Insert X between singly linked nodes \(A\to B\).
example.strategy: Preserve successor → Attach new node → Redirect predecessor

steps.title: Preserve successor
steps.explanation: Save or retain B, currently A.next.

steps.title: Attach new node
steps.explanation: Set X.next=B before overwriting the existing incoming link.

steps.title: Redirect predecessor
steps.explanation: Set A.next=X, giving A→X→B.

example.answer: The new chain is A→X→B, with constant pointer-update work when A is known.
example.verification: If A.next is changed first and B is not retained, the original suffix can be lost.

depth.body: Treat a linked-list operation as a change to graph edges between node objects. Before overwriting a link, retain every node or suffix still needed for the operation. The head is an incoming reference too, so deleting or inserting the first node requires updating it instead of an ordinary predecessor field. For reversal, maintain a reversed prefix, the current node and the untouched suffix; saving the next link is what keeps the suffix reachable. Complexity claims depend on supplied references. examples.prompt: Delete the head of singly linked list \(A\to B\)→C→null, given only head=A.
examples.strategy: Retain the successor → Redirect the entry → Remove the old head

steps.title: Retain the successor
steps.explanation: Save B from A.next before releasing or disconnecting A.

steps.title: Redirect the entry
steps.explanation: Set head=B; no predecessor node exists to update.

steps.title: Remove the old head
steps.explanation: A can now be released under the allocation model while \(B\to C\) remains reachable.

examples.answer: The list is \(B\to C\)→null, with constant pointer-update work.
examples.verification: Following head visits exactly the two retained nodes and never the removed A.

examples.prompt: Reverse singly linked list 1→2→3→null using prev=null and current=1.
examples.strategy: Reverse the first link → Reverse the next link → Complete reversal

steps.title: Reverse the first link
steps.explanation: Save next=2, set 1.next=null, then prev=1 and current=2.

steps.title: Reverse the next link
steps.explanation: Save next=3, set 2.next=1, then prev=2 and current=3.

steps.title: Complete reversal
steps.explanation: Save next=null, set 3.next=2 and set head=3 after current becomes null.

examples.answer: The list becomes 3→2→1→null.
examples.verification: All three original nodes remain reachable exactly once, and the old head is now the terminating tail.

examples.prompt: In a singly linked list of n nodes, only a pointer to its tail is supplied. Can the tail always be deleted in \(O(1)\) without changing other node identities?
examples.strategy: Find the missing information → Reject the successor-copy trick → Account for the incoming link

steps.title: Find the missing information
steps.explanation: The tail has no next node and no stored predecessor link.

steps.title: Reject the successor-copy trick
steps.explanation: There is no successor whose contents and link could be copied into the tail.

steps.title: Account for the incoming link
steps.explanation: With a head available, locating the predecessor may require traversing n−1 nodes; without it deletion may be impossible.

examples.answer: No universal \(O(1)\) deletion follows from a tail pointer alone.
examples.verification: A doubly linked node would supply a predecessor link, demonstrating the representation assumption missing here.

tutorials.title: Stacks, postfix evaluation and operand order
tutorials.body:
A stack is last-in-first-out. Push adds to the top, pop removes the top, and peek reads it without removal. example.prompt: Evaluate postfix 8 3 − 2 *.
example.strategy: First operator → Second operator → Validate stack

steps.title: First operator
steps.explanation: Pop 3 as right operand and 8 as left.

steps.title: Second operator
steps.explanation: The earlier result is the next operator’s left operand.

steps.title: Validate stack
steps.explanation: The final stack has one value and no operation underflowed.

example.verification: The corresponding infix expression is (8−3)×2. Reversing pop order at subtraction gives a wrong negative result.

depth.body: A stack models pending work whose newest unresolved item must be handled first. Write the entire stack with its top convention when tracing, because an unordered set cannot capture operand order or nesting. Parenthesis checking needs symbol types as well as counts; each closer must match the most recent unmatched opener. Expression conversion uses precedence to decide which operators remain pending, while evaluation uses the right-then-left pop order. Before every pop, establish that a value exists. A malformed expression can have balanced final size yet require an earlier underflow, so validate the sequence of operations rather than only counting net pushes and pops.

examples.prompt: Use a stack to test whether the bracket string ([)] is properly nested.
examples.strategy: Push openers → Compare the first closer → Reject immediately

steps.title: Push openers
steps.explanation: After ( then [, the stack from bottom to top is [(,[].

steps.title: Compare the first closer
steps.explanation: The closer ) requires a top (, but the actual top is [.

steps.title: Reject immediately
steps.explanation: The mismatch proves invalid nesting even though total counts of each bracket type balance.

examples.answer: The string is not properly nested.
examples.verification: The crossing pair cannot be closed in last-opened-first order; equal counts alone therefore fail as a correctness test.

examples.prompt: Convert infix 3+4*2 to postfix with an operator stack, then evaluate it.
examples.strategy: Save the pending operators → Finish the operand and drain → Evaluate in stack order

steps.title: Save the pending operators
steps.explanation: Output 3 then 4; the stack contains + then * because multiplication has higher precedence.

steps.title: Finish the operand and drain
steps.explanation: Output 2, then pop * and +, producing postfix 3 4 2 * +.

steps.title: Evaluate in stack order
steps.explanation: The multiplication result is pushed before addition consumes it.

examples.answer: Postfix is 3 4 2 * +; value is 11.
examples.verification: Direct precedence-aware infix evaluation gives 3+(4·2)=11, matching the stack computation.

examples.prompt: Evaluate postfix 5 2 −. Why does popping the first value as the left operand fail?
examples.strategy: Push operands → Assign operand roles → Apply subtraction

steps.title: Push operands
steps.explanation: The stack is [5,2] with two on top.

steps.title: Assign operand roles
steps.explanation: The top was pushed later and belongs on the operator's right.

steps.title: Apply subtraction
steps.explanation: Reversing the roles would compute a different expression.

examples.answer: The value is 3; using first pop as left incorrectly gives −3.
examples.verification: The postfix order corresponds to infix 5−2, not 2−5.

tutorials.title: FIFO queues and circular-buffer conventions
tutorials.body:
A queue is first-in-first-out: enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes at the front. An array queue can waste released prefix space if indices only move forward; a circular queue wraps them modulo capacity. A linked queue usually retains both head and tail for constant-time endpoint operations.
Full/empty representation is a design choice. If head and tail coincide when empty, using the same condition for full is ambiguous unless a count or separate full flag exists. A common alternative reserves one slot, making usable capacity N−1; that is not a universal property of every circular queue. A stored count permits all N slots and distinguishes the cases.

example.prompt: Capacity 5 with a count variable; head=3, tail=0, count=2. Dequeue then enqueue X.
example.strategy: Dequeue → Enqueue → Interpret

steps.title: Dequeue
steps.explanation: Remove the element at slot 3; head becomes 4 and count becomes 1.

steps.title: Enqueue
steps.explanation: Store X in next-free slot 0; tail becomes 1 and count becomes 2.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.explanation: The older remaining element is still removed before X, regardless of wrapped positions.

example.answer: Final head 4, tail 1, count 2.
example.verification: Indices alone may look numerically out of order, but modulo placement preserves logical FIFO order.

depth.body: A FIFO queue preserves arrival order even when its physical storage or implementation changes. Keep a logical front-to-rear sequence separate from internal arrays or stacks. A queue built from two stacks accumulates new arrivals in an input stack and removes older records from an output stack. Transfer input to output only when output is empty, reversing the current batch exactly once. Each item can be charged for one input push, one transfer pair and one output pop, giving constant amortized operations although a particular dequeue can move many items. examples.prompt: Starting empty, enqueue A, enqueue B, dequeue, then enqueue C. State the removed value and queue order.
examples.strategy: Record arrivals → Remove the oldest → Append the later arrival

steps.title: Record arrivals
steps.explanation: The front-to-rear sequence after two enqueues is [A,B].

steps.title: Remove the oldest
steps.explanation: Dequeue removes A and leaves [B].

steps.title: Append the later arrival
steps.explanation: Enqueuing C gives [B,C], with B still ahead of C.

examples.answer: Removed A; remaining order B,C.
examples.verification: Dequeuing the remaining queue would yield B then C, exactly their arrival order.

examples.prompt: Implement a queue with input/output stacks, top at the right. Enqueue 1,2; dequeue; enqueue 3; dequeue twice. Show transfers.
examples.strategy: Transfer the first batch → Preserve the older output → Transfer after output empties

steps.title: Transfer the first batch
steps.explanation: Input [1,2] becomes output [2,1] when the first dequeue finds output empty; pop one.

steps.title: Preserve the older output
steps.explanation: Enqueue three into input [3]. The next dequeue pops two from output without transferring three.

steps.title: Transfer after output empties
steps.explanation: Move three to output and pop it on the final dequeue.

examples.answer: Dequeue results are 1,2,3, with two batch transfers.
examples.verification: Every item crosses from input to output once, so three items need linear total stack operations despite a multi-item first transfer.

examples.prompt: A queue starts empty, receives X, then is dequeued twice. Is the second result another X from the old storage slot?
examples.strategy: Consume the only arrival → Check the second precondition → Separate storage from membership

steps.title: Consume the only arrival
steps.explanation: The first dequeue removes X and makes the logical size zero.

steps.title: Check the second precondition
steps.explanation: The next dequeue has no live queue element to remove.

steps.title: Separate storage from membership
steps.explanation: An old byte pattern in an array slot does not represent a current enqueued item.

examples.answer: The second dequeue must report underflow or an empty result under the API.
examples.verification: Successful dequeues cannot exceed successful enqueues for an initially empty queue.

depth.body: A circular buffer reuses released slots by reducing index updates modulo physical capacity. First specify whether rear means last occupied or next free, and whether fullness uses a count, a flag or one reserved slot. These choices change both formulas and usable capacity. Under a count convention, all physical slots are usable and equal head/rear indices can describe either empty or full. Under a reserved-slot convention, equality means empty and the next rear position colliding with head means full. Trace the logical sequence alongside indices, because numerical index order does not describe FIFO order after wrapping. Test capacity before writes and size before reads.

examples.prompt: Capacity three, count convention, head=rear=0 and empty. Enqueue P,Q,R, then dequeue once; rear is next free.
examples.strategy: Fill each slot → Recognize full equality → Remove the front

steps.title: Fill each slot
steps.explanation: P,Q,R occupy slots 0,1,2 and count becomes three.

steps.title: Recognize full equality
steps.explanation: head and rear both equal zero, but count distinguishes fullness from emptiness.

steps.title: Remove the front
steps.explanation: P is removed, rear stays zero and count becomes two.

examples.answer: Removed P; head=1, rear=0, count=2; remaining order Q,R.
examples.verification: The occupied slots are now 1 and 2, matching two remaining arrivals.

examples.prompt: Reserved-slot buffer has physical capacity four, head=3, next-free rear=1. Enqueue X, then dequeue. Find final indices and intermediate fullness.
examples.strategy: Identify occupied slots → Append and test fullness → Remove the oldest

steps.title: Identify occupied slots
steps.explanation: Slots three and zero hold the older two records.

steps.title: Append and test fullness
steps.explanation: X enters slot one; next rear would be three, equal to head, so the buffer is full.

steps.title: Remove the oldest
steps.explanation: The dequeue frees slot three; rear remains two.

examples.answer: After enqueue the buffer is full; afterward head=0, rear=2 with two elements.
examples.verification: Logical occupied positions zero and one contain the retained old record then X; usable capacity is three.

examples.prompt: A count-based capacity-five queue has head=tail=2. Can equality alone determine whether an enqueue is allowed?
examples.strategy: Construct the empty case → Construct the full case → Use the missing state

steps.title: Construct the empty case
steps.explanation: Equal indices can describe no records, so enqueue would be allowed.

steps.title: Construct the full case
steps.explanation: Five arrivals without removals wrap tail back to head, so enqueue must be rejected.

steps.title: Use the missing state
steps.explanation: Read count or an equivalent full flag; index equality supplies insufficient information.

examples.answer: No; the same equal indices can mean empty or full.
examples.verification: The two cases have identical indices but different available capacities, disproving an equality-only rule.

tutorials.title: Array insertion: capacity, indices and safe shifts
tutorials.body:
An array stores equal-sized elements in consecutive locations, so its index identifies an offset from the base address. Direct access to an existing element is constant time when the machine supports that addressing. The allocated capacity and the number of logically stored elements are separate quantities; a partly filled array can contain unused slots without those slots being members of the sequence.
Insertion at position p must preserve the order of the old suffix. First check that capacity exceeds logical length and that p is between zero and length inclusive. Shift existing elements from the end toward p, working right to left, and then write the new element. Shifting left to right overwrites values before they have been copied. Increase logical length only after constructing the expanded sequence.
Insertion near the front can move a linear number of elements even though each individual indexed read or write is constant time. Appending into available capacity moves none. Deletion uses the opposite direction to close a gap. Verify bounds, preservation of every original item, the new length and the insertion position rather than treating an array's fast indexing as proof that all its operations are constant time.

example.prompt: An array has capacity 5, logical length 4 and values [2,4,6,8]. Insert 5 at zero-based position 2.
example.strategy: Check room → Shift from the end → Fill the gap

steps.title: Check room
steps.explanation: There is one free slot and the requested position belongs to the valid insertion range.

steps.title: Shift from the end
steps.explanation: Copy the old final element first, then its predecessor, so neither is overwritten.

steps.title: Fill the gap
steps.explanation: The insertion position is now free and the logical sequence expands by one.

example.answer: The logical array becomes [2,4,5,6,8], with two shifted elements.
example.verification: All four original values remain in their original relative order, and no index outside allocated slots 0 through 4 was accessed.

depth.body: Array updates must preserve the logical sequence as well as stay inside allocated capacity. Distinguish a slot containing a leftover value from an element that belongs to the current sequence. When closing a deletion gap, copy the suffix left from low indices upward; when opening an insertion gap, copy right from high indices downward. The safe direction prevents a source from being overwritten before it is read. A sorted merge into spare capacity can also work backward because the largest remaining value belongs at the latest available destination. Establish the unread-source and completed-destination regions, then count movement from the actual affected suffix rather than assigning constant cost to every indexed operation.

examples.prompt: Delete zero-based position 1 from the logical array [5,7,9,11], capacity four.
examples.strategy: Identify the removed slot → Shift toward the front → Reduce logical length

steps.title: Identify the removed slot
steps.explanation: Seven is removed, leaving a gap before the suffix 9,11.

steps.title: Shift toward the front
steps.explanation: Assign a[1]=9 and then a[2]=11, reading sources before they are overwritten.

steps.title: Reduce logical length
steps.explanation: The trailing slot is outside the new sequence even if it still contains eleven.

examples.answer: Logical array [5,9,11]; two elements moved.
examples.verification: Every retained original element appears once in order, and the old final slot is excluded by the new length.

examples.prompt: Merge sorted B=[2,3,8] into A=[1,4,7] with three spare A slots, writing backward.
examples.strategy: Fill the largest destinations → Continue backward → Finish the merged sequence

steps.title: Fill the largest destinations
steps.explanation: Compare final unread values: place 8 at A[5], then 7 at A[4].

steps.title: Continue backward
steps.explanation: Place 4 at A[3], then 3 at A[2], then 2 at A[1]. Unread A[0]=1 remains safe.

steps.title: Finish the merged sequence
steps.explanation: All B values are consumed and A[0] is already the smallest value.

examples.verification: Each input order is preserved and the output contains the multiset union of the two inputs.

examples.prompt: Insert 9 at the front of [1,2,3] with capacity four, but copy a[j+1]=a[j] for j=0,1,2 in increasing order. What goes wrong?
examples.strategy: Overwrite the next source → Propagate the overwritten value → Write the insertion

steps.title: Overwrite the next source
steps.explanation: j=0 sets a[1]=1, destroying the original two before it is copied.

steps.title: Propagate the overwritten value
steps.explanation: j=1 and j=2 copy that same one into slots two and three.

steps.title: Write the insertion
steps.explanation: Setting a[0]=9 now produces [9,1,1,1], not the required preserved suffix.

examples.answer: The incorrect result is [9,1,1,1]; copying rightward must run from the end.
examples.verification: Original values two and three disappeared, violating the required permutation-plus-one property.

lessons.title: Trees, traversals and binary search trees
lessons.intuition: A tree is a connected acyclic structure. Rooting it introduces parents, children and subtrees. Binary search trees add an ordering invariant, so searching can discard one entire subtree at each comparison—but only balanced height guarantees logarithmic depth.

sections.title: Tree terminology and traversals
sections.body: Height in edges is the longest root-to-leaf edge count; some problems instead count nodes, so read the convention. Preorder visits root,left,right; inorder left,root,right; postorder left,right,root. A binary tree has at most two children per node. A full binary tree gives each internal node exactly two children; a complete tree fills levels left to right.

sections.title: BST operations
sections.body: For distinct keys, everything in a node’s left subtree is smaller and everything in the right is larger. Search follows one comparison-directed path. Insertion finds a null child location. Deletion handles no child, one child, or two children; the two-child case replaces the key with inorder successor or predecessor and deletes that replacement node.

sections.title: Complexity and reconstruction
sections.body: Search, insertion and deletion take O(h). Sorted insertion into an unbalanced BST can create h=n−1. Balanced trees maintain logarithmic height. Inorder traversal produces sorted keys, not insertion order. With distinct keys, inorder plus preorder or postorder uniquely determine a binary tree; preorder alone generally does not determine an arbitrary binary tree.

sections.title: Why traversal order changes output
sections.body: The recursive structure is the same for all three depth-first traversals; only the placement of visit(root) changes. Put it before the two recursive calls for preorder, between them for inorder, or afterward for postorder. On a BST, the between placement visits every smaller left key, then the root, then every larger right key, proving sorted output by induction. All three traversals visit each node once and take \(\Theta(n)\) time; auxiliary recursive space is Θ(h), which is \(\Theta(n)\) for a chain and \(\Theta(\log n)\) for a balanced tree.
sections.code:
inorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    inorder(node.left)
    visit(node.key)
    inorder(node.right)

examples.prompt: Insert 4,2,6,1,3 into a BST

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: 4 becomes root; 2 goes left; 6 goes right. Each new key follows smaller-left and larger-right from the root, so insertion order determines shape.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: 1 goes left of 2 and 3 right of 2. Once at node 2, keys 1 and 3 are compared with 2; both still belong in the left subtree of 4.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Inorder is 1,2,3,4,6; preorder is 4,2,1,3,6. Trace the visit rule rather than memorizing a shape. Inorder visits left/node/right; preorder visits node/left/right. Applying those rules yields different sequences.

examples.strategy: Insert by comparisons, then use traversal visit rules rather than the order of insertion.
examples.answer: Inorder is 1,2,3,4,6; preorder is 4,2,1,3,6. Trace the visit rule rather than memorizing a shape.
examples.verification: The inorder sequence is sorted, which checks the BST invariant. The preorder starts with root 4, as required by its visit rule.

examples.prompt: Delete root 4 from that tree using its successor
steps: The smallest key in the right subtree is 6.
Replace 4 by 6 and delete the old leaf containing 6.
The remaining root 6 has the original left subtree and no right child; the BST invariant remains true.

pitfalls: Complete, full and perfect trees are different definitions.
A BST is not automatically balanced.
revision: Perfect binary tree nodes=2^(h+1)−1 for edge-height h.

checks.prompt: What does inorder traversal of a BST with distinct keys produce?
checks.hint: Left subtree keys are smaller; right subtree keys are larger.
checks.explanation: Inorder visits left, root, right, yielding keys in increasing order under the BST invariant.

checks.prompt: Insert 1,2,3,4 into an unbalanced BST. What is its edge-height?
checks.hint: Ascending keys create a right chain.
checks.explanation: Four nodes on one path contain 3 edges.

Inorder plus preorder or postorder can reconstruct a binary tree with distinct labels; preorder plus postorder alone generally cannot uniquely determine it. A BST’s inorder sequence is sorted because of its key invariant, not because all binary trees have sorted inorder. Count nodes and edges separately when converting height formulas. A binary search tree stores smaller keys in a node’s left subtree and larger keys in its right, under a specified duplicate policy. Search compares at each node and follows one branch, giving O(h) time for height h. Insertion follows the same comparisons to an empty position. A balanced shape makes h logarithmic, but sorted insertions can create a linear-height chain.
Deletion has three cases: remove a leaf, replace a one-child node by that child, or replace a two-child node’s key by its inorder successor/predecessor and delete that replacement’s old node. The successor is the minimum of the right subtree and may itself have a right child. It is not necessarily the root’s immediate right child.
After every operation verify the invariant for whole subtrees, not just parent-child comparisons. Rotations used by balanced variants preserve inorder order but change shape. A plain BST does not rebalance automatically. GATE traces may depend on successor versus predecessor replacement and duplicate conventions, so use the stated policy instead of assuming one universal deletion result. A complete binary tree fills all levels except possibly the final level, whose occupied positions must form a leftmost prefix. A perfect tree fills every level. These definitions constrain different properties.
Compute height bottom up from child heights, and compute depth top down from the root. For shape questions, identify missing child positions rather than only counting vertices on a level. A right child with a missing left child violates completeness. Traversal order does not change any of these structural quantities. Put it before the two recursive calls for preorder, between them for inorder, or afterward for postorder. On a BST, the between placement visits every smaller left key, then the root, then every larger right key, proving sorted output by induction. All three traversals visit each node once and take \(\Theta(n)\) time; auxiliary recursive space is Θ(h), which is \(\Theta(n)\) for a chain and \(\Theta(\log n)\) for a balanced tree. A traversal order is determined by when a node is emitted relative to recursive child visits. Label the visit moment before, between or after the child calls for preorder, inorder or postorder. Missing children contribute no labels but still affect reconstruction choices. For distinct keys, preorder supplies each subtree's root and inorder partitions its left and right descendants, so together they determine a unique binary tree. Preorder and postorder lack the left-versus-right distinction for a single-child node. Reconstruction requires more than matching vertex counts: verify the proposed shape by regenerating both supplied traversals. Do not assume inorder is sorted unless a separate BST invariant is present. The BST invariant constrains every descendant, not merely a node's immediate children. Maintain an allowed key interval while descending: entering a left subtree tightens the upper limit, and entering a right subtree tightens the lower limit. Insertion adds a leaf at the first empty link on that comparison path. Verify an update by its full inorder sequence and retained key multiset. Tree counting becomes easier when each quantity is tied to a structural invariant. Every nonroot vertex has one incoming parent edge, giving n−1 edges regardless of branching pattern. For a full binary tree, counting child edges also gives twice the number of internal vertices, which relates leaves to internal vertices. Height bounds depend on whether the tree is arbitrary, complete or perfect: an arbitrary binary tree may be a chain, whereas completeness constrains the occupied positions. Always declare the edge-based or vertex-based height convention. gateGuide.recognize: Read tree shape definitions and height convention. A BST invariant enables search but does not imply balance.

For BST updates follow comparisons; handle leaf, one-child and two-child deletion separately.
Express operation cost in height h, then apply any balance guarantee. Distinct-key assumptions matter for reconstruction and ordering.

traps.claim: BST search is always logarithmic
traps.why: Ascending insertions can create a chain and linear-height search.

traps.claim: Complete means full
traps.why: A complete tree fills levels left to right; a full tree requires every internal node have two children. Neither definition can substitute for the other.

Search/insertion/deletion costs before assuming balance.

example.prompt: A tree has root A, left child B with left child D, and right child C.
example.strategy: Preorder → Inorder → Postorder

steps.title: Preorder
steps.explanation: Visit root first: A,B,D,C.

steps.title: Inorder
steps.explanation: Finish each left subtree before its root: D,B,A,C.

steps.title: Postorder
steps.explanation: Finish children before root: D,B,C,A.

example.answer: Preorder A B D C; inorder D B A C; postorder D B C A.
example.verification: Every traversal visits each node exactly once; only the visit moment changes.

depth.body: A traversal order is determined by when a node is emitted relative to recursive child visits. Label the visit moment before, between or after the child calls for preorder, inorder or postorder. Missing children contribute no labels but still affect reconstruction choices. examples.prompt: R has left child L and right child M; M has left child N. Compute all three depth-first traversal orders.
examples.strategy: Emit on entry → Emit between children → Emit on return

steps.title: Emit on entry
steps.explanation: Preorder visits R before L, then M before N, giving R,L,M,N.

steps.title: Emit between children
steps.explanation: Inorder finishes L, emits R, then visits N before M, giving L,R,N,M.

steps.title: Emit on return
steps.explanation: Postorder emits L, then N,M, then R, giving L,N,M,R.

examples.answer: Preorder R L M N; inorder L R N M; postorder L N M R.
examples.verification: Each order contains the same four labels exactly once, and M/N appear according to the stated visit moment.

examples.prompt: Reconstruct a distinct-label tree from preorder A,B,D,E,C and inorder D,B,E,A,C; give its postorder.
examples.strategy: Partition at the root → Reconstruct the left subtree → Emit completed subtrees

steps.title: Partition at the root
steps.explanation: Preorder starts with A; inorder puts D,B,E on its left and C on its right.

steps.title: Reconstruct the left subtree
steps.explanation: Its preorder root is B, with D left and E right according to the inorder partition.

steps.title: Emit completed subtrees
steps.explanation: Postorder visits D,E,B, then C, then A.

examples.answer: A has left B and right C; B has children D,E. Postorder is D,E,B,C,A.
examples.verification: Regenerating preorder gives A,B,D,E,C and inorder gives D,B,E,A,C, matching both inputs.

examples.prompt: Preorder is A,B and postorder is B,A. Must B be A's left child?
examples.strategy: Construct a left-child tree → Construct a right-child tree → Find the missing distinction

steps.title: Construct a left-child tree
steps.explanation: A with left child B produces preorder A,B and postorder B,A.

steps.title: Construct a right-child tree
steps.explanation: A with right child B produces those same two orders.

steps.title: Find the missing distinction
steps.explanation: Their inorders differ: B,A versus A,B, so the supplied orders do not choose a side.

examples.answer: No; both child placements are possible.
examples.verification: Two distinct trees satisfying both inputs are a constructive proof of nonuniqueness.

tutorials.title: BST search, insertion and deletion
tutorials.body:
A binary search tree stores smaller keys in a node’s left subtree and larger keys in its right, under a specified duplicate policy. Search compares at each node and follows one branch, giving O(h) time for height h. Insertion follows the same comparisons to an empty position. A balanced shape makes h logarithmic, but sorted insertions can create a linear-height chain.
Deletion has three cases: remove a leaf, replace a one-child node by that child, or replace a two-child node’s key by its inorder successor/predecessor and delete that replacement’s old node. The successor is the minimum of the right subtree and may itself have a right child. It is not necessarily the root’s immediate right child.
After every operation verify the invariant for whole subtrees, not just parent-child comparisons. Rotations used by balanced variants preserve inorder order but change shape. A plain BST does not rebalance automatically. GATE traces may depend on successor versus predecessor replacement and duplicate conventions, so use the stated policy instead of assuming one universal deletion result.

example.prompt: Delete 5 from BST with root 5, left 2, right 8, and 8’s left child 6.
example.strategy: Find successor → Replace root key → Remove old successor

steps.title: Find successor
steps.explanation: The smallest right-subtree key is 6, not 8.

steps.title: Replace root key
steps.explanation: Store 6 at the root while retaining both subtrees.

steps.title: Remove old successor
steps.explanation: Delete the original leaf 6 from beneath 8.

example.answer: Root becomes 6, with left 2 and right 8.
example.verification: Inorder is 2,6,8, so all remaining keys still satisfy the BST ordering.

depth.body: The BST invariant constrains every descendant, not merely a node's immediate children. Maintain an allowed key interval while descending: entering a left subtree tightens the upper limit, and entering a right subtree tightens the lower limit. Insertion adds a leaf at the first empty link on that comparison path. Two-child deletion replaces the key by a successor or predecessor, then removes that replacement from its original location, potentially reconnecting its one child. State a duplicate policy before tracing equal comparisons. Search cost follows height, so a legal BST can still perform linear work when insertions produce a chain. Verify an update by its full inorder sequence and retained key multiset.

examples.prompt: Insert distinct keys 7,3,9,5 into an empty ordinary BST, then search for five.
examples.strategy: Create the upper shape → Place the fourth key → Follow the search path

steps.title: Create the upper shape
steps.explanation: Seven becomes root; three attaches left and nine attaches right.

steps.title: Place the fourth key
steps.explanation: Five is smaller than seven and larger than three, so it becomes three's right child.

steps.title: Follow the search path
steps.explanation: Comparisons visit seven, then three, then five, where the match succeeds.

examples.answer: The search path is 7→3→5; inorder is 3,5,7,9.
examples.verification: The inorder sequence is sorted and includes each inserted key exactly once.

examples.prompt: Delete root eight using its successor. Left child is three; right child is twelve, whose left child is ten with right child eleven.
examples.strategy: Find the true successor → Replace the root key → Remove the old ten

steps.title: Find the true successor
steps.explanation: The minimum in the right subtree is ten, reached by going left from twelve.

steps.title: Replace the root key
steps.explanation: Store ten at the root, preserving the root's original two subtree links.

steps.title: Remove the old ten
steps.explanation: Reconnect twelve's left link to eleven, the old successor's only child.

examples.answer: Root ten has left three and right twelve; twelve has left eleven.
examples.verification: Inorder is 3,10,11,12. Removing eight and retaining eleven confirms both ordering and child reconnection.

examples.prompt: Insert 1,2,3,4,5 into an ordinary unbalanced BST. Is finding five guaranteed logarithmic?
examples.strategy: Follow successive insertions → Measure shape → Count the search

steps.title: Follow successive insertions
steps.explanation: Every new key exceeds all earlier ones, so each becomes a right child of the previous key.

steps.title: Measure shape
steps.explanation: Five vertices form a chain with four edges.

steps.title: Count the search
steps.explanation: Searching for five visits all five vertices; in general sorted insertion can require n comparisons.

examples.answer: No; this tree has linear-height and linear worst-case search.
examples.verification: Its inorder is still sorted, showing that the BST invariant does not itself imply balance.

tutorials.title: Tree height, leaves and complete-tree shape
tutorials.body:
A rooted tree is a connected acyclic structure with a distinguished root. Each nonroot vertex has one parent, so a tree with n vertices has n−1 edges. A vertex's depth is the number of edges from the root to that vertex. Its height is the maximum number of edges from it to a descendant leaf. Under this convention a leaf has height zero and the tree's height is the root's height; some questions instead count vertices, so state the convention.
A binary tree permits at most two children per vertex, including positions distinguished as left and right. A full binary tree gives every vertex either zero or two children. A complete binary tree fills all levels except possibly the final level, whose occupied positions must form a leftmost prefix. A perfect tree fills every level. These definitions constrain different properties.
Compute height bottom up from child heights, and compute depth top down from the root. For shape questions, identify missing child positions rather than only counting vertices on a level. A right child with a missing left child violates completeness. Traversal order does not change any of these structural quantities.

example.prompt: A has children B,C; B has children D,E; C has only a right child F; F has only a left child G. Find vertex count, leaves, height and whether the tree is complete.
example.strategy: Count structure → Follow the deepest path → Check occupied positions

steps.title: Count structure
steps.explanation: Each of B,C,D,E,F,G has one parent; the childless vertices are D,E,G.

steps.title: Follow the deepest path
steps.explanation: This path has three edges, so G has depth three and the root has height three.

steps.title: Check occupied positions
steps.explanation: At depth two, C has no left child but has right child F. Occupied positions therefore do not form a leftmost prefix.

example.answer: There are 7 vertices, 6 edges and leaves D,E,G. The height is 3 edges; the binary tree is not complete.

depth.body: Tree counting becomes easier when each quantity is tied to a structural invariant. Every nonroot vertex has one incoming parent edge, giving n−1 edges regardless of branching pattern. For a full binary tree, counting child edges also gives twice the number of internal vertices, which relates leaves to internal vertices. Height bounds depend on whether the tree is arbitrary, complete or perfect: an arbitrary binary tree may be a chain, whereas completeness constrains the occupied positions. Always declare the edge-based or vertex-based height convention. To classify a shape, inspect missing child positions as well as child counts; being full and being complete are independent requirements.

examples.prompt: A full binary tree has three internal vertices. How many leaves and total vertices does it have?

steps.title: Count child edges

steps.title: Use the tree edge invariant

lessons.title: Binary heaps and graph representations
lessons.intuition: A heap guarantees an extreme value at the root without sorting the entire collection. Graph representations instead organize many-to-many links. In both cases, choosing a representation determines which operations are cheap and which information must be searched.

sections.title: Heap invariants
sections.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree whose parent key is no larger than its child keys. In a zero-based array, left child=2i+1, right child=2i+2 and parent=floor((i−1)/2). Completeness gives height \(\Theta(\log n)\). Sibling order is unrestricted and a heap is not a BST.

sections.title: Heap updates and construction
sections.body: Insertion appends and bubbles upward; delete-min swaps the final element to the root and sifts downward. Each traverses at most the height. Bottom-up construction sifts internal nodes from the last parent backward. It is \(\Theta(n)\), since many nodes have tiny subtrees; multiplying n by the maximum sift cost overestimates aggregate work.

sections.title: Graph storage
sections.body: An adjacency matrix uses Θ(V²) space and permits \(O(1)\) edge tests, but listing neighbours takes Θ(V). Adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours proportional to degree. An undirected graph usually stores each edge twice in lists. Weighted graphs attach weights; directed graphs distinguish outgoing from incoming edges.

sections.title: Why build-heap is linear
sections.body: Only about n/2 nodes have height zero, at most n/4 have height one, at most n/8 have height two, and so on. A sift from height h costs O(h), so aggregate work is bounded by n times Σh/2^(h+1), a convergent constant sum. Thus bottom-up build is \(O(n)\), unlike repeatedly inserting n elements, whose simple worst-case bound is \(O(n\log n)\). The algorithm starts at the last internal node, floor(n/2)−1 in zero-based indexing, and visits parents backward. Each node’s child subtrees are already heaps before it is sifted, which is the key invariant.

examples.prompt: Insert 2 into min-heap array [3,5,4]

steps.title: Set up the state

steps.explanation: Parent of index 3 is 1; swap 2 with 5 to obtain [3,2,4,5]. For zero-based indexing the parent is floor((i−1)/2). Compare with that parent and swap only when heap order is violated.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Parent of index 1 is 0; swap 2 with 3 to obtain [2,3,4,5]. Heap order is restored. The second swap reaches the root. Other branches were already ordered and do not need global sorting.

examples.strategy: Append to preserve completeness, then repair heap order only along the ancestor path.
examples.answer: Parent of index 1 is 0; swap 2 with 3 to obtain [2,3,4,5]. Heap order is restored.
examples.verification: In [2,3,4,5], 2≤3, 2≤4 and 3≤5, so all parent-child inequalities hold; a heap need not be a fully sorted array.

steps.title: Append

steps.title: Matrix entries

steps.title: List entries
steps.explanation: Store 2000 neighbor entries plus 1000 vertex headers, with implementation-dependent overhead.

tutorials.title: Bottom-up heap construction and its linear work bound
tutorials.body:
A binary min-heap combines a complete binary-tree shape with a local ordering rule: every parent is at most each of its children. Its zero-based array children are 2i+1 and 2i+2. Bottom-up construction begins at floor(n/2)−1, the last internal vertex, and sifts each internal vertex downward while visiting indices in decreasing order. Leaves already satisfy heap order.
A sift compares available children, chooses the smaller one and exchanges it with an oversized parent. Continue from that child's position until heap order holds or a leaf is reached. Choosing an arbitrary child can leave the other child smaller than its parent. Previously repaired child subtrees are essential: they make a local sift sufficient for repairing the current subtree.
The total work is linear because most vertices have small height. The number of vertices able to descend at least h levels is at most floor(n/2^h); summing these possible descents over h gives less than n. Constant comparisons per descended level and one initial check per internal vertex preserve \(O(n)\). example.prompt: Build a min-heap bottom up from [9,4,7,1,6,3,2], using zero-based indices and the smaller child for each sift.
example.strategy: Start at internal index two → Repair index one → Repair the root → Explain total work

steps.title: Start at internal index two
steps.explanation: Its children contain 3 and 2; exchange 7 with 2 to obtain [9,4,2,1,6,3,7].

steps.title: Repair index one
steps.explanation: Its children are 1 and 6. Exchange 4 with 1 to obtain [9,1,2,4,6,3,7].

steps.title: Repair the root
steps.explanation: Exchange 9 with child 1, then exchange that 9 with child 4. The array becomes [1,4,2,9,6,3,7].

steps.title: Explain total work
steps.explanation: At most this many downward levels are available across all vertices; repeatedly charging every vertex a full log n height is an overestimate.

example.answer: The min-heap is [1,4,2,9,6,3,7]. This construction used four downward exchanges and has \(O(n)\) total work in general.
example.verification: The parent checks are 1≤4,2; 4≤9,6; and 2≤3,7. The array still contains exactly the original seven values and retains the complete shape.

In a min-heap, compare both children before sifting down; in a max-heap, use the larger child instead. A heap's root gives an extreme value, but no global order is promised between unrelated vertices. Keeping a small min-heap can represent the largest k values of a stream, because its root is the least competitive retained candidate. examples.prompt: Extract the maximum from max-heap [10,7,8,2,3,4]. Show root replacement and repair.
examples.strategy: Remove the extreme → Choose the larger child → Finish at the leaf

steps.title: Remove the extreme
steps.explanation: Return ten and move final value four to the root, leaving [4,7,8,2,3].

steps.title: Choose the larger child
steps.explanation: Eight is larger than seven, so swap the root with the child at index two.

steps.title: Finish at the leaf
steps.explanation: The moved four has no children in the active array, yielding [8,7,4,2,3].

examples.answer: Extracted 10; remaining heap [8,7,4,2,3].
examples.verification: Eight dominates seven and four; seven dominates two and three. Completeness follows from deleting the final slot.

examples.prompt: Maintain the largest three stream values using a size-three min-heap for arrivals 4,1,7,2,9. Show replacements.
examples.strategy: Fill the retained set → Replace the smallest retained value → Repair after nine arrives

steps.title: Fill the retained set
steps.explanation: The first three arrivals form min-heap [1,4,7].

steps.title: Replace the smallest retained value
steps.explanation: Two exceeds root one, so replacement yields [2,4,7].

steps.title: Repair after nine arrives
steps.explanation: Replace root two by nine and sift with four, producing [4,9,7].

examples.answer: The retained values are 4,7,9; the third-largest stream value is 4.
examples.verification: Sorting the whole stream gives 1,2,4,7,9, whose largest three agree with the heap contents.

examples.prompt: Is min-heap [1,8,2,9,10,3,4] invalid because sibling eight exceeds sibling two?
examples.strategy: Check the root → Check lower parents → Reject a false extra invariant

steps.title: Check the root
steps.explanation: One is no larger than either eight or two.

steps.title: Check lower parents
steps.explanation: Eight is no larger than nine and ten; two is no larger than three and four.

steps.title: Reject a false extra invariant
steps.explanation: Heap order compares parents with children, not siblings or the whole array sequence.

examples.answer: It is a valid min-heap despite being globally unsorted.
examples.verification: All six parent-child inequalities hold; the sibling pair supplies no heap violation.

example.prompt: Vertices are A,B,C,D. Directed arcs are \(A\to B\), \(A\to C\), C→B and B→B; self-loops are allowed. Find indegrees, outdegrees and vertices reachable from A.
example.strategy: Count outgoing arcs → Count incoming arcs → Follow directions → Check totals

steps.title: Count outgoing arcs
steps.explanation: The loop at B has B as its source exactly once.

steps.title: Count incoming arcs
steps.explanation: B receives arcs from A and C plus its own loop.

steps.title: Follow directions
steps.explanation: A reaches B and C. Following their arcs adds no new vertex; D is isolated.

steps.title: Check totals
steps.explanation: Each of the four arcs contributes once to each total.

example.answer: Indegrees are (0,3,1,0), outdegrees are (2,1,1,0), and the vertices reachable from A are A,B,C.
example.verification: The sums agree with four arcs. D remains in the graph even though it contributes no adjacency entries and cannot be reached from A.

examples.prompt: Undirected vertices P,Q,R have edges P–Q and Q–R. Compute degrees and verify the edge count.
examples.strategy: Count endpoint incidences → Sum degrees → Recover the edge count

steps.title: Count endpoint incidences
steps.explanation: P meets one edge, Q meets two, and R meets one.

steps.title: Sum degrees
steps.explanation: Every undirected edge was counted at both endpoints.

steps.title: Recover the edge count
steps.explanation: The handshaking identity matches the supplied edge list.

examples.answer: Degrees are 1,2,1 and there are two edges.
examples.verification: The adjacency lengths [1,2,1] provide the same incidence totals.

examples.prompt: Directed graph \(A\to B\), \(B\to C\), C→A, C→D has four vertices. Is it weakly connected or strongly connected?
examples.strategy: Inspect the underlying edges → Establish the directed core → Test the final vertex

steps.title: Inspect the underlying edges
steps.explanation: Ignoring orientation joins A,B,C,D in one component.

steps.title: Establish the directed core
steps.explanation: A,B,C reach one another through their directed cycle.

steps.title: Test the final vertex
steps.explanation: D has no outgoing arc, so it cannot return to A or reach the cycle.

examples.answer: The graph is weakly connected but not strongly connected.
examples.verification: The explicit failure D→A refutes strong connectivity, while the undirected path D–C–B–A verifies weak connectivity.

examples.prompt: An undirected graph has two parallel A–B edges and one loop at A. What are degrees A,B and the degree sum?
examples.strategy: Count parallel incidences → Count the loop correctly → Check the identity

steps.title: Count parallel incidences
steps.explanation: Each A–B edge adds one to each endpoint, giving two at A and two at B.

steps.title: Count the loop correctly
steps.explanation: The loop contributes two incidences to A, not one.

steps.title: Check the identity
steps.explanation: All three edges are accounted for.
