examples.verification: Counting the loop once would give an odd total five, contradicting the undirected degree-sum invariant.

tutorials.title: Build and traverse a directed adjacency list
tutorials.body:
An adjacency list gives each vertex a collection of its outgoing neighbors. A directed arc u→v appears in u's list; it need not appear in v's list. An undirected edge normally produces two entries, one at each endpoint. Store a list header even for an isolated vertex, whose neighbor collection is empty. Weighted graphs require a weight alongside each neighbor, and parallel-edge conventions determine whether repeated entries are allowed.
An edge list can be converted by starting with all lists empty and appending each destination to its source list. Preserve or sort neighbor order according to the stated traversal rule, because exact BFS or DFS discovery order can depend on it. The representation does not require vertices' labels to be numeric array indices; a separate mapping can connect labels to storage.
Enumerating u's neighbors costs proportional to its outdegree, and enumerating all lists costs Θ(V+E), including the empty headers. Testing whether a particular arc exists may require scanning u's list unless an additional lookup structure is maintained. Do not treat adjacency lists as giving the same constant-time membership test as a direct-access matrix.

example.prompt: Build outgoing adjacency lists in the supplied order for vertices A,B,C,D and arcs \(A\to C\), C→B, \(A\to B\). Then enumerate A's neighbors and test B→A.
example.strategy: Create every header → Append by source → Perform requested operations

steps.title: Create every header
steps.explanation: Initialize A=[], B=[], C=[], D=[] so the isolated vertex is represented.

steps.title: Append by source
steps.explanation: \(A\to C\) and \(A\to B\) give A=[C,B]; C→B gives C=[B]. The other lists stay empty.

steps.title: Perform requested operations
steps.explanation: Enumerating A visits C then B. Testing B→A scans B\'s empty outgoing list and reports absence.

example.answer: A=[C,B], B=[], C=[B], D=[]. A has two outgoing neighbors; B→A is absent.
example.verification: There are four headers and three neighbor entries, matching V+E storage. The presence of \(A\to B\) does not imply the reverse directed arc.

depth.body: Adjacency lists represent stored incidences rather than all possible vertex pairs. For directed input, outgoing lists contain one entry per arc; for undirected input, the same logical edge normally appears at both endpoints. Neighbor order is part of a trace when discovery order is requested, but it is not an additional graph edge. To remove an undirected edge, repair both endpoint lists. Membership cost depends on list lengths unless extra indexing is provided, whereas enumeration touches only actual neighbors. Include empty headers and parallel entries under the stated graph model. Compare traversal work using the total number of entries rather than assuming E always equals that total.

examples.prompt: Build undirected adjacency lists for vertices 1,2,3 and edges 1–2,1–3, listing neighbors increasingly.
examples.strategy: Add the first edge at both ends → Add the second edge at both ends → Read all lists

steps.title: Add the first edge at both ends
steps.explanation: The edge 1–2 adds neighbor 2 to vertex 1's list and neighbor 1 to vertex 2's list.

steps.title: Add the second edge at both ends
steps.explanation: The edge 1–3 adds neighbor 3 to vertex 1's list and neighbor 1 to vertex 3's list.

examples.answer: The representation has three headers and four neighbor entries.
examples.verification: The entry total is 2E=4, and every undirected incidence has its reverse entry.

examples.prompt: Directed lists are A:[B,D], B:[C], C:[], D:[C]. Enumerate reachable vertices from B and count scanned entries.
examples.strategy: Start from B → Expand C → Separate unvisited headers

steps.title: Start from B
steps.explanation: Mark B and inspect its one outgoing entry C.

steps.title: Expand C
steps.explanation: Its list is empty, so the search discovers nothing further.

steps.title: Separate unvisited headers
steps.explanation: A and D are unreachable from B and their outgoing entries are not scanned by this single-source search.

examples.answer: Reachable set {B,C}; one neighbor entry is scanned.
examples.verification: The only directed route starting at B is \(B\to C\); incoming arcs to B do not permit a reverse move to A.

examples.prompt: Undirected lists are A:[B], B:[A,C], C:[B]. Delete edge B–C by removing only C from B's list. Is the representation consistent?
examples.strategy: Remove the first incidence → Inspect the reverse incidence → Repair both endpoints

steps.title: Remove the first incidence
steps.explanation: B becomes [A], so its list no longer describes an edge to C.

steps.title: Inspect the reverse incidence
steps.explanation: C still contains B, claiming the same undirected edge exists.

steps.title: Repair both endpoints
steps.explanation: Remove B from C's list as well, making C empty.

examples.answer: No; both reverse entries must be removed.
examples.verification: After proper deletion the total entries fall from four to two, exactly twice the remaining one edge.

tutorials.title: Build an adjacency matrix and interpret its rows
tutorials.body:
An adjacency matrix reserves one entry for each ordered pair of vertices. Fix a row and column order first. In an unweighted directed graph, set M[u,v]=1 when u→v exists and zero otherwise. An undirected matrix is symmetric because each edge is usable in both directions; directed input has no such requirement. A permitted self-loop appears on the diagonal.
A row describes outgoing arcs from its vertex, while a column describes incoming arcs to its vertex. Row and column sums therefore give outdegree and indegree for a binary directed matrix without parallel arcs. A matrix for a multigraph may store counts instead, and a weighted matrix needs a no-edge marker that cannot be confused with a valid zero-weight edge.
Matrix storage is Θ(V²) regardless of edge count. A specified arc can be checked in constant time once vertex indices are known, but finding all neighbors of one vertex requires inspecting its whole row. Traversing all rows costs Θ(V²), even when most entries are zero. Verify representation choices and vertex order before reading degrees or tracing a graph algorithm.

example.prompt: Use row/column order A,B,C for directed arcs \(A\to B\), \(B\to C\) and C→B, without self-loops. Construct the matrix and find B's indegree and outdegree.
example.strategy: Initialize absent pairs → Set the directed entries → Read B\'s row and column

steps.title: Initialize absent pairs
steps.explanation: All nine ordered pairs start absent, including diagonal pairs.

steps.title: Set the directed entries
steps.explanation: Each supplied arc changes its source row and destination column only.

steps.title: Read B\'s row and column
steps.explanation: Row B has the arc to C; column B receives arcs from A and C.

example.answer: The rows are [0,1,0], [0,0,1], [0,1,0]. B has indegree 2 and outdegree 1.
example.verification: The three ones match the three arcs. M[A,B]=1 but M[B,A]=0, demonstrating why a directed matrix need not be symmetric.

depth.body: A matrix needs a fixed vertex order and an explicit meaning for every entry. Boolean entries can record simple edge existence, while counts can preserve parallel-edge multiplicity and weights need an unambiguous absent-edge marker. Matrix rows enable direct membership tests, but enumerating a sparse vertex still scans all columns. Undirected symmetry is a verification rule only under an undirected model. For a weighted shortest-path initialization, a zero diagonal represents the empty route while a genuine negative loop must remain distinguishable. Separate graph adjacency from distance closure: a matrix entry produced by a multi-edge route is not a newly supplied original edge.

examples.prompt: For undirected path X–Y–Z with order X,Y,Z, write the adjacency matrix and test X–Z.
examples.strategy: Initialize zero entries → Set symmetric pairs → Read the requested pair

steps.title: Initialize zero entries
steps.explanation: There are nine ordered-pair cells and no self-loops.

steps.title: Set symmetric pairs
steps.explanation: Each undirected edge changes two mirrored cells.

steps.title: Read the requested pair
steps.explanation: X and Z have a route via Y but no direct edge.

examples.answer: The displayed matrix represents the path; X–Z is absent.
examples.verification: Symmetry and four off-diagonal ones agree with two undirected edges.

examples.prompt: A 500-vertex matrix is used to enumerate all outgoing neighbors of each vertex, although the directed graph has only 700 edges. How many cells are inspected?
examples.strategy: Count one row → Count all rows → Compare stored sparsity

steps.title: Count one row
steps.explanation: A matrix row includes a position for every possible destination.

steps.title: Count all rows
steps.explanation: All vertices require all their row positions inspected.

steps.title: Compare stored sparsity
steps.explanation: Seven hundred actual edges change how many cells are nonzero, not how many positions are scanned.

examples.answer: 250,000 cells; Θ(V²) enumeration work.
examples.verification: Summing 500 scans over 500 rows independently yields the same count.

examples.prompt: Weighted matrix uses zero for absent edges, but graph contains edge \(A\to B\) of weight zero. Can a reader distinguish it from no edge?
examples.strategy: Encode the two cases → Attempt a membership test → Repair the representation

steps.title: Encode the two cases
steps.explanation: Both a missing pair and this valid zero-weight edge receive the same value zero.

steps.title: Attempt a membership test
steps.explanation: A test based solely on that cell cannot select the correct case.

steps.title: Repair the representation
steps.explanation: Use an additional presence bit or a distinct sentinel such as infinity for absence.

examples.answer: No; the encoding is ambiguous.
examples.verification: Two different graphs map to the same matrix cell, so no decoding rule can recover both correctly.

name: Algorithms
description: Learn to choose, prove and analyze algorithms

lessons.title: Asymptotic time, space and recurrences
lessons.intuition: Asymptotic analysis studies how cost grows with input size. It abstracts constants but must still describe the operation being measured and the case: worst-case, average-case or amortized. A bound without those assumptions can mislead.

sections.title: Bounds and cases
sections.body: f=O(g) means f is eventually at most a constant multiple of g; Ω is a lower bound and Θ is both. A worst-case time function maximizes over size-n inputs. Average-case needs an input distribution; amortized cost averages over an operation sequence without necessarily involving randomness. Best-case \(O(n)\) does not imply worst-case \(O(n)\).

sections.title: Loops and recursion
sections.body: Consecutive loops add costs; nested loops sum inner counts. A triangular loop executes Σᵢ₌₁ⁿi=\(\frac{n(n+1)}2\) operations. Halving a variable repeatedly yields \(\Theta(\log n)\) iterations. For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f with n^(log_b a) under the Master theorem’s applicable conditions; irregular recurrences may need a recursion tree or substitution.

sections.title: Space accounting
sections.body: Report input storage and auxiliary storage separately. Recursive stack memory follows the maximum active depth and frame size. Sequential calls reuse stack space once previous calls return. An algorithm can run \(\Theta(n\log n)\) total time with only \(\Theta(\log n)\) recursive stack if frames use constant additional space and divide inputs without copying.

sections.title: A recursion-tree comparison
sections.body: T(n)=T(n/2)+1 does constant work at each of \(\log_2 n\) levels, giving \(\Theta(\log n)\). T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 has increasingly many nodes and \(\Theta(n)\) total calls. \(T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\) has total n work at each of logarithmically many levels, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\). All three have logarithmic depth, demonstrating why depth is not a time bound. For an iterative doubling loop i=1;i<n;i*=2, iterations also grow logarithmically; a triangular incrementing loop instead requires summing linearly increasing counts. Specify input size in units that match the algorithm: numeric value n and bit length log n are not the same complexity parameter.

examples.prompt: Analyse for i=1..n, for j=1..i, one operation

steps.title: Express the work as a sum
steps.explanation: The inner loop length depends on i, so n×n is an upper bound but not the exact count.

steps.title: Evaluate the arithmetic series
steps.explanation: Pairing first and last terms gives average (n+1)/2 across n terms.

steps.title: Establish a tight bound
steps.explanation: Both upper and lower bounds are quadratic. Θ, rather than only O, expresses this tight order.

examples.given: For each i=1,…,n, the inner loop performs i constant-time operations.
examples.goal: Find the total operation count and tight asymptotic growth.
examples.strategy: Sum the changing inner bound; nesting alone does not specify the exact count.
examples.answer: \(n(n+1)/2\) body operations; \(\Theta(n^2)\).
examples.verification: For n=3, counts 1+2+3=6 agree with 3×4/2. Loop-control overhead has the same asymptotic order.

examples.prompt: Solve \(T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\)
steps: Each recursion level performs total n combining work.
There are \(\log_2 n\) levels before constant-size leaves.
Total is \(\Theta(n\log n)\); a balanced recursion uses \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack depth with constant-size frames.

pitfalls: Do not confuse maximum depth with total call count.
Big-O alone does not assert a tight bound.
revision: Time counts all work; auxiliary space counts simultaneous storage.

checks.prompt: A balanced recursion has \(\Theta(\log n)\) depth. Does that prove \(\Theta(\log n)\) running time?
checks.hint: Compare binary search and merge sort.
checks.explanation: Depth describes one active path. Branching and combine costs determine total running time; balanced merge sort has log depth but n log n work.
options: No; total work across all branches must be counted
Yes if it has two child calls
Time and stack depth are always equal

checks.prompt: Starting at 32, how many divisions by 2 reach 1?
checks.hint: Count powers of two.
checks.explanation: 32→16→8→4→2→1: five divisions.

lessons.concept: Asymptotic analysis studies how cost grows with input size. It abstracts constants but must still describe the operation being measured and the case: worst-case, average-case or amortized. A bound without those assumptions can mislead.
lessons.method:
A running-time function counts operations as input size grows. Worst-case T(n) maximizes that count over legal inputs of size n; best and average case are different functions. Big O bounds growth from above, Ω from below and Θ from both, after some threshold using positive constants. A tight \(\Theta(n^2)\) function is also O(n³), so “an O bound” is not necessarily its most informative one.
Separate the input distribution from the asymptotic notation. Ω does not inherently mean best case, and O does not inherently mean worst case: either can bound a chosen best, worst or average function. Ignore constant factors and lower-order terms only after deriving or bounding work.
Nested loop bounds may depend on each other; sum iteration counts rather than automatically multiplying n by n. Logarithmic work typically arises from repeatedly shrinking a range by a constant factor. Express complexity in the stated input-size measure: a numeric parameter can be exponentially large relative to its binary encoding length, which makes pseudopolynomial distinctions relevant. Space complexity describes memory needed at peak execution, not the sum of all memory ever allocated over time. Auxiliary space commonly excludes input storage but includes work structures and recursion frames; output inclusion depends on the convention. Report what is counted. An algorithm can use linear time while storing only constant extra state.
For recursion, count the longest active call chain and storage retained in each frame. Sequential recursive branches reuse stack capacity after returning; adding the full sizes of separate finished subtrees overestimates peak stack. Large local buffers can dominate even at small depth. Iterative simulation may replace call frames with an explicit stack without changing the needed information.
In-place algorithms use only limited extra storage under their defined convention; recursive quicksort can have in-place partitioning and still use stack space. Memoization adds stored subproblem results and can exchange memory for time. Distinguish \(O(1)\) references to an existing input from creating an \(O(n)\) copy of its contents; a slice or allocation’s actual semantics matter. Worst-case running time is the maximum work performed among all legal inputs of a fixed size. First define the measured operation and the input size, then derive that maximum. Big O describes an upper growth bound on the chosen function; it does not by itself say that the function is worst case. Best-case and average-case running times can also receive Big O bounds.
For a sequential search that stops at its first match, input order and target presence affect the comparison count. A target in the first position needs one equality test. A target only at the last position or absent altogether forces all n positions to be tested. Those inputs achieve the upper bound, so they justify a tight worst-case result rather than only a possible estimate.
When analyzing nested loops, recursion or graph algorithms, exhibit the pattern that makes the work large and prove that no legal input requires more. Do not infer an average by averaging the best and worst endpoints; an average needs a specified distribution. Exact counts and asymptotic classes answer different questions, so retain the concrete count before simplifying its growth. f=O(g) means f is eventually at most a constant multiple of g; Ω is a lower bound and Θ is both. A worst-case time function maximizes over size-n inputs. Average-case needs an input distribution; amortized cost averages over an operation sequence without necessarily involving randomness. Best-case \(O(n)\) does not imply worst-case \(O(n)\). Consecutive loops add costs; nested loops sum inner counts. A triangular loop executes Σᵢ₌₁ⁿi=\(\frac{n(n+1)}2\) operations. Halving a variable repeatedly yields \(\Theta(\log n)\) iterations. For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f with n^(log_b a) under the Master theorem’s applicable conditions; irregular recurrences may need a recursion tree or substitution. Report input storage and auxiliary storage separately. Recursive stack memory follows the maximum active depth and frame size. Sequential calls reuse stack space once previous calls return. An algorithm can run \(\Theta(n\log n)\) total time with only \(\Theta(\log n)\) recursive stack if frames use constant additional space and divide inputs without copying. T(n)=T(n/2)+1 does constant work at each of \(\log_2 n\) levels, giving \(\Theta(\log n)\). T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 has increasingly many nodes and \(\Theta(n)\) total calls. \(T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\) has total n work at each of logarithmically many levels, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\). All three have logarithmic depth, demonstrating why depth is not a time bound. For an iterative doubling loop i=1;i<n;i*=2, iterations also grow logarithmically; a triangular incrementing loop instead requires summing linearly increasing counts. Specify input size in units that match the algorithm: numeric value n and bit length log n are not the same complexity parameter. Big O is a quantified eventual upper bound. Choose positive constants c and n₀ so that the measured nonnegative function never exceeds c times the comparison function after n₀. One function can satisfy many upper bounds, and the tightest familiar one is usually the useful answer when a question asks complexity. Derive the operation function first; a nested loop with geometrically changing limits is not automatically quadratic. Logarithm bases differ only by constant factors for fixed bases greater than one. Check growth ratios or explicit inequalities to establish bounds, and never replace an upper-bound relation with equality of growth without also proving a corresponding lower bound. Theta expresses matching eventual upper and lower growth bounds for one specified function. Both inequalities must hold beyond a common threshold; testing several small inputs or identifying the largest written term is not by itself a proof. Summations often expose the needed bounds directly, as with dependent nested loops. A function that behaves differently on even and odd sizes may fail a proposed tight class even though it has a valid upper bound and a weaker lower bound. State the function's domain and require positive constants. Theta does not specify an exact count, nor does it imply that best, average and worst cases all share that class. Omega supplies an eventual lower bound on a chosen running-time function, and it does not inherently refer to best case. Lower bounds can come from compulsory output, inspection requirements or a decision tree with enough distinguishable outcomes. State the computational model: a comparison-sort lower bound does not prohibit faster methods with restricted integer keys. An algorithm-specific worst-case lower bound may be witnessed by one hard input family, whereas a best-case lower bound must hold even on the easiest legal inputs. Distinguish these quantifiers before translating a statement. To refute a claimed lower bound, find arbitrarily large sizes where the function-to-bound ratio becomes too small. Peak space measures objects live at the same instant. Draw allocation and release intervals rather than adding every allocation that occurs during the run. The convention for input and output storage should be explicit: total space may include them, whereas auxiliary space usually describes extra working memory. A fixed set of indices can operate on a large supplied array without copying it. Recursive algorithms add frame storage even when their array updates are in place, and retained buffers can dominate those frames. Shared references do not duplicate the referenced data, but a materialized slice does. Prove both a largest simultaneous allocation requirement and a matching upper bound before giving a tight class. A worst-case claim needs both a universal upper bound and inputs that make the algorithm approach that bound. Identify the primitive being counted, because successful comparisons, loop-condition checks and assignments have different exact totals. Input size must match the data representation; a numeric capacity is not interchangeable with its binary bit length. Structural worst cases depend on the actual policy: a sorted input is harmful to a first-pivot quicksort but useful to some other algorithms. When a loop stops early, maximize the executed prefix instead of blindly multiplying declared bounds. Separate the finite exact maximum from its eventual growth class, and avoid interpreting a loose upper bound as a tight result.

gateGuide.recognize: Identify input size, measured operation and worst/average/amortized case before simplifying growth. A recursion depth is not a total-time bound.
method: Count actual loop ranges, using summation for dependent inner bounds.
Draw recursion levels or solve a recurrence, keeping combine work and branching.
For space count simultaneously live allocations and recursive frames, excluding or including input storage as requested.

traps.claim: Nested loops always give n²
traps.why: An inner loop may halve, depend on i, or have a constant range; count its actual operations.

traps.claim: Numeric n and bit length n are interchangeable
traps.why: A capacity-W dynamic program can be polynomial in W but exponential in the bits needed to encode W.

tutorials.title: Asymptotic bounds and worst-case functions
tutorials.body:
A running-time function counts operations as input size grows. Worst-case T(n) maximizes that count over legal inputs of size n; best and average case are different functions. Big O bounds growth from above, Ω from below and Θ from both, after some threshold using positive constants. A tight \(\Theta(n^2)\) function is also O(n³), so “an O bound” is not necessarily its most informative one.
Separate the input distribution from the asymptotic notation. Ω does not inherently mean best case, and O does not inherently mean worst case: either can bound a chosen best, worst or average function. Ignore constant factors and lower-order terms only after deriving or bounding work.
Nested loop bounds may depend on each other; sum iteration counts rather than automatically multiplying n by n. Logarithmic work typically arises from repeatedly shrinking a range by a constant factor. Express complexity in the stated input-size measure: a numeric parameter can be exponentially large relative to its binary encoding length, which makes pseudopolynomial distinctions relevant.

example.prompt: Find tight growth of T(n)=3n²+5n+7.
example.strategy: Lower bound → Upper bound → Conclude

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.explanation: All terms are nonnegative for n≥1.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.explanation: Use n≤n² and 1≤n².

steps.title: Conclude
steps.explanation: Both constant-factor bounds hold.

example.answer: \(\Theta(n^2)\); O(n³) is true but loose.
example.verification: The conclusion concerns the supplied T, regardless of whether it represents worst or average case.

depth.body: Big O is a quantified eventual upper bound. Choose positive constants c and n₀ so that the measured nonnegative function never exceeds c times the comparison function after n₀. One function can satisfy many upper bounds, and the tightest familiar one is usually the useful answer when a question asks complexity. Derive the operation function first; a nested loop with geometrically changing limits is not automatically quadratic. Logarithm bases differ only by constant factors for fixed bases greater than one. Check growth ratios or explicit inequalities to establish bounds, and never replace an upper-bound relation with equality of growth without also proving a corresponding lower bound.

examples.prompt: Prove T(n)=2n \(\log_2 n\)+3n is \(O(n^2)\) for integers n≥2.
examples.strategy: Bound the logarithm → Substitute → Choose witnesses

steps.title: Bound the logarithm
steps.explanation: This valid inequality supplies a simple upper estimate.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.explanation: For n≥2, the remaining linear term is also bounded quadratically.

steps.title: Choose witnesses
steps.explanation: These constants satisfy the eventual upper-bound definition.

examples.answer: T(n) is \(O(n^2)\); this is a valid loose bound.
examples.verification: Its tighter \(\Theta(n\log n)\) growth does not contradict the proved quadratic upper bound.

examples.prompt: For n=2^k, a loop uses i=1,2,4,... while i<n and performs i operations at each value. Give a useful Big O bound.
examples.strategy: List the performed blocks → Sum their work → Bound uniformly

steps.title: List the performed blocks
steps.explanation: The iteration count is logarithmic but block sizes grow.

steps.title: Sum their work
steps.explanation: A geometric sum replaces multiplication by n at every iteration.

steps.title: Bound uniformly
steps.explanation: Choosing c=1 gives an \(O(n)\) upper bound on the counted operations.

examples.answer: Total operations n−1, hence \(O(n)\).
examples.verification: For n=8 the blocks 1,2,4 total seven, matching the derived function.

examples.prompt: T(n)=100n is \(O(n^2)\). Does that mean T(n) is \(\Theta(n^2)\)?
examples.strategy: Exhibit an upper bound → Test the missing lower bound → Give tight growth

steps.title: Exhibit an upper bound
steps.explanation: The supplied O relation is valid.

steps.title: Test the missing lower bound
steps.explanation: No positive constant fraction of n² bounds T from below eventually.

steps.title: Give tight growth
steps.explanation: Upper and lower linear factors are both exactly one hundred.

examples.answer: No; the quadratic upper bound is loose.
examples.verification: For increasingly large n, doubling n doubles T rather than quadrupling it.

depth.body: Theta expresses matching eventual upper and lower growth bounds for one specified function. Both inequalities must hold beyond a common threshold; testing several small inputs or identifying the largest written term is not by itself a proof. Summations often expose the needed bounds directly, as with dependent nested loops. A function that behaves differently on even and odd sizes may fail a proposed tight class even though it has a valid upper bound and a weaker lower bound. State the function's domain and require positive constants. Theta does not specify an exact count, nor does it imply that best, average and worst cases all share that class.

examples.prompt: Establish a tight bound for T(n)=5n+11 on integers n≥1.
examples.strategy: Keep a positive lower term → Bound the constant by a linear term → Combine witnesses

steps.title: Keep a positive lower term
steps.explanation: The additive eleven cannot reduce the linear contribution.

steps.title: Bound the constant by a linear term
steps.explanation: This holds for all n≥1.

steps.title: Combine witnesses
steps.explanation: Both positive constant factors apply from the same threshold.

examples.answer: T(n)=\(\Theta(n)\).
examples.verification: The ratio T(n)/n=5+11/n stays between five and sixteen and approaches five.

examples.prompt: An algorithm compares every pair (i,j) with 1≤j≤i≤n. Prove its comparison count is \(\Theta(n^2)\).
examples.strategy: Derive the exact count → Bound below → Bound above

steps.title: Derive the exact count
steps.explanation: Row i contributes i comparisons.

steps.title: Bound below
steps.explanation: The additional linear term is nonnegative.

steps.title: Bound above
steps.explanation: Using n≤n² produces a matching quadratic factor.

examples.verification: At n=4 the ten explicit comparisons lie between eight and sixteen, consistent with the bounds.

examples.prompt: Let T(n)=n² for even n and T(n)=n for odd n. Is T(n)=\(\Theta(n^2)\)?
examples.strategy: Confirm the upper bound → Examine odd sizes → Reject uniform lower witnesses

steps.title: Confirm the upper bound
steps.explanation: Both branches satisfy the quadratic upper bound.

steps.title: Examine odd sizes
steps.explanation: Along arbitrarily large odd n, the ratio tends to zero.

steps.title: Reject uniform lower witnesses
steps.explanation: Any proposed positive quadratic lower factor fails on a sufficiently large odd size.

examples.answer: No. It is \(O(n^2)\) and Ω(n), but not \(\Theta(n^2)\).
examples.verification: Even sizes also prevent \(\Theta(n)\), so no single argument based on only one branch establishes either proposed tight class.

depth.body: Omega supplies an eventual lower bound on a chosen running-time function, and it does not inherently refer to best case. Lower bounds can come from compulsory output, inspection requirements or a decision tree with enough distinguishable outcomes. State the computational model: a comparison-sort lower bound does not prohibit faster methods with restricted integer keys. An algorithm-specific worst-case lower bound may be witnessed by one hard input family, whereas a best-case lower bound must hold even on the easiest legal inputs. Distinguish these quantifiers before translating a statement. To refute a claimed lower bound, find arbitrarily large sizes where the function-to-bound ratio becomes too small.

examples.prompt: Why must an algorithm finding the maximum of an arbitrary unsorted n-element array inspect every element in the worst case?
examples.strategy: Assume an unread location → Change only that location → Derive compulsory work

steps.title: Assume an unread location
steps.explanation: Suppose the algorithm finishes while some array element has never been inspected.

steps.title: Change only that location
steps.explanation: An adversary can place a value larger than the reported maximum there without altering any observed value.

steps.title: Derive compulsory work
steps.explanation: Correctness on all arrays requires inspecting all n candidates.

examples.answer: The worst-case inspection work is Ω(n).
examples.verification: A single linear scan attains \(O(n)\), matching the unavoidable inspection order.

examples.prompt: A deterministic comparison sort handles four distinct keys. Derive a lower bound on its worst-case number of binary comparisons.
examples.strategy: Count possible orders → Count tree leaves → Solve the integer bound

steps.title: Count possible orders
steps.explanation: Each distinct input ordering requires a distinguishable sorted permutation.

steps.title: Count tree leaves
steps.explanation: A binary comparison tree of worst-case depth h must distinguish all orders.

steps.title: Solve the integer bound
steps.explanation: Four comparisons give only sixteen outcomes.

examples.answer: At least five comparisons in the worst case.
examples.verification: The capacity check 2^4=16<24≤32=2^5 independently confirms the threshold.

examples.prompt: Linear search has worst-case Ω(n). Must every successful search use at least a linear number of comparisons?
examples.strategy: Identify the quantified function → Construct an easy input → Separate cases

steps.title: Identify the quantified function
steps.explanation: The bound concerns the maximum comparison count among inputs of size n.

steps.title: Construct an easy input
steps.explanation: Place the target in the first slot, so search returns after one comparison for every n.

steps.title: Separate cases
steps.explanation: This constant best-case family does not affect the linear maximum attained by absent targets.

examples.answer: No; a first-slot match takes one comparison.
examples.verification: The same algorithm has best-case Θ(1) and worst-case \(\Theta(n)\), so the two functions must not be conflated.

tutorials.title: Auxiliary space, live allocations and recursion
tutorials.body:
Space complexity describes memory needed at peak execution, not the sum of all memory ever allocated over time. Auxiliary space commonly excludes input storage but includes work structures and recursion frames; output inclusion depends on the convention. Report what is counted. An algorithm can use linear time while storing only constant extra state.
For recursion, count the longest active call chain and storage retained in each frame. Sequential recursive branches reuse stack capacity after returning; adding the full sizes of separate finished subtrees overestimates peak stack. Large local buffers can dominate even at small depth. Iterative simulation may replace call frames with an explicit stack without changing the needed information.
In-place algorithms use only limited extra storage under their defined convention; recursive quicksort can have in-place partitioning and still use stack space. Memoization adds stored subproblem results and can exchange memory for time. Distinguish \(O(1)\) references to an existing input from creating an \(O(n)\) copy of its contents; a slice or allocation’s actual semantics matter.

example.prompt: A binary search is implemented iteratively with low, high and mid indices.
example.strategy: Existing input → Working state → Bound

steps.title: Existing input
steps.explanation: The array is supplied and need not be copied.

steps.title: Working state
steps.explanation: Only a constant number of numeric indices and comparison variables are live.

steps.title: Bound
steps.explanation: The number of work variables is independent of n.

example.answer: Constant auxiliary space.
example.verification: A recursive version commonly needs \(O(\log n)\) call frames unless the implementation removes them.

depth.body: Peak space measures objects live at the same instant. Draw allocation and release intervals rather than adding every allocation that occurs during the run. The convention for input and output storage should be explicit: total space may include them, whereas auxiliary space usually describes extra working memory. A fixed set of indices can operate on a large supplied array without copying it. Recursive algorithms add frame storage even when their array updates are in place, and retained buffers can dominate those frames. Shared references do not duplicate the referenced data, but a materialized slice does. Prove both a largest simultaneous allocation requirement and a matching upper bound before giving a tight class.

examples.prompt: Transpose an n×n matrix in place by swapping a[i][j] with a[j][i] for j>i, using three loop/index variables and one temporary.
examples.strategy: Keep the supplied input → Locate live working values → State the convention

steps.title: Keep the supplied input
steps.explanation: The matrix already exists and is not copied by the procedure.

steps.title: Locate live working values
steps.explanation: Only i,j,n and one temporary element are needed regardless of matrix dimension.

steps.title: State the convention
steps.explanation: Excluding the supplied matrix, working storage is constant.

examples.answer: Constant auxiliary space; the input matrix itself occupies \(\Theta(n^2)\).
examples.verification: Each off-diagonal pair is exchanged using the same temporary, whose storage is reused rather than accumulated.

examples.prompt: Balanced merge sort reuses one n-element merge buffer and has logarithmic recursion depth. Find peak auxiliary space.
examples.strategy: Count the shared buffer → Count active frames → Combine live requirements

steps.title: Count the shared buffer
steps.explanation: One allocation serves all merges rather than one fresh retained n-buffer per level.

steps.title: Count active frames
steps.explanation: Balanced recursive descent retains logarithmically many constant-sized frames.

steps.title: Combine live requirements
steps.explanation: The buffer dominates while also supplying a linear lower bound.

examples.answer: \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary space.
examples.verification: Even at maximum depth, adding logarithmic frame state cannot exceed the linear buffer order.

examples.prompt: An algorithm scans n input records with one index and writes n output records. It claims both auxiliary and total space are \(O(1)\). Assess this when output storage counts toward total space.
examples.strategy: Identify working state → Account for required output → Separate the measures

steps.title: Identify working state
steps.explanation: A streaming scan can use constant temporary state.

steps.title: Account for required output
steps.explanation: The completed n-record result must occupy linear storage under the stated convention.

steps.title: Separate the measures
steps.explanation: Excluding input/output gives constant auxiliary work storage; including output makes total space at least linear.

examples.answer: Auxiliary space can be \(O(1)\); total space is \(\Theta(n)\) if input/output records are counted.
examples.verification: The result alone supplies n simultaneously retained records, so constant total space is impossible here.

tutorials.title: Derive a worst-case function from actual inputs
tutorials.body:
Worst-case running time is the maximum work performed among all legal inputs of a fixed size. First define the measured operation and the input size, then derive that maximum. Big O describes an upper growth bound on the chosen function; it does not by itself say that the function is worst case. Best-case and average-case running times can also receive Big O bounds.
For a sequential search that stops at its first match, input order and target presence affect the comparison count. A target in the first position needs one equality test. A target only at the last position or absent altogether forces all n positions to be tested. Those inputs achieve the upper bound, so they justify a tight worst-case result rather than only a possible estimate.
When analyzing nested loops, recursion or graph algorithms, exhibit the pattern that makes the work large and prove that no legal input requires more. Do not infer an average by averaging the best and worst endpoints; an average needs a specified distribution. Exact counts and asymptotic classes answer different questions, so retain the concrete count before simplifying its growth.

example.prompt: Linear search checks indices 0 through n−1 until it finds target 8. Compare [8,1,2,3], [1,2,3,8] and [1,2,3,4], then derive worst-case equality comparisons for general n≥1.
example.strategy: Early success → Late success or failure → Generalize the maximum → Give tight growth

steps.title: Early success
steps.explanation: The first equality succeeds and terminates the search.

steps.title: Late success or failure
steps.explanation: Both inputs require checking every slot, although only one finds the target.

steps.title: Generalize the maximum
steps.explanation: No slot is checked twice, and an absent target makes all n checks necessary.

steps.title: Give tight growth
steps.explanation: The achievable lower bound and universal upper bound coincide.

example.answer: Worst-case linear search uses exactly n equality comparisons, giving \(\Theta(n)\) growth; the best case uses one.
example.verification: For n=4 the general bound predicts four comparisons, attained by both the final-match and absent-target inputs. No distribution was assumed.

depth.body: A worst-case claim needs both a universal upper bound and inputs that make the algorithm approach that bound. Identify the primitive being counted, because successful comparisons, loop-condition checks and assignments have different exact totals. Input size must match the data representation; a numeric capacity is not interchangeable with its binary bit length. Structural worst cases depend on the actual policy: a sorted input is harmful to a first-pivot quicksort but useful to some other algorithms. When a loop stops early, maximize the executed prefix instead of blindly multiplying declared bounds. Separate the finite exact maximum from its eventual growth class, and avoid interpreting a loose upper bound as a tight result.

examples.prompt: For i=1..n, an inner loop executes j=1..i with one operation. Derive the worst-case operation count.
examples.strategy: Count each row → Sum the rows → Bound the growth

steps.title: Count each row
steps.explanation: The inner counts are 1,2,3 through n; no data-dependent exit changes them.

steps.title: Sum the rows
steps.explanation: All rows execute, so this is also the maximum for size n.

steps.title: Bound the growth
steps.explanation: For n≥1 these matching quadratic bounds establish tight order.

examples.answer: Exactly \(\frac{n(n+1)}2\) operations; \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst-case time.
examples.verification: At n=3 the explicit rows 1+2+3 total six, matching the formula.

examples.prompt: Inclusive binary search on fifteen sorted distinct keys returns immediately on equality. What is the maximum number of midpoint comparisons?
examples.strategy: Build the deepest candidate path → Count tested midpoints → Translate the pattern

steps.title: Build the deepest candidate path
steps.explanation: The largest remaining lengths are 15,7,3,1 under halving.

steps.title: Count tested midpoints
steps.explanation: A target at a deepest leaf, or an appropriate absent target, requires one comparison per listed length.

steps.title: Translate the pattern
steps.explanation: The formula gives four under this convention.

examples.answer: Four midpoint comparisons.
examples.verification: A fifteen-node balanced decision tree has four levels including its root, consistent with the explicit length trace.

examples.prompt: An algorithm executes exactly n operations. A claim says its worst-case time is \(O(n^2)\), therefore it must take quadratic time. Assess the conclusion.
examples.strategy: Identify the actual function → Check the loose upper bound → Check tightness

steps.title: Identify the actual function
steps.explanation: No input changes the supplied count.

steps.title: Check the loose upper bound
steps.explanation: The \(O(n^2)\) statement is true as an upper bound.

steps.title: Check tightness
steps.explanation: No fixed positive quadratic lower factor holds.

examples.answer: \(O(n^2)\) is true, but tight worst-case growth is \(\Theta(n)\).
examples.verification: The stronger bound \(O(n)\) and lower bound Ω(n) coincide, disproving the inferred quadratic requirement.

lessons.title: Searching and sorting with invariants
lessons.intuition: A search or sort is easier to understand through its invariant: what remains true after every iteration or recursive step. Complexity then follows from how fast the unresolved region shrinks and how much work is done to combine results.

sections.title: Binary search
sections.body: Maintain a range that could contain the key in sorted data. Compare its midpoint, discard the half ruled out by ordering, and update bounds so the loop progresses. After k comparisons the candidate range is about n/2ᵏ, producing \(\Theta(\log n)\) worst-case time. Unsorted input destroys the discard argument. Boundary variants such as first occurrence need their own invariant.

sections.title: Comparison sorts
sections.body: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new key, giving \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst-case and \(\Theta(n)\) best-case on already sorted input. Merge sort recursively sorts halves and linearly merges them, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) and ordinarily \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary array storage. Heapsort builds a heap then repeatedly extracts, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) worst-case and an in-place array implementation.

sections.title: Quicksort and lower bounds
sections.body: Partition around a pivot, then recurse on both sides. Balanced partitions produce \(\Theta(n\log n)\); consistently extreme pivots produce \(\Theta(n^2)\). Randomization gives expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\), not a worst-case guarantee. General comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; counting/radix sorts exploit additional assumptions and are not counterexamples.

sections.title: Binary search with terminating bounds
sections.body: This version keeps an inclusive range [lo,hi]. On a failed comparison it removes the midpoint as well as the impossible half, ensuring progress even when one or two candidates remain. The midpoint formula avoids unnecessarily adding two large indices in fixed-width arithmetic. The returned −1 distinguishes absence from valid zero-based index 0. Sorting the input is a prerequisite; this routine does not verify that condition.
sections.code:
binary_search(a, key):
    lo = 0; hi = length(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + floor((hi-lo)/2)
        if a[mid] == key: return mid
        if a[mid] < key: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

examples.prompt: Binary-search 7 in [1,3,5,7,9]

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Midpoint index 2 contains 5; discard indices 0–2. The midpoint value is smaller than 7. Sorted order rules out the entire left part, including the tested midpoint.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: In remaining range 3–4, midpoint 3 contains 7. Using floor((low+high)/2) on [3,4] gives index 3. Equality ends the search immediately.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Return index 3. The invariant held because the array was sorted. Discarding an unsorted half would lack justification; the sorted-input precondition proves preservation of the candidate invariant.

examples.strategy: Maintain an inclusive interval containing every possible target location.
examples.answer: Return index 3. The invariant held because the array was sorted.
examples.verification: The array’s zero-based element at index 3 is 7. Every update reduces the remaining interval, ensuring termination.

steps: Compare front elements and take 1, then 2, then 3.
Take 4, then 8; one input is exhausted.
Append remaining 9. Each element is moved once, so merging six elements is linear.

pitfalls: Quicksort expected performance is not its worst case.
Binary search requires the monotonic ordering condition.
revision: Comparison sorting lower bound Ω(n log n).

checks.prompt: What is the zero-based position of 8 in the sorted array [2,4,6,8,10]?
checks.hint: Count indices from zero.
checks.explanation: The positions are 0,1,2,3,4; 8 is at index 3.

checks.prompt: Merging sorted lists of lengths 4 and 6 outputs how many elements?
checks.hint: No elements are lost.
checks.explanation: 4+6=10 output elements.

lessons.concept: A search or sort is easier to understand through its invariant: what remains true after every iteration or recursive step. Complexity then follows from how fast the unresolved region shrinks and how much work is done to combine results.
lessons.method:
Linear search examines candidates one by one and works without sorted order, taking \(O(n)\) worst-case comparisons. Binary search uses sorted order to discard approximately half the candidates after a midpoint comparison, giving \(O(\log n)\). The operation must support efficient midpoint access; repeatedly traversing a linked list changes the cost model.
For an inclusive interval [low,high], a smaller midpoint value rules out indices through mid, so set low=mid+1; a larger value sets high=mid−1. Stop when low>high. A half-open convention uses different boundaries and updates. State the invariant that any remaining target lies in the candidate interval and ensure each unsuccessful iteration shrinks it.
Duplicate targets require a modified boundary search for first/last occurrence; ordinary equality return may find any occurrence. Compute mid as low+(high−low)/2 to avoid overflowing a bounded addition. Binary search is also useful on a monotone feasibility predicate, but monotonicity must be proved. GATE trace errors commonly arise from combining two interval conventions or failing to remove the tested midpoint. Sorting arranges items by a key; a stable sort preserves the original relative order of equal keys. Merge sort splits a sequence, recursively sorts the halves, then merges by comparing the front unconsumed elements. The merge reads/moves each element at most a constant number of times, costing \(\Theta(n)\) for combined length n.
Balanced recursion gives T(n)=2T(n/2)+\(\Theta(n)\), so total work is \(\Theta(n\log n)\). A conventional array implementation uses \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary merge storage, while recursion depth is logarithmic. Stability requires choosing the left-side item first on equal keys when merging already stable halves. A different tie rule can change equal-key order.
The comparison-sorting lower bound is Ω(n log n) in the general worst-case decision-tree model; it does not rule out linear integer sorts with stronger key assumptions. GATE problems may ask comparisons for a particular merge rather than asymptotic sort time: once one side is exhausted, appending the remainder needs no further cross-side comparison. Quicksort selects a pivot and partitions items so each belongs to an appropriate side of it, then recursively sorts those sides. Partition costs \(\Theta(n)\), but exact array trace and pivot position depend on the stated scheme. Lomuto and Hoare conventions differ; one cannot assume the pivot lands in a final position under every partition algorithm.
Balanced splits give \(\Theta(n\log n)\), while repeatedly splitting into zero and n−1 gives \(\Theta(n^2)\). Random pivot selection gives expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\) under the usual model but does not remove the worst-case possibility. Sorted data is especially bad only for certain deterministic pivot choices, not for every quicksort implementation.
A conventional array partition uses constant local space but recursive stack can be \(O(n)\) under bad splits. Recursing on the smaller side and looping over the larger can limit stack depth. Standard quicksort is not stable. With duplicates, a three-way partition can isolate equal keys and avoid repeatedly reconsidering them, but complexity claims must follow the actual algorithm described. Heapsort first builds a max-heap, then repeatedly exchanges its largest root with the last active element, reduces the heap size and repairs heap order downward. After each iteration, the suffix contains finalized largest values in sorted order and is excluded from further heap operations. The active prefix remains a heap, not a fully sorted list.
Bottom-up construction is \(\Theta(n)\). Each of n removals can cost \(O(\log n)\), giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) worst-case sort time. An iterative array implementation uses constant auxiliary storage aside from the input and is conventionally unstable because swaps can reverse equal-key order. It differs from a priority queue that keeps inserting while extracting.
During a trace, heap size is separate from array length; a sift must not reintroduce elements already placed in the sorted suffix. Choose the larger child in a max-heap repair, not simply the left child. Comparison counts depend on node structure and implementation, while the asymptotic bound remains logarithmic per removal. Sorting orders records by a chosen key, while the rest of each record must remain attached to that key. A stable sort preserves the relative order of records whose keys compare equal. Sortedness alone says nothing about that relative order. Label equal-key records to distinguish them when tracing an algorithm, because replacing every record by its key can hide an unstable exchange.
Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. Take the next record, shift larger prefix records right and place the saved record into the gap. If the shift condition is strictly greater than the saved key, equal keys do not cross each other and the procedure is stable. Shifting on greater-than-or-equal can reverse equal-key records while still producing correctly ordered numeric keys.
Each insertion makes the sorted prefix one record longer. In the worst case, many prefix records move at each step, giving \(\Theta(n^2)\) time; an already sorted input can use linear comparisons in a standard implementation. Verify the ordering, that every original record appears exactly once, and the relative order of each equal-key group. Stability is a correctness requirement only when the task asks for it. Merge sort recursively divides a sequence into smaller contiguous halves until each subproblem has at most one record. Those base subproblems are already sorted. It then merges sorted children while returning through the recursion tree. A merge repeatedly compares the two first unconsumed records and takes the smaller; once either side is empty, append the remaining side without further cross-side comparisons.
To preserve stability, take a left-side record before an equal-key right-side record. Contiguous division keeps original positions on each side, and applying that tie rule at every merge preserves original equal-key order through the whole algorithm. A trace of one isolated merge does not show the recursive sort; identify both the split tree and the sequence of combined subproblems.
Balanced division creates logarithmically many levels, and every level handles a linear total number of records, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) time. A conventional array implementation needs \(\Theta(n)\) temporary merge storage in addition to logarithmic recursion depth. Exact comparison counts depend on how quickly one child is exhausted. Verify the final permutation and stability separately from its asymptotic bound. Quicksort partitions a sequence around a pivot and recursively sorts the remaining regions. Exact partition traces require an explicit scheme: different schemes use different scan directions, equal-key rules and return meanings. Lomuto partition with a last-element pivot maintains a prefix whose values are at most the pivot, followed by inspected values greater than it, followed by uninspected values and the pivot at the end.
Start boundary i one position before the subarray. Scan j from the first position through the position before the pivot. Whenever A[j] is at most the pivot, increase i and swap A[i] with A[j]. Finally swap the pivot into i+1. The returned index is the pivot's final position, so recurse on regions excluding it. The pivot does not necessarily stay where it began.
Partition requires linear work for the current subarray. Recursion cost depends on the split sizes; balanced splits give \(\Theta(n\log n)\) while repeatedly extreme splits give \(\Theta(n^2)\). Equal values can cause poor splits for this two-way scheme. Check the invariant at every movement and use the returned boundary to ensure that recursive calls shrink. Maintain a range that could contain the key in sorted data. Compare its midpoint, discard the half ruled out by ordering, and update bounds so the loop progresses. After k comparisons the candidate range is about n/2ᵏ, producing \(\Theta(\log n)\) worst-case time. Unsorted input destroys the discard argument. Boundary variants such as first occurrence need their own invariant. Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new key, giving \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst-case and \(\Theta(n)\) best-case on already sorted input. Merge sort recursively sorts halves and linearly merges them, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) and ordinarily \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary array storage. Heapsort builds a heap then repeatedly extracts, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) worst-case and an in-place array implementation. Partition around a pivot, then recurse on both sides. Balanced partitions produce \(\Theta(n\log n)\); consistently extreme pivots produce \(\Theta(n^2)\). Randomization gives expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\), not a worst-case guarantee. General comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; counting/radix sorts exploit additional assumptions and are not counterexamples. This version keeps an inclusive range [lo,hi]. On a failed comparison it removes the midpoint as well as the impossible half, ensuring progress even when one or two candidates remain. The midpoint formula avoids unnecessarily adding two large indices in fixed-width arithmetic. The returned −1 distinguishes absence from valid zero-based index 0. Sorting the input is a prerequisite; this routine does not verify that condition. Search is the task of identifying whether a desired key satisfies a membership or position condition in a representation. The permitted technique depends on guarantees such as sorted order, direct indexing and whether duplicates require the first occurrence. Linear scanning handles arbitrary order, while two sorted streams can be searched together by advancing the smaller current key. State what a successful result means and what an absent result encodes. Count comparisons along the actual path rather than a generic bound. A method that discards candidates needs a justified invariant; if an assumption is missing, it may skip a valid target even while executing perfectly valid array accesses. Binary search maintains a candidate interval justified by monotone order. Fix inclusive or half-open endpoints before computing updates. For inclusive bounds, a strictly smaller midpoint value removes indices through the midpoint, and a strictly larger value removes indices from the midpoint onward. A first-occurrence search records equality but continues into the left range instead of returning immediately. Termination needs strict interval shrinkage on every nonreturning iteration, including a one- or two-element interval. Compute the midpoint in a way that avoids bounded-integer addition overflow. Verify a result using both equality at the reported index and any extra boundary condition the question requires. Heapsort maintains two regions with different invariants: an active max-heap prefix and an increasing finalized suffix. Root extraction grows the suffix by one maximum, while sifting repairs only the shortened prefix. Keep heap length separate from physical array length; otherwise a large finalized value can be pulled back into the active structure. Bottom-up heap construction costs linear time, followed by logarithmic repairs for a linear number of extractions. Standard swaps need not preserve equal-key record order, so instability must be tested with labels rather than numeric values alone. Verify both regions after each iteration and check that the final suffix becomes the entire nondecreasing array. A sorting specification includes key order, record preservation and any stability requirement. Label records so equal keys and their original relative positions remain distinguishable. Different algorithms establish sortedness by different invariants: selection sort fixes a smallest remaining key, while stable multi-pass sorting composes orders by treating the later pass as the primary key. Comparison lower bounds assume arbitrary orderings determined by comparisons; bounded integer keys allow counting-based techniques outside that model. When verifying a result, separately test nondecreasing keys, the exact input multiset and required equal-key order. A fast method can still be incorrect for the requested tie contract, and a stable method may use extra storage. Merging requires both child sequences to be sorted before their fronts can determine the next output. The output prefix remains sorted, and every unconsumed child value is no smaller than its own front. This invariant explains correctness and the linear combine cost. It also supports applications such as counting cross inversions: a selected right value smaller than the left front is smaller than every remaining left value. Stability is a separate tie choice: take a left record first on equality to retain original equal-key order through contiguous recursive splits. Exact comparisons exclude appending a remainder after one child empties. Confirm the permutation, sortedness and any additional count derived during merging. Partitioning arranges values around a pivot but does not necessarily sort either resulting side. The returned index or boundary must be interpreted according to the specific scheme, especially when adapting recursive endpoints. Lomuto puts its pivot in a final index, while a Hoare-style boundary need not designate a final pivot location. Equal-key input can expose a poor two-way partition policy even without already sorted distinct keys. To control stack space, recurse only on the smaller side and iterate on the larger; this changes frame growth without eliminating the work of bad partitions. State pivot selection, equality handling and whether expected or worst-case cost is requested before deriving complexity.

gateGuide.recognize: Sorting questions can ask stability, auxiliary space or worst-case time. A correct answer about one property does not answer the others.
method: For binary search state the active inclusive/exclusive bounds and prove each failed comparison shrinks them.
For sorting write the invariant, such as a sorted prefix or two sorted halves being merged.
Separate expected and worst-case quicksort; count comparisons/moves under the particular algorithm, not a universal sorting formula.

traps.claim: Randomized quicksort guarantees n log n worst case
traps.why: Randomization improves expected performance but extreme partitions remain possible.

traps.claim: A sorted output implies stable sorting
traps.why: Equal keys can be reordered while numerical key order remains correct.
