State-based complexity; O(nW) is pseudopolynomial in numeric capacity.

tutorials.title: DP states, dependencies and memoization
tutorials.body:
Dynamic programming stores solutions to overlapping subproblems. Optimal substructure means an optimum can be assembled using appropriate optimal subproblem answers; overlap means naive recursion would recompute them. Define the state in a sentence before writing a table entry: it must contain enough information about the past to determine valid future decisions.
Memoization evaluates a recursive recurrence on demand and caches each state. Tabulation computes states in an order where dependencies are already available. These can implement the same recurrence with different execution and stack behavior. Base cases encode the empty/smallest problem and unreachable states must use an appropriate sentinel rather than default zero when zero might be a valid optimum.
Complexity is reachable state count times transition work, plus relevant setup. Memory compression is correct only if updates preserve dependency versions. For 0/1 knapsack, decreasing capacities keep previous-item states; increasing capacities can reuse the current item. An optimal table value need not uniquely determine a solution; reconstruction may require stored choices or comparisons along dependencies.

example.prompt: Use memoization for F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2), F(0)=0,F(1)=1, at n=5.
example.strategy: Define state → Reuse subproblems → Compute

steps.title: Define state
steps.explanation: F(k) stores the kth Fibonacci value, independent of the path that requested it.

steps.title: Reuse subproblems
steps.explanation: Each of F(0) through F(5) is computed at most once; repeated requests read cached values.

steps.title: Compute
steps.explanation: Dependencies determine each value.

example.answer: F(5)=5 with linear distinct-state work.
example.verification: Naive recursion repeats states, while memoization adds \(O(n)\) stored results and at most \(O(n)\) recursion depth.

depth.body: A DP state is a precise sentence describing what information has been fixed and what answer is still sought. Choose transitions by partitioning valid possibilities, and arrange computation so every dependency has its correct version. Counts, feasibility, minima and maxima need different base values and different unreachable sentinels. Table order can also change the problem: counting unordered coin combinations differs from counting ordered sequences, and reusing updated capacity states differs from single-use selection. Draw a small table before compressing memory, then trace representative entries back to their dependencies. Verify both the objective value and a concrete witness when possible; a plausible number does not establish that the recurrence models the intended feasible solutions.

examples.prompt: Count unordered ways to make amount four with unlimited coins one and two. Use coin-outer, increasing-amount tabulation.
examples.strategy: Initialize the empty amount → Process coin one → Process coin two

steps.title: Initialize the empty amount
steps.explanation: Set ways[0]=1 and other entries zero, representing one empty selection.

steps.title: Process coin one
steps.explanation: Amounts zero through four become [1,1,1,1,1].

steps.title: Process coin two
steps.explanation: Updates produce [1,1,2,2,3], with ways[4] adding the two ways at amount two.

examples.answer: There are three combinations.
examples.verification: The combinations are 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2 and 2+2; reordering the same coins is not counted separately.

examples.prompt: Compute Levenshtein edit distance from ab to ac with insertion, deletion and substitution each cost one.
examples.strategy: Initialize empty-prefix states → Use the matching first characters → Evaluate the final mismatch

steps.title: Initialize empty-prefix states
steps.explanation: The first row and column are 0,1,2 because empty strings require one operation per character.

steps.title: Use the matching first characters
steps.explanation: The a/a cell is zero; completing its row gives [1,0,1].

steps.title: Evaluate the final mismatch
steps.explanation: The b/c cell takes one plus the matching-prefix diagonal, giving final row [2,1,1].

examples.prompt: A one-array 0/1 knapsack update processes item (weight2,value3) in increasing capacities up to four. Why does it report an invalid value six?
examples.strategy: Update capacity two → Read the already changed dependency → Restore the correct dependency version

steps.title: Update capacity two
steps.explanation: The item is first included using the old zero state.

steps.title: Read the already changed dependency
steps.explanation: Increasing order lets the same item's new state feed a second inclusion.

steps.title: Restore the correct dependency version
steps.explanation: Decreasing capacity order reads the previous-item dp[2]=0 before it is changed.

tutorials.title: 0/1 knapsack: a complete include/exclude recurrence
tutorials.body:
A 0/1 knapsack chooses each item at most once, maximizing value under capacity W. Define dp[i,w] as maximum value using only the first i items with capacity at most w. Excluding item i gives dp[i−1,w]; including it, if wᵢ≤w, gives vᵢ+dp[i−1,w−wᵢ]. Their maximum covers both possible final decisions.
Initialize dp[0,w]=0 for nonnegative values under an at-most-capacity formulation. An exactly-filled formulation requires unreachable-state handling and different initialization. Processing increasing i makes preceding-row dependencies available. A one-array optimization uses decreasing w so included terms still refer to the old item prefix.
Time is O(nW), which is pseudopolynomial in numeric capacity because W takes only logarithmic input bits to encode. Fractional knapsack uses a different feasible set, and ratio sorting does not solve this recurrence. Recover selected items by comparing adjacent prefix rows or recording decisions; ties can give multiple optimal subsets. Verify both total weight and single-use constraints after reconstruction.

example.prompt: Capacity 4; items (2,3) and (3,4).
example.strategy: First item → Second decision → Check feasibility

steps.title: First item
steps.explanation: For capacities 2,3,4 the best value is 3; capacities 0,1 remain zero.

steps.title: Second decision
steps.explanation: Include or exclude item two.

steps.title: Check feasibility
steps.explanation: The chosen item has weight 3. Both together weigh 5 and are not feasible.

example.answer: Optimal value 4 using the second item.
example.verification: An ascending one-array update with the first item could incorrectly allow value 6 at capacity 4 by reusing it.

depth.body: Knapsack variants differ in item reuse and in whether capacity is an upper limit or an exact target. A 0/1 state must limit eligible items; an unbounded variant may keep the current item eligible after inclusion. An at-most-capacity formulation can accept unused space, whereas exact filling needs an unreachable sentinel for positive capacities with no feasible subset. Value-per-weight ranking is not sufficient for indivisible items because a locally attractive choice can block a better combination. Derive the include/exclude alternatives under the chosen variant, then reconstruct selected records and verify weight, value and multiplicity. The O(nW) table bound is pseudopolynomial because numeric W has a logarithmic-length binary encoding.

examples.prompt: 0/1 capacity five has A=(weight2,value4), B=(3,5). Compute the optimum by include/exclude decisions.
examples.strategy: Evaluate the first item → Compare choices for B → Reconstruct the subset

steps.title: Evaluate the first item
steps.explanation: A fits capacities two through five and yields value four.

steps.title: Compare choices for B
steps.explanation: Including B leaves capacity two for A.

steps.title: Reconstruct the subset
steps.explanation: Choose both A and B, each exactly once.

examples.answer: Optimal value nine with total weight five.
examples.verification: The four subsets have values 0,4,5,9 and weights 0,2,3,5, so the selected feasible maximum is verified.

examples.prompt: Capacity four and one 0/1 item (weight3,value5): compare at-most-capacity and exactly-filled formulations.
examples.strategy: Solve the at-most case → Enumerate exact possibilities → Use an unreachable state

steps.title: Solve the at-most case
steps.explanation: Selecting the item leaves one unused capacity unit and yields five.

steps.title: Enumerate exact possibilities
steps.explanation: The available subset weights are zero and three, neither equal to four.

steps.title: Use an unreachable state
steps.explanation: Exact-fill dp[1,4] stays impossible rather than inheriting zero as a feasible filled value.

examples.answer: At-most optimum five; exact fill is infeasible.
examples.verification: Enumerating the only two subsets independently confirms the different outcomes.

examples.prompt: Capacity six, indivisible items A=(4,8), B=(3,5), C=(3,5). Does descending density greedy maximize value?
examples.strategy: Compare densities → Follow its remaining capacity → Construct a better subset

steps.title: Compare densities
steps.explanation: The density rule chooses A first.

steps.title: Follow its remaining capacity
steps.explanation: After A, only two units remain and neither B nor C fits, giving value eight.

steps.title: Construct a better subset
steps.explanation: B and C exactly fill the capacity and improve value.

examples.answer: No; B,C give optimum ten while greedy gives eight.
examples.verification: All other feasible subsets are empty or singletons, so ten is also the exhaustive feasible maximum.

tutorials.title: Optimal substructure: justify each knapsack subproblem
tutorials.body:
Optimal substructure means that an optimum for a defined state can be assembled from optimal answers to the correct smaller states. The state must retain all restrictions relevant to future decisions. For 0/1 knapsack, dp[i,w] represents the maximum value obtainable using only the first i items with capacity at most w. Both the item prefix and the remaining capacity matter; a capacity-only state without item-processing context can accidentally permit reuse.
Partition feasible solutions by their decision on item i. An excluding optimum must use the best solution for dp[i−1,w]. If it includes item i, its remaining chosen items must realize dp[i−1,w−weight(i)]; otherwise replacing them by a better valid subset would improve the supposed optimum. Add the included item's value and take the larger feasible branch.
This replacement reasoning proves the recurrence rather than merely recognizing a pattern in a few table values. It differs from overlapping subproblems, which explains why caching is useful. Base states use zero value for an empty item prefix under the at-most-capacity, nonnegative-value formulation. After evaluating a state, reconstruct the choices and verify capacity and one-use constraints.

example.prompt: Capacity is 5. The first two items are A=(weight 2,value 3), B=(3,4). Add C=(2,5). Justify and evaluate dp[3,5].
example.strategy: Exclude the final item → Include the final item → Take the complete maximum → Justify use of an optimal child

steps.title: Exclude the final item
steps.explanation: The best prior-prefix subset is A,B, filling capacity five.

steps.title: Include the final item
steps.explanation: After choosing C, the remaining capacity is three and B is the best feasible prior-prefix item.

steps.title: Take the complete maximum
steps.explanation: Every feasible subset either includes C or excludes it, so no third branch is missing.

steps.title: Justify use of an optimal child
steps.explanation: If the included branch used A instead of the better fitting B, replacing A by B would increase value while retaining feasibility. Hence an optimum uses the optimal residual subset.

example.answer: The optimal subset is B,C, with total weight 5 and total value 9.
example.verification: All possibilities are covered by include/exclude. A,C has value 8 and weight 4; A,B,C has weight 7 and is infeasible. The reported subset uses each item once.

depth.body: Optimal substructure is a replacement property relative to a sufficient state. An optimal full solution must contain optimal residual answers when replacing them cannot violate constraints outside the state. Shortest paths with ordinary additive weights admit a prefix replacement, while simple-path constraints can make visited vertices relevant. A state that forgets those vertices can invalidate an otherwise convincing replacement. In string alignment, prefix boundaries isolate residual comparisons and support a clean recurrence. Prove feasibility of replacement before claiming its objective improves. Overlap is a separate property about repeated subproblems; having optimal substructure does not alone guarantee that dynamic programming will reduce an exponential number of distinct states.

examples.prompt: A shortest S-to-T route is S→\(A\to B\)→T with weights 2,3,1. If another S-to-B route costs four, what follows?
examples.strategy: Measure the alleged route → Replace the prefix → Compare the full cost

steps.title: Measure the alleged route
steps.explanation: Its prefix to B costs five.

steps.title: Replace the prefix
steps.explanation: The four-cost route to B can be followed by the same edge B→T of weight one.

steps.title: Compare the full cost
steps.explanation: The replacement contradicts the claimed shortest distance.

examples.answer: The original route cannot be shortest if a four-cost S-to-B route exists.
examples.verification: The unchanged suffix contributes one in both candidates, isolating the benefit of an optimal prefix.

examples.prompt: Find the longest common subsequence length of ABC and AC using optimal prefix substructure.
examples.strategy: Initialize empty prefixes → Process A and B → Match the final C

steps.title: Initialize empty prefixes
steps.explanation: A zero-length prefix has common-subsequence length zero with every other prefix.

steps.title: Process A and B
steps.explanation: Rows after A and B are [0,1,1] and [0,1,1]; unequal final characters use the larger adjacent prefix answer.

steps.title: Match the final C
steps.explanation: The final row is [0,1,2], taking one plus the previous A-matching prefix length.

examples.answer: LCS length is two, realized by AC.
examples.verification: AC occurs in order in both strings, and the second string has only two characters, giving a matching upper bound.

examples.prompt: Directed edges S→A=1, S→B=1, B→A=1, \(A\to B\)=100, A→T=1, B→T=1. The longest simple route is S,A,B,T. Can its S-to-A prefix be replaced by the longer S,B,A prefix?

steps.title: Compare prefix weights
steps.explanation: S→A costs one, while S→B→A costs two.

steps.title: Attempt the replacement
steps.explanation: Following the old suffix \(A\to B\)→T after S→B→A repeats B.

steps.title: Check the full constraint
steps.explanation: A simple path cannot revisit a vertex, so the replacement is infeasible despite improving prefix weight.

examples.answer: No; an endpoint-only state forgets visited vertices required by the simple-path constraint.
examples.verification: The original route weighs 102; feasible alternatives S,A,T; S,B,T; S,B,A,T weigh 2,2,3, so it is indeed longest.

tutorials.title: Memoization: trace cache misses and repeated requests
tutorials.body:
Memoization wraps a recursive subproblem solver with a cache indexed by its state. On each request, first check whether the state is already stored. A hit returns that result without recomputing its dependencies; a miss evaluates the recurrence, stores the result and returns it. Cache keys must contain every input that changes the answer, and the cached object must remain valid for the current problem instance.
For Fibonacci, state k fully determines F(k), so repeated requests for the same k can reuse one value. A left-to-right recursive evaluation still creates requests for already cached states; those requests are not new computations. Distinguish the number of distinct solved states from total function invocations and cache accesses. Whether base states are prepopulated affects the first misses but not the values.
With \(O(1)\) cache lookup and constant work per transition, solving F(n) computes only \(O(n)\) distinct states instead of an exponential recursion tree. The first descent can still create \(O(n)\) active call frames, and the cache itself has \(O(n)\) entries. Memoization saves repeated work rather than eliminating every recursive call or making every recursion use constant memory.

example.prompt: Compute F(4) using F(k)=F(k−1)+F(k−2), evaluating the left child first. Start with cached F(0)=0 and F(1)=1; check the cache at every call.
example.strategy: Descend through misses → Solve the first missing state → Resume three → Resume four

steps.title: Descend through misses
steps.explanation: Requests F(4), F(3) and F(2) miss, so their recursive evaluations remain suspended.

steps.title: Solve the first missing state
steps.explanation: Both child requests hit prepopulated entries; store F(2)=1.

steps.title: Resume three
steps.explanation: The returned F(2) result and another cache hit for F(1) complete the state; store it.

steps.title: Resume four
steps.explanation: The second F(2) request hits instead of expanding again. Seven function requests include only three missing-state computations.

example.answer: F(4)=3. The initial two base entries plus three newly computed states fill five cache entries; the evaluation makes seven requests.
example.verification: The call requests in order are 4,3,2,1,0,1,2. Repeated 1 and 2 requests reuse results; the longest active chain is 4→3→2→1, four frames.

depth.body: A cache is correct only when its key completely determines the cached result under the current input. State variables such as position, remaining resource or processed-item prefix cannot be omitted just because some calls happen to agree. On a hit, return before expanding dependencies; on a miss, compute and store after all required children are known. Count reachable distinct states for computation work, and count separate requests when measuring cache accesses. Base states may be prefilled, which changes miss counts without changing the mathematical answer. Memoization can save overlap while retaining a deep first recursion chain, and a cyclic dependency needs additional handling rather than indefinite recursive cache misses.

examples.prompt: Memoize grid-route counts F(i,j)=F(i−1,j)+F(i,j−1), with F(0,j)=F(i,0)=1. Compute F(2,2).
examples.strategy: Compute the shared interior state → Compute neighboring states → Combine the requested state

steps.title: Compute the shared interior state
steps.explanation: Both surrounding boundary states are already known.

steps.title: Compute neighboring states
steps.explanation: The second request for F(1,1) can reuse the cache.

steps.title: Combine the requested state
steps.explanation: Only one computation of the shared interior state is required.

examples.answer: Six routes; F(1,1) is reused rather than recomputed.
examples.verification: Choosing the positions of two horizontal moves among four moves gives binomial(4,2)=6.

examples.prompt: Memoize minimum coins for amount three with denominations one and three; F(0)=0 is cached and children are tried in denomination order.
examples.strategy: Descend using coin one → Store the smaller answers → Evaluate the direct-three alternative

steps.title: Descend using coin one
steps.explanation: Requests three,two,one miss in turn before the zero state is hit.

steps.title: Store the smaller answers
steps.explanation: Each result is stored after its feasible children return.

steps.title: Evaluate the direct-three alternative
steps.explanation: The second zero request hits the existing cache.

examples.answer: F(3)=1; five total requests, three newly computed states.
examples.verification: Request order is 3,2,1,0,0; one coin of value three is a concrete optimal witness.

examples.prompt: A 0/1 knapsack cache uses only capacity as its key. Item A=(2,3), B=(2,9). Compare states using first one versus first two items at capacity two.
examples.strategy: Evaluate the first prefix → Evaluate the longer prefix → Detect the key collision

steps.title: Evaluate the first prefix
steps.explanation: Only A is eligible.

steps.title: Evaluate the longer prefix
steps.explanation: B becomes eligible and is the better single item.

steps.title: Detect the key collision
steps.explanation: Both states would use capacity key two but require different answers.

examples.answer: Capacity alone is an invalid key; include the item-prefix state.
examples.verification: The distinct correct values three and nine are a direct counterexample to cache reuse across those states.

lessons.title: Graph traversal, MSTs and shortest paths
lessons.prerequisite: Graph representations, heaps and greedy proofs.
lessons.intuition: Graph traversal answers reachability; shortest paths minimize route cost; a minimum spanning tree minimizes the total cost of connecting every vertex. These objectives differ, so an MST path need not be a shortest path.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.body: BFS uses a queue and discovers vertices in layers, giving shortest edge-count paths in an unweighted graph. DFS uses recursion or a stack, finishing one branch before another. DFS supports cycle detection and topological order for directed acyclic graphs. Using adjacency lists, both inspect vertices and edges in \(O(V+E)\); mark vertices when enqueued to avoid duplicate expansion.

sections.title: MST algorithms
sections.body: For a connected undirected weighted graph, a spanning tree has V−1 edges. Kruskal sorts edges by weight and uses disjoint sets to reject cycles. Prim grows one tree by repeatedly adding a cheapest edge leaving its current vertex set. The cut property justifies these choices. Disconnected input produces a minimum spanning forest rather than one spanning tree.

sections.title: Weighted shortest paths
sections.body: Dijkstra finalizes the smallest tentative distance and requires nonnegative weights for that greedy argument. Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge repeatedly and detects a reachable negative cycle via further improvement after V−1 rounds. Floyd–Warshall permits intermediate vertices one by one and runs O(V³) for all pairs. Relaxation tests whether dist[u]+w(u,v) improves dist[v].

sections.title: Choose by the property you must preserve
sections.body: An algorithm’s invariant describes what remains true after each operation. Reachability traversal maintains a discovered set; shortest-path algorithms maintain distance estimates; MST algorithms maintain an acyclic set that can still be extended to an optimum. These are different objects even when they all store parent pointers. First translate the requested answer: “fewest hops” is unweighted distance, “minimum total cable” is a spanning-tree objective, and “prerequisites before a task” is a topological-order objective. Then test assumptions: a directed graph needs directed reachability, a disconnected undirected graph has a spanning forest rather than one spanning tree, and topological order requires a DAG. Complexity must include initialization and neighbor enumeration. With lists, summing degrees counts each directed edge once or each undirected edge twice; with a matrix, nonexistent edges still occupy positions to inspect.

examples.prompt: Triangle edges AB=1,BC=2,AC=5: find MST and A-to-C shortest path

steps.title: Build the minimum spanning tree
steps.explanation: The two cheapest edges connect all three vertices without a cycle. An MST minimizes total connecting-edge weight, not a source-to-destination distance.

steps.title: Compare both simple A-to-C routes
steps.explanation: These are the only two simple routes in this triangle. Positive weights mean adding a cycle cannot improve either route.

steps.title: Report separate results
steps.explanation: Both values are 3 here, but this is an instance-specific coincidence. A shortest-path tree can differ from an MST on another graph.

examples.verification: Changing AC to 2.5 makes the shortest A-to-C route direct, while the MST remains AB,BC with weight 3; the objectives can diverge.

lessons.concept: Graph traversal answers reachability; shortest paths minimize route cost; a minimum spanning tree minimizes the total cost of connecting every vertex. These objectives differ, so an MST path need not be a shortest path.
lessons.method:
Reachability asks which vertices can be reached; shortest path minimizes one source-to-destination route cost; a minimum spanning tree connects every vertex with minimum total selected edge weight. These are different optimization objects even though algorithms can all keep parent pointers. Decide direction, weight sign, connectivity and representation before selecting a method.
BFS supplies unweighted distances; DFS exposes nesting and ordering properties; MST algorithms apply to undirected weighted graphs; Dijkstra needs nonnegative weights; Bellman–Ford allows negative edges and reports reachable negative cycles. A disconnected undirected graph has a minimum spanning forest rather than a single all-vertex tree.
The output must include a correctness certificate appropriate to its goal: a traversal parent route, distance relaxation justification, or a cut/exchange argument. A visually short drawn edge does not specify numerical weight. Include isolated vertices when counting V. The same input can produce an MST and a shortest-path tree of different total weights, so do not substitute one objective’s answer for another. A graph traversal systematically discovers vertices through incident or outgoing edges. A search from one starting vertex covers only the vertices reachable from that start; it does not automatically visit an isolated vertex or another connected component. Maintain a visited set and mark a vertex when it is discovered, so cycles and multiple incoming routes do not repeatedly expand the same vertex.
For an undirected graph, a full traversal wraps BFS or DFS in an outer loop over all vertices. Whenever the next vertex is unvisited, start a new search and record a new component root. Discovery edges form a search forest: each nonroot discovered vertex has one parent, while already visited neighbors create no new forest edge. With c components and V vertices, the forest has V−c discovery edges.
An adjacency-list implementation checks every header and scans each neighbor entry, giving Θ(V+E) time for a full traversal. Neighbor order changes the exact discovery tree but not the component partition. Reachability, minimum spanning weight and weighted shortest paths are different tasks; simply visiting vertices does not optimize edge weights. Verify coverage explicitly when the input is disconnected. BFS uses a queue and discovers vertices in layers, giving shortest edge-count paths in an unweighted graph. DFS uses recursion or a stack, finishing one branch before another. DFS supports cycle detection and topological order for directed acyclic graphs. Using adjacency lists, both inspect vertices and edges in \(O(V+E)\); mark vertices when enqueued to avoid duplicate expansion. For a connected undirected weighted graph, a spanning tree has V−1 edges. Kruskal sorts edges by weight and uses disjoint sets to reject cycles. Prim grows one tree by repeatedly adding a cheapest edge leaving its current vertex set. The cut property justifies these choices. Disconnected input produces a minimum spanning forest rather than one spanning tree. Dijkstra finalizes the smallest tentative distance and requires nonnegative weights for that greedy argument. Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge repeatedly and detects a reachable negative cycle via further improvement after V−1 rounds. Floyd–Warshall permits intermediate vertices one by one and runs O(V³) for all pairs. Relaxation tests whether dist[u]+w(u,v) improves dist[v]. An algorithm’s invariant describes what remains true after each operation. Reachability traversal maintains a discovered set; shortest-path algorithms maintain distance estimates; MST algorithms maintain an acyclic set that can still be extended to an optimum. These are different objects even when they all store parent pointers. First translate the requested answer: “fewest hops” is unweighted distance, “minimum total cable” is a spanning-tree objective, and “prerequisites before a task” is a topological-order objective. Then test assumptions: a directed graph needs directed reachability, a disconnected undirected graph has a spanning forest rather than one spanning tree, and topological order requires a DAG. Complexity must include initialization and neighbor enumeration. With lists, summing degrees counts each directed edge once or each undirected edge twice; with a matrix, nonexistent edges still occupy positions to inspect. A traversal's coverage follows the direction and starting policy of its edges. Mark on discovery, so cycles cannot create repeated expansion before a vertex reaches the end of its scan. For a single source, unreachable headers stay unvisited. For full graph coverage, restart at each unvisited header and retain a forest of discovery parents. A directed graph's reachability set is not its undirected component, because following incoming arcs backward changes the problem. Recording discovered vertices, pending work and scanned neighbors makes the invariant visible. Count forest roots separately from vertices and verify that every nonroot has exactly one discovery parent; this gives a useful independent coverage check.

tutorials.body:
A graph traversal systematically discovers vertices through incident or outgoing edges. A search from one starting vertex covers only the vertices reachable from that start; it does not automatically visit an isolated vertex or another connected component. Maintain a visited set and mark a vertex when it is discovered, so cycles and multiple incoming routes do not repeatedly expand the same vertex.
For an undirected graph, a full traversal wraps BFS or DFS in an outer loop over all vertices. Whenever the next vertex is unvisited, start a new search and record a new component root. Discovery edges form a search forest: each nonroot discovered vertex has one parent, while already visited neighbors create no new forest edge. With c components and V vertices, the forest has V−c discovery edges.
An adjacency-list implementation checks every header and scans each neighbor entry, giving Θ(V+E) time for a full traversal. Neighbor order changes the exact discovery tree but not the component partition. Reachability, minimum spanning weight and weighted shortest paths are different tasks; simply visiting vertices does not optimize edge weights. Verify coverage explicitly when the input is disconnected.

example.prompt: Undirected graph vertices are A,B,C,D,E, edges A–B, B–C, D–E. Run a full BFS forest in vertex order A,B,C,D,E, using alphabetical neighbor order.
example.strategy: Start the first search → Finish the first component → Start the next unvisited root → Count the forest

steps.title: Start the first search
steps.explanation: A is unvisited, so mark it and begin a component. Expanding A discovers B; expanding B discovers C.

steps.title: Finish the first component
steps.explanation: The queue empties after C, giving component {A,B,C}. The outer loop skips the now-visited B and C.

steps.title: Start the next unvisited root
steps.explanation: D is unvisited, so a second search discovers E and completes component {D,E}.

steps.title: Count the forest
steps.explanation: Discovery edges are A–B, B–C and D–E, one per nonroot vertex.

example.answer: The traversal order is A,B,C,D,E and the two components are {A,B,C} and {D,E}.
example.verification: A search from A alone reaches only A,B,C. The outer loop adds exactly the missing D,E; every vertex is marked once and all three forest edges connect newly discovered vertices.

depth.body: A traversal's coverage follows the direction and starting policy of its edges. Mark on discovery, so cycles cannot create repeated expansion before a vertex reaches the end of its scan. For a single source, unreachable headers stay unvisited. For full graph coverage, restart at each unvisited header and retain a forest of discovery parents. A directed graph's reachability set is not its undirected component, because following incoming arcs backward changes the problem. Recording discovered vertices, pending work and scanned neighbors makes the invariant visible. Count forest roots separately from vertices and verify that every nonroot has exactly one discovery parent; this gives a useful independent coverage check.

examples.prompt: Traverse directed cycle \(A\to B\)→C→A from A using DFS and discovery marking; D is isolated.

steps.title: Discover the first route

steps.explanation: C sees A visited, so no new recursive expansion begins.

steps.explanation: Starting at one discovers two and three, creating two discovery edges.

steps.title: Restart at unvisited headers
steps.explanation: Four starts a second component and discovers five; six starts a singleton component.

lessons.title: BFS, DFS, cycles and topological ordering
lessons.intuition: A traversal marks each vertex once but chooses a different order for the frontier. BFS explores by distance in edges; DFS explores one path and then backtracks. That order determines what additional information you can safely infer.

sections.title: BFS levels
sections.body: Start source distance at zero, mark it visited and enqueue it. Remove a vertex, then discover its unvisited outgoing neighbours with distance one greater. Mark when enqueuing, not only on dequeue, to prevent repeated queued copies. Inductively, all distance-k vertices are processed before distance-(k+1) vertices, so first discovery gives minimum edge count in an unweighted graph.

sections.title: DFS structure
sections.body: Record a vertex as active on entry and finished on exit. A directed edge to an active ancestor is a back edge and proves a cycle. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the DFS parent is not by itself a cycle. DFS trees depend on start vertex and neighbour order, but reachability does not.

sections.title: Topological order
sections.body: A directed acyclic graph has an ordering putting every edge source before its destination. Reverse DFS finishing order gives one after confirming acyclicity. Alternatively Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices. If fewer than V vertices are removed, a cycle remains. Multiple valid topological orders may exist.

sections.title: Why traversal order proves useful facts
sections.body: BFS’s queue places newly discovered vertices after all already queued vertices. If a vertex at distance k is removed, its undiscovered neighbors are assigned distance k+1, while all shorter layers have already had a chance to discover them. That gives a shortest-number-of-edges proof, not just an implementation rule. Marking at enqueue time prevents several parents from adding the same vertex repeatedly. DFS instead keeps a chain of active ancestors. In a directed graph, an edge back to that chain closes a directed cycle; an edge to a completed vertex need not. Finishing a vertex means every recursively reachable unfinished dependency has been processed, which explains why reverse finish order is topological for a DAG. Neighbor order can change parent trees and timestamps without changing reachability or BFS distances.

examples.prompt: BFS on edges A–B,A–C,B–D,C–D from A

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Enqueue A at distance 0; discover B,C at distance 1. Mark each vertex when it is first enqueued, preventing multiple pending copies through different neighbors.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Processing B discovers D at distance 2; mark it immediately. The queue keeps earlier layers ahead of later layers. Neighbor order may change parent choices within the same layer.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Processing C does not reenqueue D. A shortest A-to-D route uses 2 edges. An assigned BFS distance counts edges from the source. This interpretation requires an unweighted or unit-weight objective.

examples.strategy: Use the queue’s first-in-first-out order to expose distance layers.
examples.answer: Processing C does not reenqueue D. A shortest A-to-D route uses 2 edges.
examples.verification: Each discovered vertex’s distance is one more than its parent’s distance; already visited neighbors should not be re-enqueued.

examples.prompt: Topological order for \(A\to C\),\(B\to C\),C→D
steps: A and B initially have indegree zero.
Remove them in either order; only then does C become available.
Remove C, then D. A,B,C,D and B,A,C,D are both valid.

In an undirected DFS, skip the parent edge in cycle detection.

For a disconnected graph, restart at unvisited vertices when finding all components, but distance-from-one-source semantics remain separate. steps.explanation: A and B have zero, C has two and D has one.

steps.title: Remove available vertices
steps.explanation: Take A then B, reducing C’s indegree to zero.

steps.title: Finish
steps.explanation: Take C then D, giving A,B,C,D.

examples.prompt: Edges \(P\to Q\),\(P\to R\),Q→S,R→S, plus isolated T. Use FIFO Kahn with initial queue [P,T] and P's neighbors Q then R.

steps.explanation: P reduces Q and R to zero indegree; queue becomes [T,Q,R].

steps.explanation: Remove T, then Q, then R; only after R does S reach zero indegree.

steps.title: Enumerate to verify

example.prompt: Run recursive DFS from A on directed lists A=[B,C], B=[D], C=[D], D=[B]. Use these neighbor orders, time initially zero and increment it on every discovery and finish.

steps.explanation: Returning resumes A\'s scan at C. C sees D black and makes no recursive call.

steps.title: Finish the remaining frames
steps.explanation: Each adjacency scan completes before its own finish event.

steps.title: Explore the first branch
steps.explanation: Discovery follows A,B,D; D and then B finish before A resumes.

steps.title: Explore the second branch
steps.explanation: A discovers C, whose neighbor D is already black and completed.

steps.title: Classify the later edge
steps.explanation: C→D connects separate explored branches; it does not point to an active ancestor.

examples.prompt: Undirected graph has only edge U–V. DFS from U reaches V, whose neighbor U is visited. Is that a cycle?

steps.title: Record the parent
steps.explanation: U is V's discovery parent.

steps.title: Recognize the reverse incidence
steps.explanation: V→U in the list is the same undirected edge just followed outward.

steps.title: Apply the correct exclusion
steps.explanation: Ignore the parent incidence in the cycle test; no other visited neighbor exists.

examples.answer: No; one undirected edge forms a tree, not a cycle.

lessons.title: Minimum spanning trees: cuts, Kruskal and Prim
lessons.prerequisite: Weighted undirected graphs and greedy proofs.
lessons.intuition: An MST connects every vertex with minimum total edge weight and no cycles. It is a global network-design objective. The cut property gives a safe local choice and makes greedy algorithms possible.

sections.title: Cut and cycle properties
sections.body: A cut partitions vertices into two nonempty sets; a crossing edge joins the sides. A lightest crossing edge is safe for some MST compatible with current choices under the standard cut argument. If it is uniquely lightest, it belongs to every MST. A uniquely heaviest edge on a cycle cannot belong to any MST. Equal weights require care: several trees may have equal optimal total weight.

sections.title: Kruskal
sections.body: Sort all edges increasingly. Maintain a disjoint-set structure for chosen components. Add an edge if its endpoints are in different components and union them; otherwise reject the cycle-closing edge. Stop at V−1 chosen edges for connected input. Sorting usually dominates at O(E log E).

sections.title: Prim
sections.body: Start at any vertex and repeatedly pick a cheapest edge connecting the current tree to an outside vertex. Maintain best connection keys using a priority queue. This resembles Dijkstra operationally but keys represent cheapest incident attachment, not full source distance. With a binary heap and adjacency lists, a common bound is O(E log V).

sections.title: Exchange arguments behind cut and cycle rules
sections.body: Consider a cut and a lightest edge e crossing it. If an MST does not contain e, adding e creates a cycle; that cycle contains another crossing edge f. Because e is no heavier than f, replacing f by e preserves or improves total weight, so some MST includes e. If e is uniquely lightest, omitting it would force a strictly worse replacement, making it compulsory. Dually, a uniquely heaviest edge on a cycle cannot belong to an MST: deleting it after adding another cycle edge yields a lighter tree. Equality matters. These arguments justify Kruskal’s component merging and Prim’s growing cut. Negative edge weights do not invalidate either algorithm; cycles, connectivity and the total-weight objective matter, rather than the nonnegative-weight restriction used by Dijkstra.

examples.prompt: Kruskal on AB=1,BC=2,AC=3,CD=4,BD=5

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Take AB then BC, connecting A,B,C. The graph and edge weights determine the candidate ordering; equal weights can permit multiple valid choices.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Reject AC because it closes a cycle within that component. Joining separate components preserves acyclicity. Reject an edge whose endpoints are already connected by chosen edges.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Take CD to attach D. Three selected edges total 1+2+4=7. A connected V-vertex tree must have V−1 edges. Sum accepted weights rather than the weights of all inspected edges.

examples.strategy: Accept edges in increasing weight only when they join different components.
examples.answer: Take CD to attach D. Three selected edges total 1+2+4=7.
examples.verification: Chosen edges must connect all vertices and contain no cycle; compare the total with the original weights, not a shortest-path distance.

gateGuide.recognize: MST questions concern a connected undirected weighted graph. Cut and cycle properties are safer than guessing from a picture.
method: For Kruskal sort edges and accept an edge only when it joins distinct components.

steps.explanation: Only then does AB,BC beat both alternatives.

steps.title: Check completion
steps.explanation: No candidate connects the two remaining components.

example.prompt: Graph edges are AB=1, AC=2, BC=3, BD=4, CD=5. Use cut {A,B}|{C,D} to justify AC, starting from spanning tree T={AB,BC,BD}.
example.strategy: Identify the crossing set → Select the unique minimum → Perform the exchange → Compare weights

steps.title: Identify the crossing set
steps.explanation: AC, BC and BD cross this cut with weights 2,3,4. AB and CD lie within the two sides.

steps.title: Select the unique minimum
steps.explanation: AC is the uniquely lightest crossing edge, so every MST must include it.

steps.title: Perform the exchange
steps.explanation: Add AC to T, creating cycle A–B–C–A. Remove crossing edge BC to recover a connected acyclic set.

steps.title: Compare weights
steps.explanation: The replacement reduces total weight while preserving all four vertices.

example.answer: AC is mandatory in every MST. The exchange yields tree {AB,AC,BD}, lowering weight from 8 to 7.
example.verification: The resulting three edges connect all four vertices without a cycle. The original T was deliberately not an MST; its improvement illustrates the contradiction that would arise if an MST omitted the uniquely lightest cut edge.

tutorials.title: Union–find: representatives and path compression
tutorials.body:
A disjoint-set structure partitions elements into nonoverlapping groups. Each group is represented by a rooted parent-pointer tree whose root points to itself. Find follows parent pointers to that root; equality of representatives establishes group membership, not equality of the original element labels. Union joins two different roots while leaving elements already in the same group unchanged.
Path compression changes each traversed parent to point directly to the root, preserving membership while shortening future searches. Union by rank or size independently limits growth when merging roots. Use the specified tie rule when exact parent arrays matter. Rank is a balancing estimate and need not equal actual height after compression; it must not be freely decremented whenever a path is shortened.
Parent links in union–find are bookkeeping links between representatives, rather than necessarily edges of the input graph. Kruskal uses finds to ask whether an edge would connect different selected-edge components, then unions those components after accepting it. A compressed parent tree can change dramatically without changing any selected graph edge. The efficient amortized bound applies to an operation sequence, not a claim that every uncompressed find takes one step.

example.prompt: Parent pointers are A→A, B→A, C→B, D→D. Run find(C) with full path compression, then union(C,D), attaching root D to root A.
example.strategy: Follow the old chain → Compress the path → Find both union roots → Attach the specified root

steps.title: Follow the old chain
steps.explanation: A points to itself, so it is the representative of C\'s set.

steps.title: Compress the path
steps.explanation: Set C.parent=A and keep B.parent=A. The elements A,B,C still belong to the same set.

steps.title: Find both union roots
steps.explanation: The roots differ, so union is required.

steps.title: Attach the specified root
steps.explanation: Every element now has representative A; a later union(B,D) would do nothing.

example.answer: The final parent pointers are A→A, B→A, C→A, D→A, forming one set.
example.verification: Compression changed only the access path to a representative. The first find performed two parent-link traversals, while a subsequent find(C) needs only C→A.

depth.body: A union–find state represents an equivalence partition, so parent-array shape can change without altering which elements are connected. Find must reach a root before union chooses which tree to attach. Attaching an arbitrary nonroot instead can undermine rank reasoning and correctness under some updates. A successful union reduces the component count by one; a redundant union does not. Path compression and rank work together, but rank remains a historical balancing bound rather than the actual height after compression. Record representatives before each union or graph-edge decision, then verify final equivalence classes independently of the particular parent links selected by tie policy.

lessons.title: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall
lessons.prerequisite: Graph relaxation, heaps and dynamic programming.
lessons.intuition: Shortest-path algorithms differ mainly in how they schedule relaxation and which edge weights their proofs tolerate. Treat unreachable distances as infinity and preserve path predecessors if you need a route rather than just its cost.

sections.title: Dijkstra finalization
sections.body: Initialize source to 0 and others to infinity. Extract the unfinalized minimum tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edges ensure no later route through a farther vertex can improve the finalized vertex. A reachable negative edge breaks that proof. Zero weights are allowed. Binary-heap adjacency-list implementations commonly take O((V+E)log V).

sections.title: Bellman–Ford
sections.body: Relax all edges up to V−1 rounds. After round k, shortest paths using at most k edges have been accounted for in the standard formulation. A simple shortest path uses at most V−1 edges when no reachable negative cycle improves it. Another improving pass identifies a reachable negative cycle; not every negative edge is a negative cycle.

sections.title: Floyd–Warshall
sections.body: Let Dᵏ[i,j] allow internal vertices only from the first k. Transition is min(Dᵏ⁻¹[i,j],Dᵏ⁻¹[i,k]+Dᵏ⁻¹[k,j]). It either avoids k or routes through k. Use k as the outer loop in the ordinary in-place implementation, with O(V³) time and \(O(V^2)\) storage. Negative diagonal values after completion detect relevant negative cycles.

sections.title: Why relaxation and finalization differ
sections.body: An actual source-to-vertex walk supplies an upper bound on the shortest distance. Relaxation improves that bound when a route through another vertex is cheaper. Dijkstra finalizes the least tentative vertex because, with nonnegative edges, any unprocessed detour cannot later yield a cheaper entrance to it. A negative edge breaks that proof even without a cycle. Bellman–Ford avoids premature finalization: after k full passes, distances are correct for shortest paths that need at most k edges, assuming each pass considers all edges. Without a reachable negative cycle, a shortest simple path uses at most V−1 edges. An improvement on the next pass therefore signals a reachable negative cycle. A DAG needs neither nonnegative weights nor repeated passes: topological order settles every predecessor before its outgoing relaxation.

examples.prompt: Dijkstra from A with AB=2,AC=7,BC=1

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: After processing A, tentative B=2,C=7. These first estimates are route costs through A; they remain tentative until the corresponding vertex is finalized.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Finalize B next and relax BC to obtain C=3. B’s distance 2 plus edge BC of weight 1 improves C’s former estimate 7 to 3. Relaxation keeps the cheaper candidate.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Finalize C at 3; predecessor route is A,B,C. Nonnegative weights justify finalization. The predecessor of C is updated to B when the improved route is selected.

examples.answer: Finalize C at 3; predecessor route is A,B,C.

examples.prompt: Edges \(A\to B\)=2,\(B\to C\)=3,C→D=1,A→D=10. Run Floyd–Warshall with intermediate order A,B,C,D and give finite final distances.
examples.strategy: Allow B → Allow C → Read the completed forward matrix

steps.title: Allow B
steps.explanation: \(A\to C\) improves to five through A,B,C; other new reverse routes remain absent.

steps.title: Allow C
steps.explanation: A→D improves to six and B→D to four using C→D.

examples.answer: Finite forward distances are AB=2,AC=5,AD=6,BC=3,BD=4,CD=1.
examples.verification: Each is the sum along its chain segment; the direct AD edge costs ten and cannot improve the six-cost chain.

examples.prompt: Vertex order A,B,C,D; edges A→D=1,D→C=1,C→B=1. A single i,j,k loop nest uses k innermost. Why can it miss \(A\to B\)?
examples.strategy: Process pair A,B too early → Discover needed pieces later → Notice no revisit

steps.title: Process pair A,B too early
steps.explanation: At that point \(A\to C\) and D→B are both infinity, so no intermediate gives a finite candidate.

steps.title: Discover needed pieces later
steps.explanation: Pair A,C later becomes two through D; row D later obtains D→B=2 through C.

steps.title: Notice no revisit
steps.explanation: The already processed pair A,B stays infinity even though the three-edge route costs three.

examples.answer: The wrong loop order can miss AB=3; keep k outermost.
examples.verification: With k outermost, allowing C produces DB=2, then allowing D produces AB=1+2=3, confirming the counterexample.

tutorials.title: Bellman–Ford: ordered relaxation passes with a negative edge
tutorials.body:
Bellman–Ford computes single-source shortest distances by repeatedly relaxing every directed edge. Initialize the source to zero and other vertices to infinity. For edge u→v, update d(v) when d(u) is finite and d(u)+weight(u,v) is smaller. An in-place pass can propagate several edges immediately if the supplied processing order permits it, so exact intermediate values depend on that order.
Without a reachable negative cycle, a shortest route can be chosen simple and therefore has at most V−1 edges. After V−1 full passes, all finite shortest distances are correct. A further improving pass proves that a negative cycle is reachable from the source. Negative edges alone are allowed; they do not by themselves create an undefined shortest distance. An entirely unreachable negative cycle does not trigger this source's improving-pass test.
Stop early if a full pass makes no changes, because all edge inequalities then already hold. Guard infinity arithmetic instead of adding a weight to an absent route. The standard time bound is O(VE); storing predecessor pointers can reconstruct routes when improvements occur. Verify a reported distance by summing a corresponding path's weights and checking that no edge can still relax.

example.prompt: Source S, vertices S,A,B,C. Process edges in this exact order on every pass: \(B\to C\)=3, \(A\to B\)=−2, S→A=4, S→C=10. Trace three passes and the extra-cycle check.
example.strategy: First pass → Second pass → Third pass → Check one more full pass

steps.title: First pass
steps.explanation: B and A are initially unreachable, so their outgoing relaxations do nothing. S→A gives 4 and S→C gives 10: distances (0,4,∞,10).

steps.title: Second pass
steps.explanation: \(B\to C\) still runs before B is improved. The pass ends with (0,4,2,10).

steps.title: Third pass
steps.explanation: The first edge now improves C, giving (0,4,2,5); no later edge helps.

steps.title: Check one more full pass
steps.explanation: Every candidate equals or exceeds its stored destination distance, so no improvement occurs and no reachable negative cycle is detected.

example.answer: Final distances are S=0, A=4, B=2, C=5. A shortest S-to-C route is S,A,B,C.
example.verification: The route weight is 4−2+3=5, below the direct edge of weight 10. Three passes equal V−1; the unchanged extra pass confirms the negative edge did not produce a reachable negative cycle.

depth.body: Bellman–Ford replaces greedy finalization with repeated checks of every directed edge. Its pass guarantee is a lower bound on how far route information has propagated; a favorable in-place order may propagate farther within the same pass. A full unchanged pass is a fixed point and allows early termination. After V−1 passes, an extra reachable relaxation signals a reachable negative cycle, whose effects must then be propagated to destinations it can reach. A negative cycle elsewhere in the graph is irrelevant to source reachability. Guard infinity before arithmetic, retain predecessor updates when reconstructing finite routes, and distinguish detecting a cycle from deciding exactly which distances are unbounded below.

examples.prompt: Process edges S→A=2,S→B=4,\(A\to B\)=−3 in that order each pass. Initialize only S to zero and run until unchanged.
examples.strategy: Relax source edges → Use the improved source state → Check the next pass

steps.title: Relax source edges
steps.explanation: The first two edges set A=2 and B=4.

steps.title: Use the improved source state
steps.explanation: The final edge improves B during the same first pass.

steps.title: Check the next pass
steps.explanation: All three candidate inequalities already hold, so no value changes.

examples.answer: Distances S=0,A=2,B=−1; stop after the second, unchanged pass.
examples.verification: The route S,A,B costs −1, and the direct S,B route costs four.

examples.prompt: Edges S→A=1,\(A\to B\)=−2,B→A=0,B→T=3. Which source distances become unbounded below?
examples.strategy: Find the cycle weight → Establish source access → Propagate destination effects

steps.title: Find the cycle weight
steps.explanation: \(A\to B\)→A decreases route cost each repetition.

steps.title: Establish source access
steps.explanation: S reaches A, so this negative cycle is reachable.

steps.title: Propagate destination effects
steps.explanation: The cycle reaches A,B and T via B→T, but has no route back to S.

examples.answer: A,B,T have no finite shortest distance; S remains zero.
examples.verification: Repeating the cycle k times lowers each affected route by 2k, while no route returning to S exists.

examples.prompt: Edges S→T=2,\(X\to Y\)=−3,Y→X=1. Source is S. Does the negative X,Y cycle make the extra Bellman–Ford pass improve anything?
examples.strategy: Initialize reachability → Skip unreachable relaxations → Check the additional pass

steps.title: Initialize reachability
steps.explanation: S=0 and T becomes two; X and Y remain infinity.

steps.title: Skip unreachable relaxations
steps.explanation: Neither \(X\to Y\) nor Y→X has a finite source distance, so they cannot create a source route.

steps.title: Check the additional pass
steps.explanation: Every reachable distance is unchanged even though the separate cycle has weight −2.

examples.answer: No extra improvement; T remains two and X,Y remain unreachable.
examples.verification: There is no edge from {S,T} to {X,Y}, independently confirming the cycle is outside source reachability.

lessons.title: Finite automata and regular expressions
lessons.intuition: Finite automata remember only which state they are in. A state should summarize exactly the past information needed to decide future acceptance. This viewpoint is more useful than memorizing transition drawings: design the meaning of states before adding edges.

sections.title: DFA and NFA semantics
sections.body: A DFA has a total transition function Q×Σ→Q, one start state and a set of accepting states. Read the entire string before deciding acceptance. An NFA may have multiple possible transitions and epsilon moves; it accepts if at least one complete path ends accepting. Epsilon moves consume no symbol. Both models recognize exactly regular languages.

sections.title: Subset construction
sections.body: A DFA state can represent a set of possible NFA states. Start with the epsilon closure of the NFA start. For a symbol, take all corresponding moves and then epsilon closure again. A subset is accepting if it contains an accepting NFA state. Up to 2ⁿ subsets exist for n NFA states, but many may be unreachable.

sections.title: Expressions and minimization
sections.body: Regular expressions use union, concatenation and Kleene star; star includes the empty string. Precedence usually places star above concatenation above union. To minimize a DFA, remove unreachable states and distinguish accepting from nonaccepting states, then refine classes when transitions lead to different classes. States are equivalent only if no suffix distinguishes their acceptance.

sections.title: What state equivalence actually means
sections.body: Two DFA states are equivalent when every possible remaining suffix leads either both to acceptance or both to rejection. Agreement on the next symbol alone is insufficient. Start by separating final from nonfinal states because the empty suffix already distinguishes them. Refine a block when members transition, under some symbol, into different blocks; repeating until stable captures longer distinguishing suffixes. Unreachable states do not affect the accepted language and should be removed when minimizing a reachable machine. In a subset DFA, a set is an information state: after reading the prefix, the NFA could be in any member. The empty subset is a valid rejecting sink, not an error. A final member makes the subset accepting because NFA acceptance is existential.

examples.prompt: Design a DFA for an even number of 1s over {0,1}

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Use E and O to remember parity; start in E and accept E. The empty input has zero ones, so the start state must be both even and accepting.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: On 0, stay in the same state because parity does not change. Appending zero preserves the count of ones; keeping the state establishes the parity invariant.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: On 1, toggle E↔O. The empty string is accepted because zero is even. Appending one flips the count’s parity exactly once. Acceptance after the whole input then corresponds to even parity.

examples.strategy: Give each state a meaning that the transition rules preserve.
examples.answer: On 1, toggle E↔O. The empty string is accepted because zero is even.
examples.verification: Trace ε, 0, 1, 11 and 101: their parity results agree with the state meanings, without counting the number of zeros.

examples.prompt: Interpret (0|1)*01
steps: The starred prefix permits any binary string, including empty.
The final symbols are specifically 0 then 1.
The expression accepts exactly strings ending in 01, including 01 itself, but not 010.

pitfalls: NFA acceptance is existential over paths, not all paths.
Complementing an incomplete DFA without a sink state can produce incorrect acceptance.
revision: DFA and NFA have equal expressive power.
Subset construction has at most 2ⁿ candidate states.

checks.prompt: An NFA accepts a string when which condition holds?
checks.hint: Acceptance is existential over full-input paths.
checks.explanation: At least one path must consume the entire input and reach an accepting state. Other failing paths do not prevent acceptance.
options: At least one complete path ends in an accepting state
It visits an accepting state before input ends
Its state count exceeds input length

checks.prompt: A 4-state NFA has how many possible subsets in subset construction?
checks.hint: Count subsets of four states.
checks.explanation: \(2^4=16\) possible subsets, not necessarily reachable.

Minimization merges states only when every future suffix gives the same acceptance outcome. Start by separating accepting from rejecting states and refine distinctions through successor blocks.

An NFA can have several next states for one symbol and may have epsilon transitions consuming no input. Epsilon closure collects states reachable by zero or more epsilon moves, including the starting states themselves.

Union allows words from either operand, concatenation joins a word from the first with a word from the second, and star permits zero or more concatenated repetitions. Star therefore always includes the empty word. The empty language and the language containing only epsilon are different.
Parentheses and precedence matter: star binds to its operand, concatenation usually binds before union. A character alphabet symbol denotes a one-character word, while an expression represents a set of words. Translating to an NFA uses branches for union, joining for concatenation and looping with an empty bypass for star.
Regular expressions and finite automata have equal expressive power. A regex can constrain finite suffixes or modular counts but cannot match arbitrary nested parentheses in the classical model. Programming-language regex libraries may add nonregular features such as backreferences, so use the mathematical definition in theory questions. Prove membership by decomposing the candidate word according to the expression, not by comparing only its length. A final member makes the subset accepting because NFA acceptance is existential. Finite-state reasoning starts by asking which facts about the consumed prefix can change future acceptance. A state summarizes those facts rather than storing the prefix itself. Two prefixes need different states if some common continuation makes one accepted and the other rejected. This also gives lower bounds on the required memory. Build transitions by updating the chosen meanings after one new symbol, then check that those meanings remain true along a run. A finite automaton can remember a suffix of bounded length or a remainder, but cannot maintain arbitrarily many distinguishable exact counts. Acceptance is evaluated after the complete input, including the special case of no symbols at all. A DFA's total transition function makes each state and input symbol determine exactly one next state. Totality matters when constructing complements, because missing transitions represent rejection but still need an explicit destination before accepting states are exchanged. State minimization compares future behavior, not names or drawing positions. First discard unreachable states, split accepting from rejecting states, and refine a block whenever its members transition to different blocks on the same symbol. A stable partition gives the quotient machine. For arithmetic languages, a state invariant such as the current remainder often supplies a direct construction: derive its update from positional notation, then trace the invariant alongside the actual number. Epsilon closure is applied before the first input and after each symbol move; it includes states reachable by zero epsilon moves as well. Acceptance is existential only at the end of the input. A branch that reaches a final state too early still needs a way to consume the remaining symbols. Determinization preserves this semantics by making each reachable active-state set one DFA state. The theoretical subset bound counts all subsets, whereas the actual construction explores only those reached from the closed start set. To understand a regular expression, describe how a member word can be decomposed into the operands of each concatenation and repetition. Union chooses one alternative for each use, while star repeats its entire operand zero or more times. Parentheses fix the repeated unit: repeating ab preserves a/b pairing, unlike independently repeating each symbol. A constructive membership proof gives a decomposition; rejection requires showing that no legal decomposition exists. For a language-design problem, separate unconstrained regions from mandatory markers and place stars only on the regions that can have arbitrary length. Classical expressions describe whole words, so there is no implicit substring search or extra surrounding text unless the expression supplies it.

gateGuide.recognize: Automata questions often ask whether two descriptions recognize the same language. Acceptance depends on the entire input.
method: State a meaning for every state, then trace transitions including epsilon closures.
For NFA-to-DFA construction treat each DFA state as a set of NFA states and mark it accepting if it intersects final states.
For minimization first remove unreachable states, then distinguish accepting/nonaccepting states and refine transitions.

traps.claim: An NFA accepts only when every branch accepts
traps.why: Existence of one accepting branch after consuming the entire input is sufficient.

traps.claim: A rejecting DFA transition can be omitted when complementing
traps.why: Complement requires a complete DFA; missing transitions must lead to a rejecting sink before final states are flipped.

Upper bound on subset states; many may be unreachable.

example.prompt: Construct a DFA over {0,1} for an odd number of ones.
example.strategy: State meanings → Transitions → Acceptance

steps.title: State meanings
steps.explanation: E means even count; O means odd count. Start in E.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.explanation: Zero preserves state; one toggles E↔O.

steps.title: Acceptance
steps.explanation: Make only O accepting; 101 has two ones and finishes E.

example.answer: Two states suffice; 101 is rejected and 111 accepted.
example.verification: The empty word has zero ones and is rejected because the start state is nonaccepting.

examples.prompt: Construct a finite automaton over {a,b} accepting exactly words ending in b, and trace aab.
examples.strategy: Choose meanings → Update the memory → Trace all input

steps.title: Choose meanings
steps.explanation: Use A for empty input or last symbol a, and B for last symbol b. Start in A; only B accepts.

steps.title: Update the memory
steps.explanation: From either state, a goes to A and b goes to B, because only the newest symbol determines the final-character fact.

steps.title: Trace all input
steps.explanation: The complete word ends in accepting B; stopping after aa would reject.

examples.answer: aab is accepted by a two-state automaton.
examples.verification: The empty word and ba end in A and reject, whereas b and abb end in B and accept.

examples.prompt: Design the smallest DFA accepting binary strings with no substring 11. Test 10110.
examples.strategy: Define three situations → Complete transitions → Run the candidate → Prove minimality

steps.title: Define three situations
steps.explanation: Use A for start/last 0, B for last 1 without a violation, and D for a violation already seen. Accept A,B.

steps.title: Complete transitions
steps.explanation: A:0→A,1→B; B:0→A,1→D; D:0→D,1→D. A violation cannot be repaired by later input.

steps.title: Run the candidate
steps.equation: A\to B\to A\to B\to D\to D
steps.explanation: Reading 10110 encounters consecutive ones on its fourth symbol and rejects.

steps.title: Prove minimality
steps.explanation: D differs from A and B by the empty suffix. A and B differ by suffix 1, accepted from A but rejected from B.

examples.answer: Three states are necessary and sufficient; 10110 is rejected.
examples.verification: 1010 never enters D and accepts. The three displayed distinguishing cases prevent any pair of states from being merged.

examples.prompt: Could finitely many states recognize {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} by remembering only whether the input is still in its a block?
examples.strategy: Choose distinct prefixes → Supply one shared continuation → Use deterministic future behavior

steps.title: Choose distinct prefixes
steps.explanation: Consider aⁱ and aʲ with i<j. A finite machine would eventually assign the same state to two such prefixes.

steps.title: Supply one shared continuation
steps.explanation: Appending bⁱ balances the first prefix but leaves excess a symbols in the second.

steps.title: Use deterministic future behavior
steps.explanation: Equal states followed by the same suffix must give equal acceptance, contradicting the different required answers.

examples.answer: Remembering the block phase is insufficient; no finite automaton recognizes this language.
examples.verification: For prefixes a and aa, suffix b gives ab versus aab. The argument extends to arbitrarily many prefixes, so adding a fixed number of phase states cannot solve it.

examples.prompt: Construct a DFA for binary numbers divisible by 3, allowing leading zeros and treating the empty word as value 0. Trace 110.
examples.strategy: Store the remainder → Select start and final state → Trace the number

steps.title: Store the remainder
steps.explanation: Appending a binary digit doubles the previous value and adds that digit.

steps.title: Select start and final state
steps.explanation: Start at remainder 0 and accept only remainder 0; the rule defines both transitions from every state.

steps.title: Trace the number
steps.explanation: The prefix values are 1,3,6, whose remainders match the states.

examples.answer: 110 is accepted because its value is 6, divisible by 3.
examples.verification: The update also sends 10 to remainder 2 and rejects it; leading zero leaves the remainder unchanged.

examples.prompt: Minimize a reachable DFA: A,B reject; C,D accept. On 0/1, \(A\to B\)/C, B→A/D, C→C/C, D→D/D; start A.
examples.strategy: Start the partition → Compare transition signatures → Form the quotient

steps.title: Start the partition
steps.explanation: Acceptance immediately separates the two blocks.

steps.title: Compare transition signatures
steps.explanation: A and B each go to the rejecting block on 0 and accepting block on 1. C and D go to the accepting block on both symbols.

steps.title: Form the quotient
steps.explanation: The partition is stable. Merge A,B into R and C,D into F; R:0→R,1→F and F loops on both symbols.

examples.answer: The minimal DFA has two states and accepts exactly words containing at least one 1.
examples.verification: All four original states are reachable: A by ε, B by 0, C by 1, D by 01. R and F are distinguished by ε, so no further merge is possible.

examples.prompt: A partial machine over {a,b} has one accepting start state q with only q --a→ q. Why does flipping q to rejecting fail to complement its language?
examples.strategy: Identify the original language → Find the missing case → Complete before flipping

steps.title: Identify the original language
steps.explanation: Every a-only word accepts; any b has no transition and rejects. The language is a*.

steps.title: Find the missing case
steps.explanation: After merely flipping q, b still has no transition and rejects, although b belongs to the desired complement.

steps.title: Complete before flipping
steps.explanation: Add sink D, send q on b to D, and loop D on a,b. Complementing then makes D accepting and q rejecting.

examples.answer: The correct complement accepts exactly words containing a b; completion needs the sink.
examples.verification: ε and aaa reject in the complement, while b and aba enter D and accept. Merely flipping the partial machine would accept no word.

tutorials.title: NFA branches and subset construction
tutorials.body:
An NFA can have several next states for one symbol and may have epsilon transitions consuming no input. It accepts when at least one complete computation consumes the whole word and ends in an accepting state; other rejecting branches do not invalidate that success. Epsilon closure collects states reachable by zero or more epsilon moves, including the starting states themselves.

example.prompt: NFA start q0 loops on 0 and on 1 goes to both q0 and final q1; q1 has no moves.
example.strategy: Initial subset → Read first 1 → Read next 0

steps.title: Initial subset
steps.explanation: No epsilon moves are specified.

steps.title: Read first 1
steps.explanation: Both nondeterministic branches are retained, so the prefix is accepted.

steps.title: Read next 0
steps.explanation: q1 contributes no transition; the branch in q0 continues.

example.answer: Word 1 is accepted; word 10 is rejected.
example.verification: An accepting intermediate state is insufficient if remaining input cannot be consumed on that branch.
