examples.prompt: NFA: q0 has ε→q1; q1 has a→q1 and b→q2; q2 is final with no outgoing moves. Trace ab.
examples.strategy: Close the start → Read a → Read b

steps.title: Close the start
steps.explanation: The epsilon move activates q1 without consuming a symbol.

steps.title: Read a
steps.explanation: Only q1 has an a move; its self-loop remains active.

steps.title: Read b
steps.explanation: All input is consumed and the active set contains the final state.

examples.answer: ab is accepted; the epsilon move is not a third input symbol.
examples.verification: The same machine rejects ε because its start closure contains no final state, and rejects aba because q2 cannot consume the final a.

examples.prompt: Determinize the NFA for words ending 01: q0 loops on 0,1 and also goes to q1 on 0; q1 goes to final q2 on 1. Other moves are absent.
examples.strategy: Name reachable subsets → Compute transitions → Check reachability and a run

steps.title: Name reachable subsets
steps.explanation: Start in A; only C contains the final q2.

steps.title: Compute transitions
steps.explanation: A:0→B,1→A; B:0→B,1→C; C:0→B,1→A. Each entry unions all moves of the current subset.

steps.title: Check reachability and a run
steps.explanation: A,B,C are reachable by ε,0,01; 011 rejects despite its accepted prefix 01.

examples.answer: Only three DFA subset states are reachable, although a three-state NFA has eight possible subsets.
examples.verification: The transitions exactly track whether the current suffix is none, 0, or 01; 101 ends in C and accepts.

examples.prompt: An NFA has start q and on a branches to final f and nonfinal d. Neither f nor d has outgoing moves. Is a rejected because one branch rejects, and is aa accepted because a prefix reached f?
examples.strategy: Read the first symbol → Decide the whole one-symbol word → Try the second symbol

steps.title: Read the first symbol
steps.explanation: Both branches exist and at least one finishes in a final state.

steps.title: Decide the whole one-symbol word
steps.explanation: For a there is no remaining input, so the branch ending at f is an accepting witness despite the branch ending at d.

steps.title: Try the second symbol
steps.explanation: Neither branch can consume another a; no complete accepting run exists for aa.

examples.answer: a is accepted and aa is rejected.
examples.verification: Acceptance needs one successful complete path, not unanimous success and not a final state reached before input exhaustion.

tutorials.title: Regular expressions: union, concatenation and star
tutorials.body:
Regular expressions describe languages using union, concatenation and Kleene star. Union allows words from either operand, concatenation joins a word from the first with a word from the second, and star permits zero or more concatenated repetitions. Star therefore always includes the empty word. The empty language and the language containing only epsilon are different.
Parentheses and precedence matter: star binds to its operand, concatenation usually binds before union. A character alphabet symbol denotes a one-character word, while an expression represents a set of words. Translating to an NFA uses branches for union, joining for concatenation and looping with an empty bypass for star.
Regular expressions and finite automata have equal expressive power. A regex can constrain finite suffixes or modular counts but cannot match arbitrary nested parentheses in the classical model. Programming-language regex libraries may add nonregular features such as backreferences, so use the mathematical definition in theory questions. Prove membership by decomposing the candidate word according to the expression, not by comparing only its length.

example.prompt: Describe (0|1)*01 and test 01,101,010.
example.strategy: Prefix language → Fixed suffix → Test words

steps.title: Prefix language
steps.explanation: The star permits any binary prefix, including empty.

steps.title: Fixed suffix
steps.explanation: Concatenation requires a final zero then one.

steps.title: Test words
steps.explanation: 01 and 101 end in 01; 010 ends in 10.

example.answer: Exactly binary words ending in 01; the first two candidates are accepted, the last rejected.
example.verification: An empty starred prefix is legal, so 01 itself must not be excluded.

depth.body: To understand a regular expression, describe how a member word can be decomposed into the operands of each concatenation and repetition. Union chooses one alternative for each use, while star repeats its entire operand zero or more times. Parentheses fix the repeated unit: repeating ab preserves a/b pairing, unlike independently repeating each symbol. A constructive membership proof gives a decomposition; rejection requires showing that no legal decomposition exists. For a language-design problem, separate unconstrained regions from mandatory markers and place stars only on the regions that can have arbitrary length. Classical expressions describe whole words, so there is no implicit substring search or extra surrounding text unless the expression supplies it.

examples.prompt: Does abccab belong to (ab|c)*? Explain the decomposition and whether ε belongs.
examples.strategy: Identify repeatable units → Decompose the candidate → Check zero repetitions

steps.title: Identify repeatable units
steps.explanation: Every repetition chooses either the two-symbol block ab or the one-symbol block c.

steps.title: Decompose the candidate
steps.explanation: All four factors are allowed, so their concatenation witnesses membership.

steps.title: Check zero repetitions
steps.explanation: The star may choose no factors at all, producing ε regardless of the nonempty alternatives.

examples.answer: abccab and ε are both members.
examples.verification: The total factor lengths 2+1+1+2 equal six, so the decomposition consumes the complete candidate.

examples.prompt: Give a regex for binary words containing exactly two 1s. Test 00100100.
examples.strategy: Place mandatory symbols → Allow only zeros around them → Match the given word

steps.title: Place mandatory symbols
steps.explanation: Exactly two 1s require two literal 1 factors, neither inside a star.

steps.title: Allow only zeros around them
steps.explanation: The three zero blocks may independently be empty or arbitrarily long.

steps.title: Match the given word
steps.explanation: The decomposition has two mandatory ones and every other symbol is zero.

examples.answer: 0*10*10* describes the language and accepts 00100100.
examples.verification: Every generated word has precisely two ones. Conversely any word with two ones uniquely splits into its before/between/after zero blocks.

examples.prompt: Are (a|b)* and a*|b* equivalent? Produce a shortest counterexample.
examples.strategy: Read the scope of star → Test a mixed word → Rule out the other language

steps.title: Read the scope of star
steps.explanation: The first expression may choose a or b anew at each repetition; the second chooses a whole all-a block or a whole all-b block.

steps.title: Test a mixed word
steps.explanation: Two repetitions choosing a and then b generate ab.

steps.title: Rule out the other language
steps.explanation: The word contains both symbols, so it is neither all a nor all b.

examples.answer: They differ; ab is a shortest counterexample.
examples.verification: Both expressions contain ε,a,b, so no word of length below two distinguishes them.

lessons.title: Regular languages, closure and pumping lemma
lessons.intuition: The pumping lemma captures a consequence of finite memory: a sufficiently long accepted run repeats a state, creating a loop. It is mainly a tool for proving nonregularity. The order of choices matters because you do not control how the opponent decomposes the string.

sections.title: Regular closure
sections.body: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation and star. Intersection can be recognized by a product automaton whose states pair the two machines' states. Complement requires a total DFA and flips accepting states. Closure can prove nonregularity indirectly by isolating a known difficult sublanguage.

sections.title: Pumping statement
sections.body: If L is regular, some p exists so every w∈L with |w|≥p can be split w=xyz with \(|xy|\le p\), \(|y|>0\), and xyⁱz∈L for all integers i≥0. The repeated DFA segment is y. This is a necessary condition; merely finding pumpable decompositions does not establish regularity.

sections.title: Proof strategy
sections.body: Assume regularity and let the opponent choose p. Choose a suitable w depending on p. Then handle every valid decomposition, not only one convenient y. Select an exponent i, often 0 or 2, that forces the pumped string out of L. Contradiction disproves the assumed regularity.

sections.title: Quantifiers and closure as proof tools
sections.body: A regular language has a finite-state machine. Reading a sufficiently long accepted word forces a repeated state in an early prefix; the intervening nonempty loop can be repeated or skipped while leaving the remainder’s acceptance unchanged. This explains the length and nonempty constraints of the pumping lemma. It also explains why the proof adversary selects the legal loop: a nonregularity argument must defeat every permitted decomposition. Sometimes closure gives a shorter proof. If an assumed regular L, intersected with a known regular filter, becomes a known nonregular language, the assumption contradicts closure under intersection. To prove regularity, provide a finite automaton, regular expression or sound closure construction. The absence of an obvious pumping counterexample is not such a construction.

examples.prompt: Prove \(\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}\) is not regular

steps.title: Accept the adversary’s pumping length
steps.explanation: p is arbitrary; we choose w after p is given. Choosing a fixed short string would not cover all possible pumping lengths.

steps.title: Constrain every legal split
steps.explanation: The entire prefix xy lies in the first p zeros. This covers all legal decompositions, rather than selecting a convenient one.

steps.title: Pump down and contradict membership
steps.explanation: Removing at least one zero leaves unequal counts. The regular pumping lemma requires every nonnegative exponent to remain in L for some legal split, and no split can satisfy that.

examples.given: Language L=\(\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}\).
examples.goal: Prove L is not regular.
examples.strategy: Assume regularity and defeat every permitted split of a carefully chosen word.
examples.answer: L is not regular.
examples.verification: The contradiction uses both \(|xy|\le p\) and \(|y|>0\). Forgetting either constraint would allow decompositions that the proof has not ruled out.

examples.prompt: Use a product DFA for two parity conditions
steps: One machine remembers parity of zeros; the other parity of ones.
Pair their states to remember both parities, giving up to 2×2=4 states.
Accept only (even,even) to recognize the intersection.

pitfalls: The opponent chooses the decomposition after your string choice.
Pumping is necessary, not sufficient, for regularity.
revision: Pick w after p; handle all valid xyz splits.

checks.prompt: In a nonregularity pumping proof, who controls a permitted decomposition xyz?
checks.hint: Track the quantifier order.
checks.explanation: After p and your selected word, you must show every allowed split fails for some pumping exponent. One failed chosen split is insufficient.
options: The proof may choose just its favourite split
The opponent; the proof must handle every valid split
Nobody because the split is unique

checks.prompt: For w=0⁵1⁵, a permitted regular-pumping y contains 2 zeros. After pumping i=0, how many zeros remain?
checks.hint: Delete the y segment once.
checks.explanation: 5−2=3 zeros remain versus 5 ones.

lessons.concept: The pumping lemma captures a consequence of finite memory: a sufficiently long accepted run repeats a state, creating a loop. It is mainly a tool for proving nonregularity. The order of choices matters because you do not control how the opponent decomposes the string.
lessons.method:
Regular languages are those recognized by finite automata. They are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation and star. Closure means an operation on regular operands produces another regular language; it does not mean an arbitrary operand becomes regular merely by intersecting with something.
A product DFA tracks a pair of component states. On each symbol update both coordinates. For intersection accept when both components accept; for union when either accepts; for difference when the first accepts and the second does not. Complement requires a complete deterministic machine. Concatenation and star are often more naturally constructed with epsilon NFAs.
Closure also supplies nonregularity proofs: assuming L regular and applying closed operations with known regular languages can produce a known contradiction. State which operands are regular and which closure rule is used. A finite language is regular because its finitely many words can be encoded by a finite machine. An infinite language can also be regular; infinity alone says nothing about unbounded memory requirements. If a language is regular, some pumping length p ensures every sufficiently long accepted word has a decomposition xyz with \(|xy|\le p\), \(|y|>0\), and xyⁱz in the language for all i≥0. A repeated DFA state along the early prefix supplies the nonempty loop y; skipping or repeating it preserves the ending state.
To prove nonregularity, assume regularity, let p be arbitrary, then choose a word depending on p. The decomposition is not your choice: prove that every legal split fails for some exponent you can select. The chosen exponent may depend on the split. A single bad split does not contradict a condition requiring existence of one good split.
The lemma is necessary, not a general sufficient criterion for regularity. Passing some pumping examples is no proof; build a finite automaton or regex for that purpose. The word must belong to the language and have length at least p. Keep all three constraints explicit, since moving y outside the early prefix or allowing empty y destroys common counting-language arguments. Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation and star. Intersection can be recognized by a product automaton whose states pair the two machines' states. Complement requires a total DFA and flips accepting states. Closure can prove nonregularity indirectly by isolating a known difficult sublanguage. This is a necessary condition; merely finding pumpable decompositions does not establish regularity. Assume regularity and let the opponent choose p. Choose a suitable w depending on p. Then handle every valid decomposition, not only one convenient y. Select an exponent i, often 0 or 2, that forces the pumped string out of L. Contradiction disproves the assumed regularity. Reading a sufficiently long accepted word forces a repeated state in an early prefix; the intervening nonempty loop can be repeated or skipped while leaving the remainder’s acceptance unchanged. This explains the length and nonempty constraints of the pumping lemma. It also explains why the proof adversary selects the legal loop: a nonregularity argument must defeat every permitted decomposition. Sometimes closure gives a shorter proof. If an assumed regular L, intersected with a known regular filter, becomes a known nonregular language, the assumption contradicts closure under intersection. To prove regularity, provide a finite automaton, regular expression or sound closure construction. The absence of an obvious pumping counterexample is not such a construction. Regularity is a property of a language, and a finite-state construction is a direct positive proof. A language may be infinite yet need only finite memory: periodic length conditions use a finite set of remainders. Equivalent presentations by automata and regular expressions let a proof choose the clearest representation. Closure rules preserve regularity when their operands meet the required assumptions; they do not automatically make arbitrary subsets regular. To establish a construction, give the invariant of its states or factors and show both directions of the language equality. To disprove an overly broad assertion, produce a regular containing language and a subset with a known finite-memory obstruction, rather than relying on the subset's size. Closure becomes useful when translated into an explicit machine operation or a precise language identity. For Boolean operations on DFAs, update both components and choose the final pairs according to the intended truth condition. Difference accepts first-yes and second-no, not exclusive-or. For contradiction proofs, an intersection with a carefully chosen regular filter can isolate a known nonregular core. Always state the filter and verify the resulting equality in both directions. Complement is straightforward for a complete DFA but fails when naively applied to NFA branches: existential acceptance does not turn into its logical negation by flipping individual final states. Determinize and complete first so every word has a single finished computation. The pumping lemma has alternating choices: a putative regular language supplies a bound, you select a sufficiently long member, and every legal decomposition must permit all exponents. A nonregularity proof therefore handles the unknown pumping segment through bounds or invariants rather than choosing its exact location. Pumping changes both length and structure, so ask which membership condition must survive and choose an exponent that breaks it uniformly. Pumping up can be more useful than pumping down for sparse length sets. A decomposition violating the prefix bound is irrelevant, and discovering one bad decomposition never refutes regularity when another good one exists. Keep the quantified bound positive and the witness dependent on it.

gateGuide.recognize: The pumping lemma is a necessary condition for regularity. Its order of quantifiers decides who chooses the decomposition.
method: Assume regularity and let the adversary choose pumping length p.
Choose a word depending on p, then cover every legal split with |xy|≤p and |y|>0.
Select a pumping exponent that forces departure from the language and explicitly explain why it fails.

traps.claim: One bad decomposition disproves regularity
traps.why: For a regular language some legal decomposition must work; to contradict the lemma all legal decompositions must fail for your chosen word.

traps.claim: Passing a few pumping examples proves regularity
traps.why: The lemma does not provide a sufficient test; a DFA, regular expression or closure construction can prove regularity.

formulas.latex: \exists p\ \forall w\in L, |w|\ge p:\ \exists x,y,z\ \forall i\ge0, xy^iz\in L
formulas.meaning: Regular-language pumping quantifiers, with w=xyz, |xy|≤p and |y|>0.

tutorials.title: Regular-language closure and product automata
tutorials.body:
Regular languages are those recognized by finite automata. They are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation and star. Closure means an operation on regular operands produces another regular language; it does not mean an arbitrary operand becomes regular merely by intersecting with something.
A product DFA tracks a pair of component states. On each symbol update both coordinates. For intersection accept when both components accept; for union when either accepts; for difference when the first accepts and the second does not. Complement requires a complete deterministic machine. Concatenation and star are often more naturally constructed with epsilon NFAs.
Closure also supplies nonregularity proofs: assuming L regular and applying closed operations with known regular languages can produce a known contradiction. State which operands are regular and which closure rule is used. A finite language is regular because its finitely many words can be encoded by a finite machine. An infinite language can also be regular; infinity alone says nothing about unbounded memory requirements.

example.prompt: Recognize binary words with even zeros and even ones.
example.strategy: Component states → Product → Acceptance

steps.title: Component states
steps.explanation: Each parity machine has E,O, updating only for its counted symbol.

steps.title: Product
steps.explanation: Track both finite facts simultaneously.

steps.title: Acceptance
steps.explanation: Start at (E,E) and accept only that pair; 0011 returns there.

example.answer: A four-state product DFA recognizes the intersection.
example.verification: The empty word has even counts of both symbols and is accepted.

depth.body: Regularity is a property of a language, and a finite-state construction is a direct positive proof. A language may be infinite yet need only finite memory: periodic length conditions use a finite set of remainders. Equivalent presentations by automata and regular expressions let a proof choose the clearest representation. Closure rules preserve regularity when their operands meet the required assumptions; they do not automatically make arbitrary subsets regular. To establish a construction, give the invariant of its states or factors and show both directions of the language equality. To disprove an overly broad assertion, produce a regular containing language and a subset with a known finite-memory obstruction, rather than relying on the subset's size.

examples.prompt: Prove {a^{4n+1}:n≥0} regular by an automaton, and test aaaaa.
examples.strategy: Use a finite length invariant → Update and accept → Trace the candidate

steps.title: Use a finite length invariant
steps.explanation: State r means the number of consumed a symbols is congruent to r modulo 4.

steps.title: Update and accept
steps.explanation: Start in 0 and accept only 1, ensuring precisely lengths congruent to 1.

steps.title: Trace the candidate
steps.explanation: Five a symbols finish in the accepting state.

examples.answer: The language is regular and aaaaa is accepted.
examples.verification: The regex a(aaaa)* generates exactly the same positive lengths 1,5,9,…; ε correctly rejects.

examples.prompt: A finite language L={ab,baa} is regular. Construct a regex for its reversal and test aab.
examples.strategy: Reverse each whole word → Union the results → Check membership

steps.title: Reverse each whole word
steps.explanation: Reversal changes symbol order, not the choice between the two words.

steps.title: Union the results
steps.explanation: The expression ba|aab is a finite union of fixed words and is regular.

steps.title: Check membership
steps.explanation: aab matches the second alternative exactly, while baa matches neither reversed word.

examples.answer: The reversed language is described by ba|aab and accepts aab.
examples.verification: Reversing ba and aab again recovers ab and baa, independently checking both alternatives.

examples.prompt: If R={a,b}* is regular, must its subset L={aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} also be regular?
examples.strategy: Check containment → Assume a pumping bound → Delete that loop

steps.title: Check containment
steps.explanation: Every aⁿbⁿ is a word over {a,b}, so L is indeed a subset of R.

steps.title: Assume a pumping bound
steps.explanation: Any valid regular-pumping y lies in the first p a symbols and contains k≥1 of them.

steps.title: Delete that loop
steps.explanation: The unequal counts contradict the required pumping property for every legal split.

examples.answer: No. A regular language can have a nonregular subset.
examples.verification: R uses a one-state accepting DFA, while prefixes aⁱ in L require arbitrarily many distinctions through continuations bⁱ.

depth.body: Closure becomes useful when translated into an explicit machine operation or a precise language identity. For Boolean operations on DFAs, update both components and choose the final pairs according to the intended truth condition. Difference accepts first-yes and second-no, not exclusive-or. For contradiction proofs, an intersection with a carefully chosen regular filter can isolate a known nonregular core. Always state the filter and verify the resulting equality in both directions. Complement is straightforward for a complete DFA but fails when naively applied to NFA branches: existential acceptance does not turn into its logical negation by flipping individual final states. Determinize and complete first so every word has a single finished computation.

examples.prompt: Construct the difference of binary languages E=words with even ones and Z=words ending in 0. Decide 11 and 110.
examples.strategy: Track both component facts → Choose the difference finals → Trace the candidates

steps.title: Track both component facts
steps.explanation: Pair parity E/O with last-zero status Y/N. Start at (E,N), since ε has no final zero.

steps.title: Choose the difference finals
steps.explanation: Accept exactly (E,N): an even count is required and ending in zero is forbidden.

steps.title: Trace the candidates
steps.explanation: 11 ends at (E,N) and accepts. Appending 0 preserves even parity but changes the second component to Y, so 110 rejects.

examples.answer: E minus Z accepts 11 and rejects 110.
examples.verification: ε also accepts because it has even ones and is not in Z, checking that difference uses first-and-not-second.

examples.prompt: Let U={aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} ∪ {words over {a,b,c} containing c}. Prove U nonregular using a regular filter.
examples.strategy: Pick the filter → Compute the intersection → Invoke closure in the correct direction

steps.title: Pick the filter
steps.explanation: This regular language contains no c and allows the required a-before-b order.

steps.title: Compute the intersection
steps.explanation: The containing-c component disappears; every equal-block word remains.

steps.title: Invoke closure in the correct direction
steps.explanation: If U were regular, its intersection with regular R would be regular, contradicting the known nonregularity of the equal-block language.

examples.answer: U is nonregular.
examples.verification: Every word in the intersection comes from the equal-block component, and every equal-block word is in both operands, verifying the equality rather than merely containment.

examples.prompt: Over alphabet {a}, an NFA start q has a→q and a→f, with only f final and no moves from f. Why does flipping final states fail to complement it?
examples.strategy: Identify its accepted words → Flip and find overlap → Determinize before complementing

steps.title: Identify its accepted words
steps.explanation: Every nonempty a-word can remain at q until its last a, then move to f. ε rejects, so the language is a+.

steps.title: Flip and find overlap
steps.explanation: Making q final allows the all-q branch to accept a, even though a already belonged to the original language.

steps.title: Determinize before complementing
steps.explanation: Only the second subset originally accepts; flipping these DFA subset finals accepts exactly ε.

examples.answer: Flipping NFA states is incorrect; the true complement is {ε}.
examples.verification: For a the original and naively flipped machines both have an accepting branch, whereas a language and its complement must be disjoint.

tutorials.title: Regular pumping lemma and the proof game
tutorials.body:
If a language is regular, some pumping length p ensures every sufficiently long accepted word has a decomposition xyz with \(|xy|\le p\), \(|y|>0\), and xyⁱz in the language for all i≥0. A repeated DFA state along the early prefix supplies the nonempty loop y; skipping or repeating it preserves the ending state.
To prove nonregularity, assume regularity, let p be arbitrary, then choose a word depending on p. The decomposition is not your choice: prove that every legal split fails for some exponent you can select. The chosen exponent may depend on the split. A single bad split does not contradict a condition requiring existence of one good split.
The lemma is necessary, not a general sufficient criterion for regularity. Passing some pumping examples is no proof; build a finite automaton or regex for that purpose. The word must belong to the language and have length at least p. Keep all three constraints explicit, since moving y outside the early prefix or allowing empty y destroys common counting-language arguments.

example.prompt: Prove L={aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} nonregular.
example.strategy: Choose word → Cover all splits → Pump down

steps.title: Choose word
steps.explanation: It belongs to L and is long enough.

steps.title: Cover all splits
steps.explanation: Every legal pumping part lies entirely in the a block.

steps.title: Pump down
steps.explanation: Counts differ for every possible k.

example.answer: L is not regular.
example.verification: The reasoning defeats every legal decomposition, not merely one selected convenient split.

depth.body: The pumping lemma has alternating choices: a putative regular language supplies a bound, you select a sufficiently long member, and every legal decomposition must permit all exponents. A nonregularity proof therefore handles the unknown pumping segment through bounds or invariants rather than choosing its exact location. Pumping changes both length and structure, so ask which membership condition must survive and choose an exponent that breaks it uniformly. Pumping up can be more useful than pumping down for sparse length sets. A decomposition violating the prefix bound is irrelevant, and discovering one bad decomposition never refutes regularity when another good one exists. Keep the quantified bound positive and the witness dependent on it.

examples.prompt: Prove the unary language {a^{n²}:n≥0} nonregular using pumping up.
examples.strategy: Choose a square length → Bound every pumping segment → Pump once more

steps.title: Choose a square length
steps.explanation: For positive pumping bound p, this member has length at least p.

steps.title: Bound every pumping segment
steps.explanation: The nonempty segment lies within the first p positions, regardless of the split.

steps.title: Pump once more
steps.explanation: The new length lies strictly between consecutive squares and cannot belong to the language.

examples.answer: The square-length unary language is nonregular.
examples.verification: The next-square gap is 2p+1, greater than every permitted k≤p, so the argument covers all decompositions.

examples.prompt: Prove L={0ⁿ1ᵐ:n>m≥0} nonregular by pumping down a suitable near-boundary word.
examples.strategy: Choose the strict-inequality witness → Locate every legal loop → Delete the loop

steps.title: Choose the strict-inequality witness
steps.explanation: It belongs to L because its zero count exceeds its one count by one.

steps.title: Locate every legal loop
steps.explanation: The prefix restriction prevents y from reaching the one block.

steps.title: Delete the loop
steps.explanation: The remaining zero count is at most the unchanged one count p, violating n>m.

examples.answer: L is nonregular.
examples.verification: Even the smallest deletion k=1 produces equal counts, and every larger deletion makes zeros fewer than ones.

examples.prompt: Someone claims a*b* is nonregular using p=2, w=aabb and y=ab straddling the boundary. Explain the invalid split and supply a valid pumpable split.
examples.strategy: Locate the proposed segment → Give a legal decomposition → Pump all exponents

steps.title: Locate the proposed segment
steps.explanation: In aabb, choosing middle ab makes x=a, so xy has length 3, exceeding p=2.

steps.title: Give a legal decomposition
steps.explanation: Its prefix length is 1≤2 and y is nonempty.

steps.title: Pump all exponents
steps.explanation: Changing the number of leading a symbols preserves the required block order.

examples.answer: The claimed proof uses an illegal split; the displayed legal split pumps successfully for every exponent.
examples.verification: a*b* itself is a regular expression. The zero-exponent result abb still lies in that regular language.

lessons.title: Context-free grammars, derivations and pushdown automata
lessons.intuition: A stack lets a machine remember arbitrarily many pending obligations in last-in-first-out order. Context-free grammars describe recursive structure, and pushdown automata recognize the same language class. Nested parentheses and matched counts are natural examples.

sections.title: Grammar mechanics
sections.body: A CFG has variables, terminals, a start variable and productions whose left side is one variable. Derivation replaces a variable using a production. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable; rightmost expands the rightmost. A parse tree records hierarchical structure, not the temporal order of independent expansions.

sections.title: PDA operation
sections.body: A pushdown automaton chooses transitions using the current state, input symbol or epsilon, and stack top. For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, push one marker per 0, then pop one per 1 and accept when input and markers are exhausted. It must prevent returning to the zero phase after ones begin. Nondeterministic PDAs recognize all CFLs; deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass.

sections.title: Ambiguity and closure
sections.body: A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two distinct parse trees, equivalently distinct leftmost derivations. A grammar can be changed while preserving its language. CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, and under intersection with a regular language; they are not closed under arbitrary intersection or complement.

sections.title: Stack discipline and parse structure
sections.body: A pushdown automaton can store an unbounded count or a nested obligation on its stack. For equal blocks, push once per first-block symbol and pop once per second-block symbol; reject an unmatched pop or remaining unmatched symbols at acceptance. Finite control records the phase so a first-block symbol cannot appear after the second block has begun. A grammar describes the same dependency by recursive nesting: each expansion adds matched symbols around a smaller instance. Ambiguity is about two structures for one terminal string, not simply two different orders of expanding independent branches. Expression grammars use separate nonterminals for precedence levels and recursion direction for associativity. Neither left-recursion removal nor left factoring alone establishes that a grammar is unambiguous or LL(1).

examples.prompt: Derive 0011 using \(S\to0S1\mid\varepsilon\)

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Start S and apply 0S1 to get 0S1. The recursive production contributes one leading zero and one trailing one, with S representing the unfinished interior.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Apply again to get 00S11. A second recursive expansion nests another matched pair; the terminals remain in zero-then-one block order.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Use S→ε to obtain 0011; each recursive expansion adds a matching outer zero and one. The epsilon production removes only S, not its surrounding terminals. This completes the terminal string.

examples.strategy: Record each sentential form and the production applied to its remaining nonterminal.
examples.answer: Use S→ε to obtain 0011; each recursive expansion adds a matching outer zero and one.
examples.verification: Two recursive expansions yield two zeros and two ones; the resulting 0011 is exactly the target string.

examples.prompt: Why E→E+E | E*E | id is ambiguous for id+id*id
steps: One parse makes + the root and groups id+(id*id).
Another makes * the root and groups (id+id)*id.
Both follow the same productions but give different structures. Add precedence levels such as E,T,F to distinguish the intended grouping.

pitfalls: Different arbitrary derivation orders do not necessarily imply different parse trees.
PDA determinism and nondeterminism differ in expressive power.
revision: CFG left-hand sides contain one variable.
CFL ∩ regular is CFL; CFL ∩ CFL need not be.

checks.prompt: Which closure claim is valid?
checks.hint: A regular restriction preserves context-free recognition.
checks.explanation: A PDA can be combined with finite-state regular constraints. Intersection of two arbitrary CFLs need not be context free.
options: CFLs are closed under arbitrary intersection
CFLs are closed under intersection with regular languages
CFLs are closed under every complement

checks.prompt: A PDA pushes one marker for each of 4 zeros. How many marker pops match four subsequent ones?
checks.hint: One pop per one.
checks.explanation: Four pushes are balanced by four pops.

lessons.concept: A stack lets a machine remember arbitrarily many pending obligations in last-in-first-out order. Context-free grammars describe recursive structure, and pushdown automata recognize the same language class. Nested parentheses and matched counts are natural examples.
lessons.method:
A context-free grammar rewrites one nonterminal at a time using productions A→α, independent of surrounding context. Starting from the start symbol, a derivation produces terminal words. The generated language contains all terminal strings attainable, not intermediate forms with nonterminals. Recursive productions can enforce unbounded balanced structure.
A parse tree records hierarchical production choices. A grammar is ambiguous if one terminal string has two distinct parse trees, equivalently two distinct leftmost derivations. Merely expanding independent branches in different orders can give the same tree and is not enough. Expression grammars often become unambiguous by assigning separate levels for precedence and recursion for associativity.
A CFL is a language with some CFG; ambiguity is a property of a chosen grammar, except when the language is inherently ambiguous across all its grammars. A grammar generating a regular language can still be written recursively, so its appearance does not automatically establish nonregularity. Verify generated strings for ordering as well as counts and include epsilon if the productions allow it. A pushdown automaton augments finite control with an unbounded stack. A transition can inspect input or epsilon, read the stack top and replace it with a string. The stack supports last-in-first-out matching obligations, allowing balanced nesting and equal ordered blocks that finite automata cannot generally count.
For aⁿbⁿ, push one marker per a, switch to the b phase and pop one per b. Reject an unmatched b, an a after the phase switch, or leftover markers at completion. A bottom marker distinguishes an empty count from losing the stack’s structural base. Acceptance by final state and by empty stack are equivalent language models for nondeterministic PDAs under suitable constructions, but a given machine’s acceptance condition must be followed exactly.
Nondeterministic PDAs recognize exactly CFLs, while deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass. One stack does not grant the full power of a Turing tape. In GATE traces, record state, remaining input and stack content at each step; stack orientation must be stated so push/pop order is unambiguous. A context-free grammar consists of terminal symbols, nonterminal symbols, a start nonterminal and productions with one nonterminal on the left. A derivation begins at the start symbol and repeatedly replaces a nonterminal by a production's right-hand side. Only strings containing terminals alone belong to the generated language. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining nonterminal; this fixes the expansion order without changing the grammar's language.
The balanced-parenthesis grammar S→(S)S | ε separates a matched outer pair from a following balanced suffix. The first S inside the parentheses describes nesting, while the second S describes concatenation. Each nonempty expansion adds a matched pair; an epsilon expansion closes an unfinished recursive obligation. Record the entire sentential form after each rewrite, including all remaining nonterminals. A parse tree stores the same production choices hierarchically. Reading its terminal leaves left to right must reproduce the target string, and every internal node must use an actual grammar production. A language is context free when some context-free grammar generates exactly its strings. A positive classification therefore needs a construction with both soundness and completeness: every generated string has the desired property, and every desired string can be generated. A grammar's recursive appearance alone does not establish that its language is nonregular, because regular languages are also context free.
Context-free languages are closed under union. To combine two grammars, first rename their nonterminals so they are disjoint, then introduce a fresh start symbol choosing one old start or the other. The choice is made for the whole derivation; it does not freely mix the component languages' terminal strings. For equal-count blocks, a production \(A\to a\)Ab adds one leading a and one trailing b together. Repeating it n times and then using epsilon gives every aⁿbⁿ and nothing else. This invariant supplies a proof for all lengths, beyond checking a few examples. The same construction can use c in place of b for another component. A CFG has variables, terminals, a start variable and productions whose left side is one variable. Derivation replaces a variable using a production. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable; rightmost expands the rightmost. A parse tree records hierarchical structure, not the temporal order of independent expansions. A pushdown automaton chooses transitions using the current state, input symbol or epsilon, and stack top. For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, push one marker per 0, then pop one per 1 and accept when input and markers are exhausted. It must prevent returning to the zero phase after ones begin. Nondeterministic PDAs recognize all CFLs; deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two distinct parse trees, equivalently distinct leftmost derivations. A grammar can be changed while preserving its language. CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, and under intersection with a regular language; they are not closed under arbitrary intersection or complement. A pushdown automaton can store an unbounded count or a nested obligation on its stack. For equal blocks, push once per first-block symbol and pop once per second-block symbol; reject an unmatched pop or remaining unmatched symbols at acceptance. Finite control records the phase so a first-block symbol cannot appear after the second block has begun. A grammar describes the same dependency by recursive nesting: each expansion adds matched symbols around a smaller instance. Ambiguity is about two structures for one terminal string, not simply two different orders of expanding independent branches. Expression grammars use separate nonterminals for precedence levels and recursion direction for associativity. Neither left-recursion removal nor left factoring alone establishes that a grammar is unambiguous or LL(1). An ambiguity witness is one terminal word with two genuinely different parse trees. Comparing leftmost derivations is a convenient way to expose those trees because expansion order is fixed. Different operator grouping changes a tree, while merely visiting independent siblings in a different order does not. A grammar may be ambiguous even when its language has another unambiguous grammar. For expressions, separated precedence levels and carefully chosen recursion remove specific grouping choices: an expression-level production handles addition, and a term-level production handles multiplication. Such rewriting changes structure while preserving the intended terminal strings. Check the same word under both proposed trees, including every terminal, rather than arguing from a vague claim that recursion causes ambiguity. A PDA's stack represents pending obligations in last-in-first-out order. Trace the state, unread input and full stack together, and declare which end of the displayed stack is the top. A stack-bottom marker protects the base and makes completion checks explicit. For nested delimiters, every opening symbol pushes an obligation and the matching close discharges the top obligation. For a marked palindrome, a separator signals when pushing must stop and comparison/popping must begin. Acceptance requires the specified machine condition after consuming the complete input; reaching an accepting configuration with unread input is insufficient. Final-state acceptance and empty-stack acceptance describe equivalent nondeterministic language classes through constructions, but cannot be exchanged silently for a particular machine. A production is a local rewriting rule, but a grammar's language includes all terminal results obtainable through any sequence of valid rules. Intermediate strings containing nonterminals are sentential forms rather than accepted words. The tree viewpoint helps separate structure from rewrite order: independent child nodes may be expanded in either order while producing the same tree. Grammar transformations need language equality, not merely matching a few sample strings. When eliminating nullable productions, first compute all nullable nonterminals, then add alternatives omitting each nullable occurrence; preserve epsilon at a fresh or permitted start symbol if it originally belongs. Keep empty-language generation distinct from the ability to derive the empty word. Context-free classification asks for some grammar or pushdown recognizer with exactly the intended language. The grammar can establish unbounded count relationships by adding linked blocks in the same recursive rule. Union, concatenation and star constructions preserve context-freeness because they combine recursive components without requiring simultaneous independent stack comparisons. Intersection with a regular language is also safe: finite-state information can accompany a PDA state without replacing its stack. Intersecting two arbitrary CFLs is different, because their separate count constraints can combine into a three-way synchronization that one stack cannot enforce. Distinguish a successful positive construction from a pumping argument, which supplies a necessary property but does not by itself prove membership in the class.

gateGuide.recognize: A CFG generates strings by derivation; a PDA uses an unbounded stack. Write the language before designing either representation.
method: Identify the dependency, such as matching counts or nested delimiters.
Trace productions or stack operations while recording consumed input and remaining obligation.
For ambiguity produce one string with two distinct parse trees or leftmost derivations; use grammar structure to enforce precedence.

traps.claim: Two derivation orders always prove ambiguity
traps.why: Expanding independent nonterminals in different orders can give the same parse tree; use distinct trees or distinct leftmost derivations.

traps.claim: Every context-free language has a deterministic PDA
traps.why: Nondeterministic PDAs are more expressive; deterministic context-free languages form a proper subclass.

formulas.meaning: Generates equal numbers of a then b, including the empty word.
A stack counts the first block and matches the second.

tutorials.title: CFG derivations, parse trees and ambiguity
tutorials.body:

example.prompt: Why E→E+E | E*E | id is ambiguous for id+id*id?
example.strategy: One tree → Second tree → Compare

steps.title: One tree
steps.explanation: Choose + at the root, giving id+(id*id).

steps.title: Second tree
steps.explanation: Choose * at the root, giving (id+id)*id.

steps.title: Compare
steps.explanation: Both yield the same terminal word but different operator grouping.

example.answer: This grammar is ambiguous.
example.verification: Two distinct structural trees, rather than two arbitrary expansion orders, establish the required witness.

Comparing leftmost derivations is a convenient way to expose those trees because expansion order is fixed. Different operator grouping changes a tree, while merely visiting independent siblings in a different order does not. A grammar may be ambiguous even when its language has another unambiguous grammar. For expressions, separated precedence levels and carefully chosen recursion remove specific grouping choices: an expression-level production handles addition, and a term-level production handles multiplication. Such rewriting changes structure while preserving the intended terminal strings. Check the same word under both proposed trees, including every terminal, rather than arguing from a vague claim that recursion causes ambiguity.

examples.prompt: Show S→SS | a is ambiguous for aaa using two leftmost derivations.
examples.strategy: Group the final two leaves → Group the first two leaves → Compare structures

steps.title: Group the final two leaves
steps.equation: S\Rightarrow SS\Rightarrow aS\Rightarrow aSS\Rightarrow aaS\Rightarrow aaa
steps.explanation: The root splits one a from a two-a right subtree.

steps.title: Group the first two leaves
steps.equation: S\Rightarrow SS\Rightarrow SSS\Rightarrow aSS\Rightarrow aaS\Rightarrow aaa
steps.explanation: The root's left child splits again, producing a two-a left subtree.

steps.title: Compare structures
steps.explanation: Both derivations are leftmost and have the same terminal leaves, but their root subtree sizes are 1+2 versus 2+1.

examples.answer: aaa has two distinct trees, so the grammar is ambiguous.
examples.verification: The two trees correspond to a(aa) and (aa)a. Two a leaves admit only one split, so the three-leaf witness is the first such ambiguity.

examples.prompt: For id*id+id, compare the ambiguous E→E+E|E*E|id with E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→id.
examples.strategy: Exhibit the ambiguous alternatives → Locate the precedence boundary → Recover the enforced grouping

steps.title: Exhibit the ambiguous alternatives
steps.explanation: The first grammar permits root + giving (id*id)+id, or root * giving id*(id+id), with identical terminal tokens.

steps.title: Locate the precedence boundary
steps.explanation: In the rewritten grammar, + can be introduced only at E level; a T cannot contain an unparenthesized +.

steps.title: Recover the enforced grouping
steps.explanation: The root must be E→E+T, with the left E producing the product through T→T*F. The grouping is (id*id)+id.

examples.answer: The rewritten grammar enforces multiplication before addition and removes this ambiguity.
examples.verification: The rightmost T generates the final id. A proposed root product would require a T or F to generate id+id, which these productions cannot do.

examples.prompt: Does S→AB, \(A\to a\), B→b become ambiguous because AB can be rewritten to aB or Ab first?
examples.strategy: Record the two orders → Inspect node choices → Apply the tree test

steps.title: Record the two orders
steps.explanation: Expanding A before B gives AB⇒aB⇒ab; expanding B before A gives AB⇒Ab⇒ab.

steps.title: Inspect node choices
steps.explanation: Both orders use exactly S→AB, \(A\to a\) and B→b; no node chooses a different right-hand side.

steps.title: Apply the tree test
steps.explanation: The only tree has ordered children A and B beneath S, with terminal leaves a and b. Reordering expansion visits leaves that tree unchanged.

examples.answer: The grammar is unambiguous; different arbitrary derivation orders are not an ambiguity witness.
examples.verification: A leftmost derivation must choose A first, so only the first displayed order is leftmost.

tutorials.title: Pushdown automata and stack-based matching
tutorials.body:
A pushdown automaton augments finite control with an unbounded stack. A transition can inspect input or epsilon, read the stack top and replace it with a string. The stack supports last-in-first-out matching obligations, allowing balanced nesting and equal ordered blocks that finite automata cannot generally count.
For aⁿbⁿ, push one marker per a, switch to the b phase and pop one per b. Reject an unmatched b, an a after the phase switch, or leftover markers at completion. A bottom marker distinguishes an empty count from losing the stack’s structural base. Acceptance by final state and by empty stack are equivalent language models for nondeterministic PDAs under suitable constructions, but a given machine’s acceptance condition must be followed exactly.
Nondeterministic PDAs recognize exactly CFLs, while deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass. One stack does not grant the full power of a Turing tape. In GATE traces, record state, remaining input and stack content at each step; stack orientation must be stated so push/pop order is unambiguous.

example.prompt: Trace a PDA for aⁿbⁿ on aabb using marker X and bottom Z.
example.strategy: Push a block → Pop b block → Completion

steps.title: Push a block
steps.explanation: After two a symbols, stack is XXZ with top at the left.

steps.title: Pop b block
steps.explanation: The first b removes one X; the second removes the other.

steps.title: Completion
steps.explanation: Input is consumed and only Z remains, satisfying the chosen acceptance condition.

example.answer: aabb is accepted.
example.verification: aab leaves a marker and is rejected; aabb a violates the phase order even if some count condition later changes.

depth.body: A PDA's stack represents pending obligations in last-in-first-out order. Trace the state, unread input and full stack together, and declare which end of the displayed stack is the top. A stack-bottom marker protects the base and makes completion checks explicit. For nested delimiters, every opening symbol pushes an obligation and the matching close discharges the top obligation. For a marked palindrome, a separator signals when pushing must stop and comparison/popping must begin. Acceptance requires the specified machine condition after consuming the complete input; reaching an accepting configuration with unread input is insufficient. Final-state acceptance and empty-stack acceptance describe equivalent nondeterministic language classes through constructions, but cannot be exchanged silently for a particular machine.

examples.prompt: Trace a balanced-parenthesis PDA on (()). It pushes X for (, pops X for ), and accepts at end with only bottom Z. Stack top is leftmost.
examples.strategy: Push opening obligations → Discharge the obligations → Check completion

steps.title: Push opening obligations
steps.explanation: Each opening parenthesis adds one X above the previous stack.

steps.title: Discharge the obligations
steps.explanation: Each closing parenthesis matches and removes the most recent unmatched opening.

steps.title: Check completion
steps.explanation: All four symbols are consumed and the stack is exactly Z, satisfying the specified acceptance test.

examples.answer: (()) is accepted.
examples.verification: The stack height above Z follows 0,1,2,1,0 and never becomes negative; )( would try to pop X when none exists and reject.

examples.prompt: Design and trace a PDA for {w#wᴿ:w∈{a,b}*} on ab#ba, with stack top at the left.
examples.strategy: Record the first half → Switch at the marker → Compare in reverse → Finish the run

steps.title: Record the first half
steps.explanation: In the push phase, store each input symbol itself so its identity remains available.

steps.title: Switch at the marker
steps.explanation: Consume # without changing baZ and enter the pop phase. No later input may be pushed as part of the first half.

steps.title: Compare in reverse
steps.explanation: Each symbol must equal the current stack top; the order naturally reverses the first half.

steps.title: Finish the run
steps.explanation: Input is exhausted and only Z remains, so accept; a mismatch or an extra marker rejects.

examples.answer: ab#ba is accepted.
examples.verification: ab#ab rejects at the first post-marker a because the required top is b. The empty first half gives #, which the same construction accepts.

examples.prompt: A PDA for aⁿbⁿ pushes X on a, then pops X on b, accepting only at end with Z. Why must aab reject even though the b phase was reached?
examples.strategy: Push the a block → Consume the available b → Apply the final condition

steps.title: Push the a block
steps.explanation: Two pending obligations are created.

steps.title: Consume the available b
steps.explanation: One obligation is discharged and the machine has correctly switched phase.

steps.title: Apply the final condition
steps.explanation: No input remains but one X still sits above Z, so the acceptance transition requiring Z is unavailable.

examples.answer: aab rejects because one a has no matching b.
examples.verification: The phase remembers ordering, while the stack remembers quantity. Satisfying the phase condition alone does not establish equal counts.

tutorials.title: Build a leftmost derivation and its parse tree
tutorials.body:
A context-free grammar consists of terminal symbols, nonterminal symbols, a start nonterminal and productions with one nonterminal on the left. A derivation begins at the start symbol and repeatedly replaces a nonterminal by a production's right-hand side. Only strings containing terminals alone belong to the generated language. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining nonterminal; this fixes the expansion order without changing the grammar's language.
The balanced-parenthesis grammar S→(S)S | ε separates a matched outer pair from a following balanced suffix. The first S inside the parentheses describes nesting, while the second S describes concatenation. Each nonempty expansion adds a matched pair; an epsilon expansion closes an unfinished recursive obligation. Record the entire sentential form after each rewrite, including all remaining nonterminals. A parse tree stores the same production choices hierarchically. Reading its terminal leaves left to right must reproduce the target string, and every internal node must use an actual grammar production.

example.prompt: Using S→(S)S | ε, give a leftmost derivation of (()) and explain the tree.
example.strategy: Open the outer pair → Nest another pair → Close the inner content → Close both suffixes

steps.title: Open the outer pair
steps.explanation: The target begins with a matched outer pair; the final S will describe any suffix after it.

steps.title: Nest another pair
steps.explanation: Expand the leftmost S, which lies inside the outer pair.

steps.title: Close the inner content
steps.explanation: Use epsilon on the leftmost S because the inner pair contains no further parentheses.

steps.title: Close both suffixes
steps.explanation: Both remaining S symbols derive epsilon, in leftmost order.

example.answer: The leftmost derivation produces (()); its tree has one pair nested inside another and empty following suffixes.
example.verification: Reading the terminal leaves gives exactly (()). Every prefix has at least as many opening as closing parentheses, and the final counts are equal.

depth.body: A production is a local rewriting rule, but a grammar's language includes all terminal results obtainable through any sequence of valid rules. Intermediate strings containing nonterminals are sentential forms rather than accepted words. The tree viewpoint helps separate structure from rewrite order: independent child nodes may be expanded in either order while producing the same tree. Grammar transformations need language equality, not merely matching a few sample strings. When eliminating nullable productions, first compute all nullable nonterminals, then add alternatives omitting each nullable occurrence; preserve epsilon at a fresh or permitted start symbol if it originally belongs. Keep empty-language generation distinct from the ability to derive the empty word.

examples.prompt: For S→aS | b, give a leftmost derivation of aab and describe its terminal leaves.
examples.strategy: Choose two recursive uses → Terminate the derivation → Check the tree

steps.title: Choose two recursive uses
steps.explanation: Each rule adds one leading a while retaining exactly one unfinished S.

steps.title: Terminate the derivation
steps.explanation: The rule S→b removes the final nonterminal and supplies the mandatory last b.

steps.title: Check the tree
steps.explanation: The root and its S child each contribute an a; the deepest S contributes b. Reading leaves yields a,a,b.

examples.answer: aab is generated; the tree contains two recursive rules and one base rule.
examples.verification: All generated words have form aⁿb. Substituting n=2 confirms the leaf order and required final symbol.

examples.prompt: Eliminate epsilon productions other than at start S from S→AB, \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\), B→b|ε. Preserve the language.
examples.strategy: Compute nullable symbols → Add omitted alternatives → Remove child epsilon rules

steps.title: Compute nullable symbols
steps.explanation: A and B derive ε directly; therefore S also derives ε through AB.

steps.title: Add omitted alternatives
steps.explanation: Omit A, B, both or neither from the original right-hand side.

steps.title: Remove child epsilon rules
steps.explanation: Only start S retains an epsilon alternative; the new unit alternatives preserve one-letter words.

examples.answer: A suitable grammar is S→AB|A|B|ε, \(A\to a\), B→b.
examples.verification: Both grammars generate exactly {ε,a,b,ab}; listing the four choices independently verifies language preservation.

examples.prompt: With S→AB, \(A\to a\) and B→b, do S⇒AB⇒aB⇒ab and S⇒AB⇒Ab⇒ab establish ambiguity?
examples.strategy: Inspect the differing order → Recover the common tree → Apply the ambiguity criterion

steps.title: Inspect the differing order
steps.explanation: One derivation expands A first; the other expands B first. Neither chooses a different production at any node.

steps.title: Recover the common tree
steps.explanation: Both use root S→AB, left child \(A\to a\) and right child B→b, so their hierarchical structure is identical.

steps.title: Apply the ambiguity criterion
steps.explanation: Ambiguity requires two distinct parse trees or two distinct leftmost derivations, not arbitrary derivation orders.

examples.answer: No ambiguity is established; this grammar has one tree for ab.
examples.verification: The second displayed derivation is rightmost rather than leftmost. There is only one production available for each of S,A,B.

tutorials.title: Establish a context-free language by constructing a grammar
tutorials.body:
A language is context free when some context-free grammar generates exactly its strings. A positive classification therefore needs a construction with both soundness and completeness: every generated string has the desired property, and every desired string can be generated. A grammar's recursive appearance alone does not establish that its language is nonregular, because regular languages are also context free.
Context-free languages are closed under union. To combine two grammars, first rename their nonterminals so they are disjoint, then introduce a fresh start symbol choosing one old start or the other. The choice is made for the whole derivation; it does not freely mix the component languages' terminal strings. For equal-count blocks, a production \(A\to a\)Ab adds one leading a and one trailing b together. Repeating it n times and then using epsilon gives every aⁿbⁿ and nothing else. This invariant supplies a proof for all lengths, beyond checking a few examples. The same construction can use c in place of b for another component.

example.prompt: Construct a CFG for {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} ∪ {aⁿcⁿ:n≥0}. Test aacc and aabc.
example.strategy: Build separate components → Choose one language → Derive a member → Rule out the mixed word

steps.title: Build separate components
steps.explanation: A generates matching a/b blocks; B generates matching a/c blocks.

steps.title: Choose one language
steps.explanation: A new start symbol makes a whole-string union without mixing the two grammars.

steps.title: Derive a member
steps.explanation: Choose the c component and apply its recursive production twice.

steps.title: Rule out the mixed word
steps.explanation: A terminal derivation through A contains no c, while one through B contains no b. The word aabc contains both and cannot be derived.

example.answer: The displayed grammar proves the union context free. It accepts aacc and rejects aabc.
example.verification: After n recursive expansions, A yields aⁿAbⁿ and B yields aⁿBcⁿ. Replacing the last nonterminal by epsilon proves exact counts and covers every member, including the empty word.

depth.body: Context-free classification asks for some grammar or pushdown recognizer with exactly the intended language. The grammar can establish unbounded count relationships by adding linked blocks in the same recursive rule. Union, concatenation and star constructions preserve context-freeness because they combine recursive components without requiring simultaneous independent stack comparisons. Intersection with a regular language is also safe: finite-state information can accompany a PDA state without replacing its stack. Intersecting two arbitrary CFLs is different, because their separate count constraints can combine into a three-way synchronization that one stack cannot enforce. Distinguish a successful positive construction from a pumping argument, which supplies a necessary property but does not by itself prove membership in the class.

examples.prompt: Construct a CFG for {aⁿb^{2n}:n≥0} and derive aabbbb.
examples.strategy: Link the counts in a rule → Derive the target → Prove exact generation

steps.title: Link the counts in a rule
steps.explanation: Every recursive use adds one a and two b symbols around the remaining S.

steps.title: Derive the target
steps.explanation: Two recursive uses and epsilon give the requested six symbols.

steps.title: Prove exact generation
steps.explanation: After n recursive uses the form is aⁿSb^{2n}; epsilon terminates it. Every n is selectable and no other production changes the ratio.

examples.answer: The grammar proves the language context free and generates aabbbb.
examples.verification: The target has two a symbols and four b symbols, matching the rule invariant 2n.

examples.prompt: Construct a CFG for the concatenation {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0}{cᵐdᵐ:m≥0}. Show aabbcd belongs.
examples.strategy: Create disjoint components → Concatenate their starts → Derive a member

steps.title: Create disjoint components
steps.explanation: The two components independently synchronize their own blocks.

steps.title: Concatenate their starts
steps.explanation: A must finish before B, giving aⁿbⁿcᵐdᵐ with n,m independently chosen.

steps.title: Derive a member
steps.equation: S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aAbB\Rightarrow aaAbbB\Rightarrow aabbB\Rightarrow aabbcBd\Rightarrow aabbcd
steps.explanation: The first component uses two paired expansions and the second component uses one.

examples.answer: S→AB with the displayed component rules generates exactly the concatenated CFL and accepts aabbcd.
examples.verification: The first component is aabb and the second is cd. Choosing either component's epsilon rule also correctly permits an empty factor.

examples.prompt: Are arbitrary intersections of CFLs context free? Consider L1={aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and L2={aᵐbⁿcⁿ}, with nonnegative indices.
examples.strategy: Verify both operands are CFLs → Combine their constraints → Use the known obstruction

steps.title: Verify both operands are CFLs
steps.explanation: L1 concatenates matching a/b blocks with c*; L2 concatenates a* with matching b/c blocks. These have direct CFG constructions.

steps.title: Combine their constraints
steps.explanation: Membership in both forces the three ordered block counts to coincide.

steps.title: Use the known obstruction
steps.explanation: The equal-three-block language violates the CFL pumping lemma: a bounded window cannot alter all three counts together.

examples.answer: No; the intersection of these two CFLs is not context free.
examples.verification: For aabbccc the first constraint holds but the second fails; for aaabbbccc both hold. This checks which equalities each operand enforces.

lessons.title: The context-free pumping lemma
lessons.intuition: Context-free pumping repeats two pieces because recursive grammar structure can surround a nested derivation. The proof pattern resembles regular pumping, but its decomposition has five parts and the two pumped parts may be separated.

sections.title: Statement and constraints
sections.body: For a context-free language L, there exists p so every w∈L of length at least p can be written uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, \(|vy|>0\), and uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for all i≥0. At least one of v,y is nonempty; neither individually must be nonempty. The bounded window vxy is important for controlling which symbol blocks can be changed.

sections.title: Proving non-CFL status
sections.body: Assume L is context free, let p be arbitrary, and select a string depending on p. Show every valid decomposition fails for some pumping exponent. Often choose a string with three synchronized blocks so the bounded window cannot alter all required counts together. If pumping disturbs symbol ordering, the string also leaves the language.

sections.title: Limits of the method
sections.body: Failure to find a useful contradiction is not a proof that a language is context free. Establish membership by constructing a grammar or PDA. Closure can simplify a difficult proof: intersecting with a regular language restricts patterns without leaving the CFL class if the original language truly is CFL.

sections.title: The bounded window and legal closure reasoning
sections.body: A sufficiently tall CFG parse tree repeats a nonterminal on one root-to-leaf path. Replacing the larger repeated subtree by the smaller one, or nesting it again, removes or repeats material on two sides of the inner subtree. That is why two substrings are pumped with the same exponent. The bounded window limits where those changes can occur; it is not a bound on the entire word. For three equal separated blocks, a window of length at most p cannot include a symbol from the first and third blocks when the middle block already has length p. Pumping must alter at least one count while leaving another unchanged, or ruin block ordering. CFL closure under intersection with regular languages can isolate a difficult pattern, but intersection with arbitrary CFLs cannot be assumed.

lessons.concept: Context-free pumping repeats two pieces because recursive grammar structure can surround a nested derivation. The proof pattern resembles regular pumping, but its decomposition has five parts and the two pumped parts may be separated.
lessons.method:
The CFL pumping lemma decomposes a sufficiently long word as uvxyz, with |vxy|≤p and \(|vy|>0\), and requires uvⁱxyⁱz in the language for every nonnegative i. Two separated pieces are pumped together because a repeated nonterminal in a parse-tree path surrounds an inner subtree. Either v or y can be empty, but not both.
For non-context-freeness, choose a word after p, cover every legal bounded window and show a pumping exponent breaks membership. A three-block equal-count language is a common example: a short window cannot affect all three widely separated counts. Boundary-straddling windows must be handled too, not just windows inside one block.
CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, and intersection with a regular language. They are not generally closed under complement or intersection with another CFL. A closure argument must use a valid operand class. As with regular pumping, the lemma is a necessary condition rather than a universal recipe for proving that a language is context-free; a grammar or PDA gives that positive proof. For a context-free language L, there exists p so every w∈L of length at least p can be written uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, \(|vy|>0\), and uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for all i≥0. At least one of v,y is nonempty; neither individually must be nonempty. The bounded window vxy is important for controlling which symbol blocks can be changed. Assume L is context free, let p be arbitrary, and select a string depending on p. Show every valid decomposition fails for some pumping exponent. Often choose a string with three synchronized blocks so the bounded window cannot alter all required counts together. If pumping disturbs symbol ordering, the string also leaves the language. Failure to find a useful contradiction is not a proof that a language is context free. Establish membership by constructing a grammar or PDA. Closure can simplify a difficult proof: intersecting with a regular language restricts patterns without leaving the CFL class if the original language truly is CFL. A sufficiently tall CFG parse tree repeats a nonterminal on one root-to-leaf path. Replacing the larger repeated subtree by the smaller one, or nesting it again, removes or repeats material on two sides of the inner subtree. That is why two substrings are pumped with the same exponent. The bounded window limits where those changes can occur; it is not a bound on the entire word. For three equal separated blocks, a window of length at most p cannot include a symbol from the first and third blocks when the middle block already has length p. Pumping must alter at least one count while leaving another unchanged, or ruin block ordering. CFL closure under intersection with regular languages can isolate a difficult pattern, but intersection with arbitrary CFLs cannot be assumed. The two pumped portions of a CFL decomposition correspond to recursive material surrounding an inner subtree. They may be separated and either one may be empty, but their combined length must be positive. The bounded span is vxy, so a short window constrains which distant blocks can change together. To disprove context-freeness, choose a member after the bound is known and cover every allowed window, including those crossing boundaries. Three synchronized blocks are difficult because any sufficiently short pumping window leaves a block count unchanged while changing another required count. The counts need not literally be equal: a fixed ratio can create the same obstruction. In a closure argument, assume the larger language is context free, intersect with a regular filter, and obtain a known non-CFL contradiction. Conversely, several visible blocks do not automatically imply non-context-freeness. If one count is independent, a grammar can finish a matching pair and then generate an arbitrary suffix with a separate component.

steps.title: Choose tightly separated counts

steps.explanation: A vxy of length at most p cannot touch both a and c, because crossing the entire b block already needs more than p symbols.

steps.title: Finish all cases
steps.explanation: At least one symbol is deleted or duplicated because \(|vy|>0\). Any ordering disruption also rejects, so every split fails some exponent.

steps.title: Restrict the pumping window

steps.title: Remove the extra component
steps.explanation: This regular filter requires at least one c, excluding every word of a*b*.

steps.title: Apply the contradiction

examples.prompt: Does {aⁿbⁿcᵐ:n,m≥0} fail to be context free merely because it has three blocks?

steps.title: Separate the constraints
steps.explanation: Only a and b counts must match; the c count is independent and requires no simultaneous matching obligation.

steps.title: Construct a grammar
steps.equation: S\to AC,\quad A\to aAb\mid\varepsilon,\quad C\to cC\mid\varepsilon

steps.title: Work a member
steps.explanation: A derives aabb with two recursive uses, and C derives ccc with three; concatenation gives aabbccc.
