lessons.title: Turing machines and undecidability
lessons.prerequisite: Automata, proof by contradiction and algorithms.
lessons.intuition: A Turing machine adds an unbounded writable tape to finite control. It models general algorithmic computation. The crucial distinction is whether a machine always halts with an answer or may run forever on some negative instances.

sections.title: Deciders and recognizers
sections.body: A decider halts on every input and accepts exactly its language. A recognizer accepts members but may reject or loop on nonmembers. Every decidable language is recognizable, but not conversely. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, interleave their steps; one must accept, giving a decider.

sections.title: The halting contradiction
sections.body: Suppose H can decide whether any machine halts on an input. Construct D that on machine code x loops if H says machine x halts on x, and halts otherwise. Running D on its own code makes either prediction contradict what D does. Thus no general halting decider exists.

sections.title: Reductions and Rice
sections.body: To show B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B: transform A instances computably so a hypothetical B decider would decide A. Reversing the reduction proves the wrong implication. Rice’s theorem states every nontrivial property of the language recognized by a machine is undecidable; syntactic facts such as the number of states are not such semantic properties.

sections.title: Halting guarantees and reduction direction
sections.body: A recognizer must eventually accept members but can reject or loop on nonmembers. A decider must halt with the correct result on both kinds of input. Complementing a recognizer by flipping its accepting and rejecting states does not fix infinite loops; complementing a decider does work. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, alternating one step of each produces a decider because exactly one eventually accepts. For an undecidability reduction, suppose a solver for your target problem exists and show how it would solve a known impossible problem. The input transformation must itself halt and preserve yes/no membership in the stated direction. Rice’s theorem concerns nontrivial semantic properties of recognized languages, not arbitrary syntactic questions such as the number of states written in a machine description.

examples.prompt: Turn two recognizers into a decider

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Run one recognizer for L and one for its complement in alternating steps on the same input. Use separate saved machine configurations and alternate their steps; both simulations receive unbounded progress.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: If the first accepts, answer yes; if the second accepts, answer no. The recognizer for the correct side eventually accepts, so its answer determines membership without needing the other to halt.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Every input belongs to exactly one side, so some recognizer eventually accepts. Running one to completion first could loop forever. Exactly one side contains any given input. This supplies the termination proof that each recognizer alone lacks.

examples.strategy: Interleave simulations to avoid waiting forever for one recognizer to reject.
examples.answer: Every input belongs to exactly one side, so some recognizer eventually accepts. Running one to completion first could loop forever.
examples.verification: For a member, the L simulation accepts; for a nonmember, the complement simulation accepts. Both cases terminate under dovetailing.

examples.prompt: Reason about a reduction A≤B
steps: Assume a computable transform maps x∈A iff f(x)∈B.
If B had a decider, first compute f(x), then call it and return the same answer.
That would decide A. If A is undecidable, B cannot have such a decider.

pitfalls: Recognizable does not mean decidable.
Reduction direction is essential.
Rice applies to semantic language properties, not all machine properties.
revision: Decider halts everywhere; recognizer need not.
Known hard A≤B establishes hardness of B.

lessons.concept: A Turing machine adds an unbounded writable tape to finite control. It models general algorithmic computation. The crucial distinction is whether a machine always halts with an answer or may run forever on some negative instances.
lessons.method:
A Turing machine has finite control and an unbounded tape whose head reads, writes and moves according to transition rules. Tape memory can be revisited and changed, unlike the restricted top access of a single PDA stack. A machine computation may halt accepting, halt rejecting or continue forever.
A recognizer for L must eventually accept every member; on nonmembers it may reject or loop. A decider must halt on every input with the correct yes/no result. Decidable languages are recognizable, but recognizable languages need not be decidable. Flipping accept/reject outcomes complements a decider, yet cannot repair a recognizer’s infinite loops.
Equivalent common machine variants describe the same computable languages despite efficiency differences. To prove decidability, provide an algorithm and a termination argument, not just plausible accepting behavior. If both L and its complement are recognizable, dovetail both recognizers; whichever accepts first determines the answer, and one must eventually accept. Simulation needs saved configurations so neither branch monopolizes execution. An undecidable decision problem has no algorithm halting with the correct answer on every permitted input. This does not mean every instance is unknowable or that no recognizer exists. The halting problem asks whether a supplied machine halts on a supplied input; a universal decider would contradict a self-referential diagonal construction.
A mapping reduction A≤ₘB transforms each input x of A into f(x) for B by an always-halting computable function, preserving x∈A iff f(x)∈B. If B were decidable, computing f then using its decider would decide A. Thus to prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B, not in the reverse direction.
The transform cannot hide an undecidable step of its own. State the constructed machine and the behavior in both source yes/no cases. Rice’s theorem concerns nontrivial semantic properties of recognized languages, not every syntactic fact about a machine description. A finite bound on simulation time decides bounded halting, a different question from unrestricted eventual halting. A Turing machine has a finite control state, a read/write tape, a head position and a transition function. A transition uses the current state and scanned symbol to choose a new state, the symbol written at that cell, and a head movement. A complete configuration records the tape, head and state. Changing only the state in a trace omits the memory operation that distinguishes this model from finite automata.
Use a two-way infinite tape with integer-indexed cells and blank symbols outside the finite input. The input alphabet here is just {1}, so every input is a unary number: n ones represent n. A unary incrementer scans right across the original ones, replaces the first blank by a one, moves left and enters a halting state. The state called q_h has no outgoing transitions. Tape blanks are part of the tape alphabet, not extra symbols in the input. Counting transitions establishes termination: n scanning steps and one writing step halt on every valid input, including the empty input representing zero. The halting problem asks whether a supplied machine eventually halts on a supplied input, whether by accepting or rejecting. A proposed decider must answer correctly and halt for every encoded machine/input pair. Simulating a machine can confirm halting when it happens, but no arbitrary finite observation establishes that a machine will run forever.
Diagonalization assumes such a total decider H exists and then builds another machine D that deliberately contradicts H on self-input. On a valid machine encoding x, D asks whether the encoded machine halts when given that same encoding x. If H predicts halting, D loops forever; if H predicts nonhalting, D halts. Invalid encodings may be handled by halting immediately, so they cause no issue. D is a finite machine description because its code just calls the assumed H and branches on its answer. Running D on its own valid encoding forces the prediction to disagree with the actual behavior in either case. The contradiction rules out H, rather than prohibiting solutions for particular machines or bounded simulation questions. A decision problem is undecidable when no algorithm halts with the correct yes/no answer on every allowed input. This is a statement about a universal solver, not about whether selected instances have easily proved answers. To prove a new problem undecidable, transform instances of an already undecidable problem into its instances and show how an assumed solver would settle the original problem.
Consider whether a Turing machine's recognized language is empty. Given a machine M and input w, construct a new machine N that ignores its own input y and simulates M on w. If that simulation ever halts, whether accepting or rejecting, N accepts y. If it never halts, N never accepts y. Thus N recognizes every string or no strings according to the original run's halting behavior. Constructing N's finite description just embeds M and w in simulation code; it does not run the simulation to completion. A decider for emptiness would therefore decide halting after reversing its answer. This separates the termination of the reduction algorithm from the possibly infinite execution of the constructed machine. A mapping reduction A≤ₘB is an always-halting computable transformation f satisfying x∈A exactly when f(x)∈B. To prove B undecidable from a known undecidable A, compute f and then invoke a hypothetical B decider. The transform must produce an instance without first answering A. A machine constructed by the transform may run forever; the algorithm writing that machine's finite description must not.
For A_TM, the source question is whether M accepts w. For HALT, the target question is whether a machine halts on its given input. These differ when M halts rejecting. Build a machine N that ignores its own input, simulates M on the embedded word w, and halts only when that simulation accepts. On simulated rejection N deliberately enters an infinite loop; on simulated nontermination it keeps simulating. Checking all three behaviors is necessary: a wrapper that simply stops whenever M stops would reduce a halting question, but would not preserve acceptance. State both the produced machine and the fixed input supplied to it in the target instance. A decider halts on every input and accepts exactly its language. A recognizer accepts members but may reject or loop on nonmembers. Every decidable language is recognizable, but not conversely. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, interleave their steps; one must accept, giving a decider. Suppose H can decide whether any machine halts on an input. Construct D that on machine code x loops if H says machine x halts on x, and halts otherwise. Running D on its own code makes either prediction contradict what D does. Thus no general halting decider exists. To show B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B: transform A instances computably so a hypothetical B decider would decide A. Reversing the reduction proves the wrong implication. Rice’s theorem states every nontrivial property of the language recognized by a machine is undecidable; syntactic facts such as the number of states are not such semantic properties. A recognizer must eventually accept members but can reject or loop on nonmembers. A decider must halt with the correct result on both kinds of input. Complementing a recognizer by flipping its accepting and rejecting states does not fix infinite loops; complementing a decider does work. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, alternating one step of each produces a decider because exactly one eventually accepts. For an undecidability reduction, suppose a solver for your target problem exists and show how it would solve a known impossible problem. The input transformation must itself halt and preserve yes/no membership in the stated direction. Rice’s theorem concerns nontrivial semantic properties of recognized languages, not arbitrary syntactic questions such as the number of states written in a machine description. Separate the machine's finite transition description from its potentially unbounded execution. A trace needs the symbol written before the head moves, because later steps may revisit that modified cell. Multi-phase algorithms use states to distinguish scanning, carrying, returning and halting; the same tape symbol may trigger different actions in different phases. Tape cells outside the input initially contain blanks, so a boundary rule is an actual transition rather than a magical stop. A terminating transducer can compute an output without discussing accepted-language membership. A recognizer's behavior on negative inputs may instead be infinite, and complementing only its halting outcomes does not repair those runs. State the initial head, tape indexing and halting convention for every trace. Halting includes both accepting and rejecting termination. Universal simulation can recognize a positive halting instance by following the supplied computation until either terminal outcome occurs, but cannot recognize nonhalting simply by waiting. A cutoff certifies only that the run has not halted yet. Many apparently narrower halting problems remain hard because an arbitrary input can be built into a new machine's finite description. When proving this, distinguish the new machine's own input from the source input being simulated. Diagonalization derives an inconsistency from a supposed universal decider; it does not claim that actual simulators give incorrect positive observations. The limitation is obtaining correct, terminating answers for every possible negative instance as well. Undecidability concerns the impossibility of one total correct algorithm for all instances of a problem. Particular machine descriptions can still have obvious answers, and restricting the question can make a different problem decidable. Semantic properties of recognized languages are distinguished from syntactic properties of machine code. Rice's theorem applies when a language property is nontrivial, meaning some recognizable language has it and another lacks it; countable states or a chosen numbering are not such properties. Reductions make hardness concrete by embedding a source simulation into a target machine and checking both yes and no behavior. The construction algorithm must terminate, even if the target computation it describes can loop forever. A reduction's correctness has two separate obligations: its transformation is effectively computable and its output preserves the source membership answer. The target solver, if assumed, comes after this construction. It is acceptable for a reduction between easy problems to compute a simple source statistic; a hardness reduction cannot secretly call an unavailable source decider. Always write the equivalence, then test a positive instance and every relevant type of negative instance. Reductions transport an available target algorithm backward to the source, so undecidability propagates from source to target. A reduction from an easy problem to a hard one does not establish that the easy problem is hard, because it may use only trivial target instances.

A Turing machine has finite control and an unbounded tape whose head reads, writes and moves according to transition rules. Tape memory can be revisited and changed, unlike the restricted top access of a single PDA stack. A machine computation may halt accepting, halt rejecting or continue forever.
A recognizer for L must eventually accept every member; on nonmembers it may reject or loop. A decider must halt on every input with the correct yes/no result. Decidable languages are recognizable, but recognizable languages need not be decidable. Flipping accept/reject outcomes complements a decider, yet cannot repair a recognizer’s infinite loops.
Equivalent common machine variants describe the same computable languages despite efficiency differences. To prove decidability, provide an algorithm and a termination argument, not just plausible accepting behavior. If both L and its complement are recognizable, dovetail both recognizers; whichever accepts first determines the answer, and one must eventually accept. Simulation needs saved configurations so neither branch monopolizes execution.

example.prompt: Given recognizers R for L and S for its complement, decide membership.
example.strategy: Interleave → Positive case → Negative case

steps.title: Interleave
steps.explanation: Run one step of R, then one of S, repeatedly on the same input.

steps.title: Positive case
steps.explanation: If R accepts, answer yes; do not require S to halt.

steps.title: Negative case
steps.explanation: If S accepts, answer no. Every input belongs to one side, guaranteeing eventual acceptance there.

example.answer: Dovetailing constructs a decider.
example.verification: Running R to completion before S could loop forever on a nonmember and would not be a decider.

tutorials.title: Undecidability and reduction direction
tutorials.body:
An undecidable decision problem has no algorithm halting with the correct answer on every permitted input. This does not mean every instance is unknowable or that no recognizer exists. The halting problem asks whether a supplied machine halts on a supplied input; a universal decider would contradict a self-referential diagonal construction.
A mapping reduction A≤ₘB transforms each input x of A into f(x) for B by an always-halting computable function, preserving x∈A iff f(x)∈B. If B were decidable, computing f then using its decider would decide A. Thus to prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B, not in the reverse direction.
The transform cannot hide an undecidable step of its own. State the constructed machine and the behavior in both source yes/no cases. Rice’s theorem concerns nontrivial semantic properties of recognized languages, not every syntactic fact about a machine description. A finite bound on simulation time decides bounded halting, a different question from unrestricted eventual halting.

example.prompt: A known undecidable A reduces to B. What follows if B has a decider?
example.strategy: Transform input → Use assumed solver → Preserve answer

steps.title: Transform input
steps.explanation: The reduction always halts.

steps.title: Use assumed solver
steps.explanation: Call B’s decider on f(x), which also always halts.

steps.title: Preserve answer
steps.explanation: Return that answer to decide A, contradicting its undecidability.

example.answer: B cannot have a decider.
example.verification: A reduction B≤A would not establish this conclusion, because B might be an easier problem.

tutorials.title: Trace a Turing machine one transition at a time
tutorials.body:
A Turing machine has a finite control state, a read/write tape, a head position and a transition function. A transition uses the current state and scanned symbol to choose a new state, the symbol written at that cell, and a head movement. A complete configuration records the tape, head and state. Changing only the state in a trace omits the memory operation that distinguishes this model from finite automata.
Use a two-way infinite tape with integer-indexed cells and blank symbols outside the finite input. The input alphabet here is just {1}, so every input is a unary number: n ones represent n. A unary incrementer scans right across the original ones, replaces the first blank by a one, moves left and enters a halting state. The state called q_h has no outgoing transitions. Tape blanks are part of the tape alphabet, not extra symbols in the input. Counting transitions establishes termination: n scanning steps and one writing step halt on every valid input, including the empty input representing zero.

example.prompt: Trace input 111 with the head at cell 0. Rules: δ(q_s,1)=(q_s,1,R) and δ(q_s,blank)=(q_h,1,L).
example.strategy: Read cell zero → Read the remaining ones → Write the increment → Inspect the halted configuration

steps.title: Read cell zero
steps.explanation: Write the same 1, retain q_s and move the head from cell 0 to cell 1; the tape is still 111 followed by blanks.

steps.title: Read the remaining ones
steps.explanation: These pairs record state and head index. Two more scanning transitions preserve cells 1 and 2 and reach the blank at cell 3.

steps.title: Write the increment
steps.explanation: Replace cell 3's blank with 1, enter q_h and move the head to cell 2.

steps.title: Inspect the halted configuration
steps.explanation: The tape now contains 1111 in cells 0 through 3; the head scans cell 2 and no further rule applies in q_h.

example.answer: The machine halts after four transitions with output 1111 and its head at cell 2.
example.verification: Three input ones caused three rightward scanning moves, and exactly one previously blank cell became 1. For n input ones the output has n+1 ones and the run takes n+1 transitions.

depth.body: Separate the machine's finite transition description from its potentially unbounded execution. A trace needs the symbol written before the head moves, because later steps may revisit that modified cell. Multi-phase algorithms use states to distinguish scanning, carrying, returning and halting; the same tape symbol may trigger different actions in different phases. Tape cells outside the input initially contain blanks, so a boundary rule is an actual transition rather than a magical stop. A terminating transducer can compute an output without discussing accepted-language membership. A recognizer's behavior on negative inputs may instead be infinite, and complementing only its halting outcomes does not repair those runs. State the initial head, tape indexing and halting convention for every trace.

examples.prompt: A machine erases unary input: δ(e,1)=(e,blank,R), δ(e,blank)=(h,blank,L); h halts. Trace 11 starting at cell 0.
examples.strategy: Erase cell zero → Erase cell one → Use the boundary rule

steps.title: Erase cell zero
steps.explanation: Read its 1, write blank and move to cell 1; state stays e and only the second input one remains.

steps.title: Erase cell one
steps.explanation: Write blank over the second 1 and move to cell 2, whose symbol was blank from the start.

steps.title: Use the boundary rule
steps.explanation: On blank at cell 2 enter h and move left to cell 1. The machine now halts with both original cells blank.

examples.answer: The input is erased in three transitions; the final head is at cell 1.
examples.verification: For n unary input symbols there are n erasing steps and one boundary step. On empty input the boundary step alone halts.

examples.prompt: Increment binary input 1011. State s scans 0/1 right unchanged; on blank it enters c moving left. In c, 1 becomes 0 and moves left; 0 becomes 1 and enters halt moving right.
examples.strategy: Locate the low-order end → Propagate the carry → Stop at the first zero → Read the output

steps.title: Locate the low-order end
steps.explanation: Four scan transitions reach blank cell 4; its boundary transition enters carry state c at cell 3.

steps.title: Propagate the carry
steps.explanation: At cells 3 and 2, the two trailing ones become zeros; the head moves left to cell 1.

steps.title: Stop at the first zero
steps.explanation: Cell 1 contains 0, so write 1, enter the halting state and move right to cell 2. The original leading 1 at cell 0 is unchanged.

steps.title: Read the output
steps.explanation: The resulting cells 0 through 3 contain 1100 after eight transitions.

examples.answer: The output is 1100, with the halted head at cell 2.
examples.verification: 1011₂ is 11 and 1100₂ is 12. The transition count is four scanning, one boundary and three carry steps.

examples.prompt: A recognizer accepts the single word 1 and loops forever on every other input. If its accepting halt is changed to rejecting, does it recognize the complement?
examples.strategy: Trace its positive input → Trace a negative input → Apply recognizer acceptance

steps.title: Trace its positive input
steps.explanation: On input 1 the changed machine now halts rejecting, so 1 is excluded as desired.

steps.title: Trace a negative input
steps.explanation: On input 0 it follows the same infinite loop as before, because no halting state is reached or changed.

steps.title: Apply recognizer acceptance
steps.explanation: 0 belongs to the complement but is never accepted. In fact the changed machine accepts no input.

examples.answer: No. The changed machine recognizes the empty language, not the complement of {1}.
examples.verification: A complement recognizer must eventually accept 0, ε and every other nonmember; merely swapping halting outcomes supplies none of those accepting computations.

tutorials.title: Prove the halting problem undecidable by diagonalization
tutorials.body:
The halting problem asks whether a supplied machine eventually halts on a supplied input, whether by accepting or rejecting. A proposed decider must answer correctly and halt for every encoded machine/input pair. Simulating a machine can confirm halting when it happens, but no arbitrary finite observation establishes that a machine will run forever.
Diagonalization assumes such a total decider H exists and then builds another machine D that deliberately contradicts H on self-input. On a valid machine encoding x, D asks whether the encoded machine halts when given that same encoding x. If H predicts halting, D loops forever; if H predicts nonhalting, D halts. Invalid encodings may be handled by halting immediately, so they cause no issue. D is a finite machine description because its code just calls the assumed H and branches on its answer. Running D on its own valid encoding forces the prediction to disagree with the actual behavior in either case. The contradiction rules out H, rather than prohibiting solutions for particular machines or bounded simulation questions.

example.prompt: Assume a total correct halting decider H(M,w). Construct D and analyze H(D,〈D〉).
example.strategy: Define the opposite behavior → Supply its own encoding → Examine a yes answer → Examine a no answer

steps.title: Define the opposite behavior
steps.explanation: On input x, D calls H on the machine encoded by x with input x. A yes answer makes D loop; a no answer makes D halt.

steps.title: Supply its own encoding
steps.explanation: The encoding is valid and refers to the very machine whose branch behavior was just defined.

steps.title: Examine a yes answer
steps.explanation: If H predicts that D on its own encoding halts, D follows the yes branch and loops forever, making the prediction false.

steps.title: Examine a no answer
steps.explanation: If H predicts that this run never halts, D follows the no branch and halts, again making the prediction false.

example.answer: Both possible answers contradict correctness, so no total halting decider exists.
example.verification: The same run is queried in H and executed by D: machine D with input 〈D〉. The argument does not confuse accepting with halting or assume the ability to obtain a nonhalting answer by simulation.

depth.body: Halting includes both accepting and rejecting termination. Universal simulation can recognize a positive halting instance by following the supplied computation until either terminal outcome occurs, but cannot recognize nonhalting simply by waiting. A cutoff certifies only that the run has not halted yet. Many apparently narrower halting problems remain hard because an arbitrary input can be built into a new machine's finite description. When proving this, distinguish the new machine's own input from the source input being simulated. Diagonalization derives an inconsistency from a supposed universal decider; it does not claim that actual simulators give incorrect positive observations. The limitation is obtaining correct, terminating answers for every possible negative instance as well.

examples.prompt: M on input 1 moves from q0 at cell 0 to q1 at blank cell 1, then enters a rejecting halt. Does the HALT recognizer accept (M,1)?
examples.strategy: Simulate the first step → Simulate the second step → Answer the outer problem

steps.title: Simulate the first step
steps.explanation: The universal simulation records M's move to q1 and head cell 1; a nonhalting state has not yet resolved HALT.

steps.title: Simulate the second step
steps.explanation: M reaches its rejecting terminal state. This is a finite termination even though M rejects its own input.

steps.title: Answer the outer problem
steps.explanation: The HALT recognizer accepts the encoded pair because it witnessed M halting, rather than copying M's language answer.

examples.answer: Yes; (M,1) is a positive HALT instance.
examples.verification: The witness is the two-transition run ending in a terminal state. HALT asks whether termination occurs, not whether M accepts 1.

examples.prompt: Prove that deciding whether a machine halts on the blank input is undecidable using general HALT.
examples.strategy: Embed the source input → Preserve halting → Use a hypothetical blank-input solver

steps.title: Embed the source input
steps.explanation: From M,w construct N that, on blank input, writes the finite word w, positions its simulation head at the start, then simulates M(w).

steps.title: Preserve halting
steps.explanation: The setup always finishes and the simulation preserves both accepting and rejecting halts.

steps.title: Use a hypothetical blank-input solver
steps.explanation: Apply it to N and return its answer for the original pair M,w. This would decide general HALT.

examples.answer: Blank-input halting is undecidable.
examples.verification: The wrapper description is computable from finite M,w. A source infinite run stays infinite after the finite setup, while either source halt yields a target halt.

examples.prompt: A proposed HALT solver simulates 100 transitions and says “never halts” if still running. Refute it with a concrete state-chain machine.
examples.strategy: Build the chain → Delay the final transition → Compare observation and truth

steps.title: Build the chain
steps.explanation: Use states q0 through q100 and terminal h. On blank, each qi with i<100 writes blank, moves right and enters q(i+1).

steps.title: Delay the final transition
steps.explanation: From q100 on blank, write blank, move right and enter h. All visited cells are initially blank.

steps.title: Compare observation and truth
steps.explanation: After 100 transitions the state is q100, so the proposed solver says never. Transition 101 reaches h and halts.

examples.answer: The cutoff solver gives a false negative on this machine.
examples.verification: The state index equals the elapsed transition count until q100. A finite chain can defeat any fixed simulation cutoff by placing its halt one step later.

tutorials.title: Show that machine-language emptiness is undecidable
tutorials.body:
A decision problem is undecidable when no algorithm halts with the correct yes/no answer on every allowed input. This is a statement about a universal solver, not about whether selected instances have easily proved answers. To prove a new problem undecidable, transform instances of an already undecidable problem into its instances and show how an assumed solver would settle the original problem.
Consider whether a Turing machine's recognized language is empty. Given a machine M and input w, construct a new machine N that ignores its own input y and simulates M on w. If that simulation ever halts, whether accepting or rejecting, N accepts y. If it never halts, N never accepts y. Thus N recognizes every string or no strings according to the original run's halting behavior. Constructing N's finite description just embeds M and w in simulation code; it does not run the simulation to completion. A decider for emptiness would therefore decide halting after reversing its answer. This separates the termination of the reduction algorithm from the possibly infinite execution of the constructed machine.

example.prompt: Use the known undecidability of HALT to prove that deciding L(N)=∅ is impossible.
example.strategy: Construct the target machine → Analyze a halting source → Analyze a looping source → Use the assumed emptiness solver

steps.title: Construct the target machine
steps.explanation: From (M,w), output code for N: ignore y, simulate M(w), and accept y if the simulation halts. This code construction always terminates.

steps.title: Analyze a halting source
steps.explanation: Every y triggers the same eventually halting simulation, after which N accepts it.

steps.title: Analyze a looping source
steps.explanation: No run of N reaches its accept action, so its recognized language is empty.

steps.title: Use the assumed emptiness solver
steps.explanation: If a total solver says empty, answer that M(w) does not halt; if it says nonempty, answer that M(w) halts. This would decide the known undecidable problem.

example.answer: Machine-language emptiness is undecidable.
example.verification: A rejecting halt of M must still make N accept, because the source question asks about halting. Inspecting that case ensures the transform preserves the intended yes/no relation.

depth.body: Undecidability concerns the impossibility of one total correct algorithm for all instances of a problem. Particular machine descriptions can still have obvious answers, and restricting the question can make a different problem decidable. Semantic properties of recognized languages are distinguished from syntactic properties of machine code. Rice's theorem applies when a language property is nontrivial, meaning some recognizable language has it and another lacks it; countable states or a chosen numbering are not such properties. Reductions make hardness concrete by embedding a source simulation into a target machine and checking both yes and no behavior. The construction algorithm must terminate, even if the target computation it describes can loop forever.

examples.prompt: Is deciding whether L(M) is finite undecidable? Apply Rice’s theorem with explicit yes/no language witnesses.
examples.strategy: Check semantic dependence → Exhibit a yes witness → Exhibit a no witness → Apply the theorem

steps.title: Check semantic dependence
steps.explanation: Finiteness depends only on the recognized language, so two machines recognizing the same language receive the same answer.

steps.title: Exhibit a yes witness
steps.explanation: A machine rejecting every input recognizes a finite language.

steps.title: Exhibit a no witness
steps.explanation: A machine accepting every input recognizes an infinite language; the property is therefore nontrivial.

steps.title: Apply the theorem
steps.explanation: Rice's theorem makes every such nontrivial semantic property of Turing-recognized languages undecidable.

examples.answer: Language finiteness is undecidable.
examples.verification: The witnesses differ in language cardinality, not their number of states, so the semantic and nontriviality requirements both hold.

examples.prompt: Assume A_TM undecidable. Prove deciding whether an arbitrary machine accepts the fixed word 101 is undecidable.
examples.strategy: Build a finite wrapper → Check the yes case → Check both no cases → Compose a supposed solver

steps.title: Build a finite wrapper
steps.explanation: Given M,w, create N that ignores its own input and simulates M on embedded w, accepting or rejecting when M does.

steps.title: Check the yes case
steps.explanation: Ignoring the supplied input ensures the fixed word triggers exactly the embedded simulation.

steps.title: Check both no cases
steps.explanation: If M rejects, N rejects 101; if M loops, N loops on 101. Neither behavior is acceptance.

steps.title: Compose a supposed solver
steps.explanation: Testing N on the fixed word with a total correct solver would decide whether M accepts w, contradicting the source undecidability.

examples.answer: Acceptance of the fixed word 101 by a supplied machine is undecidable.
examples.verification: Fixing the word does not fix the machine. N's finite code embeds both source components without first determining their acceptance result.

examples.prompt: Is “M halts within supplied bound k transitions” undecidable merely because unrestricted HALT is? Test a two-transition halting run at k=1 and k=2.
examples.strategy: Define the bounded algorithm → Evaluate the two instances → Prove termination

steps.title: Define the bounded algorithm
steps.explanation: Inspect the initial configuration for a halt, then simulate at most k transitions, checking for a halt after each.

steps.title: Evaluate the two instances
steps.explanation: A run halting after exactly two transitions gives no for k=1 and yes for k=2; neither requires waiting beyond its bound.

steps.title: Prove termination
steps.explanation: The algorithm performs a finite number of prescribed steps for every machine and finite supplied k, then returns a definite answer.

examples.answer: Bounded halting is decidable; the two answers are no and yes.
examples.verification: The no answer means no halt within k, not no halt ever. That distinction removes the infinite-wait requirement of unrestricted HALT.

tutorials.title: Construct and verify a mapping reduction
tutorials.body:
A mapping reduction A≤ₘB is an always-halting computable transformation f satisfying x∈A exactly when f(x)∈B. To prove B undecidable from a known undecidable A, compute f and then invoke a hypothetical B decider. The transform must produce an instance without first answering A. A machine constructed by the transform may run forever; the algorithm writing that machine's finite description must not.
For A_TM, the source question is whether M accepts w. For HALT, the target question is whether a machine halts on its given input. These differ when M halts rejecting. Build a machine N that ignores its own input, simulates M on the embedded word w, and halts only when that simulation accepts. On simulated rejection N deliberately enters an infinite loop; on simulated nontermination it keeps simulating. Checking all three behaviors is necessary: a wrapper that simply stops whenever M stops would reduce a halting question, but would not preserve acceptance. State both the produced machine and the fixed input supplied to it in the target instance.

example.prompt: Assume A_TM is known undecidable. Map (M,w) to a HALT instance with matching yes answers.
example.strategy: Write a finite wrapper → Check source acceptance → Check both negative behaviors → Conclude the reduction

steps.title: Write a finite wrapper
steps.explanation: N ignores its input, simulates the embedded M(w), halts on acceptance and deliberately loops on rejection.

steps.title: Check source acceptance
steps.explanation: The simulation reaches acceptance and activates the wrapper's halting branch.

steps.title: Check both negative behaviors
steps.explanation: If M rejects w, N loops after observing rejection. If M itself loops, N continues simulating forever. In either case N does not halt.

steps.title: Conclude the reduction
steps.explanation: A HALT decider composed with this terminating code transform would decide A_TM, so HALT is undecidable.

example.answer: The wrapper establishes A_TM≤ₘHALT; both source no cases map to target no cases.
example.verification: No step in constructing N needs to know whether M accepts. The deliberate rejection loop is essential, because rejecting is a source no answer despite being a halting computation.

depth.body: A reduction's correctness has two separate obligations: its transformation is effectively computable and its output preserves the source membership answer. The target solver, if assumed, comes after this construction. It is acceptable for a reduction between easy problems to compute a simple source statistic; a hardness reduction cannot secretly call an unavailable source decider. Always write the equivalence, then test a positive instance and every relevant type of negative instance. Reductions transport an available target algorithm backward to the source, so undecidability propagates from source to target. A reduction from an easy problem to a hard one does not establish that the easy problem is hard, because it may use only trivial target instances.

examples.prompt: Reduce A=binary words containing a 1 to B=nonempty unary words over {a}, using the number of ones. Map 00101 and 000.
examples.strategy: Define the transform → Verify a positive input → Verify zero and general cases

steps.title: Define the transform
steps.explanation: Scan the finite input and output one a for each 1; this always terminates.

steps.title: Verify a positive input
steps.explanation: The source contains two ones and its output is nonempty, hence belongs to B.

steps.title: Verify zero and general cases
steps.explanation: A source with no ones maps to the sole empty unary word, and the equivalence covers every input.

examples.answer: This computable transform establishes A≤ₘB; the outputs are aa and ε.
examples.verification: Counting ones independently gives 2 and 0, and B tests only whether those unary lengths are positive.

examples.prompt: Reduce HALT to machine-language universality ALL={N:L(N)=Σ*}.
examples.strategy: Construct the machine → Check source yes → Check source no → Use the equivalence

steps.title: Construct the machine
steps.explanation: From M,w output N that ignores input y, simulates M(w), and accepts y if that simulation halts in either way.

steps.title: Check source yes
steps.explanation: Every supplied y reaches acceptance after the same finite embedded simulation.

steps.title: Check source no
steps.explanation: Every y loops, so N is not universal.

steps.title: Use the equivalence
steps.explanation: A universal-language decider on N would answer the original HALT instance; therefore ALL is undecidable.

examples.answer: The construction gives HALT≤ₘALL and proves universality undecidable.
examples.verification: The wrapper must accept after a rejecting source halt as well as an accepting one. Its construction writes simulation code without executing the possibly infinite run.

examples.prompt: If the empty language A=∅ reduces to HALT, does HALT’s undecidability prove A undecidable?
examples.strategy: Build the easy reduction → Check membership preservation → Check the source algorithm

steps.title: Build the easy reduction
steps.explanation: Map every source string to one fixed machine/input pair whose machine loops forever. All target outputs are negative HALT instances.

steps.title: Check membership preservation
steps.explanation: Both sides are false for every x, so the reduction is valid.

steps.title: Check the source algorithm
steps.explanation: Rejecting every input decides A immediately. Target hardness has not made these specially chosen source instances difficult.

examples.answer: No. This valid easy-to-hard reduction has a decidable source.
examples.verification: A target decider would decide its source, but a target that lacks a decider can still have trivially negative instances used by the reduction.

name: Compiler Design
description: Follow a program from source to execution

lessons.title: Lexical analysis and tokenization
lessons.intuition: The lexer groups characters into meaningful token classes before the parser checks grammar structure. A token records a category and possibly an attribute, while the lexeme is the actual source substring. Separating them lets a grammar treat every identifier similarly.

sections.title: Token definitions
sections.body: Identifiers, keywords, numeric literals, operators and punctuation are common token classes. Regular expressions describe many lexical patterns; automata implement them. Whitespace and comments may be discarded or retained as metadata depending on the language. Symbol-table entries link identifier tokens to later declaration/type information.

sections.title: Longest match and priority
sections.body: At each input position, a lexer typically chooses the longest matching lexeme. When matches have equal length, a rule priority resolves the tie, often recognizing a keyword before a generic identifier. Thus >= is one token rather than > followed by = if the token rule allows it. A keyword prefix inside an identifier does not force splitting: whilex can remain an identifier.

sections.title: Errors and boundaries
sections.body: A lexical error is an unrecognized character sequence under the token rules. A valid token sequence can still have a parse error, such as misplaced parentheses. Nested structure is ordinarily handled by the parser, not by ordinary finite-automaton token rules. Scanner buffering must preserve character positions and handle end-of-input correctly.

sections.title: How longest match is implemented
sections.body: A lexer can continue a DFA scan while remembering the most recent accepting position and the corresponding highest-priority rule. When no transition is possible, it returns to that remembered position and emits the token. This separates longest match from tie resolution. For an identifier rule accepting letters followed by letters or digits, “ifx” has a longer identifier match than the keyword “if”; “if” alone can use keyword priority because both matches have equal length. The lexeme is the actual character slice; the token kind is its category; an attribute may hold a numeric value or symbol-table index. Syntax nesting such as arbitrarily balanced parentheses belongs to parsing, since finite-state token recognition has no unbounded stack.

examples.prompt: Tokenize sum = a + 12;

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: sum is an identifier, = an assignment operator, and a another identifier. The two identifiers are different lexemes but belong to the same token kind. Spaces separate text but are not emitted here.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: + is an arithmetic operator, 12 a numeric literal, and ; punctuation. The numeric literal is one token despite containing two digits; punctuation also contributes a token.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: There are 6 tokens if whitespace is ignored; lexemes differ from their category names. Count emitted tokens rather than characters or distinct categories. A repeated category still creates a new token occurrence.

examples.strategy: Identify maximal token lexemes, then assign token categories.
examples.answer: There are 6 tokens if whitespace is ignored; lexemes differ from their category names.
examples.verification: The token sequence is identifier, assignment, identifier, plus, number, semicolon: six occurrences.

examples.prompt: Apply longest match to a>=10
steps: Read a as an identifier.
At >, the two-character >= match is longer than the one-character > match.
Return identifier, >=, number: three tokens.

pitfalls: Longest match beats an earlier shorter token rule.
Token category and source lexeme are different.

checks.prompt: Ignoring whitespace, how many tokens are in x = 2 + 3 ; ?
checks.hint: Count identifier, operators, literals and delimiter.
checks.explanation: x,=,2,+,3,; gives 6 tokens.

checks.prompt: With >= defined as an operator, how many tokens are in x>=5?
checks.hint: Use longest match for the operator.
checks.explanation: x,>=,5 gives 3 tokens.

lessons.concept: The lexer groups characters into meaningful token classes before the parser checks grammar structure. A token records a category and possibly an attribute, while the lexeme is the actual source substring. Separating them lets a grammar treat every identifier similarly.
lessons.method:
Lexical analysis turns source characters into token occurrences. A token kind names a category such as identifier, number or operator; its lexeme is the actual source substring and an attribute can store a value or symbol-table reference. Whitespace and comments can be skipped while position tracking remains. The parser uses these tokens to determine grammatical structure.
Maximal munch selects the longest prefix matching any token rule. If several rules match the same maximum length, a priority convention selects among them. A lexer can scan forward with a DFA while remembering its last accepting position, then return there when no longer extension is possible. Keyword priority therefore does not split ifx into if and x when the whole word matches an identifier.
Regular expressions describe typical token classes; nested syntax and arbitrary balanced dependencies belong to parsing rather than a finite lexer rule. Count token occurrences, not distinct categories or characters. For GATE traces explicitly note the equal-length tie rule and whether punctuation, comments and whitespace emit tokens. A token occurrence is the lexer output for one recognized source fragment. Its kind is a category such as identifier, number, assignment or punctuation. The lexeme is the actual sequence of source characters. An optional attribute carries information needed later: an identifier can reference a symbol-table entry and a numeric token can carry its numeric value. These are related pieces of information, not interchangeable names for one object.
Token counting concerns occurrences in the input, even when their kinds or lexemes repeat. Two appearances of the same identifier still produce two token occurrences, although both can point to the same declaration entry. When whitespace is ignored it separates neighboring lexemes but emits no token. The parser usually reads token kinds to recognize grammatical structure, and semantic analysis or code generation consults attributes. To work a token-record problem, first mark the source boundaries under the specified lexical rules, then label each fragment's kind, then attach only the attributes that the question's model defines. Preserve punctuation as tokens unless its rule explicitly discards it. A classical regular expression describes a language using union, concatenation and Kleene star. In lexical analysis, this language gives the valid lexemes of a token class. A token candidate must match the whole lexeme, not merely contain a substring that matches the expression. The lexer also needs a policy for choosing among matching token rules, but that policy is separate from the language defined by one expression.

The starred suffix may have length zero, so a single letter is valid. Digits become legal only after the first character; beginning with a digit violates this rule even if later characters are letters. Such bounded position conditions are regular and can be implemented by a DFA with a start state, an accepting identifier state and a rejecting sink. When testing a candidate, decompose it according to the expression and check every character against its allowed position. Do not introduce programming-library features such as backreferences into the mathematical definition. Identifiers, keywords, numeric literals, operators and punctuation are common token classes. Regular expressions describe many lexical patterns; automata implement them. Whitespace and comments may be discarded or retained as metadata depending on the language. When matches have equal length, a rule priority resolves the tie, often recognizing a keyword before a generic identifier.
