gateGuide.recognize: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens. Maximal munch and rule priority are separate decisions.
method: Find the longest prefix matching any token rule.
If multiple rules match that same longest prefix, use the stated priority, often rule order.
Return token kind and any needed lexeme attribute; whitespace/comments may be discarded while updating position.

traps.claim: The first rule always wins
traps.why: A later rule with a longer match beats an earlier shorter match; priority resolves equal lengths.

traps.claim: A keyword embedded in an identifier becomes a keyword token
traps.why: Under typical maximal munch, ifx is a single identifier, not if followed by x.

formulas.meaning: Attribute may carry a symbol-table reference or literal value.

tutorials.title: Tokenization, maximal munch and priority
tutorials.body:
Lexical analysis turns source characters into token occurrences. A token kind names a category such as identifier, number or operator; its lexeme is the actual source substring and an attribute can store a value or symbol-table reference. Whitespace and comments can be skipped while position tracking remains. The parser uses these tokens to determine grammatical structure.
Maximal munch selects the longest prefix matching any token rule. If several rules match the same maximum length, a priority convention selects among them. A lexer can scan forward with a DFA while remembering its last accepting position, then return there when no longer extension is possible. Keyword priority therefore does not split ifx into if and x when the whole word matches an identifier.
Regular expressions describe typical token classes; nested syntax and arbitrary balanced dependencies belong to parsing rather than a finite lexer rule. Count token occurrences, not distinct categories or characters. For GATE traces explicitly note the equal-length tie rule and whether punctuation, comments and whitespace emit tokens.

example.prompt: Rules include > and >=. Tokenize a>=10.
example.strategy: Identifier → Operator → Number

steps.title: Identifier
steps.explanation: The first maximal token is a.

steps.title: Operator
steps.explanation: Both > and >= begin here, but >= consumes more characters and wins.

steps.title: Number
steps.explanation: The remaining digits form one numeric token 10.

example.answer: Three tokens: identifier(a), ≥ operator, number(10).
example.verification: Rule priority matters only if maximum lengths tie; placing > first does not beat the longer >= match.

depth.body: Lexical analysis establishes boundaries and categories before grammar analysis begins. Rules specify whether comments and whitespace emit tokens or merely separate lexemes. A scanner must retain source positions even for skipped material so later diagnostics can identify locations. Operators and punctuation are tokens in their own right; spacing is not required when the token rules determine the boundaries. Counting a program fragment means counting occurrences after these rules, not characters or distinct categories. The parser receives the resulting stream and checks which categories may follow one another. A lexically valid stream can be grammatically invalid, while an unrecognized character is a lexical failure before parsing. Keep those stages distinct when diagnosing examples.

examples.prompt: Tokenize x=/*skip me*/7; when C-style comments and whitespace are ignored.
examples.strategy: Recognize the prefix → Skip the comment → Recognize the suffix

steps.title: Recognize the prefix
steps.explanation: x is an identifier and = is an assignment operator, producing two token occurrences.

steps.title: Skip the comment
steps.explanation: The opening /* starts a comment extending through */. Its internal words and spaces emit no tokens.

steps.title: Recognize the suffix
steps.explanation: 7 is one number token and ; is one delimiter token; the complete stream is ID,ASSIGN,NUMBER,SEMI.

examples.answer: Four tokens are emitted.
examples.verification: Removing the skipped comment gives x=7;, whose same four boundaries independently confirm the count.

examples.prompt: Count tokens in while(x!=0){x=x-1;} assuming while is a keyword and != is one operator.
examples.strategy: Scan the condition → Scan the body → Combine the counts

steps.title: Scan the condition
steps.explanation: Emit while, (, x, !=, 0, ) as six occurrences; != consumes both characters as one operator.

steps.title: Scan the body
steps.explanation: Emit {, x, =, x, -, 1, ;, } as eight occurrences, retaining both braces and the semicolon.

steps.title: Combine the counts
steps.explanation: The repeated identifier x is emitted at every occurrence rather than counted only once.

examples.answer: The fragment has 14 tokens.
examples.verification: There are three x occurrences, two numeric literals, three operators, five punctuation tokens and one keyword: 3+2+3+5+1=14.

examples.prompt: With ID, + and ; all valid tokens, is x + ; a lexical error? Compare it with x @ ; when @ has no token rule.
examples.strategy: Tokenize the first fragment → Check the grammar afterward → Try the other fragment

steps.title: Tokenize the first fragment
steps.explanation: x, + and ; each match a rule, so the lexer successfully emits ID,PLUS,SEMI.

steps.title: Check the grammar afterward
steps.explanation: An expression grammar requiring an operand after + rejects the stream at ;. That failure belongs to parsing.

steps.title: Try the other fragment
steps.explanation: @ matches no lexical rule at its position, so x @ ; has a lexical error before a complete token stream exists.

examples.answer: x + ; is lexically valid but syntactically invalid; x @ ; has a lexical error.
examples.verification: Each diagnosis follows the first stage whose rules fail. A missing expression operand is not an unrecognized source character.

depth.body: Maximal munch compares all token rules beginning at the current source position and selects the greatest matched length. Only among rules tied at that maximum does priority decide the token kind. This means operator families and keyword prefixes must be considered together rather than by scanning the rule list and stopping at its first success. An implementation remembers the last accepting position while looking ahead; a later failed extension must not consume characters beyond that position. The chosen token may be a prefix of a larger source fragment, after which scanning resumes exactly where that token ended. Do not invent an undefined longer operator merely because adjacent characters look like an operator combination.

examples.prompt: Tokenize x>>=1 with operator rules >>,>,>=,= but no >>= rule.
examples.strategy: Scan the identifier → Compare available lengths → Resume after the winning token

steps.title: Scan the identifier
steps.explanation: x forms one ID token and scanning resumes at the first >.

steps.title: Compare available lengths
steps.explanation: At that position >> matches two characters, while > matches one; >= does not match because the second character is >.

steps.title: Resume after the winning token
steps.explanation: Emit >>, then = from the remaining assignment symbol, then NUMBER(1). No three-character rule exists.

examples.answer: The four tokens are ID(x), >>, =, NUMBER(1).
examples.verification: The token lexemes concatenate to x>>=1 exactly. Maximal munch selects the longest defined match, not an imagined >>= token.

examples.prompt: Rules include keyword for before ID=letter(letter|digit)*. Tokenize for forx and explain the priority decisions.
examples.strategy: Compare the first word → Compare the second word → Apply length before priority

steps.title: Compare the first word
steps.explanation: Both keyword for and ID match three characters, so this equal-length tie is decided by keyword priority.

steps.title: Compare the second word
steps.explanation: ID matches all four characters of forx; keyword for matches only its three-character prefix.

steps.title: Apply length before priority
steps.explanation: Choose ID(forx) because four is greater than three. Rule order cannot override a strictly longer match.

examples.answer: The tokens are KEYWORD(for) and ID(forx).
examples.verification: The second token must consume x with its prefix. Splitting it into keyword for plus ID(x) would violate maximal munch.

examples.prompt: A scanner with NUM=digits+ and ID=letters+ reads 123abc. Can it discard abc after looking ahead beyond the last accepting NUM position?
examples.strategy: Record the last acceptance → Observe extension failure → Restore and continue

steps.title: Record the last acceptance
steps.explanation: The NUM automaton accepts after 1,12,123; the farthest valid numeric position is after the third character.

steps.title: Observe extension failure
steps.explanation: The next a cannot extend NUM, so lookahead has found the boundary rather than consumed part of that token.

steps.title: Restore and continue
steps.explanation: Return NUM(123), leave the input position before a, and then scan ID(abc). The looked-ahead characters remain available.

examples.answer: The correct stream is NUM(123), ID(abc); lookahead must not lose abc.
examples.verification: The two lexemes reconstruct all six source characters, whereas discarding abc would silently change the source program.

tutorials.title: Convert lexemes into token kinds and attributes
tutorials.body:
A token occurrence is the lexer output for one recognized source fragment. Its kind is a category such as identifier, number, assignment or punctuation. The lexeme is the actual sequence of source characters. An optional attribute carries information needed later: an identifier can reference a symbol-table entry and a numeric token can carry its numeric value. These are related pieces of information, not interchangeable names for one object.
Token counting concerns occurrences in the input, even when their kinds or lexemes repeat. Two appearances of the same identifier still produce two token occurrences, although both can point to the same declaration entry. When whitespace is ignored it separates neighboring lexemes but emits no token. The parser usually reads token kinds to recognize grammatical structure, and semantic analysis or code generation consults attributes. To work a token-record problem, first mark the source boundaries under the specified lexical rules, then label each fragment's kind, then attach only the attributes that the question's model defines. Preserve punctuation as tokens unless its rule explicitly discards it.

example.prompt: Tokenize sum = sum + 12; ignoring whitespace. Let both occurrences of sum refer to symbol-table entry p_sum, and store integer values on NUMBER tokens.
example.strategy: Mark lexeme boundaries → Attach identifier information → Attach the remaining kinds → Count occurrences

steps.title: Mark lexeme boundaries
steps.explanation: The fragments are sum, =, sum, +, 12 and ;. The spaces emit no tokens, and the two digits form one number.

steps.title: Attach identifier information
steps.explanation: Emit this record twice, once for each sum occurrence. A shared symbol-table reference does not merge the two occurrences.

steps.title: Attach the remaining kinds
steps.explanation: The number attribute stores 12; the operators and delimiter need no additional attribute in this model.

steps.title: Count occurrences
steps.explanation: The ordered stream is ID, ASSIGN, ID, PLUS, NUMBER, SEMI: six occurrences with five distinct kinds.

example.answer: There are six token occurrences. Both ID tokens have attribute p_sum, while NUMBER has attribute 12.
example.verification: Concatenating the six lexemes reconstructs the input after removing whitespace. The repeated identifier accounts for why occurrence count six differs from distinct-kind count five.

depth.body: The token kind abstracts away spelling so grammar rules can refer to NUMBER or ID rather than enumerate every literal or name. An attribute restores the information later stages need, such as a numeric value or symbol-table handle. Distinct lexemes may share both a kind and a value: decimal 0042 and 42 can represent the same integer. Repeated names can produce multiple occurrences pointing to one declaration, while shadowed declarations with the same spelling may require different entries. Token rules also decide whether a sign belongs to a numeric lexeme; if minus is a separate operator, the parser handles unary negation. Never infer token boundaries solely from the arithmetic interpretation of the final expression.

examples.prompt: A NUMBER rule matches one or more decimal digits and stores the integer value. What record is emitted for lexeme 0042?
examples.strategy: Match the whole lexeme → Compute the attribute → Separate the representations

steps.title: Match the whole lexeme
steps.explanation: All four characters are decimal digits, so one NUMBER occurrence consumes the entire fragment.

steps.title: Compute the attribute
steps.explanation: Leading zeros affect spelling but not the integer value.

steps.title: Separate the representations
steps.explanation: The record is kind NUMBER with value 42; the lexeme remains 0042 if source spelling is retained for diagnostics.

examples.answer: One token is emitted: NUMBER with attribute 42.
examples.verification: Lexeme length is four, token count is one and numeric value is 42; these three quantities answer different questions.

examples.prompt: Tokenize x+x*y with ID attributes x→entry 0 and y→entry 1. Count total tokens, ID occurrences and distinct referenced entries.
examples.strategy: Mark the five boundaries → Attach identifier records → Count each requested quantity

steps.title: Mark the five boundaries
steps.explanation: The lexemes are x,+,x,*,y; no whitespace is necessary to separate them.

steps.title: Attach identifier records
steps.explanation: Both x occurrences refer to the same entry; y refers to another.

steps.title: Count each requested quantity
steps.explanation: There are five total token occurrences, three ID occurrences and two distinct symbol-table entries.

examples.answer: The three counts are 5, 3 and 2.
examples.verification: The operator occurrences account for the difference 5−3=2, while the repeated x accounts for the difference between three IDs and two entries.

examples.prompt: If NUMBER matches digits only and - is a separate operator, does -12 emit one negative-number token?
examples.strategy: Apply the rule at the first character → Read the following digits → Delegate expression meaning

steps.title: Apply the rule at the first character
steps.explanation: The minus matches MINUS, not the digits-only NUMBER rule, so it forms its own token.

steps.title: Read the following digits
steps.explanation: 12 matches one NUMBER token with positive attribute value 12.

steps.title: Delegate expression meaning
steps.explanation: The parser may treat the token pair MINUS,NUMBER as unary negation; that arithmetic meaning does not merge the lexer outputs.

examples.answer: Two tokens are emitted: MINUS and NUMBER(12).
examples.verification: For x-12 the same rules emit ID,MINUS,NUMBER. Tokenization is consistent regardless of whether grammar context later interprets minus as unary or binary.

tutorials.title: Use a regular expression as a whole-lexeme token rule
tutorials.body:
A classical regular expression describes a language using union, concatenation and Kleene star. In lexical analysis, this language gives the valid lexemes of a token class. A token candidate must match the whole lexeme, not merely contain a substring that matches the expression. The lexer also needs a policy for choosing among matching token rules, but that policy is separate from the language defined by one expression.
An identifier rule can require a lowercase letter first and then permit any sequence of lowercase letters or digits. Concatenation makes the initial letter mandatory. The starred suffix may have length zero, so a single letter is valid. Digits become legal only after the first character; beginning with a digit violates this rule even if later characters are letters. Such bounded position conditions are regular and can be implemented by a DFA with a start state, an accepting identifier state and a rejecting sink. When testing a candidate, decompose it according to the expression and check every character against its allowed position. Do not introduce programming-library features such as backreferences into the mathematical definition.

example.prompt: With letter={a,…,z} and digit={0,…,9}, write the identifier regex and classify x, x7a, 7x and the empty string.
example.strategy: Build the expression → Test a one-character identifier → Test a mixed suffix → Reject invalid starts

steps.title: Build the expression
steps.explanation: The first factor supplies one compulsory letter; every later symbol belongs to either allowed class.

steps.title: Test a one-character identifier
steps.explanation: The first factor matches x and the starred suffix contributes zero symbols, so x is valid.

steps.title: Test a mixed suffix
steps.explanation: The initial x is a letter and the suffix is two repetitions, digit 7 then letter a, so the entire lexeme matches.

steps.title: Reject invalid starts
steps.explanation: The candidate 7x fails the compulsory first-letter factor. The empty string also fails because only the suffix, not the first factor, can be empty.

example.answer: The rule is letter(letter|digit)*. It accepts x and x7a, and rejects 7x and the empty string.
example.verification: A three-state DFA can move from start to an accepting identifier state on a letter, loop there on letters/digits, and send other cases to a sink; this agrees with all four classifications.

depth.body: Token regex design should begin with mandatory pieces and optional groups. A one-or-more digit region is expressed classically as digit followed by digit star; a zero-or-one group is a union with epsilon. Treat punctuation that appears in the literal lexeme as a required symbol, not a metacharacter with an unintended meaning. Whole-lexeme validation and scanning a larger source are separate operations: a numeric prefix may become a token even though the complete source fragment includes an identifier afterward. A rule for a token class need not accept every concatenation of legal tokens. Verify a proposed expression by both constructing valid decompositions and testing boundary cases such as an empty required region or a dangling separator.

examples.prompt: Write a classical regex for decimal numbers with at least one digit and an optional fractional part requiring digits after the dot. Classify 0,12.5,12.
examples.strategy: Require the integer part → Make the whole fraction optional → Test the boundary cases

steps.title: Require the integer part
steps.explanation: D contains one or more digits and cannot generate ε.

steps.title: Make the whole fraction optional
steps.explanation: Either choose no fraction or a literal dot followed by another nonempty digit block.

steps.title: Test the boundary cases
steps.explanation: 0 uses the epsilon alternative; 12.5 uses integer 12 and fraction .5; 12. fails because the fraction's D cannot be empty.

examples.answer: digit digit*(ε | . digit digit*) accepts 0 and 12.5 but rejects 12.
examples.verification: The two positive examples have explicit whole-lexeme decompositions. A trailing dot cannot be absorbed by either the integer block or the empty optional alternative.

examples.prompt: Construct a token regex for hexadecimal literals beginning 0x followed by at least one symbol from H={0,…,9,A,…,F}. Test 0xAF9 and 0x.
examples.strategy: Keep the prefix literal → Require a hexadecimal digit → Validate the candidates

steps.title: Keep the prefix literal
steps.explanation: The token must begin with exactly the two symbols 0 and x; neither is optional.

steps.title: Require a hexadecimal digit
steps.explanation: The first H prevents an empty digit region, while H* permits any additional hex symbols.

steps.title: Validate the candidates
steps.explanation: 0xAF9 decomposes as prefix 0x, required A and suffix F9. The candidate 0x supplies no required H and rejects.

examples.answer: The regex is 0xHH*, accepting 0xAF9 and rejecting 0x.
examples.verification: A,F,9 all belong to H. A lowercase g after the prefix would fail the stated uppercase hexadecimal class.

examples.prompt: The NUMBER regex is digit digit*. Does matching prefix 123 prove the whole candidate lexeme 123x is a NUMBER?
examples.strategy: Apply the whole-word definition → Find the unmatched suffix → Separate scanner behavior

steps.title: Apply the whole-word definition
steps.explanation: A NUMBER lexeme must consist entirely of digits; membership requires consuming every character under the regex.

steps.title: Find the unmatched suffix
steps.explanation: The final x cannot be supplied by either required digit or digit star, so 123x is not in that token language.

steps.title: Separate scanner behavior
steps.explanation: A lexer with an ID rule may tokenize the larger source as NUMBER(123) followed by ID(x), but that creates two lexemes rather than validating one.

examples.answer: No. 123x is not a NUMBER lexeme, even if its source can be split into two legal tokens.
examples.verification: The regex accepts 123 and rejects 123x as whole words; concatenating valid token lexemes is a distinct language operation.

lessons.title: Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW and LL/LR methods
lessons.intuition: A parser discovers grammatical structure in a token stream. Predictive parsing chooses productions before seeing their full result; bottom-up parsing recognizes handles after seeing the right-hand side. FIRST and FOLLOW sets summarize where grammar decisions can be made.

sections.title: FIRST and FOLLOW
sections.body: FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α can disappear. For a sequence, continue into later symbols when earlier ones are nullable. FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can follow A in some sentential form; the start symbol includes end marker $. For A→αBβ, add FIRST(β) without ε to FOLLOW(B), and if β is nullable add FOLLOW(A).

sections.title: LL(1) prediction
sections.body: For A→α, put the production under terminals in FIRST(α); if α is nullable, also under FOLLOW(A). A conflict means the grammar is not LL(1) as written. Eliminate direct left recursion and factor common prefixes when appropriate, without assuming those changes fix every grammar. Recursive descent expands a leftmost derivation.

sections.title: Bottom-up parsing
sections.body: An LR parser tracks states representing viable prefixes, shifts input symbols and reduces a recognized right-hand side to its left-hand variable. Reductions reconstruct a rightmost derivation in reverse. Shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts signal ambiguity or insufficient parsing information for the chosen method. LR handles a wider grammar class than LL(1).

sections.title: Deriving predictive choices and LR conflicts
sections.body: FIRST records terminals that can begin a derivation, whereas FOLLOW records terminals that can legally come immediately after a nonterminal in a sentential form. If a production’s right side can vanish, the parser must choose it when the lookahead belongs to the left side’s FOLLOW set. This is why nullable prefixes propagate FIRST from later symbols. Compute these sets repeatedly until no change; a single left-to-right sweep can miss indirect dependencies. LL(1) fails when two productions demand the same table cell. LR item sets instead encode how far productions have been recognized. An LR(0) completed item proposes a reduction independent of lookahead; SLR restricts reductions using FOLLOW; LR(1) items carry their own lookaheads. A shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict must be assessed for that specific table construction.

examples.prompt: For \(S\to Ab\) and \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\), compute FIRST(S)

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: A can begin with a or vanish. FIRST(A) contains a and epsilon. Epsilon means A may contribute no terminal to the start of a derived S string.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: If it vanishes, b is the first terminal of S. The terminal after nullable A therefore supplies another possible first symbol.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: \(FIRST(S)=\{a,b\}\); ε is absent because b cannot vanish. The entire right-hand side cannot vanish because b is mandatory, so epsilon must not enter FIRST(S).

examples.strategy: Propagate FIRST past nullable prefixes until a nonnullable symbol is encountered.
examples.answer: \(FIRST(S)=\{a,b\}\); ε is absent because b cannot vanish.
examples.verification: S derives either ab or b under this grammar; their first terminals are exactly a and b.

examples.prompt: Build entries for A in that grammar
steps: \(FIRST(a)=\{a\}\), so select \(A\to a\) on lookahead a.
\(A\to\varepsilon\) uses FOLLOW(A), which includes b from \(S\to Ab\).
Select \(A\to\varepsilon\) on b. The entries are distinct and have no conflict.

pitfalls: FOLLOW sets do not contain ε.
Nullable prefixes require inspecting subsequent symbols.
revision: LL chooses a production by lookahead.
LR shifts and reduces viable prefixes.

checks.prompt: Which set can contain ε?
checks.hint: FOLLOW tracks terminals that can occur after a nonterminal.
checks.explanation: FIRST may include ε for a nullable expression. FOLLOW includes possible following terminals and sometimes the end marker, not ε.
options: FIRST, when the expression is nullable
Every FOLLOW set must contain it

checks.prompt: For \(A\to a\)A|ε, how many symbols are in FIRST(A), including ε?
checks.hint: A starts with a or disappears.
checks.explanation: FIRST(A)={a,ε}, size 2.

lessons.concept: A parser discovers grammatical structure in a token stream. Predictive parsing chooses productions before seeing their full result; bottom-up parsing recognizes handles after seeing the right-hand side. FIRST and FOLLOW sets summarize where grammar decisions can be made.
lessons.method:
Parsing checks whether a token sequence follows a grammar and builds its structure. FIRST(α) contains terminals beginning strings derived from α, plus epsilon if α can vanish. FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can appear immediately after nonterminal A in a sentential form; the end marker follows the start symbol. Compute nullable, FIRST and FOLLOW repeatedly until stable because indirect dependencies can propagate over several passes.
An LL(1) parser uses one lookahead terminal to choose a production. Place A→α under each non-epsilon terminal in FIRST(α). If α is nullable, also place it under FOLLOW(A). Two demanded productions in one cell constitute a conflict. A terminal on the stack must match the lookahead; a nonterminal selects a table action.
Nullable prefixes require looking further right when calculating FIRST. Left recursion prevents ordinary predictive descent, while left factoring can postpone a shared-prefix choice; neither transformation by itself guarantees LL(1). An unambiguous grammar can still fail LL(1). Explain why each table entry is chosen instead of memorizing a set without its dependency source. An LR parser reads input left-to-right and builds a rightmost derivation in reverse using shifts and reductions. An item A→α·β marks how much of a production has been recognized. Closure adds items for a nonterminal immediately after a dot; goto advances dots over one grammar symbol and closes the resulting set. These item sets form parser states.
A shift consumes a terminal and advances the state stack. A reduction pops the production’s right-hand-side extent and uses goto on its left nonterminal. LR(0) completed items propose reduction without lookahead restriction; SLR uses FOLLOW sets; LR(1) carries item-specific lookahead, and LALR merges suitable cores. The choice affects which grammars avoid conflicts.
A shift/reduce conflict offers both actions in one state/lookahead cell; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. Ambiguity is one possible source but parser-family limitations can also create conflicts for unambiguous grammars. Do not use all lookaheads of one completed item for every other item. Trace both grammar symbols and parser states, since a reduction changes their stack roles differently. Parsing determines whether an ordered token sequence can be generated by a grammar and, when it can, recovers a derivation or parse tree. Lexical validity alone is insufficient: every token may be individually valid while their sequence violates the grammar. A successful parse accounts for the whole input, so a valid prefix followed by leftover tokens is not enough.
In a top-down view, select a production for the start symbol and recursively parse the portions assigned to its nonterminals. In a bottom-up view, reduce suitable right-hand sides to nonterminals until the start symbol remains. Either method must respect the same grammatical structure. The grammar S→aSb | ab generates one or more a symbols followed by exactly as many b symbols. Its recursive production adds one outer a and b around a smaller instance; its base case consumes ab. The productions share an initial a, so this grammar is not an LL(1) grammar as written, and an unrestricted top-down explanation should not be mistaken for a conflict-free one-lookahead table. Check the resulting tree's leaves as well as its production labels. An LR parser reads input from left to right and constructs a rightmost derivation in reverse. lessons.example: For S→Ab and A→a|ε, compute FIRST(S)

gateGuide.recognize: Predictive parsing uses FIRST/FOLLOW; LR parsing uses viable prefixes and item states. Label the parser family before building a table.
method: Compute nullable symbols first, then FIRST and FOLLOW to a fixed point.
For A→α place it under FIRST(α) terminals; if α is nullable also use FOLLOW(A).
For LR trace closure/goto and the stated lookahead rules; identify the exact cell with multiple actions.

traps.claim: FIRST(AB) is always FIRST(A)
traps.why: If A is nullable, terminals from FIRST(B) also matter.

traps.claim: An unambiguous grammar is always LL(1)
traps.why: Left-recursive unambiguous expression grammars still fail predictive parsing; ambiguity and parser suitability are different properties.

formulas.meaning: Nullable α additionally uses FOLLOW(A).
End marker follows the start symbol.

tutorials.title: Predictive parsing, nullable prefixes and tables
tutorials.body:
Parsing checks whether a token sequence follows a grammar and builds its structure. FIRST(α) contains terminals beginning strings derived from α, plus epsilon if α can vanish. FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can appear immediately after nonterminal A in a sentential form; the end marker follows the start symbol. Compute nullable, FIRST and FOLLOW repeatedly until stable because indirect dependencies can propagate over several passes.
An LL(1) parser uses one lookahead terminal to choose a production. Place A→α under each non-epsilon terminal in FIRST(α). If α is nullable, also place it under FOLLOW(A). Two demanded productions in one cell constitute a conflict. A terminal on the stack must match the lookahead; a nonterminal selects a table action.
Nullable prefixes require looking further right when calculating FIRST. Left recursion prevents ordinary predictive descent, while left factoring can postpone a shared-prefix choice; neither transformation by itself guarantees LL(1). An unambiguous grammar can still fail LL(1). Explain why each table entry is chosen instead of memorizing a set without its dependency source.

example.prompt: \(S\to Ab\), \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\). Find FIRST(S), FOLLOW(A) and A’s table entries.
example.strategy: FIRST → FOLLOW → Predictive choices

steps.title: FIRST
steps.explanation: A either starts with a or vanishes, exposing b.

steps.title: FOLLOW
steps.explanation: The terminal after A is mandatory b.

steps.title: Predictive choices
steps.explanation: Use \(A\to a\) on a and \(A\to\varepsilon\) on b; cells do not conflict.

example.answer: \(FIRST(S)=\{a,b\}\); FOLLOW(A)={b}; two distinct A entries.
example.verification: Epsilon is absent from FIRST(S) because the trailing b cannot vanish.

depth.body: FIRST summarizes which terminal can appear first after all necessary leading rewrites. For a sequence, collect non-epsilon terminals from the first symbol, continue to the next only if that symbol is nullable, and include epsilon only when every symbol can vanish. Nonterminal cycles require solving set dependencies to a fixed point rather than following one arbitrary derivation. Computing nullable separately often prevents accidentally carrying epsilon through a mandatory terminal. FIRST belongs to a grammar symbol or sequence, whereas the lookahead selection for an epsilon production also uses FOLLOW. Verify a calculated terminal with an actual derivation beginning in that terminal, and verify epsilon with a complete derivation of the empty sequence.

examples.prompt: For \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\), B→b|ε and C→c, calculate FIRST(ABC).
examples.strategy: Inspect A → Inspect B → Stop at mandatory C

steps.title: Inspect A
steps.explanation: A contributes a and is nullable, so FIRST must continue into B.

steps.title: Inspect B
steps.explanation: B contributes b and is nullable too, so the sequence can also begin with C.

steps.title: Stop at mandatory C
steps.explanation: C contributes c and cannot vanish; therefore the whole sequence has no epsilon derivation.

examples.answer: FIRST(ABC)={a,b,c}, without ε.
examples.verification: Witnesses are abc for a, bc when A vanishes for b, and c when both A,B vanish for c.

examples.prompt: Find FIRST sets for S→Ac|d, \(A\to B\)|ε, B→b|S, including their cyclic dependency.
examples.strategy: Find nullability → Set up propagation → Iterate until stable → Check witnesses

steps.title: Find nullability
steps.explanation: A is nullable directly. B is not nullable because neither b nor S vanishes; S always retains c or derives d.

steps.title: Set up propagation
steps.explanation: B contributes b or FIRST(S); A receives FIRST(B) plus epsilon; S receives nonempty FIRST(A), exposed c and alternative d.

steps.title: Iterate until stable
steps.explanation: The initial b,c,d information flows through the cycle until no terminal is added.

steps.title: Check witnesses
steps.explanation: S⇒Ac⇒Bc⇒bc starts with b; S⇒Ac⇒c starts with c; S⇒d starts with d. A alone can choose epsilon.

examples.answer: S and B have {b,c,d}; A has {b,c,d,ε}.
examples.verification: No production introduces any other terminal, and the nonnullable mandatory c/d choices prevent epsilon from entering FIRST(S) or FIRST(B).

examples.prompt: For \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\) and B→b|ε, someone reports FIRST(AB)={a,b}. What is missing?
examples.strategy: Collect terminal beginnings → Check entire-sequence nullability → Add the exceptional member

steps.title: Collect terminal beginnings
steps.explanation: A can start with a; if it vanishes, B can start with b.

steps.title: Check entire-sequence nullability
steps.explanation: Both symbols can choose their epsilon production, so the sequence itself can disappear.

steps.title: Add the exceptional member
steps.explanation: Epsilon is included because the whole sequence vanishes, not merely because one prefix symbol is nullable.

examples.answer: The missing member is ε.
examples.verification: The four generated words are ab,a,b,ε, whose first-symbol possibilities directly reproduce the set.

depth.body: FOLLOW tracks what can appear immediately after a nonterminal in a derivable sentential form. It never contains epsilon: disappearance is represented by propagating the enclosing production's FOLLOW set when the suffix is nullable. For A→αBβ, first add non-epsilon FIRST(β) to FOLLOW(B); then, if β can vanish, add FOLLOW(A). Initialize the start symbol with the end marker and repeat propagation until stable. A dependency can travel through several nonterminals even when their own productions introduce no following terminal. Keep FIRST and FOLLOW columns conceptually separate so an empty production is selected under actual next terminals or end-of-input, rather than under a nonexistent epsilon input symbol.

examples.prompt: For S→AB, \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\) and B→b|ε, calculate FOLLOW(A) and FOLLOW(B).
examples.strategy: Initialize the boundary → Inspect A in S→AB → Inspect final B

steps.title: Initialize the boundary
steps.explanation: End-of-input can follow the start symbol.

steps.title: Inspect A in S→AB
steps.explanation: B contributes terminal b after A. Because B is nullable, the enclosing end marker can also follow A.

steps.title: Inspect final B
steps.explanation: B is at the production end and inherits FOLLOW(S).

examples.answer: FOLLOW(A)={b,$}; FOLLOW(B)={$}.
examples.verification: The derivation S⇒AB⇒aB⇒a shows $ following A when B vanishes, while S⇒AB⇒Ab exposes b after A.

examples.prompt: Compute FOLLOW in S→AB|d, \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\), \(B\to C\), C→c|ε. Explain the propagation through \(B\to C\).
examples.strategy: Expose the suffix of A → Propagate the end position → Continue through the unit production → Record the fixed point

steps.title: Expose the suffix of A
steps.explanation: FIRST(B)={c,ε}, so c follows A and B nullability also sends FOLLOW(S)={$} to A.

steps.title: Propagate the end position
steps.explanation: B is last in S→AB, hence FOLLOW(B) receives $.

steps.title: Continue through the unit production
steps.explanation: C is last in \(B\to C\); iterate after B has received the boundary fact.

steps.title: Record the fixed point
steps.explanation: No other occurrences add terminals.

examples.answer: A has {c,$}; B and C each have {$}.
examples.verification: Generated strings are d,ac,a,c,ε. Their A/B/C occurrence positions agree with the calculated boundaries, and no right-hand side puts d after a nonterminal.

examples.prompt: For S→A and \(A\to\varepsilon\), should ε appear in FOLLOW(A) because A can vanish?
examples.strategy: Separate the two facts → Locate A within S→A → Propagate only real lookahead

steps.title: Separate the two facts
steps.explanation: The production tells us that A can generate no terminal symbols.

steps.title: Locate A within S→A
steps.explanation: A is at the end of the start production, so its following context is the end-of-input marker.

steps.title: Propagate only real lookahead
steps.explanation: Epsilon is a derivation result, not a symbol that can follow A in the input.

examples.answer: FOLLOW(A) contains $ and never ε.
examples.verification: An LL parser chooses \(A\to\varepsilon\) when lookahead is $, not by trying to consume an epsilon character.

depth.body: An LL(1) table chooses the next production from the stack's leftmost nonterminal and one input lookahead. Production selection uses FIRST of its right-hand side; an epsilon alternative uses FOLLOW of the left-hand side. A table conflict can therefore arise between a nullable alternative and an ordinary alternative even when their FIRST terminal sets initially seem disjoint. Execution is separate from table construction: expand a nonterminal without consuming input, and consume a terminal only when it matches the lookahead. Declare the top-of-stack orientation and include the end marker so empty productions and successful completion can be traced. Unambiguous grammars need not be LL(1), because unique full structure does not guarantee an immediate one-symbol choice.

examples.prompt: Build the LL(1) entries for S→aS|b and parse aab with stack top at the left.
examples.strategy: Choose distinct entries → Expand and match twice → Finish the base

steps.title: Choose distinct entries
steps.explanation: M[S,a]=S→aS and M[S,b]=S→b, since the alternatives begin with different mandatory terminals.

steps.title: Expand and match twice
steps.explanation: Starting with S$, expand to aS$, match a, and repeat for the second a; input now begins b and the stack is S$.

steps.title: Finish the base
steps.explanation: Choose S→b, match b, then both stack and input reach $. No expansion consumes a token before its terminal match.

examples.answer: aab accepts under the two conflict-free entries.
examples.verification: The derivation S⇒aS⇒aaS⇒aab matches the parser expansions, and all three input symbols are consumed.

examples.prompt: For S→AB, \(A\to a\)A|ε, B→bB|ε, build the relevant LL table and parse aab.
examples.strategy: Compute selection context → Place table entries → Consume the a block → Consume the b block

steps.title: Compute selection context
steps.explanation: FIRST(S)={a,b,ε}; FOLLOW(A)={b,$}; FOLLOW(B)={$}. These account for the two nullable loops.

steps.title: Place table entries
steps.explanation: S uses AB under a,b,$. A uses aA under a and ε under b,$. B uses bB under b and ε under $.

steps.title: Consume the a block
steps.explanation: After expanding S to AB, choose \(A\to a\)A and match a twice. On lookahead b choose \(A\to\varepsilon\), leaving B.

steps.title: Consume the b block
steps.explanation: Choose B→bB, match b, then choose B→ε on $. Stack and input now share the end marker.

examples.answer: The grammar is LL(1) and aab accepts.
examples.verification: Its language is a*b*. The epsilon entries also let empty input, all-a input or all-b input complete without conflicts.

examples.prompt: For S→Aa and \(A\to a\mid\varepsilon\), why do the apparently different alternatives of A conflict in an LL(1) table?
examples.strategy: Place the terminal alternative → Place the nullable alternative → Show the competing inputs

steps.title: Place the terminal alternative
steps.explanation: \(A\to a\) must occupy M[A,a] from \(FIRST(a)=\{a\}\).

steps.title: Place the nullable alternative
steps.explanation: The following terminal in S→Aa gives FOLLOW(A)={a}, so \(A\to\varepsilon\) also occupies M[A,a].

steps.title: Show the competing inputs
steps.explanation: Input a requires \(A\to\varepsilon\); input aa requires \(A\to a\). Both present initial lookahead a, so one symbol cannot select correctly.

examples.answer: M[A,a] has a FIRST/FOLLOW conflict; the grammar is not LL(1) as written.
examples.verification: The language {a,aa} has distinct parses, demonstrating that this predictive conflict does not itself establish ambiguity.

tutorials.title: LR items, closure/goto and reduction conflicts
tutorials.body:
An LR parser reads input left-to-right and builds a rightmost derivation in reverse using shifts and reductions. An item A→α·β marks how much of a production has been recognized. Closure adds items for a nonterminal immediately after a dot; goto advances dots over one grammar symbol and closes the resulting set. These item sets form parser states.
A shift consumes a terminal and advances the state stack. A reduction pops the production’s right-hand-side extent and uses goto on its left nonterminal. LR(0) completed items propose reduction without lookahead restriction; SLR uses FOLLOW sets; LR(1) carries item-specific lookahead, and LALR merges suitable cores. The choice affects which grammars avoid conflicts.
A shift/reduce conflict offers both actions in one state/lookahead cell; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. Ambiguity is one possible source but parser-family limitations can also create conflicts for unambiguous grammars. Do not use all lookaheads of one completed item for every other item. Trace both grammar symbols and parser states, since a reduction changes their stack roles differently.

example.prompt: Item E→E·+T sees lookahead +. Is the expression E already ready for this production’s reduction?
example.strategy: Read dot position → Advance on plus → Completion condition

steps.title: Read dot position
steps.explanation: The +T suffix is still unrecognized in this item.

steps.title: Advance on plus
steps.explanation: A transition over + shifts input and moves the dot.

steps.title: Completion condition
steps.explanation: Only after T is recognized is this production complete.

example.answer: This item suggests shifting +, not reducing E→E+T yet.
example.verification: A completed item’s dot is at the far right; it is a different item from the one initially supplied.

tutorials.title: Recover grammar structure from a token sequence
tutorials.body:
Parsing determines whether an ordered token sequence can be generated by a grammar and, when it can, recovers a derivation or parse tree. Lexical validity alone is insufficient: every token may be individually valid while their sequence violates the grammar. A successful parse accounts for the whole input, so a valid prefix followed by leftover tokens is not enough.
In a top-down view, select a production for the start symbol and recursively parse the portions assigned to its nonterminals. In a bottom-up view, reduce suitable right-hand sides to nonterminals until the start symbol remains. Either method must respect the same grammatical structure. The grammar S→aSb | ab generates one or more a symbols followed by exactly as many b symbols. Its recursive production adds one outer a and b around a smaller instance; its base case consumes ab. The productions share an initial a, so this grammar is not an LL(1) grammar as written, and an unrestricted top-down explanation should not be mistaken for a conflict-free one-lookahead table. Check the resulting tree's leaves as well as its production labels.

example.prompt: Parse aabb with S→aSb | ab. Then explain why abab fails under this grammar.
example.strategy: Choose the root production → Parse the child → Read the tree leaves → Test the competing word

steps.title: Choose the root production
steps.explanation: The four-symbol input is too long for S→ab alone, so its root uses S→aSb. Match the initial a and final b, assigning the middle ab to S.

steps.title: Parse the child
steps.explanation: The child uses the base production S→ab; every nonterminal has now been expanded.

steps.title: Read the tree leaves
steps.explanation: The root's leaves are a, then its child's a and b, then the root's closing b. They consume all four input tokens in order.

steps.title: Test the competing word
steps.explanation: If abab used aSb at the root, its middle would be ba, which S cannot generate; if it used ab, two tokens would remain. Both root choices fail.

example.answer: aabb has a valid tree with one recursive node and one base node. abab is rejected.
example.verification: The grammar invariant is aⁿbⁿ for n≥1. aabb has n=2, while abab switches back to a after entering the b block and violates that invariant.

depth.body: Parsing connects a linear token sequence to recursive grammar structure. A useful walkthrough identifies which production covers each portion of input and checks that all terminal leaves appear in exactly the original order. Grammar transformations can make decisions practical: eliminate direct left recursion for predictive descent, or factor a shared prefix to defer a choice. These operations preserve the language but may require semantic actions to restore the intended associativity in an AST. Parser families also impose different decision limits. A grammar can be unambiguous while requiring more than one lookahead symbol in its current form. Distinguish failure of a particular predictive method from absence of a valid parse or ambiguity of the language.

examples.prompt: Parse ()() under S→(S)S | ε using a leftmost derivation.
examples.strategy: Create the first pair → Create the following pair → Finish and inspect leaves

steps.title: Create the first pair
steps.explanation: The enclosed first S chooses epsilon, leaving a following suffix S.

steps.title: Create the following pair
steps.explanation: The suffix uses the nonempty rule; its enclosed S again chooses epsilon.

steps.title: Finish and inspect leaves
steps.explanation: The last suffix vanishes. Reading the tree leaves consumes all four parentheses in order.

examples.answer: ()() has a valid parse with two concatenated pairs.
examples.verification: Each pair has an empty interior, whereas the final S carries concatenation. This tree differs structurally from the nested-pair tree for (()).

examples.prompt: Transform E→E+T|T, T→id to remove direct left recursion, then generate id+id+id.
examples.strategy: Separate base and repetition → Generate the desired tokens → Preserve intended semantics

steps.title: Separate base and repetition
steps.explanation: The base T occurs once, followed by zero or more +T suffixes.

steps.title: Generate the desired tokens
steps.explanation: Choose T→id three times and the nonempty E′ rule twice, then terminate E′ with epsilon, yielding id+id+id.

steps.title: Preserve intended semantics
steps.explanation: The transformed grammar preserves the token language. To retain left-associative addition in an AST, fold the suffix operands into the accumulated left expression.

examples.answer: The displayed transformed grammar generates id(+id)* and the requested word.
examples.verification: Every original derivation repeatedly appends +T to a base T; the new suffix chain lists exactly those additions without left recursion.

examples.prompt: Is S→aA|aB, A→c, B→d ambiguous because a predictive parser cannot choose its S production on lookahead a?
examples.strategy: Inspect both words → Identify the limited decision → Defer the choice by factoring

steps.title: Inspect both words
steps.explanation: The first alternative produces only ac; the second only ad. No terminal word receives both trees.

steps.title: Identify the limited decision
steps.explanation: Both alternatives have FIRST={a}, causing a one-lookahead table conflict even though their complete outputs differ.

steps.title: Defer the choice by factoring
steps.explanation: After matching a, lookahead c or d uniquely chooses the remaining production.

examples.answer: The grammar is unambiguous but not LL(1) as originally written; factoring fixes this decision.
examples.verification: ac can use only A and ad only B, independently ruling out a shared-word ambiguity witness.

tutorials.title: Construct LR states and execute shifts and reductions
tutorials.body:
An LR parser reads input from left to right and constructs a rightmost derivation in reverse. An item A→α·β records the recognized prefix α of a production. Closure repeatedly adds every production of a nonterminal immediately after a dot. The goto operation moves dots across a specified grammar symbol and then takes closure; the resulting item sets are parser states.
Augment the grammar with a fresh start production S′→S. A terminal transition creates a shift action, a completed non-start item creates a reduction, and the completed augmented item permits acceptance on the end marker. For LR(0), a reduction applies on every terminal lookahead; conflicting required actions would show that the grammar is not LR(0). The state stack begins with state 0. A shift consumes one token and pushes its destination state. A reduction by A→β consumes no input, pops as many states as there are symbols in β, and pushes goto of the newly exposed state on A. Recording both the state stack and remaining input prevents confusing a reduction with token consumption.

example.prompt: For S′→S and S→aS | b, construct the relevant LR(0) states and parse ab$. Number goto(I0,a)=I1, goto(I0,b)=I2 and goto(I0,S)=I3.
example.strategy: Close the start state → Advance and close → Identify completed states → Read table actions → Shift the input → Reduce the base → Reduce and accept

steps.title: Close the start state
steps.equation: I_0=\{S'\to\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot aS,\ S\to\cdot b\}
steps.explanation: The dot before S in the augmented item adds both S productions.

steps.title: Advance and close
steps.equation: I_1=\{S\to a\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot aS,\ S\to\cdot b\}
steps.explanation: Goto on a advances the item and closure again adds both S productions. Goto(I1,a)=I1 and goto(I1,b)=I2.

steps.title: Identify completed states
steps.equation: I_2=\{S\to b\cdot\},\ I_3=\{S'\to S\cdot\},\ I_4=\{S\to aS\cdot\}
steps.explanation: I4 is goto(I1,S). I2 reduces S→b and I4 reduces S→aS on every terminal; I3 accepts only on the end marker.

steps.title: Read table actions
steps.explanation: ACTION[0,a]=shift 1; ACTION[1,b]=shift 2; ACTION[2,$]=reduce S→b; ACTION[4,$]=reduce S→aS; ACTION[3,$]=accept. GOTO[0,S]=3 and GOTO[1,S]=4.

steps.title: Shift the input
steps.explanation: Consume a and then b. The grammar-symbol stack is ab and the remaining lookahead is $.

steps.title: Reduce the base
steps.explanation: Reduce S→b, pop one state, and push GOTO[1,S]=4. The symbol stack becomes aS and the lookahead stays $.

steps.title: Reduce and accept
steps.explanation: Reduce S→aS, pop two states, then push GOTO[0,S]=3. The stack now represents S and ACTION[3,$] accepts.

example.answer: ab is accepted after two shifts, two reductions and one accept action.
example.verification: The reversed reductions reconstruct S⇒aS⇒ab. Every reduction state contains only one completed non-start item and no shift item, so these LR(0) actions create no conflicts.

depth.body: LR item sets describe viable prefixes, not just a bag of completed expressions. Closure supplies productions for the next nonterminal without consuming input, and goto moves a dot over one grammar symbol to produce a new state. The parser's action depends on both current state and lookahead; reduction consumes no input and uses a nonterminal goto after popping the recognized right-hand side. Different LR families place reductions with different precision. LR(0) uses every terminal, SLR uses FOLLOW, and canonical LR(1) carries lookahead on individual items. A conflict in a coarser family can disappear with more context even when the grammar is unambiguous. Inspect which exact state/lookahead cell demands two actions before declaring a grammar ambiguous.

examples.prompt: Construct LR(0) states for S′→S, S→ab and parse ab$. Use I1 after a, I2 after ab, I3 after S.
examples.strategy: Close and advance → Complete the production → Execute the stack

steps.title: Close and advance
steps.equation: I_0=\{S'\to\cdot S,S\to\cdot ab\},\quad I_1=\{S\to a\cdot b\}
steps.explanation: Closure adds S's rule, and terminal a leads from I0 to I1.

steps.title: Complete the production
steps.explanation: I2 reduces S→ab; goto(I0,S)=I3 accepts on $.

steps.title: Execute the stack
steps.explanation: Shift a,b, pop two states for the reduction, push goto on S, and accept without consuming $ as a grammar terminal.

examples.answer: ab accepts with two shifts and one reduction.
examples.verification: The single reduction reconstructs S⇒ab. There are no completed items in either shift state, so no LR(0) conflict occurs.

examples.prompt: For S→L=R|R, L→*R|id, R→L, explain the SLR conflict in the state {S→L·=R,R→L·}.
examples.strategy: Find the shift demand → Compute the reduction lookahead → Find the competing demand → Locate the conflict cell

steps.title: Find the shift demand
steps.explanation: The first item has = immediately after its dot, so ACTION on = must shift.

steps.title: Compute the reduction lookahead
steps.explanation: S→L=R puts = in FOLLOW(L); L→*R propagates FOLLOW(L) to FOLLOW(R), so = belongs to FOLLOW(R).

steps.title: Find the competing demand
steps.explanation: The completed item R→L· requests an SLR reduction on every FOLLOW(R) symbol, including =.

steps.title: Locate the conflict cell
steps.explanation: On the same state and lookahead =, the table requires both shift and reduce R→L; it cannot select a unique SLR action.

examples.answer: The grammar has a shift/reduce conflict under SLR.
examples.verification: The competing actions follow from different items. Item-specific LR(1) lookahead can distinguish contexts that the global FOLLOW(R) approximation merges.

examples.prompt: For S′→S, S→Aa, A→b|ε, show why LR(0) conflicts at start but SLR can parse ba.
examples.strategy: Inspect start closure → Compare reduction policies → Trace ba under SLR

steps.title: Inspect start closure
steps.explanation: The empty-production item is already complete while another item permits shifting b.

steps.title: Compare reduction policies
steps.explanation: LR(0) reduces \(A\to\varepsilon\) on b and conflicts with shift b. FOLLOW(A)={a}, so SLR restricts that reduction to a and removes this start conflict.

steps.title: Trace ba under SLR
steps.explanation: Shift b, reduce A→b on a, use goto on A, shift a, reduce S→Aa on $, then accept.

examples.answer: The grammar is SLR but not LR(0); ba accepts under SLR.
examples.verification: On input a, SLR instead reduces \(A\to\varepsilon\) before shifting a, covering the other language member without a conflict.

lessons.title: Syntax-directed translation and runtime environments
lessons.intuition: A parse tree can carry semantic information such as expression values or types. Syntax-directed translation describes how this information moves. Runtime environments then arrange the storage needed when the translated program actually executes.

sections.title: Attributes and evaluation
sections.body: Synthesized attributes are computed from children and flow upward; inherited attributes receive information from a parent or relevant siblings. Semantic rules define dependencies, and a legal evaluation order respects that dependency graph. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit bottom-up evaluation naturally. L-attributed definitions restrict inherited dependencies for left-to-right evaluation.

sections.title: Translation actions
sections.body: An annotated syntax tree can compute expression types, values, offsets or emitted code. For E→E₁+T, a synthesized value rule may set E.val=E₁.val+T.val. Translation schemes embed actions in productions, so action placement determines execution order during a derivation. Parsing correctness alone does not guarantee the semantic actions are correct.

sections.title: Runtime storage
sections.body: An activation record can include arguments, return address, saved registers, locals and links. A dynamic link points to the caller’s frame; a static link supports lexical nesting and can point somewhere different. Stack allocation supports ordinary call-return lifetimes; heap allocation supports objects that outlive their creating call. Recursion needs separate frames even for the same function.

sections.title: Dependency graphs and environment links
sections.body: Attribute evaluation is a scheduling problem: each attribute value must be computed after the values it depends on. Synthesized attributes flow from child computations to a parent. Inherited attributes can flow from the parent or permitted siblings; not every inherited definition can be evaluated in a single left-to-right traversal. A cycle in the dependency graph prevents a simple evaluation order. At runtime, each call creates an activation record containing its own parameters, locals and return information under the calling convention. The dynamic link follows the chain of callers; the static link follows lexical nesting for nonlocal variable access. Recursive calls share the same source-level procedure but require distinct live records. Returning restores the caller’s execution context rather than reinitializing it.

examples.prompt: Evaluate attributes for expression 2+3*4

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The multiplication node synthesizes 3×4=12. The multiplication subtree is evaluated before its parent addition, because the parse groups 3*4 together.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: The addition node receives child values 2 and 12. The child attribute values are inputs to the addition node’s synthesized attribute.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: It synthesizes 14; using a different parse tree could produce a different arithmetic order. The result belongs to this parse tree. Evaluating source tokens left-to-right without precedence would incorrectly give 20.

examples.strategy: Evaluate child attributes after the parse structure fixes operator precedence.
examples.answer: It synthesizes 14; using a different parse tree could produce a different arithmetic order.
examples.verification: Independent arithmetic 2+(3×4)=14 agrees. If the grammar were ambiguous, the tree would need to be specified first.

examples.prompt: Track calls main→f→f in recursion
steps: main owns one frame; first f creates another.
Recursive f creates a third frame with its own locals.
Returning from inner f releases only its frame and restores the caller f’s state.

pitfalls: Static and dynamic links serve different relationships.
Same function code does not imply shared local variables.
revision: Synthesized flows upward; inherited receives context.
Activation records represent invocations, not functions as unique objects.

checks.prompt: For the parse tree 2+(3*4), what value is synthesized at the root?
checks.hint: Evaluate the multiplication child first.

checks.prompt: main calls f, which calls f again. How many frames are active before any return, counting main?
checks.hint: Count invocations rather than distinct names.
checks.explanation: main, outer f and inner f give three frames.

gateGuide.recognize: Keep compile-time attribute dependencies separate from runtime storage. Activation records represent individual calls, including recursive calls.
method: Classify each attribute as synthesized or inherited and draw its dependency edges.
Choose an evaluation order consistent with those edges; relate S-attributed definitions to bottom-up evaluation.
For runtime access trace lexical nesting through static links and callers through dynamic links; account for separate recursive frames.

traps.claim: Static links always point to the caller
traps.why: They point to the lexically enclosing environment; the caller can be a different procedure.

traps.claim: One variable name means one runtime memory cell
traps.why: Each recursive activation can have its own locals and parameters.

formulas.meaning: Access within a frame; finding the correct base may require following static links.

tutorials.title: Attribute dependencies and syntax-directed evaluation
tutorials.body:
Syntax-directed translation attaches semantic rules to grammar productions, computing values such as expression results, types or generated code. Synthesized attributes flow from child computations to a parent. Inherited attributes obtain information from the parent or allowed siblings, such as a declaration’s type flowing into several identifiers.
A dependency graph connects the attribute values required to compute others. A legal evaluation order must be topological; a cycle prevents straightforward evaluation for that tree. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit bottom-up evaluation. The parse tree determines grouping, and semantic evaluation must follow its dependencies rather than the unparenthesized character order. Some rules emit effects, so execution order matters in translation schemes.
