gateGuide.recognize: ER cardinality constraints and relational keys must be derived from the scenario. Tables implement entities and relationships.
method: Identify entity keys and relationship cardinalities/participation.
Map many-to-many relationships to their own relation; place suitable foreign keys for one-to-many.
For weak entities combine owner key and partial key; verify whether relationship attributes and optional participation need extra constraints.

traps.claim: A foreign key must be unique in the referencing table
traps.why: Many rows may reference the same parent in a many-to-one relationship.

traps.claim: A primary key alone enforces total participation
traps.why: A non-null foreign key plus referential integrity can enforce some participation constraints; others need additional checks.

formulas.meaning: A candidate key K functionally determines every attribute in its relation.
Referential integrity constrains referenced values, subject to allowed nulls.

tutorials.title: Entities, relationships and ER constraints
tutorials.body:
An entity is a distinguishable object in the modeled world; an entity set groups similar objects. Attributes describe entities, and a key identifies each entity. Relationships connect participating entities and can carry their own attributes, such as a grade belonging to an enrollment rather than a student alone. A weak entity needs an owner plus a partial key for identification.
Cardinality specifies how many entities can participate on a side: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. Participation specifies whether every entity must appear in the relationship, separate from its maximum cardinality. Read diagram conventions carefully because arrows and double lines vary by notation.
Map strong entities to relations; many-to-many relationships need a relation containing participating keys and relationship attributes. A one-to-many relationship can often use a foreign key on the many side, with nullability reflecting optional participation. Repeated events require an event identifier or additional term/attempt attributes; two entity keys are not automatically a unique relationship key. Derive constraints from the scenario rather than a sample diagram’s visual spacing.

example.prompt: Model students enrolling in courses, with one grade per student/course pair.
example.strategy: Entity tables → Relationship table → Key and references

steps.title: Entity tables
steps.explanation: Student(student_id,…) and Course(course_id,…) have their own keys.

steps.title: Relationship table
steps.explanation: Enrollment(student_id,course_id,grade) stores the many-to-many relationship and its grade.

steps.title: Key and references
steps.explanation: The identifier pair is the enrollment key under the one-enrollment assumption; each identifier also references its entity.

example.answer: Three relations with grade attached to Enrollment.
example.verification: If repeat attempts are allowed, the pair alone no longer uniquely identifies every enrollment event.

depth.body: ER modeling captures identity and relationship rules before tables are chosen. Ask whether an attribute belongs to an entity, to one participation, or to a repeated relationship event. Maximum cardinality and mandatory participation answer different questions: allowing only one advisor does not require every student to have one. Weak entities borrow an owner's identity and add a discriminator that is unique only within that owner. Translate the rules into keys, foreign keys, uniqueness and nullability after clarifying repetition assumptions. The examples use ordinary entity/relationship notation without relying on a particular arrow convention. Test the resulting schema using two concrete objects, because an apparently sensible identifier often fails as soon as two owners reuse the same local label.

examples.prompt: Each employee belongs to exactly one department; a department can have many employees. Design the relationship mapping.
examples.strategy: Identify independent entities → Place the many-side reference → Encode required participation

steps.title: Identify independent entities
steps.explanation: Department(dept_id) and Employee(emp_id) each need their own identifying key.

steps.title: Place the many-side reference
steps.explanation: Employee stores dept_id referencing Department, since each employee has one department.

steps.title: Encode required participation
steps.explanation: Declare Employee.dept_id NOT NULL; do not make it UNIQUE because many employees may share a department.

examples.answer: Use a nonnull department foreign key in Employee without child-side uniqueness.
examples.verification: Two employees with different emp_id values and the same dept_id satisfy the described many-to-one relationship.

examples.prompt: Order lines use line_no unique only within an order. Order 100 and 200 both have line 1. Model line identity and ownership.
examples.strategy: Locate the discriminator → Include owner identity → Enforce the owner

steps.title: Locate the discriminator
steps.explanation: line_no=1 alone cannot distinguish the two supplied lines.

steps.title: Include owner identity
steps.explanation: OrderLine(order_id,line_no,item) uses composite key (order_id,line_no).

steps.title: Enforce the owner
steps.explanation: order_id references Order; each line requires a matching owner under the weak-entity model.

examples.answer: The line key is (order_id,line_no), with a mandatory Order reference.
examples.verification: Pairs (100,1) and (200,1) are distinct keys although their local discriminator matches.

examples.prompt: Each student has at most one advisor, and some students have none. Must the Advisor relationship have total Student participation?
examples.strategy: Read the maximum rule → Read the minimum rule → Choose the mapping

steps.title: Read the maximum rule
steps.explanation: At most one limits the number of advisors for a participating student.

steps.title: Read the minimum rule
steps.explanation: Some students have none, giving minimum participation zero.

steps.title: Choose the mapping
steps.explanation: A nullable advisor_id foreign key can represent absence; NOT NULL would impose an unstated requirement.

examples.answer: Student participation is optional, not total.
examples.verification: A student with advisor_id NULL is explicitly legal under the scenario, refuting the total-participation claim.

tutorials.title: Relations, keys and integrity constraints
tutorials.body:
A relation has a schema of named attributes and a set of tuples under mathematical set semantics. A candidate key is a minimal attribute set functionally determining every attribute. A superkey also determines all attributes but may include unnecessary ones; a primary key is one chosen candidate key. Prime attributes belong to at least one candidate key, not merely the chosen primary key.
Domain constraints restrict values; entity integrity prevents null primary-key components; referential integrity requires nonnull foreign-key values to match permitted referenced keys. A foreign key need not be unique in the referencing table: many rows can name the same parent. SQL tables commonly permit duplicates unless constraints prevent them, so distinguish implementation bag behavior from mathematical relations.
Keys are constraints over every legal state, not accidental uniqueness in a small sample. A name appearing once today does not prove a schema key. Composite foreign keys should be checked as tuples with the specified null rules. Additional total participation and cardinality constraints may require uniqueness, nonnull declarations or richer checks rather than one foreign key alone.

example.prompt: Student_id uniquely identifies students. Classify {student_id} and {student_id,name}.
example.strategy: Determination → Minimality → Classification

steps.title: Determination
steps.explanation: Either set contains student_id, so both uniquely determine a legal row.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.explanation: Removing name from the larger set still preserves identification.

steps.title: Classification
steps.explanation: The singleton is a candidate key; the larger set is only a superkey unless another assumption changes minimality.

example.answer: Candidate key {student_id}; nonminimal superkey {student_id,name}.
example.verification: A key test needs both uniqueness and inability to remove an attribute while retaining it.

depth.body: A key proof needs determination and minimality over the schema constraints. Compute closure to prove determination, then remove attributes to check that no proper subset still determines everything. Attributes never appearing on any dependency right side must occur in every key unless a special empty determinant is supplied. Candidate keys may overlap and need not coincide with the chosen primary key; prime status is defined using all of them. The examples assume ordinary functional dependencies on a finite attribute set and no unlisted dependencies. Use necessary attributes to prune candidate search, but still prove sufficiency and minimality. An identifier unique in a sample gives evidence about that sample, not a guarantee for every legal database state.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\). Classify A, AB and B as candidate key, superkey or nonkey.
examples.strategy: Compute determining closure → Check the enlarged set → Check the other singleton

steps.title: Compute determining closure
steps.explanation: A determines the complete schema and is minimal as a singleton.

steps.title: Check the enlarged set
steps.explanation: AB also determines ABC but contains removable B, so it is a nonminimal superkey.

steps.title: Check the other singleton
steps.explanation: B cannot determine A and is not a superkey.

examples.answer: A is a candidate key; AB is a nonminimal superkey; B is not a key.
examples.verification: No dependency derives A, so every key must contain A, excluding B independently.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C,D,E) has A\(B\to C\),C→A,D→E. Find all candidate keys.
examples.strategy: Find necessary attributes → Supply the missing determinant → Check minimality and completeness

steps.title: Find necessary attributes
steps.explanation: B and D never occur on right sides, so every key includes BD.

steps.title: Supply the missing determinant
steps.explanation: Adding A gives ABD, while adding C gives BCD. Either closure reaches all five attributes.

steps.title: Check minimality and completeness
steps.explanation: BD alone cannot derive A or C; no other attribute supplies them. Thus ABD and BCD are the only minimal possibilities.

examples.answer: Candidate keys ABD and BCD.
examples.verification: Removing B or D loses an underivable attribute; removing A from ABD or C from BCD leaves insufficient BD.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has candidate keys A and BC. A is selected as primary key. Are B and C nonprime because they are absent from the primary key?
examples.strategy: Use the definition → Inspect both candidates → Separate selection from property

steps.title: Use the definition
steps.explanation: Prime means membership in any candidate key.

steps.title: Inspect both candidates
steps.explanation: A belongs to A, while B and C belong to BC.

steps.title: Separate selection from property
steps.explanation: Choosing A for implementation does not erase the alternate candidate key.

examples.answer: All three attributes are prime.
examples.verification: The candidate-key list itself supplies a membership witness for every attribute.

tutorials.title: A mathematical relation has set semantics
tutorials.body:
The relational model describes a relation as a set of tuples over named attributes and their domains. Attribute names identify values, while tuple order has no mathematical meaning. Because a set has no duplicate members, writing the same entire tuple twice does not create two distinct tuples in the relation. Different tuples can still have the same value for an individual attribute when another attribute differs.
SQL implementations commonly use bag semantics for query results unless duplicate elimination is requested. This difference matters when counting results after dropping attributes. In mathematical relational projection, tuples that become identical are collapsed; SQL SELECT without DISTINCT normally retains their multiplicity. Distinguish an entire-tuple duplicate from a repeated attribute value, and distinguish a relation's set definition from any additional declared key constraint. To work an example, enumerate the full tuples, perform the requested attribute operation, then apply the semantics of that operation before counting the result.

example.prompt: Consider R(A,B) with tuples (1,x),(2,x),(3,y). Compare relational projection onto B with SQL SELECT B FROM R and SELECT DISTINCT B FROM R.
example.strategy: Inspect distinct full tuples → Project under the model → Compare SQL bags

steps.title: Inspect distinct full tuples
steps.explanation: The three full tuples differ on A, so R contains three tuples even though x appears twice as a B value.

steps.title: Project under the model
steps.explanation: Dropping A produces repeated (x); set semantics retain it only once.

steps.title: Compare SQL bags
steps.explanation: SELECT B returns three rows x,x,y. SELECT DISTINCT B removes the repeated output and returns two rows x,y.

example.answer: Relational projection has two tuples; ordinary SQL SELECT has three rows; SELECT DISTINCT has two.
example.verification: COUNT(*) on the ordinary SQL result is 3 while COUNT(DISTINCT B) is 2. Repeated x does not by itself violate relation semantics because its original full tuples differ.

depth.body: The relation abstraction concerns values and constraints rather than the storage order of rows. Two instances containing the same full tuples are the same relation even if printed in a different order. Repeated values in one column do not collapse tuples whose other values differ, whereas repeating a complete tuple has no extra multiplicity in the mathematical model. Projection can make originally different tuples equal and therefore removes the resulting duplicates. SQL bags deliberately retain multiplicity unless requested otherwise. These examples assume named attributes and set-based relational operations; distinguish this from presentation sorting and implementation row identifiers. Calculate results by writing full output tuples, then applying the operation's duplicate rules, rather than counting distinct values prematurely.

examples.prompt: A printed relation R(A,B) lists (1,p),(1,p),(2,p),(2,q). How many mathematical tuples and distinct A values does it contain?
examples.strategy: Remove repeated full tuples → Retain different combinations → Count the two objects

steps.title: Remove repeated full tuples
steps.explanation: The second (1,p) repeats an existing member of the set.

steps.title: Retain different combinations
steps.explanation: (2,p) and (2,q) remain separate because their B values differ.

steps.title: Count the two objects
steps.explanation: R contains three tuples, while projection onto A contains values 1 and 2.

examples.answer: Three tuples and two distinct A values.
examples.verification: The surviving full set {(1,p),(2,p),(2,q)} explicitly contains three members.

examples.prompt: R(A,B)={(1,x),(2,x)} and S(A,B)={(2,x),(3,y)}. Compare projection onto B of their set union with SQL UNION ALL followed by ordinary SELECT B.
examples.strategy: Form the set union → Project set values → Keep bag multiplicity

steps.title: Form the set union
steps.explanation: R union S has three full tuples because (2,x) appears once.

steps.title: Project set values
steps.explanation: B values x,x,y collapse to {(x),(y)}, giving two tuples.

steps.title: Keep bag multiplicity
steps.explanation: UNION ALL retains four source rows, and ordinary SELECT B returns x,x,x,y.

examples.answer: Set projection has two tuples; the SQL bag result has four rows.
examples.verification: Source counts 2+2=4 explain the bag cardinality, while overlapping full tuple and projected x account for the set reductions.

examples.prompt: R is printed as (a,1),(b,2); S is printed as (b,2),(a,1) with the same schema. Are these different relations because row order differs?
examples.strategy: Compare schemas → Compare tuple membership → Ignore display order

steps.title: Compare schemas
steps.explanation: Both use the same named attributes and domains.

steps.title: Compare tuple membership
steps.explanation: Each full tuple in R also belongs to S, and conversely.

steps.title: Ignore display order
steps.explanation: A mathematical relation is a set, so printing order is not part of its identity.

examples.answer: R and S are the same relation.
examples.verification: Both set differences R−S and S−R are empty, independently establishing equality.

tutorials.title: Foreign keys reject missing parents and govern deletion
tutorials.body:
Integrity constraints define legal database states. Domain and check constraints restrict values; primary-key constraints require unique, nonnull identification; foreign keys preserve references to existing parent keys under their declared null and matching rules. A foreign key normally permits many child rows to reference one parent, so it does not establish uniqueness in the child table.
For a nonnull foreign-key value, compare the complete referenced key against parent rows. A missing parent makes the insert or update invalid even when the child has a new unique primary key. Deleting a referenced parent requires the declared referential action. RESTRICT prevents the deletion while references remain; CASCADE deletes matching child rows; SET NULL replaces child references and therefore requires compatible nullability. These are alternative schema choices, not actions that all occur together. Check entity integrity and referential integrity separately, and do not confuse automatic reference enforcement with arbitrary business rules such as grades being within a range.

example.prompt: Student(id PRIMARY KEY) contains 10 and 20. Enrollment(student_id NOT NULL REFERENCES Student(id), course) contains (10,OS). Test inserting (30,DB), then consider deleting Student 10 under alternative ON DELETE RESTRICT and CASCADE schemas.
example.strategy: Check the new reference → Apply RESTRICT → Apply CASCADE independently

steps.title: Check the new reference
steps.explanation: 30 matches no Student primary key. NOT NULL is satisfied but referential integrity is not, so reject the Enrollment insert.

steps.title: Apply RESTRICT
steps.explanation: Student 10 is still referenced by (10,OS). The parent deletion is rejected, preserving both original rows.

steps.title: Apply CASCADE independently
steps.explanation: In the alternative CASCADE schema, delete Student 10 and its referencing Enrollment row together. Student 20 remains; the rejected (30,DB) row never existed.

example.answer: The insert fails. RESTRICT blocks deletion of Student 10; CASCADE removes it and its enrollment.
example.verification: After each accepted operation every remaining nonnull student_id names an existing Student. SET NULL would conflict with this declared NOT NULL column unless the schema were changed.

depth.body: Constraint reasoning checks each rule against the attempted state, not against an application's intentions. A foreign key constrains the referenced values but does not generally prevent many child rows referring to one parent. Composite keys require a whole matching tuple; separate matches for each component can be insufficient. SQL check constraints and null handling also need their exact contract: a nullable value can make a predicate UNKNOWN, which ordinary CHECK accepts unless another constraint forbids null. The examples assume enforced constraints and ordinary SQL three-valued logic. Separate uniqueness, nullability, allowed domains and referential matching in the trace, then identify the particular failed rule. A rejection by one constraint does not mean every other aspect of the proposed row was invalid.

examples.prompt: Parent(id PRIMARY KEY) contains 5. Child(child_id PRIMARY KEY,parent_id REFERENCES Parent) receives (1,5),(2,5),(3,5). Is this legal?
examples.strategy: Check child identifiers → Check references → Avoid inventing uniqueness

steps.title: Check child identifiers
steps.explanation: The child keys 1,2,3 are distinct.

steps.title: Check references
steps.explanation: Every parent_id=5 matches the existing parent key.

steps.title: Avoid inventing uniqueness
steps.explanation: The foreign key imposes no UNIQUE rule on parent_id, so repeated references are permitted.

examples.answer: All three child rows are legal.
examples.verification: One parent and three distinct children is the standard many-to-one relationship a foreign key can represent.

examples.prompt: Parent has composite keys (1,A) and (2,B). Child has a nonnull composite foreign key (number,letter). Test proposed child value (1,B).
examples.strategy: Check the entire tuple → Enumerate parent keys → Reject the mismatch

steps.title: Check the entire tuple
steps.explanation: The foreign key requests parent key (1,B), not two independent component matches.

steps.title: Enumerate parent keys
steps.explanation: Neither (1,A) nor (2,B) equals the requested pair.

steps.title: Reject the mismatch
steps.explanation: The proposed child violates referential integrity even though 1 and B each occur somewhere.

examples.answer: Reject (1,B): no matching composite parent key exists.
examples.verification: Matching (1,A) would succeed; componentwise membership cannot replace tuple equality.

examples.prompt: A nullable score column has CHECK(score>=0 AND score<=100). Insert score=NULL under ordinary SQL CHECK semantics. Does CHECK alone reject it?
examples.strategy: Evaluate comparisons → Combine the predicate → Apply CHECK semantics

steps.title: Evaluate comparisons
steps.explanation: Both comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN.

steps.title: Combine the predicate
steps.explanation: UNKNOWN AND UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN, not FALSE.

steps.title: Apply CHECK semantics
steps.explanation: A CHECK rejects FALSE; UNKNOWN passes, so only an additional NOT NULL rule would forbid this value.

examples.answer: The nullable NULL value passes this CHECK.
examples.verification: A score of 101 produces FALSE and is rejected, illustrating the different treatment of FALSE and UNKNOWN.

lessons.title: Relational algebra, tuple calculus and SQL
lessons.intuition: A query describes a derived relation. Algebra describes operations to produce it, while calculus describes a logical condition on desired tuples. SQL uses related ideas but adds practical semantics for duplicates, NULL and grouping.

sections.title: Algebra and calculus
sections.body: Selection σ filters tuples; projection π keeps named columns and removes duplicates in set-based algebra. Cartesian product pairs every tuple; a join filters combinations by a condition. Union and difference require compatible schemas. Tuple relational calculus uses predicates on tuples; safe/range-restricted expressions ensure finite, domain-independent results.

sections.title: SQL order and joins
sections.body: Conceptually FROM/JOIN establishes sources, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT chooses expressions, and ORDER BY orders results. An inner join requires a match; an outer join also retains unmatched rows with NULL-filled columns. Filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE can discard the unmatched rows and change the intended semantics.

sections.title: Duplicates, aggregates and NULL
sections.body: SELECT ordinarily keeps duplicates; DISTINCT removes them. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM/AVG ordinarily ignore NULL inputs. Comparisons involving NULL usually yield UNKNOWN; WHERE retains only TRUE. Use IS NULL rather than =NULL. SQL OR/AND follows three-valued logic in such cases.

sections.title: Trace bags, nulls and grouping explicitly
sections.body: Under SQL bag semantics, a join can multiply duplicates: if a key has two matching left rows and three matching right rows, their equality join contributes six rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates at its specified stage and cannot be assumed throughout. WHERE evaluates predicates on source rows, then GROUP BY partitions survivors and HAVING filters completed groups. Null comparisons normally yield UNKNOWN, so NULL=NULL does not become TRUE; use IS NULL to test nullness. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) and AVG(column) ignore nulls. For an empty input without grouping, COUNT returns zero while many other aggregates return NULL. NOT IN can be poisoned by a null comparison; reasoning through the three-valued truth conditions is safer than blindly rewriting it as an anti-join.

examples.prompt: Count students per department with at least three students

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Group Student rows by dept. Rows with the same department value contribute to the same aggregate group.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Use SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Student GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>=3. COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group and HAVING applies the threshold to that computed group result.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count. A row-level WHERE condition cannot use the aggregate count of a group that has not yet been formed.

examples.strategy: Form groups before evaluating a predicate over their aggregate count.
examples.answer: The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count.
examples.verification: A department with two rows is absent, one with three rows appears with count 3; SELECT and GROUP BY use the same grouping attribute.

examples.prompt: COUNT semantics for values [7,NULL,9]
steps: There are three rows, so COUNT(*)=3.
Only two have non-NULL column values, so COUNT(value)=2.

pitfalls: Projection in relational algebra eliminates duplicates; SQL SELECT does not by default.
NULL is not an ordinary comparable value.
revision: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

checks.prompt: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation?
checks.hint: Group predicates require already formed groups.
checks.explanation: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters source rows before aggregation.

checks.prompt: Relations with 3 and 4 tuples have how many tuples in their Cartesian product?
checks.hint: Every tuple pairs with every tuple.
checks.explanation: 3×4=12 pairs.

lessons.concept: A query describes a derived relation. Algebra describes operations to produce it, while calculus describes a logical condition on desired tuples. SQL uses related ideas but adds practical semantics for duplicates, NULL and grouping.
lessons.method:
Relational algebra builds relations through operations. Selection σ filters tuples by a predicate and preserves attributes. Projection π keeps specified attributes and removes duplicate resulting tuples under set semantics. Cartesian product forms every tuple pairing; a theta join filters that product by a condition. Natural join matches all shared attribute names and includes one copy of each shared attribute.
Union, intersection and difference require compatible schemas/domains. Rename resolves attribute ambiguity and enables a relation to join with itself. Division expresses an “associated with every required value” query by finding candidate values with no missing required partner.
Operator order matters: projecting away an attribute before a selection that needs it makes that predicate unavailable. A natural join can accidentally match an unrelated shared name, so use explicit conditions when names do not encode the intended relationship. SQL may retain duplicates, giving different cardinalities from set algebra. GATE query-equivalence problems require the stated semantics and constraints, not just similar-looking expressions. Tuple relational calculus describes what tuples satisfy a logical condition rather than an operation sequence. A query has form {t | P(t)} with relation-membership predicates, attribute comparisons and quantifiers. Free tuple variables describe the output; bound variables express existence or universal requirements. This connects database querying to first-order logic.
A safe, domain-independent query draws results from values constrained by the database and permitted constants, so it remains finite and does not depend on an arbitrary infinite external domain. An unconstrained negation such as all tuples not in a finite relation can range over infinitely many possibilities and is unsafe. Negation becomes meaningful when candidates are bounded by a relation.
Existential predicates express matching joins; universal requirements can be rewritten as absence of a counterexample. Quantifier scope matters just as in logic: one common witness differs from a witness per candidate. For GATE, identify output variables, candidate domain and predicate meaning before translating to algebra or SQL. The calculus is declarative, but safety restrictions distinguish useful finite queries from unrestricted formulas. SQL query reasoning normally begins with FROM and joins, then WHERE row filtering, GROUP BY, HAVING group filtering and SELECT output, with DISTINCT/order/limits at their relevant stages. This is a logical model, not a guarantee of physical execution order. Aggregate predicates require the completed group and belong in HAVING rather than a row WHERE clause.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores null column values. SUM/AVG generally ignore null operands, and empty-input aggregates have specified null behavior rather than always returning zero. Comparisons involving NULL normally yield UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, while IS NULL directly tests nullness.
SQL uses bags unless duplicate removal is requested. Grouping partitions surviving rows by the grouping keys, so join multiplication can alter aggregate results. A NOT IN subquery containing NULL can produce UNKNOWN for unmatched values, unlike an appropriately correlated NOT EXISTS. Trace actual rows through each stage before counting; memorizing clause names does not reveal null or duplicate effects. An inner join emits row pairs satisfying its condition. A left outer join additionally preserves unmatched left rows, supplying nulls for right-side attributes; right/full joins preserve other sides accordingly. A self join uses aliases to compare distinct roles drawn from one table, such as an employee and manager.
Multiplicity matters under SQL bags: two left rows and three right rows with one matching key produce six joined rows. Equality of join keys does not deduplicate records automatically. Keys and foreign keys can constrain multiplicity, but only when those constraints actually exist.
A WHERE predicate on a right-side attribute after a left join can discard null-extended rows and effectively undo outer preservation. Placing the predicate in ON filters matches while still allowing unmatched left rows. Natural joins infer conditions from all shared column names, which can accidentally constrain more than intended. In GATE cardinality questions, count matching pairs per key and add unmatched preserved rows using the chosen join’s rules. Grouping partitions query rows by the values of the GROUP BY attributes. Aggregates then summarize each partition, and HAVING decides which complete groups survive. WHERE instead filters individual input rows before grouping, so moving a condition between these clauses can change both group membership and aggregate values. This is the logical evaluation model; a database optimizer may choose a different physical execution plan while preserving the result.
COUNT(*) counts surviving rows, COUNT(column) counts their nonnull values, and AVG ignores null operands under ordinary SQL behavior. Group keys can remain even when some rows are removed, provided at least one row survives for that group. To evaluate a grouped query, first enumerate rows that satisfy WHERE, form groups from those rows, compute each aggregate, apply HAVING, and produce selected values. An aggregate test such as COUNT(*)>=2 cannot ordinarily be used as a row predicate in WHERE. Join multiplication must be included before this procedure if the input came from a join. Union and difference require compatible schemas. Tuple relational calculus uses predicates on tuples; safe/range-restricted expressions ensure finite, domain-independent results. Conceptually FROM/JOIN establishes sources, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT chooses expressions, and ORDER BY orders results. An inner join requires a match; an outer join also retains unmatched rows with NULL-filled columns. Filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE can discard the unmatched rows and change the intended semantics. SELECT ordinarily keeps duplicates; DISTINCT removes them. Use IS NULL rather than =NULL. SQL OR/AND follows three-valued logic in such cases. DISTINCT removes duplicates at its specified stage and cannot be assumed throughout. WHERE evaluates predicates on source rows, then GROUP BY partitions survivors and HAVING filters completed groups. Null comparisons normally yield UNKNOWN, so NULL=NULL does not become TRUE; use IS NULL to test nullness. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) and AVG(column) ignore nulls. For an empty input without grouping, COUNT returns zero while many other aggregates return NULL. NOT IN can be poisoned by a null comparison; reasoning through the three-valued truth conditions is safer than blindly rewriting it as an anti-join. Relational algebra supplies compositional operations with explicit input and output schemas. Selection keeps columns while filtering rows; projection changes the schema and applies set duplicate elimination. Set difference requires compatible relations, and division encodes a for-every association rather than an ordinary one-match join. Before evaluating an expression, track which attributes remain available to later predicates. A plausible-looking operator order can be undefined if it drops a required column. These examples assume mathematical set semantics and attribute names rather than SQL bags. Derive intermediate relations explicitly, especially in division, where a candidate missing even one required partner must be removed. Empty divisor behavior follows the chosen candidate universe, so state where candidate identifiers come from. Tuple calculus expresses predicates over candidate tuples rather than an execution plan. The output variable must be tied to a finite relation or otherwise safely bounded; existential variables provide matching witnesses, and universal requirements can be stated as the absence of a missing witness. Scope controls whether one witness must satisfy all candidates or separate witnesses may exist for different candidates. These examples use relation membership and ordinary logical quantifiers, with student identifiers drawn from Student. Check a query by testing each candidate and exhibiting either its witness or a counterexample. Negation alone does not provide a finite domain. An unrestricted universe of possible tuples can make a superficially simple negative condition return infinitely many values unrelated to the database. SQL evaluation uses rows, nulls and three-valued predicates, so a direct translation from ordinary two-valued arithmetic can be wrong. WHERE retains TRUE only; UNKNOWN is discarded like FALSE for filtering but behaves differently under negation and constraints. Correlated subqueries bind inner comparisons to the current outer row, and ties can yield multiple maxima unless uniqueness is guaranteed. Anti-joins using NOT IN require particular care when the subquery includes NULL. These examples assume ordinary SQL semantics with no implicit ordering or duplicate removal. This makes lost preservation and duplicate multiplication visible rather than hiding them in an intuitive diagram of overlapping sets. lessons.example: Count students per department with at least three students

gateGuide.recognize: SQL uses bags by default and three-valued logic for nulls. Relational algebra commonly uses sets; keep the semantics explicit.
method: Trace FROM/join rows, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and projection; apply DISTINCT only if requested.
For null comparisons use TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN; WHERE retains TRUE rows.
For nested queries identify correlated variables and test empty inputs, duplicates and nulls.

traps.claim: COUNT(column) counts every row
traps.why: It excludes nulls in that column; COUNT(*) counts rows.

traps.claim: NOT IN is always interchangeable with NOT EXISTS
traps.why: A null in the subquery can make NOT IN UNKNOWN, while a suitable NOT EXISTS correlation behaves differently.

formulas.meaning: Select qualifying rows, then project attributes A, under relational-algebra set semantics.
Theta join; SQL duplicate counts can differ from set algebra.

tutorials.title: Relational algebra: selection, projection and joins
tutorials.body:
Relational algebra builds relations through operations. Selection σ filters tuples by a predicate and preserves attributes. Projection π keeps specified attributes and removes duplicate resulting tuples under set semantics. Cartesian product forms every tuple pairing; a theta join filters that product by a condition. Natural join matches all shared attribute names and includes one copy of each shared attribute.
Union, intersection and difference require compatible schemas/domains. Rename resolves attribute ambiguity and enables a relation to join with itself. Division expresses an “associated with every required value” query by finding candidate values with no missing required partner.
Operator order matters: projecting away an attribute before a selection that needs it makes that predicate unavailable. A natural join can accidentally match an unrelated shared name, so use explicit conditions when names do not encode the intended relationship. SQL may retain duplicates, giving different cardinalities from set algebra. GATE query-equivalence problems require the stated semantics and constraints, not just similar-looking expressions.

example.prompt: R(A,B)={(1,x),(2,x),(3,y)}. Select B=x, then project B.
example.strategy: Select → Project → Deduplicate

steps.title: Select
steps.explanation: Two rows satisfy the predicate.

steps.title: Project
steps.explanation: Both rows yield the same one-attribute tuple.

steps.title: Deduplicate
steps.explanation: Set projection contains x once, not twice.

example.answer: Result {(x)} with one tuple.
example.verification: SQL SELECT B without DISTINCT would normally preserve two x rows, demonstrating the set/bag distinction.

depth.body: Relational algebra supplies compositional operations with explicit input and output schemas. Selection keeps columns while filtering rows; projection changes the schema and applies set duplicate elimination. Set difference requires compatible relations, and division encodes a for-every association rather than an ordinary one-match join. Before evaluating an expression, track which attributes remain available to later predicates. A plausible-looking operator order can be undefined if it drops a required column. These examples assume mathematical set semantics and attribute names rather than SQL bags. Derive intermediate relations explicitly, especially in division, where a candidate missing even one required partner must be removed. Empty divisor behavior follows the chosen candidate universe, so state where candidate identifiers come from.

examples.prompt: R(A)={1,2,4}, S(A)={2,3}. Evaluate R−S and R intersect S.
examples.strategy: Test left membership → Remove shared members → Keep shared members

steps.title: Test left membership
steps.explanation: Values 1,2,4 are candidates for difference.

steps.title: Remove shared members
steps.explanation: 2 occurs in S; 1 and 4 do not, so R−S={1,4}.

steps.title: Keep shared members
steps.explanation: Intersection retains only 2, giving {2}.

examples.answer: Difference {1,4}; intersection {2}.
examples.verification: The two disjoint results partition R: {1,4} union {2}={1,2,4}.

examples.prompt: Enrollment(student,course)={(Ann,OS),(Ann,DB),(Bob,OS),(Cam,DB)} and Required(course)={OS,DB}. Evaluate Enrollment divided by Required.
examples.strategy: List candidate students → Search missing requirements → Retain universal matches

steps.title: List candidate students
steps.explanation: Ann, Bob and Cam each appear in Enrollment.

steps.title: Search missing requirements
steps.explanation: Ann has both; Bob lacks DB; Cam lacks OS.

steps.title: Retain universal matches
steps.explanation: Only Ann has a pair with every Required course.

examples.answer: The division result is {Ann}.
examples.verification: Ann's required set difference is empty, while Bob and Cam each have an explicit missing-course witness.

examples.prompt: R(A,B) is projected to A, then a selection B=7 is applied. Is sigma(B=7)(pi(A)(R)) a valid ordinary algebra expression?
examples.strategy: Track the output schema → Inspect predicate requirements → Reject the expression

steps.title: Track the output schema
steps.explanation: Projection onto A removes B.

steps.title: Inspect predicate requirements
steps.explanation: Selection B=7 needs a B attribute in its input.

steps.title: Reject the expression
steps.explanation: The required attribute is unavailable; apply selection before projection if that is the intended query.

examples.answer: The expression is undefined under the stated schema.
examples.verification: pi(A)(sigma(B=7)(R)) is well-formed because the predicate is evaluated while B still exists.

tutorials.title: Tuple relational calculus and safe queries
tutorials.body:
Tuple relational calculus describes what tuples satisfy a logical condition rather than an operation sequence. A query has form {t | P(t)} with relation-membership predicates, attribute comparisons and quantifiers. Free tuple variables describe the output; bound variables express existence or universal requirements. This connects database querying to first-order logic.
A safe, domain-independent query draws results from values constrained by the database and permitted constants, so it remains finite and does not depend on an arbitrary infinite external domain. An unconstrained negation such as all tuples not in a finite relation can range over infinitely many possibilities and is unsafe. Negation becomes meaningful when candidates are bounded by a relation.
Existential predicates express matching joins; universal requirements can be rewritten as absence of a counterexample. Quantifier scope matters just as in logic: one common witness differs from a witness per candidate. For GATE, identify output variables, candidate domain and predicate meaning before translating to algebra or SQL. The calculus is declarative, but safety restrictions distinguish useful finite queries from unrestricted formulas.

example.prompt: Express students enrolled in every required course using a counterexample formulation.
example.strategy: Bound candidates → Define missing requirement → Negate existence

steps.title: Bound candidates
steps.explanation: Choose s from Student, not all possible arbitrary tuples.

steps.title: Define missing requirement
steps.explanation: A required course c is a counterexample if no Enrollment links s to c.

steps.title: Negate existence
steps.explanation: Return s only when no such required c exists.

example.answer: Return bounded students with no missing required enrollment.
example.verification: If Required is empty, every candidate student satisfies the universal condition vacuously.

depth.body: Tuple calculus expresses predicates over candidate tuples rather than an execution plan. The output variable must be tied to a finite relation or otherwise safely bounded; existential variables provide matching witnesses, and universal requirements can be stated as the absence of a missing witness. Scope controls whether one witness must satisfy all candidates or separate witnesses may exist for different candidates. These examples use relation membership and ordinary logical quantifiers, with student identifiers drawn from Student. Check a query by testing each candidate and exhibiting either its witness or a counterexample. Negation alone does not provide a finite domain. An unrestricted universe of possible tuples can make a superficially simple negative condition return infinitely many values unrelated to the database.

examples.prompt: Student IDs are {1,2,3}; Enrollment has (1,OS),(2,DB). Evaluate bounded students for which there exists an Enrollment with matching ID and course OS.
examples.strategy: Bound output candidates → Find existential witnesses → Emit satisfying candidates

steps.title: Bound output candidates
steps.explanation: Only IDs in Student can be returned.

steps.title: Find existential witnesses
steps.explanation: Student 1 has witness (1,OS); student 2 has only DB; student 3 has none.

steps.title: Emit satisfying candidates
steps.explanation: Return 1 because its matching OS enrollment makes the predicate true.

examples.answer: Result {1}.
examples.verification: The explicit witness proves inclusion of 1; absence of an OS witness proves exclusion of 2 and 3.

examples.prompt: Student={Ana,Ben,Cid}; Required={OS,DB}; Enrollment={(Ana,OS),(Ana,DB),(Ben,OS)}. Evaluate students with no required course lacking an enrollment.
examples.strategy: Choose bounded students → Build counterexamples → Negate missing existence

steps.title: Choose bounded students
steps.explanation: Ana, Ben and Cid are the only candidates.

steps.title: Build counterexamples
steps.explanation: Ben lacks DB; Cid lacks both. Ana has no missing required course.

steps.title: Negate missing existence
steps.explanation: Only Ana satisfies NOT EXISTS(required course with no matching enrollment).

examples.answer: Result {Ana}.
examples.verification: The counterexample formulation is equivalent to requiring an enrollment for every member of Required.

examples.prompt: Student is finite. The expression {t | NOT Student(t)} ranges over an unlimited tuple universe without a positive bound. Is its result necessarily a finite database query?
examples.strategy: Inspect variable range → Apply negation → Evaluate safety

steps.title: Inspect variable range
steps.explanation: Nothing restricts t to existing database values.

steps.title: Apply negation
steps.explanation: Every tuple outside finite Student satisfies the condition.

steps.title: Evaluate safety
steps.explanation: An unlimited universe contains indefinitely many such tuples, so the expression is unsafe/domain-dependent.

examples.answer: No; unrestricted negation does not guarantee a finite, safe result.
examples.verification: Bounding t with another finite relation would change the query and make its candidate set finite.

tutorials.title: SQL evaluation order, grouping and nulls
tutorials.body:
SQL query reasoning normally begins with FROM and joins, then WHERE row filtering, GROUP BY, HAVING group filtering and SELECT output, with DISTINCT/order/limits at their relevant stages. This is a logical model, not a guarantee of physical execution order. Aggregate predicates require the completed group and belong in HAVING rather than a row WHERE clause.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores null column values. SUM/AVG generally ignore null operands, and empty-input aggregates have specified null behavior rather than always returning zero. Comparisons involving NULL normally yield UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, while IS NULL directly tests nullness.
SQL uses bags unless duplicate removal is requested. Grouping partitions surviving rows by the grouping keys, so join multiplication can alter aggregate results. A NOT IN subquery containing NULL can produce UNKNOWN for unmatched values, unlike an appropriately correlated NOT EXISTS. Trace actual rows through each stage before counting; memorizing clause names does not reveal null or duplicate effects.

example.prompt: Rows in department D have scores 7,NULL,9. Compute COUNT(*), COUNT(score), AVG(score).
example.strategy: Row count → Nonnull count → Average

steps.title: Row count
steps.explanation: All three rows exist.

steps.title: Nonnull count
steps.explanation: The null score is excluded.

steps.title: Average
steps.explanation: Use the number of nonnull values as divisor.

example.answer: 3, 2 and 8 respectively.
example.verification: Dividing 16 by 3 would incorrectly treat the unknown score as a numeric zero contribution.

depth.body: SQL evaluation uses rows, nulls and three-valued predicates, so a direct translation from ordinary two-valued arithmetic can be wrong. WHERE retains TRUE only; UNKNOWN is discarded like FALSE for filtering but behaves differently under negation and constraints. Correlated subqueries bind inner comparisons to the current outer row, and ties can yield multiple maxima unless uniqueness is guaranteed. Anti-joins using NOT IN require particular care when the subquery includes NULL. These examples assume ordinary SQL semantics with no implicit ordering or duplicate removal. Enumerate the actual rows and predicate truth values before counting output. A returned set's cardinality and an aggregate's denominator depend on which operation ignores nulls, rather than one global rule that every null is zero or always disappears.

examples.prompt: T contains values 2,NULL,5. Compare WHERE value>3 with WHERE value IS NULL.
examples.strategy: Evaluate numeric predicates → Filter TRUE rows → Evaluate null testing

steps.title: Evaluate numeric predicates
steps.explanation: 2>3 is FALSE, NULL>3 is UNKNOWN, and 5>3 is TRUE.

steps.title: Filter TRUE rows
steps.explanation: The numeric filter returns only value 5.

steps.title: Evaluate null testing
steps.explanation: IS NULL directly recognizes the null row and returns it alone.

examples.answer: value>3 returns {5}; value IS NULL returns the one NULL row.
examples.verification: Neither treating NULL as zero nor writing value=NULL reproduces the direct IS NULL predicate.

examples.prompt: Scores has (A,10),(A,20),(A,20),(B,7). Return rows whose score equals a correlated subquery MAX(score) for their own department.
examples.strategy: Bind department groups → Test each outer row → Retain bag rows

steps.title: Bind department groups
steps.explanation: For A the inner maximum is 20; for B it is 7.

steps.title: Test each outer row
steps.explanation: Both separate A rows with 20 equal their department maximum; A's 10 does not.

steps.title: Retain bag rows
steps.explanation: The result includes (A,20) twice and (B,7) once without DISTINCT.

examples.answer: Three output rows: two (A,20) and one (B,7).
examples.verification: A maximum value does not select a unique row; duplicate/tied source rows remain unless the query removes them.

examples.prompt: Candidates are 1 and 3; a NOT IN subquery returns 2 and NULL. Evaluate candidate 3 and the complete WHERE result.
examples.strategy: Compare candidate three → Negate membership → Filter the candidates

steps.title: Compare candidate three
steps.explanation: 3 differs from 2, but comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN.

steps.title: Negate membership
steps.explanation: The unresolved NULL comparison makes 3 NOT IN (2,NULL) UNKNOWN.

steps.title: Filter the candidates
steps.explanation: 1 has the same issue, so neither predicate is TRUE and the result is empty.

examples.answer: Candidate 3 is not returned; the complete result is empty.
examples.verification: A correlated NOT EXISTS checking equality to candidate IDs would return both 1 and 3 because the null matches neither.

tutorials.title: Inner, outer and self joins with duplicate multiplicities
tutorials.body:
An inner join emits row pairs satisfying its condition. A left outer join additionally preserves unmatched left rows, supplying nulls for right-side attributes; right/full joins preserve other sides accordingly. A self join uses aliases to compare distinct roles drawn from one table, such as an employee and manager.
Multiplicity matters under SQL bags: two left rows and three right rows with one matching key produce six joined rows. Equality of join keys does not deduplicate records automatically. Keys and foreign keys can constrain multiplicity, but only when those constraints actually exist.
A WHERE predicate on a right-side attribute after a left join can discard null-extended rows and effectively undo outer preservation. Placing the predicate in ON filters matches while still allowing unmatched left rows. Natural joins infer conditions from all shared column names, which can accidentally constrain more than intended. In GATE cardinality questions, count matching pairs per key and add unmatched preserved rows using the chosen join’s rules.

example.prompt: L has keys [1,1,2], R has [1,1,1,3]. Count inner and left join rows on key.
example.strategy: Matching key one → Other keys → Preserve left

steps.title: Matching key one
steps.explanation: Every qualifying left/right pair is a row.

steps.title: Other keys
steps.explanation: Left key 2 has no match; right key 3 does not contribute to an inner or left join.

steps.title: Preserve left
steps.explanation: The left join adds one null-extended row for key 2.

example.answer: Inner join 6 rows; left join 7 rows.
example.verification: The repeated key values remain multiple source rows; counting distinct keys would give the wrong result.

depth.body: A join chooses pairs according to a relationship, then applies its preservation and multiplicity rules. A self join uses aliases to express two roles from the same source without conflating them. Outer joins distinguish filters on matching pairs from filters applied after null extension, so moving a predicate between ON and WHERE can remove preserved rows. Key constraints constrain how many matches exist; without those constraints equal values do not identify unique source rows. These examples assume SQL bags and equality conditions with ordinary NULL behavior. Write the matching pairs first, add unmatched rows required by the join type, then apply later filters. This makes lost preservation and duplicate multiplication visible rather than hiding them in an intuitive diagram of overlapping sets.

examples.prompt: Employee(id,name,manager) has (1,Ana,NULL),(2,Ben,1),(3,Cid,1). Self-join employee e to manager m on e.manager=m.id. List inner-join name pairs.
examples.strategy: Assign aliases → Find manager matches → Exclude unmatched role

steps.title: Assign aliases
steps.explanation: e represents the employee role and m the manager role.

steps.title: Find manager matches
steps.explanation: Ben and Cid each point to id 1, whose name is Ana.

steps.title: Exclude unmatched role
steps.explanation: Ana's NULL manager does not equal a manager id under ordinary equality.

examples.answer: Pairs (Ben,Ana) and (Cid,Ana).
examples.verification: Every output is supported by one concrete foreign-key-like reference, and the top-level manager has no matching parent role.

examples.prompt: L IDs={1,2}; R rows={(1,active),(1,inactive)}. Compare LEFT JOIN with R.status=active in ON versus in WHERE.
examples.strategy: Filter matching pairs in ON → Filter after joining in WHERE → Compare preservation

steps.title: Filter matching pairs in ON
steps.explanation: ID 1 matches only active; ID 2 has no qualifying match and is null-extended.

steps.title: Filter after joining in WHERE
steps.explanation: The ordinary left join first adds ID 2 with NULL status, but NULL=active is UNKNOWN.

steps.title: Compare preservation
steps.explanation: ON gives (1,active),(2,NULL); WHERE gives only (1,active).

examples.answer: ON preserves two rows; WHERE returns one.
examples.verification: The missing ID 2 row is explained by its post-join UNKNOWN predicate, not by absence of the left source row.

examples.prompt: A table has two rows with key value x; B has three rows with x. Neither key column is unique. Does their equality join produce one row because only one distinct value matches?
examples.strategy: Retain source multiplicities → Enumerate matching pairs → Avoid implicit deduplication

steps.title: Retain source multiplicities
steps.explanation: Two separate A rows and three separate B rows remain distinct bag inputs.

steps.title: Enumerate matching pairs
steps.explanation: Each A row pairs with every B row carrying x.

steps.title: Avoid implicit deduplication
steps.explanation: Equality join does not apply DISTINCT or invent a uniqueness constraint.

examples.answer: The join produces six rows.
examples.verification: Labeling A rows a1,a2 and B rows b1,b2,b3 yields six explicit combinations, independently checking the product.

tutorials.title: WHERE filters rows before HAVING filters groups
tutorials.body:
Grouping partitions query rows by the values of the GROUP BY attributes. Aggregates then summarize each partition, and HAVING decides which complete groups survive. WHERE instead filters individual input rows before grouping, so moving a condition between these clauses can change both group membership and aggregate values. This is the logical evaluation model; a database optimizer may choose a different physical execution plan while preserving the result.
COUNT(*) counts surviving rows, COUNT(column) counts their nonnull values, and AVG ignores null operands under ordinary SQL behavior. Group keys can remain even when some rows are removed, provided at least one row survives for that group. To evaluate a grouped query, first enumerate rows that satisfy WHERE, form groups from those rows, compute each aggregate, apply HAVING, and produce selected values. An aggregate test such as COUNT(*)>=2 cannot ordinarily be used as a row predicate in WHERE. Join multiplication must be included before this procedure if the input came from a join.

example.prompt: Scores(dept,score) has (A,90),(A,70),(A,NULL),(B,85),(B,95),(C,60). Evaluate SELECT dept,COUNT(*),AVG(score) FROM Scores WHERE score>=70 GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>=2.
example.strategy: Filter individual rows → Form and summarize groups → Filter completed groups

steps.title: Filter individual rows
steps.explanation: A's NULL comparison is UNKNOWN and C's 60 fails. Surviving rows are A:90,70 and B:85,95.

steps.title: Form and summarize groups
steps.explanation: COUNT(*) and AVG are calculated from each department's surviving rows.

steps.title: Filter completed groups
steps.explanation: Both counts equal 2, so both groups pass HAVING. SELECT emits (A,2,80) and (B,2,90), with no guaranteed output order.

example.answer: Two result rows: A with count 2 and average 80; B with count 2 and average 90.
example.verification: The input has six rows but WHERE leaves four. Without WHERE, A would count three rows while its average still ignores NULL; the count difference demonstrates the stage ordering.

depth.body: A group is defined by equality of grouping keys among rows that survive earlier query stages. Aggregates summarize that actual input, including multiplicity introduced by joins. COUNT(*) counts group rows, COUNT(expression) counts nonnull expression results, and HAVING can reject a group after these values exist. Grouping multiple columns uses their combination, not an independent aggregation for each column. The examples assume ordinary SQL grouping and explicitly stated source rows, with no automatic DISTINCT. Make a group-to-row map before calculating, then test each group's aggregate predicate. This also exposes a common counting error after an outer join: one null-extended row represents zero matched children but still contributes one to COUNT(*).

examples.prompt: Sales(region,product,amount) has (N,A,2),(N,A,3),(N,B,4),(S,A,5). Group by region,product and sum amount.
examples.strategy: Build composite groups → Aggregate their rows → Emit summaries

steps.title: Build composite groups
steps.explanation: The distinct key pairs are (N,A),(N,B),(S,A).

steps.title: Aggregate their rows
steps.explanation: (N,A) contains 2 and 3; the other groups contain one value each.

steps.title: Emit summaries
steps.explanation: Results are (N,A,5),(N,B,4),(S,A,5).

examples.answer: Three groups with sums 5,4,5 respectively.
examples.verification: All group sums total 14, equal to 2+3+4+5 across the source.

examples.prompt: Customer IDs 1 and 2 LEFT JOIN Order on customer ID. Only customer 1 has orders IDs 10 and 11. Group by customer and compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(Order.id).
examples.strategy: Write joined groups → Count all rows → Count actual child identifiers

steps.title: Write joined groups
steps.explanation: Customer 1 has two matched rows; customer 2 has one null-extended row.

steps.title: Count all rows
steps.explanation: COUNT(*) gives 2 for customer 1 and 1 for customer 2.

steps.title: Count actual child identifiers
steps.explanation: COUNT(Order.id) ignores the null and gives 2 and 0.

examples.answer: Customer 1: (2,2); customer 2: (1,0) for the two counts.
examples.verification: Only two real orders exist, and child-identifier counts sum to two; COUNT(*) includes preservation metadata.

examples.prompt: Rows are (A,4),(A,6),(B,7). A student uses WHERE SUM(value)>8 before GROUP BY key. Correct the query and evaluate it.
examples.strategy: Identify the unavailable value → Move the group predicate → Evaluate formed groups

steps.title: Identify the unavailable value
steps.explanation: A row-level WHERE stage has no completed group sum.

steps.title: Move the group predicate
steps.explanation: Use GROUP BY key HAVING SUM(value)>8.

steps.title: Evaluate formed groups
steps.explanation: A sums to 10 and passes; B sums to 7 and fails.

examples.answer: The corrected grouped query returns A with sum 10.
examples.verification: Testing individual values>8 would return no rows and demonstrates that row filtering cannot replace aggregate filtering.

lessons.title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
lessons.intuition: Normalization controls redundancy caused by dependencies. A dependency is a rule about every valid database state, not a coincidence in one sample table. Begin by computing keys; normal-form tests depend on superkeys and prime attributes.

sections.title: Closure and inference
sections.body: \(X\to Y\) says equal values on X force equal values on Y. Attribute closure X⁺ starts with X and repeatedly adds RHS attributes whose LHS is already present. If X⁺ contains the whole schema, X is a superkey; remove redundant attributes to test minimality. Armstrong’s reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity support sound dependency inference.

sections.title: 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
sections.body: After atomic-value 1NF, 2NF rules out dependence of a nonprime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key. In 3NF, every nontrivial X→A has X a superkey or A prime, meaning in some candidate key. BCNF drops the prime-attribute exception and requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. BCNF implies 3NF, but not conversely.

sections.title: Decomposition
sections.body: Lossless join means decomposed relations reconstruct exactly the original valid relation, with no spurious tuples. For a binary decomposition into R1,R2, their intersection determining all of R1 or all of R2 under F⁺ is the usual lossless criterion. Dependency preservation permits checking original dependencies without joining. These are separate properties; a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation.

sections.title: Closure, decomposition and independent guarantees
sections.body: Attribute closure is an inference procedure: start with X, apply any FD whose entire left side is present, add its right side, and repeat to a fixed point. A key needs closure equal to all relation attributes and minimality under attribute removal. BCNF restricts every nontrivial determinant to a superkey; 3NF additionally permits a prime right-hand attribute. Lossless decomposition means every legal original relation is exactly reconstructed by joining its projections. It does not merely mean that tables share a column. Dependency preservation means constraints can be enforced within component relations without joining them. Projection includes all implied dependencies on each component, not just original FDs with visibly matching columns. A decomposition can satisfy one guarantee and fail the other, so state separate proofs.

examples.prompt: Normalize R(A,B,C) with \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\)

steps.title: Find a minimal key
steps.explanation: A determines B, then B determines C. No dependency can introduce A, so every key must contain A; A alone is the sole candidate key.

steps.title: Test the violating dependency
steps.explanation: B is not a superkey, and C is nonprime because the only candidate key is A. The nontrivial \(B\to C\) fails both BCNF and 3NF.

steps.title: Decompose and prove losslessness
steps.explanation: The shared attribute determines all of R₂, satisfying the binary lossless-join criterion. A mere shared attribute would not be sufficient.
steps.equation: R_1=AB,\quad R_2=BC,\quad R_1\cap R_2=\{B\},\quad B\to BC

steps.title: Verify preservation and resulting normal forms
steps.explanation: Each original dependency can be checked locally. A and B respectively are keys of their new relations, so both relations are in BCNF.
steps.equation: A\to B\text{ in }AB,\qquad B\to C\text{ in }BC

examples.given: R(A,B,C), with FDs \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\) and their logical consequences.
examples.goal: Find a key, violations and a lossless dependency-preserving decomposition.
examples.strategy: Compute closures before testing normal forms; verify decomposition properties independently.
examples.answer: AB and BC form a lossless, dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition.
examples.verification: Join projections of any relation satisfying the FDs: a B value can have only one C, preventing spurious alternative C values for an A.

examples.prompt: Compute closure with \(A\to B\), \(BC\to D\) and \(A\to C\)
steps: Add B and C from the two A dependencies.
Now BC is present, so add D. \(A^+=\{A,B,C,D\}\).

pitfalls: Sample rows do not prove a dependency holds universally.
Lossless and dependency-preserving are different tests.
revision: BCNF: every nontrivial determinant is a superkey.

A functional dependency \(X\to Y\) states that every pair of legal relation tuples agreeing on X also agrees on Y. It is a schema constraint, not an assertion that X values are unique unless Y includes all attributes. Dependencies can be inferred using reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity, and their consequences matter even if not listed explicitly.
Closure X⁺ starts with X and repeatedly adds an FD’s right side when its entire left side is already included. Stop at a fixed point. X is a superkey when closure includes the full schema, and a candidate key when no proper subset is a superkey. A multiattribute determinant requires all its members before applying its FD.
Dependencies inferred from one sample can fail in another legal state; given constraints govern the analysis. To compare FD sets, test whether each given dependency follows from the other set using closures. Minimal covers reduce redundant attributes/dependencies while preserving implication. Normalization and decomposition proofs require full inferred behavior, not simply checking visually present arrows. First normal form uses the relation model’s atomic attribute values. Second normal form prevents a nonprime attribute from depending on a proper subset of a candidate key. This requires finding all candidate keys; a single-attribute key has no nonempty proper subset, but another composite key still matters. Prime means belonging to some candidate key.
Third normal form permits every nontrivial X→A only when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF removes the prime-right-side exception and requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. These are definitions over all implied dependencies. A dependency chain causing a nonprime value to depend on a nonkey determinant is a common 3NF violation, but apply the precise rule rather than a slogan about “transitivity.”
Normalization separates repeated facts to avoid update, insert and delete anomalies. Decomposition still needs independent checks for lossless join and dependency preservation. A BCNF decomposition can lose preservation even when lossless, while 3NF synthesis can preserve dependencies under its algorithm. Do not rank a proposed schema solely by whether it has a chosen primary key. A decomposition projects one relation into component schemas. Lossless join means joining those projections reconstructs exactly every original relation satisfying the dependencies, with no spurious extra tuples. For a binary split, the intersection must functionally determine all attributes of at least one component. A shared column alone is insufficient.
Dependency preservation means the original constraints can be enforced using the projected dependencies within components, without joining them. Projections include dependencies implied by the original FD set, not just originally printed arrows that happen to fit. A decomposition can be lossless but not preserving, or fail losslessness despite looking more normalized.
When testing, write each component’s attributes, their intersection and the closures proving the binary criterion. Then compute the union of locally enforceable dependencies and test whether it implies every original FD. A join dependency question differs from asking whether a particular sample happens to rejoin correctly; properties must hold for every legal state. Additional new topic labels here point to explicit proofs rather than only a final split recommendation. A functional dependency \(X\to Y\) requires any two legal tuples agreeing on every attribute of X to agree on every attribute of Y. It does not require X values to be unique unless X determines the complete schema. To refute the dependency in a specific instance, find just one agreeing-left-side, disagreeing-right-side pair. Tuples with different X values impose no restriction on one another through that dependency.
A sample instance can violate a proposed dependency, but passing a sample test does not establish that the schema guarantees it in every future legal instance. The given dependency set is the source of such guarantees. Determinants can be composite: testing A\(B\to C\) requires agreement on both A and B, rather than A alone. Distinguish the tuple-level test from attribute closure, which derives what a supplied set of schema dependencies implies. Naming the determinant and searching within its equal-value groups makes a violation concrete instead of relying on accidental uniqueness or visually appealing arrows. Second normal form requires first normal form and prohibits a nonprime attribute from depending on a proper subset of a candidate key. A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key. Find all candidate keys before applying the rule: selecting a convenient primary key does not remove other candidate keys from the definition.
A partial dependency often appears when a relationship table stores a fact about only one of its participants. For example, a course enrollment may be identified by student and course while a student name depends only on the student. Repeating the name per enrollment creates update anomalies. To analyze a schema, compute candidate-key closures, determine which attributes are nonprime, and examine dependencies from proper subsets of each composite key. A single-attribute key has no nonempty proper subset, but that shortcut cannot be used when another composite candidate key exists. Separating the dependent fact can remove repetition, with losslessness and dependency enforcement still requiring their own checks. A proof for a supplied dependency cover must also respect what it implies, and showing that every attribute is prime immediately settles the right-side alternative for any implied dependency here. A violating dependency \(X\to Y\) suggests a decomposition that separates the attributes governed by X, but the properties of the resulting relations must be proved rather than assumed.
For a binary decomposition, a common sufficient and necessary FD criterion for losslessness is that the shared attributes determine one complete component under the original dependency set. For a binary decomposition into R1,R2, their intersection determining all of R1 or all of R2 under F⁺ is the usual lossless criterion. Dependency preservation permits checking original dependencies without joining. These are separate properties; a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation. Attribute closure is an inference procedure: start with X, apply any FD whose entire left side is present, add its right side, and repeat to a fixed point. A key needs closure equal to all relation attributes and minimality under attribute removal. BCNF restricts every nontrivial determinant to a superkey; 3NF additionally permits a prime right-hand attribute. Lossless decomposition means every legal original relation is exactly reconstructed by joining its projections. It does not merely mean that tables share a column. Dependency preservation means constraints can be enforced within component relations without joining them. Projection includes all implied dependencies on each component, not just original FDs with visibly matching columns. Begin with the attributes already known, and add a right side only when every attribute in its left side is known. example.prompt: R(A,B,C,D), FDs \(A\to B\),\(A\to C\),\(BC\to D\). Find A⁺.
example.strategy: Start → Use A dependencies → Use joint determinant

steps.title: Start
steps.explanation: Every attribute set determines itself.

steps.title: Use A dependencies
steps.explanation: Both right sides become available.

steps.title: Use joint determinant
steps.explanation: B and C are now both present.

example.answer: A is a superkey and, as a singleton, a candidate key assuming the empty set is not a key.
example.verification: Starting from B alone cannot use \(BC\to D\) until C is also known.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C,D,E), F={\(A\to B\),\(B\to C\),D→E}. Compute (AD)+.
examples.strategy: Initialize known attributes → Apply immediately usable rules → Continue to a fixed point

steps.title: Initialize known attributes
steps.explanation: The starting determinant knows both supplied attributes.

steps.title: Apply immediately usable rules
steps.explanation: A adds B and D adds E, giving A,B,D,E.

steps.title: Continue to a fixed point
steps.explanation: B then adds C; all attributes are known and no further expansion is needed.

examples.verification: The result contains every schema attribute, so AD is a superkey; removing D loses E and removing A loses B,C.

examples.prompt: F={\(A\to B\),\(B\to C\),\(A\to C\)}. Is \(A\to C\) redundant? Compute closure after removing it.
examples.strategy: Remove only the proposed arrow → Run the reduced closure → Compare the implication

steps.title: Remove only the proposed arrow
steps.explanation: Use Fprime={\(A\to B\),\(B\to C\)}.

steps.title: Run the reduced closure
steps.explanation: Start A, add B via \(A\to B\), then C via \(B\to C\).

steps.title: Compare the implication
steps.explanation: C remains in A closure, so the removed dependency is implied by the remainder.

examples.answer: \(A\to C\) is redundant.
examples.verification: The retained dependencies are a subset of F and derive the removed arrow, establishing equivalence of the two FD sets.

examples.prompt: F contains A\(B\to C\) only. A student starts with A and immediately adds C because A occurs in the determinant. Correct A+.
examples.strategy: Initialize the exact set → Test the whole left side → Stop without additions

steps.title: Initialize the exact set
steps.explanation: B is not initially known.

steps.title: Test the whole left side
steps.explanation: AB is not contained in {A}, so A\(B\to C\) cannot fire.

steps.title: Stop without additions
steps.explanation: No dependency applies; the fixed point remains {A}.

examples.answer: A+={A}; C cannot be inferred.
examples.verification: Starting with AB would permit C, highlighting why partial determinant matching is invalid.

example.prompt: R(A,B,C) has \(A\to B\),\(B\to C\). Determine its highest normal form under ordinary atomic attributes.
example.strategy: Keys → 2NF → 3NF and BCNF

steps.title: Keys
steps.explanation: A⁺ is ABC and no FD derives A; A is the sole candidate key.

steps.title: 2NF
steps.explanation: The singleton key has no nonempty proper part, so no partial nonprime dependency violates 2NF.

steps.title: 3NF and BCNF
steps.explanation: B is not a superkey and C is nonprime; \(B\to C\) violates both.

example.answer: The relation is in 2NF but not 3NF or BCNF.
example.verification: Checking only \(A\to B\) would miss the nonkey determinant B and incorrectly report a stronger normal form.

State atomicity first, find all candidate keys, mark prime attributes, and then examine partial dependencies and nonkey determinants.
