examples.prompt: Atomic R(A,B,C) has only \(A\to B\)C. Determine its highest form among 1NF,2NF,3NF,BCNF.
examples.strategy: Find the key → Inspect nontrivial determinants → Apply BCNF

steps.title: Find the key
steps.explanation: A is the only candidate key because no dependency derives A.

steps.title: Inspect nontrivial determinants
steps.explanation: Any determining set for B or C through the supplied dependency includes A.

steps.title: Apply BCNF
steps.explanation: Every nontrivial determinant is therefore a superkey, satisfying the strongest listed form.

examples.answer: R is in BCNF.
examples.verification: There is no nonkey determinant supplying a nontrivial dependency, so weaker forms cannot be the limiting condition.

examples.prompt: Atomic R(A,B,C,D) has A\(B\to C\) and C→D only. Determine candidate key and highest listed form.
examples.strategy: Find the necessary key → Check partial dependencies → Find the stronger violation

steps.title: Find the necessary key
steps.explanation: A and B cannot be derived, while AB reaches C then D; the sole candidate key is AB.

steps.title: Check partial dependencies
steps.explanation: Neither A nor B alone determines a nonprime attribute, so 2NF holds.

steps.title: Find the stronger violation
steps.explanation: C→D has a non-superkey determinant and nonprime D, violating 3NF and BCNF.

examples.answer: Key AB; highest form 2NF.
examples.verification: C closure is CD, missing A and B, and D appears in no candidate key, supplying both parts of the 3NF violation.

examples.prompt: Person(id,phones) has unique id, but phones is explicitly a set of independently queried phone values within one cell under a model requiring atomic scalar fields. Does uniqueness make it BCNF?
examples.strategy: Check the prerequisite → Separate key strength → Stop the classification

steps.title: Check the prerequisite
steps.explanation: The declared collection-valued cell violates the stipulated atomic-field requirement.

steps.title: Separate key strength
steps.explanation: A unique identifier does not transform the collection into a scalar domain value.

steps.title: Stop the classification
steps.explanation: The relation is not 1NF under this model, so cannot satisfy higher forms that require it.

examples.answer: It fails 1NF despite having a unique identifier.
examples.verification: Separating Phone(person_id,phone) into individual tuples addresses this representation issue; changing id alone does not.

tutorials.title: Losslessness and dependency preservation are separate proofs
tutorials.body:

Lossless join means joining those projections reconstructs exactly every original relation satisfying the dependencies, with no spurious extra tuples. Projections include dependencies implied by the original FD set, not just originally printed arrows that happen to fit. A decomposition can be lossless but not preserving, or fail losslessness despite looking more normalized.
When testing, write each component’s attributes, their intersection and the closures proving the binary criterion. Then compute the union of locally enforceable dependencies and test whether it implies every original FD. A join dependency question differs from asking whether a particular sample happens to rejoin correctly; properties must hold for every legal state. Additional new topic labels here point to explicit proofs rather than only a final split recommendation.

example.prompt: Split R(A,B,C) with \(A\to B\),\(B\to C\) into AB and BC.
example.strategy: Intersection → Losslessness → Preservation

steps.title: Intersection
steps.explanation: This is the shared attribute set.

steps.title: Losslessness
steps.explanation: The intersection determines the whole second relation.

steps.title: Preservation
steps.explanation: \(A\to B\) is local to AB and \(B\to C\) local to BC; both can be checked without a join.

example.answer: The decomposition is lossless and dependency-preserving.
example.verification: The proofs establish two distinct properties; success on one did not automatically establish the other.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has B→A. Split into AB and BC. Prove or refute losslessness.
examples.strategy: Identify the shared attributes → Compute the implication → Use the binary criterion

steps.title: Identify the shared attributes
steps.explanation: B is the natural-join agreement column.

steps.title: Compute the implication
steps.explanation: B→A plus reflexivity gives B→AB.

steps.title: Use the binary criterion
steps.explanation: The intersection determines the whole AB component, so the split is lossless.

examples.answer: The decomposition is lossless.
examples.verification: For each B the AB projection supplies only its permitted A value, preventing spurious A/C cross-combinations.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C,D) has \(A\to B\) and C→D. Split into AB and ACD, then split ACD into AC and CD. Check the final decomposition.
examples.strategy: Prove the first split → Prove the second split → Compose the reconstruction

steps.title: Prove the first split
steps.explanation: Intersection A determines AB through \(A\to B\).

steps.title: Prove the second split
steps.explanation: Intersection C determines CD through C→D.

steps.title: Compose the reconstruction
steps.explanation: Both binary operations are lossless, so joining AB,AC,CD reconstructs every legal original instance.

examples.answer: AB,AC,CD is a lossless decomposition.
examples.verification: AC retains the association between A and C; dropping that component would lose the cross-entity pairing information.

examples.prompt: With no nontrivial FDs, original R(A,B,C) contains (1,x,p),(2,x,q). Split into AB and BC and rejoin.
examples.strategy: Project the original → Join on the shared B → Identify spurious tuples

steps.title: Join on the shared B
steps.explanation: Both A values combine with both C values, producing four tuples.

steps.title: Identify spurious tuples
steps.explanation: (1,x,q) and (2,x,p) were absent from the original; shared B determines neither side.

examples.answer: The split is lossy, adding two spurious tuples.
examples.verification: The reconstructed cardinality four exceeds original cardinality two, and the two new tuples explicitly witness the failure.

Compute the dependencies projected onto each component, take their union, and test original arrows by closure under that union. A dependency need not appear verbatim inside one component to be preserved; a chain of local implications can enforce it indirectly. Conversely, a lossless join does not guarantee that separate component checks detect every cross-component violation. The examples assume complete projected FD reasoning, not merely selecting visually printed arrows. Build a small legal set of component instances to refute preservation when closure fails. That counterexample makes the enforcement cost concrete: detecting the missing constraint requires combining facts from more than one component.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has \(A\to B\),\(B\to C\). Split into AB and BC. Check preservation of both dependencies.
examples.strategy: Project onto AB → Project onto BC → Combine enforcement

steps.title: Project onto AB
steps.explanation: \(A\to B\) can be checked using only AB tuples.

steps.title: Project onto BC
steps.explanation: \(B\to C\) can be checked using only BC tuples.

steps.title: Combine enforcement
steps.explanation: The union contains both original arrows and therefore their implied \(A\to C\).

examples.answer: The split preserves the original dependency set.
examples.verification: Closure of A under the local union is ABC, independently verifying the implied chain.

examples.prompt: F={\(A\to B\),\(B\to C\),\(A\to C\)}. Components AB and BC do not contain AC. Is the explicitly listed \(A\to C\) nevertheless preserved?
examples.strategy: Collect local rules → Compute the relevant closure → Check the original arrow

steps.title: Collect local rules
steps.explanation: AB enforces \(A\to B\) and BC enforces \(B\to C\).

steps.title: Compute the relevant closure
steps.explanation: Starting from A, add B then C under those local rules.

steps.title: Check the original arrow
steps.explanation: C is in A closure, so \(A\to C\) follows even without a component containing both attributes.

examples.answer: Yes; preservation can be indirect through local dependency inference.
examples.verification: Transitivity gives \(A\to C\), so the missing AC schema is not evidence of failed preservation.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\). Split into AB and AC. Is \(B\to C\) preserved merely because the split is lossless?
examples.strategy: Establish the distinct property → Collect projected constraints → Construct a violation

steps.title: Establish the distinct property
steps.explanation: A determines AB, so the shared-A binary split is lossless.

steps.title: Collect projected constraints
steps.explanation: AB has \(A\to B\); AC has implied \(A\to C\). Starting from B adds nothing.

steps.title: Construct a violation
steps.explanation: AB={(1,b),(2,b)} and AC={(1,c1),(2,c2)} satisfy locals but their join gives one B with different C values.

examples.answer: The split is lossless but does not preserve \(B\to C\).
examples.verification: The explicit component instances pass every stated local rule and yield a concrete \(B\to C\) violation after joining.

Tuples with different X values impose no restriction on one another through that dependency.
A sample instance can violate a proposed dependency, but passing a sample test does not establish that the schema guarantees it in every future legal instance. The given dependency set is the source of such guarantees. Determinants can be composite: testing A\(B\to C\) requires agreement on both A and B, rather than A alone. Distinguish the tuple-level test from attribute closure, which derives what a supplied set of schema dependencies implies. Naming the determinant and searching within its equal-value groups makes a violation concrete instead of relying on accidental uniqueness or visually appealing arrows.

example.prompt: R(A,B,C) has (1,x,7),(1,x,8),(1,y,7),(2,z,9). Test \(A\to B\) and A\(B\to C\) on this instance.
example.strategy: Test A determinant → Test joint determinant → Interpret the evidence

steps.title: Test A determinant
steps.explanation: Tuples (1,x,7) and (1,y,7) agree on A=1 but disagree on B. They refute \(A\to B\).

steps.title: Test joint determinant
steps.explanation: Tuples (1,x,7) and (1,x,8) agree on both A and B but disagree on C. They refute A\(B\to C\).

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Both violations are pairwise witnesses. Rows with A=2 do not repair either violation; adding more rows cannot make these existing disagreements disappear.

example.answer: This instance violates both \(A\to B\) and A\(B\to C\).
example.verification: Deleting one offending row can repair a particular witness, but all remaining equal-determinant pairs must still be checked. A legal-state guarantee cannot be inferred from one repaired sample alone.

depth.body: A functional dependency expresses agreement propagation between tuples. It is directional: knowing a department identifies its manager does not imply a manager identifies just one department. Inference rules allow new dependencies without inspecting data, but each derivation must preserve the complete determinant requirement. For an instance test, group by the determinant and search for disagreeing dependent values; one such pair refutes the dependency. Passing an instance test cannot establish a universal schema rule. The examples assume classical dependencies without special SQL null complications. Contrast a tuple counterexample, a formal inference and a proposed reversal, because these are different proof tasks. Direction and joint determinants matter more than whether attribute labels sound like plausible business identifiers.

examples.prompt: DepartmentManager(D,M) contains (10,Ana),(20,Ben),(10,Cid). Test D→M.
examples.strategy: Group equal determinants → Compare dependent values → Use the witness

steps.title: Group equal determinants
steps.explanation: Department 10 occurs with both Ana and Cid.

steps.title: Compare dependent values
steps.explanation: Those two tuples agree on D but disagree on M.

steps.title: Use the witness
steps.explanation: That pair violates the required agreement implication.

examples.answer: The instance violates D→M.
examples.verification: Department 20's single row cannot repair the violating department-10 pair.

examples.prompt: Given \(X\to Y\) and YZ→W, derive XZ→W using dependency inference.
examples.strategy: Augment the first dependency → Use the joint determinant → Apply transitivity

steps.title: Augment the first dependency
steps.explanation: Add Z to both sides of \(X\to Y\).

steps.title: Use the joint determinant
steps.explanation: The second dependency requires both Y and Z, now supplied by XZ.

steps.title: Apply transitivity
steps.explanation: Combining XZ→YZ and YZ→W proves the result.

examples.answer: XZ→W follows from the given dependencies.
examples.verification: Closure of XZ contains X,Z, then Y, then W, independently confirming the inference.

examples.prompt: R(A,B)={(1,x),(2,x)} satisfies \(A\to B\). Must B→A also hold?
examples.strategy: Test the forward rule → Test the proposed reverse → Reject reversal

steps.title: Test the forward rule
steps.explanation: No two distinct rows share A, so the instance satisfies \(A\to B\).

steps.title: Test the proposed reverse
steps.explanation: Both rows share B=x but have different A values.

steps.title: Reject reversal
steps.explanation: The equal-B pair violates B→A.

examples.answer: No; dependencies cannot generally be reversed.
examples.verification: A many-to-one mapping is functional in one direction while this explicit pair disproves inverse functionality.

tutorials.title: 2NF removes partial dependencies on a composite key
tutorials.body:
Second normal form requires first normal form and prohibits a nonprime attribute from depending on a proper subset of a candidate key. A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key. Find all candidate keys before applying the rule: selecting a convenient primary key does not remove other candidate keys from the definition.
A partial dependency often appears when a relationship table stores a fact about only one of its participants. For example, a course enrollment may be identified by student and course while a student name depends only on the student. Repeating the name per enrollment creates update anomalies. To analyze a schema, compute candidate-key closures, determine which attributes are nonprime, and examine dependencies from proper subsets of each composite key. A single-attribute key has no nonempty proper subset, but that shortcut cannot be used when another composite candidate key exists. Separating the dependent fact can remove repetition, with losslessness and dependency enforcement still requiring their own checks.

example.prompt: Enrollment(S,C,N,G) has SC→G and S→N, with no other nontrivial dependencies and atomic values. Find its key, show the 2NF violation, and split the repeated student-name fact.
example.strategy: Find the candidate key → Identify the partial dependency → Separate the fact

steps.title: Find the candidate key
steps.explanation: S and C never appear on a dependency's right side, so every key must contain both. SC determines all attributes and is minimal.

steps.title: Identify the partial dependency
steps.explanation: N is nonprime and depends on a proper subset of the sole candidate key. The original relation fails 2NF.

steps.title: Separate the fact
steps.explanation: Use Student(S,N) and EnrollmentGrade(S,C,G). Their intersection S determines the whole Student component, proving this binary split is lossless.

example.answer: SC is the sole candidate key; S→N violates 2NF. The proposed split removes that partial dependency and is lossless.
example.verification: The retained dependencies S→N and SC→G can each be enforced locally, so this example also preserves its given dependencies. Two courses for one student no longer require duplicate name facts.

depth.body: Second normal form focuses on nonprime facts depending on only part of a candidate key. It does not prohibit every dependency from a key subset, because a dependent prime attribute is outside its forbidden case. Alternate composite keys remain relevant even when a single-column key was chosen as primary. Find all keys and mark prime status before testing proper subsets; otherwise a convenient primary-key shortcut can produce a false classification. The examples assume 1NF and the exact listed dependencies. A violation identifies a repeated fact whose determinant can become a separate relation, but that split still needs losslessness and preservation proofs. Use a concrete attribute membership argument rather than the informal claim that a table with any singleton key is automatically safe.

examples.prompt: Stock(W,P,City,Qty) has W\(P\to Q\)ty and W→City. W and P are underivable. Test 2NF.
examples.strategy: Find the sole candidate key → Mark the dependent fact → Apply the 2NF rule

steps.title: Find the sole candidate key
steps.explanation: WP determines every attribute and both W and P are necessary.

steps.title: Mark the dependent fact
steps.explanation: City is nonprime; W is a proper subset of WP.

steps.title: Apply the 2NF rule
steps.explanation: W→City is a partial dependency of a nonprime attribute on the key.

examples.answer: Stock violates 2NF.
examples.verification: Two products in one warehouse repeat the same City fact, providing the associated update-anomaly intuition.

examples.prompt: Atomic R(A,B,C,D) has \(A\to B\)C,BC→A,B→D. A is primary key. Determine whether the singleton-primary-key shortcut establishes 2NF.
examples.strategy: Find alternate candidates → Classify D → Test the composite key

steps.title: Find alternate candidates
steps.explanation: A closure is ABCD; BC also derives A then D, so A and BC are candidate keys.

steps.title: Classify D
steps.explanation: D belongs to neither key and is nonprime.

steps.title: Test the composite key
steps.explanation: B is a proper subset of BC and B→D, so 2NF fails despite the selected singleton primary key.

examples.answer: The relation is not 2NF; all candidate keys must be considered.
examples.verification: B closure is BD, so B is not itself a key; its dependency on nonprime D is genuinely partial.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has \(A\to B\) and B→A. Candidate keys are AC and BC. Does \(A\to B\) violate 2NF because A is a proper part of AC?
examples.strategy: Mark prime attributes → Inspect the right side → Apply the definition

steps.title: Mark prime attributes
steps.explanation: A,B,C each belong to AC or BC.

steps.title: Inspect the right side
steps.explanation: B is prime, so it is not a forbidden nonprime dependent attribute.

steps.title: Apply the definition
steps.explanation: There is no nonprime attribute and therefore no 2NF partial-dependency violation.

examples.answer: The relation satisfies 2NF; this dependency does not violate it.
examples.verification: A is not a superkey, which may matter for BCNF, but 2NF uses a different right-side condition.

tutorials.title: 3NF can allow a nonkey determinant when the result is prime
tutorials.body:
Third normal form tests each nontrivial dependency X→A using two alternatives: X must be a superkey, or A must be prime. Prime means part of some candidate key, not simply part of the selected primary key. BCNF permits only the first alternative, so a schema can satisfy 3NF while failing BCNF.
To use the exception correctly, first derive every candidate key from the supplied dependencies. Then calculate the determinant's closure rather than assuming every left side is a key. If a non-superkey determinant has a prime right-side attribute, that dependency is permitted by 3NF. If the right side is nonprime, it violates 3NF. Dependencies with multiple right-side attributes can be separated for the test. The prime exception is a precise rule; slogans about removing all transitive dependencies can misclassify examples. A proof for a supplied dependency cover must also respect what it implies, and showing that every attribute is prime immediately settles the right-side alternative for any implied dependency here.

example.prompt: R(A,B,C) has A\(B\to C\) and C→B, with no other given dependencies. Determine its candidate keys and whether it is in 3NF and BCNF.
example.strategy: Compute candidate keys → Apply 3NF → Apply BCNF

steps.title: Compute candidate keys
steps.explanation: A must occur in every key because nothing derives it. A alone does not suffice; combining A with B or C does. Thus AB and AC are the minimal keys.

steps.title: Apply 3NF
steps.explanation: A, B and C are all prime because each belongs to AB or AC. Therefore every nontrivial dependency has a prime right-side attribute, satisfying 3NF.

steps.title: Apply BCNF
steps.explanation: C→B is nontrivial but C is not a superkey, so it violates BCNF despite being allowed by 3NF.

example.answer: Candidate keys AB and AC; the relation is in 3NF and fails BCNF.
example.verification: C cannot determine A, so calling C a key would be incorrect. B is prime through candidate key AB even if AC were chosen as the primary key.

depth.body: Third normal form balances dependency enforcement with removing nonkey dependencies of nonprime facts. Test each nontrivial single-attribute right side: a superkey determinant is acceptable, and a prime dependent attribute is also acceptable. The latter exception must use all candidate keys, even if the schema includes other nonprime attributes. A synthesis-style decomposition groups dependencies into relations and must include a key-containing component for the usual lossless construction. These examples assume atomic attributes and complete reasoning from the supplied dependencies. Distinguish classification from constructing a replacement schema: proving a violation does not select a unique decomposition. Show the determinant closure and prime membership explicitly, since a dependency chain alone is not a substitute for the formal rule.

examples.prompt: Employee(E,D,City) has E→D and D→City. E is the only key. Test 3NF.
examples.strategy: Classify the determinant → Classify the dependent → Apply both alternatives

steps.title: Classify the determinant
steps.explanation: D closure is D,City, not the complete schema, so D is not a superkey.

steps.title: Classify the dependent
steps.explanation: City is absent from the sole key E and is nonprime.

steps.title: Apply both alternatives
steps.explanation: D→City satisfies neither a superkey determinant nor a prime right side.

examples.answer: The relation fails 3NF.
examples.verification: Employee identifier E determining everything does not repair the separate nonkey dependency D→City.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C,D) has \(A\to B\)C and C→D. Construct a dependency-preserving 3NF split and check losslessness.
examples.strategy: Group dependency facts → Check component keys → Check the split

steps.title: Group dependency facts
steps.explanation: Use R1(A,B,C) for \(A\to B\)C and R2(C,D) for C→D.

steps.title: Check component keys
steps.explanation: A is a key in R1; C is a key in R2, so both components satisfy BCNF and hence 3NF.

steps.title: Check the split
steps.explanation: Intersection C determines all of R2, proving losslessness; each original dependency is locally enforceable.

examples.answer: ABC and CD form a lossless dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition.
examples.verification: A full key A is contained in ABC, and the explicit binary intersection test independently supplies the recombination proof.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C,D) has \(A\to B\),B→A,AC→D. Candidate keys AC and BC. Does nonkey \(A\to B\) necessarily violate 3NF when D is nonprime?
examples.strategy: Classify attributes → Inspect the relevant dependency → Check remaining rules

steps.title: Classify attributes
steps.explanation: A,B,C are prime; D is nonprime.

steps.title: Inspect the relevant dependency
steps.explanation: \(A\to B\) has prime B on its right side, so the 3NF exception applies.

steps.title: Check remaining rules
steps.explanation: B→A also has a prime right side; AC→D has a key determinant. All given dependencies meet 3NF.

examples.answer: R is 3NF despite nonkey \(A\to B\); it fails BCNF.
examples.verification: D's nonprime status concerns dependencies producing D, where AC is a key. It does not cancel B's prime status.

tutorials.title: A BCNF split can be lossless without preserving a dependency
tutorials.body:
Boyce–Codd normal form requires the determinant of every nontrivial functional dependency to be a superkey. Unlike 3NF, it has no exception for a prime right-side attribute. A violating dependency \(X\to Y\) suggests a decomposition that separates the attributes governed by X, but the properties of the resulting relations must be proved rather than assumed.
For a binary decomposition, a common sufficient and necessary FD criterion for losslessness is that the shared attributes determine one complete component under the original dependency set. Dependency preservation is a different question: take the dependencies enforceable within individual components and test whether their union still implies every original dependency. A lossless BCNF decomposition may require a join to enforce a former cross-component constraint. Find local candidate keys and local violations to establish the normal form of each component, then use closures to examine preservation. Avoid treating a correct recombination property as proof that all business constraints remain locally enforceable.

example.prompt: R(A,B,C) has A\(B\to C\) and C→B. Decompose the BCNF violation C→B into CB and AC. Determine normal form, losslessness and preservation of A\(B\to C\).
example.strategy: Check components → Prove losslessness → Test preservation

steps.title: Check components
steps.explanation: In CB, C determines both attributes and is a key. AC has no projected nontrivial dependency, so neither component has a nonkey nontrivial determinant; both satisfy BCNF.

steps.title: Prove losslessness
steps.explanation: The common C determines the whole first component, satisfying the binary lossless criterion.

steps.title: Test preservation
steps.explanation: The only nontrivial locally enforceable dependency is C→B. It cannot derive C from AB, so A\(B\to C\) is not preserved.

example.answer: CB and AC are BCNF and form a lossless split, but the original dependency A\(B\to C\) is not preserved.
example.verification: AC can contain (a,c1),(a,c2) and CB can contain (c1,b),(c2,b), satisfying local constraints. Their join contains the same AB with two C values, a concrete preservation failure.

depth.body: BCNF asks whether a determining set is a superkey, without a prime-attribute exception. A decomposition using a violating dependency isolates its repeated fact, but the resulting pieces can trade local enforcement for stronger normal form. Compute projected dependencies rather than merely copying arrows that fit syntactically, and examine each component's own keys. A binary split is lossless when the intersection determines one whole component under the original dependencies. These examples assume standard FD-based normalization and atomic attributes. A relation with several candidate keys is not automatically BCNF: a proper part of one key can determine an attribute without determining the complete schema. Keep the three claims—normal form, losslessness and preservation—independent during verification.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has \(A\to B\) and B→A only. Determine BCNF using candidate keys AC and BC.
examples.strategy: Compute A closure → Identify the nontrivial arrow → Apply BCNF directly

steps.title: Compute A closure
steps.explanation: A lacks C and is not a superkey.

steps.title: Identify the nontrivial arrow
steps.explanation: \(A\to B\) has a nonkey determinant.

steps.title: Apply BCNF directly
steps.explanation: The determinant requirement fails even though B is prime through candidate key BC.

examples.answer: R violates BCNF.
examples.verification: B→A supplies a second symmetric nonkey violation; prime status cannot rescue either one in BCNF.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C,D) has \(A\to B\),\(B\to C\),C→D. Decompose to BCNF by removing nonkey facts.
examples.strategy: Separate C→D → Separate \(B\to C\) in ABC → Check local determinants

steps.title: Separate C→D
steps.explanation: Split into CD and ABC; common C determines CD, so this split is lossless.

steps.title: Separate \(B\to C\) in ABC
steps.explanation: Split ABC into BC and AB; common B determines BC, again lossless.

steps.title: Check local determinants
steps.explanation: Keys are C in CD, B in BC and A in AB. Each component has only key-based nontrivial dependencies.

examples.answer: BCNF components AB,BC,CD; sequentially lossless and dependency-preserving.
examples.verification: \(A\to B\),\(B\to C\),C→D each remains local, and both explicit intersection proofs establish recombination.

examples.prompt: R(A,B,C) has A\(B\to C\) and C→B. Someone declares BCNF because every attribute belongs to a candidate key. What check refutes this?
examples.strategy: Compute all key memberships → Inspect a determinant closure → Apply the stronger requirement

steps.title: Compute all key memberships
steps.explanation: AB and AC are candidate keys, so every attribute is indeed prime.

steps.title: Inspect a determinant closure
steps.explanation: C does not determine A.

steps.title: Apply the stronger requirement
steps.explanation: C→B is nontrivial with a non-superkey determinant, violating BCNF despite prime membership.

examples.answer: All-prime attributes suffice for this 3NF exception, but not BCNF.
examples.verification: The missing A in C closure is the independent witness that C is not a superkey.

lessons.title: File organization and B/B+ tree indexing
lessons.intuition: An index is an auxiliary route to data, not the data model itself. On-disk indexes use high branching factors to reduce expensive page reads. Equality and range queries can prefer different organizations.

sections.title: File layout
sections.body: Heap files place records in convenient free space and favour insertion without key order. Sorted files favour ordered scans but make insertion maintenance costly. Hash organization targets equality buckets and generally does not preserve ordering. A clustered organization aligns data placement with index order; a secondary index may require scattered data-page fetches.

sections.title: B-tree family
sections.body: B and B+ trees remain balanced and store many separator keys per page. In a common B+ design, internal nodes guide search while data entries are at leaves, which are linked for range scans. Definitions of “order” vary: read whether it means maximum children, maximum keys or minimum occupancy. Splits, redistribution and merges preserve occupancy and balance.

sections.title: Cost reasoning
sections.body: With fanout f and many entries, height grows roughly logarithmically in f. Point search follows one root-to-leaf path; a range search locates its starting leaf then walks linked leaves. Dense indexes have an entry for every relevant key/record convention; sparse indexes have selected entries and ordinarily require ordered data. Include data-page reads separately when an index does not contain the required record.

sections.title: Derive capacity from page layout
sections.body: An internal B+ tree page with f children normally needs f pointers and f−1 separator keys; a leaf page instead needs key/record entries and a next-leaf pointer, potentially with other metadata. Subtract reserved bytes before deriving each capacity. Maximum fanout is not minimum occupancy: split rules and root exceptions affect minimum and maximum tree heights. Search chooses an internal pointer using separators until a leaf, then checks the actual key. A range query locates its first leaf once and follows leaf links, but fetching records through an unclustered index can add scattered data-page I/O. A clustered layout tends to group nearby key values in nearby data pages. Counting tree levels alone estimates index traversal, not necessarily the entire query’s disk cost.

examples.prompt: Estimate maximum leaves for a B+ tree with 3 levels and fanout 4

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The root is level 1 and can point to 4 internal nodes. Level numbering starts at the root as level 1; three levels therefore contain two pointer expansions.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Each internal node can point to 4 leaves. Each of the four internal nodes can supply four independent leaf children under the maximum-fanout assumption.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Maximum leaves=4×4=16, excluding leaf entry capacity from this count. This is the maximum number of leaf pages, not the maximum records. Record capacity additionally requires entries per leaf.

examples.strategy: Count child pointers per level and keep leaf entry capacity out of leaf-node count.
examples.answer: Maximum leaves=4×4=16, excluding leaf entry capacity from this count.
examples.verification: Level counts are 1,4,16. Multiplying by four a third time would erroneously count an extra level.

examples.prompt: Range query using a B+ index
steps: Search down to the leaf containing the first key at least the lower bound.
Scan that leaf and follow next-leaf links.
Stop once the upper bound is exceeded; do not restart root search for each successive key.

pitfalls: B-tree “order” conventions are not universal.
An index-only search differs from an index lookup plus record fetch.
revision: B+ leaf links support range scans; hashing favours equality.

checks.prompt: A root with fanout 5 points directly to leaves. What is the maximum number of leaves?
checks.hint: One child pointer selects one leaf.
checks.explanation: At most 5 leaves.

checks.prompt: A disk page of 4096 bytes stores fixed-size 128-byte records without overhead. How many fit?
checks.hint: Divide page bytes by record bytes.

lessons.concept: An index is an auxiliary route to data, not the data model itself. On-disk indexes use high branching factors to reduce expensive page reads. Equality and range queries can prefer different organizations.
lessons.method:
Heap file organization places records where space is available without a key order; sorted organization arranges them by a search key and favors ordered scans. An index stores search keys with pointers to records or data regions, adding maintenance and storage to accelerate selected accesses. Hash indexing supports equality well but not general ordered ranges.
A dense index has an entry for each search-key value or record under its convention; a sparse index has selected entries, commonly one per ordered block, requiring an ordered underlying organization. A clustered organization groups data physically by the index ordering; unclustered references can fetch qualifying records from many scattered pages. A table’s primary key and its physical clustering need not be identical.
Cost includes index traversal and data-page reads, considering cache state and selectivity. An index is not always best when a query returns most rows. GATE questions need key/pointer widths, records per block, clustering and root-caching assumptions before I/O estimates. An “index lookup is logarithmic” fact alone does not count all returned-record retrieval work. A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree whose nodes fit storage pages and hold multiple keys/children. A B+ tree keeps record entries at leaves while internal separator keys route searches; leaves are commonly linked for ordered scans. Definitions of “order” vary between maximum children and maximum keys, so use the problem’s convention.
An internal node with f children normally needs f pointers and f−1 separator keys; a leaf has a different layout including record pointers and a next-leaf link. Calculate capacities separately after reserved overhead. Occupancy bounds and root exceptions affect minimum/maximum heights. Insertion splits full nodes and can propagate upward; deletion can borrow or merge under the supplied minimum rules.
All leaves remain at the same depth. Range retrieval descends once to the first qualifying leaf then follows leaf links, instead of restarting from the root for every key. Count actual page accesses and possible data fetches separately. Matching tree height alone does not prove identical range costs between clustered and unclustered layouts. File organization determines how records occupy data pages before any optional index is considered. A heap file has no search-key ordering, so an equality query without an index may scan pages until it finds the record or proves absence. A sorted file maintains key order, permitting block-level binary search when the layout and access assumptions support it. Maintaining that ordering can make inserts and updates more expensive.
An ordered file also permits continuing sequentially from the first qualifying position for a range, while a heap must examine potentially unrelated pages. These access differences depend on the actual operation: reading most records may favor a sequential scan in either organization. Count page accesses rather than abstract record comparisons, and state whether an index, cache or block directory is available. Sorted organization is not the same as having an unclustered secondary index. To make a numeric comparison, define an explicit searchable page representation, trace its probes, and contrast the unordered search's necessary inspection under the given guarantee. A B-tree is a balanced multiway search structure whose nodes hold ordered keys and child pointers. In the ordinary B-tree representation used here, record references can occur alongside keys in internal nodes as well as leaves. Compare the target against a node's keys: an equality can finish the search there; otherwise select the child interval that could contain the key and continue.
All leaves have the same depth, and minimum occupancy rules prevent long sparse chains except for the stated root exception. The term order is ambiguous across texts, so specify whether it means maximum children or keys. With at most m children an internal node normally has at most m−1 keys, while the minimum is determined by the supplied convention. Count pages actually visited, not the maximum tree height for every lookup. A B+ tree uses internal keys as routing separators and places record entries at leaves, so equal-looking internal keys do not have the same stopping rule in that different representation. A B+ tree stores record entries in its leaves, with internal separator keys guiding searches to the correct leaf. Leaves are normally linked in sorted order. A range query can therefore descend to the first possible match once and then follow successive leaf links until the upper bound is exceeded, rather than searching from the root separately for every result.
Interpret separator equality using the tree's routing convention. Internal keys are not extra result records, even when they repeat keys found in leaves. Page costs include every uncached internal and leaf page visited; separately stored records can add data-page reads, depending on whether leaf entries contain payload or pointers and whether the data are clustered. The range scan may need the next leaf to discover that no later entries qualify. State exactly which pages and bounds are given before counting. Balance guarantees a common leaf depth, but it does not mean every equality or range operation reads the same number of pages. Heap files place records in convenient free space and favour insertion without key order. Sorted files favour ordered scans but make insertion maintenance costly. Hash organization targets equality buckets and generally does not preserve ordering. A clustered organization aligns data placement with index order; a secondary index may require scattered data-page fetches. B and B+ trees remain balanced and store many separator keys per page. In a common B+ design, internal nodes guide search while data entries are at leaves, which are linked for range scans.
