Dense indexes have an entry for every relevant key/record convention; sparse indexes have selected entries and ordinarily require ordered data. Include data-page reads separately when an index does not contain the required record. An internal B+ tree page with f children normally needs f pointers and f−1 separator keys; a leaf page instead needs key/record entries and a next-leaf pointer, potentially with other metadata. Subtract reserved bytes before deriving each capacity. Maximum fanout is not minimum occupancy: split rules and root exceptions affect minimum and maximum tree heights. Search chooses an internal pointer using separators until a leaf, then checks the actual key. A range query locates its first leaf once and follows leaf links, but fetching records through an unclustered index can add scattered data-page I/O. A clustered layout tends to group nearby key values in nearby data pages. Counting tree levels alone estimates index traversal, not necessarily the entire query’s disk cost. An index trades maintained metadata for selective access to data locations. Dense and sparse representations offer different pointer granularity; sparsity usually relies on an ordered underlying file to search inside a candidate block. Traversal cost is only part of a query's I/O: qualifying records may require many data-page fetches, particularly for an unclustered index. A full scan can therefore beat indexed access when selectivity is poor. These examples assume explicit cache conditions, no covering payload unless stated, and distinct data pages counted once. Write the traversal path and the set of data pages separately, then add them. Do not infer one data access per qualifying row when several rows share a page, or assume every useful index is optimal for every query. File organization is a physical arrangement of records, and its benefits depend on the operation. A heap avoids maintaining key order but can require inspecting every page for an absent key. A rigid sorted file supports ordered access while insertion may shift records through subsequent pages. A secondary index can provide an ordered search route without making the underlying heap clustered. These examples assume explicit page packing and no compression, caching or hidden free slots. Calculate pages from record capacity, then trace the particular operation's data-page effects. Separate lookup assistance from physical adjacency: neighboring key values can still require different scattered data pages. This makes the maintenance cost and query cost of a layout visible rather than declaring one organization universally superior. A B-tree keeps search height bounded by packing several ordered keys in each node and enforcing occupancy. Page size determines maximum children through both pointer and separator costs, while insertion may split a full node and promote its median. Promotion changes the parent and can create a new root, increasing every leaf's depth together. Ordinary B-tree records may live internally, so deletion and traversal should not assume that internal keys are merely duplicated routing labels. The examples state maximum keys or minimum degree explicitly because order terminology varies. Count keys and children separately: an internal node with f children contains f−1 separators, and the root has different minimum occupancy rules from ordinary nodes. B+ trees separate routing from leaf record storage. When a leaf splits, the parent separator commonly copies the new right leaf's first key rather than removing that record from the leaf. Search equality follows the specified separator convention to a leaf, and range continuation uses leaf links. Leaf capacity and internal capacity differ because leaves contain record references and a next-leaf pointer rather than child arrays. These examples use explicit layouts and rightward routing at separator equality. Count result records at leaves only, and count data-page fetches separately if leaves store pointers instead of payload. A separator appearing both internally and in a leaf represents one record plus routing information, not two copies to emit in a query result.
lessons.example: Estimate maximum leaves for a B+ tree with 3 levels and fanout 4

gateGuide.recognize: Index questions often confuse tree order, fanout and leaf capacity. Use the definition supplied by the paper.
method: Compute internal pointer/key capacity and leaf record-entry capacity separately.
Trace lookup, split and redistribution using the specified occupancy convention.
For cost count page reads, consider root caching and distinguish clustered range scans from repeated unclustered record fetches.

traps.claim: B+ tree internal keys store every record
traps.why: Records or record pointers are normally at leaves; internal keys guide traversal.

traps.claim: An index makes every range query cheap
traps.why: An unclustered range can require many scattered data-page reads, especially when many rows qualify.

formulas.meaning: Internal fanout f with pointer size p, separator size k and available bytes B.
Balanced tree levels for L leaves under ideal fanout; occupancy changes bounds.

tutorials.title: File organizations, dense/sparse and clustered indexes
tutorials.body:
Heap file organization places records where space is available without a key order; sorted organization arranges them by a search key and favors ordered scans. An index stores search keys with pointers to records or data regions, adding maintenance and storage to accelerate selected accesses. Hash indexing supports equality well but not general ordered ranges.
A dense index has an entry for each search-key value or record under its convention; a sparse index has selected entries, commonly one per ordered block, requiring an ordered underlying organization. A clustered organization groups data physically by the index ordering; unclustered references can fetch qualifying records from many scattered pages. A table’s primary key and its physical clustering need not be identical.
Cost includes index traversal and data-page reads, considering cache state and selectivity. An index is not always best when a query returns most rows. GATE questions need key/pointer widths, records per block, clustering and root-caching assumptions before I/O estimates. An “index lookup is logarithmic” fact alone does not count all returned-record retrieval work.

example.prompt: A sorted file has block first keys 10,30,50. Sparse index is searched for key 37.
example.strategy: Find predecessor index key → Locate block → Interpret

steps.title: Find predecessor index key
steps.explanation: 30 is the largest block-first key not exceeding 37.

steps.title: Locate block
steps.explanation: Read the referenced block and search within it.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.explanation: The index entry identifies a candidate block, not necessarily a direct record pointer for 37.

example.answer: Search the data block beginning at key 30.
example.verification: Sparse index correctness depends on the file’s sorted organization and its stated block boundaries.

depth.body: An index trades maintained metadata for selective access to data locations. Dense and sparse representations offer different pointer granularity; sparsity usually relies on an ordered underlying file to search inside a candidate block. Traversal cost is only part of a query's I/O: qualifying records may require many data-page fetches, particularly for an unclustered index. A full scan can therefore beat indexed access when selectivity is poor. These examples assume explicit cache conditions, no covering payload unless stated, and distinct data pages counted once. Write the traversal path and the set of data pages separately, then add them. Do not infer one data access per qualifying row when several rows share a page, or assume every useful index is optimal for every query.

examples.prompt: A sorted file has 12 distinct-key records across four pages, three per page. Compare one-entry-per-record dense indexing with one-entry-per-page sparse indexing.
examples.strategy: Count dense entries → Count sparse entries → Interpret lookup granularity

steps.title: Count dense entries
steps.explanation: The stipulated dense representation needs one entry for each of 12 records.

steps.title: Count sparse entries
steps.explanation: The sparse representation needs the first-key pointer for each of four pages.

steps.title: Interpret lookup granularity
steps.explanation: Dense entries identify records; sparse lookup identifies a candidate ordered page that must be searched.

examples.answer: Dense: 12 entries; sparse: 4 entries.
examples.verification: Three records per page times four pages equals twelve, explaining the entry-count ratio without changing payload size.

examples.prompt: An uncached unclustered index lookup visits three index pages and returns five records on data pages [7,9,7,20,25]. Count total reads with each fetched page retained.
examples.strategy: Count traversal → Deduplicate payload pages → Combine access classes

steps.title: Count traversal
steps.explanation: Three distinct index pages are required.

steps.title: Deduplicate payload pages
steps.explanation: The five records occupy four distinct pages: 7,9,20,25.

steps.title: Combine access classes
steps.explanation: The second record on page 7 does not cause another retained-page read.

examples.answer: Seven page reads.
examples.verification: A per-record addition would give eight and double-count page 7; the actual distinct-page set supplies the check.

examples.prompt: A query needs every row of a 100-page table. A noncovering index requires three uncached traversal pages then all 100 data pages. Is index use necessarily faster than a scan?
examples.strategy: Count the scan → Count indexed retrieval → Compare selectivity benefit

steps.title: Count the scan
steps.explanation: A full table scan needs 100 data-page reads in this model.

steps.title: Count indexed retrieval
steps.explanation: Traversal plus all payload pages needs 3+100=103 reads.

steps.title: Compare selectivity benefit
steps.explanation: No data page is avoided, so the extra metadata work provides no I/O saving.

examples.answer: The scan has lower modeled I/O: 100 versus 103 reads.
examples.verification: An index benefit depends on avoiding data work or covering the query; neither is true in the supplied scenario.

tutorials.title: B/B+ trees, occupancy and range scans
tutorials.body:
A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree whose nodes fit storage pages and hold multiple keys/children. A B+ tree keeps record entries at leaves while internal separator keys route searches; leaves are commonly linked for ordered scans. Definitions of “order” vary between maximum children and maximum keys, so use the problem’s convention.
An internal node with f children normally needs f pointers and f−1 separator keys; a leaf has a different layout including record pointers and a next-leaf link. Calculate capacities separately after reserved overhead. Occupancy bounds and root exceptions affect minimum/maximum heights. Insertion splits full nodes and can propagate upward; deletion can borrow or merge under the supplied minimum rules.
All leaves remain at the same depth. Range retrieval descends once to the first qualifying leaf then follows leaf links, instead of restarting from the root for every key. Count actual page accesses and possible data fetches separately. Matching tree height alone does not prove identical range costs between clustered and unclustered layouts.

example.prompt: Internal page size 100 bytes; pointer 4 bytes; key 8 bytes; no reserved overhead. Find max fanout.
example.strategy: Layout inequality → Solve → Verify

steps.title: Layout inequality
steps.explanation: f pointers and f−1 separator keys occupy the page.

steps.title: Solve
steps.explanation: Fanout must be an integer.

steps.title: Verify
steps.explanation: Nine children fit exactly.

example.answer: Maximum fanout 9.
example.verification: Using nine keys as well as nine pointers would use a different and incorrect internal layout.

tutorials.title: Heap and sorted files have different search costs
tutorials.body:
File organization determines how records occupy data pages before any optional index is considered. A heap file has no search-key ordering, so an equality query without an index may scan pages until it finds the record or proves absence. A sorted file maintains key order, permitting block-level binary search when the layout and access assumptions support it. Maintaining that ordering can make inserts and updates more expensive.
An ordered file also permits continuing sequentially from the first qualifying position for a range, while a heap must examine potentially unrelated pages. These access differences depend on the actual operation: reading most records may favor a sequential scan in either organization. Count page accesses rather than abstract record comparisons, and state whether an index, cache or block directory is available. Sorted organization is not the same as having an unclustered secondary index. To make a numeric comparison, define an explicit searchable page representation, trace its probes, and contrast the unordered search's necessary inspection under the given guarantee.

example.prompt: An uncached file occupies 16 pages. Each sorted page holds one distinct key, pages 1…16 containing keys 1…16; there is no index. Search for absent key 17. Compare an unordered heap with block binary search using floor((low+high)/2).
example.strategy: Heap absence proof → Trace sorted probes → Terminate the ordered search

steps.title: Heap absence proof
steps.explanation: An unordered heap gives no ordering reason to skip any page, so proving key 17 absent requires reading all 16 pages.

steps.title: Trace sorted probes
steps.explanation: Start low=1, high=16. Read pages 8,12,14,15,16; each key is below 17, so move low above that midpoint.

steps.title: Terminate the ordered search
steps.explanation: The sorted search has exhausted its search interval after five reads and proves absence without inspecting the other pages.

example.answer: Heap: 16 reads. The stated sorted binary-search trace: 5 reads.
example.verification: Probe sequence 8→12→14→15→16 covers every successive candidate interval for key 17. The comparison assumes no cached pages or index, so index traversal is not silently omitted.

depth.body: File organization is a physical arrangement of records, and its benefits depend on the operation. A heap avoids maintaining key order but can require inspecting every page for an absent key. A rigid sorted file supports ordered access while insertion may shift records through subsequent pages. A secondary index can provide an ordered search route without making the underlying heap clustered. These examples assume explicit page packing and no compression, caching or hidden free slots. Calculate pages from record capacity, then trace the particular operation's data-page effects. Separate lookup assistance from physical adjacency: neighboring key values can still require different scattered data pages. This makes the maintenance cost and query cost of a layout visible rather than declaring one organization universally superior.

examples.prompt: An unindexed heap holds 950 records, 20 per page, tightly packed. Prove an equality target absent. How many data pages must be read?
examples.strategy: Count allocated pages → Use the unordered model → Complete the absence check

steps.title: Count allocated pages
steps.explanation: The final page is partially occupied.

steps.title: Use the unordered model
steps.explanation: No key ordering or index permits eliminating an unread page.

steps.title: Complete the absence check
steps.explanation: Read all 48 pages to inspect every possible record location.

examples.answer: 48 data-page reads in the uncached worst case.
examples.verification: 47 pages hold only 940 records, so a 48th page is necessary despite containing just ten records.

examples.prompt: Sorted fixed pages hold two records each: [10,20],[30,40],[50,60], all full. Maintain left-packed order while inserting 25. Compare a heap append with a new page.
examples.strategy: Keep the sorted sequence → Repack affected pages → Compare heap insertion

steps.title: Keep the sorted sequence
steps.explanation: The final record sequence is 10,20,25,30,40,50,60.

steps.title: Repack affected pages
steps.explanation: Page 1 stays [10,20]; write pages 2=[25,30], 3=[40,50], and new page 4=[60].

steps.title: Compare heap insertion
steps.explanation: An unordered heap can write new page 4=[25] without shifting existing records, under the stipulated no-free-slot layout.

examples.answer: The sorted layout writes three data pages; the heap append writes one.
examples.verification: Both store seven records in four pages; only the ordering requirement changes which existing pages must be rewritten.

examples.prompt: A heap has page P1 keys [1,100] and P2 keys [2,99]. A secondary ordered index locates keys 1 and 2. Does sorted index order imply one clustered data-page read for range [1,2]?
examples.strategy: Locate matching keys → Follow their record locations → Count physical pages

steps.title: Locate matching keys
steps.explanation: The index identifies keys 1 and 2 in order.

steps.title: Follow their record locations
steps.explanation: Key 1 lies in P1 and key 2 in P2.

steps.title: Count physical pages
steps.explanation: Both distinct heap pages must be fetched; the index did not reorder their records.

examples.answer: Two data pages, plus any specified index traversal.
examples.verification: The supplied physical layout directly separates the two neighboring keys, refuting automatic clustering.

tutorials.title: A B-tree search can finish at an internal record
tutorials.body:
A B-tree is a balanced multiway search structure whose nodes hold ordered keys and child pointers. In the ordinary B-tree representation used here, record references can occur alongside keys in internal nodes as well as leaves. Compare the target against a node's keys: an equality can finish the search there; otherwise select the child interval that could contain the key and continue.
All leaves have the same depth, and minimum occupancy rules prevent long sparse chains except for the stated root exception. The term order is ambiguous across texts, so specify whether it means maximum children or keys. With at most m children an internal node normally has at most m−1 keys, while the minimum is determined by the supplied convention. Count pages actually visited, not the maximum tree height for every lookup. A B+ tree uses internal keys as routing separators and places record entries at leaves, so equal-looking internal keys do not have the same stopping rule in that different representation.

example.prompt: A B-tree stores a record reference with every key. Its uncached root contains keys 20 and 50 with three child pointers. Root children are leaves: [5,10], [30,40], [60,70]. Count page reads for independent uncached searches for keys 50 and 40.
example.strategy: Search for 50 → Search for 40 → Complete at the leaf

steps.title: Search for 50
steps.explanation: Read the root. Its stored key 50 has the requested record reference, so the index search finishes immediately after one page read.

steps.title: Search for 40
steps.explanation: In a fresh uncached search, read the root. Since 20<40<50, follow the middle child.

steps.title: Complete at the leaf
steps.explanation: Read the [30,40] leaf and find key 40 there. This search visits two index pages, excluding any separately stored payload page.

example.answer: Key 50 needs one index-page read; key 40 needs two under the stated B-tree representation.
example.verification: Both searches respect the root's child intervals. Adding one payload read would be a different cost question; copying the B+ stopping rule would incorrectly force the 50 lookup down to a leaf.

depth.body: A B-tree keeps search height bounded by packing several ordered keys in each node and enforcing occupancy. Page size determines maximum children through both pointer and separator costs, while insertion may split a full node and promote its median. Promotion changes the parent and can create a new root, increasing every leaf's depth together. Ordinary B-tree records may live internally, so deletion and traversal should not assume that internal keys are merely duplicated routing labels. The examples state maximum keys or minimum degree explicitly because order terminology varies. Count keys and children separately: an internal node with f children contains f−1 separators, and the root has different minimum occupancy rules from ordinary nodes.

examples.prompt: An internal page has 256 usable bytes, eight-byte child pointers and eight-byte keys. Find maximum fanout, ignoring all other overhead.
examples.strategy: Write the node layout → Solve the capacity bound → Verify adjacent choices

steps.title: Write the node layout
steps.explanation: An internal node uses f pointers and f−1 keys.

steps.title: Solve the capacity bound
steps.explanation: Integer fanout is at most 16.

steps.title: Verify adjacent choices
steps.explanation: f=16 uses 248 bytes; f=17 uses 264 and does not fit.

examples.answer: Maximum fanout 16.
examples.verification: Sixteen children require fifteen keys, not sixteen; the explicit fit/nonfit test checks the rounding.

examples.prompt: A B-tree has minimum degree two, maximum three keys per node. Its root is a full leaf [10,20,30]. Insert 40 using split-before-descent.
examples.strategy: Split the full root → Choose the correct child → Insert without overflow

steps.title: Split the full root
steps.explanation: Promote median 20 into a new root; create leaves [10] and [30].

steps.title: Choose the correct child
steps.explanation: 40 exceeds 20 and enters the right leaf.

steps.title: Insert without overflow
steps.explanation: Right leaf becomes [30,40], within the three-key maximum.

examples.answer: Root [20], children [10] and [30,40]; leaf depth increases from zero to one.
examples.verification: All four keys appear once and both children meet minimum one-key occupancy; their ranges agree with separator 20.

examples.prompt: For a B-tree with maximum four children per ordinary internal node and minimum two, a nonleaf root has one key and two children. Is it underfull because it lacks two keys?
examples.strategy: Relate keys and children → Apply the root exception → Check the claimed bound

steps.title: Relate keys and children
steps.explanation: Two child pointers require one separator key.

steps.title: Apply the root exception
steps.explanation: A nonleaf root may have two children under the stated convention.

steps.title: Check the claimed bound
steps.explanation: Minimum children two does not mean minimum keys two.

examples.answer: The root is valid with one key and two children.
examples.verification: For a node with c children the separator count is c−1, so the one-key layout matches two children exactly.

tutorials.title: A B+ range scan descends once and follows leaf links
tutorials.body:
A B+ tree stores record entries in its leaves, with internal separator keys guiding searches to the correct leaf. Leaves are normally linked in sorted order. A range query can therefore descend to the first possible match once and then follow successive leaf links until the upper bound is exceeded, rather than searching from the root separately for every result.
Interpret separator equality using the tree's routing convention. Internal keys are not extra result records, even when they repeat keys found in leaves. Page costs include every uncached internal and leaf page visited; separately stored records can add data-page reads, depending on whether leaf entries contain payload or pointers and whether the data are clustered. The range scan may need the next leaf to discover that no later entries qualify. State exactly which pages and bounds are given before counting. Balance guarantees a common leaf depth, but it does not mean every equality or range operation reads the same number of pages.

example.prompt: An uncached one-level B+ root has separators 30 and 50: keys <30 use L1, 30…49 use L2, >=50 use L3. Linked leaves contain L1=[10,20], L2=[30,40], L3=[50,60]. Scan inclusive range [20,50]; leaves contain the complete records.
example.strategy: Find the first leaf → Follow the leaf chain → Finish the bounded scan

steps.title: Find the first leaf
steps.explanation: Read the root and route lower bound 20 to L1. Read L1 and emit 20 while skipping 10.

steps.title: Follow the leaf chain
steps.explanation: Read linked L2 and emit 30 and 40; no second root traversal is necessary.

steps.title: Finish the bounded scan
steps.explanation: Read L3, emit 50 and stop at 60 because it exceeds the upper bound. Total reads are one root plus three leaves.

example.answer: Results 20,30,40,50; four page reads, with no additional payload reads in this stated layout.
example.verification: Separator values 30 and 50 are emitted only from leaves, not again from the root. Four qualifying records occupy three leaves, so counting records alone would not give the I/O cost.

depth.body: B+ trees separate routing from leaf record storage. When a leaf splits, the parent separator commonly copies the new right leaf's first key rather than removing that record from the leaf. Search equality follows the specified separator convention to a leaf, and range continuation uses leaf links. Leaf capacity and internal capacity differ because leaves contain record references and a next-leaf pointer rather than child arrays. These examples use explicit layouts and rightward routing at separator equality. Count result records at leaves only, and count data-page fetches separately if leaves store pointers instead of payload. A separator appearing both internally and in a leaf represents one record plus routing information, not two copies to emit in a query result.

examples.prompt: A B+ root separator is 40; keys <40 go left and >=40 right. Left leaf=[10,20], right leaf=[40,50]. Locate equality key 40 with uncached pages.
examples.strategy: Read the root → Apply the routing convention → Read the record leaf

steps.title: Read the root
steps.explanation: Compare 40 to separator 40.

steps.title: Apply the routing convention
steps.explanation: Equality follows the right child, not the left interval.

steps.title: Read the record leaf
steps.explanation: The right leaf contains key 40, completing the lookup after two page reads.

examples.answer: Read root and right leaf; key 40 is found with two index-page reads.
examples.verification: The separator routes equality but does not itself contain the result record under the B+ representation.

examples.prompt: A B+ leaf holds at most three entries. Leaf [10,20,30] receives 25; split the four entries evenly and update its parent using first-right-key separator.
examples.strategy: Sort the overflow → Split the payload → Copy the routing key

steps.title: Sort the overflow
steps.explanation: The entries become [10,20,25,30].

steps.title: Split the payload
steps.explanation: Left leaf becomes [10,20]; right leaf becomes [25,30], with the leaf link updated.

steps.title: Copy the routing key
steps.explanation: Insert separator 25 into the parent; keep record 25 in the right leaf.

examples.answer: Leaves [10,20] and [25,30], parent separator 25.
examples.verification: Each leaf has two entries within capacity three, and all four record entries remain at leaf level.

examples.prompt: A B+ internal page contains separator 30 and its linked leaves contain records 10,20,30,40. An ordered full scan counts the separator as another record. Correct its count.
examples.strategy: Identify metadata role → Visit the leaves → Count results once

steps.title: Identify metadata role
steps.explanation: Internal 30 routes searches and is not a separate stored record.

steps.title: Visit the leaves
steps.explanation: The four leaf records are 10,20,30,40.

steps.title: Count results once
steps.explanation: Emit those four records without adding the internal copy.

examples.answer: Four records, not five.
examples.verification: The leaf sequence contains exactly one record for each supplied key; structural routing copies do not add payload multiplicity.

lessons.title: Transactions, serializability and concurrency control
lessons.intuition: Transactions group operations into a unit whose intermediate effects must be controlled. Concurrency can improve throughput, but interleavings must preserve an allowed relationship to serial execution and support recovery when work fails.

sections.title: ACID and anomalies
sections.body: Atomicity gives all-or-nothing effects; consistency preserves declared invariants when transactions themselves are correct; isolation controls interference; durability preserves committed effects after recovery. Lost updates overwrite another transaction’s changes. Dirty reads observe uncommitted writes. Nonrepeatable reads and phantoms involve changing rows or predicate result sets across reads.

sections.title: Conflict serializability
sections.body: Two operations conflict if they are in different transactions, access the same item, and at least one writes. Add Ti→Tj when Ti’s conflicting operation precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives an equivalent serial ordering. Read-read pairs create no edge. Conflict serializability is stronger than some other semantic notions of serializability.

sections.title: Locks and recovery
sections.body: Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases without acquiring new ones. It guarantees conflict serializability under the standard model but can deadlock. Strict variants retain required exclusive locks until commit/abort to prevent cascading effects. Write-ahead logging requires appropriate log records be durable before related dirty data pages are written. Recovery may redo committed work and undo uncommitted work according to its logging scheme.

sections.title: Three graphs of reasoning: conflict, reads and locks
sections.body: Conflict ordering constrains transactions when actions from different transactions touch the same item and at least one is a write. Read/read order adds no conflict edge. A directed cycle prevents any serial order satisfying all conflict constraints. Recovery instead follows which write supplied each read: committing a reader before that writer risks a committed dependency on an aborted value. Cascadeless schedules prevent reading uncommitted writes; strict schedules also prevent overwriting uncommitted writes. Two-phase locking forbids new lock acquisitions after the first release and guarantees conflict serializability, but can deadlock. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until completion, preventing dirty reads/writes of protected items; terminology for holding all locks is often called rigorous 2PL. Distinguish protocol rules from properties inferred for one particular schedule.

examples.prompt: Analyse W1(X),R2(X),W2(Y),R1(Y)

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: W1(X) before R2(X) adds \(T_1\to T_2\). A write followed by another transaction’s read conflicts, so any equivalent serial order must place T1 before T2.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: W2(Y) before R1(Y) adds \(T_2\to T_1\). The conflict on Y imposes the opposite ordering, T2 before T1.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable. No serial transaction order can satisfy both directions; the two-edge cycle is a certificate of conflict nonserializability.

examples.strategy: Build precedence edges only for same-item conflicts across different transactions.
examples.answer: The graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable.
examples.verification: Try serial T1,T2 and T2,T1: the former violates the Y constraint, the latter violates the X constraint. Commit/recovery properties are separate.

examples.prompt: Analyse R1(X),R2(X),W1(Y),R2(Y)
steps: The reads of X do not conflict.
W1(Y) before R2(Y) creates only \(T_1\to T_2\).
The graph is acyclic; serial order T1,T2 is conflict-equivalent.

pitfalls: Read-read overlap does not create a conflict.
Two-phase locking can still deadlock.
revision: WAL orders logging before corresponding data writes.

checks.prompt: Which pair creates a conflict between distinct transactions on the same item?
checks.hint: Conflict requires different transactions, same item and a write.
checks.explanation: Read/write, write/read and write/write pairs conflict. Read/read does not.
options: A pair containing at least one write
Every pair even on different items
Only writes in the same transaction

checks.prompt: A precedence graph contains \(T_1\to T_2\) and \(T_2\to T_1\). How many vertices are in this directed cycle?
checks.hint: Follow the two opposite edges.
checks.explanation: The cycle involves the two transactions.

lessons.concept: Transactions group operations into a unit whose intermediate effects must be controlled. Concurrency can improve throughput, but interleavings must preserve an allowed relationship to serial execution and support recovery when work fails.
lessons.method:
A transaction groups operations into one logical unit. Atomicity makes its effects all succeed or all roll back; consistency preserves declared database invariants when transaction logic and enforcement are correct; isolation controls what concurrent executions can observe; durability retains committed effects after failures under the system’s guarantee.
These are different properties. A serial transaction can still violate an invariant if its logic is wrong, and durability does not prevent dirty reads. Logs and recovery mechanisms support atomicity/durability, while locks or other concurrency methods support isolation. Isolation levels may allow some anomalies, so do not equate every database’s default setting with full serializability.
A schedule interleaves transaction actions while preserving each transaction’s local order. Commit and abort mark outcomes; reading another transaction’s uncommitted write creates recovery risks. In GATE, identify which guarantee a failure scenario violates rather than choosing ACID as one undifferentiated label. An attempted operation and its durable committed result have distinct points in time. Conflicting actions belong to different transactions, access the same item and contain at least one write. Their order constrains any conflict-equivalent serial schedule. Create an edge Ti→Tj when Ti’s earlier conflicting action precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this directed graph is acyclic; a topological order supplies a serial witness.
Read/read pairs do not conflict, and actions on different items do not add edges. A cycle refutes conflict serializability, not every possible view-serializability notion. Blind writes can distinguish the two classes. Keep the transaction identities attached to each operation while scanning pairs.
Recovery tracks read-from dependencies and commit order, a separate question. If Tj reads Ti’s write, recoverability requires Ti commit before Tj commits. Cascadelessness forbids reading uncommitted writes; strictness also forbids overwriting them. A graph that is acyclic can still describe a recovery-unsafe execution if commits are ordered badly. Include commits when assessing those properties. Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions to prevent disallowed anomalies. Two-phase locking divides a transaction into a growing phase with acquisitions and a shrinking phase with releases; after its first release it cannot acquire any new lock. Shared locks permit compatible reads, while exclusive locks protect conflicting writes under the lock table’s compatibility rules.
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but can deadlock and can permit recovery problems depending on release times. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort, preventing other transactions from reading or overwriting those uncommitted protected writes. Holding all locks to completion is often called rigorous 2PL, so follow the problem’s terminology.
A transaction waiting for a lock must not proceed as though acquisition succeeded. Upgrades count as acquisitions and must respect the protocol. Alternative methods such as timestamp ordering or optimistic validation have different conflict handling. In GATE traces, test both phase ordering and compatibility; a serializable particular schedule need not mean every listed protocol rule was followed. Concurrency control decides which simultaneous operations may proceed while maintaining the database's required isolation guarantees. Shared locks allow compatible readers of the same item; an exclusive lock conflicts with both shared and exclusive locks held by another transaction. A requested lock is not an acquired lock, so an operation that needs it must wait until permission is actually granted.
Two-phase locking imposes acquisition and release phases, but it does not remove all waiting or deadlocks. Transactions can each hold a lock and request another in opposite order while obeying their growing phase. A wait-for graph uses an edge from a waiting transaction to the transaction whose conflicting held lock blocks it. Under this exclusive single-owner lock model, a directed cycle identifies a deadlock. Resolve the blocked execution using the stated detector, victim abort or prevention policy; do not pretend that the conflicting operations have already executed. Serializability guarantees and progress guarantees answer different questions. ACID separates four transaction guarantees. Atomicity treats a transaction's operations as one all-or-nothing unit. Consistency requires a successful transaction and constraint enforcement to preserve the database's declared invariants. Isolation governs what concurrent transactions may observe, with serializable isolation presenting an effect equivalent to a permitted serial order. Durability preserves committed effects after failures within the system's stated guarantee.
The properties are related but cannot replace one another. Recovery can undo a partial debit without proving the transfer amount was valid. An application bug can violate a business invariant even when its writes are atomic and durable. Isolation levels weaker than serializability may permit particular anomalies, so an observation rule must name the guarantee being assumed. To classify a scenario, locate whether it concerns an incomplete operation, an invariant, concurrent visibility or a committed result after failure. A transaction's commit marks a boundary: a failure before it calls for atomic recovery, while losing its effects after a successful acknowledged commit challenges durability. Atomicity gives all-or-nothing effects; consistency preserves declared invariants when transactions themselves are correct; isolation controls interference; durability preserves committed effects after recovery. Lost updates overwrite another transaction’s changes. Dirty reads observe uncommitted writes. Nonrepeatable reads and phantoms involve changing rows or predicate result sets across reads. Two operations conflict if they are in different transactions, access the same item, and at least one writes. Add Ti→Tj when Ti’s conflicting operation precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives an equivalent serial ordering. Read-read pairs create no edge. Conflict serializability is stronger than some other semantic notions of serializability. Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases without acquiring new ones. It guarantees conflict serializability under the standard model but can deadlock. Strict variants retain required exclusive locks until commit/abort to prevent cascading effects. Write-ahead logging requires appropriate log records be durable before related dirty data pages are written. Recovery may redo committed work and undo uncommitted work according to its logging scheme. Conflict ordering constrains transactions when actions from different transactions touch the same item and at least one is a write. Read/read order adds no conflict edge. A directed cycle prevents any serial order satisfying all conflict constraints. Recovery instead follows which write supplied each read: committing a reader before that writer risks a committed dependency on an aborted value. Cascadeless schedules prevent reading uncommitted writes; strict schedules also prevent overwriting uncommitted writes. Two-phase locking forbids new lock acquisitions after the first release and guarantees conflict serializability, but can deadlock. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until completion, preventing dirty reads/writes of protected items; terminology for holding all locks is often called rigorous 2PL. Distinguish protocol rules from properties inferred for one particular schedule. A transaction has an execution lifetime and a single commit-or-abort outcome under the stated database contract. Operations may temporarily alter private or protected state before commit, while rollback restores the logical effects required by atomicity. Savepoints can undo a suffix without ending the whole transaction. A commit does not correct an invalid application decision automatically, and separate statements are not one atomic unit merely because they run consecutively. These examples assume transactional storage and explicit boundaries, rather than external irreversible side effects. Trace the state after each operation and mark which changes survive the final outcome. This distinguishes transient values, savepoint rollback and durable committed values, and exposes algorithms that accidentally split one business operation across two independent commits. Serializability compares an interleaved schedule with a possible serial execution while preserving the relevant observations or conflict orders. Conflict serializability uses same-item pairs containing a write and tests the resulting directed precedence graph. Read/read pairs add no edge, and commit placement belongs to recovery analysis rather than the conflict graph alone. View serializability preserves read sources and final writers and can differ when blind writes exist. The examples specify which equivalence is being tested. Build edges from actual ordered operations before selecting a serial order, and separately track any read of uncommitted data. Acyclic conflict order can coexist with unsafe commit order, so do not let one successful graph test answer every property of the schedule. Two-phase locking constrains each transaction's lock history, including upgrades. All acquisitions and promotions belong before the first release or demotion; later operations cannot start another growing phase. The lock point, its final acquisition, provides a serialization-order argument under the ordinary compatible-lock model. Basic 2PL does not require every lock to be held until commit, while strict 2PL specifically retains exclusive locks through completion. Holding shared and exclusive locks to the end is a stronger convention often called rigorous. These examples state mode changes explicitly, so a downgrade can be recognized as releasing exclusive permission. Verify phase order independently from compatibility and recovery: a legal acquisition phase can still block, and an early release may satisfy basic 2PL while violating strictness. Concurrency control protects acceptable interleavings, and different protocols choose different points to reject or delay conflicting work. Locks block incompatible operations before they execute; timestamp rules can reject an operation that is too old; optimistic validation can discover an invalid read set before commit. Track successful actions separately from requested actions, since a blocked write has not changed data. Logging rules support recovery but do not by themselves make faulty business logic correct.
