gateGuide.recognize: Conflict serializability, recoverability and locking guarantees measure different properties. Read-from relationships matter.
method: For the precedence graph connect different transactions when conflicting same-item actions occur in order.
Acyclicity gives a conflict-equivalent serial order via topological sorting.
For recovery track who read whose uncommitted write and compare commit order; distinguish basic, strict and rigorous 2PL.

traps.claim: Every serializable schedule is recoverable
traps.why: T2 can read T1’s write and commit before T1 aborts even if the conflict order is serializable.

traps.claim: Every cycle proves lack of view serializability
traps.why: It disproves conflict serializability; blind writes can permit view-serializable schedules outside that class.

formulas.meaning: An earlier conflicting action of Ti precedes an action of Tj on the same item; at least one is a write.
Recoverability requires writer Ti to commit before reader Tj commits when Tj reads Ti’s value.

tutorials.title: Transactions and the ACID guarantees
tutorials.body:
A transaction groups operations into one logical unit. Atomicity makes its effects all succeed or all roll back; consistency preserves declared database invariants when transaction logic and enforcement are correct; isolation controls what concurrent executions can observe; durability retains committed effects after failures under the system’s guarantee.
These are different properties. A serial transaction can still violate an invariant if its logic is wrong, and durability does not prevent dirty reads. Logs and recovery mechanisms support atomicity/durability, while locks or other concurrency methods support isolation. Isolation levels may allow some anomalies, so do not equate every database’s default setting with full serializability.
A schedule interleaves transaction actions while preserving each transaction’s local order. Commit and abort mark outcomes; reading another transaction’s uncommitted write creates recovery risks. In GATE, identify which guarantee a failure scenario violates rather than choosing ACID as one undifferentiated label. An attempted operation and its durable committed result have distinct points in time.

example.prompt: A transfer subtracts 100 from account A, then crashes before adding it to B.
example.strategy: Partial effects → Atomicity requirement → Recovery outcome

steps.title: Partial effects
steps.explanation: Without recovery, total balance drops even though the intended transfer did not complete.

steps.title: Atomicity requirement
steps.explanation: Both debit and credit must be treated as one unit, completed or undone.

steps.title: Recovery outcome
steps.explanation: An uncommitted partial transfer should be rolled back under the stated atomicity mechanism.

example.answer: Atomicity addresses the partial-transaction failure.
example.verification: Durability instead concerns retaining a transfer that had already successfully committed.

depth.body: A transaction has an execution lifetime and a single commit-or-abort outcome under the stated database contract. Operations may temporarily alter private or protected state before commit, while rollback restores the logical effects required by atomicity. Savepoints can undo a suffix without ending the whole transaction. A commit does not correct an invalid application decision automatically, and separate statements are not one atomic unit merely because they run consecutively. These examples assume transactional storage and explicit boundaries, rather than external irreversible side effects. Trace the state after each operation and mark which changes survive the final outcome. This distinguishes transient values, savepoint rollback and durable committed values, and exposes algorithms that accidentally split one business operation across two independent commits.

examples.prompt: A transaction starts with x=10, writes x=15, then aborts. No other transaction changes x. What survives?
examples.strategy: Record the original state → Apply the tentative update → Execute abort recovery

steps.title: Record the original state
steps.explanation: The pretransaction logical value is 10.

steps.title: Apply the tentative update
steps.explanation: The transaction's own work changes x to 15 before its outcome.

steps.title: Execute abort recovery
steps.explanation: Undo the transaction's effect, restoring the original value 10.

examples.answer: After abort, x=10.
examples.verification: Only the aborting transaction changed x, so retaining 15 would leave an uncommitted effect.

examples.prompt: x=10. Begin a transaction, set x=12, create savepoint S, set x=20, roll back to S, then commit. Trace final x.
examples.strategy: Establish the savepoint state → Undo only the suffix → Commit remaining work

steps.title: Establish the savepoint state
steps.explanation: At S, x=12; the earlier update belongs to the still-active transaction.

steps.title: Undo only the suffix
steps.explanation: Rollback to S removes the later x=20 update, returning x to 12.

steps.title: Commit remaining work
steps.explanation: Commit retains the pre-savepoint change to 12.

examples.answer: Final committed x=12.
examples.verification: Rollback to a savepoint differs from aborting the entire transaction, which would have restored 10.

examples.prompt: A transfer commits its debit in transaction T1, then its credit in separate T2. A crash occurs before T2 begins. Are the two commits an atomic transfer?
examples.strategy: Identify the boundaries → Locate the failure → Inspect surviving state

steps.title: Identify the boundaries
steps.explanation: T1's debit has already committed as its own unit.

steps.title: Locate the failure
steps.explanation: T2 never performs the credit, so there is no transaction containing both actions.

steps.title: Inspect surviving state
steps.explanation: The committed debit remains without its intended credit; per-transaction atomicity cannot join separate boundaries.

examples.answer: No; the business transfer is split and can leave a partial result.
examples.verification: Putting debit and credit inside one transactional unit supplies the all-or-nothing boundary that is missing here.

tutorials.title: Conflict graphs, recoverability and commit order
tutorials.body:
Conflicting actions belong to different transactions, access the same item and contain at least one write. Their order constrains any conflict-equivalent serial schedule. Create an edge Ti→Tj when Ti’s earlier conflicting action precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this directed graph is acyclic; a topological order supplies a serial witness.
Read/read pairs do not conflict, and actions on different items do not add edges. A cycle refutes conflict serializability, not every possible view-serializability notion. Blind writes can distinguish the two classes. Keep the transaction identities attached to each operation while scanning pairs.
Recovery tracks read-from dependencies and commit order, a separate question. If Tj reads Ti’s write, recoverability requires Ti commit before Tj commits. Cascadelessness forbids reading uncommitted writes; strictness also forbids overwriting them. A graph that is acyclic can still describe a recovery-unsafe execution if commits are ordered badly. Include commits when assessing those properties.

example.prompt: Schedule W1(X),R2(X),W2(Y),R1(Y).
example.strategy: Conflict on X → Conflict on Y → Cycle

steps.title: Conflict on X
steps.explanation: W1 before R2 imposes \(T_1\to T_2\).

steps.title: Conflict on Y
steps.explanation: W2 before R1 imposes \(T_2\to T_1\).

steps.title: Cycle
steps.explanation: The two edges form a directed cycle, so no serial order respects both.

example.answer: Not conflict serializable.
example.verification: This conclusion does not need commit times, while recoverability would require read-from and commit/abort information.

depth.body: Serializability compares an interleaved schedule with a possible serial execution while preserving the relevant observations or conflict orders. Conflict serializability uses same-item pairs containing a write and tests the resulting directed precedence graph. Read/read pairs add no edge, and commit placement belongs to recovery analysis rather than the conflict graph alone. View serializability preserves read sources and final writers and can differ when blind writes exist. The examples specify which equivalence is being tested. Build edges from actual ordered operations before selecting a serial order, and separately track any read of uncommitted data. Acyclic conflict order can coexist with unsafe commit order, so do not let one successful graph test answer every property of the schedule.

examples.prompt: Schedule R1(X),R2(X),W1(Y),R2(Y). Build the conflict graph and a serial witness.
examples.strategy: Ignore the read/read pair → Add the Y dependency → Topologically order the graph

steps.title: Ignore the read/read pair
steps.explanation: R1(X) and R2(X) do not conflict.

steps.title: Add the Y dependency
steps.explanation: W1(Y) before R2(Y) adds \(T_1\to T_2\).

steps.title: Topologically order the graph
steps.explanation: There is no reverse edge, so serial T1 then T2 respects every conflict.

examples.answer: Conflict serializable with witness T1,T2.
examples.verification: Only one edge exists; the same-item X operations contain no write and cannot create a cycle.

examples.prompt: Schedule W1(X),W2(X),W3(Y),R2(Y). Find all required ordering edges and a serial order.
examples.strategy: Inspect X writes → Inspect Y conflict → Choose a topological order

steps.title: Inspect X writes
steps.explanation: W1(X) before W2(X) gives \(T_1\to T_2\).

steps.title: Inspect Y conflict
steps.explanation: W3(Y) before R2(Y) gives T3→T2.

steps.title: Choose a topological order
steps.explanation: T1,T3,T2 works, as does T3,T1,T2, because T1 and T3 have no edge between them.

examples.answer: Edges \(T_1\to T_2\) and T3→T2; two valid orders are T1,T3,T2 and T3,T1,T2.
examples.verification: Both proposed orders place T2 after its two predecessors, and no other same-item cross-transaction conflict exists.

examples.prompt: Schedule W1(X),R2(X),C2,A1. Its conflict graph is acyclic. Does that ensure recoverability?
examples.strategy: Check the graph → Track the read source → Inspect the abort

steps.title: Check the graph
steps.explanation: The write-read conflict gives only \(T_1\to T_2\), so conflict serializability holds.

steps.title: Track the read source
steps.explanation: T2 reads T1's uncommitted X and commits before T1 commits.

steps.title: Inspect the abort
steps.explanation: T1 aborts after T2's commit, leaving T2 committed with a value from an aborted transaction.

examples.answer: Conflict serializable but not recoverable.
examples.verification: Recoverability requires the read-source writer to commit before the reader; here the writer never commits.

tutorials.title: Two-phase locking and strictness
tutorials.body:
Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions to prevent disallowed anomalies. Two-phase locking divides a transaction into a growing phase with acquisitions and a shrinking phase with releases; after its first release it cannot acquire any new lock. Shared locks permit compatible reads, while exclusive locks protect conflicting writes under the lock table’s compatibility rules.
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but can deadlock and can permit recovery problems depending on release times. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort, preventing other transactions from reading or overwriting those uncommitted protected writes. Holding all locks to completion is often called rigorous 2PL, so follow the problem’s terminology.
A transaction waiting for a lock must not proceed as though acquisition succeeded. Upgrades count as acquisitions and must respect the protocol. Alternative methods such as timestamp ordering or optimistic validation have different conflict handling. In GATE traces, test both phase ordering and compatibility; a serializable particular schedule need not mean every listed protocol rule was followed.

example.prompt: T1 acquires X, releases X, then requests Y. Does it obey basic 2PL?
example.strategy: Growing phase → Begin shrinking → Later request

steps.title: Growing phase
steps.explanation: The first acquisition is permitted.

steps.title: Begin shrinking
steps.explanation: Releasing X ends the period in which new acquisitions are allowed.

steps.title: Later request
steps.explanation: Acquiring Y afterward violates the two-phase rule.

example.answer: It violates 2PL.
example.verification: The prohibition is about phase order, even if no other transaction currently holds Y.

depth.body: Two-phase locking constrains each transaction's lock history, including upgrades. All acquisitions and promotions belong before the first release or demotion; later operations cannot start another growing phase. The lock point, its final acquisition, provides a serialization-order argument under the ordinary compatible-lock model. Basic 2PL does not require every lock to be held until commit, while strict 2PL specifically retains exclusive locks through completion. Holding shared and exclusive locks to the end is a stronger convention often called rigorous. These examples state mode changes explicitly, so a downgrade can be recognized as releasing exclusive permission. Verify phase order independently from compatibility and recovery: a legal acquisition phase can still block, and an early release may satisfy basic 2PL while violating strictness.

examples.prompt: T acquires shared X, upgrades to exclusive X, acquires shared Y, then releases X and Y. Does it obey basic 2PL?
examples.strategy: List acquisitions → Locate the lock point → Inspect the shrinking phase

steps.title: List acquisitions
steps.explanation: Shared X, upgrade to exclusive X, and shared Y all occur before any release.

steps.title: Locate the lock point
steps.explanation: The acquisition of Y is the final acquisition and ends the growing work.

steps.title: Inspect the shrinking phase
steps.explanation: Only releases follow, so there is no later acquisition.

examples.answer: The lock history obeys basic 2PL.
examples.verification: An upgrade counts as acquisition, but it is legal here because it occurs before the first release.

examples.prompt: T acquires exclusive X and shared Y, writes X, releases Y, commits, then releases X. Classify basic and strict 2PL.
examples.strategy: Check the two phases → Check exclusive retention → Check shared retention

steps.title: Check the two phases
steps.explanation: Both acquisitions precede the first release, and no new lock is acquired afterward.

steps.title: Check exclusive retention
steps.explanation: Exclusive X remains held through commit, protecting the uncommitted write.

steps.title: Check shared retention
steps.explanation: Shared Y is released early, allowed by strict 2PL under the stated exclusive-lock convention but not rigorous all-lock retention.

examples.answer: It follows basic and strict 2PL, but not rigorous retention of all locks.
examples.verification: The early shared release does not expose X's uncommitted write because exclusive X remains owned until commit.

examples.prompt: T acquires exclusive X, downgrades it to shared X, then acquires shared Y. A student says no lock was fully unlocked, so 2PL holds. Is that correct?
examples.strategy: Interpret the downgrade → Mark the phase boundary → Inspect later acquisition

steps.title: Interpret the downgrade
steps.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared removes exclusive permission and counts as a release/demotion.

steps.title: Mark the phase boundary
steps.explanation: The downgrade begins the shrinking phase.

steps.title: Inspect later acquisition
steps.explanation: Acquiring shared Y afterward starts new growing work and violates 2PL.

examples.answer: The history violates basic 2PL.
examples.verification: A partial mode release still ends the acquisition phase; complete unlock is not required to trigger the rule.

tutorials.title: Lock compatibility can block transactions that obey 2PL
tutorials.body:
Concurrency control decides which simultaneous operations may proceed while maintaining the database's required isolation guarantees. Shared locks allow compatible readers of the same item; an exclusive lock conflicts with both shared and exclusive locks held by another transaction. A requested lock is not an acquired lock, so an operation that needs it must wait until permission is actually granted.
Two-phase locking imposes acquisition and release phases, but it does not remove all waiting or deadlocks. Transactions can each hold a lock and request another in opposite order while obeying their growing phase. A wait-for graph uses an edge from a waiting transaction to the transaction whose conflicting held lock blocks it. Under this exclusive single-owner lock model, a directed cycle identifies a deadlock. Resolve the blocked execution using the stated detector, victim abort or prevention policy; do not pretend that the conflicting operations have already executed. Serializability guarantees and progress guarantees answer different questions.

example.prompt: T1 holds exclusive X; T2 holds exclusive Y. Before releasing anything, T1 requests exclusive Y and T2 requests exclusive X. Both use basic 2PL. Explain the outcome.
example.strategy: Check first request → Check second request → Distinguish protocol from progress

steps.title: Check first request
steps.explanation: T1 cannot acquire Y because T2's exclusive lock conflicts. Add wait edge \(T_1\to T_2\); T1 keeps its existing X lock while waiting.

steps.title: Check second request
steps.explanation: T2 cannot acquire X because T1 holds it. Add \(T_2\to T_1\), completing a cycle.

steps.title: Distinguish protocol from progress
steps.explanation: Neither has released a lock, so both remain in the allowed growing phase of 2PL. Nevertheless neither can reach its release without satisfying a blocked request.

example.answer: Both follow the stated 2PL phase rule and become deadlocked; a resolution or prevention mechanism is required.
example.verification: Abort and roll back one chosen victim before releasing its locks, or require a universal X-before-Y order from the start. Basic 2PL's serializability guarantee does not imply freedom from this cycle.

depth.body: Concurrency control protects acceptable interleavings, and different protocols choose different points to reject or delay conflicting work. Locks block incompatible operations before they execute; timestamp rules can reject an operation that is too old; optimistic validation can discover an invalid read set before commit. Track successful actions separately from requested actions, since a blocked write has not changed data. Shared locks permit multiple readers but conflict with a writer, and upgrades require checking all remaining readers. These examples state the lock compatibility or validation rule explicitly rather than assuming every implementation uses the same policy. Show a state snapshot of owners, readers, observed versions and pending operations, then derive the permitted next action from that state.

examples.prompt: T1 and T2 hold shared locks on X. T3 requests an exclusive lock on X. T1 releases, while T2 keeps reading. Can T3 proceed?
examples.strategy: Inspect compatibility → Remove one blocker → Keep the writer waiting

steps.title: Inspect compatibility
steps.explanation: Exclusive X conflicts with each existing shared holder.

steps.title: Remove one blocker
steps.explanation: T1's release removes its shared lock but T2 remains.

steps.title: Keep the writer waiting
steps.explanation: T3 can acquire only after all conflicting shared holders release.

examples.answer: T3 remains blocked until T2 also releases.
examples.verification: An exclusive owner cannot coexist with even one other shared owner; counting the remaining reader supplies the decision.

examples.prompt: An optimistic transaction reads X=5 at version 7. Another transaction commits X=9 and increments its version to 8. Validation requires every read version unchanged. May the first commit?
examples.strategy: Record the read snapshot → Inspect current metadata → Apply validation

steps.title: Record the read snapshot
steps.explanation: The transaction's read set contains X at version 7.

steps.title: Inspect current metadata
steps.explanation: Committed X now has version 8.

steps.title: Apply validation
steps.explanation: Version mismatch violates the unchanged-read rule, so abort or retry before committing.

examples.answer: The first transaction fails validation and must retry or abort.
examples.verification: The check compares versions, not whether its final write happens to look reasonable; the committed update supplies an explicit conflict witness.

examples.prompt: T1 holds shared X and requests upgrade to exclusive X while T2 still holds shared X. Does ownership of one shared lock make the upgrade immediately legal?
examples.strategy: Distinguish modes → Check other owners → Delay the upgrade

steps.title: Distinguish modes
steps.explanation: T1's shared permission permits reads, not an exclusive write.

steps.title: Check other owners
steps.explanation: T2's shared lock conflicts with T1's requested exclusive mode.

steps.title: Delay the upgrade
steps.explanation: T1 waits under the specified compatibility rule until the other shared holder leaves.

examples.answer: The upgrade must wait; holding a shared lock is not exclusive ownership.
examples.verification: If T2 releases, the incompatible other-reader set becomes empty and the upgrade can then be granted.

tutorials.title: Four ACID guarantees apply to different parts of a transfer
tutorials.body:
ACID separates four transaction guarantees. Atomicity treats a transaction's operations as one all-or-nothing unit. Consistency requires a successful transaction and constraint enforcement to preserve the database's declared invariants. Isolation governs what concurrent transactions may observe, with serializable isolation presenting an effect equivalent to a permitted serial order. Durability preserves committed effects after failures within the system's stated guarantee.
The properties are related but cannot replace one another. Recovery can undo a partial debit without proving the transfer amount was valid. An application bug can violate a business invariant even when its writes are atomic and durable. Isolation levels weaker than serializability may permit particular anomalies, so an observation rule must name the guarantee being assumed. To classify a scenario, locate whether it concerns an incomplete operation, an invariant, concurrent visibility or a committed result after failure. A transaction's commit marks a boundary: a failure before it calls for atomic recovery, while losing its effects after a successful acknowledged commit challenges durability.

example.prompt: Initially A=500 and B=300. A transaction transfers 100 from A to B under serializable isolation. Its debit occurs before its credit; another transaction asks for A+B. Consider both a crash before commit and a crash after acknowledged commit.
example.strategy: Check the invariant → Protect partial execution → Protect the committed state

steps.title: Check the invariant
steps.explanation: A completed valid transfer preserves total funds, illustrating consistency of the transaction logic.

steps.title: Protect partial execution
steps.explanation: Before commit, the debit and credit form one atomic unit. A failed transfer must be undone; serializable observers must obtain a total equivalent to a serial state, rather than treating the intermediate 700 as a completed transfer.

steps.title: Protect the committed state
steps.explanation: After a successfully acknowledged commit, recovery retains balances 400 and 400 under the durability guarantee. It does not revert a completed transfer simply because a later crash occurs.

example.answer: Atomicity handles incomplete effects; consistency preserves 800; serializable isolation protects concurrent observations; durability retains the committed 400/400 state.
example.verification: Both valid serial orders for the total-reading transaction yield 800. A post-commit recovery returning 500/300 would preserve the sum but still fail durability, demonstrating that the guarantees differ.

depth.body: ACID claims should be tested at concrete failure boundaries. Atomicity concerns all effects of one incomplete unit, durability concerns effects after an acknowledged commit, consistency depends on declared invariants and correct logic, and isolation governs concurrent observations. Logging rules support recovery but do not by themselves make faulty business logic correct. A valid committed transaction can still be reported incorrectly to a concurrent reader under weak isolation. These examples assume explicit transactional guarantees, protected database state, and the named failure timing. Identify the exact observation or surviving state that challenges a property, rather than answering every scenario with the whole acronym. Distinguishing precommit undo from postcommit preservation is especially useful because the two require opposite recovery outcomes.

examples.prompt: An atomic transaction inserts header H and two required detail rows, then aborts before completion. What should the final database contain from that transaction?
examples.strategy: Identify one unit → Locate the abort boundary → Apply all-or-nothing recovery

steps.title: Identify one unit
steps.explanation: Header and both details belong to the same transaction.

steps.title: Locate the abort boundary
steps.explanation: No successful commit occurred.

steps.title: Apply all-or-nothing recovery
steps.explanation: Remove every effect of this unit, including any header or detail already inserted.

examples.answer: None of that transaction's inserted rows survive.
examples.verification: Leaving H alone would expose a partial unit; durability does not protect an uncommitted insertion.

examples.prompt: A write-ahead log must durably store update log records before their data pages, and the commit record before acknowledging commit. Data pages are still old at a crash after acknowledgment. Is recovery allowed to forget the update?
examples.strategy: Use the ordering rule → Inspect old data pages → Redo committed work

steps.title: Use the ordering rule
steps.explanation: The acknowledged commit guarantees durable commit and preceding update records.

steps.title: Inspect old data pages
steps.explanation: Old pages indicate pending propagation, not absence of a committed transaction.

steps.title: Redo committed work
steps.explanation: Recovery uses durable log information to restore the committed effects.

examples.answer: No; durability requires recovering the acknowledged committed update.
examples.verification: The log survives by the explicit ordering rule, supplying recovery information even though data-page flushing lagged.

examples.prompt: A database declares a nonnegative account-balance invariant, but its check is absent in this hypothetical schema. Application logic atomically commits a negative balance. Does atomicity imply consistency?
examples.strategy: Inspect the unit outcome → Test the invariant → Separate guarantees

steps.title: Inspect the unit outcome
steps.explanation: All writes can succeed together, so atomicity alone may hold.

steps.title: Test the invariant
steps.explanation: A negative committed balance violates the declared nonnegative rule.

steps.title: Separate guarantees
steps.explanation: All-or-nothing execution does not prove that the committed logic preserves required invariants.

examples.answer: No; atomicity cannot establish consistency of incorrect or unenforced logic.
examples.verification: Undoing a partial write and validating a completed value are different checks; the final negative state is the explicit consistency violation.

lessons.title: Layering, switching and network performance
lessons.intuition: A network separates services into layers so each solves a manageable part of delivery. Packets share infrastructure, while circuits reserve capacity. Delay depends on several physical and queueing effects, so bandwidth and latency are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Layers and encapsulation
sections.body: An application message becomes transport data, then a network packet, then a link frame under common Internet layering. Each layer adds addressing/control information appropriate to its scope. A router forwards network-layer packets; a typical Ethernet switch forwards link-layer frames. End-to-end services and per-link services solve different problems.

sections.title: Switching models
sections.body: Circuit switching reserves a route or channel allocation, potentially with setup overhead and unused reserved capacity. Packet switching shares links among packets and can queue under load. Datagram packets can be routed independently; a virtual circuit establishes logical forwarding state before transfer, typically using a label on subsequent packets. A logical virtual circuit is not necessarily a physically reserved circuit.

sections.title: Delay and throughput
sections.body: Transmission delay=L/R for L bits on rate R; propagation delay=distance/signal speed. Processing and queueing add further delay. Store-and-forward requires a full packet before forwarding in the basic model. Bottleneck link rate constrains sustained throughput. With multiple packets and links, serialization can be pipelined; don’t multiply entire end-to-end latency by packet count automatically.

sections.title: Serialization, propagation and pipeline overlap
sections.body: A link serializes a packet by placing its bits onto the medium over L/R seconds. Once a bit is launched, propagation carries it across the link over distance/speed seconds. Doubling packet length doubles serialization but does not change an individual bit’s propagation delay. A store-and-forward router must receive the complete packet before starting its outgoing serialization. Across equal-rate links, successive packets can overlap on different links; the first packet pays the full path serialization, while later packets emerge at the bottleneck packet interval under the simplified no-queuing model. Routers replace link-layer framing for the next hop while forwarding toward the network-layer destination. Circuit setup and reserved capacity belong to a different service model than ordinary statistical multiplexing.

examples.prompt: Send a 1500-byte packet over 12 Mbps

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Convert to bits: \(1500\cdot8=12000\). The rate is given in bits per second, so leaving packet size in bytes would undercount time by a factor of eight.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Transmission delay=\(\frac{12000}{12\cdot10^6}=0.001\) s. Mbps uses decimal millions here; the resulting quotient is in seconds.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: That is 1 ms, excluding propagation and queueing. This calculation concerns serialization only. Distance or router delays cannot be inferred from packet size and link rate alone.

examples.strategy: Convert packet bytes to bits, then divide by bit rate.
examples.answer: That is 1 ms, excluding propagation and queueing.
examples.verification: 12,000 bits at 12,000,000 bits/s is 1/1000 s=1 ms, with consistent dimensions.

examples.prompt: Two store-and-forward links at the same rate, no other delay
steps: The first packet needs one transmission time on each link, total 2t.
For N packets, after the first link finishes one it can send the next while the next link forwards the previous.
Completion is (N+1)t for two equal links under these assumptions, not 2Nt.

pitfalls: Convert bytes to bits before dividing by bit rate.
Faster bandwidth does not reduce propagation distance.

checks.prompt: A 1000-byte packet uses an 8 Mbps link. What is transmission delay in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Convert bytes to bits.

checks.prompt: Propagation distance is 600 km and speed 200000 km/s. What is propagation delay in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Divide distance by speed and convert seconds.

lessons.concept: A network separates services into layers so each solves a manageable part of delivery. Packets share infrastructure, while circuits reserve capacity. Delay depends on several physical and queueing effects, so bandwidth and latency are not interchangeable.
lessons.method:
Layering divides communication responsibilities into interfaces. An upper layer uses a lower layer’s service without exposing every implementation detail; peer protocols describe behavior between corresponding layers across hosts. Application messages can be carried in transport segments, network packets and link frames, each adding its own control information.
A router forwards network packets between links and normally constructs new link framing for the next hop. Link-layer destination identifies a neighbor on that link, while the packet’s network destination generally identifies the remote host. Transport ports distinguish application endpoints at a host. These address roles should not be merged into one undifferentiated “destination.”
Encapsulation adds headers and sometimes trailers, so payload size at one layer differs from total size at the next. MTU is a link/network packet limit under the stated context, not automatically the application-message limit. GATE traces should identify which devices inspect which headers and when addresses change. Layering is a design abstraction, so protocol-specific exceptions such as tunneling or NAT need their stated rules. Circuit switching establishes a communication path with reserved resources for a session, paying setup before transfer and possibly wasting reservation during idle periods. Packet switching divides data into packets sharing link capacity statistically; queues and variable delay can arise under contention. A datagram service forwards packets independently using destination routing information.
A virtual circuit is a connection-oriented packet-switched arrangement: setup establishes state and a path/label relationship, after which packets follow that connection’s forwarding context. It is not automatically a dedicated physical circuit with guaranteed bandwidth. Labels can be locally meaningful and change between hops.
Compare setup delay, per-packet header/state, utilization and failure behavior using the model given. Statistical sharing can improve average utilization without guaranteeing zero delay. Store-and-forward means an entire packet is received before forwarding, while other switching implementations can have different timing. GATE questions often distinguish reserved resources from merely maintaining a logical connection. Transmission delay is L/R for L bits at R bits per second; it is the time to put the packet onto a link. Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed and concerns travel after a bit is launched. Queuing waits for service and processing covers local handling. End-to-end delay sums relevant path events, accounting for overlap where the model permits it.
Throughput is delivered data per time and is limited by bottlenecks, while latency is one item’s elapsed time. A bandwidth-delay product estimates bits in flight during a specified propagation/round-trip interval. Unit conversion matters: packet bytes need multiplying by eight when rates use bits/s.
Across equal-rate store-and-forward links, the first packet pays transmission on every link, while later packets can pipeline across them. Do not multiply single-packet end-to-end serialization by packet count when transfers overlap. Queue delay requires supplied load or a model; it cannot be deduced from length and rate alone. Keep one-way delay separate from RTT. Circuit switching establishes a path and reserves the stated transmission resources before a session sends its data. A reserved rate is a capacity allocation, not the number of useful bits the sender must transmit continuously. An idle session can retain its reservation, preventing another session from using that capacity under the supplied model. This distinguishes resource reservation from a virtual circuit that merely installs packet-forwarding state.
For a numerical problem, separate setup, data serialization and propagation. If setup completes before transfer starts, its delay adds to the transfer time. Serialization of L bits at reserved rate R takes L/R seconds. Add propagation only when given; do not invent packet headers or store-and-forward delays for a circuit model that excludes them.
For simultaneous reservations on a link, compare the sum of reserved rates with link capacity. A session's average useful rate can be smaller than its reservation because it pauses. Verify time units and capacity independently: fitting the data in a time interval does not establish that an additional reservation is available. Packet switching divides a message into independently transmitted packets that share link capacity with other traffic. A store-and-forward router receives a complete packet before sending that packet onward. It can receive a later packet on one link while transmitting an earlier packet on a different link, provided the model supplies independent interfaces. This overlap is the source of packet pipelining.
Draw one timeline for each link. The first packet pays serialization on every store-and-forward link, while later packets can follow at the bottleneck's packet interval. For N equal packets across k equal-rate links, with no other delays or contention, completion takes (N+k−1)L/R. This expression assumes packet length L includes all modeled transmitted bits.
Packet switching does not promise an exclusive rate for each application. Queues, headers, unequal rates and other traffic change this simple timeline and must be included when specified. Compare an actual sequence of packet completions instead of multiplying a single packet's end-to-end time by N, which would incorrectly discard permitted overlap. An application message becomes transport data, then a network packet, then a link frame under common Internet layering. Each layer adds addressing/control information appropriate to its scope. A router forwards network-layer packets; a typical Ethernet switch forwards link-layer frames. End-to-end services and per-link services solve different problems. Circuit switching reserves a route or channel allocation, potentially with setup overhead and unused reserved capacity. Packet switching shares links among packets and can queue under load. Datagram packets can be routed independently; a virtual circuit establishes logical forwarding state before transfer, typically using a label on subsequent packets. A logical virtual circuit is not necessarily a physically reserved circuit. Transmission delay=L/R for L bits on rate R; propagation delay=distance/signal speed. Processing and queueing add further delay. Store-and-forward requires a full packet before forwarding in the basic model. Bottleneck link rate constrains sustained throughput. With multiple packets and links, serialization can be pipelined; don’t multiply entire end-to-end latency by packet count automatically. A link serializes a packet by placing its bits onto the medium over L/R seconds. Once a bit is launched, propagation carries it across the link over distance/speed seconds. Doubling packet length doubles serialization but does not change an individual bit’s propagation delay. A store-and-forward router must receive the complete packet before starting its outgoing serialization. Across equal-rate links, successive packets can overlap on different links; the first packet pays the full path serialization, while later packets emerge at the bottleneck packet interval under the simplified no-queuing model. Routers replace link-layer framing for the next hop while forwarding toward the network-layer destination. Circuit setup and reserved capacity belong to a different service model than ordinary statistical multiplexing. Think of a layer as offering a service while carrying its own addressing and control information. Encapsulation changes the unit whose length is being measured: application bytes become transport payload, then network payload, then link payload. Work outward through the headers rather than counting every header repeatedly. At a forwarding boundary, ask which unit the device terminates and reconstructs. A plain Ethernet switch forwards a frame, whereas an IP router removes one link envelope and builds another. These exercises exclude tunnels, NAT, optional headers and physical coding unless explicitly supplied; those mechanisms can change the otherwise simple address and size trace. A virtual circuit combines packet transfer with installed connection state. A forwarding entry associates an incoming interface and local label with an outgoing interface and possibly a different label. The same numeric label can be reused on different links when lookup includes the interface. Trace that tuple at every hop rather than assuming one globally meaningful identifier. Setup determines forwarding context, but bandwidth reservation, reliability and recovery are independent supplied guarantees. A broken link can invalidate the established path even if the end host's destination address remains unchanged. These examples use locally significant labels and explicit setup state, without implying dedicated physical capacity. Latency measures one item's elapsed journey, while throughput measures sustained delivered data per time. They respond differently to link speed, distance and protocol waiting. Serialization depends on bits divided by bit rate; propagation depends on distance divided by signal speed. A large bandwidth-delay product means a link can carry many bits simultaneously without making each bit propagate faster. For stop-and-wait, the sender's idle acknowledgment wait can dominate utilization even on a fast link. Keep complete cycle times distinct from extra penalties and specify whether the given delay is one-way or round trip before calculating. Decimal SI units are used below. Reservation and useful transmission are separate accounting problems. A circuit can hold a share of every traversed link even while its application is silent. Admission therefore depends on the smallest available capacity along the complete path, not on one link's free rate or recent average traffic. Once admitted, transfer time uses the reserved end-to-end rate plus the explicitly serial setup and propagation components. When comparing a circuit with another service, write both complete delay expressions and solve their inequality; setup can make small transfers slower despite a better sustained rate. Decimal Mbps denotes millions of bits per second in these exercises. Packet completion is governed by service order and available interfaces. On a single nonpreemptive link, queued packets serialize one after another. Across independent store-and-forward links, different packets can occupy different links simultaneously, but a later link cannot start a packet before its full arrival or before finishing earlier queued work. Use start=max(arrival, previous completion), then add that link's serialization duration. Packetization can reduce multi-hop completion through overlap while increasing transmitted bytes through repeated headers. It does not automatically improve a one-link transfer with no overlap opportunity. These models use FIFO queues, no propagation and no competing traffic unless stated otherwise.

gateGuide.recognize: Distinguish application messages, transport segments, network packets and link frames. Delay terms are additive only along the modeled path.
method: Identify each layer’s addressing and service, then trace encapsulation across routers.
Separate serialization from propagation, queuing and processing.
For store-and-forward links account for full packet reception before forwarding; for pipelined multiple packets separate first-packet latency from steady throughput.

traps.claim: Propagation delay grows with packet size
traps.why: It depends on distance and propagation speed; serialization depends on packet length and link rate.

traps.claim: Every layer uses the same destination address
traps.why: Link destination is normally the next hop; network destination usually remains the remote host.

formulas.meaning: L bits at R bits/s.
Distance d and signal speed s in consistent units.
Sum over modeled hops; queuing must be supplied or modeled.

example.prompt: A host sends to a remote host via a router on the local Ethernet.
example.strategy: Network destination → Local link destination → Router forwarding

steps.title: Network destination
steps.explanation: The IP packet names the remote destination host.

steps.title: Local link destination
steps.explanation: The first frame names the router’s local interface, obtained through the appropriate neighbor-resolution mechanism.

steps.title: Router forwarding
steps.explanation: The router chooses the next hop and builds a frame for its outgoing link.

example.answer: First-hop link destination is the router, while IP destination is the remote host.
example.verification: The remote host’s link address is not directly used on an unrelated local Ethernet.

depth.body: Think of a layer as offering a service while carrying its own addressing and control information. Encapsulation changes the unit whose length is being measured: application bytes become transport payload, then network payload, then link payload. Work outward through the headers rather than counting every header repeatedly. At a forwarding boundary, ask which unit the device terminates and reconstructs. examples.prompt: A TCP application sends 1000 bytes. TCP and IPv4 headers are 20 bytes each; Ethernet adds a 14-byte header and 4-byte FCS. Exclude padding, preamble and interframe gap. Find each encapsulated length.
examples.strategy: Transport unit → Network unit → Link unit

steps.title: Transport unit
steps.explanation: TCP encloses the application payload once.

steps.title: Network unit
steps.explanation: The IP payload includes the complete TCP segment.

steps.title: Link unit
steps.explanation: Ethernet encloses the IP packet and appends its check field.

examples.answer: TCP segment 1020 bytes; IP packet 1040; Ethernet frame 1058.
examples.verification: Added overhead is 58 bytes, and 1000+58 independently reproduces the final length.

examples.prompt: An IPv4 path MTU is 1500 bytes. TCP has a 32-byte header and IPv4 a 20-byte header. The sender avoids IP fragmentation. What maximum application payload fits in one segment, and does an Ethernet header reduce this IP MTU budget?
examples.strategy: Identify the budget → Remove network overhead → Remove transport overhead

steps.title: Identify the budget
steps.explanation: The 1500-byte limit applies to the complete IP packet, not its Ethernet envelope.

steps.title: Remove network overhead
steps.explanation: This is the maximum TCP segment length.

steps.title: Remove transport overhead
steps.explanation: The remaining bytes can hold application data; Ethernet overhead is outside the stated IP budget.

examples.answer: Maximum application payload 1448 bytes; Ethernet does not further reduce the stated IP MTU budget.
examples.verification: 1448+32+20=1500, while adding link overhead produces a larger frame rather than an oversized IP packet.

examples.prompt: A plain learning Ethernet switch forwards a frame between two ports on one LAN. No router, NAT or tunnel is involved. Must it replace the IP destination with the next port’s address?
examples.strategy: Locate the forwarding layer → Identify the IP role → Apply the assumptions

steps.title: Locate the forwarding layer
steps.explanation: The switch selects a port using a link-layer destination address.

steps.title: Identify the IP role
steps.explanation: The enclosed IP destination names the network-layer endpoint; a port number is not a replacement IP address.

steps.title: Apply the assumptions
steps.explanation: Ordinary frame switching does not rewrite the IP destination merely because the outgoing physical port differs.

examples.answer: No; changing switch ports does not require changing the packet’s IP destination.
examples.verification: The destination host can receive the same addressed IP packet after several LAN switches, demonstrating separation of link forwarding from network addressing.

tutorials.title: Circuit, datagram and virtual-circuit switching
tutorials.body:

A virtual circuit is a connection-oriented packet-switched arrangement: setup establishes state and a path/label relationship, after which packets follow that connection’s forwarding context. It is not automatically a dedicated physical circuit with guaranteed bandwidth. Labels can be locally meaningful and change between hops.

GATE questions often distinguish reserved resources from merely maintaining a logical connection.

example.prompt: A virtual circuit is established through routers A,B,C. Does this prove an exclusive link reservation?
example.strategy: Connection state → Packet sharing → Guarantee check

steps.title: Connection state
steps.explanation: Setup installs forwarding information for the logical path.

steps.title: Packet sharing
steps.explanation: Other circuits/datagrams may still share the same physical links under the service model.

steps.title: Guarantee check
steps.explanation: A reservation or QoS contract must be explicitly supplied to infer exclusive capacity.

example.answer: A virtual circuit alone does not prove dedicated bandwidth.
example.verification: Logical path establishment and physical resource reservation are distinct concepts.

depth.body: A virtual circuit combines packet transfer with installed connection state. A forwarding entry associates an incoming interface and local label with an outgoing interface and possibly a different label. The same numeric label can be reused on different links when lookup includes the interface. Trace that tuple at every hop rather than assuming one globally meaningful identifier. Setup determines forwarding context, but bandwidth reservation, reliability and recovery are independent supplied guarantees. A broken link can invalidate the established path even if the end host's destination address remains unchanged. These examples use locally significant labels and explicit setup state, without implying dedicated physical capacity.

examples.prompt: Router R maps incoming(port 1, label 7) to outgoing(port 3, label 12). The next router S maps incoming(port 2, label 12) to outgoing(port 4, label 5). Trace one packet.
examples.strategy: Lookup at R → Rewrite for the next link → Lookup at S

steps.title: Lookup at R
steps.explanation: The incoming interface and label identify R’s established circuit entry.

steps.title: Rewrite for the next link
steps.explanation: R forwards on port 3 with local label 12, rather than retaining 7 everywhere.

steps.title: Lookup at S
steps.explanation: S uses its incoming port 2 and label 12 entry, then sends on port 4 with label 5.

examples.answer: Labels along the trace are 7→12→5; the forwarding context determines the path.
examples.verification: Every transmitted label equals the receiving router’s stated lookup label; no globally constant label was required.

examples.prompt: A router has entries(port 1, label 4)→port 3 and(port 2, label 4)→port 5. Two established circuits arrive with label 4 on the two incoming ports. Is the table ambiguous, and how many lookup contexts exist?
examples.strategy: Identify the complete key → Compare both packets → Forward independently

steps.title: Identify the complete key
steps.explanation: The model uses incoming interface together with the label.

steps.title: Compare both packets
steps.explanation: Their numeric labels match but their input interfaces differ, giving two distinct keys.

steps.title: Forward independently
steps.explanation: The port 1 packet uses port 3; the port 2 packet uses port 5.

examples.answer: The table is unambiguous and contains two distinct lookup contexts.
examples.verification: If lookup ignored the interface, the two destinations would conflict; including the stipulated interface resolves the apparent collision.

examples.prompt: A virtual-circuit service installs a fixed path but explicitly offers shared queues and best-effort delivery. A student concludes that packets cannot be dropped because the connection exists. Is that valid?
examples.strategy: List the stated guarantee → Examine queue behavior → Evaluate the conclusion

steps.title: List the stated guarantee
steps.explanation: Installed path state tells routers how to forward matching packets.

steps.title: Examine queue behavior
steps.explanation: Shared finite queues can overflow under contention; path state does not create unlimited buffering.

steps.title: Evaluate the conclusion
steps.explanation: No loss-free or reservation contract was supplied, so connection orientation alone cannot imply reliable delivery.

examples.answer: The conclusion is invalid; an established best-effort virtual circuit can lose packets.
examples.verification: A packet arriving at a full queue provides a counterexample consistent with every supplied service guarantee.

tutorials.body:

Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed and concerns travel after a bit is launched. Queuing waits for service and processing covers local handling. example.prompt: Two equal links, each taking t to serialize one packet, send three packets with no other delays.
example.strategy: First packet → Overlap → Final completion

steps.title: First packet
steps.explanation: It exits link one at t and link two at 2t.

steps.title: Overlap
steps.explanation: Link one sends packet two while link two sends packet one.

steps.title: Final completion
steps.explanation: Packets two and three then exit at 3t and 4t.

example.answer: Total 4t, not 6t.
example.verification: Three transmissions occur on each link, but their timelines overlap across different links.

depth.body: Latency measures one item's elapsed journey, while throughput measures sustained delivered data per time. They respond differently to link speed, distance and protocol waiting. Serialization depends on bits divided by bit rate; propagation depends on distance divided by signal speed. A large bandwidth-delay product means a link can carry many bits simultaneously without making each bit propagate faster. For stop-and-wait, the sender's idle acknowledgment wait can dominate utilization even on a fast link. Keep complete cycle times distinct from extra penalties and specify whether the given delay is one-way or round trip before calculating. Decimal SI units are used below.

examples.prompt: A 1000-bit packet crosses one 50 Mbps link of length 100 km with signal speed 2×10⁸ m/s. No queue or processing delays exist. Find last-bit arrival time after transmission begins.
examples.strategy: Serialize → Propagate → Add the serial stages

steps.title: Serialize
steps.explanation: This is the time to launch the last bit.

steps.title: Propagate
steps.explanation: Every bit then travels the link distance.

steps.title: Add the serial stages
steps.explanation: Last-bit arrival includes its launch delay and propagation.

examples.answer: Last bit arrives after 520 μs.
examples.verification: The first bit arrives after 500 μs, and the last follows 20 μs later, independently reproducing 520.

examples.prompt: Stop-and-wait sends 8000 data bits over 8 Mbps. One-way propagation is 4 ms; ACK serialization and processing are negligible. There is no loss. Find utilization and useful throughput.
examples.strategy: Data transmission → Complete the feedback cycle → Compute delivery rate

steps.title: Data transmission
steps.explanation: One millisecond launches the packet.

steps.title: Complete the feedback cycle
steps.explanation: The ACK returns after the forward and reverse propagation legs.

steps.title: Compute delivery rate
steps.explanation: Only the data-launch portion keeps the sender transmitting.

examples.answer: Utilization 1/9≈11.11%; useful throughput≈0.889 Mbps.
examples.verification: Multiplying link rate 8 Mbps by 1/9 gives the same throughput; omitting the return leg would exaggerate utilization.

examples.prompt: A 100 Mbps link has one-way propagation 10 ms. Another link doubles its bit rate but has the same distance and signal speed. Does this halve propagation, and how does one-way bandwidth-delay product change?
examples.strategy: Locate the propagation inputs → Compute initial in-flight capacity → Increase rate

steps.title: Locate the propagation inputs
steps.explanation: Distance and signal speed are unchanged, so propagation remains 10 ms.

steps.title: Compute initial in-flight capacity
steps.explanation: Bandwidth-delay product counts bits launched during the one-way delay.

steps.title: Increase rate
steps.explanation: The pipeline can contain twice as many bits without any bit traveling faster.

examples.answer: Propagation stays 10 ms; one-way bandwidth-delay product doubles from 1 to 2 Mbit.
examples.verification: Rate affects serialization and pipeline occupancy, whereas the supplied propagation formula contains no link bit rate.

tutorials.title: Circuit switching: reservation, setup and transfer
tutorials.body:
Circuit switching establishes a path and reserves the stated transmission resources before a session sends its data. A reserved rate is a capacity allocation, not the number of useful bits the sender must transmit continuously. An idle session can retain its reservation, preventing another session from using that capacity under the supplied model. This distinguishes resource reservation from a virtual circuit that merely installs packet-forwarding state.
For a numerical problem, separate setup, data serialization and propagation. If setup completes before transfer starts, its delay adds to the transfer time. Verify time units and capacity independently: fitting the data in a time interval does not establish that an additional reservation is available.

example.prompt: A 10 Mbps circuit needs 40 ms setup, then sends 1,000,000 bits. Ignore propagation. Its link has capacity 30 Mbps and two other 10 Mbps reservations.
example.strategy: Convert the data time → Include setup → Check reservations

steps.title: Convert the data time
steps.explanation: The reserved circuit rate determines serialization.

steps.title: Include setup
steps.explanation: Setup precedes the 100 ms data transfer.

steps.title: Check reservations
steps.explanation: The three sessions occupy all modeled reservation capacity; another 10 Mbps circuit does not fit.

example.answer: Transfer finishes after 140 ms; no fourth 10 Mbps reservation fits.
example.verification: The data uses its full reserved rate for 100 ms, while session setup accounts for the remaining 40 ms.

depth.body: Reservation and useful transmission are separate accounting problems. A circuit can hold a share of every traversed link even while its application is silent. Admission therefore depends on the smallest available capacity along the complete path, not on one link's free rate or recent average traffic. Once admitted, transfer time uses the reserved end-to-end rate plus the explicitly serial setup and propagation components. When comparing a circuit with another service, write both complete delay expressions and solve their inequality; setup can make small transfers slower despite a better sustained rate. Decimal Mbps denotes millions of bits per second in these exercises.

examples.prompt: A circuit route traverses links with free capacities 12, 9 and 15 Mbps. Every admitted circuit reserves 3 Mbps on each link. How many additional identical circuits fit?
examples.strategy: Count per-link slots → Choose the bottleneck → Test the next request

steps.title: Count per-link slots
steps.explanation: A circuit must obtain capacity at every hop.

steps.title: Choose the bottleneck
steps.explanation: The middle link runs out first.

steps.title: Test the next request
steps.explanation: A fourth reservation fails even though the other links have room.

examples.answer: Three additional circuits fit.
examples.verification: After three admissions the middle link has zero spare capacity, while the other links retain 3 and 6 Mbps.

examples.prompt: For L data bits, circuit A takes 50 ms setup plus L/4 Mbps transfer. Service B takes 20 ms fixed delay plus L/2 Mbps transfer. Ignore other costs. Find the size where A becomes no slower.
examples.strategy: Write elapsed times → Solve the comparison → Find the threshold

steps.title: Write elapsed times
steps.explanation: Both include their supplied startup costs.

steps.title: Solve the comparison
steps.explanation: Move the faster circuit’s transfer term to the other side.

steps.title: Find the threshold
steps.explanation: At this size the saved serialization time offsets the extra setup.

examples.answer: A is no slower for L≥120, 000 bits.
examples.verification: At the threshold both times are 80 ms: A is 50+30 and B is 20+60 ms.

examples.prompt: A 20 Mbps link has five active circuit reservations of 4 Mbps each. Four applications are momentarily silent. Can a sixth 4 Mbps circuit be admitted without changing existing reservations?
examples.strategy: Count reserved capacity → Distinguish utilization → Test admission

steps.title: Count reserved capacity
steps.explanation: Admission uses commitments, including silent sessions.

steps.title: Distinguish utilization
steps.explanation: Current useful traffic can be only 4 Mbps while reserved capacity remains 20 Mbps.

steps.title: Test admission
steps.explanation: The sixth commitment exceeds link capacity.

examples.answer: No under the reservation model; silence does not release a circuit.
examples.verification: If the four idle circuits were explicitly torn down, the admission result would change; merely observing no data is insufficient.

example.prompt: Split 1,000,000 bits into four equal packets over two 10 Mbps store-and-forward links. Ignore headers, propagation and other traffic.
example.strategy: Packet transmission time → Start the pipeline → Finish all packets

steps.title: Packet transmission time
steps.explanation: Every packet occupies either link for 25 ms.

steps.title: Start the pipeline
steps.explanation: Packet 1 uses link one during 0–25 ms and link two during 25–50 ms; packet 2 can use link one during 25–50 ms.

steps.title: Finish all packets
steps.explanation: Packets leave link two at 50, 75, 100 and 125 ms.

example.answer: The message finishes in 125 ms.
example.verification: Each link serializes four packets for 100 ms, and the second link starts 25 ms after the first.

Across independent store-and-forward links, different packets can occupy different links simultaneously, but a later link cannot start a packet before its full arrival or before finishing earlier queued work. examples.prompt: Three 2000-bit packets arrive together at a FIFO1 Mbps link at t=0. No other delays occur. Find their completion and queue-wait times.
examples.strategy: Service duration → Schedule FIFO → Separate wait and completion

steps.title: Service duration
steps.explanation: Each packet occupies the link for two milliseconds.

steps.title: Schedule FIFO
steps.explanation: Packet transmissions are 0–2, 2–4 and 4–6 ms because the link serves one at a time.

steps.title: Separate wait and completion
steps.explanation: Waiting before service is 0, 2, 4 ms; complete departure is 2, 4, 6 ms.

examples.answer: Completion times 2, 4, 6 ms; queue waits 0, 2, 4 ms.
examples.verification: Three service intervals total 6 ms, and each completion equals its queue wait plus 2 ms.

examples.prompt: Three equal packets take 1 ms on link A and 2 ms on link B. A store-and-forward router connects the independent FIFO links; all packets are ready at t=0. Ignore propagation. Find the last departure.
examples.strategy: Arrive at the router → Schedule the slower link → Finish the pipeline

steps.title: Arrive at the router
steps.explanation: Link A finishes the packets at 1, 2 and 3 ms.

steps.title: Schedule the slower link
steps.explanation: B serves packet 1 during 1–3 ms; packet 2 arrives at 2 but waits, then runs 3–5 ms.

steps.title: Finish the pipeline
steps.explanation: Packet 3 arrived at 3 and follows packet 2 during 5–7 ms.

examples.answer: The final packet leaves at 7 ms.
examples.verification: B sends three packets for 6 ms starting at 1 ms, so 1+6=7; multiplying three end-to-end 3 ms delays would incorrectly give 9.

examples.prompt: Send 1000 payload bytes over one 8 Mbps link. A single packet has a 20-byte header; splitting into two 500-byte packets adds 20 bytes to each. Ignore all other costs. Does splitting reduce completion time?
examples.strategy: Count the unsplit wire data → Count split wire data → Convert link time

steps.title: Count the unsplit wire data
steps.explanation: Only one header is paid.

steps.title: Count split wire data
steps.explanation: The payload stays the same but a second header is transmitted.

steps.title: Convert link time
steps.explanation: At 8 Mbps each byte takes one microsecond and there is no second-link pipeline.

examples.answer: Splitting is 20 μs slower here.
examples.verification: The extra 20-byte header explains exactly the time difference; multi-hop overlap was explicitly absent.

lessons.title: Error detection, MAC and Ethernet
lessons.prerequisite: Binary polynomials, frames and shared media.
lessons.intuition: The link layer moves frames over one link and manages its local addressing and error checks. Error detection identifies some corrupt frames; it is not automatically error correction. Shared-medium access rules matter only where senders actually contend for the same medium.

sections.title: Parity, checksums and CRC
sections.body: A parity bit detects any odd number of bit flips but can miss an even number. Internet-style checksums use one’s-complement arithmetic. CRC treats bits as polynomial coefficients over GF(2): addition/subtraction is XOR. Append r zeros for a degree-r generator, divide, and append the r-bit remainder. A receiver divides the received codeword; a nonzero remainder detects an error.

sections.title: Medium access
sections.body: ALOHA transmits with probabilistic contention; carrier-sense protocols listen before transmitting. Classic half-duplex Ethernet uses CSMA/CD, detecting collisions and backing off. The minimum frame time must support collision detection over the collision domain under its physical assumptions. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has separate bidirectional links and does not use collision detection.

sections.title: Ethernet switching
sections.body: MAC addresses identify local link interfaces. A learning switch records the source MAC and ingress port. Known destination addresses are forwarded to the corresponding port; unknown destinations and relevant broadcasts are flooded according to VLAN/topology rules. Routers separate network-layer domains; a link switch does not usually choose routes by IP prefix.

sections.title: Why sequence-space bounds prevent ambiguity
sections.body: A sender may have multiple frames outstanding while acknowledgments are delayed. Sequence numbers wrap, so a delayed old frame must not be mistaken for a new frame with the same number. Selective repeat accepts and buffers a window of out-of-order frames; disjoint old and new windows require the usual half-sequence-space bound. Go-back-N’s receiver ordinarily accepts only the next expected frame, yielding a different maximum sender window. State those receiver models before using memorized bounds. CRC treats bitstrings as polynomials over GF(2), so subtraction is XOR without borrow. Appending r zeros multiplies data by xʳ; the division remainder produces a codeword divisible by the generator. Detection guarantees depend on the error polynomial and generator, not just the remainder’s length.

examples.prompt: Detect a single flipped bit with even parity

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Suppose data has an even number of 1s and parity bit 0. The sender chooses the parity bit so the complete protected word has an even number of ones.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: One flipped bit changes overall parity to odd. One bit flip changes the number of ones by plus or minus one, which reverses its parity.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The receiver detects mismatch, but cannot locate the bad bit from parity alone. Mismatch reports inconsistency but does not identify which of the possible bit positions changed.

examples.strategy: Evaluate parity detection separately from correction capability.
examples.answer: The receiver detects mismatch, but cannot locate the bad bit from parity alone.
examples.verification: Two flipped bits can restore even parity and escape detection; the result is a single-bit detection guarantee, not an arbitrary-error guarantee.

examples.prompt: CRC using data 1001 and generator 1011
steps: Generator degree is 3, so divide appended data 1001000 by 1011 using XOR.
First XOR gives 0010000; align again and XOR to get 0000110.
Remainder is 110; transmit 1001110. Dividing this codeword by 1011 gives zero remainder.

pitfalls: CRC division uses XOR without carries.
Modern full-duplex Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD.
revision: Degree-r CRC appends r check bits.
Switch learns source MAC, forwards by destination MAC.

checks.prompt: Which statement about modern full-duplex switched Ethernet is correct?
checks.hint: Separate full-duplex links from a shared half-duplex collision domain.
checks.explanation: Full-duplex switched Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD; classic half-duplex shared-medium Ethernet does.
options: It uses CSMA/CD on every link
It does not use collision detection in the classic shared-medium sense
It routes by longest IP prefix at every basic switch

checks.prompt: An even-parity codeword suffers exactly one bit flip. What is the number of parity violations detected?
checks.hint: One flip changes parity.
checks.explanation: The single parity check fails once; it detects but does not locate the error.

tutorials.title: Frames and error-detection capabilities
tutorials.body:
The data-link layer delivers frames across one link, defining framing boundaries, link addressing and error-detection/control behavior. A receiver must identify a complete frame despite an underlying stream of bits; schemes may use lengths, delimiter patterns and escaping/bit stuffing. Checksums combine words under a specified arithmetic rule; CRC uses polynomial divisibility. A detector can fail for some structured error patterns, so “redundant bits added” does not imply perfect detection or correction.

example.prompt: Even parity protects data 1011. Add parity and consider one or two bit flips.
example.strategy: Parity bit → One flip → Two flips

steps.title: Parity bit
steps.explanation: Data has three ones, so append 1 to make four ones.

steps.title: One flip
steps.explanation: The total parity becomes odd and the error is detected.

steps.title: Two flips
steps.explanation: Parity can remain even despite corrupted data, so detection is not guaranteed.

example.answer: Parity detects single flips but does not guarantee detection of arbitrary multi-bit errors.
example.verification: The parity mismatch cannot by itself locate which bit changed, so it is not a general correction scheme.

depth.body: An error detector adds constraints to a codeword so some altered patterns fall outside the legal set. Detection succeeds when the receiver's check distinguishes the corrupted word, not merely because redundant bits exist. Simple parity depends on the number of flipped bits modulo two; it cannot determine the flipped location or catch every multi-bit change. For a linear code, an error pattern that is itself an allowed zero-syndrome pattern can transform one legal codeword into another. Use exact bit strings to demonstrate an undetected error and distinguish detection capability from correction capability. These parity exercises use an appended even-parity bit and no additional checks.

examples.prompt: Append even parity to 10100, then inspect received 101001 after one parity-bit flip.
examples.strategy: Count the data ones → Form the legal word → Check reception

steps.title: Count the data ones
steps.explanation: 10100 contains two ones, so its correct appended parity bit is 0.

steps.title: Form the legal word
steps.explanation: The transmitted codeword is 101000 with even total parity.

steps.title: Check reception
steps.explanation: 101001 contains three ones, so its parity check fails and detects corruption.

examples.answer: Transmit 101000; received 101001 is detected as erroneous.
examples.verification: The supplied corruption changes one bit, which toggles the parity of the total protected word.

examples.prompt: Use separate even parity for each 4-bit row: data rows 1010 and 0111. Find both parity bits. Then one data bit in each row flips; do both row checks detect an error?
examples.strategy: Encode both rows → Track each row independently → Apply both checks

steps.title: Encode both rows
steps.explanation: 1010 has two ones and needs 0; 0111 has three ones and needs 1.

steps.title: Track each row independently
steps.explanation: Each row experiences one flip, so each row’s total parity toggles.

steps.title: Apply both checks
steps.explanation: Both protected rows now have odd parity even though the combined frame suffered two flips.

examples.answer: Row parity bits 0 and 1; both row checks detect their respective single flip.
examples.verification: Detection depends on the protected group: two total flips do not cancel when they occur in different independently checked rows.

examples.prompt: Even-parity word 1100 is transmitted. Its first two bits flip, producing 0000. Can parity detect the corruption or locate it?
examples.strategy: Check the original → Check the corrupted word → Interpret the result

steps.title: Check the original
steps.explanation: 1100 has two ones and is a legal even-parity word.

steps.title: Check the corrupted word
steps.explanation: 0000 has zero ones, also an even count.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The check passes despite two changed bits, and a passing parity check supplies no position information.

examples.answer: This two-bit corruption is undetected; parity cannot locate or correct it.
examples.verification: Both words satisfy the same parity constraint while representing different protected data, an explicit undetected-error counterexample.

tutorials.title: CRC polynomial division without carries
tutorials.body:
CRC interprets a bit string as a polynomial over GF(2), where addition/subtraction are XOR. A generator of degree r requires r check bits. Append r zero bits to the data, divide by the generator using aligned XOR, and attach the resulting r-bit remainder to the original data. The transmitted codeword then divides with zero remainder.
At reception, a nonzero remainder detects inconsistency. An error whose polynomial is divisible by the generator can evade detection, so exact guarantees depend on generator factors and error length. The conventional nonzero constant term ensures relevant trailing behavior. CRC is normally detection, not automatic correction.
Write each XOR alignment rather than using decimal integer division or subtraction with borrows. A generator’s bit length is r+1, while remainder width is r. Keep leading zeros in that remainder to preserve field width. GATE examples may ask the codeword, remainder or whether a supplied error pattern is detected; these are related but not identical tasks.

example.prompt: Data 1001, generator 1011. Compute the codeword.
example.strategy: Append zeros → XOR division → Transmit

steps.title: Append zeros
steps.explanation: Generator degree is three.

steps.title: XOR division
steps.explanation: Aligned divisions leave remainder 110, without arithmetic borrow.

steps.title: Transmit
steps.explanation: Replace appended zeros by the remainder.

example.verification: Dividing 1001110 by 1011 using XOR gives remainder zero, verifying construction.

depth.body: CRC arithmetic is polynomial arithmetic over two coefficients: addition and subtraction are XOR, with no decimal borrow. Each leading one determines where to align the generator before canceling that term. Keep the generator degree separate from its bit-string length, and retain leading zeros when recording the check field. Reception divides the complete protected word; zero remainder means the word satisfies the code constraint, not proof that no bits changed. An error polynomial divisible by the generator has zero syndrome and can escape detection. These small examples use a nonzero constant generator coefficient and direct augmented-data construction, excluding implementation-specific initial registers or final XOR conventions.

examples.prompt: Data bits are 1101 and generator 101 (degree 2). Construct the systematic CRC codeword using two appended zeros.
examples.strategy: Augment the message → Divide with aligned XOR → Attach the check bits

steps.title: Augment the message
steps.explanation: 1101 becomes 110100 before polynomial division.

steps.title: Divide with aligned XOR
steps.explanation: 110100 XOR101000 gives 011100; XOR010100 gives 001000; XOR001010 gives 000010, so remainder is 10.

steps.title: Attach the check bits
steps.explanation: Replace the two appended zeros with 10, yielding 110110.

examples.answer: CRC bits 10; codeword 110110.
examples.verification: Dividing 110110 by 101 produces zero remainder: the final residual 001010 cancels exactly.

examples.prompt: With generator 1011 (degree 3), determine whether a burst error polynomial 10100 is detected, without needing the original valid codeword.
examples.strategy: Use linearity → Align the generator → Interpret the check

steps.title: Use linearity
steps.explanation: A valid word has zero remainder, so reception’s syndrome is the error polynomial’s remainder.

steps.title: Align the generator
steps.explanation: 10100 XOR10110 leaves 00010, giving nonzero remainder 010.

steps.title: Interpret the check
steps.explanation: The altered word fails divisibility and the error is detected.

examples.answer: Detected; the error remainder is 010.
examples.verification: Polynomial division gives 10100=(10)(1011)+010 over GF(2), independently reproducing the nonzero syndrome.

examples.prompt: Generator 101 defines a degree 2 CRC. The error pattern is 1010, exactly the generator shifted left once. Is this nonzero error always detected?
examples.strategy: Factor the error → Compute the syndrome → Apply the receiver rule

steps.title: Factor the error
steps.explanation: Its polynomial is an exact multiple of the generator.

steps.title: Compute the syndrome
steps.explanation: 1010 divided by 101 has remainder 00.

steps.title: Apply the receiver rule
steps.explanation: A zero syndrome passes the CRC even though two protected bits have flipped.

examples.answer: This error is undetected.
examples.verification: XOR of any valid codeword with a multiple of g remains divisible by g; redundancy does not guarantee detection of every pattern.
