tutorials.title: TCP bytes, ACKs and receiver flow control
tutorials.body:
TCP provides an ordered byte stream, using sequence numbers to identify byte positions. A segment with sequence s and b data bytes covers s through s+b−1. A cumulative ACK normally names the next byte expected, not the last byte received; out-of-order data beyond a gap need not advance it. SYN and FIN each consume sequence space under the protocol.
Flow control protects receiver buffering through an advertised receive window rwnd. New data must fit the permitted outstanding region, subject also to sender congestion window cwnd. Thus use min(rwnd,cwnd) and subtract bytes already outstanding; window size is not automatically additional sending allowance.
Retransmitted data reuses its original byte numbering rather than becoming a new application message. TCP segmentation boundaries do not preserve application writes. In GATE, determine whether the question asks next ACK, total in-flight limit or unused sending allowance. Preserve bytes versus bits when combining a window with RTT or bandwidth, and note whether control flags are included in sequence arithmetic.

example.prompt: SEQ=1000, payload 200 bytes, no gaps or control flags. Then window limit 1000 with 600 outstanding.
example.strategy: Covered interval → Acknowledgment → New allowance

steps.title: Covered interval
steps.explanation: Bytes are 1000…1199 inclusive.

steps.title: Acknowledgment
steps.explanation: This is the next expected byte.

steps.title: New allowance
steps.explanation: Outstanding data already occupies the window.

example.answer: ACK 1200; new sending allowance 400 bytes.
example.verification: An ACK of 1199 would name the last delivered byte rather than TCP’s next-expected convention.

depth.body: TCP flow control protects the receiving endpoint's advertised capacity. The receive window refers to bytes relative to the acknowledgment position; already outstanding bytes consume part of the sender's allowed flight. New send allowance must also respect the congestion window, and negative remaining allowance means no ordinary new data rather than permission to send a negative amount. Sequence numbers count bytes modulo two to the thirty-second power, with SYN and FIN consuming positions under their separate rules. The examples exclude those flags when tracing pure data and distinguish an advertised zero window from permanent connection failure or an instruction to discard existing queued bytes.

examples.prompt: A data segment begins at sequence 500, carries 300 contiguous bytes and has no SYN or FIN. The receiver has all earlier bytes and receives this segment completely. Find its cumulative ACK.
examples.strategy: Number the received data → Apply next-expected semantics → Distinguish last-byte numbering

steps.title: Number the received data
steps.explanation: The segment covers sequence positions 500 through 799.

steps.title: Apply next-expected semantics
steps.explanation: Acknowledgment names the first byte not yet received in order.

steps.title: Distinguish last-byte numbering
steps.explanation: 799 is the last delivered position, not the cumulative ACK value.

examples.answer: ACK800.
examples.verification: The inclusive interval 799−500+1 contains 300 bytes, matching the payload and next position 800.

examples.prompt: The sender has rwnd=12000 bytes, cwnd=8000 bytes and 7500 outstanding bytes. Ignore other sender constraints. Find additional ordinary data allowance and the effect of an ACK retiring 2000 bytes without window changes.
examples.strategy: Choose the flight limit → Find current spare room → Retire acknowledged data

steps.title: Choose the flight limit
steps.explanation: Both receiver and network constraints must be satisfied.

steps.title: Find current spare room
steps.explanation: Existing unacknowledged bytes already consume space.

steps.title: Retire acknowledged data
steps.explanation: ACK progress releases flight capacity.

examples.answer: Initially 500 bytes; after that ACK2500 bytes.
examples.verification: The allowance grows by exactly the 2000 retired bytes because both limits remain unchanged.

examples.prompt: Pure TCP data starts at sequence 2³²−100 and contains 200 bytes. All arrives in order; no control flags consume sequence space. Is the next ACK2³²+100?
examples.strategy: Compute the unwrapped endpoint → Apply sequence-field width → Preserve byte accounting

steps.title: Compute the unwrapped endpoint
steps.explanation: This arithmetic locates the next position before encoding.

steps.title: Apply sequence-field width
steps.explanation: The wire field wraps modulo 2³².

steps.title: Preserve byte accounting
steps.explanation: The wrap changes the numeric representation, not the number of acknowledged bytes.

examples.answer: The encoded ACK is 100.
examples.verification: The segment spans 100 positions before the wrap and 100 after it, totaling the supplied 200 bytes.

tutorials.title: Congestion window, slow start and loss response
tutorials.body:
Congestion control limits sender load on the network through cwnd, separate from receiver capacity rwnd. Classic slow start increases cwnd roughly exponentially per RTT while acknowledgments arrive, then congestion avoidance grows more slowly under the specified variant. A threshold determines the transition. Timeout and duplicate-ACK recovery can trigger different reductions and retransmission behavior.
Exact rules depend on the TCP variant and acknowledgment model. Reno-style additive increase/multiplicative decrease is a common exercise, but modern congestion controllers may behave differently. A loss is evidence used by the algorithm, not proof that receiver memory is full. Flow control can constrain sending even with a large cwnd, and congestion control can constrain it with a large receive window.
Trace cwnd at well-defined RTT boundaries and specify MSS/byte units. Per-ACK increments and delayed acknowledgments can alter simplified growth assumptions. A window/RTT estimate is an upper bound also limited by link bandwidth, startup and loss. GATE problems supplying an algorithm’s exact recurrence should use those rules rather than an unsupported universal “TCP doubles forever.”

example.prompt: Simplified slow start begins at 1 MSS and doubles each complete RTT until reaching 8 MSS.
example.strategy: First RTT → Second RTT → Third RTT

steps.title: First RTT
steps.explanation: All modeled acknowledgments arrive without loss.

steps.title: Second RTT
steps.explanation: Apply the same growth rule.

steps.title: Third RTT
steps.explanation: The stated threshold is reached; later rules must be specified separately.

example.answer: After three modeled RTTs cwnd reaches 8 MSS.
example.verification: Receiver window can still cap actual in-flight data below cwnd; these values do not alone determine throughput.

tutorials.title: TCP congestion control: threshold growth and two loss responses
tutorials.body:
TCP congestion control uses a congestion window cwnd to limit outstanding data according to perceived network conditions. It is separate from the receiver's advertised window rwnd; the smaller applicable window can limit transmission. Simplified RTT exercises must specify their growth and loss rules because actual TCP implementations and acknowledgment patterns vary.
In this supplied Reno-style model, reaching the slow-start threshold ssthresh changes growth to one MSS per complete loss-free RTT. On three duplicate acknowledgments, set ssthresh to half the current window, enter fast recovery at ssthresh plus three MSS, and return cwnd to ssthresh when the specified new-data acknowledgment ends recovery. A timeout instead resets cwnd to one MSS while reducing ssthresh. These are the stated exercise rules, not a universal description of every congestion controller.
Record cwnd and ssthresh separately at each event. A loss reaction does not mean the receiver ran out of buffer space, and the temporary recovery window is not the later congestion-avoidance window. Compare alternative loss events from the same pre-loss state so their different consequences are visible.

example.prompt: Use this simplified Reno-style model: cwnd=8 MSS and ssthresh=8 MSS; each complete loss-free RTT in congestion avoidance adds 1 MSS. After two RTTs, compare three duplicate ACKs with a timeout. Both set ssthresh=cwnd/2; duplicate ACKs set recovery cwnd=ssthresh+3 then cwnd=ssthresh on the new-data ACK; timeout sets cwnd=1.
example.strategy: Apply congestion avoidance → Reduce the threshold → Duplicate-ACK recovery → Timeout alternative

steps.title: Apply congestion avoidance
steps.explanation: The initial window is at the threshold, so the supplied additive rule applies.

steps.title: Reduce the threshold
steps.explanation: Both alternative loss events start from the same ten-MSS window.

steps.title: Duplicate-ACK recovery
steps.explanation: Eight is the temporary recovery window; the specified acknowledgment ends recovery at five.

steps.title: Timeout alternative
steps.explanation: A timeout restarts with the stated small congestion window instead.

example.answer: After two RTTs cwnd=10 MSS. Duplicate ACKs give ssthresh=5 and recovery cwnd 8 then 5; timeout gives ssthresh=5 and cwnd=1.
example.verification: Both loss paths halve the same pre-loss window, while only the timeout resets cwnd to one MSS under the supplied rules.

depth.body: Congestion control is a sender's response to network feedback, while flow control represents the receiver's capacity. A congestion window in segments must be converted to bytes before combining it with a byte-valued receive window. Slow start and congestion avoidance describe different growth regimes, and a loss event's exact recovery behavior depends on the stipulated TCP variant. Work at explicit RTT or acknowledgment boundaries and keep threshold, temporary recovery window and later steady window in separate columns. These examples supply simplified recurrence rules, neglect startup transfer overhead where stated, and use window divided by RTT only as a bound on sustained useful rate.

examples.prompt: A simplified sender starts cwnd=1 MSS and ssthresh=4 MSS. At each complete loss-free RTT below threshold, double cwnd capped at 4; once at threshold, add 1 MSS per RTT. Find cwnd after three RTTs.
examples.strategy: First growth → Reach the boundary → Change the rule

steps.title: First growth
steps.explanation: The initial window is below the threshold and follows doubling.

steps.title: Reach the boundary
steps.explanation: The second RTT reaches the supplied slow-start cap.

steps.title: Change the rule
steps.explanation: The third RTT starts at threshold, so congestion avoidance adds one rather than doubling.

examples.answer: Windows after RTTs 1, 2, 3 are 2, 4, 5 MSS.
examples.verification: Using exponential growth for the third RTT would incorrectly give 8 and ignore the explicitly supplied regime change.

examples.prompt: A long established TCP transfer has cwnd 20 MSS, MSS1460 bytes, rwnd 16 MSS and RTT40 ms. No other bottleneck or losses apply. Find the window/RTT useful-rate bound.
examples.strategy: Choose the limiting window → Convert time → Calculate the rate

steps.title: Choose the limiting window
steps.explanation: The receive limit is smaller than cwnd.

steps.title: Convert time
steps.explanation: Window bytes must be divided by seconds, not milliseconds.

steps.title: Calculate the rate
steps.explanation: Convert bytes to bits only at the final rate calculation.

examples.answer: Bound 584, 000 bytes/s, or 4.672 Mbps.
examples.verification: Sixteen 1460-byte segments per 40 ms reproduce the same rate; using cwnd alone would overestimate allowed flight.

examples.prompt: Under the stipulated Reno-style rules, cwnd=12 MSS when three duplicate ACKs arrive. Set ssthresh=cwnd/2, recovery cwnd=ssthresh+3, and cwnd=ssthresh after the new-data ACK. A student resets cwnd to 1. Is that the given event’s rule?
examples.strategy: Reduce the threshold → Enter and exit fast recovery → Identify the mismatch

steps.title: Reduce the threshold
steps.explanation: Use the pre-loss window as specified.

steps.title: Enter and exit fast recovery
steps.explanation: The supplied duplicate-ACK path has a temporary inflated window then a six-MSS window.

steps.title: Identify the mismatch
steps.explanation: Resetting to one belongs to a separately specified timeout reaction, not this event’s stated rules.

examples.answer: No; the specified windows are 9 during recovery and 6 after its ending ACK.
examples.verification: Neither state is 1 MSS, so applying the timeout rule contradicts the explicit duplicate-ACK contract.

tutorials.title: Socket API in this lesson: a client and server exchange bytes
tutorials.body:
A socket API exposes transport communication through operating-system objects. For a TCP server, socket creates an endpoint object, bind chooses the local service endpoint, listen prepares a connection queue, and accept returns a connected socket for a particular client. The listener remains available; an accepted socket is the channel used for that client's byte exchange.
A client creates its own socket and uses connect to request the server endpoint. Successful connection establishment precedes the application's request exchange in this simplified blocking model. Send and recv transfer byte counts, so callers must account for partial progress. TCP preserves ordered bytes but does not promise that one send is delivered by exactly one recv.
Trace listener and connected sockets as different objects. Match the client and server endpoint pairs, then count bytes still required by the application protocol. Closing a connected socket affects that connection; the listener can continue serving other clients. This local walkthrough introduces the whole workflow, while the separate socket lesson gives additional endpoint and framing examples.

example.prompt: A server binds 10.0.0.5:8080 and listens. Client 10.0.0.8:51000 connects; the server accepts. The application expects a fixed six-byte request, but its first recv returns two bytes.
example.strategy: Prepare the listener → Accept the endpoint pair → Complete the request

steps.title: Prepare the listener
steps.explanation: bind selects 10.0.0.5:8080 and listen makes it available for incoming connections.

steps.title: Accept the endpoint pair
steps.explanation: accept returns a connected socket with remote endpoint 10.0.0.8:51000; the listening socket remains available.

steps.title: Complete the request
steps.explanation: Preserve the first two bytes and continue receiving four more before processing the complete fixed-size request.

example.answer: Use the accepted socket for this client and accumulate four additional request bytes.
example.verification: Two received bytes plus four remaining bytes equals the protocol’s six-byte request; connect/accept alone did not deliver that request.

depth.body: The socket workflow translates an application's communication roles into distinct operating-system objects. A passive server endpoint waits for connections, while each accepted endpoint exchanges bytes with one peer. A client actively requests the server address and port. Keep object creation, local endpoint selection, connection establishment and application transfer as separate events; success at an earlier event does not prove later protocol success. In this overview, build the complete call sequence before reasoning about HTTP or DNS. The examples use ordinary blocking TCP with successful setup where explicitly stated, no inherited socket copies, and no implication that descriptor numbers are transmitted across the network.

examples.prompt: Put these successful server operations in a valid ordinary TCP order: accept, socket, listen, bind. Explain which operation creates the connected client channel.
examples.strategy: Create and name the endpoint → Prepare passive service → Obtain a peer channel

steps.title: Create and name the endpoint
steps.explanation: socket precedes bind because a socket object must exist before receiving its local address.

steps.title: Prepare passive service
steps.explanation: listen follows binding and marks the endpoint ready for incoming connections.

steps.title: Obtain a peer channel
steps.explanation: accept follows listen and returns a new connected socket for one queued client.

examples.answer: socket→bind→listen→accept; accept returns the connected client socket.
examples.verification: The listener was created before any client-specific channel, and it remains distinct from the socket returned by accept.

examples.prompt: One TCP listener accepts three clients, returning three separate sockets. The server keeps all four objects open and a client sends a request. Which socket should receive that client’s bytes, and how many server sockets remain?
examples.strategy: Count objects → Match the client → Choose the receive object

steps.title: Count objects
steps.explanation: The listener plus three accepted channels are separate server sockets.

steps.title: Match the client
steps.explanation: The accepted socket carrying that client’s endpoint pair identifies its stream.

steps.title: Choose the receive object
steps.explanation: Call recv on that connected socket rather than on the listener or another client’s stream.

examples.answer: Four server sockets remain; receive on the requesting client’s accepted socket.
examples.verification: Every connected socket accounts for exactly one accepted peer here, while the fourth object still serves incoming setup.

examples.prompt: A blocking TCP connect returns success, but the application never sends its intended request. Has the server necessarily received an HTTP GET?
examples.strategy: Locate the completed stage → Look for application bytes → Separate stages

steps.title: Locate the completed stage
steps.explanation: Connect success concerns establishment of the transport connection.

steps.title: Look for application bytes
steps.explanation: The premise supplies no send and therefore no encoded GET message.

steps.title: Separate stages
steps.explanation: An established socket cannot manufacture the missing application request.

examples.answer: No; connection success alone does not deliver an HTTP request.
examples.verification: A server waiting on recv without receiving any request bytes is consistent with the successful connect.

tutorials.title: DNS in this lesson: resolve a service name before connecting
tutorials.body:
DNS provides typed information about a domain name; an A lookup asks for an IPv4 address. A client stub usually delegates resolution to a recursive resolver. On a cache miss, that resolver can follow referrals through the hierarchy to an authoritative server. The returned address identifies a potential remote host, while the application's protocol separately supplies its service port.
For delay questions, determine the cache state and which exchanges occur serially. This exercise measures time after the recursive resolver receives the client's request and omits the stub-to-resolver exchange. With no cached delegation, three serial resolver exchanges require the sum of their RTTs. Valid cached results can avoid those exchanges on a later lookup until their supplied lifetime expires.
Resolution does not establish a TCP connection or complete an HTTP request. Treat naming, connection setup and application exchange as separate timeline stages. Root and top-level servers can supply referrals rather than the requested final address. Keep the requested record type explicit: a server name in an NS or MX record is not itself an IPv4 address.

example.prompt: After receiving a client’s query, an empty recursive resolver makes one serial exchange each with root, TLD and authoritative servers. Each exchange takes 20 ms; no processing time is counted. The final A record is 203.0.113.9 with TTL 60 s. A repeat query arrives 10 s later.
example.strategy: Follow referrals → Sum the resolver time → Check later reuse

steps.title: Follow referrals
steps.explanation: Root identifies the relevant TLD service, which identifies the authoritative service; the final server supplies the A record.

steps.title: Sum the resolver time
steps.explanation: The three exchanges are serial under the stated empty-cache model.

steps.title: Check later reuse
steps.explanation: With no refresh or eviction, the repeat can use the cached address and avoid these upstream exchanges.

example.answer: The initial upstream work takes 60 ms; the repeat has 50 seconds of remaining record validity.
example.verification: The 60 ms excludes the explicitly omitted client-resolver exchange and any later TCP or HTTP work.

depth.body: DNS resolves typed naming questions rather than opening application connections. Before computing lookup delay, identify who performs each remaining exchange and what that participant already caches. A delegation can be cached even if the final address is absent; an address can be returned without repeating the entire hierarchy. An authoritative negative response also differs from a timeout or a host that resolved but refuses a transport connection. This overview treats naming as one explicit stage before socket setup. The examples use valid cache entries, serial exchanges when counted, and named authoritative outcomes rather than assuming every failed website request is a DNS failure.

examples.prompt: A browser needs an IPv4 address for gate.example.test. Its recursive resolver already holds a valid A record 203.0.113.40. No policy requires revalidation. Which DNS servers must be queried upstream?
examples.strategy: Identify the requested type → Test cached validity → Return without hierarchy work

steps.title: Identify the requested type
steps.explanation: The application needs an A record for the exact name.

steps.title: Test cached validity
steps.explanation: The supplied cached A answer is still eligible for reuse.

steps.title: Return without hierarchy work
steps.explanation: The resolver can answer directly without new root, TLD or authoritative exchanges.

examples.answer: No upstream DNS query is required for this lookup.
examples.verification: The returned typed value satisfies the request; cache reuse does not imply a TCP connection to 203.0.113.40 has been opened.

examples.prompt: After receiving a query, a resolver has valid delegation and server-address data for example.test but no A record for prep.example.test. One authoritative exchange takes 30 ms; repeating root and TLD would each take 20 ms. Ignore client-resolver delay. Find the required upstream time.
examples.strategy: Use known delegation → Request the missing record → Count actual exchanges

steps.title: Use known delegation
steps.explanation: Cached authoritative location makes root and TLD discovery unnecessary.

steps.title: Request the missing record
steps.explanation: Query the known authoritative server for prep.example.test’s A record.

steps.title: Count actual exchanges
steps.explanation: Only the supplied missing-answer exchange is required.

examples.answer: 30 ms, rather than 70 ms from repeating cached discovery work.
examples.verification: The unused root/TLD costs sum 40 ms; removing that unnecessary work from 70 leaves 30.

examples.prompt: An authoritative DNS server returns NXDOMAIN for a name. A student labels this as “TCP connection refused by the website.” Is that interpretation correct?
examples.strategy: Identify the response protocol → Identify the naming result → Separate connection setup

steps.title: Identify the response protocol
steps.explanation: NXDOMAIN is a DNS outcome about the queried name.

steps.title: Identify the naming result
steps.explanation: It says that the name does not exist in the relevant authoritative answer context.

steps.title: Separate connection setup
steps.explanation: A website transport refusal would arise from a later connection attempt to an address; no such address resolution success is supplied.

examples.answer: No; this is a DNS negative naming result, not a website TCP refusal.
examples.verification: The lookup can fail before any website socket connect is attempted, so the two outcomes occur at different stages.

tutorials.title: HTTP in this lesson: separate request, response and connection time
tutorials.body:
HTTP exchanges application requests and responses. A request identifies a method and target; a response carries a status and associated headers and representation when applicable. A successful TCP connection only supplies the transport channel. The application must still send its request and interpret the resulting HTTP response.
For a timing exercise, distinguish connection setup from the request/response exchange. In the stated simplified HTTP-over-TCP model, a new connection costs one RTT to establish, then a tiny request and response cost one further RTT. Ignore DNS, TLS, transmission and processing only because the prompt excludes them. An already established persistent connection removes that first setup cost, not the remaining application exchange.
A 200 response means the request succeeded under HTTP semantics; a 404 is also an HTTP response but indicates the target was not found. Neither status should be confused with a connection failing before any response arrives. State protocol/version assumptions because HTTP/3 and different setup or parallelism models do not share every TCP timing rule.

example.prompt: An already resolved server is accessed using HTTP over a new TCP connection. RTT is 40 ms. Count one RTT for TCP setup and one RTT for a tiny GET /guide and its 200 response. Ignore TLS, transfer and processing. Compare using a connection already established.
example.strategy: New TCP setup → Get the response → Compare totals

steps.title: New TCP setup
steps.explanation: No HTTP request exchange has completed during this setup stage.

steps.title: Get the response
steps.explanation: The application request and response require the supplied additional RTT.

steps.title: Compare totals
steps.explanation: An existing connection saves setup but still performs the GET exchange.

example.answer: 80 ms with new TCP setup; 40 ms with the existing connection.
example.verification: Both cases include one application exchange, and only the new-connection case includes the extra setup RTT.

depth.body: HTTP adds request semantics and response interpretation after a usable transport channel exists. Count connection and application stages independently when building a timeline, and include discovery or security costs only when supplied. The target path tells the server which resource is requested, while the status describes the request outcome rather than the transport's health. A response body can be absent by method or status semantics, not necessarily because bytes were lost. This overview uses specified HTTP versions over TCP and simplified serial timing; the detailed HTTP lesson explores method retries, status classes, persistence and cache validation separately instead of inferring them from connection success.

examples.prompt: A client sends GET /notes HTTP/1.1 and receives HTTP/1.1 200 OK with a representation. Identify method, target and success evidence.
examples.strategy: Parse the request line → Read the response status → Keep the representation separate

steps.title: Parse the request line
steps.explanation: GET is the method and /notes is the request target.

steps.title: Read the response status
steps.explanation: 200 denotes successful handling under the response semantics.

steps.title: Keep the representation separate
steps.explanation: The response body carries content; the status is not itself the note text.

examples.answer: MethodGET; target/notes; 200 is the supplied success status.
examples.verification: The request target and response status play different roles even though they travel on the same connection.

examples.prompt: A tiny HTTP-over-TCP request requires one setup RTT and one request/response RTT. RTT is 25 ms. DNS costs 15 ms and TLS is absent. All stages are serial. Compute total time with a fresh connection.
examples.strategy: Resolve the host → Establish TCP → Exchange HTTP

steps.title: Resolve the host
steps.explanation: The supplied DNS stage costs 15 ms before connecting.

steps.title: Establish TCP
steps.explanation: Add 25 ms for the single stated setup RTT.

steps.title: Exchange HTTP
steps.explanation: The request and response add another 25 ms after setup.

examples.answer: Total 65 ms.
examples.verification: DNS15 plus TCP/HTTP50 gives 65; a previously established resolved connection would omit the first 40 ms in this model.

examples.prompt: A server returns a valid HTTP response with status 503. A student says no connection could have been established because the status is an error. Evaluate the claim.
examples.strategy: Observe an application response → Interpret the class → Check the asserted contradiction

steps.title: Observe an application response
steps.explanation: The client received an encoded HTTP response from the server.

steps.title: Interpret the class
steps.explanation: 503 describes service unavailability at the application layer, not absence of every transport exchange.

steps.title: Check the asserted contradiction
steps.explanation: An application error can travel over a functioning connection, so response status alone cannot prove setup failed.

examples.answer: The claim is false; 503 can be delivered over an established connection.
examples.verification: A valid received response is direct evidence that application bytes crossed the channel, even though the requested service did not succeed.

lessons.title: The socket API and TCP byte-stream framing
lessons.intuition: A socket is a programming interface to network communication. Establishing a connection and exchanging application messages are separate tasks. TCP delivers a byte stream, so the application must decide how to recognize message boundaries.

sections.title: Server lifecycle
sections.body: Create a socket, bind it to a local address/port, listen for incoming connections and accept. accept returns a connected socket for one peer while the listening socket remains for future connections. A server can serve multiple clients using threads, processes or nonblocking/event-driven I/O. Privileged-port and address-binding rules depend on the OS.

sections.title: Client and data transfer
sections.body: A TCP client creates a socket and calls connect to the server endpoint. send/recv may transfer fewer bytes than requested; robust code loops as needed. A recv returning zero for a TCP stream indicates an orderly peer closure after available data is exhausted. Errors and timeouts need handling rather than assuming every operation completes immediately.

sections.title: Application framing
sections.body: One send call need not equal one recv call. Define a length prefix, delimiter with escaping, fixed record size or another protocol framing scheme. Accumulate incoming bytes until one complete message is available, retain surplus bytes for the next message, and bound lengths to avoid unbounded allocation. Network byte order converts multibyte integer fields consistently.

sections.title: Message framing over a byte stream
sections.body: TCP supplies reliable ordered bytes but no boundary markers between application writes. A sender can write a length header and payload separately, while a receiver gets a combined chunk, a partial header or a partial payload. A correct receive loop accumulates enough bytes for the agreed header, validates the declared length, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes. Remaining bytes may belong to the next message and should not be discarded. A return of zero conventionally indicates orderly end of stream, which differs from a short positive read. A listening TCP socket accepts multiple connections into separate connected sockets. UDP preserves datagram boundaries under its API but does not add TCP’s ordered delivery/retransmission guarantees; an application must choose its own reliability semantics.

examples.prompt: Send a length-prefixed message “hello”

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Encode length 5 in the agreed prefix format. Both peers must agree on prefix size, byte order and length semantics before interpreting payload bytes.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Transmit the prefix and five payload bytes, allowing for partial writes. A short positive write sends only part of the buffer; continue from the first unsent byte rather than retransmitting already sent bytes.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The receiver first accumulates the complete prefix, then exactly five payload bytes, even if several recv calls are needed. The receiver accumulates exactly the declared payload length. A short read does not indicate the message ended.

examples.strategy: Frame the application message independently of TCP send and receive call boundaries.
examples.answer: The receiver first accumulates the complete prefix, then exactly five payload bytes, even if several recv calls are needed.
examples.verification: The reconstructed payload must contain five bytes spelling hello; surplus received bytes may belong to the next framed message.

examples.prompt: A recv returns 3 bytes while 8 remain in the protocol message
steps: Append the 3 bytes to the message buffer.
The remaining expected payload decreases to 5.
Call recv again as necessary; the short read alone is not a protocol failure.

pitfalls: accept returns a new connected socket.
send/recv boundaries are not message boundaries.
revision: Explicit framing and partial-I/O handling belong to the application.

checks.prompt: Does one TCP send call always correspond to exactly one recv call?
checks.hint: TCP can split or combine delivered byte portions.
checks.explanation: Applications need framing and partial-I/O handling because send and recv call boundaries are not preserved as messages.
options: No; TCP preserves bytes, not application message boundaries
Yes if the message is short

checks.prompt: One listening socket accepts 3 connections that remain open. How many socket objects are present, including the listener?
checks.hint: Count the listener plus each accepted socket.
checks.explanation: 1+3=4 sockets.

lessons.concept: A socket is a programming interface to network communication. Establishing a connection and exchanging application messages are separate tasks. TCP delivers a byte stream, so the application must decide how to recognize message boundaries.
lessons.method:
A socket is a communication endpoint exposed through an API, identified using protocol and local/remote addresses and ports as appropriate. A typical TCP server creates a socket, binds a local address/port, listens, then accepts connections. Accept returns a connected socket while the listening socket remains available for further clients. A client uses connect to establish a peer relationship.
Many accepted connections can share the server’s local port because remote endpoints distinguish flows. TCP and UDP have separate protocol namespaces, so equal numeric port values do not necessarily conflict across protocols. Binding policies and reuse flags are OS-specific details that require the stated model.
A connected socket is not interchangeable with the listener for application I/O. Connection establishment can fail or be asynchronous under the selected mode. Calls to accept/connect and the underlying packet handshake are related but not identical conceptual events. In GATE traces, label listener, connected socket and remote client separately; one server port does not imply the server can handle only one simultaneous connection. TCP preserves bytes in order but not application call boundaries. One send can be received by several recv calls, or several sends can be combined in one read. A positive short return is the amount completed, not evidence that an entire intended message has arrived. A zero-byte stream read conventionally indicates orderly end, unlike a short positive read.
Applications define framing using a length prefix, delimiter or fixed size. With a length prefix, accumulate the complete header, validate its declared length, then collect exactly that payload size; retain extra received bytes for the next message. Send loops continue from the first unsent byte rather than resending the entire buffer after partial progress.
Handle errors, closure and nonblocking would-block states according to the API. A buffer capacity limits one read call, not the network message length. UDP exposes datagram boundaries under its API but has different delivery guarantees. GATE questions about “one send equals one recv” test stream semantics, so answer from those guarantees rather than an observation on one fast local run. The bind operation assigns a socket a local address and port under the operating system's rules. A server commonly binds the service port that clients know before entering a listening state. Binding selects the local endpoint; it does not select a remote client, establish a TCP connection or consume the application's first message.
An explicit local interface address restricts the socket to that address in this exercise. A wildcard bind can allow the service on multiple local interfaces, subject to the platform and network configuration. Port zero asks the system to select an available local port; it does not advertise a well-known service port automatically. The application must discover the chosen endpoint when needed.
Check addresses and existing bindings before interpreting a failure. Two ordinary listeners cannot necessarily reserve the same local address/port with default options; address-reuse facilities require stated semantics. Distinguish the bound socket from connected sockets created later by accept. Their endpoint roles differ even when accepted connections share the listener's local service port. For TCP, connect requests a connection from a client socket to a specified remote address and port. If the client has not explicitly bound a local endpoint, the operating system ordinarily selects an appropriate local address and an available ephemeral port. The resulting connection is identified by its local and remote endpoints under the transport protocol.
In the supplied blocking, successful model, TCP's establishment exchange completes before connect returns success. That does not mean the server application has read a request. A listener can queue an established connection before the application calls accept. Accept gives the server application a connected socket for that endpoint pair; the listener remains available for further connections.
Do not confuse the server's destination service port with the client's chosen source port. Multiple clients can connect to one server port because their endpoint pairs differ. Errors, nonblocking completion and timeouts need their stated API rules. Trace connection establishment separately from application sends and receives, since an established transport is a channel rather than evidence that an HTTP or other request was processed. Create a socket, bind it to a local address/port, listen for incoming connections and accept. accept returns a connected socket for one peer while the listening socket remains for future connections. A server can serve multiple clients using threads, processes or nonblocking/event-driven I/O. Privileged-port and address-binding rules depend on the OS. A TCP client creates a socket and calls connect to the server endpoint. send/recv may transfer fewer bytes than requested; robust code loops as needed. A recv returning zero for a TCP stream indicates an orderly peer closure after available data is exhausted. Errors and timeouts need handling rather than assuming every operation completes immediately. One send call need not equal one recv call. Define a length prefix, delimiter with escaping, fixed record size or another protocol framing scheme. Accumulate incoming bytes until one complete message is available, retain surplus bytes for the next message, and bound lengths to avoid unbounded allocation. Network byte order converts multibyte integer fields consistently. TCP supplies reliable ordered bytes but no boundary markers between application writes. A sender can write a length header and payload separately, while a receiver gets a combined chunk, a partial header or a partial payload. A correct receive loop accumulates enough bytes for the agreed header, validates the declared length, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes. Remaining bytes may belong to the next message and should not be discarded. A return of zero conventionally indicates orderly end of stream, which differs from a short positive read. A listening TCP socket accepts multiple connections into separate connected sockets. UDP preserves datagram boundaries under its API but does not add TCP’s ordered delivery/retransmission guarantees; an application must choose its own reliability semantics. Socket descriptors are process-local handles for communication objects; their numeric values are not addresses shared with peers. A listener, accepted connection and unrelated client connection therefore require separate bookkeeping even when they share a service port. TCP supports bidirectional byte transfer on the same connected socket, with independent stream state in each direction. Closing or half-closing one channel does not automatically destroy the listener or all other peers. Trace object ownership and endpoint identity before using byte counts. These detailed exercises assume one process owns each supplied descriptor, ordinary connected TCP sockets and no descriptor inheritance or duplication that would change close behavior. Listen prepares a stream socket for passive connection establishment and maintains a queue according to the operating system's specified backlog behavior. It does not return a per-client connected socket or receive an application request. Backlog concerns pending connection state under a supplied model, not the total number of already accepted clients the server can ever serve. Exact queue counts differ by platform, so numerical exercises must define whether they count completed pending connections and how overflow is handled. Once accept removes an entry, pending capacity can become available while the accepted channel continues independently. The exercises use an explicit completed-connection queue model without guessing implementation details. The returned channel uses the server's local service endpoint with a particular remote endpoint, so multiple accepted sockets can share a local port without being the same connection. Depending on blocking mode, an empty queue can cause waiting or a would-block result, rather than producing a fake client socket. The exercises assume successful completed TCP setup when a queued client is supplied and explicit blocking behavior otherwise, with no descriptor duplication or inherited references. Send reports how many supplied bytes the local operation accepted under its API, so the application advances its buffer position by that returned positive count. A short write needs continuation from the first unsent byte, not repetition of the whole message. Even a complete successful send does not establish that the remote application has consumed the content; TCP acknowledgment and application-level success are separate evidence. Define framing before transmitting because stream sends do not create durable message boundaries at the receiver. These exercises assume positive return counts or a stated error, no signal interruption and a specified byte sequence, leaving nonblocking readiness handling to its supplied protocol. Recv gives the bytes available under its stream-read semantics, up to the caller's capacity, rather than guaranteeing the application record's complete size. Maintain a receive buffer and parser state separately: first collect a header, then validate its declared length, then collect exactly that payload, preserving any subsequent bytes.
